en: "One should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha; for one begins the chant with 'Om. This is its further explanation. 1.

The *Vājasaneyibrāhmaṇopaniṣad* begins with the words, "Uṣā vā aśvasya," and so forth. A brief commentary on this [text] is now commenced for those desiring liberation from saṃsāra, in order to attain the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self, which is the means for the cessation of the causes of saṃsāra. This very knowledge of Brahman is denoted by the word *upaniṣad*, because for those intent upon it, it utterly destroys (*avasādana*) saṃsāra along with its cause. Since the root *sad* preceded by the prefixes *upa* and *ni* has that meaning [destruction], the text is also called *upaniṣad* by virtue of being the means to that [knowledge].

[Connection with the preceding section: This work consisting of six chapters is called the *Āraṇyaka* because it is to be studied in the forest (*araṇya*). Because of its great extent in terms of size, it is the *Bṛhad-āraṇyaka*. The connection of this very text with the *Karmakāṇḍa* (the section on ritual action) is now stated. This entire Veda is devoted to revealing the means for attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired—objects not known through perception or inference—for all persons, since the attainment of the former and the avoidance of the latter are naturally desired by everyone.

Since the knowledge of the means for attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired within the realm of the perceptible is established through perception and inference alone, there is no need to seek it in scripture (*āgama*). Furthermore, in the absence of the cognition that an *ātman* exists as connected to other births, there could be no desire to attain the desired or avoid the undesired in those other births, because one would perceive [only] the nature of things as they appear in this life. Therefore, scripture operates with respect to both the existence of an *ātman* connected to other births and the specific means for attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired in those other births.

For, beginning with the passage, "Regarding this man who has died, there is doubt: some say 'he exists,' and others say 'he does not exist,'" a definitive conclusion is shown by such statements as, "He is indeed to be perceived as existing. And likewise, beginning with, "And according as they reach death," it continues: "Other embodied beings enter a womb for the sake of a body."

And [it says], "Others follow after a post according to their actions and according to what they have heard. And having begun with "self-luminous," it says, "Knowledge and action follow him; one becomes virtuous through virtuous action and sinful through sinful action. And having begun with "I shall make known," it says "consisting of consciousness," thus establishing the existence of a self distinct [from the body]. If it is argued that this [self] is an object of perception itself, we say no, because we observe disagreements among disputants.

For if the existence of the self, which is connected to another body, were known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then neither the Materialists (*lokāyatika*) nor the Buddhists would be our adversaries by asserting that "the self does not exist. Indeed, no one disputes a jar or similar object when it is an object of direct perception by saying, "the jar does not exist. If it is argued that this is not so because a post or similar thing is perceived as a person and so forth, we say no; for such a dispute occurs only when [the object] has not been correctly determined. For there is no dispute regarding a post or similar thing once it has been correctly determined by direct perception.

The nihilists (vaināśikas), however, even when the cognition "I" arises, maintain that there is simply no existence of anything distinct from the body. [The self is not established by inference. Therefore, because it differs in nature from the objects of perception, the existence of the self is not established through perception. Nor is it established through inference. If it is argued that this is not so because a mark (liṅga) has been shown for the existence of the self in scripture, and because a mark is itself an object of perception, we say no; for a connection with another birth is not apprehended.

Once the existence of the self has been understood through scripture (*āgama*) and through specific worldly indicators (*liṅga*) revealed in the Vedas, the Mīmāṃsakas and logicians who follow them—imagining that the indicators for the notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*) are indeed Vedic and not produced by their own intellects—declare: "The self is both perceptible and inferable."

In every respect, the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) has been commenced to make known the specific means for attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired in another body, for the sake of the seeker who holds the conviction that "the self exists in some way as connected to another body," and who desires those specific means; however, it does not remove the ignorance concerning the self—which is the cause of the desire to attain the desired and avoid the undesired, and which is characterized by the false identification with the nature of an agent and an enjoyer—by means of the knowledge of the true nature of Brahman as the Self, which is the opposite of that [ignorance].

For as long as that [ignorance] is not removed, this [individual], impelled by the natural defects of passion, hatred, and delusion regarding the fruits of action, continues to act—even by transgressing what is enjoined or prohibited by the scriptures—accumulating through mind, speech, and body those actions known as *adharma* which accomplish seen and unseen undesirable results, because the power of the natural defects is generally more forceful. From that follows a downward course of rebirth ending in the state of stationary beings (*sthāvara*). Occasionally, however, the power of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the scriptures may prevail.

Thereafter, through the mind and other faculties, one predominantly accumulates that which is called *dharma*, which is the means for accomplishing what is desired. That is of two kinds: preceded by knowledge (*jñānapūrvaka*) and purely mechanical (*kevala*). Among these, the purely mechanical has as its fruit the attainment of the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*) and so forth. That preceded by knowledge has as its fruit the attainment of everything from the world of the gods (*devaloka*) up to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). Thus says the scripture: "The self-sacrificer (*ātmayājī*) is superior to the god-sacrificer," and so on. And the Smṛti says: "Vedic action is of two kinds," and so forth. When *dharma* and *adharma* are equal, there is the attainment of the human state.

Thus, the course of transmigratory existence—beginning with Brahmā and ending with the stationary beings—is produced by merit and demerit for those possessed of innate defects such as ignorance; it has name, form, and action as its substratum. This very same world, which exists in the differentiated state of means and ends, was in a prior state, before its origination, unmanifested.

This very cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), produced by ignorance (*avidyā*)—like the sequence of seed and sprout—is characterized by the superimposition (*adhyāropaṇa*) of action, agent, and fruit upon the Self; it is beginningless, endless, and worthless. For one who has become detached from this, the *Upaniṣad* is commenced for the purpose of attaining the knowledge of Brahman, which is the opposite of that [ignorance], in order to bring about the cessation of ignorance. Furthermore, the purpose of this specific knowledge connected with the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) is that those who lack the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the horse-sacrifice may attain its fruit through this very knowledge alone.

From such scriptural passages as, "Whether by knowledge or by action," and "This indeed is the conqueror of worlds," [it may be argued that] knowledge has only action as its sphere. This is not so, because of the scriptural mention of an option: "He who sacrifices with the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha), and he who knows this thus. Furthermore, because it is recorded in the context of knowledge, and because we observe the performance of other rites [as substitutes], it is understood that the attainment of the fruit of that [sacrifice] occurs through knowledge. Moreover, among all rites, the Aśvamedha is the supreme rite.

This is because it has as its fruit the attainment of both the collective and the individual [states]. Furthermore, its mention here at the commencement of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is for the purpose of showing that all ritual actions (*karman*) belong to the sphere of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). And so he will show the fruit to consist in the state of hunger and death. If it is argued that obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) do not have the sphere of transmigratory existence as their fruit, we say no; for there is a scriptural text summarizing the fruits of all ritual actions. For every ritual action is connected with a wife.

Having shown by means of the passage, "May I have a wife," that desire is indeed the extent of all action, [the text] shows the results of the son, ritual action, and the lower knowledge to be "this world, the world of the fathers, and the world of the gods. Then, at the end, it will conclude with their consisting of the threefold food in the words, "This triad, indeed, is name, form, and action," thereby explaining that the fruit of all action is nothing but transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). This very triad, prior to its manifestation, was then unmanifested.

That very [Self] is again manifested through the power of the karma of all living beings, like a tree from a seed. This cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), consisting of both manifest and unmanifest forms, is the domain of ignorance (*avidyā*). It is superimposed as the nature of the Self by way of being composed of action, agent, and fruit; thus, it consists of ignorance itself in the form of the gross and subtle elements along with their latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Consequently, although [the Self] is distinct from that, characterized by the absence of name, form, and karma, non-dual, and by nature eternally pure, awakened, and free, it nevertheless appears through the inversion of distinctions such as action, agent, and fruit.

Therefore, for one who is detached from this very nature of the distinction between action, agent, and fruit—which consists of the forms of the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)—the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is commenced in order to bring about the cessation of ignorance, which is the seed of defects such as desire and the performance of actions, just as the cognition of a snake is removed from a rope.

"Uṣā" refers to the *brāhma-muhūrta*; the word "vai" is for the purpose of recollection, reminding one of the well-known time. "Head" is used because of its preeminence; the head is indeed the most important among the limbs of the body. "Of the horse"—that is, of the sacrificial animal fit for the *medha* (sacrifice)—the connection is that "Dawn is the head. Since the animal that is an auxiliary of the ritual must be consecrated (*saṃskartavya*), the perceptions of time and so forth are superimposed upon the head and other parts. Furthermore, its nature as belonging to Prajāpati arises from the superimposition of the perception of Prajāpati.

The superimposition of the status of Time, the World, and the Deity, as well as the making of the animal the Prajāpati, is because Prajāpati is of such a nature—just as one performs the ritual identification with Viṣṇu and others in the case of an image. The sun is the eye, because it is not separated from the head and because the sun is its presiding deity; the wind is the breath, because of its inherent nature as air; the open, wide-gaping mouth is Agni Vaiśvānara; "Vaiśvānara" is a qualification of Agni, meaning that the fire named Vaiśvānara is the open mouth, since the mouth has Agni as its presiding deity.

The year is the self (*ātman*); the year consists of twelve months or thirteen months. The "self" here means the body; and among the divisions of time, the year is the body. Furthermore, the body is the self, according to the Vedic scripture: "For it is the middle of these limbs that is the self. The phrase "of the sacrificial horse" is repeated for the purpose of applying it to every subsequent part. The sky is its back, because of their common quality of being above; the intermediate space is its belly, because of their common quality of being hollow.

The earth is the *pājasya*, which is the place of the feet (*pādasya*); the term *pājasya* is due to a transposition of syllables (*varṇavyatyaya*), meaning the location where the feet rest. The four quarters are the sides (*pārśve*), because of the horse's connection with the quarters by means of its sides. If it be argued that this is incorrect due to the disparity in number between the two sides and the [four] quarters, we say no; for there is no fault, as the horse faces all directions and is thus connected to all quarters by both its sides. The intermediate directions, such as the southeast (*āgneyī*) and so on, are the ribs (*parśavaḥ*), meaning the bones of the sides.

The seasons are the limbs, because they are parts of the year and thus share the common characteristic of being limbs; the months and half-months are the joints, due to their similarity as points of connection; the days and nights are the feet (supports), in the plural sense including those belonging to Prajāpati, the gods, the ancestors, and humans; they are "feet" because one stands by means of them—indeed, the self whose nature is time stands by means of days and nights, just as a horse stands on its feet; the stars are the bones, due to the common quality of whiteness; the sky and the clouds situated in the sky are [the internal organs], since the intermediate space has been described as the belly.

The flesh [is the earth], because of the commonality of being moistened by water and blood. The undigested food remaining in the stomach is the sand, because of the commonality of having disintegrated parts. The rivers are the veins, because of the commonality of flowing; they are plural because the word "veins" (*nāḍyaḥ*) is plural. The liver and the lungs are two pieces of flesh below the heart, to the right and left respectively; the term *klomānaḥ* is always plural even when referring to a single organ. The mountains [are the bones], because of their hardness and their height.

The small herbs are the stationary plants, and the great trees are the forest lords (*vanaspati*); the body hairs and head hairs correspond [to these] as far as possible. As the sun rises, ascending from the time of dawn until midday, it constitutes the forepart of the horse—the portion above the navel, so the meaning is. As it sets, descending from the time of midday, it is the hind part, the rear portion, because of the commonality of being "front" and "back. When it yawns—that is, when it stretches out its limbs, bending and tossing them about—that is the lightning-flash, due to the similarity with the opening of the clouds of the mouth.

When it shakes its limbs—that is, makes them tremble—it thunders, because of the commonality of the sound of roaring. When it urinates—that is, the horse voids urine—it rains, because of the commonality of the act of sprinkling (*secanasāmānyāt*). Its voice is indeed the sound itself; the meaning is that there is no further conceptualization here regarding the horse's voice. Of these elements, the earth is the essence (*rasa*); of the earth, water is the essence; of water, plants are the essence; of plants, man is the essence; of man, speech is the essence; of speech, the *Ṛk* is the essence; of the *Ṛk*, the *Sāman* is the essence; of the *Sāman*, the *Udgītha* is the essence. 2. (2) ---

Regarding the statement "Day indeed": two cups named *Mahiman*, made of gold and silver respectively, are placed in front of and behind the horse; this scriptural vision concerns them. The golden cup is the day, because of their common quality of brilliance. How is it that "the *Mahiman* was born from the horse in front"? Because the horse is Prajāpati; for Prajāpati, characterized by the sun and so forth, is indicated by the day. Having taken the form of the horse, the golden *Mahiman* cup was born, just as lightning flashes following a tree.

The eastern ocean is the womb (*yoni*)—that is, the place of deposit—of that golden cup (*graha*) in the east; there is a shift in grammatical case here. Likewise, the silver cup is the [womb] of the night, due to the similarity of color or the similarity of being secondary. After this horse, from behind—that is, from the rear—the *Mahiman* cup was born; its womb is in the western ocean. It is called *Mahiman* because of its greatness. For this is the manifestation of the horse: that both the golden and the silver cups are placed on either side of it.

These two indeed are the two "magnitudes" (mahiman), the cups named after magnitude, which came into being on both sides of the horse, having come into being with the very characteristics previously described. This repetition—stating that "thus this horse was endowed with greatness"—is for the purpose of praise. And likewise, the passage beginning with "having become a steed" (*hayo bhūtvā*) is also solely for the sake of praise. A "steed" (*haya*) is so called because it moves or strides; the meaning is that it possesses a distinguished gait, or it refers to a specific breed. It "carried the gods," meaning it brought them to the state of divinity, since Prajāpati is the source of the gods; or rather, it became the bearer of the gods.

[Objection: Is it not the case that being a vehicle is itself a reproach? [Reply: This is not a fault. Being a vehicle is natural to the horse; because it is natural, the horse’s attainment of exaltation through its connection with the gods and others is indeed a praise. Likewise, *vājī* and so forth are specific classes [of horses]; the ellipsis is “having become a *vājī*, he carried the Gandharvas”; similarly, having become an *arvan*, [he carried] the Asuras; having become a *aśva*, [he carried] human beings. “The ocean alone” refers to the Supreme Self; *bandhu* means a bond, for it is in this that things are bound (*badhyate*).

The ocean is the *yoni*—the cause with respect to its origin. Thus, it is praised as being of pure origin and pure abode. Alternatively, the ocean is well-known as the *yoni*, according to the Vedic scripture: "The horse, indeed, has its origin in the waters.
This concludes the first Brāhmaṇa of the first chapter.

Section: Mantra Chapter.
Now, it is said that when the gods and the asuras, both of whom were offspring of Prajāpati, were contending with one another, the gods took up the Udgītha, thinking, "By this we shall overcome them.

Now, the origin of the fire used for the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) is stated. This account of its origin is intended as a praise, with the desire to present a vision concerning that very subject. "In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here"—that is, in this sphere of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), before the origination of the mind and other faculties, there was not even the slightest thing (*kiṃcana*) distinguished by name and form; it did not exist (*naivāsīt*), it had not come into being.

Was it indeed only the void that existed? It must have been only the void, according to the Vedic scripture: "Nothing whatsoever was here"; neither the effect nor the cause existed. And because of the fact of origination; for a jar is produced, and therefore, prior to its production, the jar did not exist. But surely the cause does not lack existence, since we perceive the lump of clay and so forth; only that which is not perceived is non-existent. Let this be true of the effect, but not of the cause, because the cause is being perceived. No, for prior to origination, there is the non-perception of everything.
If non-apprehension is the reason for non-existence, then since neither cause nor effect is apprehended prior to the arising of the entire world, let there be the non-existence of everything.

No, because of the Vedic scripture: "This was indeed enveloped by Death. For if nothing at all existed—that which envelops and that which is enveloped—then one would not have said, "This was enveloped by Death. Indeed, it is not the case that "the son of a barren woman is covered by a sky-flower"; yet the scripture declares, "This was indeed enveloped by Death. Therefore, both that cause by which it was enveloped and that effect which was enveloped existed prior to creation, on account of the authority of the scripture and because [the matter] is inferable.

Furthermore, the existence of cause and effect prior to the production [of the effect] is inferred. For it is observed that when the cause exists, the production of an existing effect occurs, whereas when it does not exist, production is not seen; thus, the existence of the cause of the world prior to its production is inferred, just like the existence of the cause of a jar and so forth. If it is argued that even the cause of the jar and so forth is non-existent, because a jar cannot be produced without first destroying the lump of clay and the like, we say no; for clay and the like are indeed the causes.

For in that case, clay, gold, and so forth are the causes of the jar, the golden ornament, and the like; it is not the specific form of the lump, because [the effect] occurs even in the absence of that [form]. Even when the specific form of the lump is absent, the production of effects such as jars and golden ornaments is observed from the mere causal substance, such as clay or gold, alone. Therefore, the specific form of the lump is not the cause of the jar, the golden ornament, and so forth. However, since a jar, a golden ornament, and the like do not arise in the absence of the substance—clay, gold, and so forth—it is the substance of clay, gold, and so forth alone that is the cause, and not the specific form of the lump.

For every cause, in producing an effect, produces that other effect while concealing its own previously arisen effect; this is because it is contradictory for multiple effects to exist simultaneously in a single cause. Furthermore, the destruction of a previous effect does not entail the destruction of the cause's own self. Therefore, the observation of the production of an effect upon the destruction of a lump of clay and so forth is no proof for the non-existence of the cause prior to the production of the effect.

If it is argued that this is incorrect because clay and the like do not exist apart from the lump and other such forms, [we reply: it is incorrect to say that when the prior effect such as the lump is destroyed, the cause such as clay is not itself destroyed, but rather persists even in subsequent effects such as a jar; for [it is argued] that the cause such as clay is not perceived apart from the lump, the jar, and so forth. [We reply: No; for we observe the persistence of causes such as clay even when the lump has ceased upon the production of a jar and other things. If it is argued that what is observed is a continuity of similarity and not the persistence of the actual cause, [we reply: No.

Since it is the very particles of clay and so forth, as present in the lump [of clay] and elsewhere, that are perceived in the jar and other objects, it is illogical to postulate similarity and the like on the basis of fallacious inference. Furthermore, there can be no contradiction between perception and inference, because inference is preceded by perception.

Because there would be a consequence of total lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*) everywhere—if everything were momentary, then even when "this is that very same thing" is being understood, if that cognition also depended on another cognition of that [same] thing, and that [other] cognition likewise depended on yet another, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, because the cognition "this is similar to that" would also be false, there would be a state of total lack of confidence in all cases. Moreover, in the absence of an agent for both the cognitions of "that" and "this," a relationship between them is untenable. If it is argued that their relationship exists by virtue of similarity (*sādṛśya*), we say no.

This is because it is logically impossible for these two cognitions to have each other as their objects. And if there is no mutual objectivity between them, the apprehension of similarity is impossible. If it is argued that even in the absence of actual similarity, such a cognition occurs, we say no; for then the cognitions of "that" and "this" would likewise, like the cognition of similarity, result in having non-existent things as their objects. If it is argued that let all cognitions indeed have non-existent things as their objects, we say no; for this would lead to the consequence that even the cognition of a cognition would have a non-existent thing as its object. If it is argued that let that too be so, we say no.

Since all cognitions would be false, the cognition of "unreal" itself would be impossible. Therefore, this [objection] that "the cognition of that [effect] arises from similarity" is incorrect. Consequently, it is established that the cause exists prior to the production of the effect.

And because the effect has manifestation as its mark. The existence of the effect prior to its production is established; how so? Because manifestation is its mark—meaning that manifestation is its inferential sign (*liṅga*). Manifestation is the attainment of the state of being an objective support for direct cognition. For instance, when an object such as a jar, which is covered by darkness and the like in the world, attains the status of an object of cognition through the removal of the covering by means of light and the like, it does not deviate from its prior existence.

In the same way, we understand that this world also existed prior to its origination. For a jar that does not exist is not perceived even when the sun has risen. If it is argued: "No; because there is no non-existence [of the jar], it would certainly be perceived"—[we reply: No, for according to you, an effect such as a jar never exists [prior to production]; therefore, once the sun has risen, it would indeed be perceived, since it exists when the lump of clay is present and when obstructions such as darkness are absent. If this is argued, we say no; because obstruction is of two kinds.

For the effect, such as a jar, has a twofold concealment: first, darkness, walls, and so forth, which conceal the clay and other materials once they have been manifested; and second, prior to the manifestation of the clay, the configuration of the constituent parts of the clay and so forth in the form of other effects, such as a lump of clay. Therefore, because the effect—the jar and so forth—exists even before its production but is merely concealed, it is not perceived. The distinction between the verbal expressions and cognitions of "destroyed" and "produced," or "existence" and "non-existence," however, depends upon the twofold nature of manifestation and disappearance.

If it is argued that this is incorrect because the nature of the obstruction in the case of the lump and the potsherds is different—namely, that darkness, walls, and so forth, which are observed to be obstructions of jars and the like, are seen to occupy a location distinct from the jar and so forth; whereas the lump and the potsherd are not seen to occupy a location distinct from the jar—and therefore it is incorrect to say that the jar, though existing, is not perceived because it is obstructed by the lump and the potsherd due to the difference in the properties of the obstruction—if this is argued, we say no; for milk, water, and the like are seen to occupy the same location as the milk and other substances that obstruct them.

If it is argued that there is no concealment because the parts, such as the potsherds and dust, are included within the effect, such as the jar, we say no; for when they are separated, they constitute a different effect, and thus their capacity to conceal is logically established. If it is argued that effort should be directed solely toward the absence of concealment—namely, that the jar and other effects already exist in the states of the lump of clay and the potsherds but are not perceived because they are concealed—we reply: one who desires the effect, such as a jar, would then have to exert effort only toward the destruction of its concealment, and not toward the production of the jar itself; yet this is not the case.

If it is argued that, therefore, it is incorrect to say that there is non-perception because of the mere obscuration of what already exists, we say: no, because there is no such rule. For the manifestation of a jar or similar object is not invariably restricted to an effort directed solely toward its destruction; for we observe an effort, such as the lighting of a lamp, when a jar or the like is obscured by darkness. If it is argued that even this [effort] is for the sake of destroying the darkness—[we reply: the effort involved in the production of the lamp and so forth is also for the purpose of removing the darkness; once that [darkness] has perished, the jar is perceived of its own accord.

If it is argued that nothing at all is produced in the jar, we say no; for the jar is perceived as possessing light. Just as the jar is perceived as characterized by light when a lamp is brought near, it was not so perceived prior to the bringing of the lamp. Therefore, the lamp is not lit merely to remove darkness; rather, it is for the sake of providing light, since it is perceived precisely through its possession of light. In some cases, effort may indeed be directed toward the destruction of an obstruction, such as the destruction of a wall or similar barriers.

Therefore, there is no such restriction that one who desires manifestation must exert effort solely toward the destruction of the veil. This is because such a restriction would otherwise be purposeless. We have already stated that an effect existing within its cause serves as a veil for other subsequent effects. In that case, if effort were directed only toward the destruction of a previously manifested effect—whether it be a solid mass (*piṇḍa*) or a separated shell (*kapāla*)—then effects such as shards or powder would also be produced.

Even in that case, since the jar covered by it is not perceived, there must again be a dependence on further effort. Therefore, for one who desires the manifestation of a jar or the like, the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*) is indeed necessarily purposeful. Consequently, the effect exists even prior to its production. Furthermore, because of the distinction between the cognitions of "past" and "future," it is not logical that the two cognitions "the jar is past" and "the jar is future" should be without an object, just as the cognition of a present jar has an object. Moreover, there is the activity of one who seeks a future object.

For in the world, activity is never observed to occur in the absence of a desire for an object. And since the knowledge of the past and future possessed by yogins is true, if the future jar were non-existent, the Lord’s perceptual knowledge regarding that future jar would be false; yet perceptual knowledge is not treated as figurative. Indeed, we have already stated that inference [is required] when the jar exists [in the present]. Furthermore, there is a contradiction [with scripture].

If it is said that "the jar will exist," while the potter and others are occupied with the purpose of making the jar, and this has been ascertained by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then to say that at the very time when the jar is said to have its future connection, "the jar is non-existent" is a contradiction. To say "the future jar is non-existent" means "it will not exist," just as one might say "this jar does not exist [now]."

Now, if it be said that the jar is non-existent prior to its production—provided that the meaning of the word "non-existent" is that while the potter and others engaged for the sake of the jar are present there in the form of activity, the jar itself is not yet present—then there is no contradiction. Why? Because the jar exists by way of its own future form; for the state of being present belonging to the lump of clay or the shards does not belong to the jar, nor does the future state of those two belong to the jar.

Therefore, it is not contradictory to say that the jar was non-existent prior to its production while the activity of the potter and others is present. If what were being negated were the jar’s own future state as an effect, then there would be a contradiction in that negation; however, you do not negate that. Furthermore, all things possessing activity do not share one and the same presentness or futurity.

Furthermore, among the four kinds of absences (*abhāva*), the mutual absence (*itaretarābhāva*) of a jar is observed to be distinct from the jar—just as the absence of a jar is simply a cloth or the like, and not the very nature of the jar itself. Nor is the existing cloth, which constitutes the absence of the jar, of the nature of an absence; rather, it is precisely of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva*). In the same way, the prior, posterior, and absolute absences of a jar would also have to be distinct from the jar, because they are designated by means of the jar, just like the mutual absence of the jar; and likewise, the absences would possess the nature of positive entities.

This being the case, the statement "the prior non-existence of the jar" does not mean that the very nature of the jar itself does not exist prior to its production. Now, if it were argued that "the prior non-existence of the jar" refers to nothing other than the jar's own nature, then the designation "of the jar" would be untenable. If it were further maintained that this designation is applied by way of conceptual construction—just as one speaks of "the body of a stone statue"—even so, the expression "the prior non-existence of the jar" would be a designation of a merely conceptualized non-existence by means of the jar, and not of the jar's own nature itself.

Now, as for the claim that the non-existence of a jar is something different from the jar itself, this has already been answered. Furthermore: prior to its production, a jar—which is then a non-entity like the horn of a hare—cannot enter into a relation with its own cause, because a relation must reside in two things. If it is argued that there is no fault because [cause and effect] are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*), we say no; for it is impossible for existence and non-existence to be inseparably established. Indeed, whether they are separably established or inseparably established can only apply to two existing entities, but not to existence and non-existence, nor to two non-entities. Therefore, it is established that the effect exists even prior to its production.

By what characteristic is death enveloped? To this he says: "by hunger" (*aśanāyayā*). Hunger is the desire to eat; that itself is the characteristic of death. By death characterized by that—namely, by hunger. How is it that hunger is death? It is said: "For hunger is death. With the word "for" (*hi*), he indicates a well-known reason. For he who desires to eat kills living beings immediately after that desire to eat. Therefore, death is characterized by hunger; thus he says, "for hunger."

Hunger is the attribute of the intellect (buddhi). Thus, this Hiraṇyagarbha, existing in the state of the intellect, is called Death. By that Death, this effect was enveloped, just as jars and other objects might be enveloped by clay while in the state of a lump. He made that mind. "That" is a reference to the mind; that aforementioned Death, desiring to emit the effects about to be described, created—that is, brought into being—the internal organ characterized by volition and so forth, which is capable of reflecting upon those effects and is denoted by the word "mind."

With what intention did he create the mind? It is said: "May I be *ātmanvī*, that is, possessed of a self (*ātmavān*); may I become wise through this self, which is the mind"—this was his intention. That Prajāpati, being endowed with a manifested mind (*samanaska*), while worshipping (*arcan*)—that is, honoring and adoring himself with the thought "I have achieved my purpose"—performed movement (*acarat*). As that Prajāpati was worshipping and honoring, the waters, consisting of essence and forming part of the act of worship, were born.

In this context, it should be stated that for the triad beginning with space, [the creation occurs] immediately after [the creation of the Self], according to the force of another scriptural passage and because no alternative order of creation is possible. Because Death thought, "For me who was performing worship (*arcate*), water (*kam*) came into being," for that very reason, there is the *arkatva*—the nature of the *arka*—of the fire (*arka*) used in the Aśvamedha sacrifice; the meaning is that this is the cause of its being called *arka*.

This is an etymological explanation of the name *arka* for fire: because of its being worthy of worship (*arcanāt*), because it performs worship that is a cause of happiness, and because of its connection with water (*ap*), this name *arka* is an epithet of fire. He who thus knows, understands, the aforementioned nature of the *arka*—water or happiness, due to the commonality of the name—"ha vai" (indeed) are particles used for emphasis, meaning "it certainly comes to pass"; it comes to pass for such a knower, for the sake of one who knows thus.
