They meditated upon the nasal breath as the Udgītha. The Asuras pierced it with evil; therefore, one smells both the fragrant and the foul with it, for it has been pierced by evil.

Water, indeed, is the Arka. But who is this Arka? It is said: Water is indeed the Arka, because it is the constituent part of the act of praising (*arcana*), since water is the cause of fire—the Arka—and because fire is established in water. However, water is not the Arka directly, because it is not the subject of the present context, whereas fire is the subject of the context; and the text will later state: "This fire is the Arka."

Therein, that which was like the cream of water, or like the scum of curd, was condensed—that is, it underwent a process of solidification as it was cooked internally and externally by heat; or, by a change of gender, "that which was the cream of the waters was condensed. That became the earth; that mass became this very earth. The meaning is that from those waters the cosmic egg was produced. When that earth had been brought forth, that Mṛtyu, Prajāpati, became exhausted—he became overcome with fatigue.

For the entire world, having performed its task, becomes exhausted; and that great task of Prajāpati was the creation of the earth. What happened to him when he was thus exhausted? It is said: from him who was exhausted, heated, and perspiring, his *tejorasa*—that is, *tejas* (heat/energy) itself was the *rasa* (essence); *rasa* means the core essence. He emerged, meaning he issued forth from the body of Prajāpati. Who was it that emerged? Agni; he is the Virāj Prajāpati, the first-born, born within the cosmic egg as a possessor of the aggregate of effects and instruments.
As the traditional text states: "He is indeed the first embodied being."

Now, they indeed meditated upon Speech as the Udgītha. The Asuras pierced it with evil; therefore, by means of that [Speech], one speaks both the true and the untrue, for it has been pierced by evil. (3)

(3) And having been born, that Prajāpati divided himself—meaning he distributed his own self, which is the aggregate of causes and effects—into three ways, into three modes. To the question "In what way threefold?", he says: he made the sun the third, completing the number of three in relation to fire and wind; likewise, he made wind the third in relation to fire and the sun; and likewise, he made fire the third in relation to wind and the sun—this is how it should be understood, since all three are equal in their capacity to complete the number three.

This very *prāṇa*, the self (*ātman*) of all beings, is specifically divided and distributed in three ways by its own nature as death—in the forms of fire, wind, and the sun—not by the destruction of its essential nature as the *virāj*. Regarding this first-born fire, which is the *arka* utilized in the *Aśvamedha* and constitutes the piled altar (*cit*) of the *virāj*, a vision is now described, similar to that of a horse. For we have already stated that the entire previously mentioned process of origination is for the purpose of praising this [fire]—that is, to show that "its birth is thus pure."

The eastern direction is its head, because of the commonality of being pre-eminent; and those two—the north-eastern and south-eastern—are its arms (īrmā), from the root *īr*, meaning "to move. Now, for this Agni, the western direction is the tail (puccha), the hind part, because of its connection with the west for one facing east; and those two—the north-western and south-western—are its two thighs (sakthī), because of the commonality of being rear corners; and the southern and northern directions are its two sides, because of the commonality of being connected to both [the front and back].

"The sky is the back, the intermediate space is the belly," as before; "this [earth] is the chest," because of the commonality of being the lower part. This very Agni, who is of the nature of Prajāpati and consists of the worlds and so forth, is established in the waters, according to the Vedic text: "Thus these worlds are within the waters. Wherever—that is, in whatever place—he goes, there he establishes himself, that is, he finds stability. Who is this? One who knows, who understands, in this manner, the aforementioned fact of Agni’s establishment in the waters. This is the fruit of such knowledge.
Now, they venerated the eye as the Udgītha. The Asuras pierced it with evil; therefore, by means of it, one sees both the beautiful and the ugly, for it has been pierced by evil. 4.

(4) --- He desired: that which is Death created, by means of the sequence beginning with water, the Virāj—himself as the fire—possessing within the cosmic egg an aggregate of effects and instruments, and it was stated that he made himself threefold. What was his activity while creating? It is said: *sa akāmayata*; that Death desired. What? "May a second self—a body—be born for me, by which I may become embodied"; thus he desired this.

Having thus desired with the mind that had previously arisen, he brought about—performed—the union, the state of duality, with speech characterized by the three Vedas; that is, he reflected upon the three Vedas with his mind. The meaning is that he mentally reviewed the order of creation ordained by the three Vedas. Who was this? It was Death, characterized by hunger; for it has been said, "Hunger is death. He refers back to that very one so that there may be no confusion with anything else.

That which was semen at that time—in that union—was the seed consisting of knowledge and action, the cause for the birth of Prajāpati, the first embodied being, which he had perceived during his reflection upon the three Vedas as performed in a previous life. Pervaded by that state of being, having created the waters, he entered into those waters with that semen as his seed and became an embryo within the cosmic egg; he became the year, the creator of the duration of a year, and thus became Prajāpati.

Indeed, previously, before that—before the Creator Prajāpati who fashioned the year as time—the year, known as time, did not exist at all. Death bore within himself as an embryo that Prajāpati, the creator of the year-time, for as long as this well-known duration of time exists here—that is, for a period measuring so many years.

What did he do after that year which is well-known here? After that time—after the mere year—he emitted him; the meaning is that he split open the egg. When that boy had thus been born—the first embodied being—Death, because of his state of hunger, opened his mouth wide to devour him. And that boy, terrified and possessed by innate ignorance, made the sound "bhāṇ.
That itself became speech; speech became the sound.

Now, they meditated upon the ear as the *udgītha*. The Asuras pierced it with evil; therefore, by means of it one hears both what is worth hearing and what is not worth hearing, for it has been pierced by evil. (5)

(5) --- He reflected: Having seen the boy thus terrified and crying out, Death, though possessed of hunger, reflected—meaning he looked upon him—even though he was hungry: "If I should ever injure this boy"—the prefix *abhi* in *abhiman* signifies injury, meaning "I shall harm him"—"I shall make food scantier"; that is, "I shall make the food very little. Having reflected thus, he desisted from devouring him; for much food must be produced for consumption over a long period of time, not a little.

For by eating that, food would become scarce, just as there is no crop when the seed itself is consumed. Having thus reflected on the need for an abundance of food, and repeatedly entering into a state of union with that very speech previously mentioned and with that same self—the mind—he created all this, both the stationary and the moving, whatever exists here.

What are those? The *ṛc*s, the *yajus* formulas, the *sāman* chants, and the seven meters beginning with the *gāyatrī*—namely, the three kinds of mantras characterized by the *gāyatrī* and other meters which constitute the limbs of rituals such as the *stotra* and *śastra*, as well as the sacrifices accomplished by them, the progeny who perform them, and the domestic and wild animals that serve as the means for the rituals. [Objection: But it was stated that he created [the world] by means of the triple Veda (*trayi*) having entered into union (*mithunībhūtā*); how then can it be said here that he created the *ṛc*s and so forth? [Response: This is not a fault; for this union of the triple Veda is an unmanifested state of the mind.

But the external creation is the manifestation of the *Ṛg* and other Vedas, which already exist, through their application to ritual acts. That Prajāpati, having thus perceived the increase of food, resolved—that is, fixed his mind upon—whatever he created, whether an action, a means of action, or a fruit, in order to eat it, to consume it. Since he eats everything entirely, for that reason the status of Aditi is well-known for Death, who is named Aditi.

And thus says the mantra: "Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the intermediate space, Aditi is the mother, she is the father," and so forth. He becomes the eater of all this world that has become food, by means of his very self as the All; for otherwise there would be a contradiction, since no single individual is seen to be the eater of everything. Therefore, the meaning is that he becomes the Self of all. Everything becomes his food; for it is only logical that everything becomes the food of an eater who is the Self of all.
He who thus knows this Aditi-nature of Aditi, of Death, and of Prajāpati— that she is so called because she eats (ad) everything as stated— attains this fruit.

Then they venerated the mind as the Udgītha. The Asuras pierced it with evil; therefore, by means of it, one forms both what is to be formed and what is not to be formed, for it has been pierced by evil.

Regarding the statement "He desired," this is said for the purpose of defining the terms *aśva* (horse) and *aśvamedha* (horse-sacrifice). He thought, "May I sacrifice again with a greater, more magnificent sacrifice. The word "again" (*bhūyaḥ*) is used in reference to another birth; that Prajāpati performed the horse-sacrifice in another birth. Being permeated by that very state of being, he emerged at the beginning of the [new] Kalpa. Having come into existence as the essence of the action, the factors of action, and the fruit of the horse-sacrifice, he desired: "May I sacrifice again with a greater sacrifice."

Having thus desired this great task, he grew weary, as is common in the world; he performed austerity. As before, for him who was weary and had performed austerity, his fame and vigor departed; [the text] itself explains the meaning of these terms: "Fame" refers to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), such as sight and the rest, because they are the cause of fame—for when they are present, renown arises. Likewise, "vigor" is strength in this body; for one whose vital breaths have departed is neither famous nor strong.

Therefore, it is the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) alone that constitute fame and vigor within this body. Thus, that fame and vigor characterized by the vital breaths departed—that is, they went forth. When the vital breaths, which consist of fame and vigor, had thus departed and gone out from the body, that body of Prajāpati was about to swell—that is, to undergo a state of bloating—and it became impure. Even though he had emerged from the body, the mind of that Prajāpati remained in that very body;
just as the mind of someone who has gone far away remains fixed upon a beloved object, so it was in his case.

Now, they meditated upon that very vital breath which is principal as the *udgītha*. When the Asuras attacked it, they shattered it, just as a clod of earth would shatter upon hitting a stone pillar. (7)

(7) What did he do while his mind was fixed upon that very body? It is said: He desired. How? "May this body of mine be *medhya*—fit for sacrifice, worthy of the sacrificial rite (*yajñiya*); moreover, may I be *ātmanvī*—possessed of a self, embodied by means of this body. Thus he entered it. Because that body, having lost its luster and vigor through separation from him, swelled (*aśvat*), therefore it became a horse (*aśva*). Thus Prajāpati himself is praised as being directly the one named Aśva.

Furthermore, because by entering that [Prajāpati], the sacrificial horse—which was impure due to its movements, fame, and vigor—became pure, for that very reason the sacrifice named Aśvamedha obtained the name "Aśvamedha. For a sacrifice consists of action, agent, and result, and it is praised as being none other than Prajāpati himself.

The status of the horse that accomplishes the sacrifice as Prajāpati has been stated in the passage beginning with, "Verily, Dawn is the head of the sacrificial horse. Now begins the injunction for the meditative worship (*upāsana*) of that very same sacrificial horse—who is of the nature of Prajāpati—and of Agni as previously described, by way of their being unified as the essence of the fruit of the sacrifice. This meaning is understood because, in the preceding section, no injunctive verb was heard, and because the context requires a finite verb.

"Verily, he who knows this horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) sacrifice knows it—anyone at all who knows this [horse] as Agni and as the Sun (*arka*) as previously described, and as characterized by the specific attributes that will be shown hereafter in brief, he indeed knows the horse-sacrifice, and no other; therefore, it must be known in this way. How so? In this regard, he first states the perspective concerning the sacrificial animal itself."

In that regard, Prajāpati, having desired, "May I sacrifice again with a greater sacrifice," fashioned himself alone as the sacrificial animal. He considered—that is, he thought of—that animal as one not to be confined, a released animal, one whose tether was cast off without having performed the act of confinement. At the end of a full year, beyond it, he sacrificed it for himself—for his own sake; that is to say, he sacrificed it by making Prajāpati its deity. He performed the ritual slaughter.

He drove back the other animals—both domestic and wild—to their respective deities according to the specific deity of each. And because Prajāpati thought in this way, therefore another person also, having prepared himself as a sacrificial animal—a horse fit for sacrifice—according to the stated rule, should think: "While being sprinkled with water, I belong to all the deities; but while being immolated, may I belong to my own deity alone."

One should know that other animals—both domestic and wild—are sacrificed to other deities who have become constituent parts of him [the Sun]. For this very reason, sacrificial priests nowadays sacrifice an animal consecrated for all the gods (*sarvadevatya*) as belonging to Prajāpati. This indeed is the Aśvamedha which shines yonder; however, that sacrifice which has the animal as its means is here pointed out as the actual fruit itself: "This indeed is the Aśvamedha."

Who is he? He is this Savitṛ who shines and illuminates the world with his splendor. Of this very one, whose nature is the fruit of the sacrifice (kratu), the year—a specific division of time—is the self (ātman), that is, the body, because the year is brought about by him. Of that same one, whose nature is the sacrifice, this terrestrial fire is the "ark" (the sun), serving as the means of accomplishment. And of that ark, which is the sacrificial altar (citya), these three worlds are the selves—that is, the limbs of the body. And thus it has been explained [in the scripture] beginning with: "Of him, the eastern direction... and so forth.

These two, Agni and Āditya, as specifically characterized, are the Arka and Aśvamedha, which constitute the fruit of the sacrifice. That which is the earthly fire (Agni) is directly the form of the sacrifice, being of the nature of action; since the sacrifice is accomplished by means of fire, it is designated by that very form. And because the fruit is accomplished by the sacrifice, it is designated by the form of the sacrifice itself—namely, "Āditya is the Aśvamedha. These two, Agni and Āditya, who are the means and the end, consisting of the sacrifice and its fruit, become once again, moreover, a single deity. Which one is that? Death alone.

Previously, it was also one alone, divided for the sake of the distinction between action, means, and result; and thus it has been said: "He divided himself threefold. Yet, after the completion of the action, that [action] becomes once again a single deity—Death itself in the form of the result. Furthermore, he who knows this Aśvamedha as Death, the single deity—thinking, "I am indeed Death, the single deity Aśvamedha, whose forms are accomplished by means of myself, the horse, and the fire"—[attains that goal].

He conquers *punarmṛtyu*, that is, repeated death; the meaning is that having died once, he is not born again for the sake of further death. Anticipating the doubt that even though death has been conquered, death might nevertheless reach him again, [the text] says: "Death does not reach him. Why? Because death becomes the very self (*ātman*) of this one who knows thus. Furthermore, death itself, being the form of the fruit, becomes one with these deities; this is his reward. Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa of the first chapter.

Now, with reference to the deities: one should meditate upon that which shines yonder as the *udgītha*. Rising up, it indeed sings the *udgītha* for all creatures. As it rises, it dispels darkness and fear. He who knows this becomes indeed a dispeller of fear and darkness. 1.

(1) "Two" means of two kinds. The particle *ha* is a particle (*nipāta*) that indicates a past occurrence; by the word *ha*, it illuminates what occurred in a previous birth of the present Prajāpati. "Offspring of Prajāpati" (*prājāpatyāḥ*) means those who are the progeny of Prajāpati while he was in the state of his active life and birth. Who are they? They are the gods (*devāḥ*) and the asuras. How, then, do they possess the nature of gods and asuras? It is said: they are called "gods" (*devāḥ*) because they shine (*dyotanāt*), being cultivated by knowledge and action produced from the scriptures.

Those very ones are the *asuras*, because they are conditioned by knowledge and action whose purposes are perceived through innate perception and inference, and because they delight (*ramante*) in their own vital breaths (*asu*), or because they are other than the *surās* (the gods). And since the *asuras* are conditioned by knowledge and action whose purposes are perceived, therefore—*kānīyasāḥ*: "the younger ones," meaning those who are indeed smaller (*kanīyāṃsaḥ*); the suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of the word itself, resulting in the lengthening of the vowel; the gods are merely the smaller ones. The *asuras* are the greater ones (*jyāyasāḥ*), meaning the more numerous *asuras*.

For the natural inclination toward action and knowledge is stronger than the inclination toward action and knowledge produced by the scriptures, because it has visible purposes; for this very reason, the gods were inferior, since their scripture-generated activity was limited, for that [natural activity] is accomplished only with extreme effort. Those gods and Asuras, residing within the body of Prajāpati, contended—that is, they engaged in rivalry—over these worlds which serve as the objective grounds and are to be accomplished through actions and knowledge other than the natural ones.

The rivalry between the gods and the asuras consists in the emergence and suppression of their respective functions (*vṛtti*). Sometimes the function of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), consisting of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of knowledge and action produced by the sacred scriptures (*śāstra*), emerges. When it emerges, then the function of those very same vital breaths—consisting of the cultivation of knowledge and action produced by perception and inference, which has visible purposes—is suppressed by the asuric one. That is the victory of the gods and the defeat of the asuras. Sometimes, conversely, the function of the gods is suppressed and the asuric function emerges.

That was the victory of the Asuras and the defeat of the Devas. Thus, when the Devas were victorious, due to the predominance of dharma, there was an upward progression until the attainment of the state of Prajāpati. When the Asuras were victorious, due to the predominance of adharma, there was a downward regression until the attainment of the state of stationary beings (sthāvara). When both were equal, there was the attainment of the human state. Since the Devas were thus being overcome by the Asuras on account of their inferiority, what did the Devas do because of the numerical superiority of the Asuras? It is said: those Devas, being indeed overcome by the Asuras, spoke—that is, they uttered these words.

How so? "Ah! Now, in this Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, by means of the Udgītha—by taking refuge in the nature of the performer of the ritual element of the Udgītha—we shall transcend [our state]; having overcome the Asuras, we shall attain our own divine nature as revealed by the scriptures," they said to one another. And this taking refuge in the nature of the performer of the ritual element of the Udgītha is accomplished through both knowledge and action. Action refers to that which is about to be described, characterized by the recitation of mantras, and is intended to be enjoined in the words, "Therefore, one should recite these.
Knowledge, however, is precisely this very thing being defined here.

[Objection: Is this not an explanatory passage (arthavāda) supplementary to the rule for the recitation of the *abhyāroha*, and not intended to define knowledge? [Reply: No, because of the statement, "He who knows thus. [Objection: Since a past event (*purākalpa*) is heard in the context of the *udgītha*, it must be intended as a rule for the *udgītha*. [Reply: No, because it is not within that context; because the *udgītha* is enjoined elsewhere; because this [section] is a context for knowledge (*vidyā*); and because the *abhyāroha* recitation is non-obligatory (*anitya*), being to be employed by one who possesses such knowledge, whereas the knowledge itself is heard of as being obligatory (*nitya*).

This is because of the scriptural statement, "And this indeed is the winner of the worlds," and because of the mention of the purity of Prāṇa and the impurity of speech and the other organs. For if they were not objects of worship, the mention of the purity of Prāṇa and the mention of the impurity of speech and the others presented alongside it would not be appropriate; nor would the praise of the chief Prāṇa through the censure of speech and the rest be intended, nor the statement of the fruit beginning with, "Having transcended death, he shines. For that fruit—namely, the state of speech and the others becoming fire and so forth—is indeed the attainment of the very nature of Prāṇa.

"Let it be granted that there is meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*), but not as possessing qualities such as purity and so forth. [Objection: "But surely it should be so, because it is stated in scripture. [Reply: It should not be so, because when something is an object of meditation, its description of qualities is logically understood as being for the purpose of praise (*stuti*). "No," [we reply]. Because by understanding the meaning without error, the attainment of the highest good (*śreyas*) is possible, as is the case in the world. For in the world, he who understands the meaning without error attains what is desired and turns away from what is undesired, but not through the understanding of a perverted meaning.

Likewise here as well, the attainment of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) is logically established when there is comprehension of the meaning produced by words heard in scripture, and not otherwise. Furthermore, there is no evidence that the object of the cognition arising from the words heard for the purpose of meditation is unreal. Nor is any sublation (*apavāda*) of that cognition heard in scripture. Therefore, because we observe the attainment of the highest good, we conclude that it is in accordance with reality (*yathārthatā*).

Furthermore, because we observe that one incurs misfortune when there is a misconception: for in the world, it is seen that whoever perceives an object erroneously—such as taking a post for a man, or an enemy for a friend—incurves misfortune. If the apprehension of the Self, the Lord, the deities, and so forth, were likewise based on scripture through incorrect means, then this scripture would certainly result in the attainment of misfortune for the people of the world; yet this is not desired.

Therefore, the scripture causes one to grasp the self, the Lord, the deities, and so forth exactly as they are, for the purpose of worship. If it is argued that this is improper because we observe the practice of viewing Brahman in names and the like, [the reply is: the non-Brahman nature of names and so forth is perfectly clear; in those cases, the scripture is seen to cause one to grasp a view of Brahman there—just as one might grasp a false view of a person in a tree stump—which is a misconception. If it is further argued that it is therefore improper to say that spiritual welfare results from understanding things according to their true nature through the scripture, [we reply: no, because the understanding is based on a distinction, just as in the case of an image.

"You have not rightly said that the scripture teaches a perverted view by causing one to perceive Brahman in non-Brahman, such as names and so forth, just as one might perceive a person in a post. Why? Because for one who has already understood the entity of the name and so forth as distinct from Brahman, the perception of Brahman is enjoined with respect to the name and so forth, just as the perception of Viṣṇu is enjoined with respect to an image. For the understanding of the name and so forth serves as a support, just like an image; it does not mean that the name and so forth are themselves Brahman."

Just as when a post is not correctly identified, one might wrongly perceive it as "this is a man" rather than "this is a post," such a perception is erroneous; however, the perception of Brahman in names and so forth is not erroneous in that same way.

If it is argued that there is only the view of Brahman [superimposed], and that Brahman itself does not exist—by which [argument] the views of Viṣṇu and other deities, or of ancestors and others, upon images, Brāhmaṇas, and so forth, would be rendered equivalent—it is not so. This is because we observe the superimposition of the earth and other elements upon the *Ṛgveda* and so forth; for we see that it is precisely the views of existing entities such as the earth that are projected onto the subject matter of the *Ṛgveda* and the rest. Therefore, by analogy with that, it is established that the views of Brahman and others upon names and so forth have Brahman and others as their actual, existing objects.

By this, it is established that the cognitions of Viṣṇu and other deities, or of the ancestors and others, directed toward images, Brahmins, and so forth, have real entities as their objects. Furthermore, since secondary (gauna) usage depends upon a primary (mukhya) one, just as the quality of being "fire" applied to the five fires and so forth is secondary and thus implies the existence of primary fire and so forth, so too the quality of being Brahman applied to names and so forth is secondary, which establishes the existence of a primary Brahman.

And because there is no distinction between those [Vedic passages] whose purpose is action and those whose purpose is knowledge. Just as the performance of rituals such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa—having this specific fruit, this specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and its constituent parts (*aṅga*) applied in this specific order—is a non-worldly reality that is not an object of perception and the like, and is made known only by Vedic sentences; so too is the case here.

Likewise, the reality of the supreme self, the Lord, the deity, and so forth—characterized by attributes such as being "not gross" and transcending hunger and thirst—is made known by Vedic sentences alone as being thus qualified. Because it is non-empirical (*alaukika*), it must exist exactly as it is described. Furthermore, there is no difference in the capacity of sentences concerning action and sentences concerning knowledge to produce cognition. Nor does a cognition regarding the reality of the supreme self and so forth arise that is either indeterminate or erroneous.

If it is argued that [the knowledge of Brahman] is improper because there is nothing to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*), and that while the three-factored *bhāvanā*—though transcendent—is made known as something to be performed by means of sentences whose purpose is action (*kriyārtha*), no such thing to be performed exists in the case of the realization of the Supreme Self, the Lord, and so forth; therefore, the claim of similarity with sentences whose purpose is action is improper—if this is said, we reply: no, because knowledge has for its object a reality as it truly is. For the "as-it-is-ness" of the three-factored *bhāvanā* does not arise from its being something to be performed; rather, it arises from its being apprehended through a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Nor does that cognition regarding that object possess such a nature simply because its object is something to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*); what then? It is solely because it is produced by a Vedic sentence. When the reality of an object has been apprehended through a Vedic sentence, one performs it if it is qualified by being something to be performed; if it is not qualified by being something to be performed, one does not perform it. If it is argued that if there is nothing to be performed, the status of the sentence as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would be untenable—for indeed, if there were nothing to be performed, the combination of words would not be possible—[we reply: no.

However, when there is something to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*), words are combined for the sake of that performance; in that case, a sentence whose focus is the object to be performed becomes a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the form: "This is to be done by this [means] in this manner. But there is no status as a "sentence" even for hundreds of words of such a kind as "this is by this in this way," if any one of the following—*kuryāt*, *kriyeta*, *kartavyam*, *bhavet*, or *syāt* (the fifth)—is absent. Therefore, the Supreme Self, the Lord, and so forth, are not established by the authority of sentences.

If it is argued that being a category (*padārtha*) entails being an object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and therefore this [scriptural teaching] is invalid, we say no. For we observe sentences such as "Mount Meru exists, endowed with four colors," which refer to things not to be performed (*ananuṣṭheya*). Furthermore, upon hearing a sentence such as "Mount Meru is endowed with four colors," no cognition arises regarding Mount Meru or the like as something to be performed. Likewise, who can prevent the synthesis of the words in sentences that establish the Supreme Self, the Lord, and so forth—words accompanied by the term "exists" (*asti*)—through the relationship of qualifier and qualified?

If it is argued that knowledge of the Supreme Self is improper because it serves no purpose—just like the knowledge of Mount Meru and the like—it is not so; for there is the hearing of results in such texts as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" and "The knot of the heart is severed," and because we observe the cessation of defects such as ignorance, which is the seed of transmigratory existence. Furthermore, since that knowledge is not subordinate to anything else, the scriptural mention of its result cannot be treated as a mere *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), as would be the case with the ladle (*juhū*) [where the result mentioned is subordinate to another action].

Furthermore, the connection between prohibited acts and undesirable results is known from the Veda alone; nor is that [connection] something to be performed. For one who has already engaged in an action regarding a prohibited object, there is nothing else to be performed other than the non-performance [of that act]. Indeed, in the ultimate sense, the purpose of prohibitive injunctions must consist solely in the firm resolve (*niṣṭhā*) to know that [the act] is not to be done.

For one who is afflicted by hunger and conditioned by the knowledge of prohibitions, when something unfit for consumption or unfit for eating—such as *kalañja*, food of those accused of crimes, or the food of others—presents itself, the cognition arises that "this is fit to be eaten" or "that is fit to be eaten. This [cognition] is sublated by the recollection of the knowledge of the prohibition directed toward that same object, just as the cognition of drinkable water in a mirage is sublated by the true knowledge of the nature of that object. Once that natural, erroneous cognition has been sublated, the inclination toward eating or consuming that which causes harm does not occur.

There is simply the cessation of activity caused by erroneous knowledge; no further effort need be exerted once that [erroneous knowledge] is absent. Therefore, injunctions of prohibition have as their sole aim the knowledge of the true nature of reality, not even a trace of being aimed at human action. Likewise here, the injunctions regarding the knowledge of the true nature of the Supreme Self and so forth must likewise terminate in that alone.

Likewise, for one whose consciousness has been refined by that [knowledge], there would be the cessation of those activities caused by the cognition of objects contrary to reality, because they are known to be non-beneficial; for when the innate cognition caused by them is sublated by the recollection of the knowledge of the true nature of the Supreme Self and so forth, their non-existence would follow.

If it is argued: "But surely, just as the engagement in harmful acts such as eating *kalañja* and the like ceases once the natural cognition of their eatability is sublated by the recollection of the knowledge of the true nature of reality—which reveals that such acts lead to misfortune—it is not logical for there to be an absence of engagement in what is enjoined by scripture simply because it is not the object of a prohibition," we say: no; for [the two cases] are equal in terms of being caused by erroneous cognition and resulting in harmful consequences.

Just as the engagement in acts such as the eating of *kalañja* is caused by false knowledge and results in harm, so too is it with the engagements prescribed by the scriptures. Therefore, for one who possesses the realization of the true nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), even the engagements prescribed by the scriptures are equal [to worldly actions] insofar as they are caused by false knowledge and result in harm. Consequently, when false knowledge is sublated by the knowledge of the Supreme Self, their cessation is indeed appropriate. [Objection: But is that appropriate in that case?

If it is argued that for obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*), since they are based solely on scripture and lack any purposeful worldly motive, their non-performance is not logical, we say: no. For they are prescribed for one who possesses defects such as ignorance (*avidyā*), attachment (*rāga*), and aversion (*dveṣa*). Just as optional rites (*kāmya-karma*) like the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are prescribed for one possessing defects such as the desire for heaven, so too are the obligatory rites prescribed for one who possesses the defect of ignorance—the seed of all misfortune—and the defects of attachment and aversion toward the attainment of the desired and avoidance of the undesired produced by that [ignorance]; and for one impelled by those [defects] to act without distinction, seeking the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired. They are not based on scripture alone.

Furthermore, there is no inherent distinction between the optional (*kāmya*) and obligatory (*nitya*) nature of the rites—the Agnihotra, the New- and Full-Moon sacrifices, the Four-Monthly sacrifices, the Animal sacrifice, and the Soma sacrifice—within themselves. For their status as being for the sake of desire arises from the defect of desiring heaven and so forth residing in the agent; likewise, it is logical that the obligatory rites serve that same purpose for one who possesses defects such as ignorance and who seeks to obtain what is desired and avoid what is undesired by their very nature, because they are prescribed for him.

For one who possesses the knowledge of the true nature of the Supreme Self, no action is found to be prescribed other than the means of tranquility (*śama*). Indeed, the knowledge of the Self is enjoined by means of the sublation of all instruments of knowledge, such as the deities and others which are the causes of ritual action. Furthermore, the engagement in ritual action is not possible for one whose knowledge of actions, agents, and so forth has been sublated, because the commencement of action is necessarily preceded by the knowledge of specific actions, their instruments, and the like.

Indeed, there is no occasion for ritual action (*karman*) for one who maintains the realization of Brahman as non-dual, non-material, and unconditioned by space, time, and so forth. If it is argued that such an occasion might exist just as there is for activities like eating, we say no; for since activities such as eating are caused solely by defects such as ignorance (*avidyā*), their necessity is untenable in this state. Furthermore, if an act is performed at some times and not at others, being thus irregular, it cannot be considered a "constant" (*nitya*) rite.

However, because eating and other such actions would have defects as their sole cause, they would be non-obligatory (aniyata), since the arising and subsiding of defects are themselves non-obligatory, just as in the case of desires regarding the objects of desire. Furthermore, because obligatory rites depend on factors such as time prescribed by scripture, their non-obligatoriness is untenable. If it is argued that—even though defects are the cause—eating and so forth must follow fixed rules (niyama) because they are enjoined by scripture, just as the optional Agnihotra depends on the times of evening and morning due to scriptural injunction, we say no.

Since a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is not an action (*kriyā*), and since an action is not the motivator [of knowledge], it does not constitute an exception to knowledge. Therefore, because even the injunction for the knowledge of the true nature of the Supreme Self has the capacity to remove contrary cognitions such as gross duality, it effectively results in the purpose of an injunction prohibiting all ritual action; this is because the absence of engagement in action is identical [in both cases], just as in the case of a prohibition.
Consequently, like a prohibitory injunction, the scripture’s status as a presentation of reality (*vastu-pratipādana*) and its being intent upon that reality (*tatparatva*) are established.

This [breath] here and that [sun] yonder are indeed the same. This one is warm, and that one is warm; this one is called *svara* (sound), and that one is called *svara*. Because one calls this one *svara*, and that one *pratyāsvara* (echo), therefore one should meditate upon both this breath and that sun as the *udgītha*. 2.

(2) Those gods, having thus reached a firm conclusion, spoke to Vāk—the deity presiding over speech—saying: "Do thou sing for us; perform the office of the Udgātṛ. They perceived that the office of the Udgātṛ was to be accomplished by the deity Vāk, and they addressed that very deity through the mantra used for silent recitation (*japa*): "Lead me from the unreal to the real" (*asato mā sad gamaya*). And here, it is Vāk and the other deities who are intended as the agents of both the meditation (*upāsanā*) and the ritual action (*karman*).

Why? Because, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), every conventional transaction involving knowledge and action has that [Brahman] as its agent and that [Brahman] as its object. For the text will explain in detail in the sixth chapter, in the passage beginning "It meditates, as it were; it vibrates, as it were," the absence of agency in the Self. And here too, at the conclusion of this chapter, it will summarize the entire collection of actions, factors of action, and fruits beginning with the undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*)—namely, "This triad is indeed name, form, and action"—as being within the domain of ignorance (*avidyā*).

But that which is beyond the undifferentiated (avyākṛta), called the Supreme Self (paramātman), which is the object of knowledge and whose nature is not name, form, or action—that he will set apart by concluding with the negation "not this, not this" (neti neti). On the other hand, as for the transmigrating self (saṃsāryātmā) which is conceptually constructed through the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the aggregate of speech and so forth, he will show that very self to be partial toward that aggregate of speech and so forth, in the words: "Having arisen from these elements, it perishes after them."

Therefore, it is logical that speech and the other [senses] alone are intended to be the agents of knowledge and action, and the attainers of the fruit. "So be it"—having been addressed thus by the gods, Speech sang the *udgītha* for them, for the sake of those who were petitioners. But what is this specific effect produced by Speech through the act of singing the *udgītha* for the sake of the gods? It is said: it is precisely that benefit which is accomplished for the aggregate of speech and the other senses when Speech serves as the instrumental cause, through its activity of speaking and so forth.

For this enjoyment, which consists of the production of speech through the mouth, is the fruit for all [the priests]. Having assigned that enjoyment to the three *pavamāna* [stotras], the remaining nine *stotras* yield the fruit of the priestly office (*ārtvijya*) as prescribed by the text—that which is auspicious and beautiful, which one speaks, that is, which one brings forth as phonemes—that belongs to me alone. For the correct utterance of phonemes is the unique function of the deity Speech; therefore, that alone—which consists of assistance to the entire assembly—is indeed the duty of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).

There, having found an opportunity for attachment through their connection with the one of "fair face" (the Udgātṛ), those Asuras perceived a vulnerability in the deity. How so? [They thought: "By means of this Udgātṛ, he will overcome and transcend our innate knowledge and action, and by means of the light consisting of ritual knowledge and action produced by the scriptures, in the form of the Udgātṛ, he will pass us by. Having understood this, they rushed toward that Udgātṛ, approached him, and pierced him with their own evil characterized by attachment.

The meaning is that they struck and joined [the evil]. That which was the evil cast upon the speech of Prajāpati while he was in the state of his previous birth—that very thing is now made manifest. What is it? It is this very thing which one speaks here that is improper, unsuitable, and forbidden by the scriptures; that by which one is impelled to speak vulgar, loathsome, and untruthful words even against one’s will. Being followed by this effect—the speaking of what is improper—it exists within the speech of the creatures who are the effects of Prajāpati.
That very evil, which was inferred from his misshapen face, entered the speech of Prajāpati; for the effect conforms to its cause.
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.3)

Now, one should indeed meditate upon Vyāna as the Udgītha. That which one breathes out is Prāṇa; that which one breathes in is Apāna. Now, the junction of Prāṇa and Apāna is Vyāna; what is Vyāna, that is Speech. Therefore, even while not breathing out and not breathing in, one utters speech.

In the same manner, they examined the deities of the sense of smell and the others, concluding that because they bring about the *udgītha*, they are to be revealed by the mantra of recitation (*japa*) and are objects of meditation. This was the conclusion reached by the gods: "The deities of speech and the others, when examined in succession, are incapable of accomplishing the *udgītha* because of their attachment to specific beautiful objects and their connection with the evil of the Asuras. Therefore, they are not to be designated [by the mantra], nor are they to be meditated upon according to the formula 'Lead me from non-existence to existence,' because they are impure and do not pervade the others."

Thus indeed, although these deities of the skin and so forth were not explicitly mentioned, they are understood from the observation of their good and evil deeds; and just like speech and the others, it was said that "they pierced them with evil," meaning they struck them with evil, which signifies that they brought them into contact with evils.

Even though the gods were meditating upon the deities of speech and the rest, they remained without refuge for the purpose of transcending death, and proceeded in due order— [Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.4]

That which is speech is the Ṛk; therefore, without breathing out or breathing in, one utters the Ṛk. That which is the Ṛk is the Sāman; therefore, without breathing out or breathing in, one sings the Sāman. That which is the Sāman is the Udgītha; therefore, without breathing out or breathing in, one chants the Udgītha. 4. (3–6)---

In the same manner, they examined the deities of the nose and the other senses in turn, concluding that because they bring about the *udgītha*, they are to be revealed by the mantra of recitation and are to be meditated upon. This was the conclusion reached by the gods: "The deities of speech and the others, when examined in sequence, are incapable of accomplishing the *udgītha* due to their association with the evil of the Asuras, which arises from attachment to their own connection with specific beautiful objects. Therefore, they are not to be designated [by the mantra], nor are they to be meditated upon—as in the phrase 'Lead me from non-existence to existence'—because of their impurity and their lack of pervasiveness."

Thus indeed, although these deities of the skin and so forth were not explicitly mentioned, they are understood from the observation of their good and evil deeds; just as in the case of speech and the others, [the text] says that "they pierced them with evil," meaning they pierced them with evil, which signifies that they joined them with evils, brought about contact with evils.
Even though the gods were meditating upon the deities of speech and the rest, being without refuge for the purpose of transcending death, they proceeded in due order— [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.7].

Section: Mantra Chapter "Heaven is *ud*, the intermediate space is *gīḥ*, and the earth is *tham*. The sun is *ud*, the wind is *gīḥ*, and fire is *tham*. The Sāmaveda is *ud*, the Yajurveda is *gīḥ*, and the Ṛgveda is *tham*. Speech yields its milk for him who, knowing this thus, meditates upon these syllables of the *udgītha* as 'ud-gī-tha'. The milk of speech is that which is its yield; he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food. (7)

Immediately thereafter—"ha imām" is used for the purpose of indicating a gesture—they said to the *prāṇa* located in the mouth, that which exists in the mouth (*āsanya*), situated within the cavity of the face: "Do you sing the *udgītha* for us. To those who had thus approached him for refuge, that very *prāṇa*, the principal one, sang the *udgītha*, and so forth, as described previously.

Desiring to pierce—that is, wishing to strike—the Principal Breath (mukhya prāṇa), which is untouched by defects, those evils, having gained a foothold in speech and the other organs through their own inherent defect of attachment and by following after the habit of that [attachment], sought to corrupt it; however, they perished—they were destroyed and shattered.

"How so?"—thus an illustration is given: "Just as that illustration, just as in the world, having struck—that is, having reached—a stone, a clod of earth—a lump of dust—thrown against a stone for the purpose of pulverizing it, would itself be shattered, fall apart, and be reduced to powder; even so, in this very same way as this illustration, being utterly shattered (*vidhvaṃsamānāḥ*), scattering in all directions (*viṣvañcaḥ*) with various courses, they perished (*vineśuḥ*)."

Then, from that destruction of the Asuras, because they were separated from those natural evils produced by attachment which had been an obstacle to their divinity, and by virtue of relying on the Chief Vital Breath (Prāṇa), whose nature is non-attachment, the deities—the Speech and others under discussion—became what they truly were. What did they become? Their own divine form consisting of Agni and the rest, which will be described hereafter. Although they had previously indeed consisted of Agni and the rest, their knowledge had been obscured by natural evil, and they had possessed only the conceit of being limited to the physical body.

The meaning is that, through the departure of that evil, they abandoned their identification with the mere physical body (*piṇḍa-mātra-abhimāna*) and came to possess the identification with the Self consisting of speech, fire, and so forth, as established by the scriptures. Furthermore, those Asuras who were their adversaries—[the word] "were defeated" (*parābhavan*) is understood from the context; the meaning is that they were utterly destroyed.

Just as in the ancient tradition (*purākalpa*), the former sacrificer belonging to a past age—having seen this very scripture in the form of a narrative (*ākhyāyikā*) and having examined the deities such as Speech (*vāk*) and the others in that same sequence, and having set them aside because they possessed the defect of being the locus of attachment and evil—approached the primary vital breath (*mukhya prāṇa*) as his Self, being free from the locus of defects; and having abandoned the identification with a Self limited merely to the physical body (*piṇḍa*) consisting of Speech and the other internal organs, he attained the state of Prajāpati existing in the present, which consists in identifying with the cosmic body (*vairāja piṇḍa*) whose nature is Speech, Fire, and the rest.

Having entered upon that which is revealed by the scripture, this sacrificer likewise becomes, through that very rite, the self whose nature is Prajāpati. Furthermore, his enemy—the hating rival who stands as the adversary to his state of being Prajāpati—also comes into existence; for even one who is not a hater may become a rival, such as the Bharatas and others.

However, that evil which is born from attachment to the objects of the senses—the enemy and hater—because it is the cause of obscuring the ultimate nature of the Self, perishes and is shattered like a clod of earth through the embrace of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). To whom does this result belong? He says: "He who knows thus," meaning he who realizes the aforementioned *prāṇa* as the Self, just like the previous sacrificer.

Having thus presented the result, the Śruti now resorts once more to the form of a narrative to explain why one should take the *mukhya* (principal) Prāṇa alone as the Self, setting aside speech and the other organs. Now, indeed, one should worship with the thought, "Blessings, fulfillment, and approaches. One should meditate upon that *sāman* with which one intends to chant the praise.

(8) Those vital breaths (*prāṇas*), who were the sons of Prajāpati, whose divine nature had been fully attained through the principal breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), said—having reached the state of fruition—they spoke. What did they say? [The text asks: "Where, indeed? This expresses a deliberation: "Where, indeed, in what place, was he? Who was he? He who thus, in this manner, bound us—that is, he who attached us and led us to the state of divinity by making it his own self. For in the world, those who have been benefited by someone remember the benefactor.

Remembering as people do in the world and investigating, they perceived [the Self] within the very aggregate of the body and its organs. How so? "This one within the mouth"—that is, in the space (*ākāśa*) that is inside the mouth, this one exists perceptibly. For everyone in the world reaches a conclusion after investigation; so did the gods. Since this one was perceived by the gods existing within the internal space without relying on any specific identity such as speech and so forth, therefore that vital breath (*prāṇa*) is "of Āsya" (*ayāsya*).

And because it does not depend on any specific [qualities], it has designated itself as unattached with respect to speech and the other organs; for this very reason, it is the *āṅgirasa*—the self (*ātman*)—of the body and its instruments. How is it *āṅgirasa*? For this is well known: it is the *rasa*, the essence, of the limbs characterized as the body and its instruments; that is to say, it is the self. But how is there the state of being the essence of the unattached? We shall explain that it is because, upon its departure, one undergoes desiccation.

And because this [prāṇa] is the common self (*ātman*) of the organs of action and perception—due to its being the essence of the limbs and its not depending on any particular [organ]—and because it is pure, therefore, setting aside speech and the others, prāṇa alone is to be resorted to as the self; such is the meaning of the passage. For the self must be accepted as the self, since through non-perverted knowledge one attains the highest good, while in the opposite case, the attainment of the undesirable is observed.
In whichever ṛc [he recites], that ṛc; whichever seer it belongs to, that seer; and whichever deity he is about to praise, toward that deity he runs. 9.

It might be thought that the purity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is unestablished; but has this not already been refuted by the fact that, unlike speech and the other organs which are subject to attachment such as "speaking what is auspicious," there is no basis for attachment in the case of the vital breath? Certainly; however, since speech and the others are said to have the vital breath as their self through its being *āṅgirasa*, it is suspected that they may be impure—just like one who touches a corpse or one who touches someone who has touched a corpse—by way of speech and the rest. To this he says: The vital breath is indeed pure. Why? Because this deity is named "Far-off" (*dūr-nāman*); having encountered this vital breath, the Asuras were shattered like a clod of earth against a stone.

He refers to her with the word "she" (*sā*): she is this very one who resides within the body of the present sacrificer and has been identified by the gods as "this [is] within the mouth. And she must be a deity, because she is subordinate as the object of the act of meditation. Since she is named *dūr*, that is, known as "the Far One"—the word *nāma* being a synonym for "renown"—therefore her purity is well-known, owing to her name *dūr*.

He asks, "Why, then, is it called 'dūra' (far)? He says: "Because death—characterized by attachment—is indeed far from this deity of breath (*prāṇa*); since the nature of breath is non-attachment, death remains far away even though it is nearby. Therefore, its renown is 'dūra'; thus, the purity of breath has been made known. The fruit for the knower is stated: 'Death indeed becomes far from him'—from him who knows thus, from one who knows in this way. 'Thus' means: he meditates upon the breath as it has been described, endowed with the quality of purity."

What is called *upāsana* (meditative worship) consists of approaching (*upagamya*) the nature of the object of worship through the mind exactly as it is made known by the scripture in its explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and then sitting upon—that is, contemplating—it without interruption by worldly cognitions, until there is the manifestation of the conceit of identity (*abhimāna*) with that very nature of the deity, just like the worldly conceit of self-identity. This is established by such scriptural texts as: "Having become a god, he goes to the gods," and "Which deity do you have as your deity in this eastern direction? and so forth.

It has been stated: "This deity... death indeed becomes far from him. But how does death become far from one who knows thus? It is said: because of the contradiction with such knowledge. For the evil born of attachment to the contact between the senses and their objects is contradicted by one who identifies with the Self that is Prāṇa; this is because [the former] is caused by the identification with the specific selves such as speech and so forth, and because it is caused by innate ignorance, whereas the identification with the Self that is Prāṇa is produced by the scriptures.
Therefore, it is logical that for one who knows thus, evil becomes far away due to this contradiction; this very point he demonstrates:
With whatever *chandas* one is about to praise, one should lay down that *chandas*; with whatever *stoma* one is about to praise, one should lay down that *stoma*. 10.

(10) "That indeed is this deity"—the meaning has already been explained. From among these deities, speech and the rest, [he removes] evil, which is death—for it is by means of evil, born from attachment to contact with the objects of the senses through natural ignorance, that everyone dies; therefore, that is death. Having cut off and removed that [evil] from the deities whose nature consists in the conceit of being the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is said that the vital breath removes it precisely by means of the conceit of being the vital breath alone; for, due to their mutual opposition, evil becomes far removed from one who knows thus.

What, then, did he do after having struck away the evil of death from the deities? It is said: *yatra*—in which place, namely, the end (*antaḥ*) or limit of these directions, such as the eastern and so forth—he caused them to go; that is to say, he made them go there. Now, one might object: "There is no end to the directions; how then did he cause them to go to an end? It is replied: Since the directions are conceptually constructed based on the boundary of people possessing Vedic knowledge, the region inhabited by people who oppose that [knowledge] is indeed the "end" of the directions, just as one says "the forest is the end of the inhabited land."

Thus there is no fault. Having sent that [evil] there, she—the deity of breath (*prāṇadevatā*)—deposited it, that is, placed it down in various ways in a state of subordination, among these deities. By implication, this refers to the lowest-born people who are devoid of the conceit of being the self of breath; for since that evil is born from contact with the senses, it is understood to have its locus in living beings. Therefore, one should not go to that lowest-born person—that is, one should not associate with them through conversation, sight, and so forth.

In contact with them, one would come into contact with evil, for that [evil] has its locus in them. And he should not go to their dwelling-place, which is designated by the term "the end of the quarters"—that is to say, even if it is devoid of people, or even if it is people who are separated from that region; this is the intended meaning. *Ned* is a particle used in the sense of apprehension. Thinking, "In such contact with people, I might follow after evil, that is, death"—meaning "I might go after it," "I might pursue it"—he does not go to the dwelling-place of people out of fear. Thus, the connection is with what precedes.
In whichever direction he intends to praise, toward that direction he should run. 11.

(11) This very deity—this result of the knowledge and action regarding the self of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), namely that speech and the other organs have fire and the others as their true nature—is now described. "Then he carried her beyond death": because the evil that constitutes death—the evil which effects limitation within the body—is destroyed by the knowledge of the self of the vital breath, therefore that vital breath is the destroyer of evil, of death. Therefore, that very vital breath carried these deities—speech and the others—beyond the aforementioned evil, death, and brought them to their respective, unlimited forms as the deities of fire and so forth.

Having approached the Self from within, let him praise it, meditating on his desire and remaining vigilant; for that desire will quickly be fulfilled for him with which desire he praises—whichever desire he may have to praise with. Whichever desire he may have to praise with. Thus ends the third section of the first chapter.

(12) "He indeed carried speech across first"—he is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). "Speech alone" means the foremost, that is, the principal; its primacy consists in its being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) with respect to the performance of the *udgītha* rite in comparison to the other instruments. He carried that which was first; he performed the act of carrying it across.

Furthermore, it is stated what the form of that Speech (Vāk) is once she has transcended death: She is Speech. At the time when she was released from, that is, liberated beyond, evil—death—having been set free by herself, then she became that Fire. That Speech, though already Fire even before, became Fire again upon the separation from death. This, however, is the distinction regarding the separation from death: this Fire, having transcended [death], shines beyond death, on the far side of death.
Prior to liberation, being bound by death, the internal speech was not as radiant as it is now; but now, beyond death, it shines because of its separation from death.

(13) Likewise—*prāṇa*, which is the sense of smell, became *vāyu*; it blows, having transcended death. Everything else has its meaning already explained. Home>>Commentaries>>Upanishads>>Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad>>Chapter 1>>Section 3>>Mantra 14

Mantra — Chapter (15) ---
Likewise, the ear became the quarters; the quarters exist as established through the divisions of east and so forth. Chapter 1, Section 3, Mantra 16.

(16) --- The mind is the moon—it shines. Just as in the past the deity Speech and the others, by becoming Fire and the rest, carried the previous sacrificer beyond death, even so, indeed, this deity of Breath carries this present sacrificer beyond death by becoming Speech and the others, such as Fire and the rest—for one who knows the Breath as distinguished by the fivefold set beginning with Speech. This is because of the Vedic text: "In whatever way one worships it, that very thing he becomes.
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.17)

Section: Mantra Chapter (17) — Now, for himself. Just as the speech and the other organs performed the singing for the sake of the Self, so too the principal vital breath (*prāṇa*), having performed the singing common to all the vital breaths which has the fruit of attaining Prajāpati, [performed it] during the three *pavamāna* chants; then, immediately thereafter, during the remaining nine *stotra*s, he sang for himself—that is, for his own sake—the "food-and-eatable" (*annādya*), meaning both food (*anna*) and that which is to be eaten (*ādya*). It has been stated that the connection of the agent with a specific desire is based on scriptural injunction.

But how is it understood that this food and drink is brought for the sake of the self by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)? To this, he states the reason: "Whatever..."—the word "whatever" is intended to refer to food in general; "for" (*hi*) is used in the sense of a reason; because in the world, whatever food is eaten or consumed by living beings, that is [eaten] by this very *prāṇa* alone. "Ana" is a well-known name for the *prāṇa*; the word *ana* ending in a nasal (*sānta*) denotes a cart, whereas the other form ending in a vowel (*svarānta*) is a synonym for the *prāṇa*. The meaning is that it is eaten by the *prāṇa* alone.

Furthermore, it is not merely that food is eaten by the vital breath (*prāṇa*); rather, the vital breath is established here upon that very food which has been transformed into the form of the body. Therefore, food is brought in by the vital breath for the sake of its own support. Even that act of eating performed by the vital breath is solely for the purpose of its own support; thus, unlike in the case of speech and the other organs, no possibility of sin arising from attachment to pleasant things exists in the vital breath.

(18) "Those gods. Now, is it not improper to state the restriction, "It is eaten by the breath alone," since we observe that speech and the other organs also receive assistance from food? This is not a fault, because that assistance to them is mediated through the breath. To demonstrate how the assistance to speech and the others, produced by food, is mediated by the breath, he says: "Those gods"—speech and the rest—are called "gods" (*devāḥ*) because they illuminate (*dyotana*) their respective objects. They said to the principal breath: "This is only this much; there is nothing more than this. The particle *vā* is used for the sake of recollection; [the meaning is: "All this is only this much."

"What is it? [The answer is: Whatever food is eaten in the world that sustains the life of living beings—all that you have sung for yourself, "you have taken unto yourself" by means of your singing; this is the meaning. And we are not able to remain without food. Therefore, after this—include us, us, in this food which is for yourself, your own food; the omission of the causal suffix (*ṇic*) is a Vedic license; "make us sharers in the food."

The other [organs] said: "If you indeed desire food, do not enter me—do not settle down all around me, facing toward me. When Prāṇa had spoken thus, they said, "So be it," and they settled down all around him; that is, they entered him decisively from every side, meaning they settled down surrounding that Prāṇa.

For those who have entered [the body] in this manner, by the permission of the vital breath (prāṇa), food that sustains the vital breath becomes a source of satisfaction for them precisely through that vital breath; there is no independent connection with food for speech and the other organs. Therefore, the restriction—"it is eaten by this alone"—is indeed appropriate.

And he says that very thing: "Therefore," because the deities of speech and the other senses are established through the permission of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) precisely by being dependent upon it, "therefore," whatever food the world eats with this vital breath, by that food these [deities] of speech and the others are satisfied. He who knows the vital breath as the support of speech and the others—namely, that "speech and the others are dependent on the five vital breaths"—him too, in this very way, his own kinsmen approach and enter, just as speech and the others enter the vital breath.

The intention is that he becomes one who is to be resorted to by his kinsmen. And for his own people who are settled together—just as speech and the other organs are to the vital breath—he becomes their supporter with his own food; likewise, he is their leader; he goes before them, at the forefront, just as the vital breath goes before speech and the others; likewise, he is an eater of food, meaning he is free from disease; and he is the sovereign, the protector ruling over them, an independent lord, just as the vital breath is over speech and the others. For one who knows the vital breath in this way, these aforementioned fruits accrue.

Furthermore, whoever among one's own kinsmen wishes to be an adversary—that is, to act in opposition—to one who knows thus, who knows the vital breath (prāṇa), such a person, like the Asuras who were rivals of the vital breath, is certainly not capable, nor is he sufficient, for those who are to be supported; that is to say, he is unable to maintain them.

Furthermore, he who among his kinsmen follows this one who knows thus—just as speech and the other organs follow the vital breath (prāṇa)—or he who, following and conforming to this one who knows thus, desires to support his own dependents and wife, just as speech and the others desired to support themselves by following the vital breath; he indeed becomes capable and sufficient for those who are to be supported, his dependents, to provide for them, and not another who acts independently. All this has been stated as the fruit of the knowledge of the qualities of the vital breath.

In order to establish that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the self of the body and its organs, its nature as *Āṅgirasa* was introduced with the words, "This is Ayāsya Āṅgirasa. However, the reason why it is *Āṅgirasa* has not yet been stated; therefore, this section is commenced to establish that reason. For the status of the vital breath as the self of the body and its organs depends upon the establishment of that reason. Furthermore, the dependence of speech and the other organs upon the vital breath was mentioned immediately before; he now explains how that dependence is to be justified. [Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.19] "And because, when the vital breath departs from these limbs, they fall down, therefore it is called *Aṅgirasa*. (19) When the vital breath departs from these limbs—namely, the hands, feet, and so forth—they fall down. Because of this, it is called *Aṅgirasa*. The word *aṅga* means "limb" (*aṅga*), and *rasa* means "essence" (*sāra*). Therefore, since it is the essence of the limbs, it is *Aṅgirasa*. Alternatively, the limbs themselves are the *aṅgas*, and the vital breath is their *rasa* (juice/essence); thus it is *Aṅgirasa*. Or else, the limbs are the *aṅgas*, and because it is the essence (*rasa*) of those limbs, it is *Aṅgirasa*. In all these cases, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule [Pāṇini 4.3.130]. Thus, by demonstrating that the vital breath is the essence of the limbs, its status as the self of the body and its organs is established. And since the vital breath is the self of the body and its organs, it is the self of all beings. Therefore, it is the supreme Brahman. Thus, the purpose of the entire chapter is fulfilled. Therefore, it is said: [Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.20] "That is the Brahman, that is the Immortal, that is the Self. Entering it, one is freed from sin, shakes off good and evil, and becomes a possessor of the true nature of light, attaining the highest identity in the worlds of Brahman. (20) "That" refers to the aforementioned vital breath. That is Brahman, that is the Immortal, that is the Self. Entering into that Self, one is freed from sin—that is, from all evil—and shakes off both good and evil deeds. Having shaken them off, one becomes a possessor of the true nature of light, meaning one becomes of the nature of light. And having become such, one attains the highest identity in the worlds of Brahman. That is, one attains the state of being identical with the highest Brahman. This is the fruit for one who knows the vital breath in this manner. Thus, the purpose of the entire chapter is fulfilled. Therefore, it is said: [Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.21] "Now, concerning the meditation on the fivefold Sāman: the earth is the *Hinkāra*, fire is the *Prastāva*, the atmosphere is the *Udgītha*, the sun is the *Pratihāra*, and the heaven is the *Nidhana*. This is the Sāman resting upon the worlds. (21) "Now," that is, after the meditation on the vital breath, "concerning the meditation on the fivefold Sāman": the earth is the *Hinkāra*, fire is the *Prastāva*, the atmosphere is the *Udgītha*, the sun is the *Pratihāra*, and the heaven is the *Nidhana*. This is the Sāman resting upon the worlds. The word "this" refers to the Sāman consisting of the five parts beginning with *Hinkāra*, which has just been described. "Resting upon the worlds" means that it rests upon the worlds, namely the earth and the others. The phrase "the earth is the *Hinkāra*" and so forth indicates that the Sāman is to be meditated upon as the earth and the other worlds. The word "this" is used to show that the Sāman previously mentioned is the same as the one here described. The word "now" (*atha*) is used to indicate a sequence. The meaning is: "After the meditation on the vital breath, one should perform the meditation on the fivefold Sāman as follows. The rest is as explained. [Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.22] "The *Hinkāra* is the past, the *Prastāva* is the future, the *Udgītha* is the day, the *Pratihāra* is the night, and the *Nidhana* is food. This is the Sāman resting upon time. (22) "The *Hinkāra* is the past," that is, the *Hinkāra* part of the Sāman is to be meditated upon as the past. "The *Prastāva* is the future," that is, the *Prastāva* is to be meditated upon as the future. "The *Udgītha* is the day," that is, the *Udgītha* is to be meditated upon as the day. "The *Pratihāra* is the night," that is, the *Pratihāra* is to be meditated upon as the night. "The *Nidhana* is food," that is, the *Nidhana* is to be meditated upon as food. "This is the Sāman resting upon time. The meaning is that this Sāman, consisting of the five parts beginning with *Hinkāra*, is to be meditated upon as time. The word "this" is used to show that the Sāman previously mentioned is the same as the one here described. The word "now" (*atha*) is used to indicate a sequence. The meaning is: "After the meditation on the Sāman resting upon the worlds, one should perform the meditation on the Sāman resting upon time as follows. The rest is as explained. [Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.23] "The *Hinkāra* is fire, the *Prastāva* is the wind, the *Udgītha* is the sun, the *Pratihāra* is the constellations, and the *Nidhana* is the moon. This is the Sāman resting upon the deities. (23) "The *Hinkāra* is fire," that is, the *Hinkāra* is to be meditated upon as fire. "The *Prastāva* is the wind," that is, the *Prastāva* is to be meditated upon as the wind. "The *Udgītha* is the sun," that is, the *Udgītha* is to be meditated upon as the sun. "The *Pratihāra* is the constellations," that is, the *Pratihāra* is to be meditated upon as the constellations. "The *Nidhana* is the moon," that is, the *Nidhana* is to be meditated upon as the moon. "This is the Sāman resting upon the deities. The meaning is that this Sāman, consisting of the five parts beginning with *Hinkāra*, is to be meditated upon as the deities. The word "this" is used to show that the Sāman previously mentioned is the same as the one here described. The word "now" (*atha*) is used to indicate a sequence. The meaning is: "After the meditation on the Sāman resting upon time, one should perform the meditation on the Sāman resting upon the deities as follows. The rest is as explained. [Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.24] "The *Hinkāra* is the *Ṛk*, the *Prastāva* is the Sāman, the *Udgītha* is the Uktha, the *Pratihāra* is the Yajuṣ, and the *Nidhana* is the Brahman. This is the Sāman resting upon the Vedas. (24) "The *Hinkāra* is the *Ṛk*," that is, the *Hinkāra* is to be meditated upon as the *Ṛk*. "The *Prastāva* is the Sāman," that is, the *Prastāva* is to be meditated upon as the Sāman.

Section: Mantra Chapter (19) The passage beginning with "This very one is Āṅgirasa" and so forth is taken up exactly as it was introduced for the sake of what follows. The sentence ending with "Prāṇa, indeed, is the essence (*rasa*) of the limbs" serves to remind us once again of the meaning already explained. How so?—"Prāṇa, indeed, is the essence of the limbs. For Prāṇa—indeed, the word "indeed" (*hi*) indicates what is well-known—is the essence of the limbs. It is well known that Prāṇa is the essence of the limbs, and not speech or the other organs; therefore, the reminder "Prāṇa, indeed" is appropriate.

But how is its well-known status established? To this he says: therefore the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) is connected as a concluding term (*upasaṃhārārtha*). From which [limb]—from whichever unspecified limb—from whatever limb, from any part of the body without distinction, when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) departs and withdraws, that very limb withers, becomes sapless, and undergoes drying up. Therefore, "this indeed is the essence (*rasa*) of the limbs"—this is the conclusion.

Therefore, it is established that the Self of the organs and the body is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). For if the Self were to depart, the remainder would be death. Consequently, all living beings live by means of it. Thus, setting aside speech and the other [organs], the vital breath alone is to be meditated upon; this is the collective meaning.

Furthermore, this vital breath is not only the Self of the body and the organs—which constitute its form and function—but what else? It is the Self of the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman* verses, which constitute its name. Praising the vital breath as the Self of everything, the text magnifies it for the purpose of being an object of meditation.
