Mantra — Chapter (20) ---
This very one who is under discussion is Āṅgirasa Bṛhaspati. How so is he Bṛhaspati? It is said: Speech indeed is the Bṛhatī; [she is] the Bṛhatī meter.

The *anuṣṭubh* consists of thirty-six syllables, and speech (*vāk*) is the *anuṣṭubh*; how so? Because of the Vedic revelation (śruti): "Speech, indeed, is the *anuṣṭubh*. And that speech, as the *anuṣṭubh*, is included within the *bṛhatī* metre; therefore, it is appropriate to speak of it as established fact, saying, "Speech, indeed, is the *bṛhatī*. Furthermore, all *ṛc*s (verses) are included within the *bṛhatī*, because it is praised as the vital breath (*prāṇa*); for another scriptural passage states: "One should know that the *bṛhatī* is the vital breath, and the *ṛc*s are the vital breath. Since the *ṛc*s have speech as their essence, they are included within the vital breath.

To the question "How so? he says: This *prāṇa* is the lord (*pati*) of that speech, which is the *bṛhatī* verse, because it brings it forth; for the *ṛc* is indeed produced by the wind impelled by the digestive fire within the belly. Or, he is the lord of speech because of its protection; for speech is protected by *prāṇa*, since one who lacks *prāṇa* has no capacity for the utterance of sound. Therefore, the meaning is that *Bṛhaspati*—the *prāṇa*—is the self (*ātman*) of the *ṛcs*.

(21) The same applies to the *yajus* formulas. How so? This very [breath] is indeed *Brahmaṇaspati*. Speech (*vāk*) is indeed *brahman*—and *brahman* is the *yajus*; moreover, that is simply a particular form of speech. Of this speech, of this *yajus*, of this *brahman*, he is the lord (*pati*); therefore he is *Brahmaṇaspati*—as before.

How, then, is it understood that the *bṛhatī* and the *brahman* possess the nature of *ṛc* and *yajus*, and not some other meaning? It is said: because at the end [of the section on] *vāk* (speech), there is a designation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *sāman*, namely, "Speech indeed is *sāman*. And likewise, since there are the statements "Speech indeed is *bṛhatī*" and "Speech indeed is *brahman*," it is logical that the *ṛc* and *yajus* are coreferential with speech. Furthermore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*): when *sāman* has been mentioned, only *ṛc* and *yajus* remain. Moreover, because they are specific forms of speech: for *ṛc* and *yajus* are indeed specific varieties of speech.

Therefore, it is appropriate that those two [terms] stand in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇatā*). Furthermore, because otherwise there would be the consequence of non-distinction—since "Sāman" and "Udgītha" clearly function as specific designations, it is likewise appropriate that the words "Bṛhatī" and "Brahman" function as specific designations; otherwise, there would result the futility of terms whose specific referents are not determined, and if the designation of a specific were merely a matter of words, there would be redundancy in both cases; moreover, such a sequence of the words *ṛk*, *yajus*, *sāman*, and *udgītha* is observed in the Śrutis themselves.

Mantra — Chapter (22) ---

This very thing is indeed *sāman*. How so? He says: Speech (*vāk*) is *sā*; whatever is denoted by feminine words is speech. For the word *sā*—a pronoun—is used with reference to all objects denoted by feminine words. Likewise, this breath (*prāṇa*) is *ama*; the word *ama* is used with reference to all objects denoted by masculine words. This is known from another scriptural passage: "By what do you obtain my masculine names? "By breath," he should say. "By what my feminine names? "By speech. Thus, this word *sāman* consists of the designations of speech and breath.

In this way, *gīti*—which is merely a collection of vowels and so forth brought about by the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—is denoted by the word *sāman*. Therefore, there is nothing called *sāman* apart from speech and breath, because vowels, syllables, and the rest are produced by the vital breath and are dependent upon it. This very breath is indeed the *sāman*. Since it is both *sā* (speech) and *ama* (breath), making up the essence of speech and breath, therefore the nature of being *sāman* belongs to that *sāman*—the collection of vowels and so forth in the form of song—and that is what is sung on earth.

Furthermore, because it is equal (*sama*)—that is, identical—in every respect with all that is about to be stated, it is connected with the phrase "therefore, indeed, it is *sāman*. The word "or" (*vā*) is to be understood through the force of indicating another mode for obtaining the designation "Sāman."

In what manner, then, is the equality of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) stated? It is said: equal to a *pluṣi* (a tiny insect) in the body of a *puttikā*; equal to a gnat in the body of a gnat; equal to a *nāga* (elephant) in the body of an elephant; equal to these three worlds in the body of Prajāpati belonging to the triple world; and equal to this entire universe in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha. This equality of the vital breath consists in its being fully present in its entirety within the bodies of the *puttikā* and others—just as "cowness" (*gotva*) is fully present in every individual cow—and not merely by having the same dimensions as the body itself.

Because [the self] is formless and all-pervading, its equality within bodies is not like that of a lamp in a jar or a palace, which expands or contracts according to the size of those objects. For the scripture states: "Therefore, all these are indeed equal; all are infinite. However, for that which is all-pervading, there is no contradiction in its obtaining a function within bodies that corresponds to the dimensions of those bodies.

Thus, for one who knows the *prāṇa* called *sāman* because of its equality—its greatness being revealed by the Veda—the fruit is this: he attains (*aśnute*), that is, pervades, the *sāyujya*, which is the state of union with the *prāṇa* as *sāman*, characterized by having the same body, senses, and self-identification; or else he attains *sālokya*, residence in the same world, depending on the particularity of his contemplation. This applies to one who thus knows this *prāṇa* as the *sāman* described above—that is, he worships it until the manifestation of the identification with the nature of *prāṇa*.

Section: Mantra Chapter (23) This, indeed, is the Udgītha. The Udgītha is a specific part (*bhakti*) of the Sāman, not the act of singing (*udgāna*), because the context concerns the Sāman. How is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) the Udgītha?

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed "ut," for by means of the vital breath this entire world is *uttabdha*—meaning held up, supported, and sustained from above. This syllable "ut" illuminates the sense of being supported and denotes the quality of the vital breath; therefore, the vital breath is "ut. Speech alone is the *gīthā*, because the *udgītha* portion is a particular kind of sound; since the root *gai* has the meaning of "sound," that [portion] is indeed speech.

For no form whatsoever is perceived for the *udgītha*-portion apart from sound; therefore, the restriction "speech alone is the *gīthā*" is appropriate. Breath is "high" (*ud*), and speech is dependent on breath as its *gīthā*; thus both are denoted by the single word *udgītha*. Mantra Chapter (24) Furthermore, regarding this matter already stated, there is also a traditional narrative (ākhyāyikā) that is heard. Brahmadatta by name, the son of Cikitāna—thus Caikitāneya, his grandson—while consuming the Soma at a sacrifice, said to the King: "May the head—the skull—of me, who has spoken untruth, fall off clearly as I consume this King [Soma] residing in this cup!"

The substitution of *tātaṅ* for *ta* occurs in the imperative (*loṭ*) expressing a blessing—thus, "may he cause to fall" (*vipātayatāt*); the meaning is, "if I should be a speaker of untruth. But how is the possibility of speaking untruth established? It is said: "If (*yat*), from this aforementioned vital breath (*prāṇa*) conjoined with speech, Ayāsya—the one who was the Udgātṛ at the sacrificial session (*satra*) of the ancient seers (*pūrvarṣi*), the creators of the universe, and who is designated by the term *Āṅgirasa* which denotes the chief vital breath—had sung the *udgītha* by means of another deity distinct from speech and breath, [then he would have fallen]. The word *udagāyat* refers to the act of singing the *udgītha*.

"If I have done this, then I would be a speaker of untruth; may the deity strike off the head of me, who has thus acted with a perverted understanding"—in making such an oath, he demonstrates the firmness of conviction regarding the necessity of performing the act of faith.

The Śruti concludes this very matter, which was determined through the narrative, in its own words: "By means of speech, which has breath as its primary essence, and by means of breath, which is his own self, that Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, the Udgātṛ priest, sang the Udgītha"—this is the meaning established by the oath.

Mantra — Chapter (25) ---

Regarding the phrase "of this very one": the word "this" connects back to the *prāṇa* under discussion; the expression "of this very one" points specifically to the principal *prāṇa* by means of a demonstrative gesture. Of that *sāman*—that is, of the *prāṇa* denoted by the word *sāman*—he who knows what is its own property (*svam*); what indeed would happen to him? To him it surely becomes his own property. Having enticed and drawn him forward with this result, [the teacher] says to the one desiring to hear: "Of that *sāman*, the tone (*svara*) alone is its own property. By "tone" is meant the sweetness residing in the throat; that alone is its own property, its ornament.

Therefore, the singing (udgāna) is observed to be adorned by prosperity. Since this is so, one who is about to perform the office of the *ṛtvij*—that is, the work of the *udgātṛ* singer—should desire a tone (*svara*) in relation to speech, or rather, a tone dependent upon speech. This is intended for the *udgātṛ* who wishes to effect the richness of the *sāman* by means of the tone. However, this is prescribed as a secondary or incidental rule (*prāsaṅgika*).

The meaning is that when the perception of the Sāman’s possession of proper tone must be produced through its sweetness of sound, since such sweetness does not arise by mere wish alone, one must perform acts such as cleaning the teeth and drinking oil according to one's capacity. With speech thus purified and endowed with the correct tone, one should perform the priestly office (*ārṭvijya*).

Therefore—since *svara* (accent) is the very nature (*svabhūta*) of the *sāman*, the *sāman* is adorned by its own [nature]; for this reason, people at a sacrifice truly desire to see (*didṛkṣante*) the *udgātṛ* who possesses *svara*, just as people in the world desire to see a wealthy man. For it is well known in the world: "Moreover (*atho*), they desire to see him who possesses his own wealth—that is, a wealthy man. Thus, the connection between the established knowledge of the quality and its fruit is concluded: "He indeed comes to possess his own [wealth], he who thus knows this *sva* (own property/nature) of the *sāman*."

Mantra — Chapter (26) ---

Now, another quality characterized by "goldenness" (*suvarṇatva*) is enjoined. This too is simply excellence of tone (*sausvarya*). The distinction is this: the former was sweetness residing in the throat; this, however, is defined by the word "gold" (*suvarṇa*). Regarding that very *sāman*, he who knows its goldenness obtains gold for himself; this is because of the commonality of the word "gold" between sound and precious metal. The meaning is that ordinary gold itself becomes the fruit of knowing this quality. Indeed, for him, the tone itself is the gold.
"He indeed possesses a beautiful armor who thus knows this beauty of the Sāman"— all this is as explained previously.
Chapter 1, Section 3, Mantra 27.

(27) Likewise, desiring to teach the quality of its foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), [the text] says: "He who knows the foundation of this very Sāman—[it is called] 'foundation' because one is established (*pratitiṣṭhati*) upon it—that foundation is speech (*vāk*); he who knows that foundation as a quality of the Sāman, he indeed becomes established. Since the scripture states, "As they meditate upon it, so they become," it is logical that it possesses that quality. To those who, having been enticed by the result as before, wish to know what the foundation is, [the text] says: "Of that Sāman, speech itself is [the foundation]. "Speech" is the designation for the places of articulation such as the root of the tongue; that alone is the foundation.

Regarding this, he says: "For speech is the foundation. Because this Prāṇa, being established in speech—specifically in the root of the tongue and other parts—is sung, that is, it attains the state of song (*gīti*), therefore speech is the foundation of the Sāman. Others say: "It is sung as being established in food"; however, it is more appropriate to say "it is established here [in speech]. Since the view of the others is not censured, one should cultivate the knowledge of the quality of the foundation through the alternative: either speech is the foundation, or food is. Section: Mantra Chapter (28) Thus, the ritual of recitation (*japa-karma*) is intended for one who possesses knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). That knowledge, by virtue of which one is qualified for the ritual of recitation, has already been explained. Now, immediately following that, because the ritual of recitation performed by such a knower results in the fruit of ascending to the state of a deity, it is therefore prescribed here.

Since these [mantras] would apply everywhere due to their connection with the *udgītha*, and since the statement "of the *pavamānas*" establishes that they are to be performed during all three *pavamāna* chants, the text further restricts the time: "The *prastotṛ* indeed sings the *sāman*. At whatever time—that is, at which moment—the *prastotṛ* should begin to sing the *sāman*, at that time he should mutter these. And the name of this act of muttering is "ascent" (*abhyāroha*).

*Abhyāroha* (the ascent) is that by which, through this very act of recitation (*japa*), one causes the self to ascend toward such a divine state in a direct manner. Because of the plural number in the word *etāni* ("these"), there are three *yajus* formulas. Due to their being indicated in the accusative case and because they originate from the Brāhmaṇa portion of the Veda, the accentuation must be employed exactly as it is read [in the Saṃhitā], and not according to the *mantra*-accent. This is the recitation-act belonging to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).

These are those very *yajus* formulas: "Lead me from non-existence to existence," "Lead me from darkness to light," and "Lead me from death to immortality. Since the meaning of the mantras becomes obscured, the *Brāhmaṇa* itself explains the meaning of the mantras: "That mantra," which means what has been stated; if it is asked what that meaning is, it is said: "Lead me from non-existence to existence. Non-existence (*asat*) is indeed death—death is said to be one's natural karma and ignorance; for non-existence is the cause of the ultimate downward state.

"Sat" means the real—the knowledge of scriptural action—and "amṛta" (immortal) because it is the cause of immortality. Therefore, from the unreal—from improper action and ignorance—lead me, who am the real, to the real; that is to say, lead me to the state of selfhood which is the means for attaining divinity. Regarding this, he states the meaning of the sentence: "He says this very thing: 'Make me immortal. Likewise, "From darkness, lead me to light."

Death is indeed darkness (*tamas*). For all ignorance, being of the nature of an obscuration, is darkness; and that very thing, because it is the cause of death, is death. Light is the immortal, the divine essential nature which is the opposite of what was previously described. Because its nature is luminosity, knowledge is light; and that very thing is the immortal, because its nature is indestructible. Therefore, "Lead me from darkness to light" means: as before, "Lead me from death to immortality," and so forth. He says this effectively: "Make me immortal"—that is, lead me to the state of fruition belonging to the divine Prajāpati.

"May the first mantra cause that which is by nature not a means to attain the state of being a means; may the second, however, cause that which is already a means but is of the nature of ignorance to attain the state of being the goal. "Lead me from death to immortality"—this is simply the combined meaning of the two preceding mantras expressed by the third mantra; its meaning is well-known. In this third mantra, there is no form of meaning that is hidden or concealed as it might appear to be in the case of the two preceding mantras; the meaning is exactly as it is heard.

Having performed the *udgāna* for the sake of the sacrificer during the three *pavamāna* chants, he should thereafter sing for himself food and nourishment (*annādya*) during the remaining chants that follow—provided the *udgātṛ* is a knower of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), being himself of the nature of the vital breath, just like the vital breath itself. Since this very *udgātṛ* knows the vital breath as described, he is therefore capable of accomplishing that desire just like the vital breath; therefore, while those chants are being performed, the sacrificer should choose a boon.

Whatever desire one might desire, that very desire as a boon one should choose—that is, one should pray for it. Because he is such a knower, the word "Udgātṛ" (the chanter) is to be connected even before the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*). Whatever desire the Udgātṛ desires—whether for himself or for the sacrificer—and whatever he wishes for, that he brings about through his singing; he accomplishes it by means of his chant.

Thus far it has been stated that through both knowledge and ritual action one attains the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇātman*); in that regard, no possibility of doubt arises. Therefore, a doubt is raised as to whether or not the attainment of the vital breath occurs upon the cessation of ritual action; to remove that doubt, he says: "That, indeed, this very thing is world-conquering. That is to say, this very vision of the vital breath—even when isolated and devoid of ritual action—is "world-conquering," meaning it is indeed a means for attaining the worlds. There is certainly no "hope"—that is, expectation or prayer—for the state of being "non-worldly" (or unworthiness for the worlds). There is simply no such hope at all.

For one who has developed the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) with respect to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is impossible to hope for its attainment. Indeed, a person living in a village does not hope, as one living in the forest might, "When shall I reach the village? Hope is directed toward an object that is not already present and is not the self; it cannot occur with respect to one's own self. Therefore, there is no such hope as: "May I never fail to attain the state of being the vital breath."

To whom does this belong? It belongs to one who thus knows this *sāman* as the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—whose greatness has been determined as described: "I am the pure *prāṇa*, invincible by the demonic evils consisting of attachment to the objects of the senses; and the pentad beginning with speech, because it rests upon me, has the nature of fire and the other [deities]."

It is free from the defect of the evil of the Asuras, which arises from attachment to the objects of the senses produced by the intellect arising from one's own nature; and there is the bond of the consumption of food based on Me among all beings. Furthermore, I am the Self of all beings because of My being the *Āṅgirasa*; and I am the Self of Speech, which consists of the Ṛk, Yajus, Sāman, and Udgītha, because of Its pervading that speech and because of bringing it about. For me, as the Sāman attains the state of being sung, external wealth is the ornament of good voice (*sausvarya*); even more internal than that is the excellence of gold (*sauvarṇya*), which is figuratively termed "good voice."

"The places such as my throat, which belong to me as I undergo the state of being song, are my foundations. Possessing such qualities, I am fully and entirely present even in bodies such as those of gnats, because of my incorporeality and omnipresence"—until such an identification is manifested, this is what one meditates upon according to the Veda.
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa of the first chapter.

Section: Mantra Chapter.
"Om"—one should meditate upon this syllable as the Udgītha, for one chants the Udgītha with "Om. Here follows its detailed exposition.

"In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone. The attainment of the state of Prajāpati through the combination of knowledge and action has already been explained, as well as through the contemplation of Prāṇa alone, by the passage beginning with "That, verily, is the winner of worlds. This section is now commenced for the purpose of describing the excellence of the fruit of Vedic knowledge and action by means of a description of the majesty of Prajāpati—the very embodiment of that fruit—consisting in his sovereignty over the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world.

And by this, a praise of knowledge and action as prescribed in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) would be established through implication. However, what is intended here is this: all this fruit of knowledge and action is merely *saṃsāra*, because it is heard to be joined with fear, discontent, and so forth; because it is characterized by the body and the organs; and because its objects are gross, manifest, and non-eternal. Furthermore, this is for the sake of the subsequent portion, which is that pure knowledge of Brahman to be described hereafter is the cause of liberation.

For one who is not detached from the sphere of transmigratory existence—characterized by the distinction between means and ends and so forth—there is no qualification for the subject matter of the knowledge of the oneness of the Self, just as there is none for a thirsty person regarding drinking. Therefore, the description of the excellence of the fruits of knowledge and action is for the sake of what follows. And thus [the author] will say: "This is the path leading to that," and "This is dearer than a son," and so forth.

"The Self alone was the Self"—thus Prajāpati, the first embodied being born from the egg, is designated. He, who is the fruit of Vedic knowledge and action, was indeed this entire collection of diverse bodies, undifferentiated from that body of Prajāpati, at the beginning, prior to the production of other bodies. And he was "of the form of a person," meaning of the nature of a person, characterized by a head, hands, and so forth; he was Virāj.

He alone, having first come into being, looked around—having performed an investigation, thinking, "Who am I, or what am I characterized by? He saw nothing else whatsoever other than himself, who consists of the vital breath and the physical body, and is of the nature of the effects and instruments [of action]; he did not perceive anything else. Rather, he perceived only the Self, the Self of all. Thus, refined by the Vedic knowledge from his previous birth, he first proclaimed: "I am that Prajāpati; I am the Self of all."

Therefore, from that—because he first designated himself as "I" (aham) due to the impressions of his previous knowledge—he came to have the name "Aham"; the scripture will later state that his secret name (upaniṣad) is indeed "Aham," as shown by the Veda.

Therefore, because this occurred regarding Prajāpati as the cause, for that reason, among the living beings who are his effects, even at this present time, when addressed and asked "Who are you?", one first says "I am this one," designating oneself by means of the name of the causal self; and subsequently, when there is a desire to know the specific name, one then declares the designation of the particular body, such as "Devadatta" or "Yajñadatta"—whatever the name of this particular body may be.

It is that which was performed by the parents, and he speaks of it. And he is Prajāpati; because, in a previous birth, during his state as a seeker (*sādhakāvasthā*) through the practice of the cultivation of right action and knowledge, since he—being the first among all those desiring to attain the status of Prajāpati through the practice of the cultivation of action and knowledge—burned, consumed [the impurities] at the very beginning.

What [did he do]? He burned away all evils characterized by attachment and ignorance, which serve as the causes for obstructing the state of Prajāpati. Because it was so, therefore he is called "Puruṣa"—one who has burned away (*apūrvam auṣat*) [the evils]. Just as this Prajāpati, having burned away all obstructive evils, became the Puruṣa-Prajāpati; so too [does the sacrificer].

In the same way, another person also burns—that is, reduces to ashes—by means of the fire of the practice of knowledge, action, and meditation, or solely by the power of knowledge. Whom does he burn? It means: him who, being prior to this knower—that is, the first Prajāpati—desires to become [Prajāpati]. He shows who that is: "he who knows thus"; by implication, one who possesses the excellence of the cultivation of knowledge. Now, one might object: the desire to attain the state of Prajāpati leads to misfortune, if such a person is burned by one who knows thus.

This is not a fault, because burning consists merely in the initial failure to attain the status of Prajāpati due to the absence of excellence in the cultivation of knowledge. One who possesses superior means attains the status of Prajāpati first, while one with inferior means does not; thus it is said that the former "burns" the latter. However, it is not the case that the other is physically burned by the superior means in a literal sense—just as in the world, among those racing in a contest, he who first reaches the goal renders the others as if burnt, depriving them of their capacity; so it is here.

That is to say, the fruit of knowledge and ritual action prescribed in the *karmakāṇḍa*, characterized by the state of Prajāpati—which was desired for praise—did not at all transcend the sphere of saṃsāra; intending to demonstrate this point, he says:
[The text continues].

The gods, indeed, being afraid of death, entered the threefold knowledge; they covered themselves with the meters (*chandāṃsi*). Because they covered themselves with these, that is the "metrical nature" (*chandaḥ-tva*) of the meters.

He was afraid. That Prajāpati—himself being that first embodied one described as having the form of a person—was afraid, just like we and others; thus it is said. Because this person, possessing a body and the instruments of action, was afraid due to a perverted perception regarding the destruction of the self, therefore, by virtue of that similarity, even today one who is alone is afraid. Furthermore, just as in our own case, the cause for removing the perverted perception that is the source of fear is the vision of the Self as it truly is.

This Prajāpati performed *īkṣā*, that is, he made an act of seeing. How? He says: "Since there exists nothing other than me—no other entity distinct from my self that stands as an adversary—in the absence of any cause for the destruction of the self, why indeed should I fear? From that very realization of the self as it truly is, fear departed from this Prajāpati; it clearly vanished.

He states that whatever fear belonged to that Prajāpati was caused solely by ignorance (*avidyā*) and is untenable in the light of the vision of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*): "From what indeed would he have been afraid? Why did he become afraid? The intention is that, upon the investigation of ultimate reality, fear is simply not possible. For fear arises only from a second thing, another entity; and that second entity is presented only through ignorance.

For that which is not perceived cannot be the cause of fear, according to the Vedic verse: "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness? And it is logical that he dispelled fear through the perception of oneness; why? Because fear arises from a second thing, from another entity; since that perception of a second thing has been removed by the perception of oneness, fear no longer exists.

Regarding this, they raise the following objections: From what did Prajāpati’s vision of oneness arise? Who instructed him? Or did it manifest spontaneously without instruction? If so, the same would follow for people like us. If, on the other hand, it was caused by impressions (*saṃskāra*) formed in previous births, then the vision of oneness would be rendered purposeless.

Just as Prajāpati, even though he had transcended the state of birth, did not cast off the cause of bondage—ignorance—despite his vision of oneness, because he was born still joined with ignorance and was afraid; in the same way, the vision of oneness for all beings would result in being purposeless. If it is argued that only the final [vision] is the remover [of ignorance], we say no; because, as before, it would recur again, thus lacking definitiveness. Therefore, the vision of oneness is indeed purposeless.

This is not a fault; for it arises from superior causes, as is seen in the world. Just as it is observed that when one is born with a body and organs produced by meritorious deeds and free from defects, there is clarity of wisdom, intelligence, memory, and confidence, so too the birth of Prajāpati is superior, being endowed with body and organs purified by the burning away of all evils—the causes contrary to virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty. And it is logical that the realization of oneness belonging to Prajāpati should arise spontaneously from that [superior birth], even without being taught.

And so says the Smṛti: "Whose knowledge is unimpeded, as well as the dispassion, sovereignty, and virtue of Prajāpati—this quartet is co-existent. If it is argued that fear is impossible given this state of being co-existent, we say no; for the statement regarding their co-existence does not refer to something taught by another [source], just as darkness does not arise together with the sun.

If it be argued that faith, devotion, prostration, and so forth are not causes [of knowledge]—that is to say, if it be thought that those causes of knowledge prescribed by Śruti and Smṛti, such as "The man of faith obtains knowledge, being intent upon it and with senses restrained," and "Know that through prostration," etc., are not causes because knowledge has as its cause the merit (dharma) performed in another birth, just as in the case of Prajāpati—[we reply: No, for there is the possibility of distinctions based on the variation of instrumental conditions, their combination, and whether they possess excellence or lack it.

In the world, indeed, the distinction between the causes of various effects produced by those who perceive signs (*naimittika*) is conceptualized in many ways, as is the combination of such causes. Furthermore, among those causes—whether conceptualized individually or combined—there exists a further distinction based on whether they possess excellence (*guṇavat*) or lack it (*aguṇavat*). For example, regarding the effect that is the cognition of form (*rūpa-jñāna*), which is itself dependent on a cause: for nocturnal creatures, the contact between the eye and form in the absence of light is the cause for the cognition of form; for yogis, the mind alone is the cause for the cognition of form.

In our case, however, there are various instrumental causes combined with proximity and light, as well as the different types of light from the sun, moon, and so forth; likewise, there may be distinctions based on whether they possess the specific quality of light or lack it. In the same way, even regarding the knowledge of the unity of the Self, in some cases karma performed in a previous birth serves as the instrumental cause, as in the case of Prajāpati; in other cases, austerity (*tapas*) is the cause, according to the Vedic scripture: "Seek to know Brahman through austerity."

In certain places, based on such scriptural and traditional texts as "A man who has a teacher knows," "One who possesses faith attains knowledge," "Know that through prostration," "Verily, from the teacher alone [is it obtained]," and "He is to be known, to be seen, and to be heard," it is established that faith and the other qualities are the means for the attainment of exclusive knowledge, because they serve as the cause for the removal of obstacles such as demerit (*adharma*); furthermore, this is because the hearing, reflection, and meditative concentration upon the Vedāntas have the knowable reality itself as their direct object.

And when the obstacles such as evil have been destroyed, there occurs [the union] of the self and the mind, because their inherent nature is to be the cause of knowledge of reality as it is. Therefore, knowledge is never without a cause; [it does not arise solely from] faith, prostration, and so forth.

Section: Mantra. Chapter.

There Death beheld them, just as one might see a fish in water, within the *Ṛg*, the *Sāman*, and the *Yajus*. Having discovered them, they ascended from the *Ṛg*, the *Sāman*, and the *Yajus* and entered into the very Svara itself. 3.

Moreover, the state of Prajāpati pertains only to the realm of *saṃsāra*, because that Prajāpati "indeed did not find delight" (*naiva reme*), meaning he was possessed by discontent (*aratyāviṣṭaḥ*), just like ourselves and others; for even now, due to possessing such qualities as being alone, one who is alone does not find delight—that is, does not experience pleasure. Delight (*rati*) is play born from union with desired objects. Discontent (*arati*) is said to be the agitation of the mind arising from the separation from those desired objects to which one is attached.

In order to dispel that dissatisfaction, he desired—and became greedy for—a second object of desire, a woman, which was capable of removing that dissatisfaction. As he thus became greedy regarding the object of a woman, his state of being became as if embraced by a woman. Because of his longing for truth, he became (*āsa*) of such a size, of this very measure (*etāvān*). Indeed, he became so.

As to what its size was, he says: "Just as in the world a man and a woman, when embraced for the sake of dispelling passion, might be of a certain size, so of that same size it became"—this is the meaning. Being of such a size, he caused this very self to fall into two parts, i.e., into two modes. The restrictive phrase "this very" is intended to distinguish [the self] from the Virāj, the root cause. It was not the case that the Virāj became this much by the total destruction of everything, like milk becoming curd through the total destruction of itself.

What then? It was the Virāj himself, established as the Self, who, by virtue of his power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*), became another body of a different dimension, embraced by a woman and a man. And that very Virāj, having become thus—on account of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the passage "He was of such a size"—therefrom, from that falling apart, he became both husband and wife; this is the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the worldly couple.

Therefore, for that reason—because this woman is a half that has become separate from the Self itself—for that reason, this body is the "half-fragment" (*ardhabṛgalam*) of the Self; that is, it is both a half (*ardham*) and a fragment (*bṛgalam*), a split-off piece (*vidalam*), meaning it is like a half-fragment. It is called a "half-fragment" because, prior to the taking of a wife, it was [merely] one's own Self.

Thus he spoke, namely Yājñavalkya—the son of Yajñavalkya (whose patronymic is Yājñavalkya); the meaning is that he is the descendant of Devarāti, not the offspring of Brahmā. Since this half of a person is empty like space, it is filled again by a female half through remarriage, just as a split half of a shell is restored by being joined back together.

That Prajāpati, known as Manu, united with his own daughter named Śatarūpā, whom he had intended for the state of wife; that is, he entered into sexual union with her. From that union, human beings were born.

Or, when one encounters a *ṛc*, one utters "Om" as its over-tone; likewise for the *sāman* and likewise for the *yajus*. This syllable is indeed the over-tone (*svara*); it is immortal and fearless. Having entered into it, the gods became immortal and fearless. 4. (4) ---

She was indeed Śatarūpā; she, remembering the Smṛti prohibition against approaching one’s own daughter, reflected: "How indeed can this be an improper act—that he, having produced me from his very self, should approach me? Even if he is merciless, well then, let me now become concealed by another species. Having thus reflected, she became a cow.

Having brought them forth, as she was impelled again and again by the karma of living beings, that very same thought occurred to Śatarūpā and Manu. Then the other became a bull (*ṛṣabha*). He united with her, and so on as described previously. From that, cows were born. Likewise, the other became a mare (*baḍabā*) and the other a stallion (*aśvavṛṣa*); similarly, the other became a she-ass (*gardabhī*) and the other a donkey (*gardabha*). There, from the union of the mares, stallions, and so forth, the three species known as horses, mules, and donkeys—characterized by having a single hoof or a single hoofed foot (*ekaśapha*)—were born.

In the same way, he became a female goat (*ajā*), and the other was a male goat (*basta*). Likewise, he became a female sheep (*avī*), and the other was a ram (*meṣa*). He united with each one—*tāṃ tāṃ* is a distributive repetition meaning "with each one"; the sense is that he coupled with that female goat and that female sheep. From that, goats and sheep (*ajāvayaḥ*) were born. In this very manner, whatever exists here, whatever pair characterized by male and female, even down to the ants (*ā pipīlikābhyaḥ*), he created all that by this same principle; he brought forth the world.

He who, knowing it thus, utters this very syllable—this very syllable which is tone, immortal, and fearless—enters that. Having entered it, he becomes immortal, just as the gods are immortal. 5. Thus ends the fourth section. 4.

(5) That Prajāpati, having created this entire world, realized: "How so? It is I alone who am the creation. By "creation" is meant the world that is being created; thus it is said, "I am the creation. Whatever world was created by me, because it is non-different from me, it is indeed I myself and does not exist apart from me. Why is this so? Because I have created (asṛkṣi) this entire world; such is the meaning.

Because Prajāpati designated himself by the word "creation" (sṛṣṭi), therefore he became creation—that is, he came to have the name "creation. In this world, in this very creation, that person becomes a creator like Prajāpati of the world which is non-different from his own self. Who is he? He who knows, as Prajāpati did, that the world—consisting of the internal self (adhyātma), the elements (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaiva)—is "I am this world," being non-different from his own self.

Mantra — Chapter (6) ---

Thus, having created this world consisting of pairs, that Prajāpati, desiring to create the deities who govern the castes such as the Brāhmaṇas and so forth, first—[the two words] "atha" and "iti" being for the purpose of demonstrating a gesture—placed his hands upon his mouth in this manner and churned it, performing a churning directed toward himself.

Having rubbed his face with both hands, he created fire—the benefactor of the Brāhmaṇa caste—from his mouth and from his two hands, that is, from the two sources (yoni). Since both of these, the hands and the mouth, were the source of the burning fire, therefore both of them are hairless, being devoid of hair; but not entirely so, for they are hairless only on the inside. For indeed, there is a commonality between these two and the female organ.

Why? Because the womb of women is hairless within; likewise, the Brāhmaṇa was born from the very mouth of Prajāpati. Therefore, due to this common origin, the younger is favored by the elder—just as the Brāhmaṇa is favored by Agni. Thus, it is established by Śruti and Smṛti that the Brāhmaṇa has Agni as his deity and his strength resides in the mouth. Likewise, from the two arms, which are the seat of power, [Prajāpati created] Indra (Balabhid) and others, as well as the Kṣatriya caste and the protection against injury (kṣatitraya).

Therefore, it is understood from both Śruti and Smṛti that the Kṣatriya belongs to Indra and possesses strength of arm; likewise, the Vaiśya is the ruler of the people (viś), who are characterized by wealth and so forth, because their activity and effort (īhā-ceṣṭā) reside in the thighs; thus, the Vaiśya is devoted to agriculture and the like, and has the Vasus and other deities as his presiding gods. Similarly, he created the Śūdra from the feet as one fit for service, having Pūṣan—the deity of the earth—as his presiding god; this is well-known from Śruti and Smṛti.

In this context, for the sake of proclaiming the completeness of the creation, he concludes—as if it were already stated—what was not explicitly mentioned here regarding the creation of the Kṣatriyas and other deities, though it will be discussed later. Just as this Śruti is established, so the determined meaning is that Prajāpati alone is all the gods; for created beings are non-different from their creator, and the gods were created by Prajāpati himself. Now, since the meaning of the section is thus established, there is introduced a censure of the views of the ignorant with the intent of praising it. The censure of one thing is for the purpose of praising another.

In that context, regarding the section on ritual action, there are certain ritualists who, at the time of sacrifice, utter such words as, "Sacrifice to this Agni," "Sacrifice to this Indra," and so forth. The intention is that they say this because they consider each deity, such as Agni and the others, to be distinct, owing to the differences in their names, *śastra* recitations, *stotra* chants, and ritual acts. One should not understand it in that way; for all that diversity of deities is merely the manifestation (*visṛṣṭi*) of this very Prajāpati. Indeed, this very Prāṇa, who is Prajāpati himself, is all the gods.

Regarding this, there are conflicting views: some maintain that Hiraṇyagarbha is indeed the Supreme [Brahman]; others hold that he is a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*). However, he is indeed the Supreme, on account of the wording of the mantra: "They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni"—so says the Śruti; and also from the Śruti: "He is truly Brahman, he is Indra, he is Prajāpati, and all these gods"; and from Smṛti as well: "Some call him Agni, others Manu, and others Prajāpati," and: "He who is beyond the senses, ungraspable, subtle, unmanifest, and eternal."

And it is said: "Consisting of all beings, inconceivable, he himself shone forth. Alternatively, he might be a transmigrating being (saṃsārī), because of the Vedic text: "He burnt away all evils"; for there is no possibility of the burning away of evil for one who is not a transmigrator. Furthermore, there is the hearing of his connection with fear and aversion; and from the mantra texts: "Then, being mortal, he created the immortals," and "Behold Hiraṇyagarbha being born."

And from the *Smṛti*, in the context of the process of the ripening of karma: "Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest—these the wise call the highest *sāttvika* goal. Now, if it is argued that because such contradictory meanings are untenable, there is a subversion of its authoritative status (*prāmāṇya*)—

No, for there is no contradiction, as another conceptualization is possible. Due to the connection with specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), another conceptualization of distinction arises. From such scriptural passages as, "Seated, he goes far; lying down, he goes everywhere. Who, other than me, is able to know that God, who is both intoxication and non-intoxication?", it follows that transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) is due to the influence of limiting adjuncts, not in the ultimate sense. By its own nature, it is indeed non-transmigratory. Unity and plurality both belong to Hiraṇyagarbha, and likewise to all individual souls (*jīva*), according to the scripture, "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*).

The declarations of the Śruti and Smṛti proceed on the basis that, with respect to the excellence of the purity of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of Hiraṇyagarbha, he is for the most part indeed the Supreme (para). However, they show his state of being a transmigrator (saṃsāritva) only in certain instances. But because of the abundance of impurity residing in the limiting adjuncts of individual souls (jīvas), their state of being transmigrators is generally predicated. Yet, with respect to the exclusion of all distinctions of limiting adjuncts, every soul is designated as the Supreme by the declarations of the Śruti and Smṛti.

However, by logicians who have abandoned the authority of scripture and who, through much contradictory reasoning—such as "it exists," "it does not exist," "there is a creator," or "there is no creator"—the meaning of the scriptures has been thrown into confusion. Consequently, the ascertainment of that meaning is difficult to attain. But for those who follow the scriptures alone and are free from pride, the meaning of the scriptures concerning deities and other such matters is as certain as an object of direct perception.

In this context, it is intended that a distinction characterized by the eater and the food exists within the single deity Prajāpati—there, Agni was described as the eater; now Soma is described as the food. Whatever moist, liquid substance there is here in the world, that he created from his own seed, which is semen; for the scripture says, "From semen comes water. And Soma is liquid by nature. Therefore, whatever moist thing was created by Prajāpati from his semen, that is indeed Soma. This whole world is just this much, not more than this.

What is that? Food is indeed Soma, because it is nourishing due to its liquid nature; and fire is the eater of food, due to its heat and dryness. In this regard, it is determined as follows: Soma alone is the food—the meaning is that whatever is eaten is Soma; and whoever is the eater is Agni. This restriction follows from the force of the context. Even fire, when being offered as an oblation, belongs to the side of Soma; and even Soma, when being worshipped, is indeed Agni, because he is the eater. Thus, one who perceives the world as consisting of the nature of Agni and Soma does not become tainted by any fault.

And he becomes Prajāpati. This is that "over-creation" (atisṛṣṭi) of Brahmā Prajāpati, which is even superior to himself. To the question "What is it?", he says: because he created the gods—who are more excellent, that is, more praiseworthy—than himself, therefore the creation of the gods is called an "over-creation."

How, then, is there the creation of something superior to oneself? To this he says: "Now, because," being mortal—that is, subject to death—he created the immortals, those whose nature is not to die, having burnt away all his own evils by means of the fire of ritual action and knowledge; therefore, this is a "super-creation" (*atisṛṣṭi*), meaning it is the fruit of exalted knowledge.
Therefore, he who knows this super-creation, which is the very self of Prajāpati, becomes like Prajāpati in this super-creation; that is, he becomes a creator just like Prajāpati.

Therefore, at that time, this was undifferentiated. All Vedic means of accomplishment—characterized by knowledge and action, dependent upon various factors such as the agent, and culminating in the fruit of Prajāpati-status—are limited to this much: namely, this differentiated world-process of saṃsāra.

Now, he wishes to point out that state of this very manifested world—characterized by the relationship between the goal and the means—which existed prior to its manifestation, like the seed-state of a tree inferred from its effects such as the sprout and so forth. For this tree of transmigratory existence must be uprooted along with its roots, having karma as its seed and ignorance as its field. Indeed, the uprooting of that tree is the complete fulfillment of the purpose of human life. Thus it has been said in the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad*: "With roots above and branches below"; and in the *Gītā*: "With roots above and branches below"; and in the *Purāṇa*: "The eternal tree of Brahman."
