Mantra — Chapter (7) ---

"That indeed was this. "That" refers to the world in its state as a seed prior to its origination; "then" means at that time. It is denoted by the pronoun "that," which is an indirect designation for something not present to the senses, because the world, though yet to be manifested, is connected with past time. The particle "ha" is used in the sense of tradition (*aitihya*) for the sake of easy comprehension; when it is said, "Thus, indeed, it was then," one easily understands that state of the world as its seed, even though it is beyond direct perception—just as when it is said, "Yudhiṣṭhira, indeed, was once a king."

The term "this" (*idam*) refers to that which has been described as consisting of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), characterized by the relationship between the goal and the means; it denotes the world in its manifest state. Since the two words "that" (*tat*) and "this" (*idam*)—which respectively denote the world in its unmanifest and manifest states—are used in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the oneness of the world in both its unmanifest and manifest states is understood: "That indeed is this," and "This indeed was that unmanifest. This being so, it is established that there is no origination of the non-existent, nor the destruction of the existent, with respect to the effect.

Thus, this world, being in an undifferentiated state (*avyākṛta*), was differentiated by name and form—that is, by name alone and by form alone. Regarding the expression "was differentiated" (*vyākriyata*), because it is used in the reflexive passive construction (*karmakartṛ-prayoga*), it means that it was differentiated by itself, by its own self—*vi-ā-kriyata*: it attained a state of manifestation characterized by the clear determination of specific names and forms. This is implied by the force of the context as having a controller, an agent, instruments, action, and causes. By using the pronoun "this" (*asau*)—which denotes a name without specifying particulars—he designates it merely as "name."

"His name is Devadatta or Yajñadatta"—thus he is "one who has such a name. Likewise, "this"—there is no distinction among white, black, and so forth. "This is his form, whether white or black"—thus he is "one who has this form. This very undifferentiated entity, even at this present time, is differentiated by name and form alone—as "he is one who has such a name and this form."

That for whose sake all scriptures are commenced; upon which, through innate ignorance, the superimposition of agent, action, and fruit has been made; which is the cause of the entire world; in whose nature name and form—like froth from clear water or impurity from it—are differentiated within the undifferentiated; and which is distinct from those two, name and form, being by its own nature eternally pure, conscious, and free—it is this very [Self] that, while differentiating name and form which constitute its own unmanifested state, has entered here into bodies beginning with Brahmā and ending with a blade of grass, which are the substrates of the fruits of karma and possess hunger and other such traits.

But has it not been stated that the undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*) differentiates itself? How, then, is it now said that the Supreme Self alone, differentiating the undifferentiated, entered here? This is not a fault, because the Supreme Self is also intended [here] as having the undifferentiated world as its essence. For we have already stated that the undifferentiated world differentiates itself, presupposing a controller, an agent, and an action. Furthermore, this is so because the word "undifferentiated" is used in grammatical coordination with the word "this" (*idam*).

Just as this manifest world (*vyākṛta*) is characterized by various distinctions such as having a controller, multiple causal factors, and so forth, so too is that unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) not devoid of any one of those very same distinctions. The only difference lies in the mere state of being manifest or unmanifest. Furthermore, it is observed in common worldly usage that the employment of words depends upon the speaker's intention; for instance, in the expressions "the village has arrived" and "the village is empty," sometimes, when there is an intention to refer merely to the dwelling place by the word "village," the expression "the village is empty" occurs.

Sometimes, when there is a desire to express only the inhabitants, one says "the village has arrived"; sometimes, even when there is a desire to express both, the word "village" is used, as in "he should not enter the village. In the same way, here too, when there is a desire to express the non-difference between the Self and the non-Self, there occurs the designation "this world is both manifest and unmanifest. Likewise, there is the designation of the world alone, such as "this world consists of origination and destruction.
Similarly, there is the designation of the Self alone, such as "the great unborn Self," "neither gross nor subtle," and "He is 'not this, not this,'" and so forth.

But surely, the other, the Expositor, has declared that the world is everywhere pervaded at all times; how then can he be conceived here as having entered? For only a space not already occupied can be entered by something limited, such as a village and so forth by a person; nothing can be entered by space, because it is eternally present there. If it is argued that this is like a stone-serpent or similar cases—that is, by means of another attribute (*dharmāntara*)—then it might be said: the Supreme Self did not enter by its own very form.

What then? It is that very [Brahman] which, while remaining in its own state, arises through another attribute (*dharmāntara*); by virtue of that, it is figuratively designated as "having entered. This is not like a snake naturally inherent within a stone, or water within a coconut—no, for the Śruti says, "Having created that, He entered into it. For it is heard in scripture that the Creator, without having undergone any change into a different state of being, created the effect and subsequently entered it.

Just as in the expression "he goes after eating," there is a mutual separation between the two actions of eating and going occurring at prior and subsequent times, yet the agent remains the same, so too might it be here; however, this is not possible if it refers to the production of another state within that very [agent] itself. Nor is an entry characterized by disjunction from one location and conjunction with another location observed for that which is partless and undivided. If it is argued that entry must belong only to something possessing parts because of the scriptural mention of entry, we say no.

For [the Self is] "divine, indeed, formless, the Person" and "partless, actionless," according to such scriptural passages, as well as from those scriptural passages which negate all specific qualities that could serve as designations. If it is argued that [the entry of the Self] is like the entry of a reflection, we say no; for it is impossible for there to be a spatial separation [of the Self] from another real entity. If it is argued that it is like the entry of a quality into a substance, we say no; because [the Self] is not dependent. It is only a quality that is inherently dependent and rests upon something else that is metaphorically said to "enter" a substance.

However, such an entry by Brahman is not tenable because of the scriptural declarations of its absolute independence. If it is argued that it is like a seed entering a fruit, we say no; for that would entail the consequence of Brahman possessing parts, as well as the properties of growth, decay, birth, destruction, and so forth. But Brahman does not possess such properties, as this would contradict scripture and logic, such as the texts stating "He is unborn and undecaying. If it is argued that it is some other transmigrating being, limited in nature, that has entered here, we say no.

This is because scripture declares that very deity to be the agent of both entering and manifesting names and forms, beginning with "That deity thought" and continuing with "Let me manifest names and forms. Likewise: "Having created that, He entered into it"; "He, having split open this very aperture, entered through this door"; "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and made their names, sits calling them by those names"; "You are a boy, or perhaps a girl; you are an old man tottering with a staff"; "He made bodies with two feet"; and "Every single form."

There is no entry of another [Self] into that which is other than the Supreme (Parā), on account of the words of the Mantras. If it be argued that because those who have entered [the Supreme] are mutually distinct, there must be a multiplicity of Supreme Selves, we say: no. This is known from such scriptural passages as: "The one God is established in many ways," "Being one, he manifests himself in many ways," "You are one, having entered into many," and "The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings. Thus, according to these and other Śruti texts, there is no plurality of the Supreme.

As for the objection that "entry" is either possible or impossible—let that stand for now—if it is argued that because those who have entered [the body] are subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*), the Supreme Self must also be subject to transmigratory existence due to its non-difference from them, we say: no; because there is no scriptural statement regarding hunger and other such afflictions [belonging to the Self]. If it is argued that this is not so because we observe happiness, suffering, and so forth [in the Self], we say: no; because of the scriptural text: "It is untouched by the suffering of the world, being external. If it is argued that this is untenable because it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge, we say: no; because perception and the rest have as their objects only those specific distinctions produced by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). As it is said: "One cannot see the seer of seeing."

From such scriptural passages as "By what, my dear, should one know the knower? and "The knower is unknown," the cognition whose object is the Self [in its true nature] does not exist. What then? The immediate cognition such as "I am happy" or "I am miserable" has as its object merely the reflection of the Self in the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect (buddhi). This is because there is a figurative identification (sāmānādhikaraṇya-upacāra) of the subject with the object in the form "this is I," and because of the negation of any other seer in the passage, "There is no other seer but this."

Furthermore, because pleasure and pain are predicated of specific parts of the body, they are attributes of the object [of experience]. If it is argued that this is incorrect because of the scriptural statement, "But for the sake of the Self" (*ātmanastu kāmāya*), which establishes them as being for the sake of the Self, we say no; for the passage "where there is, as it were, something else" (*yatra vā anyadiva syāt*) accepts that they are for the sake of the Self within the domain of ignorance (*avidyā*). Moreover, since their negation is established within the domain of knowledge (*vidyā*) by such passages as "then by what should one see whom? (*tat kena kaṃ paśyet*), "there is not even the slightest diversity here" (*neha nānāsti kiṃcana*), and "what delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness? (*tatra ko mohaḥ kaḥ śoka ekatvamanupaśyataḥ*), they cannot be attributes of the Self.

If it is argued that this is untenable because it contradicts the tenets of the logicians (*tārkika*), we say no; for even by reason, the suffering of the self (*ātman*) is impossible. For the self cannot be qualified by suffering which is an object of perception, since the self is not itself an object of perception. If it is argued that the self’s state of suffering is like space’s possession of the quality of sound, we say no; for it is impossible for them to be objects of a single cognition. Indeed, it is not possible for the self—which is always to be inferred—to be made an object of a cognition that perceives pleasure and is itself an object of perception.

Furthermore, if that [suffering] were made an object, then because the self is one, it would follow that there is no subject (the knower). If it is argued that a single entity can be both the object and the subject—just like a lamp—it is not so; for this is impossible simultaneously, and because it is illogical for the self to possess parts. By this, the status of consciousness as both the grasped and the grasper is refuted. Moreover, there is no inference to establish that suffering and the self are respectively quality and possessor of quality, because suffering is always an object of direct perception and because [suffering] is co-referential with color and other qualities.

Even if suffering arises in the self through its conjunction with the mind, it would follow that the self possesses parts, is subject to modification, and is non-eternal. For nowhere is a substance seen to undergo the arrival or departure of any quality without itself being modified; nor is anything seen anywhere to be modified while remaining partless, or to be eternal while serving as the substratum for non-eternal qualities. Furthermore, space is not accepted as eternal by those who follow the scriptures, and there exists no other illustrative example [to the contrary].

If it is argued that even when undergoing modification (*vikriyamāṇa*), the self remains eternal because the cognition of it does not cease, we say no; for modification is impossible unless there is a change in the constituent parts (*avayava-anyathātva*) of a substance. If it is argued that it can still be eternal despite having parts, we say no; for that which has parts must be preceded by the conjunction of its parts, and thus the disjunction of those parts is possible. If it is argued that this is not so because it is not observed in the case of diamonds and the like, we say no; for the fact of being preceded by conjunction is a matter of inference. Therefore, it is not possible for the self to be the substratum of impermanent qualities such as suffering.

If it is argued that, in the absence of another who is not suffering and in the absence of any other sufferer, the commencement of the treatise for the sake of pacifying suffering would be purposeless, we say no; for its purpose is to remove the delusion of being a sufferer superimposed by ignorance—just as one removes the delusion of being the "thirteenth" person when there are only twelve in a group—and because we accept the existence of a self that is a sufferer only through conceptual construction (*kalpita*).

The entry of the Self is like the reflection of the sun in water and so forth; it is perceived within the manifested effect, just as a reflection appears. Prior to creation, the Self was unperceived, but afterwards, once the effect has been produced and manifested, it is perceived within the intellect (*buddhi*). Having created the effect, it is pointed out as if having entered it—just as the reflection of the sun and other luminaries appear in water and similar media—being observed as "having entered here," as in: "Having created that, He entered into that very thing" and "He, having pierced this very opening, [entered] through this door."

[The Self] entered by means of such passages as: "That deity reflected: 'Well, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman)'" and so forth. However, for that which is all-pervading and partless, an entry characterized by moving away from one direction, place, or time to reach another is never possible. Nor is there any seer other than the supreme Self, as we have already stated based on such scriptural texts as: "There is no other seer than this," and "There is no other hearer than this."

Furthermore, because the statements concerning creation, entry, maintenance, and dissolution have as their purpose [the attainment of] realization; for it is heard that realization is the goal of man from such scriptural passages as: "He knew only himself" (ātmānamevāvet), "Therefore, he became all this" (tasmāttatsarvamabhavat), "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (brahmavidāpnoti param), "He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (sa yo ha vai tatparamaṃ brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati), "The man who has a teacher knows" (ācāryavānpuruṣo veda), and "For him, there is delay only so long" (tasya tāvadeva ciram).

This is also supported by such Smṛti passages as: "Then, having known Me in truth, he enters into Me immediately thereafter," and "For that is the foremost of all sciences, for through it immortality is attained. Furthermore, because of the refutation of the perception of difference, it is established that the statements concerning creation and so forth have as their purpose the realization of the oneness of the Self. Therefore, the very fact of being perceived while abiding in an effect is figuratively designated as "entry."

"Down to the tips of the nails"—consciousness of the self is perceived even as far as the limits of the nail-tips. To the question, "How exactly has it entered there?", he says: just as in the world, in a razor-case (*kṣuradhāna*)—that in which a razor is placed, namely the barber's equipment case—a razor is perceived as being situated within; that is, it is deposited or inserted there. Or, just as the fire called *viśvambhara*—"bearer of all," so named because it sustains the universe—is deposited in its nest (*kulāya*), that is, in wood and such, within the fire-pit (*nīḍa*).

The word "syāt" (it may be) carries over from the previous context; for it is there [in the body] that he is perceived when being sought. Just as a razor is situated in one part of a razor-case, and just as fire is situated pervading wood and other materials on all sides, so too the Self is situated pervading the body both generally and specifically; for it is there that he is perceived as possessing activities such as breathing and as possessing activities such as seeing.

Therefore, they do not see—that is, they do not perceive—that Self which has thus entered therein and is characterized by activities such as breathing. [Objection: But this is a prohibition of something that was not previously introduced, since "they do not see it" refers to seeing, which was not the subject under discussion. [Reply: This is not a fault; for since the passages concerning creation and so forth have as their purpose the realization of the oneness of the Self, its being seen is indeed the subject at hand, as indicated by the Vedic verse: "He became the counterpart of every form; that is his form for the sake of perception."

In this regard, he states the reason for viewing [the Self] as characterized by the activity of breathing and so forth: "He is *akṛtsnaḥ*, meaning incomplete (*asamastaḥ*), because (*hi*) that [Self] is characterized by the activity of breathing and so forth. But why is it incomplete? It is said: "Only while breathing"—that is, performing only the activity of breathing—does one become what is called "Prāṇa," namely, designated as Prāṇa and named Prāṇa. For it is because of being the agent of the activity of breathing that one is called "Prāṇa" (the Breather), not when performing any other activity—just as one is called a "reaper" or a "cook" [only when performing those respective actions].

Therefore, because that [Self] is not brought forth as qualified by other functions, it is incomplete. Speaking—that is, performing the act of speaking—is "speech" (*vāk*); seeing—that is, the seer who performs the act of seeing—is "the eye" (*cakṣus*); hearing—that is, the hearer who performs the act of hearing—is "the ear" (*śrotra*). By these two statements, "breathing indeed is breath" and "speaking is speech," the emergence of the power of action is demonstrated.

By the two phrases "seeing with the eye" and "hearing with the ear," the emergence of the power of consciousness (*vijñāna-śakti*) is demonstrated, because the power of consciousness has name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as its object. The ear and the eye are the instruments for consciousness, while consciousness itself is the instrument for name-and-form; for there is no object of cognition apart from name-and-form. Furthermore, the eye and the ear are the instruments for the perception of those two. And action, which is accomplished through name-and-form, resides in the vital breath (*prāṇa*); speech is the instrument for the manifestation of that action, which has the vital breath as its substrate.

Likewise, there are those called the hands, feet, anus, and genitals; speech serves as the representative for all of them. For this entire world has been thus differentiated—indeed, he will later state: "This triad is indeed name, form, and action. As for the mind (*manas*), it is so called because it thinks (*manute*); the mind is the common instrument for the expansion of the powers of cognition—it is that by which one thinks. However, the person (*puruṣa*), being the agent, is called the "mind" when he is thinking.

These, namely "prāṇa" and so forth, are the names of this Self based on its actions; they are names born of action (*karmanāmāni*), indeed nothing but names derived from action, and not referring to the mere substance itself. Therefore, they do not illuminate the entire reality of the Self—yet even so, this Self is manifested and revealed through the process of differentiation (*vyākriyamāṇa*) by means of the functions such as breathing and the names and forms (*nāmarūpa*) produced by those very functions.

He who, from this aggregate of activities such as breathing and so forth, meditates upon—thinks of—one specific vital function, such as the eye, as "this is the Self," while not withdrawing the other specific functions that constitute its nature, does not know, he does not understand Brahman. Why? Because this Self is incomplete and not whole; for it is distinguished by only one particular attribute from this aggregate of breathing and so forth, due to the non-inclusion of the other remaining attributes. Thus it remains partial.
As long as one knows this—namely, "I see," "I hear," or "I touch"—as characterized by the activity of one's own nature, so long does one not directly know the entire Self.

But how does one perceive it? To this he says: "As the Self indeed, as the Self. That which possesses those qualifiers—such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth—which have been mentioned, is called the "Self" when it attains them. Thus, by incorporating all these specific attributes, it becomes the Whole (*kṛtsna*). For, in its form as pure Being alone, it pervades the qualifiers produced by the specific activities of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the vital breath. And thus he will say later: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were. Therefore, one should worship it as the Self alone.

Thus, this whole [Self] is indeed grasped in its own essential form. Anticipating the question "Why is it 'whole'?", he says: for in this Self—which is without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*)—just as the various reflections of the sun in water do not differ from the sun itself, these aforementioned distinctions produced by limiting adjuncts such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which are designated by names arising from the functions of the vital breath and so forth, become one; that is, they attain non-difference.

The injunction "one should meditate [on the Self] as the Self" is not an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), because [the meditation] is already established in certain cases. Through such scriptural passages dedicated to establishing the nature of the Self—such as "Brahman which is immediate and direct," and "Which is the Self? ... that which consists of consciousness"—knowledge regarding the Self has been produced. By that very knowledge of the true nature of the Self, ignorance (*avidyā*)—which consists of the superimposition of the notions of agency and so forth, and of the results of actions, upon that [Self], namely the cognition of "I-ness" directed toward the non-Self—is removed.

When that [notion of non-self] has been set aside, since defects such as desire cannot arise, the contemplation of the non-self is no longer possible; by the principle of elimination, it is necessarily the contemplation of the Self alone. Therefore, in this view, the meditation on that [non-self] need not be enjoined, as it is already established.

Let us set aside for now the question of whether the attainment of the meditation on the Self (*ātmopāsanā*) is optional or obligatory. It must be an *apūrva-vidhi* (an injunction for what was previously unestablished), because knowledge (*jñāna*) and meditation (*upāsana*) are one and the same, and thus [meditation] has not been previously established as a duty. This is understood from the fact that, having introduced "knowledge" with the words "He does not know," the text states "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self alone" (*ātmetyevopāsīta*), thereby showing that the words "know" (*veda*) and "meditate" (*upāsīta*) have the same meaning. Furthermore, from such scriptural passages as "For by this one knows all this" and "He knew the Self alone," knowledge is indeed meditation. Since this is not already established, it is fit to be the object of an injunction. Nor...

The engagement of a person is possible only when there is a description of something not yet known; therefore, this is indeed an *apūrva-vidhi* (an injunction for what was previously unknown). Furthermore, because of its general similarity to injunctions regarding ritual acts—just as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) and "one should offer oblations" (*juhuyāt*) are injunctions regarding ritual acts—no distinction is perceived between those and this injunction regarding the meditation on the Self, such as "one should meditate [on the Self] as the Self alone" (*ātmety evopāsīta*) or "the Self, my dear, is to be seen" (*ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ*).

And because consciousness is a mental activity—just as a mental action is enjoined in such passages as, "To whichever deity the oblation has been taken, that one he should meditate upon mentally when about to utter the *vaṣaṭ*," likewise in such passages as, "One should venerate [the Self] as the Self alone," and "It is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon," an action consisting of knowledge itself is enjoined. Thus we have stated that the words *veda* (to know) and *upāsana* (veneration) have the same meaning.

And because the three constituent parts of the *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) are established—just as in the *bhāvanā* expressed by "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the three parts are understood as the means for removing the expectancy regarding what is to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) and so forth, namely: "What?", "By what means?", and "In what manner?"—so too, when the *bhāvanā* expressed by "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*) is enjoined, there arises the expectancy: "What should one meditate upon?", "By what means should one meditate?", and "In what manner should one meditate? [The answer is: "One should meditate upon the Self with the mind, joined with the performance of duties such as renunciation, celibacy, tranquility, self-control, withdrawal from sense objects, and forbearance."

The three components [of an injunction] are established by such scriptural passages as these. Just as the entire section concerning the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices serves as the basis for the injunctions regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa and so forth, so too the section concerning the meditation on the Self taught in the Upaniṣads serves specifically as the basis for the injunctions regarding the meditation on the Self. Passages such as "not this, not this," "neither coarse nor fine," "one only, without a second," and "beyond hunger and so forth," serve their purpose by imparting the specific nature of the Self that is to be meditated upon.
And the fruit is liberation, or the cessation of ignorance.

Others explain as follows: through meditation (*upāsana*), one should cultivate a distinct, superior cognition (*vijñāna*) concerning the Self; by that, the Self is known, and that [superior cognition] alone is the remover of ignorance, not the cognition produced by Vedic sentences concerning the Self. There are scriptural statements to this effect, such as: "Having known, let him practice wisdom" (*vijñāya prajñāṃ kurvīta*); "He is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (*draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ*); and "He is to be sought, He is to be desired to be known" (*so'nveṣṭavyaḥ sa vijijñāsitavyaḥ*).

No, because there is no other matter [to be accomplished]. Nor is "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self" an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*). Why? Because, apart from the knowledge produced by the statement that negates the non-Self in order to describe the true nature of the Self, there is no other matter—whether mental or external—that remains to be performed. For an injunction is fruitful only where human activity is understood to follow after the knowledge produced merely by hearing the injunctive sentence—as, for example, in:

In such cases as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices," the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices is not identical to the cognition produced by the injunctional sentence regarding those sacrifices. Furthermore, that performance is experienced as dependent upon qualifications [such as desire for a result] and so forth. However, apart from the cognition produced by sentences establishing the Self—such as "Not this, not this"—no human activity like that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices is possible; for the cognition produced by those [Upanishadic] sentences is the cause for the cessation of all activity.

For neutral knowledge does not produce activity. Furthermore, because sentences such as "One only, without a second" and "That thou art" serve to remove the knowledge of non-Brahman and the non-Self, once that [false] knowledge is removed, activity is no longer possible due to contradiction. If it is argued that the removal of the knowledge of non-Brahman and the non-Self does not occur through the mere knowledge produced by the sentence, we say no.

Because such statements as "That thou art," "Not this, not this," "All this is indeed the Self," "One only, without a second," "This immortal Brahman alone," "There is no other seer than this," and "Know that very thing to be Brahman" proclaim that [Brahman]. If it is argued that these sentences merely serve to present the object for the injunction to see, we say no.

Because this has already been answered by the statement "due to the absence of any other object"—since the vision of that [Reality] is accomplished at the very time of hearing through sentences such as "That thou art" which impart the true nature of the reality of the Self, there is no further performance of the injunction to "behold" to be undertaken; thus, this has already been answered. If it is argued that one does not engage in the realization of the Self merely through the description of its nature without an injunction, we say: no.

Because the knowledge of the Self is produced by hearing the words of one who maintains the doctrine of the Self—what, then, is the purpose of [another] injunction? If it is argued that even upon hearing that [injunction], one does not engage [in action], we say no; for this would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Just as one does not engage in hearing the meaning of the words of the proponent of the Self without an injunction, so too one would not engage in hearing the meaning of the injunctive sentence without an injunction, and thus there would be a requirement for another injunction; and since the same would apply to hearing the meaning of that [subsequent injunction], an infinite regress would result.

If it is argued that the continuous stream of recollection of the knowledge of the Self produced by the statement is something distinct from the mere cognitive awareness (*vijñāna*) arising from hearing [the scripture], we say no; because this is already implied by the meaning itself. For as soon as the cognitive awareness having the Self as its object arises from hearing the statement that establishes the Self, that very arising cognition arises precisely by subverting the false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) regarding that same object. And when the false cognition regarding the Self is subverted, the natural recollections—which have as their objects the distinctions of non-Self entities—no longer occur, as they are born of that [false cognition].

And because of the realization that [everything else] is disadvantageous: for when the Self is realized, every other object is understood to be disadvantageous, since it possesses many defects such as impermanence, suffering, and impurity, whereas the reality of the Self is of a nature contrary to those; therefore, the cognitions and memories of the non-Self would result in non-existence once the realization of the Self has occurred. By the method of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*), the continuous stream of cognition and memory regarding the oneness of the Self exists as a matter of course (*arthataḥ*); thus, it cannot be an object of injunction.

Furthermore, because the remembrance of That (Brahman) removes defects such as sorrow, delusion, fear, and exhaustion—since defects like sorrow and delusion arise from erroneous knowledge—the following scriptural passages confirm this: "In that state, what delusion can there be?", "The wise man fears nothing," "O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness," and "The knot of the heart is severed. Thus say the Śruti texts.

If it is argued that cessation (*nirodha*) is therefore a different entity—namely, that because the cessation of mental fluctuations is a distinct entity from the knowledge of the Self produced by Vedic statements, and because it is understood as something to be performed in other systems (*tantra*), it must be something to be enjoined (*vidheya*)—we say no, because it is not understood as a means to liberation (*mokṣa*).

For in the Vedāntas, nothing other than the knowledge of the Self as Brahman is understood to be the means for attaining the supreme goal of man—based on hundreds of such scriptural passages as: "The Self alone he knew; therefore, all this became his"; "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"; "He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself"; "The person who has a teacher knows [it]"; "For him, there is delay only so long [as he is not liberated]"; and "Truly, he who knows thus becomes the fearless Brahman."

And because cessation has no other means of accomplishment—for there is indeed no means for the cessation of mental fluctuations apart from the stream of self-knowledge and its recollection—this was stated while provisionally accepting [other means]. However, no means for liberation other than the knowledge of Brahman is perceived. Furthermore, due to the absence of any further desire, there is an absence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

As for what was said—that just as in injunctions such as "one should sacrifice," where there is an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) regarding the *bhāvanā* as to "what?", "by what means?", and "how?", the removal of that expectancy occurs through the [mention of] the fruit, the instrument, and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), so too is it possible here in the injunction for the knowledge of the Self—this is incorrect; because at the very moment of understanding the meaning of such sentences as "One only, without a second," "That thou art," "Not this, not this," "Without interior, without exterior," and "This Self is Brahman," all expectancy ceases.

Furthermore, one does not engage in the comprehension of the meaning of such sentences impelled by an injunction (*vidhi*). And we have already stated that if engagement were impelled by another injunction, there would be the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Moreover, no injunction is perceived in sentences such as "Brahman is one only, without a second," because they terminate solely in the descriptive explanation of the nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*).

If it is argued that [the Upanishads] lack authority because they are merely descriptive accounts of the nature of things (*vastu-svarūpa-anvākhyāna-mātra*)—that is, if it be further argued that just as in passages such as "He wept; because he wept, that is the Rudra-nature of Rudra," there is a lack of authority because they are merely descriptive accounts of the nature of things, so too it is for the Upanishadic sentences concerning the Self (*ātman*)—we say: no, because there is a distinction. It is not whether a sentence is a description of a thing or a description of an action that is the cause of its being authoritative or non-authoritative; rather, it is its capacity to produce a certain knowledge that has a fruitful result.

Therefore, that in which [the object] exists is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); that in which it does not exist is invalid (*apramāṇa*). Furthermore, sir, we ask you: in sentences devoted to explaining the nature of the Self, does a fruitful and certain cognition arise, or not? If it does arise, how can there be invalidity?

Or do you not see that the fruit of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*) is the cessation of the defects that are the seeds of *saṃsāra*, such as ignorance, grief, delusion, and fear? Or do you not hear hundreds of Upaniṣadic passages such as: "What delusion, what grief can there be for one who perceives oneness? and "I am indeed a knower of mantras, but not a knower of the Self; therefore, O Blessed One, I grieve. May the Blessed One carry me across to the further shore of this grief"? Likewise, does there exist in passages such as "He wept" (*so 'rodīt*) a certain and fruitful higher knowledge? If it does not exist, [then...]

Let it be that [the Upanishads] lack authority. But if they lack authority, why should that which produces a certain cognition of a result—which is itself fruitful—lack authority? And if that lacks authority, what confidence can there be in the sentences concerning the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) and the like? Now, one might argue: "The sentences concerning the New and Full Moon sacrifices lack authority because they produce a cognition that prompts human activity, whereas in the sentences regarding the cognition of the Self, that is not the case. This is true; however, this is not a fault, because the grounds for authority are established. And the grounds for authority are exactly as previously stated, and nothing else.

Furthermore, this is an ornament [to our position]: that the sentences establishing the Self produce a consciousness that results in the cessation of the seeds of all worldly activity, and thus they do not possess the cause of invalidity. As for what was said—that statements such as "having known, one should practice wisdom" (vijñāya prajñāṃ kurvīta) have the purpose of meditation (upāsana) distinct from the knowledge of the sentence-meaning—this is true; however, they do not serve the purpose of an original injunction (apūrva-vidhi), but rather serve as restrictive injunctions (niyama) for that which is already established in some cases.

But how can meditation (upāsana) be subject to this contingency, given that it has been stated that, by the method of elimination, the continuous stream of mindfulness regarding the knowledge of the Self is indeed eternal? True—though this is so, nevertheless, because the karma that initiated the present body has its fruit fixed, activity of speech, mind, and body necessarily continues even upon the attainment of perfect knowledge, owing to the greater force of karma that has already begun to operate—just like the initial movement of a released arrow; therefore, the weakness of the operation of knowledge is established as a possibility.

Therefore, by relying on the strength of the means such as renunciation and dispassion, one must emerge from the continuous stream of mindfulness regarding the realization of the Self; it is not something to be newly produced, because it has already been attained—as we have stated. Consequently, statements such as "having known, one should exercise discernment" (*vijñāya prajñāṃ kurvīta*) are intended to enjoin the regulation of the continuous stream of mindfulness regarding that which has already been attained, since no other purpose is possible. [Objection: But surely this is a meditation on the non-Self, because of the use of the word "iti."

Just as in passages such as "One should meditate on this as the dear" (*priyam*), it is not the qualities like "dear" that are to be meditated upon, but rather the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth which possess those qualities; so too here, because of the use of the words "this" (*iti*) and "the Supreme Self" (*parātman*), it is understood that the non-self entity possessing the qualities of the Self is to be meditated upon. Furthermore, this is distinct from sentences where the Self itself is the object of meditation—as the author will state later: "One should meditate on the Self alone as the world."

And in that sentence, it is the Self alone that is intended as the object of meditation, because the accusative case is heard in the phrase "the Self alone" (*ātmānam eva*). But here, the accusative is not heard, and the word "Self" is used in the nominative—as in "One should meditate [on Him] as 'I am the Self'" (*ātmety evopāsīta*). Therefore, it is understood that the Self is not the object of meditation, but rather some other quality of the Self. No, for in the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), the Self is understood to be the object of meditation.

In the remainder of this very passage, the Self alone is understood as the object of worship: "This is the track to be followed of all this, namely this Self"; "That which is more internal than this, namely the Self"; and "He knew only the Self. If it is argued that [the Self] cannot be the object of worship because seeing it is prohibited for one who has entered, we reply: it is precisely that Self whose entry was mentioned whose seeing is forbidden, because the subject under discussion is taken up in the phrase, "They do not see Him."

If it be argued that, for this reason, the Self is simply not to be meditated upon—[we reply: no, because of the fault of incompleteness (*akṛtsnatva*). The prohibition of [seeing] the Self is intended on account of the fault of incompleteness, not for the purpose of prohibiting the meditation on the Self; for [the text] qualifies [the Self] by means of its association with specific activities such as breathing and so forth. If the meditation on the Self were not intended, then the statement regarding the incompleteness of the Self when qualified by each individual activity, such as breathing, would be meaningless—namely: "For this one is incomplete, being [defined] by only one [activity] at a time."

Therefore, it is established that the Self, characterized by many and one, is indeed to be meditated upon in its entirety. As for the subsequent use of the word "Self" (ātman) as a pronoun, it is intended to make known that the reality of the Self is, in the ultimate sense, not an object of either the word or the cognition of "Self"; otherwise, he would have simply said, "one should meditate on the Self," and in that case, by implication, the word and the cognition regarding the Self would have been permitted.

And that is undesirable, because of such scriptural passages as: "Not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6); "By what, my dear, would one know the knower? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15); "The knower is itself unknown" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.2); and "From whence words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach it" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9.1). As for the statement, "One should meditate on the Self alone as the world," that is intended solely to preclude the practice of meditating on what is not the Self; it is not a separate injunction.

Because they share the common characteristic of being unknown, both the Self (*ātman*) and the non-Self (*anātman*) are to be known. In that case, why is effort directed toward the meditation on the Self alone—as in "One should meditate [on it] as the Self"—and not toward the knowledge of the other? To this it is said: That very thing which is under discussion here is what is to be reached, what is to be attained, and nothing else. The genitive case in the phrase "of all this" (*asya sarvasya*) has the sense of specification; the meaning is "in this entire [world]. That which is this Self—that which is this reality of the Self—is what must be known. Is it not the case that everything else is simply not to be known? No.

What then? Even though it is something to be known, it does not require a separate cognition other than the knowledge of the Self. Why? Because by means of this Self being known, one knows all this—that is, everything else that has originated from the non-Self, all of it in its entirety. [Objection: But surely one thing is not known through the knowledge of another. We shall provide the answer to this with the passage beginning with "the drum" (*dundubhi*).

But how is this to be understood as "to be found by means of a footprint"? It is said: just as in the world, a place marked by the hoofprints of cows and other animals is called a "footprint" (*pada*); by means of that footprint, one searching for a lost animal that one wishes to find, would find or obtain it; in the same way, when the Self is attained, one attains everything—this is the meaning.

[Objection: Since it has been stated that "when the Self is known, everything else is known," and knowledge is the subject under discussion, why is "attainment" (lābha), which is not the subject, being mentioned? [Reply: No, because the intended meaning is that knowledge and attainment have the same referent. For the non-attainment of the Self is simply ignorance; therefore, knowledge itself is the attainment of the Self. The attainment of the Self is not characterized by the acquisition of what was previously unobtained—as is the case with the attainment of the non-Self—because there is no distinction between the attainer and the object to be attained. Indeed, where the non-Self is to be attained by the Self, there the Self is the attainer and the non-Self is the object to be attained.

Furthermore, that [attainment] is unobtained and mediated by actions such as production; it must be acquired by performing specific actions through the employment of specific causal factors (*kāraka*). That [attainment], characterized by the reaching of what was previously unobtained, is impermanent because it originates from the activity of desire produced by false knowledge—just like the acquisition of a son or other things in a dream. This Self, however, is the opposite of that. Precisely because it is the Self, it is not mediated by actions such as production. Even though its essential nature is eternally attained, there is only the veil of ignorance (*avidyā*) as an obstruction.

Just as even when mother-of-pearl is being perceived, its non-perception as such due to the appearance of silver is merely an intervention by erroneous cognition, so too its perception is merely cognition itself, since the purpose of cognition is to remove the intervention of erroneous cognition; likewise here also, the non-attainment of the Self is merely an intervention by ignorance. Therefore, its attainment through knowledge is merely the removal of that [ignorance], and nothing else is ever possible.

Therefore, we shall explain that once the self has been attained through knowledge, any means for achieving something other than that is useless. Consequently, wishing to state without any doubt that the attainment of knowledge and the attainment [of the Self] have the same purpose, he says—referring to knowledge—"one should find" (*anuvindet*), because the root *vid* signifies "attainment."

This is called the fruit of the knowledge of qualities—as follows: this Self has attained manifestation through its entry into name and form, [being designated] by names such as "Self" and so forth, and it has reached the state of being a "verse" (śloka) through the aggregate of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the rest. He who knows thus attains—meaning he obtains—fame (*kīrti*), which is renown, and the "verse," which is the aggregate together with his loved ones. Alternatively, he who knows the reality as described attains the knowledge of unity, denoted by the word "fame," which is required by those seeking liberation, and he obtains the fruit thereof, which is liberation, denoted by the word "verse. Thus, this is indeed the primary fruit.

For what reason is it that the reality of the Self alone is to be known, while everything else is disregarded? To this he says: "This very reality of the Self is dearer than a son. For in the world, a son is well known to be dear; [the text states] it is dearer even than him—thus he demonstrates its state of being unsurpassedly dear. Likewise, [it is dearer] than wealth, such as gold and jewels; likewise, than whatever else is well known in the world as dear—the meaning is: than all of that.

Why is it that the reality of the Self alone is dearer than the vital breaths and so forth? It is said: because it is "more internal. For the aggregate of the vital breaths and the physical body is more internal—that is, closer and more intimate—than external things such as children and wealth. Even more internal than that is this Self, which is the reality of the Self. For whatever is most beloved in the world must be obtained through every effort; and thus, this Self is the dearest of all things beloved in the world.

Therefore, the meaning is that one should apply great effort toward its attainment—setting aside even the effort required for other desired gains when such [attainment] has become a duty. But why, when there is the possibility of choosing between the pleasure of oneself and the pleasure of another by abandoning the pleasure of one or the other, is the abandonment of the other always made by choosing the pleasure of oneself, and not the reverse? To this it is said: Suppose someone were to speak of another specific non-self entity, such as a son or the like, as being dearer than oneself; then a speaker who speaks what is pleasing to oneself would say to him:

"What?"—[the question is: "What is dear to you," meaning that which is desired, characterized by sons and so forth—"it will obstruct," meaning it will encounter an obstruction, it will reach a state of the suspension of breath, it will perish. Why does he speak thus? Because the Lord (*īśvara*) is capable, competent, and able to say this; therefore, it must be exactly so. As for what was said—"it will reach the suspension of breath"—he is indeed a speaker of things as they truly are; therefore, he is the Lord (*īśvara*) in the sense of being one who speaks. Some maintain that the word *īśvara* signifies swiftness.

If it were so, then such a realization would exist. Therefore, having abandoned other objects of affection, one should worship the Self alone as dear. He who worships the Self alone as dear realizes that the Self alone is dear and there is nothing else; having determined that all other worldly objects of affection are indeed non-dear, he worships—that is, he contemplates—this. For such a knower, his object of affection does not become *pramāyuka*, meaning prone to perish. This is merely a restatement, because for the knower of the Self, there exists no other thing that is either dear or non-dear.

Or [the suffix] is for the purpose of praising the grasping of what is dear to the self; or it is for the purpose of enjoining the fruit consisting of the quality of being dear to those who perceive the self only dimly, due to the employment of the suffix denoting habit (*tācchīlya*). [End of] Mantra 9, Section 4, Chapter 1, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.

(9) The science of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) has been aphoristically stated in the words, "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self alone," for the sake of which the entire *Upaniṣad* exists. Desiring to explain this aphorism and wishing to state its purpose, [the author] prepares the ground by saying: "They say"—that is, the Brāhmaṇas—[they speak of] Brahman, the reality to be illuminated in the immediately following sentence, indicated by the word "That" (*tat*).

Those desiring to know (*vividiṣavaḥ*), having approached a Guru who serves as a boat for crossing the shoreless great ocean whose waters consist of the suffering and exhaustion caused by wandering in the wheel of the continuous cycle of birth, old age, and death—desiring to reach that shore, being weary of the nature of means and ends characterized by merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) and their fruits, and seeking the eternal, unsurpassed, supreme good (*śreyaḥ*) which is distinct from that [cycle]—what do they say? He says: "That which [is attained] through the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*)."

Brahman is the Supreme Self; that by which It is known is Brahma-vidyā (the knowledge of Brahman). By means of that Brahma-vidyā, all things without exception—regarding which humans think, "We shall become," "we shall exist"—[are attained]. The mention of "humans" is for the purpose of making known their specific qualification; the intention is that humans alone are specifically qualified for the means of attaining worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

Just as they consider the attainment of results from ritual actions to be certain, so too do they consider the attainment of the fruit of universal selfhood through the knowledge of Brahman to be equally certain, since the authority of the Veda is no different in both cases; yet, in that regard, a contradictory matter is perceived.

Therefore, we ask: what is that Brahman, by the knowledge of which humans think they shall become everything? What did it know, by virtue of which knowledge that Brahman became all? For it is heard in scripture that "Brahman is all"; if it became all without knowing anything, then let it be so for others as well.

"What is the use of the knowledge of Brahman? For if one becomes everything after having known [it], then, because it is accomplished through knowledge, the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman—namely, the state of being everything—would be equal to the fruit of ritual action, which entails the consequence of impermanence. Furthermore, there is the fault of infinite regress: that too became everything after knowing something else, and before that, it must have become everything after knowing yet another thing. "It did not become everything without having known [it], for that would entail the fault of contradicting the meaning of the scriptures. Then, is there the fault of the impermanence of the fruit? "No, not even a single fault exists, because a specific meaning is logically established."

If that Brahman became all this only after knowing something, we ask: what was that Brahman which, by not knowing, became all this? When thus questioned, he offers a reply untainted by any such defect: "O Gārgī, the Brahmins and Kshatriyas who have not heard this [teaching] from their teacher, they, indeed, are like cattle. He among them who knows it thus becomes the possessor of cattle. [The opponent asks: "Is there anything else beyond this space? [Yājñavalkya replies: "O Gārgī, do not question too far, lest your head shatter. Do not question about the Brahman, O Gārgī! You are questioning about the Brahman, O Gārgī! Thereupon, having praised her for her inquiry, he said: "O Gārgī, truly, the Brahmins and Kshatriyas here venerate this as the Imperishable (Akṣara). It is neither gross nor fine, neither short nor long, neither red nor fluid, neither shadow nor darkness, neither air nor space. It is without stickiness, without taste, without smell, without eyes, without ears, without speech, without mind, without light, without breath, without mouth, without measure, and has no interior or exterior. It does not consume anything, nor is it consumed by anyone. Verily, O Gārgī, through being established in and supported by this Imperishable, this vast space is woven back and forth. Now, O Gārgī, that which is above heaven, that which is below the earth, and that which is between these two, heaven and earth, as well as that which people call the past, the present, and the future—verily, all this is woven back and forth on this Imperishable.
