(10) — The "Brahman" here must be the lower Brahman, because it is logical that the attainment of all states of being is something to be accomplished. Indeed, the attainment of all states of being by the higher Brahman is not something to be accomplished through knowledge; yet the text speaks of the attainment of all states of being as being accomplished through knowledge in the passage, "Therefore, that became all. Therefore, in the phrase "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman," it is appropriate that the lower Brahman is intended here.

Or rather, because the qualification for this [knowledge] belongs to human beings, he would be a Brāhmaṇa destined to become that [Brahman]; for it is said, "All men think they shall become [Brahman]," and thus human beings are the subject under discussion. And it has been stated that they alone have the specific qualification for the means to attain worldly prosperity and the supreme good (abhyudaya-niḥśreyasa), neither for the Supreme Brahman nor for the lower Prajāpati. Therefore, one who—through the knowledge of the lower Brahman characterized by both duality and unity, combined with ritual action—has attained the state of the lower Brahman, turned away from the world of objects of enjoyment, and whose bonds of desire and karma have been severed through the attainment of all things, is designated as "Brahman" because he is destined to become the Supreme Brahman due to the cause of Brahma-knowledge.

Furthermore, the use of words based on a future state is observed in the world—such as "he cooks the rice"—and in the scriptures—as in "the wandering mendicant [gives] the gift of fearlessness to all beings," and so forth; likewise here, some explain that the person who is destined for the state of Brahman is a "Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*).

That is not so, because it would entail the attainment of all states of being, which carries the defect of impermanence. Indeed, there exists nothing in the world that, by virtue of a cause, attains another state of being and yet remains eternal. Likewise, if the attainment of all states of being were produced by the knowledge of Brahman as its cause, it would be contradictory for it to be eternal. Furthermore, if it were impermanent, the aforementioned defect would apply, namely, that it would be equal to the fruit of ritual action (*karma*).

If you consider the cessation of non-universality caused by ignorance and the attainment of the state of universality by the mind to be the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman, then the conceptualization of a person who becomes Brahman would be useless. Even prior to the realization of Brahman, every living being is eternally already in the state of universality due to being Brahman from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); it is only through ignorance that non-Brahmanhood and non-universality are superimposed—just as silver is superimposed on mother-of-pearl, or as surface and impurity are superimposed on the sky.

If you think that here, in this case, the non-Brahmanhood and non-omnipresence superimposed upon Brahman by ignorance are removed by the knowledge of Brahman, then it is logical to say that what was in reality the Supreme Brahman—the primary referent of the word "Brahman"—is what is spoken of in the statement, "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman," because the Veda speaks of things as they truly are.

However, this conception is not tenable—that a person who is to become Brahman, though contrary to the meaning of the word "Brahman," is called "Brahman"—because it involves abandoning what is heard in scripture and imagining what is not heard, which is improper. If it is argued that even in the absence of some other greater purpose, non-Brahmanhood and non-omnipresence actually exist as distinct from Brahman due to the creation of ignorance, we say no; for it is impossible for such [non-Brahmanhood] to be removed by the knowledge of Brahman.

For nowhere is it observed that the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) directly removes or produces any real property of an entity; rather, it is seen everywhere as the remover of ignorance (avidyā). Thus, here too, non-Brahmanhood and non-omnipresence—which are produced by ignorance alone—must be removed by the knowledge of Brahman; however, the knowledge of Brahman cannot create or remove an ultimately real entity. Therefore, the abandonment of what is stated in scripture and the postulation of what is not so stated are entirely futile.

If it is argued that ignorance is impossible in Brahman, we say no, because knowledge is enjoined with respect to Brahman. For when silver is superimposed upon mother-of-pearl, the true nature of the mother-of-pearl is not made known—while it has come within the range of the eye—in the form: "This is mother-of-pearl, not silver."

Likewise, the realization of the oneness of Brahman—expressed as "All this is indeed Being," "All this is indeed Brahman," "All this is indeed the Self," and "This duality does not exist apart from Brahman"—need not be enjoined, provided that there is no superimposition of ignorance upon Brahman. We do not say that there is no superimposition of non-Brahman attributes upon Brahman, as there is [the superimposition of silver] upon mother-of-pearl; rather, we mean that Brahman is not the cause for the superimposition of non-Brahman attributes upon its own self.

Regarding the phrase "and ignorance is the agent": it is indeed so that Brahman is neither the agent of ignorance nor deluded. However, it is not the case that there exists some other non-Brahman who is the conscious agent of ignorance and is deluded. This is known from such scriptural passages as: "There is no other knower than this," "There is nothing else but this that knows," "That thou art," "One should know only the Self," "I am Brahman," and "He who thinks 'that one is one and I am another' does not know. And so forth.

And from the Smṛtis: "The same in all beings," "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa," "In the dog and even in the outcaste"; and from the Vedic mantras: "He who [sees] all beings [as himself]," and "In whom all beings [exist]. If it is argued that, in this way, the instruction of the scripture (śāstra) would be purposeless, we reply: certainly it is so; once [the truth] is realized, there is indeed purposelessness. If it is asked whether there is also purposelessness regarding the realization itself, we say no, because the cessation of non-realization is observed. If it is argued that even the cessation of that [non-realization] is untenable in the state of oneness, we say no, because that would contradict what is observed.

For it is observed that the cessation of non-comprehension occurs precisely from the cognition of oneness; to say that what is being perceived is nevertheless untenable would constitute a contradiction with experience (*dṛṣṭavirodha*). And a contradiction with experience is not accepted by anyone. Furthermore, there is no such thing as "the untenability of what is seen," precisely because it has been seen. If it is argued that the perception itself is untenable, the same reasoning applies there as well.

From such scriptural passages and traditional authorities as, "One becomes virtuous by virtuous action," "Knowledge and action follow him," and "The person is the knower, the perceiver, the agent, the self consisting of consciousness," a transmigrating being is understood to be distinct and different from the Supreme. And the Supreme is distinct from that [transmigrating being], according to such scriptural passages as, "This one is 'not this, not this'," "He transcends hunger and so forth," "The Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless," and "By the command of this Imperishable."
Furthermore, in the systems of logic such as those of Kaṇāda and Akṣapāda, God is established through reasoning as distinct from the transmigrating soul;

for it is clearly understood that the transmigrating soul is different from God because we observe his engagement in activity due to the desire to remove the suffering of saṃsāra, and because of the Śruti and Smṛti texts such as "He is beyond speech and disregard" and "I have nothing [to gain], O Pārtha."

Furthermore, there are indications of both the object and the agent of action in such passages as: "He is to be sought, He is to be desired to be known"; "Having known Him, one is not tainted"; "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"; "This is to be viewed as one alone"; "O Gārgī, he who does not know this Imperishable"; "The wise man, having fully understood that very [Self]"; and "The Praṇava is the bow, the Self is the arrow, and Brahman is said to be its target. Moreover, there is the instruction regarding the specific path and destination for the seeker of liberation.

If there were no difference [between the individual self and Brahman], for whom and from what source could there be any movement? And in the absence of that [difference], the distinction between the southern and northern paths would be untenable, as would the destination to be reached. However, all this is logically consistent if the transmigrating self is distinct from the Supreme Self. Furthermore, because of the instruction regarding the means of action (*karman*) and knowledge (*jñāna*): if the transmigrator were non-different from Brahman, the teaching of action and knowledge as the means to the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) would be appropriate for him, but not for the Lord (*īśvara*), since his desires are already fulfilled.

If it is argued that it is therefore logical to say "Brahman" refers to the person who is destined to become Brahman—this is not so, because it would result in the futility of the instruction regarding Brahman. For if the transmigrating being, while not yet Brahman, becomes Brahman by knowing the Self alone through the realization "I am Brahman," and thereby becomes everything, then since the fruit of becoming the Self of all is already accomplished simply through the knowledge of the transmigrating Self, the instruction regarding the Supreme Brahman would certainly become purposeless.

If it is argued that because the cognition of that [Brahman] is not employed for the accomplishment of any human goal, this instruction—"I am Brahman"—is intended solely for the sake of producing the state of being Brahman in one who is still a transmigrating soul; [we reply: if the true nature of Brahman is not already known, what could one produce by saying "I am Brahman"? For the realization (*saṃpat*) can only be effected when Brahman’s characteristics are already known—as in: "This Self is Brahman," "That which is immediate and direct is Brahman," "The Self," "That is Truth, that is the Self," and "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme."

From the very beginning, through thousands of instances of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the words "Brahman" and "Self"—such as in the passage, "From this very Self..."—it is understood that they possess exactly one and the same referent. For the superimposition (*saṃpat*) of one thing upon another is performed when they are distinct, not when they are identical. Furthermore, the text, "All this is what this Self is," demonstrates the oneness of the very Self under discussion, which is to be seen. Therefore, the superimposition of Brahmanhood upon the Self is not tenable. Nor is any other purpose for the instruction regarding Brahman perceived.

Because of the scriptural declarations regarding the attainment of that [Brahman], such as: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," "For you have attained fearlessness, O Janaka," and "Indeed, one becomes the fearless Brahman. If it were a case of merging (*saṃpatti*), there would be no such attainment; for it is not possible for one thing to become another. If it is argued that, on account of the scriptural statement, even through merging there is the attainment of that state, we say no; for merging is merely a mental conception (*pratyayamātra*). And we have already stated that cognition has no other function than the removal of false knowledge.

Furthermore, a word does not produce the capacity of a thing; for the established principle is that a scripture is indicative (*jñāpaka*), not productive (*kāraka*). And in such sentences as "He has entered here," it is established that it is the Supreme [Self] alone who enters. Therefore, the conception of a person who will become Brahman is not tenable.

And because it subverts the desired object: the knowledge that Brahman is "without interior or exterior, a single essence, like a mass of salt"—this is the intended meaning to be established in every Upaniṣad, as is understood from the final determinations in both sections [of the Veda]: "This is the instruction" and "This much indeed, my dear, is immortality. Likewise, in all the Upaniṣads of every Śākhā, the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman is the settled meaning.

In this regard, if it were imagined that the transmigrating soul, being other than Brahman, "knew itself," then there would be a subversion of the intended meaning; and thus the scripture would be rendered inconsistent by imagining a contradiction between its opening and its conclusion. Furthermore, the designation [of the knowledge] would be untenable: if the transmigrating soul were imagined as the one who "knew itself," then the designation "knowledge of Brahman" (brahmavidyā) would not apply, because it would be the transmigrating soul alone that is established as the object of knowledge.

If it is argued that "the Self" (ātman) is stated to be something other than the knower, we say no, because of the qualification "I am Brahman. If the object of knowledge were something else, one would qualify it as "this is that," but not as "I am. Because of the qualification "I am" and the restriction in the phrase "he knew the Self alone," it is understood with certainty that the Self itself is Brahman. This being the case, the designation "knowledge of Brahman" is appropriate, and not otherwise; for otherwise, it would merely be the knowledge of a transmigrating being (saṃsārī).

Furthermore, both being Brahman and not being Brahman cannot logically belong to one and the same thing from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because they are as contradictory as darkness and light in relation to the sun. Nor is it appropriate to apply the definitive designation "knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyā*) when it is caused by both [ignorance and knowledge], for in that case, it would be both the knowledge of Brahman and the knowledge of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Moreover, it is not proper to conceive of a real entity as being like a "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīya*) when the intention is to convey the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*); for in such a case, doubt would arise in the listener.

Furthermore, certain knowledge is held to be the means for accomplishing the goals of human life, according to the Śruti and Smṛti: "He who has this [knowledge] truly and has no doubt," and "The one whose self is full of doubt perishes. Therefore, one who seeks the welfare of others should not state the meaning of a sentence in a manner that is subject to doubt.

If it is argued that the conception of Brahman as an agent (*sādhakatva*) is as improper as [the conception of agentship] in the case of people like us—based on such passages as "It knew only itself, therefore It became all"—we say no, because this is found in the scripture (*śāstra*). For this is not our own fabrication; rather, it was composed by the scripture. Therefore, this is a critique of the scripture; and one who desires to accomplish what is beneficial for Brahman should not abandon its own meaning by fabricating a contrary interpretation of the scriptural sense. Nor is it reasonable for you to be so intolerant regarding this much alone.

For all diversity is merely imagined within Brahman, as established by hundreds of scriptural passages such as: "It should be viewed as one alone," "There is not even the slightest diversity here," "For where there is duality, as it were," and "One only, without a second. Indeed, the entire worldly transaction is imagined within Brahman itself and is not ultimately real; therefore, it is a trifle to say that this very [worldly] imagination is clever.

Therefore—that which entered as the Creator-Brahman is indeed that Brahman; the word *vai* is for the purpose of emphasis. This which is perceived as residing in the body was, even before [the attainment of] enlightenment (*agre*), nothing but Brahman, and all this is Brahman. However, due to a lack of enlightenment, because of the superimposition upon the Self of the notions "I am not Brahman" and "I am not the All," one superimposes: "I am the agent, I am the doer, I am the enjoyer of fruits, I am happy, I am miserable, I am a transmigrating being. But in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), it is Brahman alone, distinct from that [superimposed nature].

And all that has been somehow awakened by the compassionate Teacher with the words, "You are not a transmigrating being"; the meaning of the word "alone" (eva) is that one should know the Self itself as natural, devoid of the distinctions superimposed by ignorance.

"Tell me, what is this innate self (*ātman*) which Brahmā knew? But surely you do not remember the self; for it was shown to you as that which, having entered here, breathes in, breathes out, breathes pervasively, breathes upward, and breathes evenly. "But surely that [self] is designated by you as 'this is a cow' or 'that is a horse'; you do not point to the self through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). "In that case, he who is the seer, the hearer, the thinker, and the knower—that is the self."

"Is it not the case that here too you do not show the nature of the agent of the acts of seeing and so forth to be perceptible? For movement (*gati*) is not the very nature of the mover, nor is cutting (*chidi*) the nature of the cutter. If that is so, [the Upanishad says]: 'He who is the seer of seeing, the hearer of hearing, the thinker of thought, the knower of knowing—that is the Self. But what is the distinction here regarding the seer? Whether he is the seer of seeing or the seer of a jar, in every way he is simply a seer. Yet you state a distinction by saying 'the seer of seeing'."

Whether the seer is the seer of seeing or the seer of the jar, he remains simply the seer. No, for a distinction is established—there is indeed a distinction here: that which is the seer of seeing, if it is itself seeing, then it sees seeing eternally; seeing is never at any time not seen by the seer. Therefore, the seer must possess eternal seeing.

If the seer were impermanent, then that vision which is the object of seeing would never be seen—just as an object such as a jar is not seen by an impermanent vision. Yet, unlike that, the seer of vision never fails to see the vision. Are there then two visions for the seer—one eternal and invisible, and another impermanent and visible? Certainly; the impermanent vision is well-established, since we observe the difference between being blind and not being blind. If it were eternal alone, everyone would necessarily be non-blind.

But for the seer, vision is eternal—according to the scripture, "For there is no loss of the vision of the seer"; and also from inference: even for a blind person, a vision whose objects are the appearances of jars and so forth is perceived in a dream; that vision, therefore, does not perish when other visions perish; that is the vision of the seer.

By means of that unimpaired, eternal vision—which constitutes its own essential nature and is designated as self-luminous—one perceives the other, impermanent vision (consisting of the impressions and cognitions of the states of dream and waking) as being eternally [of the same nature]; thus one becomes the "seer of vision. This being so, vision alone is its essential nature, like the heat of fire; it is not, as the followers of Kaṇāda maintain, a separate conscious seer distinct from vision.

That Brahman knew itself alone—its nature being eternally seeing and devoid of superimposed notions such as non-eternal seeing. [Objection: But is this not contradictory, given the Śruti text, "One should not seek to know the knower of cognition"? [Reply: No, there is no contradiction in knowing it in this way; for in this manner, it is indeed known as the "seer of seeing."

And because it does not depend on any other knowledge: once it is understood that the seer’s vision is indeed eternal, one does not seek another vision whose object would be the seer; for the desire for a vision having the seer as its object ceases precisely because such a vision is impossible. Indeed, no one develops a desire for an object that does not exist. Nor is it possible for the vision, being itself an object of sight, to take the seer as its own object, such that one might desire it. Furthermore, there can be no desire for one's own nature directed toward itself.
Therefore, what was stated—“He knew only himself”—refers solely to the cessation of the superimposition of ignorance, and not to the making of the Self an object.

To explain how he knew that, the text says: "I am the seer of seeing; I am the Self, I am Brahman. Regarding "Brahman": it is that Self which is immediate and direct, the innermost of all, beyond hunger and so forth, characterized as "not this, not this," "neither gross nor subtle," and so on; that very one I am, and not another who is a transmigrating being, just as you have stated. Therefore, from such realization, that Brahman became everything—because the superimposition of non-Brahman has been removed, and with the cessation of its effect, the state of being non-universal, it became everything.

Therefore, it is indeed appropriate that men think: "By the knowledge of Brahman, we shall become everything. As for what was asked—"What is that Brahman, by knowing which he became all this?"—that has been resolved: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself, thinking 'I am Brahman'; therefore, it became all this."

In that regard, whoever among the gods awakened—that is, who realized the Self according to the method described—became that very Brahman which is the awakened Self. Likewise among the seers (*ṛṣis*) and likewise among human beings. The mention of "among the gods" and so forth is made with reference to worldly perspective, not with the intent of asserting their actual nature as Brahman; for we have already stated that "the Person entered into the bodies," meaning that Brahman alone has entered everywhere.

Therefore, with reference to the worldly perspective produced by limiting adjuncts such as the body, it is said, "of the gods," and so forth; but in the ultimate sense, in each instance, Brahman alone existed in the beginning prior to awakening, appearing otherwise within the bodies of gods and others. Then, it knew itself alone, and thus became everything.

To strengthen this point—that the fruit of this knowledge of Brahman is the attainment of all states of being—the Śruti cites certain mantras. How so? Seeing that very Brahman as "I am this Self," the seer named Vāmadeva indeed attained it—yes, he truly realized it through that very vision of Brahman. Established in this realization of the Self as Brahman, he beheld these mantras beginning with, "I was Manu, I was the Sun."

In the phrase "perceiving this very Brahman," the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is referred to; by the statement "I was Manu, I was the Sun," and so forth, he refers to the attainment of all states of being as the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman. From this usage—"perceiving [it], he attained the state of being the Self of all"—he shows that liberation is to be accomplished by means of the auxiliary instruments of the knowledge of Brahman, just as one says, "eating, he becomes satisfied. This is that...

One might think: "In the past, the attainment of all states of being through the knowledge of Brahman occurred for the great ones, such as the gods, due to their extraordinary vigor; but it does not happen now for those of this age, especially for human beings, because of their meager vigor. To dispel that notion, he says: "This very Brahman under discussion, which has entered into all beings and is indicated by seeing, acting, and so forth—even now, at this present time, whosoever, having turned away from external longings, knows the Self alone thus: 'I am Brahman'..."

—having set aside those distinctions, which are worldly attributes superimposed by the erroneous cognition produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), [one realizes]: "I am indeed the absolute Brahman alone, without interior or exterior, untouched by the qualities of transmigratory existence"—then, through the knowledge of Brahman, which brings about the cessation of non-universality created by ignorance, this [Self] becomes all this. For there is no distinction in Brahman, nor in the knowledge of it, whether among those of great heroism such as Vāmadeva and others, or among men of the present day who possess little heroism.

However, since it might be suspected that among men of the present day there is a lack of certainty regarding the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman, he says: "Of him who has realized Brahman according to the aforementioned method, even the gods of great power (*mahāvīryāḥ*) are not capable (*neśate*), that is, they are not able (*na paryāptāḥ*), of effecting his non-existence (*abhūtyai*), i.e., the cessation of his state as Brahman which is the being of all; how much less others?"

As for the doubt that gods and others might have the power to create obstacles to the attainment of the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman—it is said in response: because mortals are in a state of debt toward the gods and others. For the Śruti declares that a person is born already burdened with debts: "By studentship (brahmacarya) to the sages, by sacrifice to the gods, and by progeny to the ancestors."

Moreover, based on the illustration of cattle and the scriptural passage from common worldly usage beginning with "Now this one indeed... (atho ayaṃ vā...), it is entirely reasonable to suspect that the gods, like those who do not pay debts, might create obstacles for human beings—who are dependent upon them—in the attainment of immortality, out of a desire to protect their own livelihood. For the gods protect [humans] as they would their own cattle or their own bodies; indeed, the text will later show that the gods and others regard each individual person as equivalent to many cattle, since the gods' superior livelihood is dependent upon ritual action.

For it will be stated later: "Therefore, that is not dear to them which men might know," and, "Just as one would desire safety for one's own world, even so do all beings desire safety for one who knows thus. From these two statements regarding what is "not dear" and "safety," it is understood that when one possesses the knowledge of Brahman, there is an end to being subservient to others, and consequently, there is neither the state of being their "world" nor the state of being their "cattle. Therefore, the gods would certainly create obstacles against the knower of Brahman attaining the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman;
for they possess great power.

[Objection: But if this were so, then in the case of other attainments of the fruits of action as well, the gods’ creating obstacles would be equivalent to drinking wine; alas, there would then be no confidence in the performance of the means for attaining worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Likewise, because the Lord possesses inconceivable power, he has the capacity to create obstacles; the same applies to time, karma, mantras, herbs, and austerity, for their status as causes for the attainment or failure of results is well-known both in the scriptures and in the world. Therefore, there would also be no trust in the performance of the meaning of the scriptures. [Reply: No.

Because all things arise from specific causes and materials, and because the diversity of the world is observed, and because both of these would be untenable under the theory of inherent nature (*svabhāva*), it is established that action (*karman*) is the cause of results such as pleasure and pain; this position being accepted by the Vedas, the Smṛtis, logic, and the world, neither gods, nor the Lord (*īśvara*), nor time (*kāla*) can be the agents who subvert the fruits of actions, since actions bring about their desired effects— for auspicious and inauspicious action does not depend upon gods, time, the Lord, or other such causal factors to produce its own result.

Even that which has attained its own nature is incapable of yielding a fruit, for action, by its very nature, requires the employment of multiple causal factors such as the agent and so forth. Therefore, since gods, lords, and others are merely subordinate to action, there is no confidence whatsoever in the attainment of results from ritual acts alone. Furthermore, even these [deities] are sometimes subject to the power of actions, because their own capacity cannot be set aside.

The relative predominance or subordination among action, time, destiny, material substances, and so forth, as well as their intrinsic natures, is不定 (aniyata, indeterminate) and difficult to discern; thus, the world is deluded by this. Some hold that action alone is the agent in the attainment of results and nothing else; others that it is destiny alone; some that it is time; some that it is the nature of material substances and so forth; and others that all these together constitute the cause.

In this regard, accepting the primacy of action (*karman*), there are declarations in the Vedas and Smṛtis such as: "One becomes virtuous through virtuous action and sinful through sinful action. Although among these [factors] there may be the emergence of the primacy of one within its own domain and the temporary suppression of the power of primacy of the others, nevertheless, there is no uncertainty regarding the attainment of results by action, because the primacy of action has been definitively established by scripture and logic.

No, because the fruit of attaining Brahman consists merely in the removal of ignorance. Regarding what was said—that the gods might create obstacles to the fruit of attaining Brahman—in that case, the gods have no power to create obstacles. Why? Because the fruit of attaining Brahman is not separated by any interval from the time of knowledge. How so?

Just as in the world, at the very moment the eye of the observer comes into contact with light, there is the manifestation of form; even so, at the very moment consciousness has the Self as its object, there must be the disappearance of ignorance regarding that object. Therefore, since the effects of ignorance are untenable when the knowledge of Brahman exists—just as the effects of darkness are not when a lamp is present—who could obstruct whom? For in that state where the knower of Brahman realizes the identity of the gods with the Self, what obstruction could the gods possibly offer?

This is what he says: the Self (*ātman*), which is one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) and that which is to be meditated upon, is Brahman, who is to be known through all the scriptures; for indeed, because of this, he becomes a knower of Brahman at the very same moment as the knowledge of Brahman arises—[namely] for these gods.

We have already stated that, just as in the case of mother-of-pearl appearing as silver, its true nature as mother-of-pearl is revealed upon the removal of the veil of mere ignorance. Therefore, it is impossible for the gods to exert effort toward what is contrary to the Self. For when a result is non-self, separated by space, time, and other causal conditions, then the gods may effectively employ effort to create obstacles regarding that non-self object; but this is not the case here, because the result is coeval with knowledge, is of the nature of the Self, and is not separated by space, time, or causal conditions—since no such opportunity exists.

If that is so, then because there is no continuity of the cognition of knowledge (*vidyā*), and because the erroneous cognition and its effects are observed [to persist], it follows that only the final cognition of the Self (*ātmapratyaya*) is the remover of ignorance (*avidyā*), and not the preceding ones. This is not so, because the first [cognition] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For if the first cognition regarding the Self does not remove ignorance, then the final one likewise would not, since they have the same object (*viṣaya*). If that is the case, then it must be a continuous [series of cognitions] that removes ignorance, not one that is interrupted.

No, because when life and so forth exist, a continuous stream [of knowledge] is impossible. For as long as there is a cognition caused by life and the like, a continuous stream of the cognition of knowledge cannot arise, due to their mutual contradiction. If it is argued that the continuous stream of knowledge persists until death precisely by setting aside the cognitions of life and so forth, we say no; for there would be the fault of failing to determine the meaning of the scripture, since one would not ascertain the sequence of cognitions. That is to say, without determining that "a stream of this many cognitions brings about the cessation of ignorance," the meaning of the scripture would remain undetermined.

And that is undesirable. If it is argued that [the cessation] occurs only when the mere continuity has been determined, we say no, because there is no distinction between the beginning and the end—since there would be no difference whether the first continuity of the cognition of ignorance ends at death or not, the two previously mentioned defects would apply to both the initial and final cognitions. If it is then argued that [the knowledge] does not bring about cessation at all, we say no, on account of the scriptural text, "Therefore, he became all this," and from such texts as, "The knot of the heart is severed" and "What delusion is there then? and so forth.

If it is argued that this is merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), we say no, because it would follow that all the Upaniṣads of every Vedic branch are likewise mere eulogies; for all the Upaniṣads of every Vedic branch are exhausted in having just this much as their purpose. If it is argued that [the Self] truly exists because its nature is an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), we say no, because the refutation has already been stated: namely, that the cessation of defects such as ignorance, grief, delusion, and fear is itself directly perceived. This is the refutation that has been stated.

Therefore, it is not to be questioned whether [knowledge] is initial, final, continuous, or non-continuous; for knowledge culminates in the fruit of the cessation of defects such as ignorance. Since we accept that whatever cognition brings about the fruit of the cessation of defects like ignorance—whether it be initial, final, continuous, or non-continuous—is itself knowledge, there is not even a scent of a valid objection here.

As for what was said regarding "the observation of erroneous cognition and its effects," that is not so, because it serves as the cause for the persistence of the remainder [of karma]. That karma by which the body was initiated has the capacity to yield its fruit only when it is of such a nature—namely, when it is conjoined with the defects of erroneous cognition; therefore, until the fall of the body, it projects only that much erroneous cognition and defects such as passion, merely as a subordinate factor for the experience of the fruit—just like a released arrow.

Because the karma caused by that [ignorance] has already begun to bear fruit, knowledge does not cause its cessation, as there is no contradiction between them. Rather, from its own locus, knowledge obstructs that effect of ignorance which is about to arise, because that [future effect] has not yet come into being; for the other [past effect] has already passed away.

Furthermore, a contrary cognition does not arise in one who possesses knowledge (*vidyā*), because it lacks a real objective basis. Indeed, a contrary cognition arises only by resorting to a mere generality (*sāmānyamātra*) whose specific nature as an object has not been determined, as in the case of [perceiving] silver in mother-of-pearl. And that [contrary cognition] cannot occur as before for one who has ascertained the specific nature of the object, because the latent impressions (*āśaya*) of all contrary cognitions have been destroyed; this is seen from the fact that such a cognition is no longer observed once a correct cognition has arisen regarding mother-of-pearl and similar objects.

In some cases, however, due to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by erroneous cognitions that arose prior to knowledge, memories arise in which erroneous cognitions appear; these produce the delusion of erroneous cognition all at once—just as, for example, one who has already correctly understood the directions may suddenly experience the confusion of a reversal of directions.

If, even for one who possesses right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), a contrary cognition were to arise as before, then because there would be no confidence even in right knowledge, activity toward the understanding of the meaning of the scriptures and so forth would be improper; furthermore, every means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would become invalid, since no distinction between valid and invalid cognitions could be established. By this, the question of why the body does not fall away immediately after right knowledge is answered.

The destruction of those karmas—accumulated in this life, in previous lives, or in future births—which have not yet begun to bear fruit, prior to, after, and at the very moment of the arising of knowledge, is established by the scriptural texts themselves that prohibit obstacles to the attainment of the fruit.

This is also established by such scriptural passages as: "And his actions are exhausted," "For him there is delay only so long," "All evils are burnt away," "Having known Him, one is not tainted by evil action," "These two do not cross over Him," "Neither what is done nor what is left undone afflicts Him," "Verily, this does not afflict Him," and "He fears nothing at all"; as well as by such traditional texts (smṛti) as: "The fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes."

As for the claim that [liberation] is obstructed by debts, that is not so, because it refers to the subject who possesses ignorance (*avidyā*). For one who possesses ignorance is a debtor, since agency and the like are possible for him; as the text will later state: "But where there is, as it were, another, there one might see another. This shows that when the non-dual reality called the Self appears, due to ignorance, as if it were something else—like a second moon produced by a visual disorder—then action such as seeing, which depends on various factors produced by ignorance, and the fruit resulting from that action, are manifested.

In that context, [the text] says "one would see another," and so forth; whereas when knowledge has arisen and the delusion of manifoldness produced by ignorance is abandoned, it shows the impossibility of action with the words, "then by what means would one see whom? Therefore, the state of being a debtor exists only for one who possesses ignorance, because action is possible there, and not in the other case. We shall demonstrate this in detail through the very passages that are intended to be explained further on.

To explain this very point: suppose here someone who does not know Brahman worships some deity other than his own self—approaching that deity through praise, salutation, sacrifice, offerings, oblations, mental application, meditation, and so forth, remaining in a state of subordination to it. With the conviction, "That one is another, not the Self; it is distinct from me; I am another, one who is authorized [to act]; I must repay my debt to it like a debtor"—if he worships while holding such a notion, he does not truly know or understand in this way.

This is the truth. He is not merely such an ignorant person, possessed of the defect of nescience (*avidyā*); rather, just as an animal, such as a cow, is utilized for various services like carrying loads and yielding milk, so too is he to be enjoyed through many services, such as being used by each of the gods and others individually. Therefore, the meaning is that, like an animal, he is entitled to perform all ritual actions (*karma*).

For this ignorant person—who possesses the distinctions of caste, stage of life, and so forth, who is qualified for action, and who performs the actions prescribed by the scriptures either in conjunction with knowledge or independently—the result is an upward progression beginning from the human state up to the level of Brahman. Conversely, the result of that which is contrary to the scriptural injunctions and is merely natural is a downward degradation beginning from the human state down to the level of stationary objects. How this is so, we shall explain in its entirety in the remainder of this chapter, starting with the passage, "Now, there are indeed three worlds," and so forth.

Furthermore, it has been shown in brief that the effect of knowledge is the attainment of the state of being the Self of all. Indeed, this entire Upaniṣad is exhausted by demonstrating the distinction between knowledge and ignorance. And we shall demonstrate how this meaning applies to the whole scripture.

Since this is so, therefore, with respect to a person possessed of ignorance (*avidyā*), the gods are indeed capable of both creating obstacles and bestowing grace; this is what is being shown. Just as in the world many animals, such as cattle and horses, serve and protect their master—their own controller—so too each ignorant person, who stands in the place of many animals, "serves" and "protects" the gods. The mention of "the gods" is intended to include the ancestors (*pitṛ*) and others; [it means] these others, Indra and the rest, [are served].

The intention is as follows: "They are my masters; like a servant, I shall propitiate them through praise, salutation, worship, and so forth, and thereby obtain the fruit bestowed by them—both worldly prosperity and the supreme good."

In this world, just as for one who possesses many cattle there is great displeasure when even a single animal is taken away or carried off by a tiger or some other predator, so too, when a single person—who stands in the place of many cattle—rises above the state of being a mere beast, it becomes a source of displeasure to the gods. What is surprising about this? It is like the grief of a householder at the loss of his many cattle. Therefore, that is not dear to them: namely, that human beings should somehow come to know or realize this true nature of Brahman as the Self.

And likewise, there is a traditional teaching (smaraṇa) by the blessed Vyāsa in the *Anugītā*: "For the world of the gods, O son of Kuntī, is filled with those who perform ritual actions; and this is not desired by the gods—that mortals should dwell above them. Therefore, the gods wish to create obstacles to the knowledge of Brahman for men, as if they were beasts [kept away] from tigers and other predators, thinking, "Let them not rise up [from their state], lest they cease to be objects of our enjoyment. However, those whom they wish to liberate, they will endow with faith and its like, while those of the opposite sort they will endow with lack of faith and its like.

Therefore, one who desires liberation should be intent on propitiating the gods, devoted to faith and devotion, disciplined, and vigilant—this is shown by the ironic statement "unpleasant to the gods" (devāpriya), implying that such qualities are essential for the attainment of knowledge.

The meaning of the treatise has been set forth in the aphorism: "One should meditate [on the Self] as 'I am the Self'. And for that [aphorism], which is intended to be explained, the connection and purpose have been stated along with an explanatory statement (arthavāda) beginning with, "Regarding this they say: 'By the knowledge of Brahman... Furthermore, the fact that ignorance is the cause for one's involvement in transmigratory existence has been declared by the passage beginning with, "Now, he who worships another deity... In that context, it was stated that the ignorant person is like a debtor or a beast, dependent upon others due to the necessity of performing duties toward the gods and other beings.

What, then, is the cause for the necessity of performing duties such as those of the gods? It is the castes (*varṇa*) and the stages of life (*āśrama*). To this end, the following is commenced: [to explain] by what cause, when connected with ritual actions, this person—being entirely dependent [on others]—is authorized [to act] and transmigrates. To demonstrate this very point, the creation of Indra and the others was not mentioned immediately after the creation of Fire; rather, the creation of Fire was shown for the purpose of completing Prajāpati’s creation. And this creation of Indra and the others is to be understood in that very context, because it is supplementary to it.
But here, that very same [Self] is designated for the purpose of demonstrating the cause of the ignorant person’s entitlement to perform ritual action.
Chapter 1, Section 4, Mantra 11.
Section: Mantra; Chapter.

(11) --- "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman" — that is, Brahman which, having created Agni, had assumed the form of Agni — is designated as "Brahman" due to its identification with the *brāhmaṇa* caste. Indeed, this entire collection of classes, beginning with the *kṣatriya*, was Brahman alone, undivided, being one only; there was no distinction of *kṣatriya* and so forth. That single Brahman, being devoid of protectors such as the *kṣatriya* and others, did not flourish (*na vyabhavat*); the meaning is that it was not capable of manifesting for the sake of action.

Then that Brahman—desiring to perform action motivated by the caste of the Brāhmaṇa, thinking "I am a Brāhmaṇa; thus must I act"—for the sake of manifesting the agency of the Self in action, created, indeed created preeminently, that which is of the nature of *śreyaḥ*, the auspicious form. But what was it that was created? It was the *kṣatra*, the Kṣatriya caste. He demonstrates this through its individual manifestations: those well-known in the world as the *kṣattrāṇi* among the gods (*devatrā*)—in the alternative view where the term denotes a genus.

The plural number is used either because of the traditional teaching of the plural form (*bahuvacana-smaraṇāt*) or due to the figurative attribution of plurality based on the multiplicity of individual instances (*vyakti-bahutvāt*). To the question "Which are these?", he says: therein, those who have been consecrated (*abhiṣikta*) are specifically pointed out—Indra is the king of the gods, Varuṇa of the aquatic creatures, Soma of the Brāhmaṇas, Rudra of animals, Parjanya of lightning and so forth, Yama of the ancestors, Mṛtyu of diseases and so forth, Īśāna of lights; such are the *kṣatra* (ruling powers) among the gods.

Following that, it should be understood that the human *kṣatriyas*—those belonging to the lunar and solar lineages, beginning with Purūravas—who are presided over by deities such as Indra and others, were indeed created. For it was for this very purpose that the creation of the divine *kṣatriyas* was introduced. Since the *kṣatra* was created by Brahmā as something preeminent, there is nothing higher than that *kṣatra*, even for the Brahmin caste, as its controller.

Therefore, although the Brāhmaṇa is the cause, he remains below the Kṣatriya and attends upon him who stands above—where? At the Rājasūya sacrifice. Therein, he bestows—that is, establishes—the Kṣatriya’s own glory, which consists of renown, as "Brahman. When the king, consecrated by the Rājasūya and seated upon the throne, addresses the officiating priest as "O Brahman," the priest replies to him: "O King, you are Brahman."

This is what is being stated: "He places that glory in the Kṣatriya alone. This very Brahman is the source (*yoni*) of the Kṣatriya under discussion. Therefore, even though the king attains—that is, reaches—the state of supremacy, which is the specific quality of the Rājasūya consecration, he nonetheless, at the end—that is, at the conclusion of the ritual—rests upon, takes refuge in, the Brahman, that is, the Brāhmaṇa caste; he places his own source before him, meaning he appoints a domestic priest (*purohita*).

But he who, out of pride in his power, harms—that is, injures by looking down upon—his own source, namely the Brāhmaṇa caste or a Brāhmaṇa, he reaches his own very source; he cuts off and destroys his own progeny. Having done this, he becomes more sinful, even more wicked than before; for although the Kṣatriya was already sinful due to his cruelty, he becomes even more so by injuring his own offspring.
Just as in the world one becomes more wicked after harming and insulting someone superior and more praiseworthy, so it is here.

Even after the *kṣatra* (the ruling class) was created, he did not prosper; nor did the *brahman* (the priestly class) thus prosper for the sake of ritual action, because there was no one to acquire wealth. He created the *viś* (the commoner class) for the acquisition of wealth, which is the means for performing rituals. But who is this *viś*? It refers to those classes born of the gods—the suffix *niṣṭhā* is used here in its own sense—meaning these various divisions of the divine race; they are called by their names in groups, for the *viś* are generally composed of groups.

Generally, those who are joined together are capable of acquiring wealth, not those who are alone—such as the Vasus, a group of eight; likewise the eleven Rudras; the twelve Ādityas; the Viśvedevas, thirteen being the offspring of Viśvā; or all the gods; and the Maruts, seven groups of seven. (13) Because he lacked attendants, he again did not prosper. He created the Śaudra caste—the Śūdra himself is the Śaudra; the suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense, resulting in the lengthening of the vowel. But who is this Śaudra caste that was created? Pūṣan—Pūṣan is so called because he nourishes (*puṣyati*). But who is this Pūṣan? He specifies him by way of distinction: "This earth is Pūṣan. He provides the etymological derivation himself: for this [earth] nourishes all this, whatever exists here.

Mantra — Chapter (14) ---

Even after creating the four social orders (*varṇas*), he did not find stability because of the ferocity of the ruling power (*kṣatra*) and the resulting fear of its lack of restraint. Therefore, he created that which is a superior form—what is it? Dharma. This very thing created as a superior form is the "ruler of the ruler" (*kṣatrasya kṣatram*), the controller even of the ruling power, more fierce than the fierce—that is, Dharma. Because it is the controller even of the ruling power, there is nothing higher than Dharma; for by it all things are restrained.

How is this so? It is said: Furthermore, even one who is weaker, more feeble, may hope for and desire to conquer by means of the power of *dharma* even one stronger than himself, more powerful than himself—just as in the world a householder [may do so] against a king who is the most powerful of all. Therefore, it is established that because *dharma* is more powerful than everything, it is the controller of all. That which is indeed *dharma*, characterized by legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) and being transacted by people in the world—that is truly *satya*.

"Truth" (*satya*) means being in accordance with the meaning of the scriptures; that very same thing, when being practiced, becomes what is called "dharma," while when it is known as the meaning of the scriptures, it is "truth. Because this is so, they say at the time of legal proceedings to one who speaks according to the scriptures: "Speak the truth."

Those standing nearby, who understand both [types of conduct], say of one who speaks "dharma" that he is speaking a well-known worldly principle (*nyāya*); likewise, conversely, they say of one who speaks what is contrary to dharma or worldly convention that he is speaking the truth, or that he is speaking in accordance with the scriptures (*śāstra*). Thus, that which is both known and practiced becomes dharma itself. Therefore, that dharma—characterized by knowledge and practice—governs all others, including those known through the scriptures.

Therefore, there is no ruling power even for the Kṣatriya. Consequently, the ignorant person, out of self-identification with that [body], conceives of distinctions based on Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra for the purpose of performing their specific duties; and these [distinctions] are by their very nature the causes for eligibility to perform ritual actions.
[End of Chapter 1, Section 4, Mantra 15]

(15) This fourfold order was created—the Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra; this is a summary for the sake of what follows. That which is the creating Brahman became, among the gods, the Brahman—that is, the Brāhmaṇa caste—by means of Agni alone and not by any other form; it became the Brāhmaṇa among men in the very form of a Brāhmaṇa.

In the other castes, having undergone a transformation, [the Brahmin] became a Kṣatriya through the Kṣatriya—presided over by deities such as Indra—a Vaiśya through the Vaiśya, and a Śūdra through the Śūdra. Since the Brahmin alone remains untransformed in the fire as the creative Brahman, whereas in the Kṣatriya and others there has been a modification, therefore they desire the world—the fruit of action—among the gods, specifically in the fire; the meaning is that they do so by performing actions connected with the fire.

For that very purpose, that Brahman exists in the form of fire as the locus for ritual action; therefore, it is logical that by performing action in that fire, they seek its fruit. Regarding the Brāhmaṇa among humans—among men, moreover, when there is a desire for the fruits of action, there is no requirement for activities based on fire and so forth; rather, the fulfillment of the human goal is achieved simply by obtaining the essential nature of one's own birth.

But where the accomplishment of the human goal depends upon the gods, there indeed is a requirement for rituals connected with fire and the like. And from Smṛti: "A Brāhmaṇa shall attain perfection through recitation alone; of this there is no doubt. Whether he performs other rites or not, he who is friendly is called a Brāhmaṇa. This is also evident from the observation of the life of wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya). Therefore, it is among humans who possess the status of a Brāhmaṇa that people desire the world as the fruit of action. For it was through these two—the Brāhmaṇa and Agni, which constitute the agent and the locus of action—that Brahman, as the Creator, directly manifested itself.

However, some maintain that here one desires the world of the Supreme Self (paramātman) in the fire and in the Brāhmaṇa. That is incorrect, because the division of social classes (varṇa) has been introduced for the purpose of establishing the qualification for ritual action within the context of ignorance (avidyā), and because of the subsequent qualification; for if the Supreme Self alone were meant by the word "world" (loka) here, the subsequent qualification—"not having seen his own world"—would be redundant.

If the "world" under discussion—which is being sought because it is dependent on fire—is one distinct from one's own world, then the qualification "one's own" (*sva*) is appropriate, as its purpose is to exclude the previously mentioned other-world. Furthermore, the world of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is never subject to the deviation of "belonging to oneself," whereas worlds produced by ignorance are subject to such deviation; indeed, the text declares the deviation of worlds created by karma with the words, "it surely perishes."

The castes were created by Brahmā for the sake of action (*karman*); and that action, known as *dharma*, governs all [castes] as something to be performed and is the means for accomplishing the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Therefore, if their own world—the Supreme Self—is attained even without being known through action, why is that very [Self] made the object to be reached? To this he says: "Now" (*atha*), which serves to set aside the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Whoever, indeed, from this worldly state characterized by the assumption of a physical body—which has ignorance, desire, and action as its causes—whether due to the conceit of performing rituals dependent on the sacrificial fires or the conceit of performing the duties of the Brāhmaṇa caste alone, departs—that is, dies—without having seen his own world called the Self as the Self, because it is non-deviating [from him], thinking "I am Brahman."

Although that [Self] is one's own world, it does not benefit—meaning it does not protect—one who is unaware of it because it is veiled by ignorance, appearing as if it were not one's own; just as in the world, the Veda, if not recited—that is, not studied—does not benefit by making known the rituals and other matters; or just as any other worldly activity such as agriculture, if not performed—that is, not manifested by oneself—does not benefit by bestowing its own fruit, so too is the Self one's own.

The world, not manifested by its own eternal nature of the Self, is indeed not enjoyed [by one] as long as ignorance and the like have not been abandoned. Now, one might ask: "What is the use of protecting [the means] for the sake of seeing one's own world? Since the attainment of the fruit of action is certain, and since actions that serve as the cause for desired fruits are numerous, the protection for their sake will be inexhaustible. This is not so; because that which has been performed is subject to exhaustion, he says this: "In this very cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), even some great-souled person who, like a marvel, does not know thus his own world..."

According to the aforementioned method, an ignorant person performs great and abundant meritorious acts such as the Aśvamedha sacrifice, which yield desired fruits, doing so continuously with the thought, "By this alone my [merit] will become infinite. Yet, for that ignorant person, that action is indeed exhausted in the end—that is, at the conclusion of the enjoyment of its fruit—because it is caused by ignorance and desire born of ignorance, like the illusory manifestation produced in a dream-vision. This is established because, due to the instability of its causes, namely ignorance and desire, there is the certainty of destruction once they have been spent.

Therefore, there is indeed no hope for the preservation of the fruits of meritorious deeds. Hence, one should meditate upon the Self alone as one's own world—"the Self" being used in the sense of "one's own world," because "one's own world" is the subject under discussion and the word "own" (*sva*) is not explicitly used here. As for him who meditates upon the Self alone as his world—what happens to him? It is said: "His work (*karman*) does not perish. This is a restatement of a constant truth, since there is simply an absence of further work to be done.

The meaning is that the suffering of saṃsāra, characterized by the exhaustion of karma, exists continuously for the ignorant, but it does not exist for him in that same way—just as it is said: "Even when Mithilā is ablaze, nothing of mine is burning."

Others describe that for the wise man who meditates on his own self as the world (*svātmaloka*), action itself does not perish due to its connection with knowledge (*vidyā*). They indeed postulate two kinds of meanings for the word "world" (*loka*) as inherent in action: one is the world called Hiraṇyagarbha, which exists in the state of manifestation and is the substratum of action. For him who meditates on that manifested, limited world which is inherent in action—for that one who perceives the self as consisting of limited action—action indeed perishes.

If one were to meditate upon that very world—which is inherent in action—in its unmanifest state as the causal form, then because such a person perceives the Self as consisting of unlimited action, their karma would not perish. This is indeed a plausible conception, yet it is not supported by scripture (*śrautī*), because the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) under discussion is denoted by the word "one's own world" (*svaloka*). Having introduced the subject with "one's own world" (*svaṃ lokam*), the text subsequently discards the word "own" (*sva*) and substitutes the word "Self" (*ātman*) to refer back to that same entity: "One should meditate upon the Self alone as the world" (*ātmānam eva lokam upāsīta*).

In that context, there is simply no occasion for the conceptualization of a world as being inherent in action (*karma-samavāyin*). Furthermore, because it is qualified by the opponent’s [view] which refers exclusively to the sphere of knowledge—namely, "What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self is this world?"—it distinguishes this world from those worlds produced by sons, ritual acts, and lower knowledge, stating, "This Self is our world," and, "His world is not measured by any action whatsoever; this is his supreme world."

It is appropriate that these [qualities] with their qualifiers form a single syntactical unit with this [text], because here too we see the qualifier "his own world" (*svaṃ lokam*). If it is argued that the phrase "from him he creates whatever he desires" is improper—given that it is established here that "his own world" is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and that through meditation upon Him one becomes that very Self—it would be improper to speak of a fruit other than the attainment of that Self, such as "whatever he desires, he creates from this Self"—we say no. This is because the passage is intended as a praise of the meditation on one's own world.

The meaning is that everything desired is accomplished from this very world itself; nothing else need be prayed for as a gift, because his desires are already fulfilled—just as in another scriptural passage, "From the Self comes breath, from the Self comes hope," and so forth. Or, as before, this is intended to demonstrate the state of being the Self of all. For if he indeed becomes the Supreme Self, then the use of the word "Self" in the phrase "from this very Self" is appropriate; its meaning is "from this very world that is the Self under discussion."

Otherwise, he would have stated "from the world of karma" with a qualification—specifying it as being in its unmanifest state—in order to exclude the world of the Supreme Self under discussion and to exclude its manifest state; for when this [world] has been qualified in this way, it is not possible to understand an intermediate state that has not been heard.

Now, this indeed is the Self. It has been stated that here, the ignorant person—possessing the conceit of caste, stage of life (*āśrama*), and so forth—is constrained by *dharma* and, being subject to the performance of duties toward the gods and others, is dependent like a beast. But what are those duties, by the performance of which he becomes dependent like a beast? And who are those gods and others to whom he renders service like a beast through his actions? Both of these points are now elaborated upon. [Mantra 16] Chapter 1, Section 4. Mantra 16. Commentary. Home > Commentaries > Upanishads > Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad > Chapter 1 > Section 4 > Mantra 16. (16) Now, the word *atha* is used here for the purpose of introducing the statement. This very person under discussion—the householder authorized to perform ritual action (*karma*), the ignorant one characterized by the aggregate of body, senses, and so forth, who is called the "body-self" (*piṇḍātman*)—is the world, that is to say, the object of experience (*bhogya*), and the self of all beings from the gods down to the ants; this is because he is benefited by the actions prescribed for all the social classes (*varṇas*) and stages of life (*āśramas*).

By which specific actions, while benefiting which specific beings, does one obtain the world [of those beings]? This is explained as follows: When that householder offers oblations (*juhoti*) and performs sacrifices (*yajate*)—sacrifice being the renunciation of ownership directed toward a deity, and that same act with the addition of pouring liquid being an oblation (*homa*)—by means of that action characterized as oblation and sacrifice, which must necessarily be performed, his world is secured for the gods, who are dependent upon him like cattle. Furthermore, when he recites the *anuvāka* and studies the *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) day after day, by that [action] he secures the world of the *ṛṣis*.

Now, as for that which he offers to the ancestors—namely, the funeral cakes, water, and so forth—and that for which he desires offspring, making an effort for the sake of progeny (the word "desire" being intended to indicate actual production)—that is to say, he procreates offspring—by means of that rite, which is an obligatory duty, [he attains] the world of the ancestors.

The world is dependent on others as an object of enjoyment. Now, when one causes humans to dwell in one's house by providing land, water, and so forth, and when one gives food to those who are there, whether they are staying or passing through and are in need, by that act it belongs to humans. Furthermore, when one provides grass and water for animals, by that act it belongs to animals. And whatever beasts of prey, birds, and even ants, along with them, subsist upon the crumbs, offerings, and the washing-water in one's houses, by that act it belongs to them.

Since he benefits the gods and others by performing these actions, therefore, just as in the world one would desire security—that is, non-destruction and the non-falling away from one's own state—for one's own world, namely for one's own body, and would protect it on all sides through nourishment, guarding, and so forth, out of fear of falling away from that state of ownership; so too [should one act].

Thus, for one who knows this—who has conceived of himself in this manner, thinking, "I am the object of enjoyment for all beings; in this way, I must necessarily repay them like a debtor"—all beings, beginning with the gods as previously mentioned, desire his non-injury (ariṣṭim), that is, his non-destruction, and they protect him on all sides so that his ownership [of them] does not lapse, just as householders protect their cattle. Therefore, it was said: "Therefore, that is not dear to them."

This very point—that the aforementioned rites must necessarily be performed like a debt—is known from the section on the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), and has been examined and deliberated upon as a duty in the section on the sacrificial portions (*avadāna*).

[The text states: "In the beginning, this was only the Self. If one knows Brahman, one is liberated from that state of being a sacrificial animal, which consists of the bondage of duty. [One might ask: By whom is he impelled to proceed as if involuntarily within the jurisdiction of the bondage of ritual action, rather than entering the jurisdiction of knowledge (*vidyā*), which is the means for liberation from it? Now, it has already been stated that "the gods protect [him]."

"Certainly—those [entities] protect only those who have ascended to their own respective spheres of authority within the domain of *karma*; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the acquisition of what was not earned (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and the loss of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*). But they do not protect a mere person in general who has not ascended to a specific qualification (*adhikāra*); therefore, that [cause] must exist by which one, being impelled and truly helpless, becomes turned outward from one's own world. [Objection: "But surely it is through ignorance (*avidyā*); the ignorant person here becomes turned outward and engages [in action]. [Reply: Even that is not the actual motivator (*pravartikā*); for its nature consists in the veiling of the true essence of reality (*vastusvarūpa*)."

But it is established that [desire] is the seed of activity, being the cause for engaging in activity such as falling into a pit, just like blindness [is the cause for such a fall]. Well then, let this be stated: what is that which is the cause of activity? To this it is replied here: desire (*eṣaṇā*) is that [cause]; for the *Kaṭhaka-śruti* says, "The ignorant, abiding in innate ignorance, pursue outward desires," and in the *Smṛti*: "This is desire, this is anger," and so forth, and in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "All activity has desire alone as its cause.
This very subject shall be demonstrated here in detail until the end of the chapter.

Section. Mantra. Chapter (17). ---

In the beginning, this was the Self alone. The Self alone—natural, ignorant, characterized by the aggregate of causes and effects, and designated as "Self" prior to the union with a wife—is what is meant here. Therefore, there existed nothing separate from that Self in the form of desired distinctions such as wife and so forth. He alone was one—he alone existed, possessing the ignorance that serves as the seed for the desire for a wife and the rest.

Perfumed by the latent impressions of ignorance (*avidyāvāsanā*), which consist in the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) upon his own self of the nature of agents, actions, and fruits—characterized by its inherent [duality]—he "desired" (*akāmayata*), that is, he willed. How so? "May there be a wife for me," he thought—a wife being the cause for eligibility (*adhikāra*) to perform ritual action (*karman*); for without her, I would be ineligible for ritual action. Therefore, let there be a wife for the sake of attaining eligibility for ritual action. "And may I be procreated"—that is, may I myself be born in the form of offspring. "And may I have wealth"—wealth characterized by cattle and other such means for performing ritual action.

Now, I shall perform the action that is the means for attaining worldly prosperity and the supreme good—by which, having become free from debt, I may attain the worlds of the gods and others; that action I shall perform.

And "desires" (*kāmyāni*) refers to the means for attaining sons, wealth, heaven, and so forth. The meaning is that desire is limited to this much; that is to say, the object of desire is precisely this much: namely, the three worlds—the world of men, the world of the fathers, and the world of the gods—which are the results of this "seeking of means" (*sādhanaiṣaṇā*) consisting of wife, son, wealth, and ritual action. For the seeking of means, characterized by wife, son, wealth, and ritual action, exists solely for the sake of those [worlds].

Therefore, that which is the desire for worldly objects (*loka-eṣaṇā*) is itself the one and only desire. Although it is a single desire, it is twofold because it depends upon means for its accomplishment. Hence, [the text] will later determine: "For both of these are indeed desires. Since every undertaking has the attainment of results as its purpose, the desire for worldly objects is already implied and thus stated—this is restricted by the words, "Desire is only this much. Just as when food is mentioned, satiety need not be mentioned separately, because satiety is for the sake of that food.

These two pursuits, characterized as the goal and the means, constitute desire (*kāma*). Impelled by this, the ignorant man, being utterly helpless like a silkworm, envelops himself—directing his very self toward the path of action, becoming outward-turned, he does not recognize his own world. Thus it is said in the *Taittirīyaka*: "Like one deluded by fire, exhausted by smoke, he does not recognize his own world. But how can the extent of desires be determined as being merely this much, given their infinity?

"Desires are indeed infinite"—anticipating this doubt, he states the reason: "Because even though one desires (*na-icchan-cana*), that is, even if one were to desire, one would not find (*na vindet*), nor obtain, anything further (*bhūyaḥ*) or more than this [world] characterized as the means to the fruits [of action]. For in the world there exists nothing to be obtained—whether seen or unseen—that is distinct from the means to the fruits; since desire has as its object only that which is to be obtained, and since no such thing exists apart from this [world], it is correct to say: 'Desire is indeed of this extent.'"

This is what is meant: desire is the twofold pursuit characterized by the means and ends of action, whether for visible or invisible results, which pertains to the domain of persons under the influence of ignorance; therefore, one who knows this must renounce it. For in this way, the ignorant person who desires the non-Self pursued such desires in the past, and so did those even further back; such is the nature of worldly existence.

And such was the creation of Prajāpati: he was afraid because of his ignorance; then, impelled by desire, being alone and finding no pleasure, he desired a wife for the sake of removing that lack of pleasure; he united with her, and from that this creation came into being—so it has been said. Therefore, regarding that creation, even now at this present time, being alone before the performance of marriage, one desires: "May I have a wife, then may I procreate, then may I possess wealth, then may I perform ritual acts"—this sentence expresses the aforementioned meaning.

He—desiring thus and seeking to acquire a wife and the rest—so long as he does not obtain even one of these aforementioned things, namely the wife and so forth, considers himself "incomplete" or "imperfect"; only when, by process of elimination, he acquires all of them together does he attain completeness.

But when one is unable to achieve completeness, then, for the sake of achieving that completeness for such a person who conceives of incompleteness, it is said: "This very completeness comes about for him. How so? This aggregate of the body and the organs is analyzed.

In this context, because all other groups of effects and instruments follow the mind, the mind—due to its preeminence—is designated as the "Self," just as the master of a household is the "Self" for his wife and so forth, since the fourfold group beginning with the wife conforms to him. Likewise here, the mind is conceived as the Self for the sake of achieving completeness. Similarly, speech is the wife, due to the commonality of following after the mind.

Speech (*vāk*)—meaning sound characterized by injunctions and the like—is grasped, determined, and employed by the mind through the door of the ear; thus, speech is like a wife born of the mind. And from those two, speech and mind, which stand in the relation of wife and husband, *prāṇa* is produced for the sake of action; thus, *prāṇa* is like offspring. In that regard, action characterized by the movement of *prāṇa* and so forth is accomplished by means of sight and wealth; therefore, sight is human wealth. That wealth is of two kinds: the human and the other.

Therefore, he specifies "human" in order to exclude other forms of wealth. For cattle and the like are human wealth, perceivable by the eye, and serve as means for ritual action (*karma*); thus, the eye stands in their place, and because of that connection, the eye is human wealth. For by means of the eye, one finds—that is, perceives—this human wealth, such as cattle and so forth. What, then, is the other wealth? The ear is divine wealth; because cognition has the gods as its object, cognition is divine wealth.

In this context, the ear alone is the object of attainment. Why? Because by means of the ear one hears that divine wealth, which is knowledge (*vijñāna*); therefore, since knowledge is dependent upon the ear, the ear itself is that [wealth]. But what is the ritual action (*karman*) to be accomplished here by these [elements] beginning with the self and ending with wealth? It is said: "The self alone. Here, "self" refers to the body. How, then, is the self the locus of the ritual action? Because it is the cause of the ritual action.

How is it that action has its cause in this? For one performs action with the self through the body. Since he previously possessed the conceit of incompleteness, this completeness is now achieved for him—just as [completeness] exists in external things characterized by wife and so forth. Therefore, this very sacrifice is *pāṅkta*, accomplished by means of five; it is a *pāṅkta* sacrifice accomplished merely through vision, even for one who does not perform ritual actions.

But how, by the mere attainment of fivefoldness (*pañcatva*), does this [sacrifice] possess the nature of a sacrifice (*yajña*)? It is said: because even an external sacrifice is accomplished by means of animals (*paśu*) and persons (*puruṣa*), and both that animal and that person are indeed fivefold (*pāṅkta*), owing to their connection with the fivefold set beginning with the mind (*manas*), as has been stated. Thus it says: "The animal, such as the cow and so forth, is fivefold; the person is fivefold. Although he is an animal, the person is distinguished by his being the one authorized [for the rite]; hence the separate mention of the "person."

What need is there for much? All this—whatever this is, whatsoever exists—is fivefold, consisting of both the means of action and the fruit. He who thus accomplishes the sacrifice as the fivefold Self attains all this world as his own Self—he who knows thus.
Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa of the first chapter.

Section: Mantra Chapter Now, that which is the *udgītha* is the *praṇava*; that which is the *praṇava* is the *udgītha*. This sun, indeed, is the *udgītha*, and this is the *praṇava*; for as "Om," he goes forth sounding.

Regarding the passage beginning with "The seven kinds of food [he creates] by means of intelligence," ignorance has been introduced there. In that state, the ignorant person worships another deity, thinking, "He is one and I am another. Such a person, identifying with the caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), being bound by the sense of duty regarding ritual actions, performs sacrifices and other rites impelled by desire, thereby benefiting the gods and so forth. It has thus been stated that he belongs to the world of all beings.

And just as this world was created by each and every being through its own respective actions as an object of enjoyment, so too did he create all beings and the entire universe as objects of his own enjoyment through the fivefold rites such as the *homa* sacrifice; thus, according to the nature of their own actions and knowledge, each individual is both the enjoyer and the enjoyed of the entire universe, and every one is both the agent and the effect of everything—this is the meaning.
