And we shall explain this very point in the section on knowledge (*vidyā-prakaraṇa*) regarding the Madhu-vidyā: "Everything is honey for everyone" is for the purpose of realizing the unity of the Self. That world which he created as food for himself through the fivefold ritual action involving the *juhoti* oblation and other rites performed with desire, and through knowledge—that entire world, when divided sevenfold according to the relationship of cause and effect, is called the "seven foods" because they are objects of enjoyment. Therefore, he is the father of those foods.
These mantras are like threads (*sūtra-bhūta*) for these foods along with their applications, because they reveal them in brief.
"I approached that very one; therefore, you are my only son," so said Kauṣītaki to his son. "Worship the rays; then many sons indeed will be yours. This is with regard to the deities. (2)

(2) Regarding the phrase "the seven kinds of food"—the words "that which he generated" (*yad ajanayat*) function as an adverbial modifier. [The generation was] "by means of *medhā*, *prajñā*, *vijñāna*, and *tapas*. For it is knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*karman*) alone that are denoted by the terms *medhā* and *tapas*, because these two are the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*). It does not refer to other forms of intelligence or austerity, as those are not the subject here. Action consisting of five factors has its means in the wife and so forth; furthermore, immediately following [this], knowledge is the subject under discussion in the words, "He who knows thus. Therefore, one should not entertain the suspicion that the terms refer to the commonly known [external] intelligence and austerity.

Therefore, the completion of the sentence is: "We shall now explain those seven kinds of food which the Father produced through knowledge and action. In this context, because the meaning of the *mantras* is generally difficult to understand due to its being obscured, the *brāhmaṇa* proceeds to provide an exposition of that meaning. Regarding the question, "What is the meaning of the statement: 'The Father produced seven kinds of food by means of wisdom and austerity'?", it is said in reply: He explains it by the very word *hi*, which indicates a well-known fact.

The meaning of this mantra is indeed well-known; for by the mantra "that which he generated," its status as having a well-known meaning is revealed through the form of a restatement (anuvāda). Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa says without any hesitation: "For with wisdom and austerity, the Father generated [him]."

Now, one might ask: "How is this meaning well-known? It is said in reply: First of all, the fatherhood of those things beginning with the wife and ending with ritual action—which are the means for achieving worldly results—is indeed directly perceived. And this has been stated [in the scripture] with the words, "May I have a wife," and so forth. Furthermore, it has been stated there that divine wealth, knowledge, ritual action, and a son are the means for the creation of the worlds that constitute the fruits; and what is about to be described is likewise well-known. Therefore, it is appropriate to say, "by means of intelligence," and so on.

For *eṣaṇā* (the desire for acquisition) is well known in the world as having results as its object; and it has been stated that "desire consists of [the wish for] a wife and so forth" by the passage, "So great indeed is desire. Furthermore, in the sphere of the knowledge of Brahman, since all is one, desire is impossible. By this, it is shown that the creation of the world through natural, non-scriptural wisdom and austerity is indeed [excluded]; for everything up to the stationary state is caused by karma and [false] cognition, which result in undesirable fruits.

However, what is intended here is precisely the relationship of means and end as established by the scriptures; for, with the desire to impart knowledge of Brahman, detachment from that [world] is what is intended—since this entire cycle of transmigratory existence, characterized by the manifest and the unmanifest, is impure, impermanent, consisting of means and ends, painful, and the domain of ignorance, knowledge of Brahman must be undertaken by one who is detached from it.

In this regard, the application of foods through their classification is stated: "One [part] of his is common" is a word of the mantra; its explanation is: "This very thing is his common food," as it has been said—referring to the community of eaters. What is that? That which is eaten and consumed day after day by all living beings—that common food was fashioned for the sake of all eaters by the Father after creating it.

He who meditates upon this food, which is common to all living beings, which sustains them, and which is being consumed—this means he becomes intent upon that. For in the world, "meditation" (upāsana) is observed to mean "devotion," as in such expressions as "he attends upon his teacher" or "he attends upon the king. Therefore, the meaning is that he is primarily devoted to the enjoyment of food for the sake of maintaining the body, and not primarily devoted to actions whose purpose is the unseen (adṛṣṭa); such a person does not turn away from evil, that is, from unrighteousness—he is not liberated from it.

And thus says the Vedic mantra: "In vain does he obtain food," and so forth; and there is also the Smṛti: "One should not cook food for oneself alone," "He who eats without giving to these [others] is indeed a thief," and "The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the eater of the food," and so on.

Why, then, does one not turn away from evil? For this [food] is mixed—it belongs to all, being undivided among those beings who consume it. Precisely because it is for the consumption of all, even a morsel that, when placed in the mouth, is seen to cause pain to another, is such that everyone has their hope fixed upon it, thinking, "May this be mine. Therefore, it is impossible to swallow it without causing pain to others. This is also supported by traditional texts (smṛti) such as: "For the misdeeds of men... and so forth.

Some maintain that the food called *vaiśvadeva* is that which is set aside day after day by a householder. That is not correct. It is not evident that the food known as *vaiśvadeva* is common to all eaters in the same way that the food being eaten by all living beings is common to them; nor is there a scriptural statement favorable to that view, such as "that which is eaten here."

Furthermore, because the food called *vaiśvadeva* is included within the food consumed by all living beings, it is appropriate that the food eaten by dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and others is also grasped; for we observe food eaten by dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and others even apart from the *vaiśvadeva* offering. In that case, the statement "that which is eaten here" is appropriate. For if that were not grasped, it would follow that the food was not created by the Father nor assigned [for consumption] by him, due to the word "common" (*sādhāraṇa*). Yet, it is indeed intended that the entire class of food was created by Him and assigned by Him.

Furthermore, for one performing the rite called Vaiśvadeva as prescribed by the scriptures, it is not logical that there should be no cessation of evil; nor is there any prohibition against it. Nor is this act inherently loathsome like the work of a fisherman or the like, because it is carried out by the learned (śiṣṭas) and because a transgression is heard to occur from its non-performance. This is not the case with other acts, as indicated by the mantra-verse: "I am the food; I eat the eater of food."

"Two he assigned to the gods"—this is the mantra phrase. Regarding the two foods which, having been created, he assigned to the gods: what are those two? It is said: the *huta* and the *prahuta*. *Huta* is the offering into the fire; *prahuta* is the offering of the *bali* after having performed the *homa*.

Since the Father assigned these two kinds of food—the *huta* and the *prahuta*—to the gods, therefore even now householders offer oblations at the proper time to the gods; they offer them thinking, "This food is being given by us to the gods," and they offer secondary oblations (*prajuhati*), which means that after making the primary offering, they perform the ritual distribution of portions (*baliharaṇa*). Now, others say: the two foods assigned by the Father to the gods were not the *huta* and the *prahuta*, but rather the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsau*).

The first position is that [the two refer to] *huta* and *prahuta*, because there is no distinction in the mention of "two" and because they are extremely well-known. Although duality is possible for *huta* and *prahuta*, nevertheless, it is more widely established that the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices themselves—being mentioned in the Veda—are the food of the gods, since they are revealed by the mantras; furthermore, when both a subordinate and a principal element are present, the principal is understood first; and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices possess primacy in comparison to *huta* and *prahuta*.

Therefore, it is logical that only those two [the new and full moon sacrifices] are mentioned: "He assigned two to the gods. Since these two foods called the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* were prepared by the father for the sake of the gods, one should not be a "frequent performer of *iṣṭis*"—meaning one whose habit is to perform *iṣṭis*—in order to avoid obstructing their purpose for the gods. By the word *iṣṭi*, it is said, optional (*kāmyā*) sacrifices are meant; this is a well-known usage in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*. Because of the use of the suffix denoting habit (*tācchīlya*), the meaning is that one should not be primarily devoted to performing optional sacrifices.

"He gave one to the animals"—as for that food which the father gave to the animals, what indeed was it? It was milk. How, then, is it understood that animals are the owners of this food? To this he says: "For, first of all—at the very beginning—both humans and animals subsist upon milk alone. For that food is appropriate for them; otherwise, how could they subsist upon that alone as a rule at the outset?

How is it said that even today people subsist on that very same [food] at the beginning? Because both humans and animals subsist on that very food even now, just as the application was made by the Father in the beginning; therefore, when a boy or child is born, members of the three higher castes cause him to lick or consume clarified butter mixed with gold during the *jātakarman* rite; or they cause him to suckle the breast, or subsequently feed him other things as appropriate.

To others than humans, they first cause the breast to be sucked by the animals. Then, when asked regarding a newborn calf, "How large is the calf?", they reply, "He is a non-grazer" (*atṛṇāda*), meaning that he does not yet eat grass; the sense is that he is so very young that he still subsists on milk alone. Furthermore, whether they subsist on clarified butter (*ghṛta*) during the birth-rite and other ceremonies, or on milk alone as others do, in every case they subsist on milk alone; for even clarified butter, being a modification of milk, is indeed milk.

But why is the seventh "being," which is the food of cattle, explained as the fourth? Because it is a means for action (*karman*). For action—such as the *agnihotra* and others—is dependent upon milk as its means; and that action, being a means, is to be accomplished by wealth (*vitta*) for the sake of the "food to be accomplished" (the fifth) which is about to be mentioned, just as the previously mentioned *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are for the sake of the two kinds of food. Therefore, because it belongs to the category of action, it is taught together with action as a single unit. Furthermore, since there is no difference in their status as means and they are connected in purpose, mere immediate succession is not the reason [for their grouping].

And because of the ease of understanding in the exposition: for foods can indeed be explained continuously and easily, and once explained, they are easily comprehended. As for the meaning of the statement, "In that everything is established—whatever breathes and whatever does not," it is said: in that food, which is the animal and the milk, the entire universe characterized by the internal (adhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), and the celestial (adhidaiva) is established—namely, whatever breathes, possessing vital activity, and whatever does not, such as the stationary mountains and so forth.

For this has already been explained by the word *hi* itself, which indicates what is well-known. How is it that the substance of milk (*payodravya*) is the support of all things? Because its status as a cause is established; and its being a cause consists in its being inherent in rituals such as the *agnihotra*. Furthermore, there are hundreds of scriptural and traditional statements establishing that the entire world consists of the transformation of the oblations of the *agnihotra* and other rites. Therefore, the explanation by means of the word *hi* is entirely appropriate.

Regarding this, it is said in other Brāhmaṇas: "One who offers oblations of milk for a year overcomes repeated death. For it is said that in a year there are three hundred and sixty oblations, plus seven hundred and twenty, which, when they become the *yājuṣmatī* bricks, correspond to the days and nights of the year; thus, they attain the year, Agni, and Prajāpati.

"By performing it in this manner and offering oblations for a year, one overcomes recurrent death—the meaning being that having departed from here and been reborn among the gods, one does not die again—so say the declarations of the Brāhmaṇas. One should not know it thus; it should not be viewed in that way. On the very day one offers the oblation, on that very day one overcomes recurrent death; it does not depend upon a practice continued for a year."

Knowing thus—that which was said, namely, that "all this is established in milk because everything consists of the transformation of the milk-oblation"—one attains the state of being the Self of the universe in a single day. This is expressed as follows: he "overcomes repeated death," meaning repeated dying; having died once, the knower, being separated from the body, becomes the Self of all and does not again take up a limited body for the sake of dying. This is the meaning.

What, then, is the reason that one overcomes death by attaining all selves? It is said: because he offers all—that is, everything—consisting of food and the like, as sacrificial oblations in the evening and morning, to all the gods. This is appropriate: having made himself an ātman consisting of all oblations, having attained a state of identity with all the gods by way of being the food of all the gods, and having become composed of all the gods, he does not die again.

Furthermore, this has also been stated by the Brāhmaṇa: "Brahman, the Self-existent, performed austerity. He reflected: 'Indeed, there is no infinity in austerity; come now, let me offer myself as a sacrifice in all beings, and all beings in myself. Having offered himself as a sacrifice in all beings and all beings in himself, he attained preeminence, sovereignty, and lordship over all beings."

"Why are they not exhausted, even though they are being consumed at all times? Since the father, having created the foods, bestowed them separately upon the seven distinct eaters from that very moment onward, they have been consumed by those eaters "always," that is, continuously—since their continued existence is dependent upon them—and because it is logical that what is produced must eventually perish, their exhaustion would be expected; yet they are not exhausted, as we observe the world persisting with its form entirely unimpaired; therefore, there must be a cause for their inexhaustibility.

Therefore, the question is asked: "Why, then, do they not perish? The answer to this is: "The person (*puruṣa*) is indeed imperishable. Just as he was formerly the creator of foods, the father, and the enjoyer through wisdom (*medhā*) and the fivefold ritual (*pāṅkta-karman*) connected with wife and so forth, so too those to whom the foods were given, while being the enjoyers of those foods, are also fathers—since they generate those very foods through wisdom and austerity (*tapas*).

This is now explained: the person who is indeed the eater of foods is the imperishable, the cause of non-destruction. How is it that he possesses this quality of imperishability? It is said: for he, by means of each successive act of intelligence—that is, the specific wisdom arising at each respective time—and by means of actions consisting of the activities of speech, mind, and body, repeatedly and ever again produces and brings forth this sevenfold aggregate characterized by the body and its instruments, which consists of the fruits of action.

If one were not to perform even for a moment this sevenfold food that has been described—both through wisdom and through ritual actions—it would be cut off; because it is being consumed, it would indeed perish due to lack of continuity. Therefore, just as this person, the enjoyer, acts with regard to foods continuously according to his wisdom and according to his karma, so too is the person imperishable (*akṣiti*), because of his continuous agency. Thus, the meaning is that even while being consumed, the foods do not perish.

Therefore, the entire world—characterized by the relationship between means and ends, consisting of the fruit of activity, and mounted upon a continuum defined by wisdom and action—is momentary, impure, and devoid of essence. Because it is held together by the stream of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the collective karma of many sentient beings, it is like the flow of a river, the flame of a lamp, or a succession of moments; it is as insubstantial as the trunk of a plantain tree, and equal to foam, an illusion, a mirage, water in a dream, and so forth. Yet, to those whose views are fixed upon its nature, it appears as if it were permanent and substantial, even though it is never truly dispersed.

This is stated for the sake of dispassion: "Whatever one generates with each thought through actions—if one were not to perform this [work], it would perish. For it is toward those who are dispassionate regarding this that the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is to be undertaken, beginning with the Fourth [State]. "He who knows this imperishability," it is said.

Since the three kinds of food that are about to be described have already been explained on this occasion, their fruit—consisting in the knowledge of their true nature—is now being concluded: "He who knows this imperishable one (akṣiti), the cause of non-destruction, as it has been described"—that is, the Person (*puruṣa*) is indeed the imperishable one, for he produces this food by means of every thought and by means of ritual acts; for if he were not to do so, it would perish. Now, the meaning of the phrase "he eats food with his face" (*pratīkena*) is stated: "the face" (*mukham*) refers to the state of being the mouth, that is, preeminence or primacy.

Primarily, he who knows that the father of foods is the imperishable Person (*puruṣa*) eats food, not being subordinate to food as the ignorant man is. The wise man, being the very self of foods, becomes solely the eater and does not fall into the state of being eaten. "He goes to the gods, he lives upon strength"—this which was said is a praise; there is no other new meaning [beyond this].

Now, with reference to the self (*adhyātma*), one should meditate upon that which is this principal vital breath (*mukhya prāṇa*) as the *udgītha*; for it moves along sounding "Om. The three kinds of food that were introduced as the fruits of the fivefold ritual (*pāṅkta karma*) are distinct from and superior to the previous foods, because they are effects (*kārya*) and because their scope is extensive. The subsequent text, up to the end of the Brāhmaṇa, is intended to explain them. Regarding the statement, "He made three for himself," the meaning is explained as follows: mind (*manas*), speech (*vāk*), and vital breath (*prāṇa*)—these are the three foods.

The Father, having first created them, made the mind, speech, and breath for himself—that is, for his own sake. Since there is doubt regarding the existence and nature of that mind, he says: "In the first place, there exists a mind distinct from the external organs such as the ear."

Since this is well known: even when there is a connection between the external sense organ, its object, and the self, one does not perceive the object that has appeared before one. When asked, "Did you see this form? one says, "My mind was elsewhere; I was absent-minded (*anyatramanā*), I did not see it. Likewise, when asked, "Did you hear these words of mine? one says, "I was absent-minded, I did not hear it"—that is, I did not hear it.

Therefore, it is understood that there exists another internal organ called *manas*, which connects with all the senses and their objects; for when this [organ] is absent, even though the eyes and other organs are capable of grasping form and so forth, the cognition of form, sound, and the rest does not occur upon contact with their respective objects, whereas it does occur when this [organ] is present. Hence, the entire world perceives "with the mind alone" and hears "with the mind," because when the mind is distracted, perception and the like do not take place.

Once the existence of the mind is established, this is stated for the sake of its specific nature: *kāma* (desire) is the longing for sexual union with women and so forth; *saṃkalpa* (volition) is the conceptualization of objects presented to it, according to distinctions such as white or blue; *vicikitsā* (doubt) is knowledge characterized by uncertainty; *śraddhā* (faith) is the conviction regarding unseen matters such as ritual actions and deities; *aśraddhā* (lack of faith) is the cognition contrary to that; *dhṛti* (fortitude) is the sustaining or uplifting of the body and other faculties when they sink; *adhṛti* (lack of fortitude) is the opposite of that; *hrī* (modesty) is shame; and *dhī* (intellect) is wisdom.

Fear, terror, and all such states as these are the mind alone; these are the forms of the mind, which is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Another reason for the existence of the mind is stated [124]: Therefore, there exists an internal organ called "mind" (*manas*), because even when something touches one from behind, outside the range of vision, one perceives with discrimination, "This is the touch of the hand," or "This is the touch of the knee. If there were no internal organ called "mind" to effect this discrimination, how could such discriminative perception arise from the skin alone? That which is the cause of this discriminative perception is the mind.

The mind exists, and its essential nature has been understood. Here, three kinds of food resulting from ritual actions—known as mind, speech, and breath—are intended to be explained with respect to the self (ādhyātmam), the elements (adhibhūtam), and the divine (adhidaivam). Among these, the mind among the internal [factors] of speech, mind, and breath has now been explained.

Now begins the exposition on Speech (*vāk*): Whatever sound (*dhvani*) exists in the world—whether it is manifested by the palate and other organs as characterized by phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth by living beings, or otherwise produced by instruments such as drums—all such sound is indeed Speech; this, first of all, is the stated nature of Speech. Now its function is described: For this Speech is dependent upon, that is, follows along with, the "end" (*anta*), which is the limit of the signified object, the determination of what is to be expressed.

Furthermore, this [Speech] is not itself to be manifested like the object to be expressed, but rather it is solely the manifester of the object to be expressed, because its nature is that of light, like a lamp and so forth. For the light of a lamp and the like is not manifested by another light; likewise, Speech is solely a manifester and is not itself manifested. Thus the Śruti avoids an infinite regress: "For this is not to be manifested," meaning that the very function of Speech is to be the manifester.

Now, *prāṇa* is explained: *Prāṇa* is the function of the heart that moves through the mouth and nose; it is called *prāṇa* because of its leading forward (*praṇayana*). *Apāna* is the downward-moving function that carries away urine, feces, and so forth; it is located from the navel downwards. *Vyāna* is so called because its action is pervasive distribution (*vyāyamana*); it is the junction between *prāṇa* and *apāna*, and it is the cause of vigorous actions. *Udāna* is the cause of excellence, upward movement, and so forth; it is located from the soles of the feet to the head and has an upward-moving function. *Samāna* is so called because it leads things equally; it is located in the stomach and is the digester of food and drink. *Ana*... [text ends]

Thus, the function common to these specific functions, which is connected with the general movements of the body—namely, this entire collection of functions beginning with *prāṇa* as described—is indeed *prāṇa*. Here, *prāṇa* refers to the internal possessor of the function (*vṛttimān*). Its action has been explained precisely through the demonstration of the distinctions among its functions. The internal "foods" known as mind (*manas*), speech (*vāk*), and breath (*prāṇa*) have been explained. This [body] consists of them and is a modification (*vikāra*) thereof, being composed of these [organs] belonging to Prajāpati: speech, mind, and breath.

What is this aggregate of causes and effects, this "sheath" (*kośa*)? It is the "body" (*piṇḍa*), which is conceived by the undiscriminating as the nature of the Self (*ātman*). Having stated generally that [the body] consists of these, there is now a specific clarification: "consisting of speech," "consisting of mind," and "consisting of the hands. The physical expansion of those very foods belonging to Prajāpati is now described:

Kauṣītaki said to his son, "I have approached this very one; therefore, you are my only sheath. [He further instructed: "Let the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) sing praises to the abundance (*bhūmāna*); then indeed they shall become many for me. (4)

(4) — The three worlds known as Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar are these very things: speech, mind, and breath. Therein lies this distinction: speech is this world (the earth), the mind is the intermediate world (the atmosphere), and breath is that world (the heavens). Now, indeed, that which is the Udgītha is the Praṇava, and that which is the Praṇava is the Udgītha. For by means of it, one may even rectify a poorly sung chant from the seat of the Hotṛ priest—yes, one may rectify it. Thus ends the fifth section. 5.
(5–7) Likewise, sentences such as "the three Vedas" have a straightforward meaning.

The known, the object of inquiry, and the unknown—these are precisely those [three forms]. Therein lies the distinction: whatever is known, clearly understood—that is the form of speech (*vāk*). Regarding this, he himself states the reason: for speech is the knower, because its nature is luminosity (*prakāśātmakatva*); how could that which makes others known itself be unknown? For it will be said later: "O King, by speech alone is a kinsman recognized."

This fruit is declared for one who knows the excellence of speech: speech itself, having become known to him—him who knows the aforementioned glory of speech—protects and sustains him; the meaning is that food becomes fit to be eaten by him precisely through the form of that knowledge.

Likewise, whatever is to be desired to be known—that is, whatever is intended to be clearly understood—is all of the form of the mind (*manas*). For it is because the mind has the nature of being in a state of doubt that it is "to be desired to be known. As before, the result for one who knows the manifestation of the mind is as follows: that which is to be desired to be known becomes this very mind and protects him; it attains the state of being food precisely by means of its own nature as that which is to be desired to be known. (10)

Likewise, whatever is unknown—that which is beyond the range of cognition and not subject to doubt—is the form of Prāṇa. For Prāṇa is indeed unknown, because its nature is unknown, as stated in the scriptural passage "Prāṇa is undefined" (*anirukta*). Since the division of speech, mind, and breath is established through the distinction between the known, the object of inquiry, and the unknown, the assignments such as "the three worlds" and so forth are merely based on the explicit words of the text. Because these forms—the known and so on—are observed everywhere, this restriction must be understood as being derived solely from the scriptural statement.

The vital breath (*prāṇa*), having become that, protects him—the meaning is that his vital breath becomes his food in an unperceived form. For teachers, fathers, and others are seen to provide assistance even when that assistance is doubted or not clearly understood by their pupils, sons, and so forth; likewise, it is possible for the mind (*manas*) and the vital breath to function as food even while being doubted or not clearly understood.
The extension of speech, mind, and vital breath in their objective, material aspect (*ādhibhautika*) has been explained; now begins this section concerning their divine aspect (*ādhidaivika*).

Of that very speech of Prajāpati which has been presented as food, the earth is the body—the external support—and the fire belonging to the earth is the instrument consisting of light, which is the luminous essence supported by the earth. For the speech of Prajāpati is twofold: the effect, which is the non-luminous support, and the instrument, which is the luminous supported. Both of these, the earth and the fire, are indeed the speech of Prajāpati.

In this regard, to whatever extent and of whatever measure speech exists—being differentiated by internal and external elements—to that same extent does the earth exist as its substratum in all those cases, becoming the effect. To that same extent is this fire, the object to be supported—the instrument in the form of light—which has entered into the earth, existing as precisely that much. The subsequent portion is the same.

Now, for this very mind—which has been described as belonging to Prajāpati—the sky (the celestial world) is the body, the effect, and the substratum; and that Āditya is the light-form, the instrument, and the superstratum. In this regard, to whatever extent the mind exists—whether with respect to the internal self (adhyātma) or the external world (adhibhūta)—to that same extent, to that same width, and to that same measure, the sky stands established as the substratum for the mind, which is the light-form instrument; and to that same extent is that Āditya, the light-form instrument, the superstratum.

Then those two, Fire and the Sun—the divine Father and Mother, Speech and Mind—united as a couple, coming together in sexual union, that is, in mutual contact, between the two worlds (Heaven and Earth). Impelled by the father, the Sun, through the mind, and manifested by the mother, Fire, through speech with the thought, "I shall perform action," [the offspring was produced]. From the very union of those two, Prāṇa, the Wind, was born for the sake of movement and action. He who was thus born is Indra, the Supreme Lord.

It is not only Indra who is *asapatna*—one for whom no rival (*sapatna*) exists. But what indeed is a "rival"? A second person who has come forward as an adversary is called a "rival. Therefore, even though speech and mind are second to him, they do not possess the status of rivals; for with respect to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), they have entered into a state of subordination, just as in the case of the internal self (*adhyātma*). In this context, the incidental fruit of the knowledge that [the breath] is without a rival is this: no rival or adversary arises for this knower who knows the vital breath as described above to be without a rival. (13)

Now, regarding this aforementioned prāṇa belonging to Prajāpati—that is, the prāṇa not mentioned as "offspring" (prajā) but immediately specified—the waters are its body, being the effect and the substratum for the instruments. As before, that moon is its form of light. In that regard, to whatever extent the prāṇa exists—whatever its measure it may be across the various divisions of the internal self (adhyātma) and so forth—to that same extent the waters pervade it, possessing that same measure. To that same extent, that moon is indestructible, having entered into those waters as an instrument, pervading them to the same extent both internally and externally.

These three foods—namely speech, mind, and breath—were created by the Father through the fivefold rite (*pāṅkta* karma). By means of these, the entire universe, both with respect to the self (*adhyātma*) and with respect to the elements (*adhibhūta*), is pervaded; there exists nothing else beyond or apart from them, whether consisting of effects (*kāryātmaka*) or consisting of instruments (*karaṇātmaka*). All these together—these very speech, mind, and breath—are entirely equal and equivalent, possessing pervasive power; they remain pervading everything within the range of living beings, including both the self and the elements.

For this very reason, they are infinite, existing as long as saṃsāra persists. Indeed, saṃsāra is not understood through the rejection of the body and the senses; for it has been stated that those [entities] consist of the body and the senses.

Whoever indeed worships these [beings] as having an end and being limited—whether in their form as the internal self (*adhyātma*) or in their form as external elements (*adhibhūta*)—wins a world that is likewise limited and finite according to the nature of that worship; he becomes limited himself and does not become one with their true self. On the other hand, whoever worships these as infinite, as the self of all, and as the self of all living beings, being unlimited—he wins an infinite world.

It has been stated that the Father, having created seven kinds of food by means of the fivefold rite (*pāṅkta-karman*), set aside three kinds of food for his own sake; these very foods, which are the fruits of the fivefold rite, have now been explained. How, then, are these the fruits of the fivefold rite? It is said: because the fivefold nature is perceived even in those three kinds of food, since both wealth (*vitta*) and action (*karman*) are also present therein.

In this context, it has been explained that Earth and Fire are the mother, Heaven and the Sun are the father, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) that exists between these two is the offspring. Now begins the section concerning how wealth and ritual action are to be brought about:

This very one is the year—that Prajāpati, consisting of threefold food, who was introduced as the subject—is here specifically designated by way of his nature as the year. He is "sixteen-parted," meaning he whose constituent parts (*kalā*) are sixteen; this is the year, the self of the year, the embodiment of time. And of that Prajāpati, whose nature is time, the nights alone—the days and nights, which is to say the lunar days (*tithi*)—are the fifteen parts.

The sixteenth part, which completes the sixteen, of this Prajāpati is indeed constant and eternally established. It is by means of the nights—the lunar days (*tithi*)—referred to as "parts" (*kalā*), that it is filled and diminished. For the Moon, who is Prajāpati, is filled during the bright fortnight; he increases through the parts that are accumulating until his orb is full on the day of the full moon.

By those very digits (kalās) being diminished, he wanes during the dark fortnight until, on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), only one fixed digit remains. That Prajāpati, whose nature is Time, on every new moon night—by means of that fixed digit which has been described as remaining—he enters into all this world of living beings. Having pervaded everything by means of that sixteenth digit in the form of the plants—both what they drink and what they eat as herbs—he dwells upon the new moon day.

Having remained during the night, he is then born on the following day at dawn, joined with a second digit (*kalā*). Thus, Prajāpati consists of five parts: the sky and the sun are the mind, the father; the earth and the fire are speech, the wife, the mother; and their offspring is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The lunar days (*tithis*) are the digits (*kalās*), which constitute his wealth, because they possess the nature of increase and decrease, like wealth; and the function of those digits, which are divisions of time, is to cause the transformation of the world.

Thus, this entire Prajāpati has come to be as the fruit of the fivefold rite (*pāṅkta-karman*), precisely according to that desire: "May I have a wife, then may I procreate, then may I have wealth, then may I perform ritual action. For even in the world, it is an established principle that the effect conforms to its cause.

Because this moon dwells during this night with its fixed digit (*dhruvā kalā*) having entered into the entire multitude of living beings, for that reason, on this new-moon night (*amāvāsyā*), one should not cut off the life-breath of any living being—that is, one should not cause any creature to perish—even that of a chameleon (*kṛkalāsa*). For the chameleon is by its very nature a sinful soul who is harmed by living beings, as it is considered inauspicious even when merely seen.

But is it not the case that injury to living beings has indeed been prohibited by the rule: "Not injuring any living beings, except at the sacred fords"? Certainly it is prohibited; nevertheless, this statement is not intended as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to injury on occasions other than the new moon, nor does it concern the lizard. What then? It is for the sake of honoring—that is, for the worship of this deity Soma. (15)

That Prajāpati, the year consisting of sixteen parts, who was indeed described as being beyond direct perception, should not be considered entirely imperceptible, because he is perceived here directly as this very person. Who is this person? It is that man who knows Prajāpati—who consists of the three kinds of food as previously described—as his own self; such is the man who possesses this knowledge.

On what basis is he called Prajāpati? That is now explained: for this person who knows thus, his wealth consisting of cattle and so forth is indeed the fifteen digits (*kalā*), because it is subject to increase and decrease; and ritual action is accomplished by means of wealth. For the sake of his completeness, his very self—his physical body alone—is the sixteenth digit, which stands as the constant element. Like the moon, it is filled and diminished by wealth alone; this is well known in the world.

This is "nabhya," which means beneficial for the nave (*nābhi*); it is called *nabhya* because it is fit for the nave, or because it deserves the nave. What is that? It is this very self (*ātman*), this physical body (*piṇḍa*). The rim (*pradhi*) is external wealth, standing in the place of an encircling felly—just as the spokes, the felly, and so forth belong to a wheel.

Therefore, even if one suffers a total loss—that is, the seizure of all one's property and falls into exhaustion—if he lives by means of his "self," which stands in the place of the nave of a wheel, then they say of him: "This man has gone away, he is wasted away"—just as a wheel deprived of its spokes and rim. The intention is that if he remains alive, he may be replenished again by means of wealth, which stands in the place of the spokes and the rim.

Thus, it has been explained that through action associated with the fivefold [sacrifice], wealth, knowledge, and the divine, one becomes Prajāpati, who consists of the three foods. Immediately thereafter, it was stated that wife, wealth, and progeny constitute the retinue. In that context, it was understood only in a general sense that son, ritual action, and the lower knowledge are means for attaining the worlds; however, there was no specific rule regarding the particular relationship between the son and the other means with respect to the fruit of attaining the worlds.
Therefore, the subsequent section is composed to state this specific relationship between the means, such as the son, and their respective results:

The word "atha" (now) serves to introduce the statement. "Three"—the particle "vāva" has the sense of restriction—meaning that there are exactly three worlds worthy of being attained through the means taught in the scriptures, neither fewer nor more. Which are they? It is said: the world of men (*manuṣyaloka*), the world of the fathers (*pitṛloka*), and the world of the gods (*devaloka*). Of these, this world of men is to be won, to be conquered, to be accomplished, by the means of a son alone. We shall explain later how it is to be won by a son, and not by any other action or by knowledge; such is the remainder of the sentence.

The world of the ancestors is to be won by action alone, characterized by the Agnihotra and other rites, neither by a son nor by knowledge. The world of the gods is won by knowledge, neither by a son nor by action. Indeed, among the three worlds, the world of the gods is the best and most praiseworthy; therefore, because it is the means to attain that [world], they praise knowledge.

Thus, there are three means of accomplishment—known as son, ritual action, and knowledge—each assigned according to the distinction between the three worlds to be attained as their respective fruits. The wife, however, is not mentioned separately as a distinct means of accomplishment because she exists for the sake of ritual action and the son. Nor is wealth mentioned as a separate means, since it serves as a means for performing ritual action. It is well known that knowledge and ritual action are the causes for conquering the worlds precisely through the attainment of one's own self. But as for the son, since he is not of the nature of an action, it is not understood by what manner he becomes a cause for conquering the worlds.

Therefore, that must be explained; thus, what follows is commenced immediately after: *saṃprattiḥ* means "bestowal. *Saṃprattiḥ* is the name of the rite about to be described; for in this manner the father effects the bestowal of his own self-activity upon the son, and therefore this rite is designated as *saṃpratti*.

To the question of at what time this should be performed, he says: when that father, at whatever time, thinking "I am about to die," "I shall die," perceives through the sight of omens of death (*ariṣṭa*) and the like, then at that time he calls his son and says: "Thou art Brahman, thou art the sacrifice, thou art the world. Thus addressed, the son replies; for he, having been previously instructed, knows: "This must be done by me. Therefore he says these three statements: "I am Brahman, I am the sacrifice, I am the world."

Thinking that the meaning of this is obscure, the Śruti proceeds to provide an explanation: "Whatever indeed remains"—that is, whatever has been spoken and whatever has not been spoken, whether studied or unstudied—all of that finds its unity, its oneness, in this very word "Brahman. The meaning is: that activity of study which was my duty for all this time concerning the Vedas, from now on, you are that Brahman; it is your duty, not mine.

Likewise, whatever sacrifices were to be performed by me—whether they have been performed or not—all of them are unified in this single term "sacrifice" (*yajña*). The meaning is: those sacrifices which had me as their agent, from now on let them have you as their agent; you are the sacrifice. Whatever worlds were to be conquered by me—whether they have been conquered or not—all of them are unified in this single term "world" (*loka*). From now on, you are the world; they are to be conquered by you.

"From this point forward, my duty regarding study, sacrifice, and the conquest of the worlds has been entrusted to you; I am indeed released from the bond of duties pertaining to that ritual. And because he had been so instructed, the son accepted everything exactly as it was. Regarding this intention of his father, the Śruti declares: "All this is indeed of such a measure—namely, that which must be done by a householder: the Vedas are to be studied, sacrifices are to be performed, and the worlds are to be conquered."

"May he not abandon me from this world"—thinking thus, "May he protect me," [the father entrusts himself]. The *laṅ* is used here in the sense of the future (*lṛṭ*), since in Vedic there is no restriction regarding time. Because the son, having become thus perfected, will release the father from this world—that is, from the bondage of duties—therefore the Brahmins say that a son who has been instructed is "worldly" (*lokya*), meaning beneficial for the world, for his father.

For this very reason, fathers instruct their son, thinking, "May he be one who belongs to our world. When that father, at whatever time, being one who knows this and having entrusted the performance of duties to his son, departs from this world—that is, dies—then at that time he enters his son; he pervades the son by means of these very same speech, mind, and breath that have been mentioned.

Due to the disappearance of the cause of internal limitation, the father’s speech, mind, and vital breaths enter into everything by means of their own divine forms—consisting of earth, fire, and so forth—just as the light of a lamp enters all objects within a broken jar. Along with those vital breaths, the father also enters, because the father is essentially composed of speech, mind, and vital breaths; for the father has cultivated the realization: "I am the infinite speech, mind, and vital breaths, expanded through the distinctions of the internal, external, and so on."

Therefore, it is rightly said that the father's continuity through the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) occurs: "He enters the son together with these very vital breaths. For he becomes the self (*ātman*) of all, including the son. This is what is meant: the father whose son has been thus instructed exists in this very world in the form of his son; the meaning is that he should not be considered dead. And so it is stated in another Śruti: "This other self remains here for the sake of meritorious deeds."

Now, he states the etymological definition of "son" (*putra*): That son, if at any time there remains something unperformed by this father—something that ought to be done, whether through negligence, from a corner, or from within—that is, from all that which ought to be done and which constitutes an obstacle to the attainment of the world, the son releases him, liberates him, by personally performing and completing it all. Since he protects his father by means of such completion (*pūraṇa*), he is therefore called a "son" (*putra*).

This is the true sonship of a son—that he protects by filling the deficiency of his father. Such a father, through such a son, even though dead, becomes immortal and is established in this very world. In this way, the father conquers this world of men by means of a son; not so the worlds of the gods and the fathers through knowledge and ritual action, which are won merely by the existence of one's own nature.

For knowledge and action do not become causes for the conquest of the worlds by depending on any other operation—such as that of a son—beyond the mere attainment of their own nature. Now, once the father has performed the transmission (*saṃpratti*), these vital breaths (*prāṇas*)—speech and the rest—which are divine, belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha, and immortal, characterized by the nature of non-death, enter him.

He will explain how this is so: "And for the earth, him... and so forth. Thus, the Śruti itself has demonstrated that the son, ritual action, and the lower knowledge have as their goals the accomplishment of the world of men, the world of the fathers, and the world of the gods, respectively. Regarding this, certain disputants—being ignorant of the specific meanings stated by the Śruti—assert that the means such as the son and the rest have liberation as their goal.

Having heard this, the following was made as a covering for their mouths: by beginning with "May I have a wife," etc., it is shown that the fivefold ritual action is performed out of desire; and by concluding with the specific application of sons and so forth to particular goals, it is established that the scriptural injunction regarding debts refers to the unenlightened and not to the knower of the Supreme Self. And the text will later say: "What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self is this world?

However, some maintain that even the conquest of the world of the fathers and the world of the gods is simply a turning away from those worlds; therefore, [liberation is attained] through sons, rituals, and the lower knowledge.

They maintain that by performing these three together, one becomes detached from these three worlds and attains liberation through the knowledge of the Supreme Self; thus, they hold that the means such as sons and so forth have liberation as their ultimate purpose. To silence even them, this very subsequent Śruti has been set forth to demonstrate the fruit for one who has performed his duties, who possesses a son, who is a performer of rituals, and who knows the science of the threefold food.

Nor can it be said that this very fruit is the fruit of liberation, because of its connection with the three kinds of food, because the foods are produced from meditation and austerity, because of the observation that [the Self] "produces them again and again," because of the scriptural mention of decay in the passage, "If he did not do this, it would indeed perish," because the statement "the body is of the nature of light" establishes its status as an effect and an instrument, and because of the concluding summary in the passage, "These three indeed," which identifies it as consisting of name, form, and action.

Nor can it be understood from this very sentence that these three means, when combined, lead to liberation for some and result in the fruit consisting of the three foods for others; for the sentence is exhausted merely by showing that the means such as a son result in the fruit consisting of the three foods.

From the earth and from the fire, divine speech—consisting of the deities and pertaining to the supreme self—enters him who has performed the *saṃpratti* rite. For divine speech, characterized by earth and fire, is the material cause of all speech; it is indeed obstructed by defects such as attachment in the case of the individual self (*ādhyātmika*). When those defects depart for the knower, it pervades him like water when its confinement is broken, or like the light of a lamp. This is what is meant by the statement: "Divine speech enters him from the earth and from the fire."

And that divine speech is pure, free from defects such as untruth; by whatever he speaks with that divine speech—whether for himself or for another—that very thing comes to pass. The meaning is that his speech becomes unfailing and unimpeded.

(19) Likewise, the divine mind enters him from heaven and from the sun. And that divine mind, because of its natural purity, is such that by means of it he becomes truly blissful, truly happy; moreover, he does not grieve, because of the absence of contact with the causes of sorrow and the like.

(20) Likewise, the divine vital breath (*prāṇa*) enters him from both the sun and the moon. What are the characteristics of that divine *prāṇa*, it is said: it is that which, while moving among the various classes of living beings, does not move—whether in its collective or individual form—or else, while moving among mobile creatures, does not move among immobile ones; it does not suffer, meaning it is not joined with fear caused by pain; and furthermore, it is not harmed, it does not perish, and it does not undergo injury.

He—who thus knows this very vision of the Self as the threefold food—he becomes the Self of all beings, he becomes the vital breath of all beings, he becomes the mind of all beings, and he becomes the speech of all beings; the meaning is that, by being the Self of all beings, he becomes omniscient—and indeed, the doer of all.

Just as this deity Hiraṇyagarbha is established from of old, even so there is no obstruction whatsoever to his omniscience or his omnipotence; "he" is the reference to the subject of the illustration. Furthermore, just as all beings protect, sustain, and worship this deity Hiraṇyagarbha through sacrifices and other rites, even so do all beings protect him who knows this—meaning they constantly offer him worship characterized by sacrifice and the like.

Now, this objection may be raised: it has been stated that [the Self] is the Self of all living beings; and if it were the Self that performs the actions and experiences the effects for all living beings, it would consequently be connected with the pleasure and pain of all living beings. This is not so, because its intelligence is unlimited (*aparicchinna-buddhi*). For it is observed that those whose self-conception is limited experience connection with suffering upon being reviled and the like, thinking, "I am being reviled by this person."

But for this one who is the Self of all, since there is no distinction in the cognition of selfhood regarding either the one who is reviled or the one who reviles, suffering caused by that [reviling] does not arise. And it is like the suffering of death because of the absence of a cause—just as when someone has died, suffering arises in someone else because of the cause of a son or a brother, thinking "he was my son" or "he was my brother," yet in the absence of such a cause, no suffering arises even for one who witnesses that death; so too it is for the Lord, whose self is undivided.

Because of the absence of defects such as false knowledge—which is the cause of suffering characterized by notions like "mine-ness" (mamatva) and so forth—suffering does not arise at all. This is what is expressed [in the text]: "Whatever these creatures grieve, that suffering, which has grief and so forth as its cause, becomes conjoined with those very creatures, because it is produced by a limited intellect; but for the Universal Self (sarvātman), with what could it be conjoined or from what could it be disjoined?"

But as for him who abides in the station of Prajāpati—merit alone, that is to say, auspiciousness alone, being the intended fruit; "merit" here refers to that unsurpassed merit he has performed, and by virtue of that, he goes only to its fruit. Indeed, evil does not go to the gods, because there is no occasion for the fruit of evil; the meaning is that he does not go to the suffering that is the fruit of evil.

"‘All these indeed are equal, all are infinite’—thus the meditation on speech, mind, and breath has been taught without distinction, and no specific preference for any one among them has been stated. Should this be understood exactly as it stands, or is some distinction to be found when investigated regarding the practice of meditation? To this it is replied:

Now, therefore, follows the inquiry (*mīmāṃsā*)—meaning the deliberation regarding the ritual duties of worship (*upāsana*). This inquiry proceeds as to which among these vital breaths (*prāṇas*) should be maintained as the primary duty. In this regard, Prajāpati—"ha" being a particle used in the sense of "it is said"—Prajāpati, it is said, having created living beings, created the organs such as speech and so forth, which are called "actions" (*karma*) because they exist for the sake of action; that is to say, he created the instruments such as speech.

Once created, they contended with one another—that is, they engaged in rivalry and competition. How so? Speech took up its vow, thinking: "I shall indeed speak; I must not cease from my own function. It held fast to this resolve, thinking: "If there is anyone else equal to me who is capable of not ceasing from his own function, let him too display his own prowess. Likewise, the eye [took up its vow], thinking: "I shall see," and the ear, thinking: "I shall hear."

In this way, other actions and instruments—whatever action belongs to each, according to its action—Death, the slayer, having become weariness in the form of fatigue (*śrama*), seized them; he gathered them together. How so? He reached those instruments as they were engaged in their own respective functions by appearing in the form of weariness; and having reached them, Death confined them—he obstructed them, meaning he caused them to fall away from their own functions.

Therefore, even today, speech, engaged in its own function, indeed tires and, joined with death in the form of fatigue, falls away from its own task; likewise the eye tires, and the ear tires. But death in the form of fatigue did not reach this very chief vital breath—this middle vital breath. Therefore, even today, it proceeds in its own function without ever tiring.

Those other organs resolved and fixed their minds upon knowing him, thinking: "He indeed is the best among us, the most praiseworthy, the superior one, because he neither suffers nor is harmed while moving and not moving. Come now, let us all assume his very form; let us recognize this Prāṇa as our own self. Having thus decided, they all assumed his form alone—they took the form of Prāṇa itself as their self.

They resolved upon the vow of the vital breath alone, thinking: "Our own vows are not sufficient to ward off death. For by means of the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the other organs possess form—through its nature as movement and through its own nature as light. Indeed, apart from the vital breath, the existence of the nature of movement is not possible;

for they are always observed to be preceded by the activity of movement in their own respective functions. Therefore, these [organs] such as speech and the rest are designated—that is, called—by this name of the vital breath: they are called "the vital breaths" (*prāṇāḥ*).

Whoever thus knows the state of being the self of breath for all the organs, and their denotability by the word "prāṇa"—by that very knowledge, indeed, worldly people designate that family in which that wise man was born; that family becomes renowned by the name of the wise man alone, as "this is the family of so-and-so," just as [one says] "the Tāpatya. This is the fruit for one who knows as stated—that speech and the other organs have the nature of breath and are designated by the name "prāṇa."

Furthermore, whoever indeed competes with one who knows thus—that is, with the seer of the Self as Prāṇa—being his adversary, he withers away in this very body; having withered away, that is, having reached a state of desiccation, he finally dies at the end, not dying suddenly without prior affliction. Thus has been stated the vision of the Self as Prāṇa with reference to the internal self (*adhyātma*); this concludes what was said for the purpose of demonstrating the vision with reference to the divine (*adhidaivata*).

Next, immediately following this, the vision concerning the deities (*adhidaivata*)—that is, the domain of the gods—is set forth. It is deliberated upon which specific deity’s observance of vows (*vratadhāraṇa*) is more excellent. Everything is to be understood as it was in the case of the self (*adhyātma*). Agni resolved: "I alone shall burn"; Āditya: "I shall give heat"; Candramas: "I shall shine"; and so did the other deities, each according to their respective nature.

Just as among these vital breaths (*prāṇas*) such as speech and the rest, the middle *prāṇa* is not overtaken by death—that is, it is not displaced from its own function—and thus remains one whose vow is unbroken by virtue of its own *prāṇa*-vow; even so is Vāyu among these deities such as Agni and the others. While they "set"—that is, they go to their setting and cease from their respective functions—just as the other deities within the body, such as speech and the rest, or the external deities such as Agni and the others do; Vāyu does not set, just like the middle *prāṇa*.

Therefore, this very deity that does not set is Vāyu—this which is Vāyu. Having thus investigated with respect to both the internal self (*adhyātma*) and the divine realm (*adhidaiva*), it is determined: "The vow of Prāṇa and Vāyu is unbroken.
(23) Now, there is this verse, a mantra, which illuminates this very same meaning: from which Vāyu the sun rises, goes upward; and [with respect to] the internal self...

The eye [arises] from the self and from the breath; and where it goes to rest—in the wind and in the breath—at the time of the evening twilight and at the time of sleep for a person—that very thing the gods made; that is, the gods, such as Speech and the others, and Fire and the others, having deliberated in the past, established the vow of the breath and the vow of the wind. That very same thing is followed today, even now, and will be followed in the future time by the gods; this is the intended meaning.

Regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa explains the mantra in brief: "From breath indeed this sun rises; into breath it sets. The gods made that their law (dharma); that is today, and that will be tomorrow. What is the meaning of this? It is said: whatever vow these—namely speech and the others, as well as fire and the others—undertook at that time or on that occasion, namely the vow of breath and the vow of air, they perform that very same thing even today, they follow it, and they will continue to follow it; the vow of those two remains unbroken.

As for the vows regarding speech and the other senses, as well as the vows regarding fire and the other deities, they are indeed broken; for at the time of their setting and at the time of sleep, they are seen to merge into the wind and the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Thus it is said elsewhere: "When a person sleeps, then speech merges into the vital breath, the mind merges into the vital breath, the eye merges into the vital breath, and the ear merges into the vital breath. When he awakens, they are born again from the vital breath alone. This refers to the internal (microcosmic) level. Now, with respect to the divine (macrocosmic) level: "When the fire goes out, it merges into the wind."

"Therefore they say, 'He has entered into water,' for when the sun sets, it enters into Vāyu, and the moon enters into Vāyu; in Vāyu the quarters are established, and from Vāyu alone they are born again. Since this very vow—namely, the nature of vibration belonging to both Vāyu and Prāṇa, which is followed by all the gods—is common to speech and the other [senses] as well as to fire and the other [elements], therefore another person too should observe this one single vow.

What is that? It would breathe—that is, it would perform the function of inhalation—and it would exhale—that is, it would perform the function of exhalation; for there is no cessation of the activity of inhalation and exhalation characterized by breathing in and breathing out.

Therefore, one should observe that very same single vow, abandoning the activity of the other senses—[thinking] "lest the evil one, death in the form of exhaustion, should reach me. The word *na* is used in the sense of fear (*paribhaye*). The intention is that, terrified [with the thought], "If I should fall away from this vow, I am already swallowed by death," one should maintain the vow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). If at any time one should undertake—that is, begin—the vow of the vital breath, one should desire to complete it—to wish for its fulfillment.

For if one were to desist from this vow, the vital breaths (prāṇas) and the gods would be disregarded; therefore, one must certainly complete it. By means of that very vow—through the realization of the self as the vital breath—one [realizes] that among all beings, speech and the other senses, as well as fire and the other deities, are indeed of my nature; "I am the vital breath, the self, the sole agent of all movement. Thus, by maintaining this vow, one attains—depending on the degree of one's understanding—either *sāyujya*, which is union or identity of essence with this very deity of the vital breath, or *salokatā*, which is residence in the same world, or dwelling in the same place. One conquers, that is, one attains this.

Thus ends the fifth Brāhmaṇa of the first chapter. This very earth is the Ṛg, fire is the Sāman; this Sāman is supported upon that Ṛg. Therefore, the Sāman is sung as being supported upon the Ṛg. This [earth] is *sā*, and fire is *ama*; that constitutes the Sāman. 1. (1)---

This threefold world—consisting of name, form, and action—which was introduced as the object of ignorance and characterized by the relationship of means and ends, including even the fruit that culminates in the attainment of the self consisting of vital breath (*prāṇa*); and that state of it prior to its manifestation, denoted by the term "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta*) like the seed of a tree—all this triad is indeed non-self (*anātman*), not the Self (*ātman*) which is Brahman, immediate and direct.

The passage beginning with "Or rather, the triad" is commenced for the purpose of causing detachment from this [world]. For the intellect of one whose mind has not turned away from this non-Self cannot proceed toward meditating on the Self alone as the world—realizing "I am Brahman"—because there is a contradiction between the outward-turned activity and the inward-turned Self. Thus it is said in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "The Self-existent pierced the openings of the senses outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner Self.
But some wise man, desiring immortality, looked within the inner Self with his eyes turned back," and so forth.

Furthermore, how can it be established that this saṃsāra—which consists of actions, agents, and fruits, and is both determinate and indeterminate—is composed solely of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and karma, and does not possess the nature of a self (*ātman*)? It is in order to make this possible that [the following is said].

To this it is replied: regarding those names as they have been presented—"Speech" (*vāk*) refers to the universal of sound (*śabda-sāmānya*), because it has been stated, "Whatever sound there is, that is indeed speech. That which is the referent of this word "speech"—namely, the mere universal of sound—is the *uktha*, the cause, the material source of these specific names, just as a mountain of rock salt is the source of individual grains of rock salt.

Thus he says: "For from this [Supreme] Name-sāmānya, all names—distinguished as Yajñadatta, Devadatta, and so forth—emerge, arise, and are differentiated, like grains of salt from a mountain of salt; and the effect is not distinct from its cause. Likewise, because particulars are included within the universal (sāmānya)—as to how there can be the relation of universal and particular—it is this 'Name-sāmānya' that is the *sāman* of these particular names; it is called *sāman* because of its equality (*samatvāt*), meaning it is the universal."

For this [Brahman] is equal to all names, that is, to all particular manifestations of the Self. Furthermore, because there is no distinction in the acquisition of their own nature (*ātmalābha*): whatever acquires its own nature from something else is seen to be non-different from that source, just as jars and other objects are non-different from clay. How is it said that the acquisition of the nature of particular names comes from speech? It is said: because for these [names], the reality denoted by the word "speech" is Brahman, the Self; for from that [Brahman] comes the acquisition of the nature of names, since a distinct essential form apart from sound is impossible.

He explains this: "For this universal sound (*śabdasāmānya*) bears—that is, sustains—all particular sounds (*śabdaviśeṣa*), all names, by providing them with their own form. Thus, because the relationship of cause and effect is established, the relationship of the general and the particular is established, and the relationship of providing its own self is established, it is proven that the particular names are nothing but sound. In the same way, everything should be applied to the two subsequent cases as stated: "The intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) itself is the *ṛc*, the wind (*vāyu*) is the *sāman*. This *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*; therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being supported upon the *ṛc*. The intermediate space itself is 'Sā', and the wind is 'Ama'; that is the *sāman*. (2) (2)

Now, regarding forms such as white, black, and so forth—the term "the eye" (*cakṣus*) denotes the generality of the objects of sight, which is what is expressed by the word "eye"; it refers to the generality of form (*rūpasāmānya*), which is mere luminosity. For from this all forms arise; this is their *sāman*, for this is equal to all forms; this is their *brahman*, for this sustains all forms. The sky (*dyauḥ*) is indeed the *ṛc* and the sun (*ādityaḥ*) is the *sāman*. This *sāman* is mounted upon this *ṛc*; therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being mounted upon the *ṛc*. The sky is indeed the *sā* and the sun is the *ama*; that is the *sāman*. 3. (3)

Now, the inclusion of all specific actions—whether consisting of mental perception or consisting of physical motion—within the mere generality of action (*kriyāsāmānya*) is being stated. How so? For all specific actions, the "self" (*ātman*) is the body, which is the common locus; thus, the action of the self is called "the self. For it has been said that one performs action by means of the body, the self; and in the body, every action is manifested.

Therefore, by virtue of being located therein, the action is designated by that term—namely, "the Uktha" and so forth, as before, referring to the mere generality of action. Thus, this triad of name, form, and action, as described, is mutually dependent, the cause of mutual manifestation, and the locus of mutual dissolution; joined together like the support of a tripod, they constitute the one Being.

By what means is the oneness with the Self stated? It is said: this Self and this body—the aggregate consisting of the organs and their functions—have been explained in the section on the three foods by such passages as, "This Self indeed consists of this. For all this that has been manifested and the unmanifested is just this: name, form, and action. This very Self, being one, exists as this triad of name, form, and action, established in the form of the internal self (adhyātma), the elements (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaiva). This is what is about to be explained.

He states the meaning of the statement "Amṛta is covered by satya": "Prāṇa is indeed amṛta"—that which consists of the instruments [of perception], the internal supporter, the essential self, the immortal, the imperishable. "Satya" refers to name and form, which consist of effects and exist in the state of the body. Prāṇa, however, whose nature is action, is the supporter of those two; it is "covered" by the two external forms consisting of the body, which are subject to birth and destruction and are mortal—that is, it is rendered unmanifest. This very reality of transmigratory existence, which is the domain of ignorance, has thus been demonstrated.
Therefore, the fourth [chapter] is commenced with the aim that the Self, which is the object of knowledge, must be realized hereafter.
Thus [ends the work] of the venerable teacher of the Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka order, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
The first chapter in the commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavat.

Now, with reference to the self: speech is the *ṛc* and breath is the *sāman*. This *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*; therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being supported upon the *ṛc*. Speech is *sā*, and breath is *ama*; that is the *sāman*. There were three men who were skilled in the *udgītha*: Śilaka Śālāvatya, Caikitāyana Dālbhya, and Pravāhaṇa Jaibali. They said, "We are indeed skilled in the *udgītha*; come, let us have a discussion on the *udgītha*."

"What is the goal of this world? "Space," he said. "Indeed, all these beings arise from space alone; they return to space at the end. Space is indeed greater than these; space is the ultimate resort. While the Kurus were being devastated by hailstorms, Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa lived as a beggar with his wife Āṭikī in Ibhyagrāma. Then a patron said to him, "I wish to know you, O Blessed One. He replied, "I am Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa."
Now, therefore, follows the Udgītha of the dogs. Baka Dālbhya—or Glāva Maitreya—went out to study his sacred recitation (svādhyāya).

"The world here is indeed the syllable *hā-u*; the wind is the syllable *hā-ai*; the moon is the syllable *atha*; the self (*ātman*) is the syllable *iha*; and fire is the syllable *ī*. Indeed, the meditation on the Sāman in its entirety is excellent. For what is good, they call "Sāman"; and what is not good, they call "Asāman."

(1) In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) was Gārgya—a knower of Brahman within the scope of ignorance, namely Dṛptabālāki. "Dṛpta" means proud; he was proud precisely because his knowledge of Brahman was incomplete. "Bālāki" means the offspring of Balākā; thus, "Dṛptabālāki" refers to one who is both proud and a descendant of Balākā. In this narrative, the particle *ha* signifies tradition (*aitihya*). He was "anūcāna," meaning capable of reciting [the Vedas] or eloquent in speech. "Gārgya" indicates his lineage. He existed at a certain particular time.

He [Uddālaka Āruṇi] said to Ajātaśatru, the King of Kāśī named Ajātaśatru, having approached him: "I shall tell you Brahman; I shall speak of Brahman to you. Being addressed thus, Ajātaśatru said: "We shall give a thousand cows for this speech—namely, for the words 'I shall tell you Brahman' which you have spoken to me. The intention is that the giving of a thousand cows is the sole motive for this.

Why is the direct statement of Brahman itself not accepted as the cause for the gift of a thousand cows? It is said that this very speech, "I shall tell you Brahman," is required as the cause—because the Śruti itself expresses the king's intention through the two statements, "Janaka is the giver" and "Janaka is the hearer," wherein the word *janaka* is repeated twice; the particle *vai* is used to indicate well-known renown.

"Janaka is one who wishes to give; Janaka is one who wishes to hear"—thus people who desire to hear the Brahman, who wish to speak it, and who wish to grasp it run toward and approach him. Therefore, you have attributed all that to me as well. Regarding this, they also say: "He has approached him with *sāman* (gentleness)" means "He has approached him with what is good"; "He has approached him without *sāman*" means "He has approached him with what is not good. 2.

(2) When the king had thus become attentive and was facing him, Gārgya said to him: "That very one who is the single presiding deity in the sun and in the eye, who has entered here into the heart through the door of the eye, and who exists [there] with the thought 'I am the enjoyer' and 'I am the doer'—it is this very one that I perceive as Brahman; I meditate upon Him within this aggregate of causes and effects. Therefore, I declare that Person to you as Brahman; meditate upon Him."

Thus addressed, Ajātaśatru replied, warding him off with his hand: "No, no! Do not speak to me regarding this Brahman that is to be known. The repetition of "no, no" is for the sake of emphasis. "In this way, while the object of our knowledge is the same, you would be contradicting us by presenting it as if we were ignorant; therefore, do not speak to me regarding this Brahman. If you know anything else, you may speak of that Brahman, but not of that which is already known to me."
Now, if you think—"You know only Brahman alone, but not its specific fruits of worship"—that should not be thought; for I know all this that you speak.

How so? "Atiṣṭhāḥ" means he stands transcending all beings; he is the head and the summit of all beings, the king—indeed, a king because he is endowed with the quality of radiance. Distinguished by these attributes, this Brahman is the agent and the enjoyer within this aggregate of body and organs. Thus one should meditate upon it, thinking, "I am this. The fruit for one who meditates with such distinctions is as follows: "He who meditates upon it thus becomes *atiṣṭhā*, the head and the king of all beings."
For the fruit is indeed in accordance with the quality of the worship, according to the Vedic revelation: "In whatever way they worship it, that very thing they become.

Furthermore, they say: "It is *sāman* for us, alas! when something is good; they mean "it is truly good" when they say "it is *sāman* for us, alas! And they say: "It is not *sāman* for us, alas! when something is not good; they mean "it is truly not good" when they say "it is not *sāman* for us, alas! 3. (3) ---

When the Brahman in the sun was refuted through this dialogue, Gārgya proceeded to another Brahman in the moon for Ajātaśatru. "That person who is one and the same in the moon and in the mind—the enjoyer and the agent," with these qualifiers as before—"he who is vast, great, and whose garment is white (pāṇḍaravāsas), because the vital breath (prāṇa) presiding over the moon has no physical body; he who is King Soma, the moon, and that which, being food, is pressed as a creeper in the sacrifice—unifying these, I meditate upon him alone as Brahman."

For one who meditates upon the Sāman as possessing the qualities described above, day after day the Soma is pressed at his sacrifice; it is "prasuta," meaning it is excellently and most abundantly pressed in its modification—the sense being that he possesses the capacity to perform both types of sacrifice. Furthermore, food never fails for him who meditates on the Self consisting of food. He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the Sāman as "good" (sādhu)—verily, soon indeed may good dharmas come to him and bow down before him. Thus ends the first section. (4) 1. (4)

Likewise, there is one deity in lightning, in the skin, and in the heart; "radiant" is the qualifying attribute. Its fruit is this: he becomes radiant, and his offspring become radiant. Because the multiplicity of lightnings is accepted, there is a multiplicity of fruits both for oneself and for one's offspring.

Likewise, there is one deity in space, in the space of the heart, and in the heart itself; it is characterized by two attributes: "full" (*pūrṇam*) and "non-moving" (*apravarti*). The result of the attribute of fullness is this: "one is filled with offspring and cattle. The result of the attribute of non-movement is: "his offspring does not depart from this world," meaning that the lineage of offspring is never interrupted. (6)
