Likewise, there is one deity in the wind, in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and in the heart. Its qualification is as follows: Indra is the Supreme Lord; Vaikuṇṭha is the invincible; and "unconquered" refers to his army, which has never before been defeated by others—this being well known from its status as a host of Maruts. The fruit of this meditation is also stated: he becomes victorious, that is, of a nature inclined toward conquering; unconquerable, meaning his own nature cannot be overcome by others; and a subduer of adversaries, meaning he is of a nature inclined toward defeating enemies who oppose him. (7)

In fire, in speech, and in the heart, there is one deity. Its qualification is: *viṣāsahiḥ*, meaning "enduring" or "overpowering others. Due to the multiplicity of fires, the abundance of results is as previously described.

(8) In water, in semen, and in the heart, there is one deity. Its qualification is: *pratirūpaḥ*, meaning "conformable," that is, not contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti. As for the result: that which is conformable—namely, exactly in accordance with the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti—approaches and reaches him, and not its opposite; furthermore, from him, another is likewise born.

(9) In a mirror whose nature is clarity, and elsewhere in such things as a sword, and within the heart whose inherent nature is the purity of being (*sattva*), there is a single deity. Its qualification is: "radiant," meaning its nature is luminosity; and the fruit is that very same thing, with the multiplicity of fruits resulting from the multiplicity of the bases for that radiance. (10)

Regarding the sound that follows one who is going or walking from behind, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which is the cause of life within the body—having unified these two, he says: "The *asu* is the *prāṇa*, the cause of life"; this is its quality. As for its fruit: "He goes through his entire lifespan in this world"—meaning that even when he is afflicted by diseases and the like, the *prāṇa* does not abandon him before the time of his lifespan, which is determined by his past actions and limited by the results of those actions.

In the quarters, in the two ears, and in the heart, there is one deity: the two gods Aśvinī, whose nature is inseparable. Its quality is "being accompanied by a second," which consists in non-separation and mutual inseparability, both among the quarters and between the two Aśvinīs, because they possess such attributes. And that very thing is the fruit for the worshiper: non-interruption of his attendants and being accompanied by a second. (12) In shadow—meaning external darkness—and in the internal, in ignorance consisting of obscuration, and in the heart, there is one deity; its qualification is "Death. The fruit is entirely as before; the distinction is the absence of affliction from disease and so forth, due to the non-arrival of Death.

(13) — There is one deity in the self (*ātman*), in Prajāpati, in the intellect (*buddhi*), and in the heart. Her qualification is "possessing a self" (*ātmanvī*) or "self-possessed" (*ātmavān*). The result is: he indeed becomes self-possessed, he becomes self-possessed; his offspring becomes self-possessed. The distinction is that this accomplishment occurs among the offspring because of the abundance of intellect. When the [various] Brahman-conceptions had been thus successively rejected by him through his own thorough understanding, Gārgya, his knowledge of Brahman exhausted and unable to provide a further reply, remained silent.

Observing Gārgya in such a state, Ajātaśatru said to him: "Is it only this much?"—meaning, "Is Brahman fully known by this much alone, or is there more? The other replied: "It is only this much. Ajātaśatru said: "Brahman is not truly known by knowing only this much. Why are you so proud? I shall tell you about Brahman. [Gārgya asks: "Is it being said that what has been known in this way is not actually known at all? [Ajātaśatru replies: "No; for we hear of a knowledge that bears fruit."

Nor is it possible to understand these sentences as being merely explanatory (arthavāda); for each instruction on meditation, the sentences are observed to be intent upon enjoining something not previously established—for instance, "He is the pre-eminence of all beings," and so forth—and corresponding fruits are heard mentioned everywhere in distinct terms. This would be inconsistent if they were merely explanatory statements.

How then is it that [the truth] is not understood by this much? This is no fault, because it depends on the specific context: for Gārgya, who knew only the secondary Brahman, proceeded to instruct Ajātaśatru, who was desirous of hearing about the Supreme Brahman. It was entirely appropriate for Ajātaśatru, the knower of the Supreme Brahman, to say to Gārgya, the knower of the secondary Brahman: "That Supreme Brahman about which you set out to speak, you do not know."

If even the knowledge of the non-primary Brahman were to be rejected, then [the teacher] would not have said, "It is only this much," but rather would have said, "Nothing at all has been known by you. Therefore, there are these many Brahmans within the sphere of ignorance (*avidyā*). Furthermore, because the knowledge of the supreme Brahman is attained through these very means of knowledge, it is entirely appropriate to say, "By this much alone, [Brahman] is not known. That these [Brahmans] are objects of knowledge within the sphere of ignorance, and that their nature consists of name, form, and action, has been demonstrated in the third chapter.

Therefore, by saying, "It is not known by this much alone," it is shown that there is further Brahman to be known. And since that must not be told to one who has not approached [as a disciple], Gārgya, knowing the rules of proper conduct, said of his own accord: "I will come to you as a pupil"—that is, "I will approach you," just as any other pupil approaches a teacher.

Ajātaśatru said: "This is contrary and inverted. What is it? That a Brāhmaṇa—one belonging to the highest caste and authorized to be a teacher—should approach a Kṣatriya, who by nature is not a teacher, in the manner of a disciple, thinking, 'He will tell me the Brahman. This is forbidden in the treatises on the rules of conduct. Therefore, remain as you are, a teacher."

"I shall indeed inform you [of that] wherein, when known, Brahman becomes known—that which is the primary Brahman to be realized. Observing Gārgya with embarrassment, [Ajātaśatru], in order to inspire confidence, took him by the hand—seizing him—and rose up. Those two, Gārgya and Ajātaśatru, went to a certain place in the royal palace where a man was asleep.

Having approached that sleeping man, he addressed him with these names—"O Bṛhan! O Pāṇḍaravāsa! O Soma! O Rājan!"—with these [names]. Even though thus addressed, the sleeping man did not rise. Pressing him repeatedly with his hand, he caused him to wake; he awakened him, and by that means he rose up. Therefore, he whom Gārgya intended was not the agent, the enjoyer, or Brahman within this body.

But how is it understood that, through the man's sleeping, his departure, his being awakened, and his not rising, it is made known that the Brahman favored by Gārgya is not truly Brahman? Just as during the waking state the person intended by Gārgya—the agent and enjoyer who is Brahman—is present within the senses, so too is the person intended by Ajātaśatru present as its master, like a king among his servants. However, the cause for determining the distinction between the servant and the master—between those intended by Gārgya and Ajātaśatru—is not perceived because their specific qualities remain undistinguished due to their being intermingled.

That which is the state of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtva*) belongs only to the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), not to the object of sight (*dṛśyatva*); and that which is the state of being an object of sight belongs only to the non-enjoyer, not to the seer. Since both of these are intermingled here, it is impossible to demonstrate them by distinguishing them; therefore, there is the going to the sleeping man. Now, one might object: even when a man is asleep, if he is addressed by specific names, the enjoyer alone will respond, not the non-enjoyer—thus, no definitive conclusion would be reached.

No, because the specific characteristics intended by Gārgya have been determined: for that very Prāṇa, who is the immortal Self hidden by truth, who does not set while speech and the other organs are setting, whose body is water, who is clad in white, who is "Great" (Bṛhat) due to being without rival, and who is King Soma consisting of sixteen parts—he remains with his own functions engaged, exactly as previously identified, possessing a nature that never sets. Furthermore, at that time, no activity of any other entity opposed to him is intended by Gārgya.

Therefore, one ought to wake up when addressed by one's own name; yet he did not wake up. Consequently, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it follows that Brahman is not the enjoyer as intended by Gārgya. For if its nature were that of an enjoyer, it would surely enjoy its own object when it has reached it. Indeed, fire—which possesses the nature of burning and the nature of illuminating—does not fail to burn combustible things such as grass and reeds when they have reached its domain, nor does it fail to illuminate what is to be illuminated.

If fire does not burn or illuminate its own object when it has reached it, it is determined that it is not fire, nor a burner, nor an illuminator; likewise, if this Prāṇa intended by Gārgya is of the nature of a perceiver of objects such as sound that have been reached, then he would perceive his own object—namely, the words "Bṛhat," "Pāṇḍaravāsa," and so forth—just as fire invariably burns and illuminates grass, reeds, and the like when they have been reached.

Therefore, because it does not recognize the sound and other objects when they are presented to it, it is determined to have the nature of a non-experiencer (*abhoktṛ*); for that whose nature has been ascertained never deviates from it at any time. Thus, the non-experiencing nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is established.

If it is argued that its lack of recognition is due to the failure to grasp the connection with a specific name used for the purpose of addressing it—namely, that one might think: "Just as when many people are sitting together, because the connection with one's own specific name is not grasped, a person being addressed hears the call but does not specifically understand 'this person is addressing me'—" [the reply follows].

If it is argued that the vital breath (prāṇa) does not grasp the word used for addressing because it has not grasped the connection that "these names, such as 'Bṛhan' and so forth, are my names," and not simply because it lacks the capacity for cognition—this is not so; for if one accepts [the vital breath] as a deity, its failure to grasp [the name] would be untenable. For one who accepts that the vital breath within the body is the enjoyer whose deity is the one presiding over the moon and so forth, a connection with specific names must necessarily be grasped for the sake of mutual communication.

Otherwise, worldly transaction regarding summoning and so forth would be untenable. If it is argued that [the opponent's position] is also incorrect because there is no comprehension even in the case of the view that [the self] is distinct—[we reply: for one who holds that the enjoyer is distinct from the vital breaths, comprehension would indeed be logical when addressed by names such as "Great One" (*bṛhan*), since at those times the names "Greatness" and so forth would have that [distinct self] as their referent; yet, we never observe anyone being addressed with words such as "Greatness" and then comprehending [it].

If it is argued that, therefore, the failure to respond to the address is not a reason for [the Self] not being the enjoyer—[we reply: no, because for one who possesses those [organs], such a limited conceit (abhimāna) is untenable. He for whom there is an enjoyer distinct from the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is a living being (*prāṇin*) endowed with the instruments such as the vital breath; he does not have a conceit consisting merely in the deity of the vital breath, just as [one does not identify oneself] with the hand. Therefore, when addressed by the name of the vital breath, the failure to respond is entirely appropriate for one who has a conceit in the whole [body], but not for the vital breath itself when addressed by its own specific name. Furthermore, this is because the Self does not conceive of itself as having the nature of a deity.

If it is argued that this is incorrect because we observe a lack of comprehension even when one's own name is used—just as a person in deep sleep sometimes does not respond even when addressed by his worldly name such as "Devadatta," and likewise the vital breath (*prāṇa*), though it is the experiencer, does not respond—it is not so, because a distinction between being asleep and awake is established for the self (*ātman*) and the vital breath. Due to its state of deep sleep, the self, with its organs ceased through being swallowed by the vital breath, does not comprehend its own name even when it is being employed.

However, it is not logical that while the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is awake and acting as the experiencer, its organs should be inactive or that it should fail to perceive being addressed. If it is argued that addressing someone with names that are not well-known is improper—since there are indeed well-known names such as "breath" (*prāṇa*) and so forth pertaining to the vital breath—it is improper to set those aside and address it with unfamiliar names like "the Great One" (*bṛhat*), because this would contravene common worldly practice.

If it is argued that, for this reason, there is simply no perception of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which is itself the enjoyer—[we reply: no, because the purpose is to refute [the claim regarding] the deity. Since the non-enjoyership of the internal vital breath is established merely by the lack of perception when addressed alone, the fact that he is addressed with names pertaining to the lunar deity is intended to refute Gārgya’s specific conviction that the lunar deity is the enjoyer in this body.

For it is not possible to address it by means of a worldly name; because, by the very rejection of the vital breath (prāṇa), the other organs are swallowed up by the vital breath, their activity becomes impossible, and thus the suspicion that it might be an enjoyer is untenable. Furthermore, there is no other deity [to which it could belong].

If it be argued that the distinction between deities possessing qualities is shown by the passage beginning with "He is without support" and ending with "possessing a self," we say no; for in all the Śrutis, through the illustration of the nave and spokes, it is admitted that the vital breath (prāṇa) alone is one, and because nothing other than the vital breath is admitted as the enjoyer, as seen in such passages as "He is covered by truth" and "The vital breath, indeed, is immortality."

Furthermore, because it is established that all the gods are one in Prāṇa, as stated in the passage: "For he indeed is all the gods; which one god? Prāṇa. Likewise, there can be no suspicion regarding a difference in the instruments [the senses], for just as in the case of different bodies, the synthesis of memory, knowledge, desire, and so forth would be impossible; for one person does not remember, know, desire, or synthesize what was seen by another. Therefore, a suspicion of being an enjoyer based on a difference in the instruments, or one based on mere consciousness, is never tenable.

[Objection: Let the aggregate itself be the enjoyer; what is the use of postulating something distinct? [Reply: No, because a distinction is observed upon pressing. For if the enjoyer were merely the aggregate of the vital breaths and the body, then, since there would be no difference between the mere aggregates, there would be no difference in the state of consciousness between one who has been pressed and one who has not been pressed.

However, if there were an enjoyer distinct from the aggregate, then a distinction [between states] would be logical, because of the multiplicity of specific relations with the aggregate, and because of the possibility of differences in the fruits of actions—superior, middling, and inferior—resulting in pleasure, pain, and delusion, as well as the resulting sensations of crushing or not crushing; but this is not the case for the aggregate alone, since neither a relation nor a difference in the fruits of action is possible therein.

A distinction is appropriate; likewise, there is a distinction caused by the sharpness or dullness of the senses regarding sound and so forth. And this distinction exists: for this reason, Ajātaśatru awakened the sleeping man—who was not waking up from mere touch—by repeatedly pressing him with his hand.

Therefore, it is established that he who was awakened by the pressing—blazing as it were, quivering as it were, appearing as if coming from somewhere, and transforming the body into something contrary to its previous state by endowing it with specific features such as the activity of consciousness—is distinct and separate from the Brahman favored by Gārgya. Furthermore, because it is a composite entity, the Prāṇa's subservience to another is logically established.

We have already stated that the vital breath (*prāṇa*), acting as an internal supporter for the body like the pillars of a house, is a composite of the body and its constituents—just as in the case of the spokes and the rim of a wheel, and just as everything is centered in this [body] which stands in the place of the nave. Therefore, we understand that, like a house or similar structures, it is composed of parts that are distinct from the collection of its own constituent members.

Having observed that the constituent parts of a house—such as pillars, walls, grass, and wood—possess their existence and so forth independently of their own birth, growth, decay, destruction, name, form, and function, and exist for the sake of the seer, hearer, thinker, and knower who perceive them; we likewise conclude that the constituent parts of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and their aggregate possess their existence and so forth independently of their own birth, growth, decay, destruction, name, form, and function, and exist for the sake of the seer, hearer, thinker, and knower who perceive them.

It must be so. If it is argued that since the deity possesses consciousness, it would be equal [to the individual soul] and thus could not attain the status of being subordinate—[we reply: its possession of consciousness is accepted because we see it being addressed by specific names; and if it is further argued that since it possesses consciousness, its subordination to another (the individual soul) is untenable due to their equality—we say no, because it is the unconditioned, absolute Self that is intended to be made known. For the nature of the Self as consisting of action, factors of action, and results is produced by the limiting adjuncts of name and form and is superimposed through ignorance.

The world’s cycle of existence (saṃsāra), characterized by the conceit of action, agent, and fruit, has that [ignorance] as its cause; it must be removed by the knowledge of the nature of the Self which is free from limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika). Therefore, with the desire to make known that very nature, the Upaniṣad begins—starting with "I shall tell you of Brahman" and "By this much it is not known," and concluding with "This much indeed, my dear, is immortality. Furthermore, there is nothing else intended or stated in the interval between these two.

Therefore, the objection that "because of their equality, the status of quality and qualified cannot be admitted" is out of place. For the relationship of quality and qualified exists for the sake of conventional usage only in the case of that which possesses distinctions and is conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), not in the opposite case. Indeed, that which is intended to be made known in every Upanishad is the indefinable (*nirupākhya*), as seen from the concluding statement, "He is 'not this, not this'. Therefore, it is established that there is another, distinct from these [beings] consisting of intelligence—such as the Sun and others who are themselves composed of intelligence—the one who consists of pure consciousness (*vijñānamaya*).

Having thus established the existence of a self distinct [from the body], Ajātaśatru said to Gārgya: "At what time—namely, when this person consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) has fallen into this sleep and slept prior to being awakened by the clapping of hands—the term 'consisting of consciousness' (*vijñānamaya*) refers to that which is made of, or predominantly composed of, the internal organ called the intellect (*buddhi*), so defined as 'that by which one cognizes' (*vijñāyate*); and what constitutes its being 'predominantly composed' of that? It consists in being perceived within it, being perceived by it, and being the perceiver."

But how, when the suffix *mayaṭ* has multiple meanings, is it understood that it has the sense of "mostly consisting of" (*prāya*) alone? Because in such passages as "This Self, which is indeed Brahman, consists of knowledge (*vijñānamaya*), consists of mind (*manomaya*)," we observe its usage in the sense of "mostly consisting of"; because it is not well-known for [the Self] to be a modification (*vikāra*) of supreme knowledge; because the statement "this which consists of knowledge" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of something already established; and because the senses of "component part" (*avayava*) and "analogy" (*upamā*) are impossible here—by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it has the sense of "mostly consisting of" alone.

Therefore, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which consists of volition, doubt, and so forth, is made of that [intellect]; the person (puruṣa) is so called because he dwells in the city [of the body]. The question, "Where was this [person] then? is intended to make known his true nature—that before awakening, the Self has a nature contrary to action, agent, and fruit—and thus it is sought to be shown through the absence of any effect; for prior to awakening, no effect such as action or pleasure is perceived at all.

Therefore, because [the soul] is not joined with action, its very nature as such is understood—that nature which it possessed when it was not yet transmigrating, and from which nature it has fallen away to become a transmigrating being characterized by a different nature. With this intention, he questions Gārgya, who lacked immediate insight, in order to awaken his intellect: "Where was this [person] then? Whence did he come? Both of these points ought to have been asked by Gārgya himself; nevertheless, since Gārgya did not ask them, Ajātaśatru does not remain indifferent.

He proceeded with the thought, "I must certainly awaken him," for he had pledged, "I shall indeed make him understand. Thus, although Gārgya was being instructed, he did not comprehend either of these two things—that where this Self was prior to awakening, and from whence it came when it returned; Gārgya did not know, nor did he understand, whether to speak or to ask.

(17) Then Ajātaśatru spoke in order to deliver the intended meaning: "Where was this person, consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), when he was thus asleep? Where was he then, and from whence did he come?"

Listen to what is being said regarding that which we asked—"Whence did this come?"—at the time when he was thus asleep: at that time, having taken by means of *vijñāna*—that is, by the specific consciousness residing in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) produced by the nature of the limiting adjuncts—the *vijñāna* of these vital breaths such as speech, meaning having grasped the capacity of speech and the others directed toward their respective objects, [he entered] that which is within, in the middle, in the heart; the space of the heart—that which is called "space" refers to one's own supreme Self.

He lies in that very Self, which is space—both the innate and the acquired. It is not merely in space alone, according to the force of another scriptural passage: "Then, my dear, he becomes merged in the hundred. The intention is that, having cast off the specific nature of the individual self created by the connection with the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the subtle body (liṅga), he abides only in the absolute, innate Self, which is devoid of distinctions. How is it understood that when he casts off his lordship over the body and senses, he then abides in his own Self? By the well-known usage of the term.

He asks: "What is this well-known designation? He replies: When—that is, at which time—he grasps or takes up those cognitions of speech and the other senses, then at that time this person has the name "he sleeps" (*svapiti*); this name of this person becomes well-known then. This is merely a figurative name for him; he is called "he sleeps" because he goes back to (*api-gacchati*) his own self (*svam*).

Anticipating the objection that the nature of the Self as distinct from the attributes of transmigratory existence is understood merely through the conventional expression "he himself sleeps," and that there is no logical reasoning for this here, [the author] says: "In that state, at the time of sleep, the breath is indeed withdrawn"; by "breath" (prāṇa) is meant the olfactory organ, because the context concerns speech and the other organs; for when there is a connection with speech and the rest, its possession of the attributes of transmigratory existence is indicated due to those being its limiting adjuncts (upādhi); and speech and the others are indeed withdrawn by it at that time.

How so? Speech is withdrawn, the eye is withdrawn, the ear is withdrawn, and the mind is withdrawn. Therefore, when speech and the other senses are withdrawn, because the nature of action, agent, and fruit ceases to exist, it is understood that the Self remains established in its own Self.

But surely, even in the dream state characterized by mere perception, when there is a dissociation from the body and its organs, this self is seen to possess the attributes of transmigratory existence—just as in the waking state it is happy or miserable, separated from kinsmen, grieves, and is deluded. Therefore, this self is indeed possessed of the qualities of grief and delusion; its grief, delusion, happiness, misery, and so forth are not merely superimposed through the error produced by the conjunction of the body and the organs.

No, because it is false. When that aforementioned Self moves—that is, exists—by means of the dream-state characterized by seeing, then those worlds of his are the fruits of his actions. What are they? At that time, he becomes, as it were, a great king; this world of his is like the state of being a great king, but it is not the actual state of being a great king as in the waking state.

Likewise, O Great Brahmin, he enters into various high and low states—high such as divinity and the like, and low such as the state of an animal and the like, as if they were high and low—even though these worlds, such as that of a great king, are entirely false, because of the use of the word "as if" (*iva*) and because of the observation of their deviation from reality. Therefore, in a dream, one is not truly bound by grief, delusion, and so forth, born of separation from kinsmen and other such causes.

Now, when one is in deep sleep—or when one moves about in a dream—even then this [Self] is indeed pure. Furthermore, when, having abandoned the state of dreaming characterized by perception, at whatever time one is in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), that is, well-sleeping, one has attained *saṃprasāda*, which is one's own inherent nature—just as water becomes clear by abandoning the turbidity caused by contact with other things, so too it becomes serene through its own inherent nature. When does one become in deep sleep? At whatever time one does not know anything of anyone—that is, one perceives nothing.

Or rather, one must supply the words: "he does not know any other related object whatsoever, such as sound and so forth"; however, the former [interpretation] is more logical, because it is the absence of specific cognition that is intended when one is asleep. Thus far, it has been stated that one becomes deep in sleep (suṣupta) upon the absence of specific cognition.

Now, by what sequence does one become fast asleep? It is said: there are the channels called *hitā*—so named because they are beneficial—which are vessels (*sirā*) consisting of the transformation of the essence of food within the body. They number seventy-two thousand—that is, seventy thousand plus two thousand; these seventy-two thousand [channels] extend from the heart. The "heart" is a lump of flesh, shaped like a lotus; they say that the *purītat* is the membrane surrounding this lump of flesh.

The body characterized by that [heart] is intended here by the word *purītat*—the meaning of "they rest upon the *purītat*" is that they extend outwards like the veins of an ashvattha leaf, pervading the entire physical body. In this context, the heart is the location of the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); and the other external organs are dependent upon the intellect situated there.

By that [intellect], the intellect (*buddhi*)—under the influence of karma—extends the ears and other organs through those channels (*nāḍīs*), like a fisherman’s net, from their locations such as the ear-cavities; having extended them, it presides over them during the waking state. The one consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) pervades that [intellect] by means of the manifestation of the radiance of its own self-consciousness; and at the time of its contraction, it contracts along with it. This is the sleep of this one consisting of consciousness; the experience of the expansion of the waking state is its enjoyment (*bhoga*).

For it conforms to the nature of the limiting adjuncts of the intellect (*buddhi*), just as the reflection of the moon and other objects conforms to water and the like. Therefore, following the withdrawal of that waking intellect through those channels (*nāḍīs*), it goes forth and lies—that is, remains—in the *purītat*, which is the body; the meaning is that it exists pervading the body without distinction, like fire pervading a red-hot lump of iron.

Although [the Self] exists in its own essential nature, it is said to "lie in the pericardium" (purītat) because it follows the tendencies of the intellect which is permeated by karma. For at the time of deep sleep, there is no connection with the body; as the text will later state: "For then he has crossed beyond all the sorrows of the heart."

Regarding this state as being free from all the sufferings of *saṃsāra*, there is an illustration: just as a young prince, or an extremely young child, or a great king whose subjects are entirely submissive, or a great Brahmin who has reached the highest maturity and is endowed with learning and discipline—having attained and entered that state of bliss which is "all-destroying" (*atighnī*), meaning it destroys suffering to the utmost degree—that state of happiness, he would lie down, remaining therein.

Furthermore, for these [beings] such as children who remain in their natural state, unsurpassed happiness is well-known in the world; for when they undergo modification, it is suffering that arises, not [happiness] by nature. Therefore, their natural state is taken as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) because it is well-established. It is not their sleep alone that is intended [as the example], because sleep is what is intended to be the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*), and because there would be no distinction [otherwise]. For if there were a distinction, there would be a difference between the example and the thing illustrated.

Therefore, sleep is not an illustration for them—just as this illustration [shows]: "this one consisting of consciousness lies down on this bed"—the word *etat* (this) is used for the purpose of qualifying the action; thus, during the time of sleep, he exists in his own natural Self, which transcends all attributes of transmigratory existence.

The answer to the question, "Where was this [self] then? has been stated; and by this resolution of the question, the natural purity and non-transmigratory nature of the one consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) have been declared. Now begins the undertaking for the purpose of resolving the question, "From where did it come? But surely, when someone resides in a certain village or city, when he goes elsewhere, he goes from that very village or city, not from somewhere else; such being the case, let the question simply be, "Where was this then?"

Since it is well known that its coming was from that very place where it was, the question "whence did this come? is indeed purposeless—is the Śruti being censured by you? No; rather, I wish to hear a different meaning for the second question, and therefore I urge its lack of purpose. In that case, the sense of "whence" is not taken as denoting the *apādāna* (the point of departure); for if it had the sense of *apādāna*, there would be redundancy, but not if it has another meaning.

"Let it be, then, that the question is for the sake of the cause—asking 'whence did this come? meaning 'for what purpose has it come here? It cannot even be for the sake of the cause, because of the incongruity with the answer; for in the answer, the origin of the entire world from the Self is heard, like sparks from a fire. Indeed, fire is not the cause for the scattering of sparks; rather, it is their point of departure."

Likewise, the Supreme Self is heard in scripture as the material cause (*apādāna*) of the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), in the statement "from this Self" (*asmād ātmanaḥ*). Therefore, because of the contradiction with the answer, it is impossible to describe the question "whence? as having the sense of a mere occasion (*nimitta*). [Objection: But even in the case of the *apādāna* interpretation, the fault of tautology remains exactly the same.

This is not a fault, because by means of the two questions, the intended aim is the negation of the nature of action, agent, and fruit with respect to the Self. For here, the objects of knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are presented: "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self alone," "He knew only the Self," and "One should meditate on the Self alone as the world"—these are the objects of knowledge; likewise, there is also the object of ignorance.

The fivefold ritual action, its fruit, and the three kinds of food consist of name, form, and action. Regarding that, everything that needs to be said concerning the sphere of ignorance (*avidyā*) has been stated. However, the Self (*ātman*), which is the sphere of knowledge (*vidyā*), has been introduced as something absolute, yet it has not been definitively determined. To determine it, the teacher began by saying, "I shall tell you of Brahman," and "I shall make it known. Therefore, that Brahman, which is the object of knowledge, must be made known according to its true nature.

And its true nature is intended here as being devoid of the distinctions of action, agent, and fruit, absolutely pure, and non-dual. Therefore, questions corresponding to that [nature] are raised by the Śruti: "Where was this then? Whence did it come? In this context, that in which something exists is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and that which exists is the thing located (*adhikartavya*); and in the world, a distinction between these two—the locus and the thing located—is observed.

Likewise: that from which something comes is the *apādāna* (ablative point); he who comes is the agent (*kartṛ*), and one different from him is observed. Similarly, the notion arises—just as in the world—that the self was previously another in another place, or came from somewhere else as another, by means of some distinct instrument or other factor. That notion must be set aside by the reply: "This self was not another elsewhere, nor did another come from another, nor is there any other instrument in the self."

Rather, it was already within its own self—as in the scriptural passages: "He has entered into his own self," "Then, my dear, he becomes united with That," "Embraced by the conscious Self (prājña-ātman)," and "He is established in the Supreme Self. For this very reason, nothing comes from anything else; this is demonstrated by Scripture itself in the words, "from this Self," because there is no other entity apart from the Self. [Corresponds to ASS edition p.

269] Now, one might object that there is another entity distinct from the Self, such as the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth—but no, for the vital breath and the rest are produced from that very Self.
To explain how that is so, it is said:
(2.1.20) — there is an illustration for this: just as in the world a spider (*ūrṇanābhi*), well known as a single being, might go forth or emerge by means of a thread not distinct from its own self;

And there is no other causal factor distinct from itself for its emergence—just as from a single fire of one form, small sparks, fragments, or parts of fire issue forth, or rather, they emerge variously and diversely—just as these two examples demonstrate activity even in the absence of a difference in the causal agent, and how prior to that activity there is unity by nature—so too is the true nature of this Self consisting of consciousness prior to awakening.

Therefore—this is the meaning—all the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), such as speech and the rest; all the worlds, such as the earth and the rest; all the fruits of action; all the gods, such as Agni and others, who are the presiding deities over the vital breaths, the worlds, and so forth; and all beings, the entire range of living creatures from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—“all these very selves” (in this reading, the meaning is: the selves whose specific characteristics are being awakened through contact with limiting adjuncts)—they “issue forth.”

Since this entire world of moving and non-moving beings issues incessantly from this Self like sparks from fire, dissolves back into it like bubbles in water, and exists during its period of maintenance having that very Self as its essence—for that Self, which is Brahman—the *upaniṣad*—so called because it is a word that "brings near" (*upa-nigamayati*) [the meaning]—is the expressive term by virtue of the authority of the scripture; for through the power of this word, a specific quality is understood, namely, the state of being that which brings [the reality] near.

He states what the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the saffron robe is: "The truth of truth. For that secret doctrine is everywhere difficult to understand because its meaning is non-worldly; therefore, he explains its meaning: "The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed truth, and of them, this [Self] is the truth. To provide an explanation of this very statement, there will follow the two subsequent Brāhmaṇas.

Let it be that the two subsequent Brāhmaṇas are for the purpose of explaining the Upaniṣad, as it was stated, "Its Upaniṣad is..."; however, in this regard we do not know: does this Upaniṣad belong to the transmigrating self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), who was previously mentioned and arose from the clapping of hands and enjoys sound and other objects, or rather to some other transmigrating being?

What follows from this? If [the Self] is a transmigrating being (*saṃsārin*), then it is the transmigrating being alone that is to be known; through the knowledge of that alone comes the attainment of everything, and that very being is what is denoted by the word "Brahman," and the knowledge of that is "Brahma-vidyā. On the other hand, if it is a non-transmigrating being, then the knowledge whose object is that is Brahma-vidyā, and from that knowledge of Brahman comes the attainment of the state of all things. All of this will come to pass through the authority of the scripture (*śāstra*).

However, on this view, the scriptural texts that establish the identity with the Supreme Brahman—such as "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self alone" and "He realized the Self alone as 'I am Brahman'"—would be contradicted; furthermore, if there were no transmigrating soul other than [the Supreme], instruction would be rendered purposeless. Since this is a point of great delusion even for the learned, being a subject regarding which neither answer nor question has been explicitly stated, we shall therefore investigate it to the best of our ability for the sake of clarifying the intellect of those desiring to know Brahman, based upon the passages that expound the knowledge of Brahman.

First of all, there is no other being outside of saṃsāra—because scripture declares the origination [of the world] from that which is distinguished by a different state, namely the one who enjoys sound and other objects, who was awakened by the pressing of the hands; nor does there exist another supreme being who is a ruler free from hunger and other such afflictions.

Why? Because, having made the promise "I shall make Brahman known," the Śruti awakens the sleeping person by a touch of the hand, shows him as characterized by being the enjoyer of sound and other objects, and then, by means of the dream state, leads him to another state called deep sleep; from that very Self characterized by the state of deep sleep, the Śruti demonstrates the origin [of beings] through the two examples of sparks from a fire and the spider and its web, with the words "In this very way, from this... and so forth.

Furthermore, no other cause of the origin of the world is heard of in the intervening context; for the subject matter (prakaraṇa) concerns that which consists of consciousness (vijñānamaya) alone. Moreover, in another scriptural text belonging to the same context—the Kauṣītakins—after introducing the persons such as the one in the sun and so forth, [Ajātaśatru] says: "O Bālāki, he who is the maker of these persons, and whose work this is, he indeed is to be known. This shows that it is the awakened one consisting of consciousness who is to be known, not some other entity.

And likewise, after stating, "But for the sake of the Self, everything becomes dear," the text shows that it is precisely this well-known dear Self which is that which is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. Furthermore, at the time of introducing knowledge, there would be consistency with such statements as "One should worship [it] as the Self alone," "This is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth," and "He knew the Self alone, saying, 'I am Brahman,'" provided that a supreme [Self] exists.

And it will say: "If a person were to know himself, [realizing] 'I am this'. In all the Vedāntas, it is shown that the inner self (pratyagātman) alone is to be known—as "I"—and not as something external to be known like sound and so forth, in the manner of "That is Brahman. Likewise, in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad itself, through the passage beginning with "One should not seek to know speech, but should know the speaker," it shows that the agent who is distinct from the instruments such as speech is the very one to be known.

If it is argued that [the transmigrating soul] becomes non-transmigrating when distinguished by a different state—namely, if it be thought that the one consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) who experiences sound and other objects in the waking state is the very same entity that, having entered another state called deep sleep, becomes the non-transmigrating Supreme Ruler, distinct and other than before—we say no, because such a thing is not observed. Indeed, no object possessing such properties has ever been observed, except for the doctrines of the Nihilists (*vaināśika*). For in the world, a cow remains a cow whether standing or walking; it does not become a different species, such as a horse, merely by lying down.

And by logic as well: whatever property a given object is known to possess through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it possesses that very same property even in other places, times, and states; if it were to deviate from that possession of such properties, all practical discourse based on valid cognition would collapse. Thus, the experts in logic—the Sāṃkhyas, Mīmāṃsakas, and others—demonstrate through hundreds of arguments the non-existence of anything that is not subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*).

If it is argued that [the transmigrating soul] is unfit [to be the agent], because even for a transmigrating being there is an absence of the knowledge that constitutes agency over the acts of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world—namely, that which you have established with such great elaboration, that the transmigrating being itself, while enjoying sound and other objects, is the agent of the world here when distinguished by a different state—that is incorrect; for the absence of the means and the capacity for the knowledge of agency over the acts of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world is evident to all people in the case of the transmigrating being.

If it is argued that this is untenable because how could a transmigrating being like us create a world characterized by the specific arrangement of the earth and other elements—something impossible even for the mind to conceive—[we reply]: No, because of scripture (*śāstra*). Scripture shows the origin and so forth of the world from a transmigrating being, stating, "In this very way, from this Self... Therefore, everything should be accepted with faith; such is one position.

"He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving"; "He who transcends hunger and thirst"; "Unattached, for he does not cling"; "By the command of this Imperishable One"; "He who, dwelling within all beings... the Inner Controller, the Immortal"; "He who, having cast those persons aside, passed beyond"; "Verily, this is the Great Unborn Self"; "This is the bridge, the supporter"; "The ruler of all, the lord of all"; "The Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless"; "That [Being] emitted heat (tejas)"; "Verily, the Self alone was this in the beginning."

"He was indeed the first," "He is untouched by the suffering of the world, being external to it"—from hundreds of such scriptural passages, and from the Smṛti passage, "I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds"—there exists a Supreme Being who is beyond transmigratory existence, according to Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning; and He is the cause of the universe.

If it is argued that the phrase "from this very Self" shows the origin of the transmigrating soul alone—no, for since the Supreme is the subject under discussion in the words "this space within the heart," the reference in "from this Self" is rightly understood as referring to the Supreme alone. Furthermore, as an answer to the question "Where was he then? the Supreme Self, denoted by the word "space," is stated in the passage: "He lies in that space which is within the heart."

From such scriptural passages as, "Then, my dear, he becomes united with the hundredfold [Brahman]," "Day after day they go to this world of Brahman and do not find it," "He is completely embraced by the conscious Self (prājña-ātman)," and "He is established in the Supreme Self," it is determined that the word *ākāśa* refers to the Supreme Self; furthermore, because the word *ātman* is used for that very same thing after introducing it as "The small *ākāśa* within this [heart]," it is the Supreme Self alone that is the subject under discussion.

Therefore, it is logical that the statement "from this very Self" refers to the creation of the Supreme Self alone; for we have already stated that the transmigrating soul lacks the capacity for knowledge regarding the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the world]. Furthermore, here the knowledge of Brahman is introduced in the passages, "One should meditate on it as the Self alone" and "He knew the Self alone as 'I am Brahman'"; and since the cognition of Brahman has Brahman as its object, the work was commenced with the words, "I shall tell you of Brahman" and "I shall make Brahman known."

In this regard, Brahman—which is beyond transmigratory existence, the cause of the world, transcending hunger and other such needs, and whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free—is of a nature entirely opposite to that of the transmigrating self. Therefore, one should not grasp [the identity] "I am Brahman"; for how could one who is lowly, by remembering the Supreme Lord, the Ruler, as being the transmigrating self, not become a partaker of fault? Consequently, it is not logical to say "I am Brahman."

Therefore, one should seek to propitiate [Brahman] through offerings of flowers, water, handfuls of water, salutations, oblations, recitation, meditation, yoga, and so forth. By propitiating [Him], one comes to know Brahman as the Lord of all; but one should not contemplate the non-transmigrating Brahman as having the nature of a transmigrating self—just as one would not contemplate fire as coldness or space as possessing form. Even the scripture that teaches the identity of the self with Brahman will then be merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). In this way, there will be no contradiction with any system of logic, worldly conventions, or reasoning.

No, because its very entry is heard from the declarations of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas. Having begun with "He made the bodies," [the text continues] "The Person entered the bodies," and "He became the counterpart of every form; that was his form for the sake of perception"; and "Having fashioned all forms and made names, the Wise One sits calling them by those names. Thus, in all the Vedic branches, there are thousands of mantra-declarations showing that the creator of the world alone—the one who is not subject to transmigratory existence—enters the body.

Likewise, there are the declarations of the Brāhmaṇas: "Having created that, He entered into that very thing"; "He, having split open this very aperture, entered through this door"; "This deity... having entered these three deities by means of this living self (jīva-ātman)"; "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth"—and so forth.

Since the word "Self" (ātman) is employed for Brahman in all the Vedas, and since the word "Self" denotes the innermost Self, and because of the scriptural statement, "He is the inner Self of all beings," there is no transmigrating soul apart from the Supreme Self; and because of such scriptural passages as "One only, without a second," "Brahman alone is this," and "The Self alone is this," it is indeed proper to ascertain that "I am Brahman."

Since the meaning of the scripture stands thus, it follows that the Supreme Self is subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*); and this being the case, the futility of the scripture results. Alternatively, if it were not subject to transmigratory existence, the futility of the instruction would follow as a manifest defect. If, first of all, the Supreme Self—the inner self of all beings—were to experience the sufferings produced by contact with all bodies, then the transmigratory nature of the Supreme would clearly be established.

And in that case, the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and all logical arguments (nyāyas) which establish that the Supreme is not subject to transmigratory existence would be contradicted. Even if it could somehow be established that he is not connected with the sufferings born of his connection with the body of vital breath (prāṇa), the defect of the futility of instruction regarding the Supreme Self—since there is nothing for him to achieve or avoid—cannot be averted. On this point, some offer a solution: the Supreme Self has not entered into beings directly in his own essential form.

Rather, having entered into a state of modification, it attained the nature of the cognizing self (*vijñānātman*); and that cognizing self is both different from and non-different from the Supreme. Insofar as it is different, it is connected with transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*); insofar as it is non-different, it is fit to be determined as "I am Brahman. In this way, everything will be free from contradiction.

In that regard, concerning the position that the conscious self (*vijñānātman*) is a modification, these are the possible courses: the supreme self (*paramātman*), which is composed of many substances and possesses parts like the substance of the earth, undergoes a transformation in one part, and the conscious self is that [part], like a jar or similar object; or else, a single part of the supreme self, while remaining in its prior configuration, undergoes modification, like hair or saline soil; or the entire supreme self undergoes transformation, like milk or similar substances.

In that case, when some particular substance within a collection of multiple substances of the same genus attains the nature of consciousness, then because of their being of the same genus, their oneness is merely figurative and not in the ultimate sense; and such being the case, there is a contradiction with the established doctrine.

Now, suppose the supreme Self is a whole (*avayavin*) consisting of parts that are eternally and inseparably established (*nityāyutasiddha*), and that a single part of it in that state is the conscious self (*vijñānātman*) which transmigrates—even then, because the whole is permeated by all its parts, whatever defect or quality resides in a part belongs to the whole itself. Thus, the supreme Self would be connected with the defect of the transmigratory nature of the conscious self; this too is an undesirable hypothesis. Furthermore, in the view that [the Self] undergoes all transformations like milk, there is a contradiction with all the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, and that is undesirable.

"All these positions are contrary to the Śruti, Smṛti, and logic, as evidenced by such passages as: 'Partless, actionless, and tranquil'; 'For the divine Puruṣa is formless, existing both within and without, and unborn'; 'Like space, he is omnipresent and eternal'; 'Verily, this great unborn Self is undecaying, immortal, and deathless'; 'He is never born, nor does He ever die'; and 'This is unmanifest,' and so forth."

It has been stated that if the conscious self (*vijñānātman*) were a mere part of the immovable Supreme Self (*paramātman*), its transmigrating to the regions where the fruits of karma are experienced would be impossible; or else, the Supreme Self itself would become subject to transmigratory existence. If it is argued that a part of the Supreme Self—like a spark from a fire—breaks off and the conscious self thus transmigrates, even so, by the breaking off of a limb of the Supreme, it would incur injury; and upon its transmigration, there would result a vacuity due to the rearrangement of the parts in another region of the Supreme Self, which contradicts scriptural texts declaring it to be without wound (*avraṇa*).

Since there is no space devoid of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) for the transmigrating conscious self (*vijñānātman*), which is a constituent part of that [Supreme Self], the Supreme Self would incur suffering through the pushing and displacing of other parts, like a piercing pain in the heart. If it is argued that this fault does not apply because of scriptural texts citing analogies such as sparks from a fire, we say no; for scripture serves only to make things known. Scripture is not intended to alter the nature of entities, but rather to make known those things as they truly are, which were previously unknown. What follows from this? Listen, and then you shall see what results.

The properties of entities, such as the formed and the formless, are well-known in the world as they truly are. Therefore, the scripture, having set out to make known another reality that is not in contradiction with those [worldly things] by employing worldly examples, does not employ a worldly example for the purpose of making known something in contradiction with worldly things; for even if such an example were employed, it would be useless due to its lack of correspondence with the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*).

For it is not possible, even by means of a hundred examples, to establish that fire is cold or that the sun does not burn, because the nature of the thing has been apprehended otherwise through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); nor does one means of valid cognition contradict another, for one means of valid cognition merely makes known the very object that is the domain of another means of valid cognition. Furthermore, apart from relying on worldly words and word-meanings, it is not possible for scripture (*āgama*) to cause one to understand any other unknown reality.

Therefore, for one who follows established reasoning, it is impossible to demonstrate that the Supreme Self possesses parts or is composed of parts and their whole from the perspective of ultimate reality. If it is argued that this is heard in scripture and recorded in tradition—such as "minute sparks" and "a part of Me alone"—we say no, because these passages are intended to convey the sense of oneness. For in the world, a spark of fire is seen to be fit for the cognition of oneness with fire itself, saying "it is indeed fire"; and likewise, a part is fit for the cognition of oneness with the whole.

This being so, those words which express that the conscious self (vijñānātman) is a modification or a part of the Supreme Self (paramātman) are intended to establish the realization of its identity with the Supreme Self. Furthermore, this is evident from the beginning and the conclusion [of the texts]: for in all the Upaniṣads, having first proposed the doctrine of unity, and having established that the world is a modification or a part of the Supreme Self through illustrations and reasons, they finally conclude once again with unity.

For example, right here [in this very text], having first made the proposition "All this is what this Self is," and having established the reasons for the notion of oneness—such as the nature of the modified and the modifier—through arguments concerning the causes of origination, maintenance, and dissolution, and through illustrative examples, [the text] will conclude with "Without interior or exterior" and "This Self is Brahman. Therefore, by both the opening and the conclusion, this meaning is determined: that the statements teaching origination, maintenance, and dissolution are intended to strengthen the realization of the oneness of the Supreme Self.

Furthermore, otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). For it is undisputed among all proponents of the Upaniṣads that in every Upaniṣad, the realization of the identity of the individual self (*vijñānātman*) with the supreme self (*paramātman*) is enjoined. And since it is possible for those [passages concerning] origination and so forth to form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*) with that injunction, there is no evidence for assuming them to be separate sentences; moreover, one would have to postulate a different result [for them]. Therefore, the scriptural texts on origination and so forth are intended solely to establish the unity of the Self.

And regarding this, those who know the tradition relate a story: it is said that a certain prince was abandoned by his parents immediately after birth and raised in the house of a hunter; not knowing his own lineage, he identified himself as belonging to the hunter caste and followed only the duties of the hunter caste, rather than identifying "I am a king" and following the duties of the royal caste.

Furthermore, when someone who is supremely compassionate, recognizing that the prince is worthy of attaining royal splendor, awakens him to his true identity, saying: "You are not a hunter; you are the son of such-and-such a king; you have somehow entered the house of a hunter"—once thus awakened, he abandons the actions conditioned by his birth as a hunter and follows his own ancestral path, thinking, "I am a king."

Thus, it is said that this [Self], like a spark from a fire, being of the same nature as that [Supreme Self], has become differentiated and entered here into the thicket of the body, senses, and so forth; though itself non-transmigratory, it conforms to the transmigratory attributes of the body, senses, and so forth—thinking, "I am the aggregate of body and senses," "I am thin," "I am stout," "I am happy," "I am miserable"—because it does not know its own identity as the Supreme Self.

When one has been enlightened by the teacher that "you are not of this nature; you are indeed the Supreme Brahman, beyond saṃsāra," and having abandoned the pursuit of the three desires, one realizes, "I am Brahman. In this regard, the realization of Brahman becomes firm—just as a prince [realizes his true status]—upon being told, "Like a spark, you have fallen from the Supreme Brahman," because a spark is seen to be identical with fire even before its fall from the fire.

Therefore, the analogies of gold, a gem, iron, fire, and sparks are intended to strengthen the conviction of oneness, not to establish distinctions such as origination and so forth. This is because, like a mass of salt, there is the determination of a continuous, single flavor of designation, as expressed in the text: "It should be viewed as one alone. Furthermore, if it were intended to demonstrate that Brahman possesses a manifold variety of attributes such as origination—like a variegated painting or like trees and oceans—it would not have been described as "of a single flavor, without interior or exterior, like a mass of salt."

If [the world] were not withdrawn [into Brahman], He would not have declared, "It is to be seen as one alone," nor would there be the condemnatory statement, "He who sees here as if there were multiplicity. Therefore, in all the Vedānta texts, the conceptualization of origination, persistence, dissolution, and so forth, is solely for the purpose of strengthening the realization of the oneness of the single form, not for the purpose of producing that [conceptual] cognition itself.

Furthermore, it is not logical to conceive of a single part of the partless Supreme Self as being subject to transmigratory existence when that Self is inherently free from transmigration; for the Supreme Self is by its very nature devoid of spatial location (*adeśa*). If one were to conceive of the partless Supreme Being as having a portion that is subject to transmigration, it would effectively result in the conception that the Supreme Being Himself is the transmigrator. If it is argued that a portion of the Supreme Being is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), like the space within a jar or a water-pot, even then, the notion does not arise in the minds of the discerning that a specific part of the Supreme Self constitutes a separate entity engaged in worldly transaction.

If it is argued that a figurative cognition (*upacaritā buddhiḥ*) is observed for both the non-discriminating and the discriminating, we say no; because for the non-discriminating, it is a false cognition (*mithyābuddhi*), and for the discriminating, it serves merely as a basis for conventional usage (*saṃvyavahāramātra*). For example, even among the discriminating, when one occasionally speaks of "the black sky" or "the red sky," the attribution of blackness or redness to the sky is understood to serve merely as a basis for conventional usage; in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the sky cannot possibly be black or red.

Therefore, the wise should not entertain notions regarding the realization of the nature of Brahman such as that of part and whole, part and possessor of parts, or modification and the modified, for all the Upaniṣads have as their ultimate purport the removal of all conceptual constructions. Hence, having abandoned all conceptualization, one should realize its featureless nature, like space, on the basis of hundreds of scriptural passages such as: "All-pervading and eternal like space," and "It is not tainted by the suffering of the world, being external to it."

One should not conceive of the Self as distinct from Brahman—like a cold spot within fire, which is essentially hot, or like a patch of darkness within the sun, which is essentially light—for all the Upaniṣads have as their ultimate purport the removal of all such conceptual constructions and the realization of the essential reality.

Therefore, all worldly transactions regarding the Self—which is by nature free from the attributes of transmigratory existence—are caused solely by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). This is known from such Vedic mantras as: "He assumed a form corresponding to each form," and "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and created names, sits calling them by those names. Thus, the transmigratory state of the Self is not intrinsic; it is merely an illusion, like the perception of redness in a crystal produced by contact with an adjunct such as lac-dye, and does not exist in ultimate reality.

From such scriptural texts and traditional authorities as "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were," "It does not increase by action, nor does it become less," "It is not smeared by evil action," and "Abiding in tranquility toward all beings—even toward a dog and an outcaste"—it follows that the Supreme Self is indeed partless (*niṣkala*). Therefore, when its lack of parts is accepted, one cannot specifically entertain the alternatives of whether the individual soul (*vijñānātman*) is a part, a modification, a power, or something else entirely.

We have already stated that scriptural and traditional declarations concerning [the Lord’s] portions (*aṃśa*) and so forth are intended to establish unity, and do not aim to demonstrate difference, because they form a single syntactical whole (*ekavākya*) whose intended meaning is one. Now, if all the Upaniṣads are devoted solely to making known the oneness of the Supreme Self, for what purpose is a contrary doctrine—the difference of the individual self (*vijñānātman*)—imagined? Some say it is to avoid contradicting the authority of the Ritual Section (*karmakāṇḍa*); for the sentences teaching ritual action depend upon various actions, instruments, results, enjoyers, agents, and substrates.

For if there were no distinction between the individual self (*vijñānātman*) and the Self, and the supreme Self (*paramātman*) were the only one that does not transmigrate, how could [the scriptures] impel one toward actions with desired fruits or turn one away from actions with undesired fruits? Or for whose sake—being bound—would the Upaniṣads be commenced? Moreover, in the view of those who maintain the oneness of the supreme Self, how could there be an instruction regarding that oneness of the supreme Self? And what would be the fruit of receiving such an instruction? For instruction is intended for the destruction of the bondage of one who is bound.

In the absence of that [the Self], the Upaniṣadic scripture would indeed be without a subject matter. If this is so, then the path of objection and resolution for the position of the Upaniṣadic proponents is identical to that of the proponents of the ritual section (Karmakāṇḍa): by which [reasoning], in the absence of difference, the ritual section finds no support for itself regarding its authority, just as the Upaniṣads do as well. If this is so, then let the authority belong only to that ritual section whose authority does not involve a contradiction of its own meaning.

However, if one were to assume the authority of the Upaniṣads, there would be a contradiction with their own literal meaning; thus, let them not possess authority. For the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), being authoritative, cannot become non-authoritative; indeed, a lamp does not illuminate what is to be illuminated and yet fail to illuminate it. Furthermore, because of the contradiction with means of knowledge such as perception—Upaniṣads, in establishing the oneness of Brahman, do not merely contradict themselves, but also subvert the authority of the ritual section.

Furthermore, they contradict those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish distinctions through perception and other such means. Therefore, the Upaniṣads must either lack authority altogether, or have some other purpose; they certainly cannot have the realization of the oneness of Brahman as their purpose. This is not so, because the answer has already been stated. For whether a means of knowledge is authoritative or non-authoritative depends on its capacity to produce or fail to produce a valid cognition (*pramā*); otherwise, it would follow that pillars and the like would possess authority with respect to objects of knowledge such as sound. What follows from this? If the Upaniṣads indeed produce a valid cognition regarding the oneness of Brahman, how could they be considered non-authoritative?

If you argue that they do not perform [their functions] at all—just as fire does not produce cold—you who speak thus must be asked: Does your statement, intended to negate the authority of the Upaniṣads, not itself fail to negate the authority of the Upaniṣads? Or does fire fail to illuminate form? If it does perform [its function], then let your statement be a valid means of knowledge for the purpose of negation, and let fire be an illuminator of form.

If the authority of prohibitive statements is established, then the authority of the Upaniṣads is indeed established. Let your honors state: what is the solution to this? [Objection: But surely here, in my statement, there is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the comprehension of the meaning of the prohibition of the authority of the Upaniṣads, and in the case of fire, there is the perception of the manifestation of form as a valid cognition (*pramā*); so why this hostility of yours toward the Upaniṣads which are found to produce direct perception as a valid cognition regarding the realization of the oneness of Brahman? [Response: Because such a prohibition is untenable.

We have already stated that the cessation of sorrow, delusion, and so forth is the perceptible fruit produced through the successive stages of realizing the oneness of Brahman. Therefore, since this has been answered, there is no ground for doubting the authority of the Upaniṣads.

As for the claim that [the Upaniṣads] lack authority because they subvert their own meaning, that too is not correct, because there is no sublation of the understanding of their intended meaning. For from the Upaniṣads, there is no such comprehension as "Brahman is one only, without a second, and yet it is not so"—in the way that a dual, contradictory meaning is comprehended from the sentence "Fire is hot and cold. And we have stated this while merely conceding the point for the sake of argument.

However, this principle does not apply at the time of establishing the authority of a sentence—namely, that a single sentence may have multiple meanings. For if there were multiple meanings, there would be both its own primary meaning and another contradictory meaning that subverts it. But this is not the case; for those who hold sentences as authoritative, the established rule is that a single sentence conveys neither the contradictory nor the non-contradictory [simultaneously], because unity of sentence arises from unity of meaning. Indeed, the unity of a sentence is due to the singleness of its sense.

Furthermore, no Upaniṣadic passages negate the oneness of Brahman. As for the worldly statement—"Fire is hot and cold"—there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) therein, because one part of it merely restates an object already within the domain of other means of knowledge; "Fire is cold" constitutes one sentence, whereas "Fire is hot" is a reminder of an experience from another means of knowledge and does not itself convey a new meaning.

Therefore, this [sentence] does not form a single syntactical unit with "fire is cold," because its purpose is exhausted merely by reminding one of an experience established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As for the view that this sentence expresses a contradictory meaning, that is an illusion caused by the employment of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word "fire" and the words "cold" and "hot"; for neither in common worldly usage nor in Vedic usage does a single sentence have multiple meanings.

As for what was said—that the Upaniṣadic statements subvert the authority of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa)—that is not so, because they have a different purpose. For the Upaniṣads are intent upon establishing the oneness of Brahman; they do not preclude the instruction of means for attaining desired ends, nor do they forbid the injunction of a person toward such ends, precisely because it is impossible for them to have multiple purposes. Furthermore, it is not the case that no valid cognition arises regarding the literal meaning of the statements in the ritual section. If a statement produces a valid cognition regarding its own unique subject matter, how could there be a contradiction with another?

If it is argued that because Brahman is one, no valid cognition (*pramā*) arises at all due to the absence of an object, we say no, because valid cognition is directly perceived. From such sentences as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" and "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," a direct valid cognition is produced; if it were inferred that this [cognition] would simply not exist because the Upaniṣads intend to teach the oneness of Brahman, then that inference would find no authority when it contradicts direct perception.

Therefore, it is said that this is simply non-existent—that valid cognition (*pramā*) itself does not arise. Furthermore, by relying upon the very agency, action, and fruit presented by ignorance (*avidyā*) as they are ordinarily perceived, the Śruti—instructing one who is engaged in the general means for attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired, yet remains ignorant of their specific details—neither asserts the reality nor denies the unreality of the distinctions between action, agent, and fruit as they are well-known in the world.

This is because [the scripture] is devoted to prescribing the means for attaining desired fruits and avoiding undesired ones. Just as the Veda, when engaged in rites for specific desires (*kāmya*), prescribes only the means for those very desires as they are encountered—even though those desires arise from false knowledge—it does not, on that account, fail to prescribe them by declaring that "desires are undesirable because they arise from false knowledge. Nor does it [declare them to be undesirable].

Similarly, the scripture concerning the obligatory *agnihotra* and other rites also prescribes such rituals as the *agnihotra* and so forth, seeing some purpose—either the attainment of a particular desired end or the avoidance of a particular undesired one—by taking for granted the distinction between action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka-bheda*) which arises from false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). It does not fail to operate because it has as its object unreal things within the domain of ignorance (*avidyā*), just as it does not fail to operate in the case of optional rites (*kāmya-karma*). Nor is it the case that persons possessed of ignorance would not engage in them, for they are seen to do so, just like those driven by desire.

If it is argued that only those possessing knowledge (*vidyā*) have the qualification for ritual action (*karma*), we say no; for it has already been stated that there is a contradiction between the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the qualification for ritual action. By this same reasoning, the objection—that because the oneness of Brahman is devoid of objective content, there would be the fault of the teaching having no result in its comprehension—should be understood as refuted. Furthermore, due to the diversity of human desires, passions, and so forth: for indeed, the desires of men are manifold, and defects such as passion are diverse; consequently, the scripture is not capable of turning back one whose mind has been carried away by passion and other defects toward external objects.

Nor is it possible to turn the mind, which by its very nature is detached from external objects, toward those objects. Rather, from scripture there occurs only this much: the manifestation of the specific relationship between means and ends, namely, "this is the means to achieve the desired" and "this is the means to achieve the undesired"—just as a lamp, for instance, makes visible forms and other objects in the dark. Scripture does not, however, forcibly restrain or compel one like servants; for people are seen transgressing even scripture due to the weight of passion and other such afflictions.

Therefore, with regard to the diversity of human intellects, [the scripture] teaches the various specific relationships between means and ends in many ways. In this regard, individuals engage in specific means according to their own inclinations; the scripture, however, remains indifferent, like the sun or a lamp. Likewise, for some, even that which is a supreme human goal appears as if it were not a human goal; whatever a person’s perception is, they perceive the human goal in that form and seek to adopt the means corresponding to it.

And likewise, there is even an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "Three sons of Prajāpati lived the life of a student (*brahmacarya*) with their father Prajāpati," and so forth. Therefore, the Vedāntas, intending to make known the oneness of Brahman, do not sublate the scripture of injunctions (*vidhiśāstra*). Nor does the scripture of injunctions become devoid of subject matter by this much. Furthermore, the scripture of injunctions does not negate the authority of the Upaniṣads regarding the oneness of Brahman with respect to the aforementioned distinctions of factors of action (*kāraka*) and so on. For means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are bold within their own respective domains, like the sense of hearing and the others.

In this regard, some who consider themselves wise, by the power of their own minds, regard all means of valid cognition as mutually contradictory; likewise, they raise objections regarding the contradiction with perception and so forth concerning the oneness of Brahman—claiming that sound and the other objects of the senses are indeed perceived through direct perception as distinct, and therefore, for those asserting the oneness of Brahman, there would be a contradiction with perception.
