Likewise, by means of the ears and other senses, perceivers of sound and so forth, who are the agents of merit and demerit, are inferred to be distinct in every body as transmigrating beings; thus, for those asserting the oneness of Brahman, there is a contradiction with inference. Furthermore, they cite a contradiction with scripture: from such statements as "one desiring a village should sacrifice," "one desiring cattle should sacrifice," and "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," it is understood that those who desire villages, cattle, heaven, and so on, as well as those who perform the means to attain them, are distinct.

To this it is replied: those wretched outcasts among the *brāhmaṇa* and other castes, whose internal organs are corrupted by fallacious reasoning, are to be pitied, for their intellects have lost the tradition regarding the meaning of the scriptures. How so? Those who claim that the oneness of Brahman is contradicted by sound and the other objects perceived through direct perception via the doors of the ears and other senses, should be asked: "Is the oneness of space contradicted by the diversity of sound and the rest? If it is not contradicted, then there is no contradiction with direct perception.

As for what was said—that distinct perceivers of sound and so forth, as well as agents of merit and demerit, are inferred for each body, and thus, if Brahman were one, there would be a contradiction with inference—it must be asked by whom these distinct entities are inferred. If they should reply, "By all of us who are skilled in inference," then being asked, "Who are you who are skilled in inference? what would be their answer?

If you claim that, regarding each of the body, the senses, the mind, and the self, you have rejected proficiency in inference [only for yourselves], yet maintain: "We selves, whose instruments are the body, senses, and mind, are proficient in inference, because actions are accomplished by multiple causal factors"—then, in that case, it follows that there must be a plurality of you selves; for you yourselves have admitted that an action is accomplished by multiple causal factors, and inference is indeed an action.

It was previously asserted that this [action] is accomplished by the self as the agent, with the body, senses, and mind as the instrumental means (*kāraka*); now, by saying "we are experts in inference," you would be admitting that each of us selves possesses the body, senses, and mind as instruments and that we are many. Oh, what skill in inference has been displayed by these logician-bulls who lack even tails and horns!

For how could one who does not even know the Self—being thus deluded—know its difference or non-difference? In that case, what could he infer, or by what mark (liṅga)? Indeed, there is no mark whatsoever that establishes the difference of the Self from itself, by which mark one might prove the difference of the Self.

Those signs characterized by name and form which they put forward to prove the difference of the Self are merely adjuncts (*upādhi*) belonging to name and form—just as jars, water-pots, rooms, and cavities in the earth are adjuncts of space. When one perceives a sign of difference in space, then he might likewise find a sign of difference in the Self; for even by hundreds of logicians who accept distinctions based on something other than the Self, it is impossible to demonstrate a sign of difference in the Self.

But from its own side, it is indeed far removed, because the Self is not an object [of perception]. For whatever another accepts as a property of the Self, that is accepted by him as being of the nature of name and form (*nāmarūpa*); and since the Self is accepted as being distinct from name and form—according to the Śruti: "Space, indeed, is the revealer of name and form; that which is within them is Brahman"—and also according to "Let me manifest name and form"—for name and form consist of origination and dissolution, whereas Brahman is of a different character from them.

Therefore, since inference itself has no object [in this case], how can there be a contradiction with inference? By this, contradiction with scripture (*āgama*) is also refuted. As for what was said—that because the unity of Brahman lacks both the recipient of instruction and the fruit of receiving instruction, the teaching of unity is purposeless—that too is not so; for while a question may arise regarding actions accomplished by multiple factors (*kāraka*), there is no instruction, no instructor, and no fruit of receiving instruction in the case of the one, unconditioned (*nirupādhika*) Brahman.

Therefore, the point that the Upaniṣads are purposeless has already been admitted. Now, if it is objected that they are purposeless because they concern multiple causal factors (kārakas), we say no; for those who maintain the existence of a self (ātmavādins), this contradicts their own fundamental tenets.

Therefore, this fortress of fearlessness—unapproachable by the rogue-soldiers of logicians, inaccessible to those of small intellect, and unreachable by those devoid of the grace of the scriptures and the Guru—is [the domain of the Lord]. For it is said in the scriptural and traditional declarations that He is attainable only through the grace of His boon: "O God, who other than I can know that Lord who is both intoxicated and free from intoxication? "Even the gods have doubted this in the past," and "This wisdom is not to be attained through logic. Thus, it is to be reached only through the favor of His supreme boon.

This is also evident from Vedic verses that reveal its possession of contradictory attributes, such as: "It moves, and it moves not; it is far, and it is near. And in the *Gītā*: "All beings abide in Me," and so forth. Therefore, there is no other distinct entity whatsoever called a "transmigrating soul" apart from the Supreme Brahman.

Therefore, it is well said: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself as 'I am Brahman'—there is no other seer than this, there is no other hearer than this," and so on from hundreds of such scriptural passages. Therefore, the supreme Upanishad of the supreme, true Brahman is the name "the Truth of Truth.

Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa of the second chapter. One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in the worlds: the Earth is the *hiṅkāra*, Fire is the *prastāva*, the intermediate space is the *udgītha*, the Sun is the *pratihāra*, and Heaven is the *nidhana*—thus in the ascending order. (1)

(1) Whoever knows the child together with its support, its counter-support, its pillar, and its bond—this is his reward. What is it? He holds back seven—seven in number—those who hate him, the haters, the rivals; for rivals are of two kinds: those who hate and those who do not hate. Among them, he holds back those rivals who hate him.

The seven vital breaths located in the head are the gateways for the perception of objects; the attachments to those objects, arising from them, are "enemies" because they are innate. For these [attachments] turn one's vision, which resides in one's own Self, toward the realm of objects; therefore, they are enemies and haters, because they act as obstacles to the vision of the inner Self. As it is said in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "The Self-existent pierced the openings outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner Self," and so forth.

In this regard, he who knows the child and so forth—that is, who ascertains their true nature—shuts out, opens away, and destroys these rivals. To him, who has been made attentive by the hearing of this result, [the teacher] says: "This, indeed, is the child."

What are the two sheaths? It is this middle vital breath (*prāṇa*), the vital breath within the body which is the subtle body (*liṅgātman*), that which has entered the body in five ways—spoken of as "the great one, clad in white, King Soma"—in whom the organs such as speech and mind are fastened, according to the illustration of the sixfold pinning-block (*ṣaḍvīśaśaṅku*). This very [breath] is like a child, because it lacks the proficiency found in other organs regarding sense-objects; thus it is called "the child who is being trained."

What, then, is the "placing" (*ādhāna*) of that infant-like self consisting of the instruments? This very body is its "placing"—that is, its effect-natured locus; for it is "placed" (*ādhīyate*) in this, hence it is called the locus (*ādhāna*). Indeed, this body is the substratum for that infant-like vital breath (*prāṇa*); for it is in this [body] that the instruments, having attained their own nature, become gateways for perception, but they do not remain merely attached to the vital breath alone.

For this has been shown by Ajātaśatru: when the organs are withdrawn, that which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) is not perceived; but when the organs are distributed throughout the body, that which consists of consciousness is perceived as being present. And this was demonstrated by the awakening through the pressing of the hand. This "resting place" (*pratyādhāna*) refers to the head; it is called a "resting place" because it is supported (*prati-ā-dhīyate*) in various specific locations. Breath (*prāṇa*) is the pillar—the power generated by food and drink; "breath" and "strength" (*bala*) are synonyms.

For the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the support by strength within this body—according to the scriptural vision: "When this self, having fallen into weakness, enters as it were into a state of confusion"—just as a calf is supported by a pillar. Some say that the vital breath, which sides with the body, is the pillar, while food is the rope. For food, once consumed, undergoes a threefold transformation: that which is the gross transformation becomes these two and enters this [body]—namely, urine and feces.

That which is the medium rasa, by means of the sequence beginning with blood, nourishes its own effect—the body composed of the seven constituent elements (dhātus); for the body is built up through the arrival of food, which is its own source, because it consists of food; in the opposite case, it diminishes and falls away.

That which is the subtlest essence—called *amṛta*, *ūrj*, and *prabhāva*—having reached the region of the heart from above the navel and having entered the seventy-two thousand channels branching out from the heart, becomes the cause of stability for that subtle body (*liṅga*) known as the "child" (*śiśu*), which consists of an aggregate of organs; by generating strength, it is called the "pillar" (*sthūṇā*). By means of this, food becomes the bond between the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the body, like a calf tied on both sides by a rope.
Now, regarding the re-placement of that very same infant who has been carried [into the womb], certain secret doctrines (*upaniṣad*) concerning the eye are stated:
Now, when the breaths have returned, heaven is the *hiṅkāra*, the sun is the *prastāva*, the intermediate space is the *udgītha*, fire is the *pratihāra*, and the earth is the *nidhana*.

These seven imperishables attend upon him—that prāṇa consisting of the instruments, which is bound to food within the body and established in the eye. These seven imperishables (*akṣitayaḥ*), so called because they are the causes of imperishability, attend upon him as will be described. Although the root *sthā* preceded by *upa* takes the middle voice when used with a mantra as the instrument, here too the names of the seven deities function as mantras; therefore, the middle voice for the root *sthā* is not contradictory in this context either.

What are these called "akṣitayas"? In this context, those well-known red streaks or lines (*lohinyaḥ rājayaḥ*) in the eyes (*akṣan akṣaṇi*), which serve as gateways—through them Rudra is *anvāyattaḥ*, meaning he follows or is connected with this central vital breath (*madhyamaṃ prāṇam*). Furthermore, those waters (*āpaḥ*) in the eyes that are manifested through contact with smoke and other elements—through those waters serving as gateways, Parjanya, the deity, is *anvāyattaḥ*; the meaning is that he follows and attends upon it.

And that [food], having become food, is the imperishable support of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), according to another scriptural passage: "When Parjanya rains, the vital breaths become joyful. Through the *kanīnakā*—the power of vision—as its door, the Sun attends upon the middle vital breath (*madhyama-prāṇa*). That which is black in the eye, by that Agni attends upon it; that which is white in the eye, by that Indra attends upon it. By the lower eyelash (*vartanī*) as the door, the Earth is connected to it, due to the commonality of being "lower" (*adhara*).

Regarding this matter, there is this verse as a mantra beginning with: "The cup with its mouth downward... To explain the meaning of that mantra, the Śruti says: "The cup with its mouth downward and its bottom upward. But what is this cup with its mouth downward and its bottom upward? It is this very thing; for the head has the shape of a cup. How so? Because this [head] has its mouth downward, since the mouth is of the nature of an opening (*bila*), and because the head has the form of a bottom, it is "bottom-upward" (*ūrdhvabudhna*).

"In that [head] glory is deposited, multiform"—just as Soma is in the cup, so too in that head glory, which is multiform (of various forms), is deposited and resides. What, then, is that? Glory—glory is indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the multiform; the vital breaths such as hearing and so forth, and the Maruts, the winds, which have spread out through them in seven ways—that is what the mantra calls "glory," because it is the cause of the cognition of sound and other objects.

"Of that [unborn one], there are seven seers on the shore"—the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), whose nature is movement, are indeed these seers; it is of the vital breaths that this mantra speaks. "Speech is the eighth, attaining union with Brahman"—by entering into dialogue with Brahman, speech becomes the eighth; he states the reason for this: "For speech, as the eighth, attains union with Brahman. (4)

"Who, then, were the sages sitting on the rim of that cup?"—"These two, namely Gotama and Bharadvāja, are the ears: this one is Gotama and this one is Bharadvāja, the right and the left, or vice versa. Likewise, pointing to the eyes, he said: "These two, namely Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni, are the eyes: the right is Viśvāmitra and the left is Jamadagni, or vice versa. Pointing to the nostrils, he said: "These two, namely Vasiṣṭha and Kaśyapa, are the nostrils."

The southern channel is Vasiṣṭha; the northern is Kaśyapa—as before. Speech itself is Atri, so called because of its connection with the act of eating; for by speech food is eaten. Therefore, "Atri" is indeed a well-known name: it means "the eater" (*attri*) because of his being an eater, and though he is actually the eater (*atti*), he is called "Atri" cryptically. By this knowledge of the etymology of Atri, one becomes the eater of all this variety of food belonging to Prāṇa.

It is said that he himself becomes that [food] and is not perceived again as something else; this means that everything becomes his food. He who knows this true nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as it has been described—he, having become the middle *prāṇa* and being situated within the primary and secondary receptacles, becomes solely the enjoyer, not the object of enjoyment; the meaning is that he turns away from the object of enjoyment.
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa of the second chapter.

One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in rain: the preceding wind is the *hiṅkāra*, the cloud arises that is the *prastāva*, it rains that is the *udgītha*, it lightens that is the *pratihāra*, and it thunders that is the *nidhana*.

In this regard, it has been said: "The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed truth. Those secret doctrines (*upaniṣad*) concerning the vital breaths have been explained in connection with the secret doctrine of Brahman, as well as the statement: "These are your vital breaths."

It must be stated what their nature is and how their reality is established; therefore, this Brāhmaṇa is commenced for the purpose of determining the true nature of the five elements—which are real and consist of effects and instruments—by means of which the true essence of Brahman is intended to be defined through the removal of specific limiting adjuncts (upādhi) by the formula "not this, not this" (neti neti).

In this regard, Brahman is of two forms: that which is connected with the body and organs produced from the five elements, known as the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*), having the nature of mortal and immortal, consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by those [elements], being all-knowing, all-powerful, and possessing designations; and that which consists of action, agent, and fruit, serving as the basis for all worldly transactions.

That very same Brahman, when free from all specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), becomes the object of perfect vision—undecaying, immortal, fearless, beyond the reach of both speech and mind due to its non-duality—and is indicated as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).

In that regard, that Brahman which is indicated by way of negation as "not this, not this" has these two forms—indeed, the word *vāva* is for the purpose of emphasis, meaning "these two alone"—the two forms of Brahman, the Supreme Self. By means of these two, the formless Supreme Brahman is made to appear as having form through superimposition by ignorance. What are those two? They are the formed (*mūrta*) and indeed the formed itself; likewise, the formless (*amūrta*) and indeed the formless itself. This is the meaning.

The two, namely the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*), are determined as such by having their own specific qualifications (*viśeṣaṇa*) included within them. What, then, are those qualifications of the formed and the formless? They are stated as follows: "the mortal" (*martya*)—that which is subject to death—and "the immortal" (*amṛta*)—its opposite; "the stationary" (*sthita*)—that which is limited, fixed, and preceded by motion; and "that which moves" (*yat*)—the all-pervading, unlimited, and the opposite of the stationary; and "the existent" (*sat*)—that which possesses its own unique, distinguishing attributes that differentiate it from others.
And that which is the opposite of that—namely, "atyat"—is always fit for designation as something remote (*parokṣa*).

He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the rain, takes hold of that [rain] as its conclusion; rain falls for him, and he causes rain to fall. Thus ends the third section. (2) 3.

In that context, there is the "formed" (mūrta), characterized by four specific attributes, as well as the "formless" (amūrta). Here, they are distinguished: which are the attributes of the formed, and which are the others? This "formed" means having compacted parts, with parts interpenetrating one another—meaning it is dense and solid. What is that? It is "that which is other. Other than what? Other than the two elements, wind and space—by process of elimination, the triad of elements beginning with earth.

"This is mortal"—that which is called "embodied," consisting of these three elements, is mortal, characterized by death. Why? Because it is situated; for that which is limited is subject to contradiction when it comes into contact with another object—just as a jar is contradicted by a pillar, a wall, or the like. Likewise, the embodied is situated and limited, and being related to other objects, it is mortal due to its contradiction with those other objects.

This "Being" (sat) possesses a qualified, non-common attribute; for it is therefore defined, and because it is defined, it is mortal; hence it is corporeal. Or, because it is corporeal, it is mortal; because it is mortal, it is situated; and because it is situated, it is Being. Thus, since these four attributes do not deviate from one another, their relationship as qualifier and qualified, as well as their relationship as cause and effect, may be demonstrated according to one's preference. In any case, however, the three elements (bhūtas), characterized by these four qualifiers, constitute the corporeal form of Brahman.

In this regard, since one of the four qualifiers has been grasped, the others are indeed grasped as qualifiers as well; thus he says: "Of this embodied one, of this mortal one, of this stationary one, of this existent one"—the meaning is "of these three elements characterized by the fourfold attributes. This is their *rasa*, meaning their essence; for the Sun is the most essential (*sāriṣṭha*) of the three elements, and the three elements have him as their essence, because they possess the specific forms that are differentiated and manifested by him.

This is the form of the cosmic (ādhidaivika) effect: namely, that orb which the Sun (Savitṛ) shines as. For it is grasped as the essence (*rasa*) of the three elements (*bhūta*) that have come into being (*sat*); for this Savitṛ shines as a formal entity (*mūrta*), and he is the most substantial (*sāriṣṭha*). As for the cosmic instrument (*karaṇa*) within that orb, we shall explain that later. (3)

Now, as for the formless (amūrta): now the formless is being described. Wind and the intermediate space (antarikṣa)—these two remaining elements—this is the immortal (amṛta), because of its lack of form; it is non-static, and therefore not obstructed by anything; it is immortal, having the nature of not dying. This which is the opposite of the static, all-pervading, and undivided; since this has no distinguishable particularity that can be separated from others, it is therefore "that" (tyat)—fit only for a remote designation, as before.

Of this formless, immortal, moving, and distinct entity—characterized by these four attributes—this is the essence (rasa). What is it? It is that person who is in this orb—the Hiraṇyagarbha, consisting of the instruments of perception, who is designated as Prāṇa. He is the essence of the two formless elements, being their most excellent extract, just as before.

And these two formless elements constitute the essence of that Person. For the manifestation of the two elements from the unmanifested occurs for the sake of initiating the subtle body (*liṅga*) of Hiraṇyagarbha; therefore, because they serve that purpose, the two elements have him as their essence. Indeed, this is his "savor" (*rasa*): since the Person who resides within the orb is not perceived as having the same form as the orb, yet he is the essence of the two elements, there is thus a commonality between the Person residing in the orb and the two elements.
Therefore, it is appropriate to employ a well-known reason, namely: "for this is his savor."

Some maintain that *rasa* (the essence) is the cause, namely the conscious *Hiraṇyagarbha*, whose nature is knowledge (*vijñānātman*). In their view, the action (*karman*) of this *Hiraṇyagarbha*-knowledge-self is the impeller of wind and space; that action, being supported by wind and space, becomes the impeller of the other elements. Thus, because he is the impeller of wind and space through his own action, *rasa* is said to be the cause of those two. This is not so, because it is not analogous to the "essence of form" (*mūrtarasa*).

The essence (*rasa*) of the three gross elements (*mūrta*), which are of the same genus as those elements, is seen to be a gross sphere (*maṇḍala*); it is not conscious. Likewise, the two subtle elements (*amūrta*) must also be endowed with an essence of the same genus as they are, because the operation of the scriptural statement is identical. For just as the fourfold attributes of the gross and the subtle are distinguished, so too must there be a corresponding distinction between the gross and the subtle as possessors of essence and essence respectively; a partial inconsistency is not appropriate.

If it is argued that even in the case of a material substance (*mūrtarasa*), the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is intended to be conscious—this is stating far too little; for in every instance, both the material and the immaterial are intended to be of the nature of Brahman.

If it is argued that the word "puruṣa" (person) is inappropriate in reference to the altar, we say no; for we observe the use of the word "puruṣa" for a sacrificial fire-altar characterized by limbs such as wings and a tail, as in the passage: "Or, being thus, we shall not be able to produce offspring; let us make these seven persons into one person," and so on, as well as the use of the word "puruṣa" in other scriptural passages regarding those consisting of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*) and others.
"Thus far with respect to the deities" (*ity adhidaivatam*) is a conclusion of what has been said, intended to introduce the description of the division with respect to the self (*adhyātma*).

Now, the internal division between the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*) is being stated. What is that which is formed? It is this very [body]. And what is this? Whatever is other than the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the wind (*vāyu*), and that which is this space (*ākāśa*, *kha*) within—inside the self (*ātman*); and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) situated in the body—excluding these two, whatever else constitutes the three elements that originate the body; this is mortal, and so forth, the rest being the same as before. For of this Being (*sat*), this is the essence (*rasa*)—namely, the eye.

This is the essence, the core, of the internal effect that initiates the body; for by means of that core, this entire body becomes substantial—just as the celestial sphere is substantial by means of the solar orb. Furthermore, because of its priority: "The eyes alone are the first to be formed," according to the indicative mark from the text, "From fire, light as its essence issued forth. For the eye is composed of fire (*taijasa*). This triad of elements is the internal essence; "for this is the essence of Being" is the reason for its being the core of material form (*mūrtatva*). (5)

Now, that which is formless is being described. That which remains—the two elements, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and this space within the self (*antarātman*)—this is the formless. The rest is as before. Of this [formless], this is the essence (*rasa*), the core: namely, this person (*puruṣa*) who is in the right eye. The specific mention of "in the right eye" is because it is directly perceived through scripture (*śāstra-pratyakṣatvāt*); for the scripture's direct perception is that the subtle body (*liṅga*) presides specifically over the right eye, as such usage is seen in all the Vedas.
"For this is indeed its essence," as before; because it is not specifically grasped [as having form], the meaning of the reason is simply its being formless and its being the essence.

(6) — The division of the two, the formed and the formless, which serve as the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of Brahman and are denoted by the word "Truth" (*satya*), has been explained through their distinction as effects and instruments in the internal self (*adhyātma*) and in the divine realm (*adhidaivata*).

Now, we shall describe the form of this very person who consists of the instruments—the subtle body (*liṅga*). It is composed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), produced by the conjunction of the conscious self with the impressions of the formed and the formless; it is variegated like a painting on a canvas or a wall, comparable to magic, a juggler’s trick, or a mirage, and is the locus of all delusion. It is here that the nihilistic Vijñānavādins are mistaken, asserting that "the Self is merely this much. Likewise, the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas hold that this very form of latent impressions is an attribute (*guṇa*) of the substance (*dravya*) that is the Self, just as color is an attribute of a cloth.

Those who have accepted [this view] are the Sāṃkhyas, who hold that this threefold, independent *pradhāna*, which exists for its own sake, proceeds for the sake of the *puruṣa* as its cause, depending upon the *pradhāna*.

Even some who consider themselves followers of the Upaniṣads construct a system as follows: there is one aggregate consisting of the formed and the formless; there is a supreme aggregate, which is the Supreme Self; and distinct from these two is this third, intermediate aggregate, namely the collection of knowledge, action, and prior experience, together with the "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya) which was awakened by Ajātaśatru. Furthermore, they posit an agent, which is the aggregate of actions; that which is to be acted upon, which is the aforementioned aggregate of formed and formless elements; and the instrument. In this regard, they enter into a compromise with the logicians.

Having stated that "this mass of karma has the *liṅga* as its substratum," those who are again terrified by the fear of being [accused of] Sāṃkhya doctrine say: "The entire mass of karma—just as fragrance, though separated from the flower, comes to reside in the oil within a vessel—likewise, even upon separation from the *liṅga*, it takes refuge in a portion of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). That portion of the Supreme Self, although inherently devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), becomes possessed of qualities (*saguṇa*) through the quality of karma arriving from elsewhere; it is that [portion] which is the agent, the enjoyer, and that which is bound and liberated."

They follow the Vaiśeṣika view as well, asserting that the self is consciousness (*vijñānātman*); and they follow the Sāṃkhya view through this conceptualization: that the mass of karma is adventitious to the mass of elements, for [the self], being a portion of the Supreme Self, is inherently devoid of qualities; and that ignorance, though arising spontaneously and not adventitious, is not a property of the self, like saline soil (*ūṣara*).

Logicians view all this as agreeable by attempting to reconcile it with their own systems, yet they fail to perceive the true doctrine of the Upaniṣads and its contradiction of all reason. How so? First of all, if the Supreme Self possessed parts, the aforementioned defects would arise: it would be subject to transmigratory existence, it would be vulnerable, and its wandering to the regions where the fruits of karma are experienced would be impossible. Furthermore, if there were an eternal difference between the individual self and the Supreme, their oneness could not be established.

If it is argued that [the soul] resides in the *liṅga* (subtle body) alone—which is imagined as having a location attributed to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) like the space within a jar, a water-pot, or a hole in the ground—then such a conception is entirely untenable. For even when separated from the *liṅga*, it would imply that the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) resort to the location of the Supreme Self, or that they arise spontaneously like saline soil; this kind of imagination is impossible. Furthermore, it is not possible even for the mind to conceive of the latent impressions migrating to another entity apart from the location of the object being perfumed (*vāsya*).

Nor do the scriptural texts understand [the Self] in this way; for there are such passages as: "Desire, volition, and doubt," "For forms are indeed in the heart," "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were," "The desires that reside in the heart," and "For then one has crossed beyond all the sorrows of the heart. Nor is it proper to assume a meaning other than what is heard in these scriptures, because they are intended to establish that the Self is the Supreme Brahman, and because the purpose of all the Upanishads is exhausted in this much alone.

Therefore, all those who are skilled in imagining meanings not intended by the scripture interpret the meaning of the Upaniṣads otherwise. Nevertheless, if it should be the meaning of the Veda, let it be so; I have no aversion to that. Furthermore, the statement "There are indeed two forms of Brahman" would not be consistent with the theory of three groups.

But when the formed and the formless, as well as the latent impressions produced by them, constitute two forms, and Brahman is the third form possessing form—there being no other fourth form in between—then this restrictive determination, "Brahman has only two forms," is appropriate. Otherwise, one would have to assume that these two forms belong either to a portion of Brahman, namely the individual self (*vijñānātman*), or to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) by means of the individual self. In that case, the dual number in the phrase "only two forms" (*rūpe eva*) would be inconsistent.

The plural form "forms" (*rūpāṇi*) would be more appropriate when taken together with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*); that is, the two—the formed and the formless—and the latent impressions as the third. If it is argued that the formed and the formless alone are the forms of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), while the latent impressions belong to the individual self (*vijñānātman*), then this way of speaking—that the Supreme Self undergoes modification through the medium of the individual self—would be purposeless, since the fact that the latent impressions also operate through the medium of the individual self remains unchanged.

Furthermore, it cannot be conceived—even in a primary sense—that one entity is modified through the medium of another entity. Nor is the conscious self (*vijñānātman*) a different entity from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), for such a conception would result in the abandonment of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). Therefore, these and similar conceptions arising from their own minds belong to those who are deluded regarding the meaning of the Veda; they lie outside the literal teaching. Indeed, that which lies outside the literal teaching is neither the meaning of the Veda nor an aid to the meaning of the Veda, because the Veda is independent with respect to its authority. Consequently, the conception of three heaps is inconsistent.

The "Person in the right eye" introduced as the *liṅga-ātman* within the microcosm (*adhyātma*), and the "Person in this orb" within the macrocosm (*adhidaiva*)—by the reference "of him," it is that very same one who is taken up, namely, the essence (*rasa*) of that which is formless, and not the one consisting of cognition (*vijñānamaya*).

Now, one might ask: why do these forms not belong to the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) itself, since the self consisting of consciousness is also the subject under discussion, and the word "his" (*tasya*) refers back to that very subject? It is not so, because the self consisting of consciousness is intended to be made known as being formless. For if these forms, such as saffron-colored cloth and the rest, were indeed the forms of that self consisting of consciousness, then there could be no instruction regarding it as having an indefinable nature through the words "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).

[Objection: But surely this designation refers to something else, and not to that which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). [Reply: No, because at the end of the sixth chapter, after introducing that which consists of consciousness with the words, "By what, my dear, could one know the knower?", he concludes with, "This is the Self—'not this, not this'."

And because the promise "I shall make it known" possesses meaning— for if it were intended to make known the very nature of the Self, which consists of consciousness alone and is beyond empirical transaction, with all specific limiting adjuncts destroyed, then this promise would be meaningful: by which, once made known, he would know the Self alone, thinking "I am Brahman," reach the culmination of the scripture, and fear nothing whatsoever.

If, on the other hand, the one consisting of consciousness were one thing and the one designated as "not this, not this" were another, then a misconception would have been grasped—namely, that Brahman is something else and "I am another"—and not the realization, "I have known the Self alone: I am Brahman. Therefore, these forms belong to the *liṅga-puruṣa* (the subtle body) itself, referred to by the words "of this very [one]. Furthermore, when the true nature of the Supreme Self—the truth of truths—is to be explained, the truth must be stated in its entirety; and the specific forms of that truth are the latent impressions (*vāsanās*). These forms of them are now being described.

These are the forms of this aforementioned person, whose nature is the subtle body (*liṅga-ātman*). What are they? It is said: just as in the world there is *mahārajana*—that which is dyed with turmeric (*haridrā*)—or as there is cloth in the world, so too, upon contact with objects such as women, a corresponding form of latent impression (*vāsanā*) arises in the mind in the shape of passion (*rañjana*), by which that person is called "passionate," just like a garment or the like. And just as in the world there is *pāṇḍvāvikam*—this belonging to a sheep (*āvika*), such as wool—and just as that is pale (*pāṇḍura*).

Likewise, there is another form of latent impression (*vāsanā*): just as in the world the *indragopa* insect is extremely red, so too is this person's form of latent impression—sometimes varying in intensity according to a particular object, and sometimes according to the mental state of the person. Just as in the world the flame of a fire is radiant, so too is the form of latent impression for someone in a certain case; and just as a white lotus exists, so too does the form of latent impression exist for someone else.

Just as a flash of lightning occurs once, and just as a single flash of lightning in the world becomes an illuminator everywhere, so too, in view of the increase of the light of knowledge, a certain form of latent impression (*vāsanā*) arises for someone. Of these forms of latent impressions, neither the beginning, the end, nor the middle, nor their number, nor their location, time, or cause can be determined—because the latent impressions are innumerable and because the causes of those latent impressions are infinite. And thus he will state in the sixth chapter: "Consisting of this, consisting of that," and so forth.

Therefore, the examples—such as "like a saffron-colored garment" and so forth—are not intended to determine the specific nature or number [of impressions]; rather, they are intended to demonstrate the manner [in which they appear], meaning that the forms of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are of such a kind. As for what was stated at the end regarding the form of the impression—"like a single flash of lightning"—that is because, when Hiraṇyagarbha emerges from the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), his manifestation occurs all at once, like a flash of lightning.

He who knows that form of latent impressions belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha—for him, indeed, just as at a single flash of lightning, so indeed (the particle *ha vai* being for emphasis), his glory and renown come to be in this very way; that is to say, just as [it is] for Hiraṇyagarbha—so too for one who knows this aforementioned final form of latent impressions.

Having thus described the nature of Truth in its entirety, this [instruction] concerning Brahman is now commenced for the purpose of determining the specific nature of that which we called "the Truth of Truth": *atha* (now), immediately after the description of the nature of Truth, because that alone remains which is the Truth of Truth—*ataḥ* (therefore), we shall describe the nature of the Truth of Truth; *ādeśaḥ* (instruction) means the description of Brahman.
What, then, is this description? It is said: the description is "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).

Now, one might ask: how is it that by these two words, "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), the "Truth of truths" is intended to be pointed out? It is said: by the exclusion of all specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). In that [Brahman] there is no distinction whatsoever—neither name, nor form, nor action, nor difference, nor genus, nor quality; for it is through these that the application of words occurs, and none of these distinctions exists in Brahman.

Therefore, it cannot be pointed out as "this is that," in the manner that things are pointed out in the world, such as "that is a cow, it moves, it is white, it has horns. Rather, Brahman is pointed out by means of superimposed names, forms, and actions through words such as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" and "Brahman, the Self, is a mass of consciousness. However, when its very own nature—devoid of all specific limiting adjuncts—is intended to be pointed out, then it cannot be pointed out by any means whatsoever.
In that case, this is the only means: namely, the teaching "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) by way of negating whatever has been pointed out.

And these two negative particles (*na-kāra*) are for the purpose of pervasion through repetition; whatever is apprehended is each time negated. This being so, any suspicion regarding the Brahman that has not yet been specified is removed. Otherwise, if only the two things under discussion were negated by the two negatives, then as for that Brahman which is other than the two things already mentioned and negated, it would not have been specified, and the suspicion—"What indeed is its nature?"—would not be dispelled.

And thus, that instruction would be purposeless, because it does not bring about the desire to know in the person; furthermore, the statement "I shall make you know Brahman" would have an incomplete meaning.

But when the desire to know all directions, time, and so forth has been turned back by means of the removal of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then—like a single mass of salt—the mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*) is of a single flavor, without interior or exterior, the reality of realities; at that point, the desire to know ceases entirely with the realization "I am Brahman," and wisdom becomes established in the Self alone. Therefore, the two negations in the phrase "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) are for the purpose of repetition.

Now, one might ask: having prepared such a great effort with the binding of the preparatory equipment (*parikarabandha*), is it indeed appropriate to define *brahman* in this way? Certainly; why? Because—namely, because of the phrase "not thus, not thus" (*neti neti*)—by the word "thus" (*iti*), the various modes of what is to be pervaded are indicated as the objects of the two "nots" (*na*), just as in the expression "every village is beautiful. There is no other way of defining it beyond this; therefore, this alone is the definition of *brahman*.

As it has been said: "Its secret name (*upaniṣad*) is 'the Truth of truth. In this manner, that which is the Truth of truth is the Supreme Brahman; therefore, it is rightly stated that this is the name of Brahman—*nāmadheya* meaning simply "name. What is that "Truth of truth"? "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed truth; He is their truth.
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa of the second chapter.

One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in all waters: that which is the gathering of clouds is the *hiṅkāra*; that which rains is the *prastāva*; those [rivers] which flow eastward are the *udgītha*; those which flow westward are the *pratihāra*; and the ocean is the *nidhana*. 1. (1) ---

"Maitreyī," said Yājñavalkya—the sage named Yājñavalkya addressed his own wife, Maitreyī—"I am about to depart, that is, I am going upward to another stage of life called wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya). 'Are' is a term of address. I am desirous of departing from this state, this stage of life, namely the householder's life; therefore, I ask for your permission."

Furthermore: "I shall bring about an end—a separation—for you with this second wife, Kātyāyanī. I shall effect a severance of that relationship which existed between you two while you were united through your husband; having divided the property, I shall depart from you after distributing the wealth.
"He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in all waters does not perish in water; he becomes possessed of water. (2) Thus ends the fourth section. (4) (2)

Thus addressed, she said: "If"—the word *anu* here denotes deliberation—"this earth of mine, O Venerable Sir (*bhago*), were entirely filled with wealth and riches, surrounded by the ocean; how so? The sense is either a negation, meaning 'not at all,' or a question. [The connection is with the distant clause: 'Could I, by means of that ritual action—such as the *agnihotra*—which is accomplished through wealth filling the earth, become immortal?'"

Yājñavalkya replied: "How so? If this was intended as a challenge, it was an expression of assent, [to which] Yājñavalkya said, "No. If, however, it was a question seeking an answer, [the response would be: "You would certainly not be immortal; rather, your life would be exactly like that of those in the world who possess means—that is, those who possess the instruments for achieving happiness through the enjoyment of pleasures. But there is not even a mental hope for immortality through wealth, that is, through ritual action accomplished by means of wealth.

Maitreyī said: Having been addressed thus, Maitreyī replied—"If it were so, what would I do with that wealth by which I could not become immortal? Tell me, O Venerable One, only that which you know to be the sole means of immortality; that alone, tell me.

Yājñavalkya said: When the means for attaining immortality achievable through wealth had thus been rejected, Yājñavalkya, satisfied with the fulfillment of his own intention, said—"He said": "O dear one"—he spoke with compassion using the term "dear" (*priyā*)—"Alas! O Maitreyī, you who were already dear to us before, now speak even more agreeably, in accordance with our hearts."

Therefore, come; sit down—be seated—and I shall explain: I will tell you that which is desired by you, the knowledge of the Self which is the means to immortality. Furthermore, while I am explaining—that is, while I am performing the exposition—you must practice profound reflection (*nididhyāsasva*), meaning you should desire to meditate with certainty upon the meanings of these statements.

He said this—desiring to teach detachment as the means to immortality—he produces a dispassion toward wife, husband, children, and so forth, for the sake of renouncing them. "Na vai"—the word *vai* is used for the purpose of recalling what is well-known; it is indeed well-known in the world that a husband is not dear to the wife for the sake of the husband’s own desire or purpose; rather, the husband is dear to the wife only for the sake of his own self’s desire or purpose.

Likewise, "Verily, not through a wife," and so forth, the rest is the same: "not through sons," "not through wealth," "not through the Brahman [caste]," "not through the Kṣatriya [caste]," "not through the worlds," "not through the gods," "not through beings," "not through everything. Each preceding item is mentioned as a means for producing affection, because detachment arises more intensely toward each subsequent one. The mention of "everything" includes both what has been specifically stated and what has not been stated.

Therefore, this is well-known in the world: the Self alone is dear, and nothing else. That which was introduced in the passage, "This Self is dearer than a son," has here been elaborated as its detailed exposition. Consequently, because they are means for attaining pleasure in the Self, affection for other things is secondary; affection for the Self alone is primary. Therefore, "the Self, indeed, my dear, must be seen"—it is worthy of being seen, and must be brought within the range of vision; first, it must be heard from a teacher and from the scriptures; afterwards, it must be reflected upon through reasoning.

Therefore, it must be meditated upon (*nididhyāsitavya*), that is, it must be contemplated with certainty; for it is only when these means—listening, reflection, and meditation—have been brought to completion that this [Brahman] becomes truly seen. When these have reached a state of unity, then the right vision (*samyagdarśana*) whose object is the oneness of Brahman becomes clear, and not otherwise by listening alone.

That which consists of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama), characterized by the causes of action such as Brahminhood and Kṣatriyahood—which is the object of notions superimposed upon the Self through ignorance, consisting of action, agent, and fruit, and being the object of the notion of ignorance, like the various perceptions [superimposed] upon a rope—he speaks for the purpose of subverting that: "Verily, Maitreyī, when the Self is seen, heard, thought, and known, all this becomes known and understood.

Now, one might ask: how can that which is known when something else is known? This is not a fault. For there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from the Self; if there were, it would not be known. But there is nothing else; the Self alone is everything. Therefore, when the Self is known, everything becomes known. But how is it that the Self alone is everything? This the scripture declares: "Brahman"—meaning the Brāhmaṇa caste—"would despise" (parādāt), would cast aside, would treat with contempt, that person."

Whom? One who knows that this Brāhmaṇa caste is other than the Self—that is, apart from the nature of the Self—and thinks, "This Brāhmaṇa caste is not the Self," [the Supreme Self] would abandon him, thinking, "This Brāhmaṇa caste views me as something other than its own true nature"; for the Supreme Self is indeed the Self of all. Likewise the Kṣatra—the Kṣatriya caste—likewise the worlds, the gods, the beings, and everything.

"This is Brahman"—all those things which have been enumerated are the Self alone. That which is this Self—this very Self that has been introduced as "is to be seen, is to be heard"—from which [the world] is born, into which it is dissolved, and which consists of the Self during the time of its existence, because nothing is perceived apart from the Self; therefore, the Self alone is everything.

But how, then, can it be grasped now that "all this is indeed the Self"? Because of the pervasive presence of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) everywhere, it is understood that everything has the very nature of consciousness. In this regard, an illustration is stated: in the world, it is observed that when one thing cannot be apprehended apart from the essential nature of another, the former is of the same nature as the latter. This is the illustration: "just as that."

Just as in the world, when a drum, a kettledrum, or the like is being struck—that is, beaten with a stick or similar instrument—one would not be able to grasp the external sounds, that is, the specific sounds distinct from the general sound of the drum; yet, by grasping the drum itself—by way of its general and specific nature as "these are the sounds of the drum"—the specific sounds become grasped, because they do not exist apart from the general sound of the drum.

Or, as in the case of the "striking of a drum"—*āghāta* means the striking of a drum—by perceiving the general property of sound characterized by the striking of the drum, its specific particulars are thereby grasped; however, those particulars cannot be grasped separately [from that general property], because they do not exist as distinct entities. In the same way, apart from consciousness (*prajñāna*), no specific object whatsoever is perceived in either the dreaming or waking states. Therefore, it is logical that these [states] have no existence apart from consciousness.
Likewise, just as when a conch shell is being blown—being joined with sound and being filled—one would not be able to perceive external sounds; and so forth, as previously described.

Likewise, "for the lute being played" means for the lute that is being played. The employment of numerous examples here is for the purpose of demonstrating the multiplicity of universals (*sāmānya*); for there are indeed many distinct universals and particulars, both conscious and unconscious. It is intended to show how their inclusion within a single Great Universal occurs through a successive process, as in the case of the mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*). How indeed is this to be demonstrated?

Just as the general and specific qualities of the sounds of a drum, a conch, and a lute are included within the universal property of "soundness," so too, during the period of manifestation, because the general and the particular are not distinct from one another, the oneness of Brahman can be understood.

Thus, at the time of origination, it can be understood that [the world] was indeed Brahman prior to its origination. Just as in the case of fire, before the separation of sparks, smoke, embers, and flames, there is only fire and thus the oneness of fire exists, so too it is logical to grasp that the world—though modified by name and form—is, prior to its origination, nothing but a mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*). This is what is stated: "Just as, from a fire with wet fuel"—that is, a fire kindled with wet fuel is a "fire with wet fuel"—from that [fire] when fuel is added, various smokes emerge separately... separate.

"In various ways"—the mention of smoke is for the purpose of illustrating sparks and so forth; smoke, sparks, and the like "issue forth," that is, they go out. "In this manner"—just as in this illustration—"O Maitreyī, this is the breath of this Great Being, the Supreme Self under discussion"; "breath" means like a breath; just as a person's breath occurs without effort, even so, O Maitreyī, is it with this.

What was born from that, as if it were his breath? It is said: the fourfold collection of mantras—the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvāṅgirasa; the *itihāsa*, such as the dialogue between Urvaśī and Purūravas, beginning with "Urvaśī, the Apsaras," which is indeed the Brāhmaṇa; the *purāṇa*, beginning with "In the beginning, this was non-existent" (*asad vā idam agre āsīt*); the *vidyā*, the knowledge of the divine beings; the *veda* itself, beginning with "This is that Veda"; the *upaniṣads*, beginning with "One should meditate on [Brahman] as the Beloved" (*priyam ityetad upāsīta*); and the *ślokas*.

The *mantras* originate from Brahmins, such as "These are the verses" (*tad ete ślokāḥ*) and so forth; the *sūtras* are summary statements of the subject matter found in the Veda, such as "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self alone" (*ātmeti evopāsīta*) and so forth; the *anuvyākhyānas* are commentaries on the *mantras*; and the *vyākhyānas* are explanatory passages (*arthavādas*). Alternatively, the *anuvyākhyānas* are commentaries on the summary statements—such as that of the fourth chapter regarding "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self alone," or that regarding "He who thinks 'the other is one and I am another' does not know, being like a beast."*

This very remainder of the chapter consists of the explanations and commentaries on the mantras; thus, the Brāhmaṇa is of eight kinds. In this way, there is the inclusion of only the Mantra and the Brāhmaṇa. The Veda, which exists with its fixed arrangement, is manifested like the breath of a person, and it is not preceded by human intellect or effort. Therefore, it is an independent authority regarding its own subject matter. Consequently, whatever is stated by it must be accepted exactly as such by those desiring their own welfare—whether it be knowledge or action. For the state of transformation of form occurs through the power of the manifestation of names.

For it is precisely name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which serve as the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the Supreme Self and are being manifested, that constitute *saṃsāra* in all its states—being indefinable either as identical to or different from reality, like water and foam. Therefore, it is said that name alone is the "breath" (exhalation) [of Brahman], since by that statement alone the status of the other [form] as a breath is established. Alternatively, it has been stated that the entire realm of duality is the object of ignorance (*avidyā*), as in: "Brahman would abandon him who would declare this All to be other than the Self; for all this is what this Self is."

On that basis, one might suspect that the Veda lacks authority; therefore, this was said in order to dispel such a suspicion: the Veda is authoritative because it arises without effort, like the breath of a person, unlike other compositions.

Furthermore, it is not only because the world does not exist apart from consciousness during the times of its persistence and origination that the world is Brahman; it is also so at the time of dissolution. Just as water-bubbles, foam, and the like do not exist apart from water, so too name, form, and action—which are its effects—do not exist apart from consciousness when they are being dissolved back into it. Therefore, one should realize that Brahman alone is a single mass of consciousness, of a single essence. To demonstrate this dissolution, he provides an illustration.

The word "sa" refers to the illustration; "yathā" means in whatever manner the ocean (*abdhi*) is the "ekāyana"—meaning the single point of convergence, the single destination, and the single dissolution—of all waters located in rivers, ponds, lakes, and so forth, such that they reach a state of non-distinction.

Just as this illustration shows, so too for all tactile sensations—whether soft, rough, hard, slippery, and so forth—which have wind as their essence, the skin is the single point of convergence. "Skin" refers here to the mere generality of touch that is the object of the skin; the specific varieties of touch enter into it—just as waters enter the ocean—and apart from it, they cease to exist, for they were merely its particular configurations.

In the same way, that generality of touch denoted by the word "skin" enters into the mental conception—the mere generality of the object of the mind—and, being non-existent apart from it, becomes identical with it; just as specific touches are non-existent apart from the generality of touch as an object of the skin. Likewise, the object of the mind also enters into the mere generality of the object of the intellect, and being non-existent apart from it, becomes identical with it; having become mere consciousness, it dissolves into the supreme Brahman, which is a mass of pure intelligence, just as water dissolves into the ocean.

In this way, through a successive process, when sound and the other objects, along with their corresponding perceivers and instruments, have dissolved into the mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*), then, due to the absence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), Brahman remains as a single-flavored, infinite, boundless, and continuous mass of consciousness, like a block of salt (*saindhavaghana*). Therefore, it should be understood that the Self alone is the one non-dual reality. Likewise, for all odors—which are specific qualities of earth—there is the sense of smell in the nose, which is the commonality of the objects of olfaction.

Likewise, among all tastes, which are specific forms of water, there is the generality that is the object of the sense of taste. Likewise, among all forms, which are specific forms of fire, there is the eye, which is the generality that is the object of sight. Likewise, the generality that is the object of hearing among sounds is as described before. Likewise, the generalities that are the objects of the ear and other senses merge into the volition, which is the generality that is the object of the mind; the generality that is the object of the mind merges into the mere consciousness, which is the generality that is the object of the intellect; and having become mere consciousness, it dissolves into the supreme mass of pure intelligence.

Likewise, the specific objects of the organs of action—speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and sexual pleasure—are subsumed within their respective general activities and do not exist as distinct entities, just as specific waters are subsumed in the ocean. These generalities, moreover, consist of mere vital breath (*prāṇa*); and vital breath is nothing but consciousness (*prajñāna*) itself, as the Kauṣītakins recite: "That which is vital breath is indeed consciousness; that which is consciousness is vital breath. Now, it may be objected that in all these cases the dissolution of the object alone has been stated, and not that of the instrument.

Regarding this, what is the intended meaning? Certainly; however, the Śruti considers the instrument (*karaṇa*) to be of the same genus as its object (*viṣaya*), not of a different genus. The instrument is simply another configuration (*saṃsthānāntara*) of the object itself, acting as the grasper of its own self—just as a lamp, which is a specific configuration of a particular form, is the instrument for the illumination of all forms; likewise, the instruments are other configurations of all specific objects themselves, acting as the illuminators of their own specific selves, like a lamp.

Therefore, no separate effort need be made for the dissolution of the instruments (karaṇas); since they consist of the nature of their respective objects, their dissolution is established by the dissolution of the objects themselves.

In this regard, it was asserted that "all this is what this Self is. Therein, the reason was stated: its identity with the Self, its birth from the Self, and its dissolution into the Self. Therefore, because there is no existence apart from consciousness at the times of its origin, subsistence, and dissolution, that which was asserted—"Consciousness is Brahman" and "All this is indeed the Self"—has been established through reasoning. The Paurāṇikas say that this dissolution is natural (svābhāvika).

But that dissolution which is preceded by conscious knowledge, belonging to those who know Brahman and caused by the knowledge of Brahman—this they call "absolute," occurring through the cessation of ignorance; for that purpose, this specific undertaking [of the following verses] is begun.

In this regard, an illustration is adduced: "Just as that... A *saindhavakhilya*—*saindhava* is a derivative of *sindhu*; by the word *sindhu*, water is denoted, for it is called *sindhu* because of its flowing (*syandana*). A *saindhava* is either a derivative of that or something produced therein; being both *saindhava* and a *khilya*, it is a *saindhavakhilya*. *Khilya* is simply *khila*, with the suffix *-ya* added in the sense of the same meaning. When thrown—that is, cast—into the water, which is its own source, it dissolves into that very water.

It dissolves; that which was the attainment of hardness by the lump [of salt] due to contact with the earth and fire departs through contact with its own source—this is the dissolution of the water, and thus it is said that "the lump of sea-salt dissolves accordingly. This is what he says: "it would dissolve accordingly into water alone. "Not indeed" (na ha) means not at all; no one, however skillful, would be able to grasp this lump—that is, to lift it up and seize it as before. The word "iva" (as if) is meaningless here.

It is not at all capable of being grasped. Why? Because from whichever place one might take that water, having taken it and tasted it, that water would have only the taste of salt, and not the state of being a solid mass.

Just as with this illustration, even so, O Maitreyī, is this Great Being called the Supreme Self—from which Great Being you have become separated by ignorance (avidyā), and through connection with the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the body and organs, have fallen into the state of a fragment (khilya). You are mortal, possessed of the attributes of transmigratory existence such as birth, death, hunger, thirst, and the like, and consisting of name, form, and their effects—thinking, "I am the descendant of such-and-such. That state of being a fragment of yours, born from the delusion caused by contact with the limiting adjuncts of the body and organs, [is dissolved] in the Great [Being].

He has been made to enter the Supreme Self—the source of all beings, comparable to the great ocean, undecaying, immortal, fearless, pure, of a single flavor like a mass of rock salt, a solid mass of consciousness, infinite, shoreless, without interval, and devoid of the distinctions produced by the delusion of ignorance.

When that [individual soul] has entered and been swallowed by its own source, such that the state of being a fragment caused by ignorance—the state of duality—has been destroyed, there remains this one Great Being (*mahadbhūtam*). It is "Great" because it is greater than all else, and it is "Being" (*bhūtam*) because it does not deviate from its essential nature throughout the three periods of time; thus, the suffix of completion (*niṣṭhā-pratyaya*) indicates that it is eternally established. Furthermore, it is the cause of ether and the other elements.

Alternatively, the word *bhūta* signifies the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); thus the meaning is "great" and "ultimately real. For although something may be great in a worldly sense, if it is produced by dreams or illusions—like the Himalayas and other mountains—it is not an ultimately real entity. Therefore, he distinguishes it: "but this is both great and real. It is "infinite" (*ananta*) because no end to it is found; lest it be thought that this might be merely relative, he further qualifies it as "without limit" (*apāra*).

Manifestation is consciousness (*vijñāna*), and that which is a mass of this consciousness is the "mass of consciousness" (*vijñānaghana*). The word "mass" (*ghana*) is intended to exclude any other distinct category (*jātyantara*), just as in the cases of "a mass of gold" (*suvarṇaghana*) or "a mass of iron" (*ayoghana*). The word "only" (*eva*) is for the purpose of restriction, meaning that no other distinct category exists in the interval.

If this one non-dual reality is, from the perspective of ultimate truth, pure and untouched by the sufferings of saṃsāra, for what reason is this fragmentary state of the Self said to exist—characterized by being born, dying, being happy, being miserable, "I," "mine," and so forth, and afflicted by the manifold attributes of saṃsāra? [It is said: "from these elements"—those which have transformed into the forms of bodies and organs, consisting of name and form, comparable to foam and bubbles on water, belonging to the pure Supreme Self who is like water.

For those whose limits are the objects of the senses, it has been stated that their dissolution occurs within Brahman—the dense mass of wisdom—through the knowledge of ultimate discrimination, like rivers [merging] into the ocean; having emerged from these elements which serve as causes and are denoted by the word "truth," like a lump of salt [dissolving], or as the reflection of the sun, moon, and so forth arises from water, or as a clear crystal assumes redness and other colors due to limiting adjuncts such as lac-dye, so too [does the Self emerge] from the limiting adjuncts of the elements existing as cause and effect.

Having arisen as a distinct individual fragment (*viśeṣātmakhilya*), having truly arisen—when those elements from which one has arisen, those elements that have transformed into the forms of the body, the organs, and sense-objects, which serve as the cause for the state of being a distinct individual fragment, are dissolved by means of the knowledge of Brahman through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, and perish like foam and bubbles on water, then, upon their perishing, this state of being a distinct individual fragment perishes along with them.

Just as when the causes such as water, lac, and so forth are removed, the reflection of the sun, moon, crystal, and so forth perishes, and only the true nature of the moon and so forth remains in the ultimate sense, even so, that which is a mass of pure consciousness—endless, boundless, and transparent—remains.

"Thereafter, for one who is liberated from the aggregate of the body and its instruments, there is no specific cognition (viśeṣasaṃjñā). Thus, O Maitreyī, I say to you: "There is no specific cognition. Such characteristics as "I am this person," "I am the son of so-and-so," "this is my field," "this is my wealth," "I am happy," "I am miserable," and so forth, arise because they are produced by ignorance (avidyā). Since ignorance has been destroyed without remainder by the knowledge of Brahman, how could specific cognition possibly arise for the knower of Brahman, who abides in his own nature of pure consciousness?

"Even for one abiding in a body, a specific designation is not possible; how much less so for one who is entirely liberated from the body and its instruments? Thus indeed did Yājñavalkya speak—namely, he spoke this vision of the supreme truth to his wife Maitreyī.

Thus enlightened, Maitreyī indeed spoke as follows: "By the Blessed One, by declaring that this very same single reality, Brahman, possesses contradictory attributes, my confusion has been created. Therefore she said: 'In this very matter, the Blessed One, the worshipful one, has bewildered me. How did he state the possession of contradictory attributes? It is said: having first asserted, 'It is indeed a mass of consciousness,' he then stated again, 'After death, there is no consciousness.'"

"How can he be a mere mass of consciousness? Or how can it be that there is no perception after death? For fire is not both hot and cold at once; therefore, I am confused about this. Yājñavalkya said: "Indeed, Maitreyī, I do not speak what is confusing"—the meaning is that I do not utter a delusive statement. [Maitreyī asked: "But how did you state two contradictory properties—a mass of consciousness and the absence of perception? [Yājñavalkya replied: "I have not attributed these to a single substratum."

It is you alone who, through delusion, have grasped this single reality as possessing contradictory properties; it was not stated by me. What I have said is this: when that state of fragmentation (*khilyabhāva*) of the Self—which is brought about by ignorance and consists in the relationship between cause and effect—is destroyed by knowledge, then the specific notion (*viśeṣasaṃjñā*) caused by it—namely, the perception of difference characterized by the connection with the body and so forth—is destroyed once the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the aggregate of cause and effect has been dissolved, due to the absence of its cause.

Just as the reflection of the moon and so forth, along with its attendant light and other qualities, perishes upon the destruction of its substratum such as water, there is no destruction of the nature of the Brahman that is beyond transmigratory existence—the mass of consciousness (vijñānaghana)—in the manner of the ultimate reality of the moon or the sun. This is why it is called the "mass of consciousness. That Self is the soul of the entire world; in the ultimate sense, it is not subject to destruction because of the non-destruction of the real. However, the state of being a limited fragment (khilyabhāva) produced by ignorance is perishable, according to another scriptural passage: "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name."

But this is the ultimate reality: "Verily, this Self is indestructible. Therefore, it is sufficient, indeed, for the purpose of knowing—that is, for understanding—this great being, which is infinite and boundless, as has been explained. For it will be said later: "For there is no loss of the knower's knowledge, because of its imperishability.

How then is it said that "after death there is no consciousness"? Listen: in that state—wherein, in this particularized self produced by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the aggregate of causes and effects imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*), and which is a mere fragmentary existence—for what reason is duality perceived? That is to say, although in reality Brahman is non-dual, a duality as if distinct from the Self—as if it were another entity—is observed. [Objection: But surely, because it is compared with duality, duality must be ultimately real.

No, because of other scriptural passages such as "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name," and "One only, without a second," and "All this is indeed the Self"—therefore, since duality appears there, that other self which is like a fragment of the Supreme Self is not ultimately real, just as the reflection of the moon and so forth in water is not the moon itself; thus, one who is different smells an object of smell that is different by means of a sense of smell that is different.

The phrase "one [smells] the other" is for the purpose of demonstrating the grammatical factors (*kāraka*), while "he smells" is the designation of both the action and its result—just as in the case of "he cuts. Just as in the expression "he cuts," both the repeated raising [of the tool] and the falling upon it, as well as the splitting into two of that which is to be cut, are designated by the single word "cuts"—because the action culminates in its result and because that result is not perceived apart from the action.

The one [the knower] smells the other [the object of smell] by means of the other [the sense of smell]—thus everything is as before—he cognizes; this is the state of one possessed of ignorance (*avidyā*). But where ignorance has been brought to destruction by the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), there is no existence of anything else apart from the Self.

In that state where, for this knower of Brahman, all names, forms, and so forth have been dissolved into the Self alone and have become the Self itself—wherein everything has thus become the Self alone—by what instrument could one there smell what is to be smelled, or who would smell? Likewise, how could one see, or how could one know? For in every case, action is accomplished by means of its factors (kārakas); therefore, in the absence of the factors, action is impossible, and in the absence of action, there is an absence of its fruit.

Therefore, the conventional usage of action, agent, and fruit exists only when ignorance prevails, but not for the knower of Brahman—for everything is indeed the Self. Apart from the Self, there exists neither an agent nor an action or its fruit. Furthermore, nothing that is non-Self can ever become the Self for anyone. Therefore, the state of being non-Self is merely imagined through ignorance; in ultimate reality, nothing exists apart from the Self.

Therefore, in the realization of the oneness of the Self from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the notions of action, agent, and fruit are untenable. Consequently, due to this contradiction, for the knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*), there is an absolute cessation of ritual acts and their means. The statement "by what, whom? is intended as a rhetorical negation (*kṣepārtha*) to demonstrate the impossibility of any other mode [of action]; that is to say, since no agent, instrument, or other factor of action is possible in any manner whatsoever, one should not smell anything by any means.

Even in that state of ignorance where one perceives another, by what could one perceive that by which one perceives all this? For that instrument by means of which one perceives is already engaged with the object to be known; and the desire to know belongs to the knower only regarding the object to be known, not regarding the Self. Furthermore, the Self cannot be an object of the Self, as fire is not its own object; and it is not possible for a knower to have knowledge of that which is not an object.

Therefore, by what instrument could one know that knower by whom all this is known, or who else could know him? But when, for the knower of Brahman who has discerned the ultimate reality, there remains only the solitary, non-dual Knower—then, O Maitreyī, by what could one know that Knower?
Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa of the second chapter.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in the seasons: Spring is the *hiṅkāra*, Summer is the *prastāva*, the Rainy season is the *udgītha*.
Autumn is the prelude, and winter is the finale...

This earth is the honey for all beings—this earth is the honey, the effect, for all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, just as honey is produced by many bees; just as a single honeycomb is fashioned by many bees, so too is this earth fashioned by all beings. Likewise, all beings are the honey—the effect—for this earth.

Furthermore, this person who exists on this earth—consisting of light, consisting of the radiance of pure consciousness, consisting of immortality, and characterized by the nature of being deathless—and this person who exists within the self (adhyātma), namely the embodied one (śārīra) existing in the body, likewise consisting of light and consisting of immortality as before—that person, who identifies with the subtle body (liṅga), is honey by virtue of being beneficial to all beings, and all beings are honey for him, according to the force of the word "and" (ca).

Thus, this tetrad is first of all one effect of all beings, and all beings are its effects; therefore, it has a single cause as its antecedent. Since this has arisen from a single cause, that alone is the one Brahman in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*); everything else is an effect, a mere modification consisting of speech-activity and name-only. This is, in brief, the meaning of all the honey-sections (*madhuparyāya*). This is precisely that which was proposed in the statement: "All this is what this Self is."

This is the immortal—namely, that knowledge of the Self which was declared to Maitreyī as the means to immortality; this is that immortal. This is Brahman—that which was introduced at the beginning of the chapter with the words, "I shall tell you Brahman," and "I shall make it known to you," and the knowledge concerning which is called the "knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyā*). This is everything—for from the knowledge of Brahman, everything comes to be. "The seasons indeed become favorable for him, and he becomes possessed of the seasons, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the seasons. (2) Thus ends the fifth section. (5) (2)
Likewise, water: within the self, water is especially situated in semen. (3) Likewise, fire: fire is especially situated in speech.

(4) Likewise, there is wind; internally, it is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). It possesses the nature of honey because it assists living beings by forming their bodies; it also possesses the nature of honey because it assists the elements contained within those bodies—such as that which consists of light—as their instruments of action. And so it has been said: "Of that speech, the earth is the body, and this fire is its form consisting of light.
Likewise, the sun is honey; internally, it is the eye.

(6) Likewise, the quarters are honey. Although the ear is the internal [aspect] of the quarters, at the time of hearing a sound, it becomes particularly present; thus, internally, it is the *prātiśrutka*—the *prātiśrutka* being that which exists (*bhava*) in an echo (*pratiśrutkā*), that is, at the time of hearing.
