(7) Likewise, the moon; internally, it is the mind.
Likewise, lightning; that which exists in the luster of the skin is *taijasa* with respect to the self.

(9) Likewise, thunder; although that which exists in sound is *śābda* with respect to the self, nevertheless, because it occurs specifically in the tone (*svara*), it is *sauvara* with respect to the self.
(10) Likewise, there is space; internally, there is the space within the heart.

It has been stated that the groups of elements beginning with earth, as well as the groups of deities—all of which consist of the aggregate of effects and instruments—act as honey by providing benefit to each embodied soul. That by which they are impelled to connect with the embodied souls and thus function as honey must now be explained; therefore, this [section] is commenced.

(11) --- "This is Dharma" --- although this Dharma is not itself perceptible (*apratyakṣa*), it is designated as "this is Dharma" by means of its effect, which is produced by it and is perceptible, just like something that is directly perceived. Furthermore, Dharma has been explained as being characterized by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*; it is the restrainer even of the Kṣatriyas and others; it is the cause of the diversity of the world, because it is the cause of the transformation of the earth and other elements; and it exists in the form of actions performed by living beings. And thus, there is the designation "this is Dharma" by means of what is perceptible.

In the case of *satya* (truth) and *dharma*, they have been taught by the author as non-different, characterized respectively as scriptural injunction and right conduct; however, here they are designated as distinct even though they are one, because they initiate effects in the form of a distinction between the seen and the unseen. That *dharma* which is unseen and termed *apūrva* initiates its effect through an unseen form consisting of both general and particular aspects: in its general form, it becomes the impeller of the earth and other elements, and in its particular form, it acts within the self upon the aggregate of the body and the instruments of action.

In that regard, concerning the agent of earth and the other elements: "that which is this fiery [quality] in this dharma"; likewise, with respect to the internal agent of the aggregate of the body and its instruments, it is "dhārma" (pertaining to dharma).

(12) Likewise, when practiced through visible conduct in the form of ritual observance, it becomes what is called "truth" (*satya*); that itself is dharma. That too is of two kinds, consisting of a general and a specific nature: the general form is inherent in earth and the other elements, while the specific form is inherent in the aggregate of the body and its instruments.

In that regard, existence (*bhava*) is real (*satya*)—both in the form of present activity inherent in earth and the other elements, as well as internally, inherent in the aggregate of the body and its instruments—as another Vedic scripture states: "By means of the Real, the wind blows.

This specific aggregate of causes and effects is impelled by both *dharma* and *satya*. That particular species with which it becomes associated—such as the human species and so forth—is the "species" (*jāti-viśeṣa*). In this regard, all classes of living beings are seen to exist in a state of mutual assistance and cooperation, distinguished precisely by their human and other species. Therefore, the human species and others are also honey for all beings. In that context, the human species and so forth are designated in two ways: as external and as internal. (14)

That aggregate of causes and effects (kāryakaraṇasaṃghāta) which is distinguished by the human and other species—that is this Self (ātman), the honey of all beings. [Objection: But was this not already indicated by the term "embodied" (śārīra) in the section concerning the earth? [Response: No, because in that context only the earthly element was grasped; here, however, it is the aggregate of causes and effects characterized by the hosts of deities of all beings, with all particularities—pertaining to the self, the elements, and the divine—completely set aside, that is called "this Self."

In this very Self, the person consisting of light, consisting of immortality, the essence of the formless, the universal Self, is pointed out; however, He was pointed out only partially in relation to earth and the other elements, and here, because there is no specific internal distinction [to be described], He is not pointed out in that way. But that which remains—the one consisting of consciousness, for whose sake this aggregate of the body and the subtle body exists as the Self—is what is called "this Self.

That Self (*ātman*) into which the "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*), remaining in the final stage (*paryāya*), has been introduced—that is this very Self. When that [Self], which was previously characterized by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the aggregate of effects and instruments produced by ignorance, has been introduced into the ultimate Self through the knowledge of Brahman, it is described as such: without interior or exterior, whole, and consisting of a single mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*). Indeed, he—this very same Self, the conscious individual (*vijñānātman*) who was designated in the immediately preceding stage as "consisting of light" (*tejomaya*) and so forth—is the learned one, the Self of all beings.

"Worshipped by all"—he is the lord (*adhipati*) of all beings, independent of all beings—not like a prince or a minister. What then? He is the king of all beings. The term "lord" (*adhipati*) is a specific qualification of "king": there may be someone who, by adopting the conduct appropriate for a king, is a king but not a lord; therefore, he specifies "lord. Thus, the knower who is the self of all beings becomes liberated as a knower of Brahman.

As for what was said—"Human beings think, 'By means of the knowledge of Brahman we shall become everything'; yet what is that Brahman, unknown, by which all this has become?"—this has been explained as follows: having heard from both the teacher and the sacred tradition that the Self alone is the Self of all, having reflected upon it through reasoning, and having realized it directly in this manner, just as it is shown in the Madhu Brāhmaṇa; therefore, even prior to such realization of Brahman characterized in this way, one was already Brahman itself, though through ignorance one was non-Brahman.

And all that was real was indeed non-real. But having cast aside that ignorance through this knowledge, the knower of Brahman, being Brahman itself, became Brahman; he, who is the All, became the All. The purpose of the scripture, for which it was commenced, is now fully accomplished.

Regarding this very point—that the entire world is established within the knower of Brahman, who is the Self of all and the universal Self—an illustration is provided: "Just as all the spokes are established in the nave and the felly of a chariot wheel"—this is a well-known fact—"even so, in this Self who has become the Supreme Self, the knower of Brahman, all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, all the gods beginning with Agni, all the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, and all the vital breaths beginning with speech [are established]."

All these selves enter into each body like the moon reflected in water; they are fashioned by ignorance, and the entire world is contained within this [Self]. As it was said—that Vāmadeva, the knower of Brahman, realized: "I became Manu and the Sun"—this state of being the Self of all has been explained. This very knower, the knower of Brahman, becomes everything, possessing all limiting adjuncts and being the Self of all.

It is without limiting adjuncts, indefinable, without interior or exterior, a single mass of pure consciousness, unborn, undecaying, immortal, fearless, immovable, and characterized by such attributes as "not this, not this," neither gross nor subtle. Not understanding this reality, certain logicians and even those who consider themselves learned among the knowers of scripture—misconceiving the meaning of the sacred texts and engaging in conceptualizations—fall into profound delusion.

These two mantras express this very meaning: "The one that moves not is swifter than the mind," and "It moves; it moves not. Likewise, in the Taittirīyaka: "Than which there is nothing higher," "Singing this Sāman he sits," and "I am food, I am food, I am food," and so forth. Similarly, in the Chāndogya: "Eating, playing, rejoicing," "If he is desirous of the world of the fathers," "Possessing all fragrances, possessing all tastes," "All-knowing, all-perceiving," and so forth.

And in the Atharva Veda: "It is far away and yet very near here. Also in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest"; "Who is that God, the great wonder?"; and "While others run, It stands surpassing them."

Likewise, in the Gītā: "I am the sacrifice, I am the ritual," "I am the father of this world," "He does not take on the sin of anyone," "Peace toward all beings," "Undivided among the divided," and "Devouring and procreative"—those who, considering such scriptural meanings to be seemingly contradictory, deliberate for the sake of determining the truth by the power of their own intellects, [conclude]: "The self exists" or "the self does not exist"; "It is an agent" or "it is a non-agent"; "It is liberated" or "it is bound"; "It is momentary" or "mere consciousness."

Conceptualizing in this way, "It is empty," they do not reach the further shore of ignorance, because they perceive contradictory attributes everywhere. Therefore, only those who follow the path shown by the scriptures and the teacher reach the further shore of ignorance; only they shall cross over this fathomless ocean of delusion, and not others who follow the cleverness of their own intellects.

The knowledge of Brahman, which is the means for attaining immortality, has been completed—that very knowledge which Maitreyī asked of her husband, saying, "Tell me that alone, O Blessed One, which you know to be the means of immortality. This narrative has been introduced for the purpose of praising this knowledge of Brahman. To briefly illuminate the meaning of that narrative, there are these two verses:

For thus, because it has been praised by both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas, the fact that the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is the means for attaining immortality and all things is made manifest and brought onto the royal road—just as the rising sun dispels the darkness of night. Moreover, the knowledge of Brahman is praised in this way: that which is guarded by Indra is difficult to attain even for the gods; since even from the two unpropitious divine physicians, the knowledge guarded by Indra was obtained only with great effort.

Having cut off the head of the Brahmin and joined it with the head of a horse, and when that [horse-head] was subsequently cut off by Indra, he rejoined his own head; through that very head of his own, the Brahmin heard the entire science of Brahman (brahmavidyā) as it was spoken. Since there has never been, nor will there ever be, any means for achieving the goals of human life superior to this—let alone anything existing at present—there is no praise higher than this.

Moreover, the knowledge of Brahman is praised in this way: it is well known in the world that action is indeed the means for all human goals, and such action is accomplished through wealth; therefore, there is no hope even for immortality [through action]. Yet, this very immortality is attained through the exclusive knowledge of the Self, independent of action.

Since, although it was expected to be mentioned in the section on ritual action (*karmaprakaraṇa*), it has instead been stated in the section on the *Pravargya* rite—having transcended the context of ritual action because it is incompatible with such rites—as being accompanied by absolute renunciation for the sake of attaining immortality; therefore, there is no means for the supreme human goal beyond this. Moreover, the knowledge of Brahman is thus praised: for the entire world delights in pairs of opposites, as the scripture declares, "He indeed did not find delight; therefore, one does not delight when alone."

Although Yājñavalkya was common to the world, by the power of self-knowledge he abandoned attachment to the cycle of worldly existence—consisting of wife, children, wealth, and so forth—and became one satisfied with wisdom and delighted in the Self. Furthermore, thus has this knowledge of Brahman been praised: because even while departing from the path of worldly existence, it was spoken by Yājñavalkya solely for the sake of pleasing his beloved wife, as indicated by the words, "You speak what is dear; come, sit here. (16)

In this regard, we have stated that this is a narrative for the purpose of praise; what, then, is that narrative? It is said: the word "this" (*idam*) points to what has been immediately mentioned, because it is present in the intellect; the particle "vai" (*vai*) is for the purpose of recollection; the word "that" (*tat*), referring to what was concluded in the narrative and mentioned in another context as something remote, is pointed out here while recalling it by means of the particle "vai."

That which was indicated in the section on the Pravargya rite, but not explicitly revealed as "honey," is this very honey pointed out here immediately following—"this earth," and so forth. How was it indicated there in another context? [It says: "Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa indeed taught these two the Brāhmaṇa text named 'Honey. That is their beloved abode; by this [teaching], he approaches that very abode of theirs. He (Dadhyañc) said: "I have been told by Indra: 'If you should teach this to anyone else, he shall cut off your head from its very base.'"

"Therefore, I am indeed afraid that he might cut off my head; I shall bring you both [the head] near. They said, "We two shall protect you from him. [He asked,] "How will you protect me? [They replied,] "When you bring us [the head], then we shall cut off your head, carry it away, and set it aside. Then, having brought the head of a horse, we shall replace yours with it. With that, you will recite [the Veda] for us. When you have recited for us, then Indra will cut off that head of yours."

"Then," they said, "we shall bring our own head and replace it for you. "So be it," he replied, and he initiated them both. When he had initiated them, they cut off his head and set it aside elsewhere. Then, having brought the head of a horse, they replaced it for him. With that [head], he recited the Veda to them both. When he had recited it to them, Indra then cut off that head of his. Then, having brought his own head, they replaced it for him.

However, only that which constitutes the honey forming a part of the Pravargya ritual was mentioned there, and not the "secret" (kakṣya) knowledge known as the knowledge of the Self. The narrative told therein is presented here for the purpose of praise: "This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa declared to the two Aśvins through this detailed exposition. Regarding this, the seer—the mantra—seeing, that is, perceiving, this very ritual action, spoke; he uttered it.

How so? That deed (*daṃsaḥ*) is connected with the distant word [in the verse]; *daṃsa* is the name for an action. And what is that deed qualified as? It is *ugraṃ*, meaning cruel, belonging to you two (*vām*), O *narā*, O you two who have the form of men, O Aśvins. And for what purpose is that action? For gain (*sanaye*); for even in the world, one greedy for gain performs a cruel deed, and these two are perceived in exactly the same way as people in the world. Therefore, I make manifest (*āviḥ kṛṇomi*), I reveal, that which was performed by you two in secret.

It is asked: "In what way? It is said: "Like the thunderer," that is, like Parjanya. The particle *na* is used here in the Veda in the sense of comparison (*upamārthīya*), not for negation—as in the expression *aśvaṃ na*, meaning "like a horse. The connection is as follows: "Just as Parjanya, like a thunderer, makes rain manifest through sounds such as thundering, so do I make manifest your cruel deed."

[Objection: But how could these two mantras be for the purpose of praising the two Aśvins? For these are words of censure. [Reply: This is not a fault; this is indeed praise, not words of censure. Because even while performing such an extremely cruel deed, not even a single hair of yours is diminished—indeed, nothing at all is lost. Thus, these two become praises; for people in the world remember that censure can take the form of praise, and likewise, censure in the form of praise is well-known in the world.

Dadhyañc by name was a descendant of Atharvan; *heti* is an expletive particle. That honey characterized by the knowledge of the Self (*ātman*), which the descendant of Atharvan proclaimed to you two with the head of a horse—that honey he proclaimed—*īm* is an expletive particle.

The passage beginning with "This indeed is that honey" is as before, for the purpose of showing another mantra. Likewise, another mantra follows that same narrative: "Dadhyañ by name, the son of Atharvan"—he specifies this because there is another [son] of Atharvan—namely, Dadhyañ by name, the son of Atharvan; "to him, Dadhyañ, the son of Atharvan," O Aśvinā, these are the words of the seer of the mantra.

The "equine" (*aśvyam*) is that which belongs to the horse by nature: the head. When the Brahmin's head had been cut off, having severed the horse's head and performed such an exceedingly cruel deed, you two caused the equine head to go toward the Brahmin; and that Ātharvaṇa [the horse] declared to you both that honey which he had previously promised—"I shall speak."

For what purpose did he speak thus, having placed his life in jeopardy? It is said: desiring to fulfill that truth which was previously promised as his vow (*ṛtāyan*); for this is an indication that the preservation of truth and dharma is weightier even than one's own life.

What is that honey which he spoke? It is said: "That which belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ. Tvaṣṭṛ is Āditya; that which pertains to him is the honey belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ. When the head of the sacrifice was severed by Tvaṣṭṛ, the Pravargya rite was performed for the purpose of rejoining it. The knowledge that constitutes a constituent part of that Pravargya rite is the honey belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ—the vision concerning the severing and rejoining of the head of the sacrifice is the honey belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ.

"O Dasras, O Dasras"—that is, you two who destroy the forces of adversaries and are the slayers of enemies. Furthermore, it is not only the honey related to the *Tvaṣṭṛ* sacrifice that he has declared to you both; moreover, the secret, hidden knowledge concerning the Supreme Self—which is like the "honey" described in the Madhu-brāhmaṇa and revealed in these two chapters—he has likewise declared to you both (*vām*). This is understood from the phrase "he has declared to you" (*pravocat*) which carries over [from the previous verse].

"This indeed is that honey," as before. Two mantras have been stated which conclude the narrative related to the *pravargya* rite; the meaning of the two chapters concerning the *pravargya* ritual has been illuminated by these two mantras in the form of a narrative. However, since the meaning of the two subsequent chapters concerning the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) must be revealed by the following two verses, the next section proceeds.

Regarding what was said by the youthful Atharvaṇa, "The honey that is within the girth-belt [is for you two]": it is asked, "What, then, is that honey? It is explained as follows: "He made the cities"—that is, the cities, which are bodies—since this is the process of the manifestation of the unmanifested. That Supreme Lord, while manifesting the unmanifested name and form, first created the worlds beginning with Bhūr, and then "made" (cakre), i.e., fashioned, the bipeds—the human bodies characterized by having two feet—and the bodies of birds.

Likewise, he created bodies before him—bodies of four-footed animals, characterized by having four feet. "Before" means in front. That Lord, becoming a bird—that is, the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*)—entered the bodies that were before him. The Śruti explains the meaning of the phrase "the Person entered the bodies": "This very Person is one who lies in all cities (bodies), in all bodies; because he lies in the city (*puri śete*), he is called 'one who lies in the city' (*puriśaya*), and thus he is called the 'Person' (*puruṣa*). By him, nothing at all remains uncovered or unenveloped.

Likewise, there is nothing whatsoever by which he is enclosed or entered within—neither by what is external nor by what is internal is he obstructed. Thus, he alone is established as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), through the distinction of interior and exterior, in the form of the body (*kārya*) and the instruments of action (*karaṇa*). The meaning is that the mantra beginning with "He made the cities" (*puraścakre*) teaches, in brief, the oneness of the Self (*ātmaikatva*).

"This indeed is that honey," and so forth, as before. "He became the counterpart (*pratirūpa*) to every form"—the meaning is that he became a different form corresponding to each form. That is to say, he is the counterpart or the conformable one; whatever the configuration of the mother and father, the son is born with that very configuration and in conformity with it. For indeed, a four-footed being is not born from a two-footed one, nor a two-footed one from a four-footed one. It is that very Supreme Lord, manifesting names and forms, who became the counterpart to every form.

Why, then, is it said that his coming is "in accordance with form"? It is for the purpose of manifesting—that is, making known—this form of his own self. For if name and form were not differentiated, then this form of the self, called the "mass of consciousness" (*prajñānaghana*) which is free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), would not be made known. But when name and form are differentiated through the nature of the body and the organs, then his form is made known.

Indra, the Supreme Lord, by means of his powers of illusion (*māyābhiḥ*), that is, by means of his powers of wisdom (*prajñābhiḥ*)—or rather, by means of false identifications with names and forms produced [by ignorance]—and not in reality, is perceived as having many forms (*pururūpaḥ*, *bahurūpaḥ*). Although he is in truth of a single form, a mass of pure consciousness (*prajñānaghanaḥ*), he is perceived through the powers of ignorance and wisdom.

For what reason, then? Because they are yoked like horses to a chariot for the purpose of illuminating their own respective objects. For "his" (asya) "bay steeds" (harayaḥ)—so called because they carry [the senses]—are the sense organs (*indriyāṇi*). They are "hundreds," meaning hundreds, and "ten" as well; they become "hundreds and ten" because of the great diversity of living beings. Therefore, due to the multiplicity of the objects of the senses, these [organs] are yoked solely for the purpose of illuminating those objects, not for the purpose of illuminating the Self. For it is said in the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad*: "The Self-existent pierced the openings outward."

Therefore, [the Lord] is perceived through those very forms of objects, not through His own nature as a single, uniform mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*). If this is so, then it would follow that the Supreme Lord is one thing and the *haris* (rays/manifestations) are another; to this it is replied: "He indeed is the *haris*, He indeed is ten and thousands, many and infinite," because of the infinity of the distinctions among living beings.

What more need be said? This very Brahman is the Self (ātman). It is "without prior" (apūrva), meaning that no cause exists prior to it; it is "without posterior" (anapara), meaning that no effect exists subsequent to it; it is "without interior" (anantara), meaning that no other kind of entity exists within its midst; likewise, it is "without exterior" (abāhya), meaning that nothing exists outside of it. What, then, is this uninterrupted Brahman? It is this very Self.

The two sheaths? That which is the inner self—the seer, the hearer, the thinker, the knower, the perceiver, the all-experiencer—[the "all-experiencer" being so called because it experiences everything through its entire self]—this is the instruction, this is the teaching of all the Vedāntas; this is the summarized meaning of all the Vedāntas; this is the immortal, the fearless; and thus the purpose of the scripture is fully completed. Thus ends the fifth Brāhmaṇa of the second chapter. One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in animals: goats are the *hiṅkāra*, sheep are the *prastāva*, cows are the *udgītha*, horses are the *pratihāra*, and man is the *nidhana*. (1)
The Commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
Second Chapter.
Sixth Brāhmaṇa.

Now follows the lineage (*vaṃśa*) of the Madhu-section, which deals with the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), for the purpose of praising that knowledge. This mantra is intended for the study of the sacred text (*svādhyāya*) and for its recitation (*japa*). In this context, "lineage" (*vaṃśa*) is so called because it is like a bamboo cane (*veṇu*); just as a bamboo cane is split joint by joint, so too this lineage extends from the tip down to the root. The succession of teachers for the four chapters is called the "lineage. In this regard, the word ending in the nominative case denotes the disciple, while the word ending in the ablative case denotes the teacher.

Parameṣṭhin is Virāj; [he arose] from Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha; beyond him, there is no further succession of teachers. That which is Brahman, however, is eternal and self-existent; salutation to that self-existent Brahman. Thus ends the sixth Brāhmaṇa of the second chapter.
Thus [ends the work] of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya...
In the commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
The second chapter.
Animals indeed become his, and he becomes rich in animals, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in animals. 2. Thus ends the sixth section.

One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman, which is higher than the high (*parovarīyas*), in the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). For the vital breath is the *hiṅkāra*, speech is the *prastāva*, the eye is the *udgītha*, the ear is the *pratihāra*, and the mind is the *nidhana*. These [vital breaths] are indeed higher than the high. 1.

Now, one should meditate upon the sevenfold Sāman in speech. Whatever in speech is "hum," that is the *hiṅkāra*; whatever is "pra," that is the *prastāva*; whatever is "eti," that is the *ādi*. Furthermore, one should meditate upon yonder sun as the sevenfold Sāman. It is always the same with its totality; it is the Sāman because it is the same with everything through its totality. Furthermore, one should meditate upon the sevenfold Sāman, which is commensurate with the self and transcends death: *hiṅkāra* has three syllables, *prastāva* has three syllables; thus they are equal.

The mind is the *hiṅkāra*, speech is the *prastāva*, the eye is the *udgītha*, the ear is the *pratihāra*, and the breath is the *nidhana*. This *Gāyatra* chant is woven upon the vital breaths. When one rubs [the fire-sticks] together, that is the *hiṅkāra*; when smoke arises, that is the *prastāva*; when it blazes, that is the *udgītha*; when it becomes embers, that is the *pratihāra*; when it subsides, that is the *nidhana*; and when it is completely extinguished, that is the *nidhana*. This *Rathantara* chant is woven upon the fire.

He beckons—that is the *hiṅkāra*. He makes himself known—that is the *prastāva*. He lies with a woman—that is the *udgītha*. He lies with a woman against her will—that is the *pratihāra*. He passes the time—that is the *nidhana*; he reaches the end—that is the *nidhana*. This *Vāmadevya* chant is interwoven in sexual union. The rising sun is the *hiṅkāra*; the risen sun is the *prastāva*; midday is the *udgītha*; afternoon is the *pratihāra*; and the setting sun is the *nidhana*. This *Bṛhat* chant is interwoven in the sun.

The clouds gather—that is the *hiṅkāra*; the cloud forms—that is the *prastāva*; it rains—that is the *udgītha*; it lightens and thunders—that is the *pratihāra*; it ceases—that is the *nidhana*. This *vairūpa* [sāman] is woven into Parjanya. Spring is the *hiṅkāra*, summer is the *prastāva*, the rainy season is the *udgītha*, autumn is the *pratihāra*, and winter is the *nidhana*. This *vairāja* [sāman] is woven into the seasons. The earth is the *hiṅkāra*, the intermediate space is the *prastāva*, the sky is the *udgītha*, the quarters are the *pratihāra*, and the ocean is the *nidhana*. These...

The Śakvarī verses are woven into the worlds: goats are the *hiṅkāra*, sheep are the *prastāva*, cows are the *udgītha*, horses are the *pratihāra*, and man is the *nidhana*; these Revatī verses are woven into animals. Greed is the *hiṅkāra*, skin is the *prastāva*, flesh is the *udgītha*, bone is the *pratihāra*, and marrow is the *nidhana*; this Yajñāyajñīya is woven into the limbs.

Agni is the *hiṅkāra*, Vāyu is the *prastāva*, Āditya is the *udgītha*, the constellations are the *pratihāra*, and the moon is the *nidhana*. This is the *rājana* [Sāman] woven upon the deities. The threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*) is the *hiṅkāra*; these three worlds are the *prastāva*; Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya are the *udgītha*; the constellations, birds, and rays of light are the *pratihāra*; and the serpents, Gandharvas, and ancestors are the *nidhana*. This Sāman is woven upon everything. "I choose the resonant (*vinardi*) Sāman, which is beneficial for cattle"—this refers to the *udgītha* of Agni. That which is unexpressed (*anirukta*) belongs to Prajāpati; that which is expressed (*nirukta*) belongs to Soma; and that which is soft (*mṛdu*) belongs to Soma.

The smooth sound belongs to Vāyu, the powerful to Indra, the krauñca-like to Bṛhaspati, and the apadhvānta to Varuṇa; one may employ all of these, but one should avoid that of Varuṇa. There are three branches of duty: sacrifice, study, and charity constitute the first; austerity alone is the second; and the student who dwells in the teacher’s house is the third, exhausting himself completely in the teacher’s house. All these attain worlds of merit, but he who is established in Brahman attains immortality.

The exponents of Brahman say: "What belongs to the Vasus is the morning pressing; what belongs to the Rudras is the midday pressing; and what belongs to the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas is the third pressing. Yonder sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods. Of it, the sky itself is the crosswise frame, the atmosphere is the cake, and the rays are the sons.

There was indeed a king named Janaka, the sovereign of the Videhas; one born there is called a Vaideha. He performed a sacrifice with many sacrificial fees—either a sacrifice known in another Vedic branch by the name "Bahudakṣiṇa," or the Aśvamedha, which is here called "Bahudakṣiṇa" due to the abundance of its sacrificial fees—with that he sacrificed.

At that sacrifice, Brāhmaṇas from the lands of the Kurus and the Pañcālas—invited there or desiring to see it, for they were renowned as being numerous among the learned—had gathered together and assembled. Having seen that great assembly of scholars there, a desire to know specifically who among them was the most proficient in Brahman (*brahmiṣṭha*) arose in Janaka, the King of Videha, who was the patron of the sacrifice. It is said that he wished to discern this distinction.

"How so? Who indeed among these Brahmins is the most learned (*anūcānatama*)—for all of them are learned; who among them is pre-eminently learned? Thus, having conceived a desire to know regarding the one most learned, he, for the sake of finding the means to ascertain that, enclosed a thousand cows of the first age within a cow-pen.

What kind of cows were those that were confined? It is said: a "pāda" is a fourth part of a pala of gold; ten pādas were bound to each of the horns of every single cow—five pādas on each horn. Those rays of his which extend toward the east are his eastern honey-cells. The Ṛgvedic verses are the honey-makers, the Ṛgveda itself is the flower, and those are the immortal waters. Indeed, these are the Ṛgvedic verses... 2 ... (2)

Having thus penned the cows, he said to those Brahmins: "O venerable Brahmins," he addressed them— "Whosoever among you is the most learned in the Veda (*brahmiṣṭha*)—for you are all indeed Brahmins—he who is the most preeminent in Vedic knowledge among you, let him drive these cows away toward his own home. Those Brahmins did not dare; indeed, having been addressed in this manner, those Brahmins did not venture to claim for themselves the status of being the most learned in the Veda; they became lacking in confidence.

When the Brahmins became disheartened, Yājñavalkya then spoke to his own pupil, a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī): "O gentle one (somya), drive these cows back toward our home, O Sāmaśrava. Because he hears the rules of the Sāman, Yājñavalkya was by implication a knower of the four Vedas. He then drove those cows back toward the teacher's house.

By accepting the wager for being the most proficient in Brahman (*brahmiṣṭha*), Yājñavalkya had claimed for himself the status of being the most proficient in Brahman; therefore, those Brāhmaṇas became enraged. [The text] describes the intent of their anger: "How can he say 'I am the most proficient in Brahman' to us, each of whom is preeminent? Now, while the Brāhmaṇas were thus enraged, there was a Hotṛ priest named Aśvala belonging to Janaka, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

He, the King—who was proud of being the most proficient in Brahman (*brahmiṣṭha*) and bold because of his royal status—questioned Yājñavalkya. How so? "Are you indeed, O Yājñavalkya, the most proficient in Brahman among us? The protracted vowel (*pluti*) is used here for the purpose of reproach. Yājñavalkya said: "We pay homage to the one most proficient in Brahman; at present, we are merely desirous of cattle.

Then, toward him who had thus made the claim of being the most proficient in Brahman, the Hotṛ Aśvala set his mind upon questioning him, precisely because of that acceptance of the wager regarding proficiency in Brahman.

He brooded over this Ṛgveda. From it, thus brooded upon, there was born its essence: fame, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food. 3. "O Yājñavalkya," he said. In that section on the Madhu-kāṇḍa, the transcendence of death by the sacrificer through the fivefold ritual combined with contemplation was explained briefly in the Udgītha section; since this present portion is an examination of that very same subject, this detailed exposition is now commenced for the purpose of explaining the specific contemplations contained therein.

This collection of means for this rite—such as the officiating priests, the sacrificial fire, and so forth—is "attained" (āpta), that is, pervaded (vyāpta), by Death, characterized by action and accompanied by innate attachment; it is not only pervaded but also "assailed" (abhipanna), meaning it has been brought under the control of Death. By what kind of means characterized by vision does the sacrificer overcome this attainment of Death—that is, transcending the domain of Death—and become liberated, independent, and no longer subject to Death? This is the meaning.

"Is it not the case that it was already stated in the section on the *udgītha* that one is liberated by means of the vision of the Self as the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*)?"—Certainly, this was said; however, there is no fault here, because this present undertaking is for the purpose of explaining those specific details that were not mentioned therein. Yājñavalkya says: "By the Hotṛ priest, by the fire, and by speech."

He explains the meaning of this: "Who, then, is the Hotṛ by whom one transcends death? It is said: Speech indeed belongs to the sacrificer of the sacrifice, according to the Vedic revelation, "The sacrificer is indeed the sacrifice. That which is the speech of the sacrificer of the sacrifice is itself the Hotṛ with respect to the sacrifice (*adhiyajña*). How so? That which is this speech of the sacrificer of the sacrifice is this well-known Agni with respect to the deities (*adhidaivata*); this has been explained in the section on the three foods (*tryanna-prakaraṇa*).

And that fire is the Hotṛ priest, according to the Vedic revelation: "Agni indeed is the Hotṛ. These two means of the sacrifice—the Hotṛ priest as the officiant with respect to the sacrifice (*adhiyajña*), and speech with respect to the self (*adhyātma*)—both of these means are limited and seized by Death; they are brought under its control by action prompted by innate ignorance and attachment, which undergoes transformation at every moment due to that Death.

Thus, being perceived by this Agni in his form as the presiding deity (*adhidaivata*), it leads to the sacrificer’s liberation from death at the sacrifice. This is what is stated: "He is liberation; he is the Hotṛ priest, Agni. Liberation is indeed the very perception of the true nature of Agni. For when one perceives these two means [the Hotṛ and the sacrificial fire] in the form of Agni, at that very moment one is liberated from natural attachment—that is, from death consisting of the internal (*ādhyātmika*) limited form and the external (*ādhibhautika*).

Therefore, that Hotṛ priest, when viewed in the form of Agni, is liberation (*mukti*)—the means of liberation for the sacrificer. That is "transcendent liberation" (*atimukti*); the meaning is that whatever constitutes liberation, that itself is transcendent liberation, being the means to transcendent liberation. Liberation is that vision of the two limited means of attainment in their unlimited form as Agni, by way of the divine aspect (*adhidaivata*).

That liberation which is the vision of the divine (adhidaivata) is itself—having transcended death, which has its locus in the limbs consisting of the distinctions between the internal self (adhyātma), the elements (adhibhūta), and their objects—it is the attainment of the state of the divine, namely the state of Agni, which constitutes the fruit; that is called "transcendence" (atimukti). Since liberation itself is the means for that transcendence, he calls that [liberation] "transcendence. For it has been explained in the section on the Udgītha that for the sacrificer who has attained transcendence, there is the transformation of speech and the other organs into Agni and the other deities.

In that [preceding section], the mere vision of the principal vital breath (*prāṇa*) in its general aspect was stated as the means to liberation, but not its specific details; here, however, the specific meditation on speech and the other organs as fire and so forth is described. Furthermore, the transcendence of death—which is the very fruit explained in the *Udgītha-brāhmaṇa* by the passage beginning "Having transcended death, he shines"—is precisely this [result]. "That flowed out; it took refuge all around the sun. That indeed is the red form of the sun... Thus ends the first section. (4) 1. (4)

"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "the liberation from death characterized by action—which is prompted by natural ignorance and attachment—has been explained. Now, that which is the cause of the transformation of time, which is the substratum of that death consisting of action along with its attachments and is the means for performing rites such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices—from that time, liberation must be described as distinct. This [section] is commenced to show that even apart from the performance of ritual acts, [time is the cause] both before and after the act, by virtue of being the cause of the transformation of the means."

Because time is observed through its activity, liberation from it must be explained as distinct from time; therefore, he says: "All this that is obtained by day and night"—and that time is of two forms: characterized by days and nights, etc., and characterized by lunar days (tithis), etc. Regarding that, he first states liberation from what is characterized by days and nights: for by day and night everything is born, grows, and perishes, as does the means for sacrifice—the eye of the sacrificer and the Adhvaryu priest.

The remaining syllables are to be understood as before: the eye of the sacrificer and the Adhvaryu priest constitute a pair of means. When these two, having abandoned the limitations of the individual self (*adhyātma*) and the physical elements (*adhibhūta*), are perceived as the nature of the deities (*adhidaivata*), that is liberation (*mukti*). That Adhvaryu, when perceived as being of the nature of Āditya, is liberation; and that very liberation is "transcendence" (*atimukti*), as explained previously. For one who has attained the state of being the Self of Āditya, day and night do not exist. (5)

Now, liberation beyond the characteristics of the lunar days (*tithi*) and so forth is described: all this [universe] has the sun as its agent during the undifferentiated day and night, but not during the lunar days such as the first day (*pratipad*). However, because they undergo increase and decrease, the moon is the agent of those lunar days beginning with the *pratipad*. Therefore, by attaining that [state of the moon], there is the transcendence of the bright and dark fortnights, just as there is the transcendence of day and night by attaining the state of the sun.

In this regard, it is understood in the *Udgītha-brāhmaṇa* that "the breath (*prāṇa*) of the sacrificer is Vāyu, and he himself is the Udgātṛ," and it is determined that "he sang the Udgītha with speech and with breath. Furthermore, it is stated that "water is the body of this breath, and its form of light is that moon. Since there is identity between the breath, Vāyu, and the moon, there would be no difference whether the conclusion were made by means of the moon or by means of Vāyu; thinking thus, the Śruti concludes by means of Vāyu in his form as the presiding deity (*adhidaivata*).

Moreover, the waxing and waning of the moon are indeed caused by the wind (*vāyu*); therefore, the wind is the agent, or rather the instigator, even of time characterized by the new moon and so forth. Consequently, it is most reasonable that one who has attained the form of the wind transcends time consisting of lunar days and the like. Thus, in another scriptural passage, meditation on the wind in the form of the moon constitutes liberation and further liberation (*atimukti*); whereas here, for the followers of the Kāṇva school, meditation on the two means in their causal form as the self of the wind constitutes liberation and further liberation—there is no contradiction between these two scriptural texts.

The liberation of the sacrificer from death and time has been explained. By what support does he, while being liberated, transcend death—which consists of limitation—and attain the fruit? It is said that he is "liberated" (atimucyate) by means of this well-known intermediate space (antarikṣa), the ether (ākāśa). The word "as it were" (iva) implies that there is indeed a support there, but the point is that it is not known.

As for that unknown support, it is asked by means of the pronoun "by what," because otherwise the attainment of the fruit would be impossible; the object of the question is: "By what support, by what ascent, does the sacrificer, while attaining the fruit of his action, become liberated?"—that is, "By what ascent does the sacrificer ascend to the heavenly world?"—the meaning being that he reaches the heavenly world as his fruit and thereby becomes liberated.

"Brahmā as the officiating priest through the mind, with Candra"—the arrangement of these syllables is as before. In that regard, that which is well-known as the mind of the sacrificer in the context of the sacrifice is this very Candra in the context of the deities (adhidaiva); for it is well known that "mind is the internal self (adhyātma) and the moon is the presiding deity (adhidaivata). That same moon is Brahmā the officiating priest; by him—[he] perceives both of these, namely the limited form of Brahmā in the objective world (adhibhūta) and the mind in the internal self (adhyātma), as the unlimited form of the moon.

The meaning is that by means of that moon as a mental support, one attains the world of heaven as the fruit of karma and is thereby liberated. The word "iti" is used for the purpose of conclusion; that is to say, these are the various modes of liberation from death. Since all the different types of views concerning the components of the sacrifice have been stated on this occasion, there is a conclusion: "these are the liberations"—meaning, the liberations are of such a kind. Now, regarding the "correspondences" (*saṃpadaḥ*): now, at this point, the correspondences are being explained.

"Accomplishment" (*sampad*) refers to the securing of the fruit for fruitful rites such as the *agnihotra* by means of some commonality, or it is the fruit itself; for those striving with all their energy to perform the means of attaining the fruit, there may be an impossibility due to some deficiency. Therefore, one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), taking up whatever rite is possible among the *agnihotra* and others as a basis, and being possessed of knowledge regarding the fruits of action, accomplishes precisely that which he desires as the fruit of his action.

Otherwise, even for those of the three higher castes who are entitled to perform the *rājasūya*, *aśvamedha*, *puruṣamedha*, and *sarvamedha* sacrifices, these would be impossible; their recitation would be merely for the sake of private study (*svādhyāya*) if there were no means whatsoever to attain their fruits. Therefore, the attainment of those fruits occurs through meditative identification (*saṃpat*) alone; thus, since even such identifications possess fruitfulness, the meditative identifications are now commenced.

"O Yājñavalkya," he said, in order to draw his attention: "With how many *ṛc*s will this Hotṛ priest perform the recitation (*śastra*) at this sacrifice today?"—that is, with how many, by what number, types of *ṛc*s will this Hotṛ priest, the officiating minister, perform and recite the *śastra* in this sacrifice? The other replied: "With three types of *ṛc*s. To him who had spoken thus, the other replied: "Which are those three? This question concerns the objects to be numbered, whereas the previous one concerned the number itself.

Regarding the *puronuvākyā*: those *ṛc* verses which are employed prior to the time of the sacrifice are called the *ṛc*-class known as the *puronuvākyā*; those *ṛc* verses which are employed for the purpose of the sacrifice are the *ṛc*-class known as the *yājyā*; those *ṛc* verses which are employed for the purpose of the *śastra* recitation are the *ṛc*-class known as the *śasyā*; and all *ṛc* verses whatsoever—whether they are *stotriyā*s or others—are entirely subsumed within these three classes of *ṛc*.

"What does he conquer by means of those [verses]?"—namely, "whatever there is here that possesses breath. And because of this commonality of number, whatever collection of living beings there is, he conquers all of that; he accomplishes that entire range of fruits through the commonality of number and other such factors.

"O Yājñavalkya," he said, as before. "How many kinds of oblations will this Adhvaryu priest offer today in this sacrifice?"—"How many types of oblations are there?"—"Three."—"Which are those three?"—as before. The other replied: "Those which, when offered, blaze up are the oblations of fuel-sticks and clarified butter (*samid-ājya*); those which, when offered, overflow with sound, making a great noise, are the oblations of meat and so forth; those which, when offered, lie down—that is, having gone beneath the earth—they lie upon it, are the oblations of milk and Soma. What does one win by means of them?"

What does one conquer by means of these oblations thus prepared? Those oblations which, when offered, blaze—that is, are endowed with brilliance—and the fruit called the world of the gods is likewise brilliant; because of this commonality, he brings about the following identification: "These blazing oblations being prepared by me are the very form of the world of the gods, the fruit of action; thus, the fruit known as the world of the gods itself is being prepared by me. In this way, he effects the correspondence.

Those oblations which are offered with excessive noise—he conquers the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*) by means of them, due to the commonality of being the producers of contemptible sounds. For in the city of Saṃyaminī, which is connected to the world of the ancestors, there arises among those being led away by Vaivasvata the cry, "Alas, we are destroyed! Release us, release us! Such too are the oblations of the portions cut off (*avadāna*). Therefore, because of this similarity to the world of the ancestors, he brings about the identification: "The world of the ancestors itself is being accomplished by me."

Those oblations which lie upon the fire-altar, by means of them he conquers the world of men, because of the commonality of their connection with the surface of the earth; for the world of men is indeed "below" (adhaḥ), in relation to the higher worlds of the Sādhyas, or else in relation to downward movement. Therefore, at the time of performing the oblations of milk and Soma, he brings about the realization: "The world of men itself is being accomplished by me.

"O Yājñavalkya," he said, as before. This officiating priest, the Brahman, seated on his seat to the south, protects the sacrifice. "By how many deities does he protect it?"—this plural number is used incidentally, for he protects it by means of only one deity; once this is known, a question using the plural would not be appropriate for one who already knows.

Therefore, having observed the sequence in the questions and answers of the two preceding sections—namely, "By how many? and "By three," and "Three"—here too the inquiry is commenced with the plural number. Alternatively, the plural is used for the purpose of confusing the opponent. The other says: "By one"; that deity is one, by whom, standing to the south, he protects the sacrifice on the seat of Brahman. "Which is that one?"—"The mind alone"; the mind is that deity.

For Brahmā functions through the mind alone by means of meditation, according to another Vedic text: "Of that sacrifice, the mind and speech are the two paths; of these two, the Brahmā perfects one by means of the mind. Therefore, the mind itself is the deity; for by that mind, Brahmā protects the sacrifice. And that mind is infinite due to its various modifications (vṛtti); the word *vai* serves to indicate what is well-known; the infinity of the mind is well-established. The gods are those who possess the conceit (abhimāna) of that infinity.

For there is another scriptural passage stating, "The All-gods are indeed infinite—wherein all the gods become one," and so forth; therefore, because of that commonality of infinity, he wins an infinite world by means of that [offering].

"O Yājñavalkya," he said, as before. "How many *stotriyās* will this Udgātṛ chant? A *stotriyā* is a collection of verses (*ṛk*) belonging to a *sāman*, consisting of several verses. Whether they are *stotriyās* or *śasyās*, whatever verses there may be, he says that they are all indeed three; and these have been explained—namely, the *puronuvākyā*, the *yājyā*, and the *śasyā* as the third. In this regard, it was previously stated: "Whatever exists here that is endowed with breath, he conquers all of that"—by what commonality is that so?

It is said: "Which are those three *ṛc*s that exist with reference to the self (*adhyātma*)? Breath (*prāṇa*) itself is the *puronuvākyā*, because of the commonality of the word "forward" (*pura*). Exhalation (*apāna*) is the *yājyā*, because of immediate succession—for it is through exhalation that the deities swallow the oblation offered, and sacrifice is the act of offering. The pervasive breath (*vyāna*) is the *śasyā*, according to another scriptural passage: "Without breathing out and without breathing in, one utters the *ṛc*. What one conquers by means of them has already been explained.

In this regard, the general principle of specific connection has not yet been stated and is now being declared here; everything else has already been explained. By means of the general connection with the world, one conquers the earth-world (*pṛthivīloka*) by the *puronuvākyā* verse; the intermediate space-world (*antarikṣaloka*) by the *yājyā* verse, because of the commonality of being in the middle; and the heavenly world (*dyuloka*) by the *śasyā* verse, because of the commonality of being upward. Then, from that resolution of the question regarding the Self, that Hotṛ priest Aśvala desisted, thinking, "This is beyond our reach. Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa of the third chapter.
Now, those which are its southern rays are its southern honey-cells; the Yajus formulas themselves are the honey-makers, the Yajurveda itself is the flower, and those are the immortal waters. 1.

Now, regarding him—here the particle *ha* signifies tradition (*aitihya*). Immediately after Aśvala had ceased, Ārtabhāga, born of the Jaratkāru lineage (a *Jāratkārava*), the son of Ṛtabhāga, questioned Yājñavalkya, who was the subject under discussion. He addressed him as "O Yājñavalkya," saying "thus" (*iti*) in order to draw his attention. The question was as before: "How many are the *grahas* (seizers) and how many are the *atigrahas* (over-seizers)? The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the sentence. In this regard, the question might be asked either when the *grahas* and *atigrahas* have already been identified, or when they have not yet been identified.

If the *grahas* and *atigrahas* are already known, then since their number—which is a quality belonging to them—is also known, a question regarding the scope of that number, such as "How many *grahas* are there? How many *atigrahas*? would be inappropriate. On the other hand, if they are not known, then the question must concern the objects to be numbered; one should ask "Which are the *grahas*? Which are the *atigrahas*?", rather than asking "How many *grahas* are there? How many *atigrahas*?"

Moreover, a question arises for the sake of specific knowledge only regarding things whose general nature is already known—for example, "Which ones here are the Kaṭhas? Which ones here are the Kālāpas? But in this case, no entities named "grasping" (graha) and "over-grasping" (atigraha) are well-known in the world, such that there would be a question for the sake of specific knowledge.

But has it not been stated that "he is released"? For release belongs to one who was seized by a *graha*; since it was stated twice—"this is release (*mukti*), this is further release (*atimukti*)"—it follows that both *grahas* and *atigrahas* have been reached. Now, in that context too, four *grahas* and four *atigrahas* were specifically identified: speech, sight, breath, and mind. Therefore, the question "How many? is inappropriate because they have already been identified. Not so, for the purpose is not to establish a definite number; indeed, the number four was not intended there.

In this context, however, regarding the vision of the *grahas* (seizers) and *atigrahas* (over-seizers), the question "How many? is indeed appropriate, as there is a desire to express the quality of their being eight. Therefore, since "this is liberation (*mukti*), that is over-liberation (*atimukti*)" mentions liberation and over-liberation twice, the *grahas* and *atigrahas* are also established [as a pair]. Consequently, he asks: "How many are the *grahas*, or how many are the *atigrahas*? The other replies: "There are eight *grahas* and eight *atigrahas*. [The questioner asks: "Which of those eight *grahas* mentioned are to be understood as the specific ones to be grasped?"

These very *yajus* formulas heated this *Yajurveda*. From it, thus heated, there was born its essence (*rasa*)—its fame, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food. Regarding this, it is said: "The *graha* is indeed the *prāṇa*. Here, "prāṇa" refers to the sense of smell, because of the context; it is accompanied by air (*vāyu*). "By means of the *apāna*" means by means of odor (*gandha*); because it is associated with the *apāna*, the *apāna* is called "odor. For the whole world smells an odor brought forth by the *apāna* through the nose. Thus it is said: "For one smells odors by means of the *apāna*."
That flowed forth; it took refuge around the sun. That indeed is this white form of the sun. This is the second section.

Speech, indeed, is the *graha* (seizer). For by speech—which is limited to the internal self, which is the locus for objects of attachment, and which is occupied with speaking what is untrue, false, vulgar, loathsome, and so forth—the world is seized and carried away; therefore, speech is the *graha*. That [speech] is seized by name as the *atigrāha*. That *graha* called speech is seized by "name" (*nāmnā*), that is, by its object, which is that which is to be spoken; the lengthening in the word *atigrāheṇa* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). For speech exists for the sake of the meaning to be expressed.

Speech is employed for that purpose—the object to be spoken—and is thus brought under its control. Without performing that task, there can be no release from it; therefore, speech is said to be "seized by the over-seizer" (*atigrāha*) that is name. For, engaged through attachment to what is to be spoken, one becomes joined with all misfortunes. The rest is the same. Thus, these eight, ending with the skin, are the "seizers" (*graha*), and these eight, ending with touch, are the "over-seizers" (*atigrāha*). (10)

When the *grahas* and *atigrahas* had been withdrawn, he spoke again: "O Yājñavalkya," he said, "as for all this which is food for death—as for all this that is differentiated, all of it is food for death; everything is born and perishes, being seized by death characterized as the *grahas* and *atigrahas*. What indeed might be that deity, that deity for whom even death would be food? For another Vedic text says: "Death is the condiment for him."

This is the intention of the questioner: if death were to speak of death, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); but if it does not speak of it, liberation from this death characterized by the "seizers" (*graha*) and "over-seizers" (*atigraha*) would not be possible. For liberation occurs only upon the destruction of death in the form of the seizers and over-seizers. If there were a death even of death, then the destruction of death—characterized by the seizers and over-seizers—would be possible. Thinking the question to be difficult to answer, he asks: "Who, indeed, is that deity? There certainly exists a death of death.

[Objection: But would this not lead to an infinite regress—since for that [death] there would be yet another death? [Reply: There is no infinite regress, because it is impossible for the death of all deaths to have another death. How, then, is it known that there is a death of death? Because it is observed. Fire, for instance, is seen to be the death of everything because it is a destroyer; yet that fire is consumed by water. That fire is the food of water. Therefore, grasp this: there is a death of death. By that death of death, the entire collection of grasping (*graha*) and over-grasping (*atigraha*) is consumed.

When that bondage has been destroyed and devoured by Death, liberation from saṃsāra becomes possible; for it has been stated that bondage is characterized by the *grahas* and *atigrahas*, and it has been established that liberation from them is indeed possible. Therefore, human effort toward the release from bondage becomes fruitful; thus, one overcomes death once again.

When death has been swallowed by the higher Death—the realization of the Supreme Self—and the wise one, Yajñavalkya, is liberated, at what time does this person die? Do the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*)—the *grahas* such as speech and the *atigrahas* such as name, which exist within as latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and are the instigators—depart upward from this knower of Brahman who is dying, or do they not? "No," said Yājñavalkya; "they do not depart."

Right here, in this very [Supreme], the effects and the instruments attain non-distinction from the Supreme Self; they are merged into their own source, which is the true essence of the Supreme Brahman—they are dissolved into it through a state of oneness, meaning they are absorbed like waves into the ocean.

And thus another scriptural passage shows the dissolution of the vital breaths—which are denoted by the word "parts" (kalā)—into the supreme Self: "In this very way, these sixteen parts of this observer, which have the Person as their goal, reach the Person and go to their setting. This demonstrates that they attain non-distinction from the supreme Self. [Objection: In that case, one is not dead. [Reply: No; for...

And this [body] is dead—because it swells, that is, it undergoes inflation; it distends, being filled with external air like a leather bag; thus inflated, the dead person lies motionless. The meaning of the sentence is that upon the destruction of its bonds, there is no going anywhere for one who is liberated.

"Does only the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of the liberated one merge [into its source], or does everything that motivates it also [merge]? Or is it only the vital breaths and not everything that motivates them? If the motivator remains, there would be the consequence of the vital breaths returning again; but if everything—including desire, action, and so forth—merges, then liberation becomes possible. For this purpose, the next question was asked: "Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person dies, what does not leave him? The other replied: "The name (*nāman*)."

The meaning is that everything is completely merged [into the name]; however, the name itself does not dissolve, because of its connection with form. For the name is eternal; indeed, the name is infinite. The infinity of the name is precisely its eternity. Those who are entitled to that infinity—the Viśvedevas are indeed infinite—he wins an infinite world by means of that; having approached the Viśvedevas, who are entitled to that infinity of names, as his very self, he wins an infinite world through that vision of infinity.

The bondage consisting of the *grahas* (seizers) and *atigrahas* (over-seizers) has been described as being of the nature of death. And for that death, both the existence of further death and liberation are possible. That liberation consists in the dissolution right here of those things known as *grahas* and *atigrahas*, like the extinguishing of a lamp. To determine the essential nature of that which impels this bondage—which is called *graha* and *atigraha* and is of the nature of death—this [section] is commenced. "Yājñavalkya," he said.

On this point, some describe it as follows: even when the graspers (*graha*) and over-graspers (*atigraha*), together with their causal agents (*prayojaka*), have been destroyed, one is indeed not yet liberated. Remaining only as a name, separated from the Supreme Self by ignorance—which stands in the place of barren soil and originates from one's own self—and excluded from the world that is to be enjoyed, one persists in the intermediate state with desire and karma eradicated. For such a person, the perception of duality must be removed by means of the vision of oneness with the Supreme Self; therefore, the vision of the Supreme Self must now be commenced. Thus they say.
Thus, having postulated this intermediate state called "liberation," they establish the connection with the subsequent text.

In this regard, it must be asked: how can there be seeing, hearing, reflecting, and meditating upon the Supreme Self for one who is bodiless when the instruments [of perception] have fallen apart? For they say that such a person has his vital breaths completely withdrawn and nothing remains but a mere name; indeed, it is said, "He lies dead. This cannot be established even by way of imagination. If, on the other hand, it is postulated that while still living, he is freed from the objects of enjoyment with only ignorance remaining, then it must be stated what the cause of that is.

If it were argued that this is the means for attaining the self which is the unity of all duality, that has already been refuted. A knower endowed with the vision of the self as the unity of duality, accompanied by ritual action (*karman*), would—upon death and the dissolution of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)—attain either the state of being the world-self or the nature of Hiraṇyagarbha. Alternatively, one whose vital breaths have not dissolved might, while still living, turn away from the objects of enjoyment, become dispassionate, and be oriented toward the vision of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). However, both of these goals cannot be achieved through a single means accomplished by a single effort.

If it is a means for attaining Hiraṇyagarbha, it is not a means for turning away from him; if it is a means for turning away from the objects of enjoyment in order to direct one toward the Supreme Self (paramātman), it is not a means for attaining Hiraṇyagarbha—for that which is a means for reaching a destination is not also a means for the cessation of that journey. Furthermore, if one were to die and reach Hiraṇyagarbha, and then, with the vital breaths withdrawn and nothing remaining but the name, be qualified for the knowledge of the Supreme Self, then the instruction on the knowledge of the Supreme Self would be useless for people like us.

For the knowledge of Brahman is taught for the sake of the human goal (puruṣārtha) for all beings, according to such scriptural passages as, "Whosoever among the gods... Therefore, this conception is utterly base and stands outside the scriptures. We shall, however, proceed with the subject at hand.

In this regard, with the desire to determine by what cause the bondage characterized by the *grahas* (seizers) and *atigrahas* (over-seizers) is instigated, [the text] says: "When this person—who lacks right vision (*asamyagdarśin*), possesses a head, hands, and so forth, and has died—his speech enters fire, his breath (*prāṇa*) enters the wind, and his sight enters the sun"; the phrase "enters" is to be connected everywhere [in the following cases]: "the mind [enters] the moon, the hearing [enters] the quarters, the body [enters] the earth, and the self (*ātman*) [enters] space. Here, the term "self" refers to the substratum, namely the space within the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*).

It goes even into space; the body hairs go into the plants; the hair of the head goes into the trees; blood and semen are deposited in the waters—this is a sign of their being taken up again; for in all cases, by words such as "speech" and so forth, the deities are intended, and it is not the mere instruments that depart prior to liberation.

In this regard, it is asked: since the instruments (karaṇas), when not presided over by deities, are comparable to an axe or other tools laid aside, and the person (puruṣa) who is the agent is bodiless and lacks independence, upon what does he depend? The question is: "Where does this person exist then?"—that is, "Upon what does the person depend then?"—referring to that substratum by resorting to which he again takes up the aggregate of the body and the instruments, and by means of which the bondage characterized by the "graspers" (graha) and "over-graspers" (atigraha) is applied. What is that? Such is the question.

To this it is replied: [Theories] such as inherent nature (*svabhāva*), chance (*yadṛcchā*), time (*kāla*), action (*karman*), fate (*daiva*), consciousness-only (*vijñānamātra*), and emptiness (*śūnya*) have been postulated by various disputants. Therefore, because there are many points of disagreement, no determination of the reality can be reached through the method of mere debate (*jalpanyāya*). If you desire a determination of the reality here, then, my dear Ārtabhāga, take my hand; the two of us alone shall know—that which is to be known regarding what you have asked—and we shall investigate it.

Why? Because this matter cannot be determined by us two in the midst of people, in a crowd of men; therefore, we shall go to a secluded place for deliberation. "Those two," and so forth, is the statement of the Śruti. It is said what those two, Yājñavalkya and Ārtabhāga, did after going to a secluded place: "Having departed from that place where people were gathered, they two deliberated; at first, they reflected upon each of the positions of the worldly disputants."

Listen to what those two said after deliberating and setting aside all prima facie objections: they stated that action alone is the recurring basis—the cause for the appropriation of the body and the senses—and that it is not merely that.

When Time, Karma, Destiny, and the Lord were proposed as causes, those two praised Karma alone—they praised it because it has been determined that the repeated appropriation of the body, the senses, and the objects of perception is impelled by Karma; therefore, one indeed becomes meritorious through meritorious action prescribed by the scriptures, and conversely, one becomes its opposite, namely sinful, through sinful action. Thus, when the questions had been resolved by Yājñavalkya, then—
Because Yājñavalkya was impossible to shake, Ārtabhāga, the son of Jaratkāru, ceased questioning.
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa of the third chapter.
Now, those rays of his which go westward are its western honey-cells; the Sāmans are the honey-makers, the Sāmaveda is the flower, and those are the immortal waters. 1.

(1) Immediately after Jāratkāra had ceased speaking, Lāhyāyani—the son of Lāhya, whose personal name was Bhujyu—questioned him. He said, "O Yājñavalkya. At the outset, the vision of the Aśvamedha was mentioned; and the Aśvamedha sacrifice, which yields both collective and individual fruits, whether combined with knowledge or accomplished through knowledge alone, is the supreme limit of all ritual acts. For the traditional authorities remember: "There is nothing higher than the killing of an embryo and the Aśvamedha among merit and demerit."

Therefore, he attains both the aggregate (*samaṣṭi*) and the individuals (*vyaṣṭi*). Among these, the individuals are well-known as pertaining to the interior of the cosmic egg (*antaraṇḍa*), being the fruits of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*); it is said: "Death becomes the self of these deities; he becomes one among them. And Death—characterized by hunger—is the first-born aggregate consisting of the intellect (*buddhyātman*), namely Vāyu, the Thread (*sūtra*), Truth (*satya*), and Hiraṇyagarbha.

Its defined domain must be stated: that which constitutes the nature of all duality, who is the inner self of all beings, the mark (*liṅga*), the formless essence, upon whom depend the actions of all beings, and who is the supreme goal and the highest fruit of actions and of the cognitions connected with those actions. To what extent is its range, and how great is its all-encompassing pervasion? When that is explained, the entire sphere of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*)—the realm of bondage—will have been explained.

And in order to demonstrate the extraordinary nature of that vision of the Self as both the aggregate and the individual, he relates his own personal narrative; by means of this, he thinks, "I shall confound the intellect of my opponent."

"In the Madra country—Madra being the name of a region—we, being *carakas*—so called because we practice vows for the sake of study, or perhaps because we are *adhvaryu* priests—wandered about. While wandering, we went to the house of one named Patañjali, of the Kapi lineage (*kāpya*). He had a daughter possessed by a Gandharva—that is, taken over by some non-human being."

The fire-altar (agni) called Dhiṣṇya is determined to be the Gandharva, the deity who is the officiating priest (ṛtvij), because of his distinguished knowledge; for such knowledge is not possible for a mere being. Surrounded by all of us, we asked him: "Who are you?"—that is, "Who are you? What is your name? What is your true nature? He replied that he was a Gandharva, Sudhanvan by name and Āṅgirasa by lineage.

When we asked him about the ends, the limits, of the worlds—at which time, while all those engaged in seeking knowledge of the dimensions of the universe were praising themselves, we questioned him—how so? "Where did the Pārikṣitas go? That Gandharva told us everything. The intention is: "By that [knowledge] I have obtained divine wisdom; you do not possess it; therefore, you are defeated."

Thus, being endowed with knowledge and having received the traditional lore from a Gandharva, I ask you, Yājñavalkya: "Where did the Pārikṣitas go? Do you know that? O Yājñavalkya, speak; I ask you: "Where did the Pārikṣitas go? These very Sāmans, indeed, heated the Sāmaveda. From that which was thus heated, fame, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and the essence of food were produced. 2. (2)

Yājñavalkya said: "He indeed spoke"—the word *vai* is used for the sake of recollection—indeed he, that Gandharva, spoke to you. "The Pārikṣitas indeed went there"—where? To where the performers of the Aśvamedha sacrifice go. Having thus resolved the question, he asks: "Where, indeed, in what place, do the performers of the Aśvamedha sacrifice go?"

With the intention of describing their movement, he states the measurement of the cosmic egg (*bhuvanakośa*): "Indeed, thirty-two"—that is, thirty-two more than thirty; "indeed, thirty-two," meaning *devarathāhnyāni*. *Deva* refers to the Sun (*āditya*); his chariot is the *devaratha*. The extent of space delimited by the movement of that chariot in one day is a *devarathāhnya*. Thirty-two times that is *devarathāhnyāni*. This world is of such a magnitude, encircled by the Lokāloka mountain—wherein the Vairāja [abides].

The body, wherein the fruits of the actions of living beings are experienced—that is this world. This much is the world; beyond this is the non-world (*aloka*). Encircling that world on all sides—from its circumference with a dimension twice as great as the extent of the world—the earth stands surrounding it. In the same way, surrounding that earth on all sides with a dimension twice as great, the ocean stands encircling it, which the experts in the Purāṇas call Ghanoda.

In this context, the measurement of the opening between the two halves of the cosmic egg is stated—the opening by which way those who have performed the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) emerge and pervade the exterior. Therein, as great as the edge or point of a razor is, or as subtle as the wing of a fly, so great is that space, the aperture, between the two halves of the egg; "by that space" means by this opening.

When those descendants of Parikṣit, who had performed the horse-sacrifice, arrived there, Indra—the Supreme Lord, who is the fire piled in the horse-sacrifice and who is the *suparṇa* (the well-winged one) concerning whom it was said in the vision, "The eastern quarter is his head," and so forth—becoming a *suparṇa*, that is, becoming a bird consisting of wings and tail, delivered them to Vāyu; for because of his embodied form, the Self has no movement there.

Vāyu, having placed those Pārikṣitas within himself—having established them there and made them one with his own self—led them to that place. Where? To where the former Pārikṣitas who had performed the Aśvamedha sacrifices had gone. "In this very way"—that is, in this same manner—that Gandharva praised Vāyu alone as the goal of the Pārikṣitas. The narrative is concluded; however, setting aside the narrative and returning to its own form as revealed scripture (*śruti*), the text explains the meaning derived from the narrative to us.

Since Vāyu is the inner self of all beings, both stationary and moving, and he alone is also outside them, therefore that which is the manifold pervasion (*vividhā vyāpti*) by way of the states of the individual self (*adhyātma*), the elements (*adhidaiva*), and the deities (*adhibhūta*), is Vāyu alone; likewise, the collective pervasion (*samaṣṭi*) as the mere thread-self (*sūtrātman*) is Vāyu alone. To one who thus approaches Vāyu as the self consisting of the nature of both the collective and the individual—that is, who knows this—what is the fruit? He says: "He conquers death again; having died once, he does not die again.
Then, following the resolution of the question regarding the Self, Bhujyu Lāhyāyani ceased [asking further questions].

Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa of the third chapter. Now, those rays of his which point northward are its northern honey-cells; the Atharva-Aṅgirases are the honey-makers, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are the flower, and those are the immortal waters. 1.

(1) Then, Uṣasta by name, the son of Cakra (Cākrāyaṇa), questioned this very Yājñavalkya who was present there: "That Brahman which is immediate, not separated from the seer by anything, direct—not figurative like the 'Brahman that is the ear' and so forth—what is it? It is the Self—the innermost of all, the one within everything; for by the word 'Self' (ātman), the inner self (pratyagātman) is meant, as that is the well-known meaning of the word."

"If by the words 'that' and 'which' you mean the well-known Self is Brahman—then explain that Self to me," he said. "Explain it clearly, as one shows a cow by seizing it by the horns; tell me 'this is it,' such is the meaning. Being addressed thus, Yājñavalkya replied: "This is your Self, the innermost of all (sarvāntaraḥ), existing within everything. The term "innermost of all" is used to indicate all its specific attributes and characteristics.

That which is the immediate, unmediated, non-indirect, and non-figurative Brahman—the Supreme, the Greatest, the Self of all, existing within everything—endowed with all these qualities, who is this Self of yours? That aggregate of causes and effects which constitutes you, and by which [Self] that [aggregate] possesses a self—that indeed is your Self; the meaning is: it is the Self of your aggregate of causes and effects.

In that context, there is the body (*piṇḍa*); within it is the self consisting of the subtle body (*liṅgātman*), which is the aggregate of the instruments (*karaṇasaṃghāta*); and thirdly, that which is being doubted. When it was asked, "Among these, which one is intended by you as my innermost Self?", the other replied: "That which breathes—that is, performs the activity of breathing—by means of the *prāṇa* (the vital air) moving through the mouth and nose; the meaning is that by which the *prāṇa* is led forth—that is your Self, consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), within the aggregate of your body and instruments. The rest is the same [as before].
