"He who breathes in with the in-breath (apāna), he who breathes out with the inter-breath (vyāna)"—the lengthening [of the vowels] is a Vedic usage. All activities such as breathing and so forth, which pertain to the aggregate of the body and the organs, are performed by him, just like those of a wooden machine. For indeed, the activities of breathing and so forth do not exist in a wooden machine unless it is presided over by a conscious being.

Therefore, presided over by the one consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya), who is distinct [from the body], the aggregate attains the activity of breathing and so forth, like a wooden machine. Consequently, there exists that which is distinct from the aggregate of the body and the organs, and which causes it to act.
These very Atharvans and Aṅgirasas brooded upon this Itihāsa-Purāṇa. From it, thus brooded upon, there was born its essence: fame, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food.

Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa said: "Just as someone might first make one promise and then, having changed his mind, speak otherwise—saying, for instance, 'That is a cow' or 'That is a horse,' when it is actually moving or running—having first promised, 'I shall show you the object directly perceived,' he subsequently identifies it by means of signs such as its movement; in exactly this same way, this Brahman has been identified by you through signs such as breathing and so forth."

"What more need be said? Setting aside the pretext of the thirst for the cow, explain to me that very Brahman which is immediate and direct, the Self that is within all. The other replied: "I am indeed following through on the promise I made at the outset—that the Self has such-and-such characteristics—and it is exactly as I have stated. As for what you said, 'Make that Self an object of perception like a jar or other things,' that cannot be done because it is impossible."

Why, then, is that impossible? He says: because of the very nature of things (*vastusvābhāvya*). What, then, is this nature of things? It is the state of being the seer of seeing and so forth; for the Self is indeed the seer of seeing. Seeing is of two kinds: worldly (*laukikī*) and ultimate (*pāramārthikī*). Among these, the worldly is the modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) conjoined with the eye; it is produced, meaning it is born and perishes.

That which is the vision of the Self, like the heat and light of fire, because it is the very nature of the seer, neither arises nor perishes; yet, through its association with the conditioned adjunct that undergoes modification, it is designated as "the seer" and appears as if distinct—as "the seer" and "vision."

This worldly vision, which arises colored by form through the gateway of the eye, is as if already conjoined with the eternal vision of the Self; it is born as if permeated by its reflection and perishes in the same way. Therefore, the Seer is figuratively described as "always seeing," yet as "seeing" and "not seeing"; however, there is never any change whatsoever in the vision of the Seer.

And so it will be stated in the sixth chapter: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were," and "For there is no loss of the vision of the Seer. He states this very point: you would not see the Seer—who pervades with His own eternal vision—that very worldly vision which has become an object; for that worldly vision, being an object, is colored by form and manifests form, but it does not pervade the Self, who is its own pervader and the inward-facing reality.

Therefore, you should not see that inner Self as the seer of seeing; likewise, you should not hear it as the hearer of hearing; likewise, you should not conceive of it as the pervader of mere mental activity (manas); likewise, you should not cognize it as the pervader of mere intellectual activity (buddhi). This is the very nature of reality; therefore, it cannot be shown like a cow or other such objects.

Regarding the phrase "not the seer of seeing" (*na dṛṣṭerdraṣṭāram*), some explain the words differently: "Do not look for the seer of seeing—that is, the agent of seeing—without making a distinction between [different kinds of] seeing, [but rather for] the agent of mere seeing. Here, the genitive case in *dṛṣṭeḥ* is used in the sense of the object (*karma*); that seeing, while being performed, becomes an object like a jar. By the suffix *-tṛ* in *draṣṭāram*, the word expresses that seeing is the agency of seeing. Thus, the intention of those commentators is that he is the seer of seeing, the agent of seeing.

In this regard, they do not perceive the fault that the inclusion of the word "of vision" (*dṛṣṭeḥ*) in the genitive case is purposeless; or, even if they do perceive it, they show no concern, thinking it either redundant or a careless reading. How, then, is there redundancy? Since the agency of seeing is already established by the suffix *-tṛ* itself, the term "of vision" (*dṛṣṭeḥ*) is superfluous; in that case, one should have said simply, "you would not see the seer. For the suffix *-tṛ* is prescribed to denote the agent of the action expressed by the verbal root from which it follows.

For only this much is actually employed in speech: "it leads the goer" or "it leads the breaker"; one does not say "the goer of going" or "the breaker of breaking" when there is no specific meaning [to be conveyed]. Nor should it be discarded as a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) when a literal sense exists. Nor is it a corrupt reading, since there is no disagreement among all [reciters]. Therefore, the deficiency lies only in the understanding of the commentators, not in the negligence of the students.

However, as we have explained—that the Self, distinguished from the worldly perspective by the eternal perspective, must be demonstrated—so too is the twofold use of the word "vision" (dṛṣṭi) justified as a qualifier of both the agent and the object for the purpose of determining the true nature of the Self; furthermore, this is consistent with the syntactic unity of the statement from another section, "for there is no cessation of the vision of the Seer."

And thus, consistency with another scriptural passage—namely, "The eyes see" and "This ear has heard"—is established. This is also supported by logic: for the eternity of the Self is only possible in the absence of modification; and it is a contradiction to say that something which undergoes modification is eternal. Furthermore, the words of the scripture—"It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were," "For there is no loss of the vision of the seer," and "This is the eternal glory of the Brāhmaṇa"—cannot be interpreted otherwise.

[Objection: But surely such words as "the seer," "the hearer," "the thinker," and "the knower" would not apply if the Self were immutable. [Reply: No, because those words merely repeat worldly expressions as they are commonly used; they do not aim at defining the true nature of the Self. Since phrases such as "not the seer of seeing" cannot possibly have any other meaning, it is understood that their purpose is precisely as stated. Therefore, it was only due to a lack of understanding that the qualification "of seeing" was discarded.

"This Self of yours is distinguished by all the aforementioned attributes; therefore, anything other than this Self is afflicted—whether it be the body as an effect, or the subtle body (*liṅga*) consisting of the instruments [of perception]. This alone is the one that is unafflicted, indestructible, and immutable. Thereupon, Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa desisted. Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa of the third chapter.
Now, those rays which go upwards are its upward honey-cells; the secret instructions are the honey-makers, and Brahman itself is...
The flower, those waters are the *amṛta*...

(1)... Then indeed Kahola by name, the son of Kuṣītaka—Kauṣītakeya—questioned him. He said, "O Yājñavalkya," as before—"Explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all, knowing which one is released from bondage. Yājñavalkya said: "This, for you, is the Self."

Is one and the same Self questioned by both Uṣasta and Kahola, or are two distinct Selves with identical characteristics being questioned? It is more reasonable that they are distinct, because it is thus that the non-redundancy of the two questions is logically established. For if one and the same Self were intended in the questions of both Uṣasta and Kahola, then since that [Self] would have been apprehended by the first question alone, a second question concerning that same subject would be purposeless. Furthermore, the sentence cannot be considered a mere explanatory or laudatory statement (arthavāda).

Therefore, some explain that these two selves called the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) and the *paramātman* (the supreme self) are distinct. That is not so, because of the initial proposition "those"; for in the reply, "This is your self," that which was proposed is reaffirmed. Furthermore, it is not possible for a single aggregate of body and organs to have two selves; for one aggregate of body and organs possesses its selfhood through one self alone.

Furthermore, the Self of Uṣasta is not one thing and that of Kahola another, distinct by nature; for it is impossible for both to be non-figurative, the Self, and the innermost of all. If one is the non-figurative Brahman, the other must necessarily be figurative. Likewise, regarding being the Self and being the innermost of all—since these attributes of things are mutually exclusive: if one is the innermost Brahman, the primary Self, the other must necessarily be non-innermost, a non-Self, and secondary.

Therefore, the fact that one and the same [subject] is heard twice is due to the intention to state a specific distinction. As for the second question being stated in a manner identical to what was previously said, that much is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the former; it is intended so that some unstated specific detail regarding that very same subject may be expressed.

What, then, is this distinction? It is stated as follows: In the first question, it was asked whether there exists a distinct Self for whom this bondage, along with its cause, has been described; but in the second, the distinction is stated to be that very Self's transcendence of the attributes of transmigratory existence, such as hunger and so forth—by the thorough knowledge of which distinction, accompanied by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), one is liberated from the aforementioned bondage. Therefore, the two questions and their respective answers, ending with the words "This is your Self," have indeed the same meaning.

Now, one might object: "How can there be the coexistence of contradictory attributes in the very same Self—namely, its being beyond hunger and so forth, and its possessing those very qualities? This is not so, for we have already refuted this objection. We have stated more than once, in the course of explaining contradictory scriptural passages, that the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) is merely an illusion produced by contact with the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), characterized as the aggregate of name, form, modifications, and effects.

Just as a rope, a mother-of-pearl shell, the sky, and so forth, appear as a snake, silver, or impurity when characterized by attributes superimposed by another, yet the rope, the shell, the sky, and so forth remain in themselves merely what they are—there is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that objects can possess the coexistence of such contradictory attributes.

If it be argued that if names and forms exist as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then scriptural texts such as "One only, without a second" and "There is not here any diversity whatsoever" would be contradicted—the answer is no, because this has already been resolved through the analogies of water and foam, as well as the analogies of intoxication and the like.

But when, from the perspective of ultimate reality, name and form—being investigated as distinct from the reality of the Supreme Self by those who follow the Śruti—are found not to exist as separate entities in truth, just like the modifications of clay and the like, or indeed like the modifications of water, foam, and jars, then, in relation to that [Supreme Self], the world attains the status of being the object of the vision of ultimate reality, as expressed in such passages as "one only, without a second" and "there is no diversity whatsoever here."

Just like a form, that which exists in its own nature, though its essence is untouched by anything else, is not perceived as distinct from the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of name and form and the resulting body and organs; rather, the perception of the adjuncts of name and form itself becomes its natural state. At that time, all this worldly transaction regarding the existence of other things occurs. And this false transaction based on differentiation exists for those for whom an object is found to exist as something other than the reality of Brahman, and for those for whom it does not so exist.

However, when those who speak of the ultimate truth (paramārtha) investigate the reality in accordance with the sacred revelation (śruti)—as to whether a thing exists in reality or does not exist—they determine that Brahman alone is non-dual, devoid of all empirical transaction (saṃvyavahāra). Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever. For we do not admit the existence of any other entity when we are intent upon the determination of the ultimate truth, according to the scriptural texts: "One only, without a second" and "Without interior or exterior."

Nor is it denied that at the time of the conventional usage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), there is no conventional discourse regarding action, agent, result, and so forth for those who lack discrimination. Therefore, all worldly and scriptural conventional discourse exists in dependence upon knowledge and ignorance; hence, there is no suspicion of contradiction whatsoever. Even for all proponents of philosophical systems, this conventional discourse based on the ultimate and the conventional is unavoidable.
In that regard, with reference to the nature of the Self as the ultimate reality, the question is asked again: "O Yājñavalkya, which one is the innermost of all? The other replies:

"He who transcends hunger and thirst"—*aśanāyā* is the desire to eat, *pipāsā* is the desire to drink; he who transcends these two, hunger and thirst—this is the connection with what is to be said hereafter. Just as the sky, though perceived by the undiscriminating as if possessed of a surface and impurities, actually transcends that surface and those impurities because its essential nature is in reality unconnected with them—so too Brahman, though perceived by the deluded as possessing hunger, thirst, and so forth (in the thought, "I am hungry," "I am thirsty")—those [two].

It transcends [them] indeed from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), because its essential nature (*svabhāva*) is unconditioned by those two; for the Śruti says, "It is not tainted by the suffering of the world, being external"—the meaning is: by the suffering superimposed upon it by the ignorant world. Hunger and thirst are mentioned as a compound because they share the same characteristic of belonging solely to the vital breath (*prāṇa*). "Sorrow and delusion"—here, "sorrow" refers to desire (*kāma*); that dissatisfaction which arises in one who reflects upon a desired object is the seed of desire for one overcome by craving, for by means of it, desire is inflamed.

Delusion (*moha*), however, is non-discrimination (*aviveka*) arising from perverted cognition; it is error. And that is ignorance (*avidyā*), the seed for the production of all misfortune. Because their functions are distinct, grief and delusion are not compounded [into a single term]. Both have the mind as their locus; likewise, they have the body as their locus. One transcends both old age and death: "old age" refers to the transformation of the aggregate of causes and effects, characterized by signs such as wrinkles and graying hair.

"Death" is the cessation of that [life], ending in transformation; he transcends both old age and death, which have the body as their locus. Those [states] beginning with hunger, which have the vital breath, the mind, and the body as their loci and which exist incessantly among living beings like day and night or like the waves of the ocean, are called "saṃsāra" (transmigration) among living beings.

The Self (Ātman), which is characterized as "the Seer of the seer" and so forth, is directly perceived, immediate, non-figurative, and the innermost of all; this Self, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is never touched by the attributes of transmigratory existence such as hunger and thirst—just as the ether is not affected by impurities like clouds—and having known, that is, realized, this very Self as one's own true nature, thinking: "I am this Supreme Brahman, eternally free from all transmigratory existence and ever-satisfied," [the] Brāhmaṇas [attain liberation].

The qualification for renunciation belongs only to Brahmins; therefore, there is the mention of "Brahmin"—having renounced, that is, having risen up by turning away from worldly life. Why? He says: "from the desire for sons"—the desire for a son is the longing for a son as a means for conquering this world, expressed as "May I conquer this world through a son"; this desire is the taking of a wife. The meaning is: without having taken a wife.

And regarding the quest for wealth (*vittaiṣaṇā*): it is the acquisition of cattle and other means for performing ritual action, with the thought, "Having performed this rite, I shall conquer the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*)," or the world of the gods (*devaloka*) through knowledge conjoined with action, or the world of the gods through the divine wealth consisting solely of the knowledge of Hiraṇyagarbha. Some maintain that there can be no renunciation (*vyutthāna*) from divine wealth at all, because it is said that renunciation occurs by its power; however, that is incorrect, since divine wealth is included among the objects of desire (*kāma*) in the scriptural passage, "Desire is indeed of this extent."

Knowledge concerning deities such as Hiraṇyagarbha is called "wealth" (vitta), because it is a cause for attaining the world of the gods; for the knowledge of Brahman, which has as its object the undifferentiated mass of pure consciousness (prajñānaghana) free from all limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika), is not a cause for attaining the world of the gods, according to the scriptural texts: "Therefore, that became all" and "He becomes the Self of these. Indeed, by the power of that [knowledge of Brahman], there is renunciation (vyutthāna), as indicated by the specific statement: "Having known this very Self..."

Therefore, having risen above these three objects of desire—which are the means for attaining worlds that are not the Self—the meaning is: having ceased to harbor thirst for this manifold means of attaining worlds that are not the Self. For all desire for the means is indeed desire for the fruit; therefore, the Śruti explains: "Desire is one alone. How so? That which is the desire for a son is the same as the desire for wealth, because they are equal in being means for attaining visible results.

That which is the desire for wealth is the desire for worlds; it is solely for the sake of a result. For everyone, being impelled by the aim of a result, takes up every means of accomplishment. Therefore, there is only one single desire, namely the desire for worlds, since that cannot be accomplished without means; thus, because of the distinction between the goal and the means, both of these are indeed merely desires.

Therefore, for the knower of Brahman, there is neither action nor any means of action. Consequently, those Brāhmaṇas who have transcended [this state] abandon all action and all means of action—including the sacrificial thread and so forth, which are intended for the gods, the ancestors, and men; for by means of these, the rites for the gods, the ancestors, and men are performed, as stated in such Vedic texts as, "The *nivīta* [wearing mode] is for men."

Therefore, the ancient Brahmins who knew Brahman, having renounced ritual acts and the instruments of those acts such as the sacrificial thread and so forth, and having entered the state of the wandering mendicant of the highest order (*paramahaṃsa-pārivrājya*), practiced the life of begging—*bhikṣācaryam* meaning they moved about for the sake of alms—they abandoned the marks prescribed by the Smṛtis, which are merely the means of subsistence for those who take refuge in the stage of life alone and serve to manifest their status as wandering mendicants.

The wise man is devoid of external marks (*liṅga*), according to such Smṛti texts as, "Therefore, the knower of Dharma, being without marks, has unmanifested marks and unmanifested conduct," and according to Śruti texts such as, "Now the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*), wearing discolored garments, shaven-headed, and without possessions," and also, "Having shaved the hair except for the top-knot, he should cast away the sacred thread."

Now, one might object: since the statement "Then, having risen, they wander for alms" is a description in the present tense (*vartamānāpadeśa*), it is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*); no injunctive suffix—whether *liṅ*, *loṭ*, or *tavya*—is heard here. Therefore, by means of an explanatory praise alone, it is not possible [to establish] the necessity of the sacrificial threads and other implements prescribed in the Śruti and Smṛti.

It is intended to cause [the abandonment] to be relinquished; for it is said: "One should study, officiate at sacrifices, or perform sacrifices while wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavītin*). Furthermore, study is prescribed even for the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*), as in: "By renouncing the Veda one becomes a *śūdra*; therefore, one should not renounce the Veda," and Āpastamba states: "Even when renouncing all else, one should not abandon Vedic recitation. Moreover, because the fault of abandoning the Veda is heard in such passages as: "Neglecting the Veda, reviling the Veda, giving false testimony, killing a friend, eating forbidden food or drink, and drinking liquor—these six are equal to the drinking of liquor."

"In the service of teachers, elders, and guests; during the fire-oblation, the recitation of prayers, eating, sipping water, and Vedic study, one should wear the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavītī*)"—since these activities, such as serving the teacher, Vedic study, eating, and sipping water, are enjoined as duties to be performed for wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) in both Śruti and Smṛti, and since the sacrificial thread is prescribed as an accessory (*aṅga*) to the service of the teacher and so forth, its abandonment cannot possibly be understood [as permissible].

Although renunciation from the pursuits (*eṣaṇā*) is indeed enjoined, nevertheless, this renunciation is only from the three pursuits beginning with offspring, and not from all ritual action (*karman*) and the means of ritual action (*karmasādhana*). If everything were abandoned, that which is not prescribed would be performed, and that which is prescribed—such as the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth—would be lost. Thus, a great transgression would be committed, caused by the non-performance of what is enjoined and the performance of what is prohibited. Therefore, the abandonment of the signs such as the sacred thread is merely a blind tradition.

No, because of the scriptural text: "The ascetic (yati) should renounce all that, including the sacred thread and the Vedas. Furthermore, since the entire Upaniṣad is devoted to the knowledge of the Self—given that it begins with the statement, "The Self is to be seen, heard, and reflected upon"—it is well established that this very Self must be known as such: immediate, non-mediated, the innermost of all, and devoid of the attributes of transmigratory existence such as hunger and so forth.

Since this entire Upaniṣad has such a purpose, it cannot be a subordinate part of another injunction; therefore, it is not a mere *arthavāda* (laudatory statement), because the knowledge of the Self is something to be accomplished. Furthermore, the Self must be known as distinct from both the means and the fruits of action, being devoid of attributes such as hunger and so forth.

Consequently, the non-differentiation of the Self [from the body] is ignorance (*avidyā*), according to such scriptural passages as: "He who thinks 'this one is one and I am another' does not know," "He goes from death to death," "He who perceives here as if there were diversity," "It is to be seen as one alone," "One only, without a second," and "That thou art."

Action, its fruit, and the means of accomplishment—all these, which are other than the Self that transcends the attributes of transmigratory existence such as hunger and so forth, fall within the domain of ignorance (*avidyā*). This is established by hundreds of scriptural passages such as: "For where there is duality, as it were," "He thinks, 'I am another, he is another,'" "He does not know," and "But those who know otherwise than this. Furthermore, knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) cannot coexist in a single person due to their mutual contradiction, just like darkness and light.

Therefore, for the knower of the Self (*ātmavit*), no qualification (*adhikāra*) within the sphere of ignorance—which consists of the distinctions of action, agent, and fruit—should be observed. This is because such a sphere is censured in passages such as, "He goes from death to death" (*mṛtyor na mṛtyum āpnoti*). Furthermore, since all actions, their means, and their fruits belong to the sphere of ignorance, they are intended to be abandoned by the knowledge of the Self, which is the opposite of that ignorance. Moreover, the sacrificial thread and other such implements have that [sphere of ignorance] as their domain. Therefore, the desire for objects other than the Self—which is by nature devoid of means and fruits—is distinct [from the knowledge of the Self].

For both of these—the means and the fruit—are indeed forms of desire (*eṣaṇā*), because the sacred thread and so forth, as well as the rituals to be accomplished by them, constitute the means; this is established by the restrictive statement of the reason: "for both of these are indeed desires. Since the sacred thread and other such means, as well as the rituals to be accomplished by them, fall within the domain of ignorance (*avidyā*), consist of the nature of desire, and are therefore of the nature of things to be abandoned, renunciation (*vyutthāna*) is precisely what is intended to be enjoined.

[Objection: "But surely, since the Upaniṣads have as their primary purpose the knowledge of the Self, the scriptural mention of 'emerging' (vyutthāna) is for the sake of praising that [knowledge], not an injunction. [Reply: No, because we hear of a common agent with the knowledge intended to be enjoined; for it is never possible in the Veda to hear of a common agency between that which is not to be performed and that which is to be performed.

For just as there is an auditory statement regarding the acts that must be performed—namely, pressing, offering, and consuming, in the form "having pressed, having offered, they consume"—so too there would be an auditory statement regarding the common agency of those very acts that must be performed: self-knowledge, renunciation of desires, and the mendicant's life. If it is argued that the abandonment of the sacrificial thread and so forth is already established by implication because it falls within the domain of ignorance and constitutes a form of desire, and thus need not be enjoined as part of the injunction for self-knowledge—that is not so.

Furthermore, the strengthening of that which is enjoined by the very rule for the knowledge of the Self is established through the scriptural mention of a common agent; the same applies to the practice of begging for alms. As for what was said—that because it is stated in the present tense, it is merely an explanatory praise (arthavāda)—that is not so, for there is no fault, as it is similar to injunctions such as that regarding the *audumbara* sacrificial post.

If it is argued that by the phrase "having emerged, they wander for alms," wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) is enjoined, and since the sacrificial thread and other implements as well as the [ascetic] marks are prescribed for the stage of wandering mendicancy by both Śruti and Smṛti, therefore this "emerging" must mean emerging from something other than that [stage], even though it is a state of seeking—[we reply: no.

Because there arises another form of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) distinct from that wandering mendicancy characterized by rising above desires—which shares the same agent as the knowledge of the Self—since that wandering mendicancy characterized by rising above desires is an auxiliary to the knowledge of the Self, consisting in the renunciation of desires that are opposed to the knowledge of the Self, and because desire has ignorance as its object;

and because, apart from that, there exists a wandering mendicancy in the form of a stage of life (*āśrama*) which is a means for attaining results such as the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), and for which there are injunctions regarding implements such as the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and the assumption of specific marks (*liṅga*).

Furthermore, when the undertaking of means consisting of desire is possible within the state of wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) merely by virtue of its being an ascetic duty (āśramadharma), it is not proper to subvert the knowledge of the Self (ātmajñāna) enjoined in all the Upaniṣads; for if there were a desire to undertake means consisting of desire—such as the sacrificial thread—which fall within the sphere of ignorance (avidyā), then the realization "I am Brahman," which is of the nature of neither a means nor a fruit and is devoid of the transmigratory attributes such as hunger, would necessarily be subverted.

Nor is such a sublation (of the injunction) logical, because all the Upaniṣads have that [liberation] as their ultimate purpose. If it is argued: "The Śruti itself sublates [the injunction for renunciation], since by saying 'they lead a life of begging,' it enjoins the practice of begging"—even so, having prescribed the rising above desires, the Śruti, by enjoining the practice of begging which is but a portion of desire, would thereby enjoin other things connected to it as well—if this is the argument, we say no, because begging is not the primary motive, just like the eating that follows an oblation.

Because it is a ritual act belonging to the remaining duties (*śeṣapratipattikarma*), that [eating] is indeed not a motive; and because it does not effect a refinement (*asaṃskārakatvāt*). Eating might indeed be a refinement for the person, but begging for alms is not. Furthermore, even the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the rule is undesirable for one who knows Brahman. If it is asked, "If the unseen merit of the rule is undesirable, what is the use of begging for alms?"—the answer is no, because renunciation (*vyutthāna*) has been prescribed as having other means. If it is further asked, "Even so, what is the point of that [alms-begging]?"—if it were to exist, very well; for that is indeed admitted.

Those statements prescribed for the life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*), such as "one should study while wearing the sacred thread" (*yajñopavītī*) and so forth, have been set aside as referring only to the mendicancy of one who lacks knowledge; for it has already been stated that otherwise there would be a contradiction with the knowledge of the Self. [As it is said: "One who is free from desire, free from undertaking, free from salutation, and free from praise..."

The Smṛti demonstrates the absence of all action for the knower in the passage: "The gods know him as a Brāhmaṇa who, though his actions have been exhausted, remains unexhausted [in his true nature]," and further: "The knower is devoid of marks (liṅga)," and "Therefore, the knower of dharma is without marks. Therefore, one who knows the Self should indeed undertake the wandering life of a Paramahaṃsa, characterized by renunciation, which consists in the abandonment of all means of action.

Because the ancient Brahmins, having realized this Self—which is by nature devoid of means and fruits—rose above all forms of seeking characterized by means and fruits, and wandered as mendicants, abandoning both action for the sake of seen and unseen results and the means to that action; therefore, even today, a Brahmin who knows Brahman, having fully understood this "pāṇḍitya"—that is, the state of being a scholar, which is the knowledge of this Self—having known it completely and without remainder, [should abandon it]. Having known the knowledge of the Self exhaustively...

The meaning is "having done so"—that is, having risen above the desires (eṣaṇā) through both the teacher and the scripture. For that scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*) culminates precisely in the rising above desires, because it arises from the rejection of desires and is opposed to them. Indeed, the arising of scholarship whose object is the Self does not occur without rejecting desires; thus, the rising above desires is enjoined by the very knowledge of the Self, as confirmed by the scriptural use of the *ktvā* suffix, which indicates a common agent for the acts of knowing the Self and rising above desires.

Therefore, having risen above these desires, one should desire to abide in "childhood" by means of the state of possessing the power of knowledge; for the strength of others—those who do not know the Self—consists in relying upon means and their fruits. Abandoning that strength, the knower should rely solely on the very nature of the realization of the Self, which is devoid of both means and fruits. For when one relies on that, the senses are no longer able to carry him away and establish him within the sphere of desires.

For the organs impel this deluded person, who is devoid of the power of knowledge, toward the very pursuit of objects both seen and unseen. "Power" (bala) indeed means the setting aside of the vision of all objects through self-knowledge. Therefore, one should abide in that state of "childhood" (bālya); for according to another Vedic text, "By the Self one finds strength," and also, "This Self is not to be attained by one devoid of strength. Having thoroughly mastered both childhood and wisdom—having brought them to completion—one then becomes a sage (muni), a yogi, by virtue of contemplation (manana).

For this much alone is to be done by a Brahmin, namely, the complete setting aside of all notions of the non-Self; having accomplished this, the yogi becomes one who has fulfilled his task. Having thoroughly performed both "non-mauna"—which consists of the knowledge of the Self and the setting aside of notions of the non-Self, designated respectively as "panditya" (scholarship) and "balya" (childlike simplicity)—there arises the fruit called "mauna," which is the culmination of the setting aside of notions of the non-Self. Having realized that as well, he then becomes a Brahmin who has fulfilled his task—the realization arises: "Brahman alone is everything."

That brahmin has accomplished what was to be done; therefore, he is a brahmin. For at that time, his status as a brahmin is attained in its primary, non-figurative sense. Therefore, it is said: "By what would he be a brahmin? By what conduct (*caraṇa*) would he exist?"—by whatever conduct he might exist, by that very [conduct] he is of such a kind. That is to say, by whatever conduct he may exist, by that very [conduct] he becomes a brahmin of the aforementioned characteristics.

The phrase "by whatever means" is for the purpose of praise; it is this state of Brahman-hood that is being praised, not a disregard for conduct (*caraṇa*). Therefore, from this state of Brahman-hood—which is the nature of the Self transcending hunger and so forth, and which is eternally satisfied—there is another thing, characterized by desire, which is the domain of ignorance. That other thing is afflicted, perishable, seized by suffering, and like the water of a dream, a magic show, or a mirage; it is devoid of essence. Only the Self is one, absolute, and eternally liberated.
Thereupon, Kahola Kauṣītakeya ceased questioning. This concludes the fifth Brāhmaṇa of the third chapter.
Now, that which is the first nectar, the Vasus subsist upon it with Agni as their mouth. Indeed, the gods neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by seeing this nectar.

That Brahman which has been described as being directly perceived, not hidden from view, and as the Self within all—beginning from this point up to the Śākalya Brāhmaṇa, the text is commenced for the purpose of attaining knowledge of the true nature of that Innermost Self. For the elements, beginning with earth and ending with space, are established in a relationship of inner and outer.

Having repeatedly realized and then set aside each successive external layer of those [elements], the Seer—the innermost Self of all, non-figurative, and entirely free from all the attributes of transmigratory existence—must be shown. This is the undertaking: Then Gārgī by name, the daughter of Vācaknu (Vācaknavī), questioned him; she said, "O Yājñavalkya..."

That is to say, this entire collection of earthly elements is woven warp and woof within the waters—woven lengthwise like the threads of a long cloth, woven crosswise like the threads across it, or otherwise—the meaning being that it is pervaded on all sides, internally and externally, by the waters; otherwise, it would fall apart like a handful of flour.

This, first of all, is the inference set forth: that which is an effect—limited and gross—is seen to be pervaded by a cause that is unlimited and subtle, as for example, the earth is pervaded by water; likewise, each preceding element must be pervaded by each succeeding one that is more pervasive. This is the meaning of the question leading up to the Self within all. In this regard, the five elements, being indeed composite, exist in their successive order as increasingly subtle, pervasive, and causal in nature.

Furthermore, there is no other entity apart from the Supreme Self prior to it, according to the Śruti: "The Truth of truth. Here, "truth" refers to the five elements, and "the Truth of truth" is the Supreme Self. [The text asks: "In what, indeed, are the waters woven warp and woof? Since these too are effects, gross, and limited, they must necessarily exist somewhere in a state of being woven warp and woof. Where, then, is their state of being woven warp and woof? In this manner, the sequence of successive questions is to be applied.

"In air, O Gārgī. [The opponent objects: "Surely it should have been said, 'In fire'—this is not a fault. For fire, like the other elements, has no acquisition of its own self through independence without depending on an earthly or watery constituent; therefore, the state of being woven across and lengthwise is not taught with respect to it. [The question is asked again: 'But in what, indeed, is air woven across and lengthwise? [The answer is: 'In the worlds of the intermediate space, O Gārgī. These very elements, when combined, are the worlds of the intermediate space."

And those [subtle elements] also—[as] Gandharva-worlds among the Gandharva-worlds, Āditya-worlds among the Āditya-worlds, Candra-worlds among the Candra-worlds, Nakṣatra-worlds among the Nakṣatra-worlds, Deva-worlds among the Deva-worlds, Indra-worlds among the Indra-worlds, Prajāpati-worlds among the Prajāpati-worlds which consist of the elements that originate the body of Virāj, and Brahma-worlds among the Brahma-worlds—which are the elements that originate the cosmic egg; [all these are the subtle elements].

For everywhere, the elements—transformed into the forms that serve as the substrata for the enjoyment of living beings—are joined together in a subtle gradation, and it is these very five [elements] that take the plural form [in the word *bhūtāni*]. "In what, indeed, are the worlds of Brahmā woven to and fro? Yājñavalkya said: "O Gārgī, do not ask beyond your own question. The meaning is: do not, by overstepping the method of reasoning, ask about the deity who is to be known through scripture by means of inference.

"And as you ask me, may your head not shatter—may it not fall off clearly! The deity regarding which your question concerns the realm of scripture (āgama); Gārgī’s question has overstepped that realm of questioning, because it is based on inference (ānumānika). That deity whose question is asked is 'one beyond questioning' (atipraśnyā); 'not beyond questioning' (anatipraśnyā) means she is not beyond questioning, but rather restricted solely to the realm of her own [scriptural] question, meaning she is accessible only through scripture. You are indeed asking about that deity who is not beyond questioning. Therefore, Gārgī, do not ask beyond [that]; unless you wish to die. Thereupon, Gārgī Vācaknavī ceased.
Thus ends the sixth Brāhmaṇa of the third chapter.
Now, as for that second nectar, the Rudras subsist upon it through Indra as their mouth. Indeed, the gods neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by beholding this very nectar. 1.

Now, since the most internal *sūtra* of the worlds of Brahman must be declared, this section begins for that purpose. And since that must be inquired about through scripture (*āgama*) itself, the scripture is introduced by means of a historical narrative (*itihāsa*): "Then Uddālaka by name, the son of Aruṇa (Āruṇi), questioned him; 'O Yājñavalkya,' he said."

We lived and resided in various regions, studying the ritual science (*yajña*) in the house of one named Patañjala—who was by name Patañjala and belonged to the Kapi lineage (*kāpigaotra*)—while performing our studies of the sacrificial scriptures. His wife was possessed by a *gandharva*; we asked him, "Who is he? He replied, "He is named Kabandha, a descendant of Atharvan (*ātharvaṇa*)."

That Gandharva said to Patañjala Kāpya and his disciples who were performers of sacrifices: "Do you know, O Kāpya, that Sūtra? What is it? By which Sūtra this world—this present birth—and the other world—the future birth to be attained—as well as all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, are strung together, woven together, and held fast like a garland by a thread? Do you know that Sūtra?"

Being thus questioned, Kāpya replied: "No, indeed, O Venerable One; I do not know that Sūtra," saying this as a mark of reverence, "O Venerable One. Then the Gandharva spoke again to the teacher and to them: "Do you, Kāpya, know that Inner Controller—the one who is specifically designated as the 'Inner Controller'—who, being within and internal to this world, the other world, and all beings, controls and governs them like a wooden puppet?"

"It causes them to revolve, making each perform its own appropriate function. Having been addressed thus, Patañjala Kāpya replied, "I do not know him, O Blessed One," speaking while offering his respects. Then the Gandharva spoke again:

The knowledge of both the Sūtra and the Inner Ruler contained within it is praised: "O Kāpya, whoever should know this Sūtra—that is, should understand it—and should know that Inner Ruler who is contained within the Sūtra, the controller of that very Sūtra—in the manner thus described—he indeed is a knower of Brahman, a knower of the Supreme Self; he knows the worlds, such as the earth and others, which are governed by the Inner Ruler; he knows the gods, such as Agni and others, who inhabit those worlds; and he knows the Vedas."

He knows all those who have become authoritative means of knowledge; he knows the beings beginning with Brahmā, held by the thread and governed by the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) residing within them; he knows himself as characterized by agency and enjoyership, being governed by that very same Inner Controller; and he knows the entire world to be likewise constituted. When the knowledge of the Thread and the Inner Controller was thus praised, Kāpya became covetous and turned toward it, and we did so as well.

And to us, who had turned toward them, the Gandharva spoke concerning the Sūtra and the Antaryāmin; having received this tradition from the Gandharva, I know that knowledge of the Sūtra and the Antaryāmin.

"O Yājñavalkya, if that is the sacred thread and if you do not know that Inner Controller—if, being ignorant of Brahman, you drive away the cows of a Brahmin (brahmagavīḥ), that is, if you unjustly drive away the cows belonging to those who know Brahman—then, consumed by my curse, your head shall clearly shatter. Thus addressed, Yājñavalkya said: "I know it, O Gautama," referring to his lineage, "that sacred thread which the Gandharva told you."

"And that Inner Controller whom you have known from the Gandharva, that Inner Controller I know too"—when this was said, Gautama replied: "If some ordinary person were to say what you have said—'I know, I know,' thus praising himself—what is the use of that boasting? Show it by its effect; tell me how you know it.
"They enter into this very form and they emerge from this form.

Yājñavalkya said: "The worlds of Brahman are woven to and fro within it during the present time, just as the earth is woven upon the waters; that thread must be declared as something to be known through scripture. For this purpose, another question was raised; therefore, in order to resolve it, he said: "Vāyu indeed, O Gautama, is that thread; nothing else."

Regarding "wind" (*vāyu*): it is subtle like space, the supporter of earth and the other elements; that of which the seventeenfold *liṅga* (subtle body) of living beings consists—which is the substrate of the impressions of karma; which exists as both a collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) and as individuals (*vyaṣṭi*); and whose external divisions are the seven groups of winds each numbering seven, like waves upon the ocean—that very principle of wind is designated as the "thread" (*sūtra*).

"By the thread of air, O Gautama, this world, the other world, and all beings are held together and bound together—this is well known. And there is a common saying in the world: how so? Because air is the thread and everything is supported by air, therefore, O Gautama, they say of a deceased person: 'The limbs of this man have fallen apart, they have become disintegrated.'"

For it is observed that when a thread is removed, gems and other such things strung upon it fall away; in this way, the wind is the thread. If its limbs were strung upon it like gems, then it would be logical that they should fall away when the wind is gone. Therefore, he concludes: "Indeed, O Gautama, they are bound together by the thread of the wind. "It is exactly so, Yājñavalkya," [Gautama replied]. "The thread has been correctly explained; now, however, tell me of the inner controller, the Antaryāmin, who dwells within that very thread. Thus addressed, he said:
He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Rudras, becomes satisfied by seeing this very nectar through Indra as his mouth; he enters into this very form and emerges from this form. 3.

He who dwells in the earth is the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*). To avoid the over-extension that "everyone dwells in the earth," he specifies: "interior to the earth" (*pṛthivyā antaraḥ*), meaning within it. At this point, one might think that the deity Earth itself is the Inner Controller; therefore, he says: "that Inner Controller whom even the deity Earth does not know—[thinking], 'someone else exists within me.'"

For whom the earth is the body—meaning for whom the earth itself is the body and nothing else—whose body is precisely that which is the body of the deity Earth; and the mention of "body" is intended as an illustration, for both the effect and the instrument of the earth belong to him, since the effect and the instrument of the deity Earth are indeed impelled by her own karma.

Because he lacks personal karma, because the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) is eternally liberated, and because his very nature consists in acting for the sake of another, whatever action or instrument belongs to the Supreme—that alone belongs to him, not by his own initiative. Thus it is said: "He whose body is the earth. For the activity and cessation of the deity's organs would occur through the necessary proximity of the Lord as their witness alone.

This Lord named Nārāyaṇa, who, dwelling within as the inner controller, governs and regulates the earth—the deity of the earth—in its own functions: He is your Self, and this is intended to include mine and that of all beings; He is the Inner Controller about whom you asked, and He is the Immortal, devoid of all the attributes of transmigratory existence.

"As long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, twice that long it shall rise in the south and set in the north; for so long shall he attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Rudras. Thus ends the seventh section.

The rest is the same. He who dwells in the waters, in fire, in the intermediate space, in the wind, in the sky, in the sun, in the quarters, in the moon and stars, in the ether, in the darkness consisting of external obstruction, and in the light which is its opposite—the general term for luminosity: such is the vision regarding the deities, concerning the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) within the divine powers. Now, as for the "with respect to beings" (*adhibhūta*): the vision of the Inner Controller among all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is that which pertains to beings. (15–23)

Now, with respect to the internal self: He who is in the breath—that is, in the sense of smell accompanied by the vital air (prāṇa)—who is in speech, in the eye, in the ear, in the mind, in the skin, in discernment, in the intellect, and in the semen, the organ of procreation. For what reason, then, do the highly exalted deities of earth and the other elements not perceive the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), the restrainer of the self, who dwells within themselves like human beings? To this he says: "Unseen" (*adṛṣṭaḥ*)—he is not seen, nor has he become an object for the vision of anyone; yet, because he himself is present within the eye, he is the seer (*draṣṭā*), being of the nature of sight itself.

Likewise, it is "unheard" (*aśruta*), meaning it has not entered the range of the hearing of anyone; yet it is itself the "hearer" (*śrotā*) because its power of hearing is undiminished and it is present within all ears. Similarly, it is "unthought" (*amata*), meaning it has not become an object of mental volition (*manaḥ-saṃkalpa*); for everyone forms volitions only regarding what has been seen or heard, whereas this is "unthought" precisely because it has not been seen or heard. Nevertheless, it is the "thinker" (*mantā*) because its power of reflection is undiminished and it is present within all minds.

Likewise, while it is "unperceived"—meaning it has not entered the sphere of objective determination—just like form (*rūpa*) or pleasure (*sukha*), it is itself the "perceiver" because its power of consciousness is never lost and because of its proximity [to all things]. In this regard, from the statements "whom the earth does not know" and "whom all beings do not know," it follows that there are other perceivers who are to be governed, and another who is the governor, the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*).

To dispel the suspicion that it might be something else, it is said: "Not other than this"—not other than this internal ruler (antaryāmin), there is no other seer; likewise, there is no other hearer than this; there is no other thinker than this; there is no other knower than this.

Because there is no other seer, hearer, thinker, or knower beyond him—he who is the unseen seer, the unheard hearer, the unthought thinker, the unknown knower, the immortal, devoid of all the qualities of transmigratory existence, and the ordainer of the distribution of the fruits of action for all those subject to transmigration—this is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. Other than this Ātman, the Lord, everything is subject to suffering. Thereupon, Āḍḍālaka Āruṇi ceased questioning.
Thus ends the seventh Brāhmaṇa of the third Adhyāya.

Now, as for that third nectar, the Ādityas subsist upon it through Varuṇa as their mouth. Indeed, the gods neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by seeing this nectar. Then Vācaknavī spoke. Having been previously forbidden by Yājñavalkya and having desisted out of fear of the loss of her head, she now requested permission from the Brāhmaṇas to ask further questions: "O venerable and worshipful Brāhmaṇas, listen to my words! Well then, I shall ask this Yājñavalkya two more questions, provided you grant me your consent."

"If he shall speak—that is, if he shall somehow, at any time, ever—among you, no one at all shall be a conqueror of this Yājñavalkya in a theological debate (*brahmodya*), a discourse on Brahman"—when he had spoken thus, the Brāhmaṇas gave their permission, saying, "Ask, Gārgī.
They enter into this very form; from this form they emerge. 2.

Having obtained permission, she said to Yājñavalkya: "I shall indeed ask you two questions"—this is the syntactical connection. When the desire arises as to what those two are, he states them, preceded by an illustration, to show their difficulty to answer: "O Yājñavalkya, just as in the world a Kāśya—one born in Kāśī—or a Vaideha—a king of the Videhas—of noble lineage, meaning one whose father is a hero, with his bow strung..."

Having strung the bow from which the string had been removed—that is, having made it ready for use by fixing the string upon it again—he should take two "bāṇavats," meaning two arrows (the term *bāṇa* refers to the bamboo shaft that is fitted to the tip of the arrow; he specifies "two bāṇavats" because an arrow can exist even without that part). He should take those two arrows, which are "exceedingly piercing of the enemy"—meaning they cause extreme pain to the foe—and placing them in his hand, he should rise up and show himself nearby, thinking: "In this very way, I [shall overcome] you."
"I have approached you with two questions that are like arrows; I have stood before you. Answer those for me," [said Gārgī], provided she is a knower of Brahman. The other said, "Ask, Gārgī.

"He who knows this immortal state thus—having become one of the Ādityas, through Varuṇa as his mouth—he, having seen this very immortal state, becomes satisfied. He enters into this very form and emerges from this form. 3. (3)

She said: "That which is above, beyond the upper shell of the cosmic egg; that which is below, beneath the earth, under the lower shell of the cosmic egg; that which is in between, in the midst of heaven and earth—that is, these two, heaven and earth themselves; that which has been, the past; that which is, the present existing in its own activity; and that which will be, the future to be inferred by signs occurring at a time subsequent to the present—all this which they declare and speak of according to tradition—*all that*."
The meaning is that in which all that has arisen as duality becomes one—that which was previously called the *sūtra*—in what is it woven lengthwise and crosswise, like the element of earth in water?

As long as the sun rises in the south and sets in the north, twice as long will it rise in the west and set in the east; for so long he shall attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Ādityas. Thus ends the eighth section. (4) 8.

The other said: "O Gārgī, as for what you have said—that which they call the 'Thread' (sūtra), extending upwards from heaven and so forth—that Thread, in which this manifest world consisting of the Thread is woven like warp and woof within the unmanifest space (avyākṛtākāśa), like the element of earth in water, exists throughout all three times: at its origin, its duration, and its dissolution.

Again she said: "Homage be to you" (*namaste'stu*), etc., in order to demonstrate the difficulty of answering the question. "You have answered (*vyavocaḥ*)"—that is, you have specifically resolved—this question of mine. The reason for its difficulty is this: even the *sūtra* itself is incomprehensible and difficult for others to explain; how much more so that in which [the world] is woven across and lengthwise? Therefore, "homage be to you. "Maintain yourself (*dhārayasva*)" for the second question—that is, fortify yourself. "Ask, Gārgī," the other replied. (6)

The rest has been explained. She said: "That which is above, Yājñavalkya," and so forth—the question and the answer are stated again for the purpose of confirming the very meaning already expressed; no new or different matter whatsoever is being stated.

Having repeated everything exactly as it was stated by Gārgī, Yājñavalkya confirmed that very same previously mentioned point: "It is indeed space (*ākāśa*). Gārgī said: "In what, then, is space woven across and lengthwise? Thinking that space itself is difficult to describe because it transcends the three periods of time, and that the Imperishable (*akṣara*) is even more difficult than that—in which space is woven across and lengthwise—it is therefore indescribable—she did not understand. This lack of understanding is called a "point of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*) known as "non-apprehension" (*apratipatti*) in the system of logicians.

Now, even if he were to speak what is unspeakable, that too would be the point of defeat called "contradiction" (*vipratipatti*), for it is a contradictory apprehension to speak of that which is unspeakable; therefore, Gārgī considers this a question that is difficult to answer.

Desiring to avoid both of those faults, Yājñavalkya said: "This indeed is that which you asked about—'In what, then, is space woven to and fro? What is that? It is the Imperishable (akṣara)—that which does not perish, or which does not decay, is the Imperishable. That Imperishable, O Gārgī, the Brāhmaṇas who know Brahman declare."

By stating that he would address the Brahmins, he avoids two faults: namely, that he might speak what should not be spoken, or that he might fail to provide an answer. When the question has thus been cleared away, Gārgī’s reply is to be seen: "Tell me, what is that syllable which the Brahmins address? Being thus addressed, he said: "It is not gross; it is other than the gross. "In that case, is it subtle? "It is not subtle. "Then let it be short? "It is not short."

If that is so, then it is long—nor is it long, nor is it short. Thus, by these four negations of measurement, the property of a substance (*dravyadharma*) is negated; the meaning is that this syllable is not a substance. Let it then be the quality of redness—it is other than that, being non-red. Redness is the fiery quality; let it then be the viscidity of water—it is not without viscidity. Let it then be shadow—it is other than even shadow, because shadow cannot be definitively specified in any way whatsoever.

Let it then be darkness—yet it is not darkness; let it then be air—yet it is not air; let it then be space—yet it is not space; let it then be something of the nature of attachment like lac—yet it is unattached; let it then be taste—yet it is tasteless; likewise, let it be smell—yet it is odorless; let it then be the eye—yet it is eyeless, for no instrument of sight exists for it, and thus it is "eyeless," according to the Vedic mantra: "He sees without eyes."

Likewise, it is without ears; "he hears without ears. Let it then be without speech—speechless; likewise, it is without mind; likewise, it is without luster—*atejaska*, meaning that luster does not exist in it; for it possesses no luster such as the light of fire and so forth. It is without breath—the internal vital air (*prāṇa*) is negated by the term "without breath. Then its mouth must be the door—it is without a mouth (*amukha*).

"Without measure"—that by which something is measured is a "measure" (*mātra*); that which is "without measure" (*amātra*) does not possess the nature of a measure, for nothing whatsoever is measured by it. Let it then be like space (*chidra*)—"without interval," meaning there is no interval within it. Let it then exist externally—"not external. Let it then be an eater—"it eats nothing at all. Let it then be the food of someone—"no one eats it. The meaning is that it is devoid of all qualifications.
For it is indeed one without a second; by what could it be qualified? (9)

Although the existence of the Imperishable has been established by the Śruti through the effort of negating numerous qualifications, nevertheless, with regard to the common understanding of people, a doubt may still arise; therefore, he sets forth inference as a means of knowledge for the sake of establishing its existence: "Of this, indeed, the Imperishable... [and so on].

This which has been realized—the imperishable (*akṣara*), the innermost of all, Brahman directly and non-empirically perceived, the Self that transcends the attributes of hunger and so forth—under the governance of this very imperishable: just as a kingdom remains orderly and undisturbed under the governance of a king, even so under the governance of this imperishable, O Gārgī, do the sun and the moon—the sun and the moon being the lamps of the world for day and night—exist by virtue of that governor, through them...

And regarding their creation by one who possesses the knowledge of the purposes of the world being brought forth, these two [the sun and moon] would exist—because they provide illumination and benefit for all living beings in common, like a worldly lamp. Therefore, that exists by which the two Lords, being independent, remain created and supported; they proceed with rising and setting, increase and waning, according to fixed place, time, and cause. Thus, there exists for these two a ruler, the Imperishable (akṣara), like the maker and supporter of a lamp.

"Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth—heaven and earth, though possessing parts and thus naturally subject to disintegration, though by their heaviness naturally subject to falling, and though by their conjunction naturally subject to separation, and though seemingly independent because they are presided over by conscious deities—exist under the governance of this Imperishable, held apart and remaining [in their places]. For this Imperishable is the bridge that supports all order and the sustainer of all boundaries."

Therefore, the governance of this Imperishable does not transcend heaven and earth; hence, the existence of this Imperishable is established. For that sign—namely, that heaven and earth remain governed—is indeed infallible. This would not be possible without a conscious ruler who is not subject to transmigratory existence, according to the Vedic mantra: "By whom the mighty heaven and the earth were made firm."

"Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, these divisions of time—moments (*nimeṣas*) and *muhūrtas*—are the reckoners of everything born, whether past, future, or present. Just as in the world a calculator appointed by a lord counts all income and expenditure with vigilance, so too is this controller of the divisions of time the one who stands in the place of a lord."

Likewise, the eastern rivers—those flowing eastward, moving toward the eastern direction—flow and stream forth from the white mountains, such as the Himavat and others; these rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, proceed exactly as they have been set in motion, fixed in their course even though they might otherwise be capable of flowing differently. This is a sign of the Ruler. Other rivers, such as the Sindhu and others, flow westward, heading toward the western direction.

Furthermore, whatever direction they have followed, they do not deviate from it; that too is a mark [of its truth]. Moreover, even men who are knowers of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) praise one who gives—bestowing gold and other gifts—even while inflicting pain upon themselves. In that regard, the meeting and dissolution of those things given, those who give, and those who receive are seen here in this very world through direct perception; however, the supreme meeting [with the result] is unseen.

Nevertheless, humans, seeing that those who give are joined with the fruit of their gift, praise them because they understand the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And that [joining] would not occur if there were no ordainer (*praśāstṛ*)—the agent who joins [others] with the fruit of their action—one who knows the distribution of the fruits of actions; for the act of giving perishes perceptibly. Therefore, there exists one who joins the givers with the fruit. If it is argued that this is the *apūrva* (unseen force), we say no, because no proof for its existence is established.

If it is argued that this applies even to the case of a ruler (*praśāstṛ*), we say no, because the purport of the scripture (*āgama*) has been established; for we have already stated that scripture has as its object real entities (*vastu*). Furthermore, if one were to postulate an unseen principle (*apūrva*), there would be an abandonment of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), since the matter can be explained otherwise—as seen in the case where the fruit of service is obtained from the one served—and because service is an action, and since sacrifices, gifts, and oblations share that same nature, the attainment of results from the Lord or other objects of service is logically consistent.

Since it is logically consistent to postulate the attainment of a result without abandoning the observed efficacy of the nature of the action, it is not reasonable to abandon that observed efficacy of the nature of the action. Furthermore, this involves an excessive proliferation of assumptions: one must postulate either God or the *apūrva*. In that regard, the attainment of a result from service is observed to be the very nature of the action itself, but not from the *apūrva*.

Furthermore, nothing unprecedented has been observed there that would require one to postulate an unseen principle (*apūrva*), nor its capacity to bestow results, nor even the act of giving itself, once that capacity is assumed. In this case, however, one need only postulate the mere existence of the Lord as the object of service; one does not need to postulate His capacity to bestow results or His status as a giver, since we observe that the attainment of results occurs through the one being served. Moreover, inference has already been shown: "Heaven and earth stand held apart," and so forth.

And likewise, the gods, though they are lords, have followed the sacrificer for the sake of their own livelihood, with the purpose of subsisting on the *caru*, *puroḍāśa*, and other offerings; for they could have lived otherwise, yet they remain by resorting to this wretched and miserable mode of life—this is due to the command of the Ruler (*praśāstṛ*). Similarly, the ancestors also follow that same purpose; "attached to the ladle" (*darvīm anvāyattāḥ*) means they are dependent upon the *darvī-homa* sacrifice. Everything else is the same as before. (10)

For this reason also that Imperishable exists: because the occurrence of transmigratory existence is certain when it is not known. It must indeed exist, since its cessation results from the knowledge of it, as is logically established.

If it be argued that its cessation might occur through ritual action alone, we say no—for it is said: "O Gārgī, whoever in this world offers oblations, performs sacrifices, or practices austerities without knowing, without having realized this Imperishable, even if they do so for many thousands of years, their fruit is merely finite; at the end of the enjoyment of that fruit, their actions are simply exhausted."

Moreover, that through the knowledge of which there is the transcendence of wretchedness and the cessation of saṃsāra, and in the absence of the knowledge of which the performer of action becomes wretched—a mere enjoyer of the fruits of his deeds, mounted upon the continuous cycle of birth and death, and transmigrates—that is the Imperishable (akṣara), the Ruler. This is what is said: "O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is wretched, like a slave bought for a price. But he, O Gārgī, who departs from this world having known this Imperishable, he is a Brāhmaṇa."
Just as fire possesses the inherent qualities of burning and illuminating, one might think that this power of presiding over all belongs inherently to this [Self] even though it is insentient;

therefore, he says: (11) "That indeed, O Gārgī, is this Imperishable. It is unseen, for it is not seen by anyone, because it is not an object [of perception]; yet it is itself the Seer, because its nature is seeing. Likewise, it is unheard, because it is not an object of the ear; yet it is itself the Hearer, because its nature is hearing. Likewise, it is unthought, because it is not an object of the mind; yet it is itself the Thinker, because its nature is thinking. Likewise, it is unknown, because it is not an object of the intellect; yet it is itself the Knower, because its nature is knowing."

Moreover, there is nothing other than this imperishable syllable (*akṣara*). There is no seer—that is, no agent of the act of seeing—other than this; this very syllable is the agent of the act of seeing everywhere. Likewise, there is no hearer other than this; that very syllable is the hearer everywhere. There is no thinker other than this; that very syllable is the thinker everywhere through all the doors of the mind.

There is no other knower than this who is the agent of the act of knowing; that very Imperishable (*akṣara*) is the agent of the act of knowing through the medium of all the faculties of cognition, and not the insentient *pradhāna* or anything else. "In this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, the ether is woven like warp and woof.

That which is Brahman, immediate and direct, the Self that is within all, transcending the attributes of transmigratory existence such as hunger and so forth—in which the ether is woven like warp and woof—this is the supreme goal, this is the supreme attainment, this is the highest Brahman, and this is the reality of the reality of everything from the earth up to the ether.

She said: "O venerable Brahmins, listen to my words; you should hold them in high esteem. What are they? That you may be released from this Yājñavalkya by means of salutation—that is, having offered him salutation, you should hold that very thing in high esteem. His victory, moreover, is not even to be wished for in thought, much less in action. Why? Because among you there is never, at any time, a victor over this Yājñavalkya in debate concerning Brahman."

"If he answers my two questions, he will certainly not be the victor"—this was already promised by me beforehand; even today, this remains my firm conviction: that there is no one equal to him regarding the discussion on Brahman. Thereupon, Maitreyī Vācaknavī ceased speaking.

In this Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa, it is stated: "Him whom the earth does not know, him whom all beings do not know," and so forth; [it speaks of] that Inner Controller (antaryāmin) whom they do not know, those who do not know Him, and that Imperishable (akṣara) which is said to be the essence of consciousness for all, as the agent of actions such as seeing. Now, what is the distinction among these, or what is their commonality?

Regarding this, some explain as follows: of the Supreme Brahman—the imperishable (akṣara) which is like the great ocean and whose nature is unmoving—there is the state of being slightly moved, which is the Inner Controller (antaryāmī); and the state of being completely moved is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who does not know that Inner Controller. Likewise, they postulate five other states, and say that thus there are eight states of Brahman. Others say that these are the powers (śaktis) of the Imperishable, and that the Imperishable possesses infinite powers.

Others, however, say that [these] are modifications (*vikāra*) of the Imperishable (*akṣara*). But both states (*avasthā*) and powers (*śakti*) are untenable, because of the scriptural teaching that the Imperishable transcends the attributes of transmigratory existence such as hunger and so forth. For it is not possible for one and the same thing to simultaneously possess both the state of transcending hunger and so forth and the state of possessing those very attributes like hunger; likewise, it is not possible for it to possess powers. Furthermore, the faults regarding [the Imperishable] being a modification or having parts have already been demonstrated in the fourth [chapter]. Therefore, all these conceptual constructions are unreal.

What, then, is the distinction between these? We say it is one produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); there is no distinction or non-distinction among them in themselves, because their essential nature is a single, uniform mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*), like a block of salt, as stated in the Śruti: "Without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior," and "This Self is Brahman"—and also in the Ātharvaṇa: "For He is without interior or exterior, unborn. Therefore, since the Self devoid of adjuncts is indefinable, devoid of attributes, and one, it is designated as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).

The Self, when characterized by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the body and organs distinguished by ignorance, desire, and action, is called the transmigrating individual soul (jīva). The Self, when characterized by the limiting adjunct of the power of eternal and unsurpassed knowledge, is called the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) or the Lord (īśvara). That same Self, when devoid of all adjuncts, absolute, pure, and established in its own essential nature, is called the Imperishable (akṣara) or the Supreme (para). Likewise, when distinguished by the limiting adjuncts of the effects and instruments—such as Hiraṇyagarbha, the unmanifest (avyākṛta), deities, species, bodies, humans, animals, ghosts, and so forth—it becomes designated by those names and takes on their forms.

Thus, [the statement] "It moves, yet It does not move" has been explained. Likewise, scriptural passages such as "This is your Self," "This is the inner Self of all beings," "This is hidden in all beings," "That thou art," "I indeed am all this," "The Self alone is all this," and "There is no other seer but This," are not contradicted. Under any other conceptualization, these scriptures would not be consistent.

Therefore, their distinction arises solely through the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and not otherwise, because of the definitive assertion in all the Upanishads that "It is one only, without a second.
Thus ends the eighth Brāhmaṇa of the third chapter.
Now, as for that fourth nectar, the Maruts subsist upon it with Soma as their mouth. Indeed, the gods neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by seeing this nectar.

Then Śākalya—the descendant of Śakala, named Vidagdha—questioned him: "How many gods are there, O Yājñavalkya? Yājñavalkya, it is said, determined the number by means of this very *nivid* (enumeration) which was about to be spoken, the very number that Śākalya had asked about.

"However many," meaning however numerous, "are the gods" mentioned in the *nivid* of the *vaiśvadeva* recitation—the *nivid* being certain mantra-words expressing the number of deities that are recited during the *vaiśvadeva* litany, and which are designated as *nivid*; "as many gods as are heard" in that *nivid*, so many are the gods.

What, then, is that *nivid*? Those *nivid* verses are now shown: "Three and three hundred"—that is, three gods and three hundred gods; again likewise, "three and three thousand"—so many are the gods. Śākalya said, "Yes. Thus, their intermediate number has been correctly known.

Furthermore, he asks for the number of those very deities in their contracted state: "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya?"—"Thirty-three, six, three, two, one and a half, and one. Having asked about the number regarding the contraction and expansion of the deities, he asks again about the nature of those who are numbered: "Who are those 'three and three hundred and three and three thousand'?"—It is into this very form that they enter, and from this form that they emerge.

The other said: "They are the glories (*mahimānaḥ*), the manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) of these thirty-three gods—namely, 'these three and three hundred,' and so forth; but in the ultimate sense, there are only thirty-three gods. It is asked: "Which are those thirty-three? It is replied: "The eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, and the twelve Ādityas—those are thirty-one; Indra and Prajāpati are the thirty-second and thirty-third, completing the number thirty-three."
He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Maruts alone, becomes satisfied upon seeing this very nectar with Soma as his mouth; he enters into this very form and emerges from this form. 3.

"What are the Vasus?"—thus their individual nature is asked. "Agni and Pṛthivī," etc.—these [entities] beginning with Agni and ending with the Nakṣatras are the Vasus. Because they transform into the form of the aggregate of causes and effects (the body) as the substratum for the fruits of the actions of living beings, and because they serve as their dwelling place, they cause this entire world to dwell (*vāsayanti*) and they themselves dwell (*vasanti*); since they cause [beings] to dwell, they are therefore called Vasus.

"As long as the sun rises in the west and sets in the east, twice as long will it rise in the north and set in the south; for so long will he attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Maruts. Thus ends the ninth section.

"What are the Rudras? These ten are in the person: the organs of action and the organs of perception, together with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). The self (*ātman*) and the mind (*manas*) are the eleventh—the one that completes the eleven. When these vital breaths depart from this mortal body at the exhaustion of the enjoyment of the fruits of the living beings' karma, they then cause those related to them to weep. Because they cause those relatives to weep (*rodayanti*) in that situation, they are therefore called "Rudras. (5)

"What are the Ādityas? The twelve months are well known as the constituent parts of the year, which is time; these are the Ādityas. How so? Because they, revolving again and again, go—meaning they proceed—taking, seizing, and appropriating the lifespans and the fruits of the actions of living beings. Since they go while thus taking all this, they are therefore called Ādityas. (6)

"What is Indra? What is Prajāpati? "Indra is indeed the thunder, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice. "What is the thunder? "It is the lightning bolt (*aśani*).
