The lightning bolt is the thunderbolt (*vajra*), the heroic power, and the strength that causes living beings to perish; that is Indra, for that is the work of Indra. "What is the sacrifice? "It is the sacrificial animals (*paśu*). For sacrificial animals are the means (*sādhana*) of the sacrifice; because the sacrifice is formless and because it depends on the sacrificial animals as its means, the sacrificial animals are called the sacrifice. (7)

"What are the six? These same [deities] enumerated as *vasus*, beginning with Agni, become six when excluding the moon and the stars—that is, they are characterized by the number six. For all that was mentioned, beginning with the thirty-three, these very ones constitute the six; the meaning is that the entire expansion of the *vasus* and so forth is contained within these six alone.

"Which are those three gods? [The answer is: "These very three worlds—namely, by unifying the earth and fire, there is one god; by unifying the intermediate space and wind, there is a second; and by unifying the sky and the sun, there is a third. These indeed are the three gods. For since all gods are included within these three gods, therefore these alone are the three gods—such is the position of certain etymologists (nairuktas).
"Which are those two deities?"—food and breath; these are the two deities, for within these two all that has been mentioned is included. "Which is the one-and-a-half?"—this wind that blows.

Regarding this, they say and raise this objection: "Since this wind blows as one alone, how can it be called 'Adhyardha' (the One-and-a-Half)? [The answer is: "Because in this, all this has prospered. When this wind exists, all this has prospered—it attains growth (*ṛddhi*)—therefore it is called Adhyardha. "Which is the one god? "Prāṇa."

That vital breath (*prāṇa*) is Brahman—because it consists of the essence of all the gods, it is the Great Brahman (*mahadbrahma*). Therefore, they call it "Brahman" and "That" (*tyad*); they call that Brahman by the word "That" (*tyad*), which is a term used for what is beyond direct perception. This is both the unity and the diversity of the gods: the inclusion of infinite gods within those characterized by the number *nivit*; and their further inclusion, from thirty-three and so on, in each subsequent group until they are contained within the single vital breath; and the entire expansion from the infinite number belongs to this one vital breath alone.

Thus, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is one, infinite, and distinguished by intermediate numbers. And therein, for a single deity, there is a differentiation of names, forms, actions, qualities, and powers due to the difference in their respective offices (*adhikāra*).
Now, the eightfold division of that very Brahman, which is the *prāṇa*, is further taught:

The deity whose abode or support is the earth itself; whose world is fire—“world” (*loka*) meaning that by which one sees (*lokayati*), i.e., he sees by means of fire; whose light is the mind—he who performs functions such as volition and conceptualization by means of the mind as his light, he is "mind-light" (*manojyoti*). The meaning is: the deity who has the earth as his body, who perceives through fire, who wills with the mind, who identifies with the earth, and who possesses the aggregate of causes and effects (the body and organs).

Whoever should thus know—that is, understand—that distinguished Person as the supreme goal (*parāyaṇa*), the ultimate refuge of the self of all, namely the aggregate of the internal body and its instruments: He indeed would be the knower. For He is the supreme resort of that which is born of the mother—consisting of skin, flesh, and blood, which stands in the place of the field—for that which stands in the place of the seed, consisting of bone, marrow, and semen, which is born of the father; and He is also the resort of the self of the instruments. He indeed would be the knower.

The intention is that he who knows this thus would indeed be a learned knower. The intention is that you, Yājñavalkya, while not knowing him, merely pride yourself on being learned. [Yājñavalkya says: "If such learning is obtained through the knowledge of him, then I indeed know that Person—whom you say, whom you speak of, as the ultimate resort of every self. In this regard, Śākalya’s words are to be understood: "If you know that Person, tell me what his specific attributes are."

Listen, as to what its qualification is—that which is this "bodily" (śārīra) one: "bodily" means existing in the earthly portion of the body, that is to say, consisting of the three maternal sheaths. This very deity is the one you asked about, O Śākalya; however, there is another qualification to be stated regarding it, so ask about that now, O Śākalya.

Thus provoked and overcome by indignation, he spoke like an elephant struck by a goad: "What deity is there for that body of the god—from which it is produced? What deity presides over it?"—this is what is intended in this context. He replied, "The Immortal. "The Immortal" refers to the essence (*rasa*) of the food consumed, which is the cause of the production of the blood derived from the mother; for from that essence of food, blood is produced and takes refuge in the woman, and from that, the body consisting of blood, which is the substratum for the seed, comes into being. The rest is the same. (11)

"Desire alone is his abode. Desire means the longing for sexual union with women; the meaning is that desire is his body. "The heart is the world"—he sees by means of the heart, that is, by means of the intellect. This very person who consists of desire, even in relation to the self (*adhyātman*), consists of desire alone. "What is his deity?"—"Women," he said; for from women arises the kindling of desire. (12)

"Form itself is its sphere. Forms are white, black, and so forth. That very person who is in the sun—the person in the sun being the most distinguished effect of all forms—[the questioner asks] "What is his deity? [Yājñavalkya] said, "Truth. By "truth," the eye is meant; for from the eye as the internal principle (*adhyātma*) arises the sun as the divine principle (*adhidaivata*).

"Space itself is his abode. That which exists in the ear is the auditory [element]; since it occurs specifically at the time of hearing, it is called the "pratiśrutka" (the echo). "What is its deity?"—"The quarters," he said; for from the quarters this internal [element] is produced. (14) "Darkness itself is his abode. By "darkness" is meant the gloom of night and so forth; internally, it is the person consisting of shadow, consisting of ignorance. "What is its deity?"—"Death," he said; death is the presiding deity (*adhidevata*) and the cause of its production.

(15) — For whom visible forms alone are the sphere (*āyatana*). Previously, common visible forms were mentioned; here, however, specific visible forms that act as illuminators are intended. The specific sphere of the deity of the form-sphere (*rūpāyatana*) is the substratum for reflections, such as a mirror and so forth. "What is its deity?"—"It is *asu*," he said. The manifestation of that person known as the reflection arises from *asu*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*). (16) —

"Water alone is its abode. All waters in common constitute the abode; it has its specific location within the waters residing in ponds, wells, tanks, and so forth. "What is its deity? "Varuṇa. From Varuṇa come those who effect the aggregation; within the body, water itself is the cause for the production of the waters found in ponds and such.

"Seminal fluid indeed is its abode; that which consists of the son is the specific abode of that which has seminal fluid as its abode—namely, the son. And [the son's] bones, marrow, and semen are born from the father. What is its deity? "Prajāpati," he said—"for Prajāpati is called the father, since the son's birth is from the father.

Each individual deity, having divided itself threefold and threefold according to the distinction between the world of the gods and the world of men, exists as eightfold; each one is designated for the purpose of meditation as a specific manifestation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Now, in order to bring about the withdrawal [of these] into the Self, which is divided fivefold according to the divisions of the directions, Yājñavalkya spoke to Śākalya—who had become silent—as if possessing him with a spell, saying: "Śākalya," said Yājñavalkya.

The word *tvāṃ svid* expresses a conjecture (*vitarke*): "Surely these Brāhmaṇas have made you into a charcoal-remover (*aṅgārāvakṣayaṇa*)—that is, a pair of tongs or similar tool in which coals (*aṅgārāḥ*) are extinguished (*avakṣīyante*). Surely the Brāhmaṇas have made you such; but you do not perceive it—that is, you do not realize that you yourself are being burned by me. This is the intended meaning. (19)

"Yājñavalkya," said Śākalya, "since you have spoken over these Brāhmaṇas of the Kurus and Pañcālas—you have spoken too much—[they], being themselves afraid, have made you a 'charcoal-pit' (aṅgārāvakṣayaṇa). Being a knower of Brahman, why do you thus insult the Brāhmaṇas? Yājñavalkya replied: "This much, at least, is my knowledge of Brahman. What is it? I know the quarters; I possess knowledge concerning the quarters."

And that [knowledge] does not concern the directions alone, but the directions together with the gods (*sadevāḥ*), that is, together with the presiding deities of the directions; furthermore, it includes the foundations (*sapratiṣṭhāḥ*), together with their foundations. The other says: "If you know the directions together with the gods and the foundations—if such is the knowledge you have claimed to possess, then it is indeed fruitful.

"Whose deity are you? What is the deity of you who have become this quarter? For Yājñavalkya had divided his own self, the heart, fivefold among the quarters, having identified the entire world with the self through those quarters and established himself in the thought, "I am the self of the quarters," facing the east—as is evident from the mention of his "support. Just as was Yājñavalkya's declaration, so he asks: "Whose deity are you in this quarter?"

For throughout the Veda, it is said that whichever deity one worships here, having become that very being, one attains that deity; and thus it will be stated later: "Having become a god, he goes to the gods. Regarding this eastern direction, which deity presides over you who are the self of the directions? The meaning is: by which deity have you been endowed with the form of the eastern direction? The other replies: "The deity Āditya"; in the eastern direction my deity is Āditya, and thus I am "one whose deity is Āditya" (ādityadevataḥ).

It has been stated that [the world] is "together with the gods," but it must now be stated that it is "together with its foundation. Thus he asks: "On what is that sun founded? [The answer is: "In the eye"; for the declarations of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas state that the sun is produced from the eye—such as, "From the eye the sun was born" and "From the eye the Āditya"—and indeed, an effect is founded upon its cause. [He asks again: "On what, then, is the eye founded? [The answer is: "In visible forms."

For the eye, being of the nature of form, is engaged with form in order to grasp form; indeed, the eye is undertaken for the purpose of grasping its own self by means of those very forms with which it is engaged. Therefore, the eye, together with the sun and the eastern direction, along with all things situated therein, is established in forms. The entire eastern direction, together with the eye, consists of form. And as to where those forms are established—“In the heart,” he said; “Forms are originated from the heart.”

For the heart has been transformed into the form of visible objects (*rūpa*); because it is by means of the heart that the entire world cognizes forms. The term "heart" (*hṛdaya*) is a designation made by unifying the intellect (*buddhi*) and the mind (*manas*). Therefore, it is in the heart alone that forms are established; for it is by means of the heart that there is the recollection of forms which exist in the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Thus, the meaning is that forms are established in the heart. "It is exactly so, Yājñavalkya. (21)

"Which deity belongs to you in this southern direction?"—as before—"Which deity is yours in the southern direction? "Yama is my deity"—Yama is the deity for me who am situated in the southern direction. "In what is that Yama established? "In the sacrifice"—Yama, together with the direction, is established in the cause that is the sacrifice. But how is it said that Yama is the effect of the sacrifice? It is because the sacrifice is accomplished by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

By means of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the sacrificer ransoms the sacrifice from them; by that sacrifice, he is born together with Yama into the southern direction. Because Yama is to be accomplished through that sacrifice, he is established therein along with the southern direction. "In what, then, is the sacrifice established? "In the sacrificial fee"—for it is by means of the sacrificial fee that the sacrifice is ransomed; therefore, the sacrifice has the sacrificial fee as its function.

"On what, then, is the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā) established? "On faith (śraddhā)," he replied. Faith is the desire to give, a conviction of the truth accompanied by devotion. How is the sacrificial gift established on that? Because when one has faith, then one gives the sacrificial gift; one does not give the sacrificial gift without having faith. Therefore, the sacrificial gift is indeed established on faith.

"On what, then, is faith established? "On the heart," he said. "For faith is a function of the heart, since one knows faith by means of the heart; and a function is established in that which possesses the function. Therefore, faith is indeed established in the heart. "It is just so, Yājñavalkya. (22)

"Which deity resides in this western direction? "Varuṇa is its presiding deity for me. "In what is that Varuṇa established? "In the waters," [he replied]. For Varuṇa has the waters as his effect, according to the Vedic revelation: "The waters are indeed faith," and "From faith he created Varuṇa. "In what are the waters established? "In semen," [he replied]. For the waters were created from semen, according to the Vedic revelation. "In what is semen established? "In the heart," [he replied]; because semen is the effect of the heart.

"Desire is the function of the heart; for from the heart of one who desires, semen flows forth. Therefore, people in the world say of a son born who resembles his father: 'This son has slipped out, emerged from the very heart of this father,' as if he were fashioned from the heart, just as an earring is fashioned from gold. Therefore, it is in the heart indeed that the semen is established. "It is even so, Yājñavalkya. (23)

"Which deity presides over this northern direction? "The Moon (Soma) is its deity."—here, the plant *soma* and the deity *Soma* are mentioned by identifying them as one. "On what is that Soma established? "On consecration (*dīkṣā*)."—for it is the consecrated sacrificer who purchases the *soma*; having sacrificed with the purchased *soma*, the man of knowledge reaches the northern direction, which is presided over by the deity Soma and is auspicious (*saumya*).

"On what is initiation (*dīkṣā*) established? "On truth."—"How so?"—"Because initiation is established on truth, therefore they say of one who has been initiated: 'Speak the truth,' lest there be a failure in the effect due to a failure in the cause. For initiation is indeed established on truth. "On what is truth established? "On the heart," he said. "For by the heart one knows the truth; therefore truth is indeed established on the heart. "It is just so, Yājñavalkya. (24)

"What deity is presiding over this fixed (dhruvā) direction? [The answer is: "Because it abides unswervingly all around Mount Meru, the upward direction is called 'the fixed' (dhruvā). "Agni is its deity"—for in the upward direction there is an abundance of light, and Agni is light. "On what is that Agni established? "On speech. "On what is speech established? "On the heart. In this regard, Yājñavalkya has attained all the directions as his own self through the heart, which extends throughout all the directions.

The quarters, together with the gods and their foundations, became the very self of that Yājñavalkya, who had become the essence of name, form, and action. That which was his form, along with the eastern quarter, became the heart of Yājñavalkya. And whatever was his pure action—characterized by the procreation of sons as well as accompanied by knowledge, together with its fruit and the presiding deities—the southern, western, and northern quarters, consisting of the fruits of action, entered into his heart alone.

Together with the fixed direction, everything called by name enters into the heart alone through the door of speech; for all this is only this much: namely, form, action, or name—all that is indeed the heart. That heart, which is the self of all, is now questioned: "In what, then, is the heart established? (25)

"Ahallika! said Yājñavalkya—thus he addressed him by another name. "If you think that at some time this heart, the self of this body, exists elsewhere, somewhere other than us—if indeed this heart were elsewhere than us, then dogs would eat this body, or birds would tear it apart, mangle it, and drag it away."
Therefore, the meaning is that my heart is established within the body. Since the body itself consists of name, form, and action, it is established in the heart.

Thus, the mutual dependence of the heart and the body, as the effect and the instrument, has been explained. Therefore, I ask you: "In what, then, are you and the body—the self and your heart—both established? "In the vital breath (prāṇa). The body and the self would both be established in the vital breath, that is, in the function of the vital breath. "But in what is the vital breath established? "In the downward breath (apāna). For even that function of the vital breath would have departed earlier, were it not held back by the function of the downward breath.

"On what is the apāna established? "On the vyāna. If that function of the apāna were not held back by the middle function of the vyāna, it would simply move downward, just as the function of the prāṇa moves upward. "On what is the vyāna established? "On the udāna. If all three functions were not bound to the udāna, which stands like a pillar, they would go in all directions. "On what is the udāna established? "On the samāna. For all these functions have the samāna as their foundation.

This is what is meant: the body, the heart, and the vital airs are mutually dependent; they function as a fixed aggregate, impelled by objects consisting of consciousness. This entire complex—by which it is regulated and in which it is established, woven like warp and woof up to the limit of space—is that Brahman, free from all limiting adjuncts, immediate and direct. It is for the purpose of providing an instruction regarding that Brahman that this undertaking begins.

This very one—He who was pointed out in the Madhu-kāṇḍa by the words "not this, not this"—is this very Self. He is ungraspable (*agṛhya*); that is, He cannot be grasped. Why? Because He transcends all qualities of effects (*kāryadharma*); therefore He is ungraspable. Why? Because He is indeed not grasped. For whatever object is within the range of the instruments of perception (*karaṇa*) and is differentiated (*vyākṛta*), that falls within the range of grasping; but this reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is the opposite of that. Likewise, He is indestructible (*aśīrya*). For whatever is material and composite, such as the body and so forth, that is subject to destruction; but this Self is the opposite of that.

Therefore, it does not decay. Likewise, it is unattached (*asaṅga*): for that which has form, when coming into contact with another thing possessing form, becomes attached; but this [Self] is the opposite of that, and therefore it is not attached. Likewise, it is unbound (*asita*): for that which has form is bound; but because this is the opposite of that, it is unbound. Because it is unbound, it does not suffer; therefore, it does not perish. The meaning is that, being devoid of the properties of grasping, dissolution, attachment, and bondage, it does not perish—that is, it does not undergo injury or destruction.

Having bypassed the sequence and departed from the narrative concerning the Puruṣa of the Upaniṣads, the Śruti has provided a direct instruction in its own form with urgency; then, returning once more to the narrative itself, it says: "These which have been mentioned—the eight abodes beginning with 'the earth indeed is his abode,' the eight worlds beginning with the world of Agni, the eight deities beginning with 'He said, "Immortality,"' and the eight persons beginning with 'the person in the body'—whosoever [among them]..."

Having drawn out those persons beginning with the embodied self (śārīra), having led them away with certainty—that is, having established the order of the world through the division of the eight groups of four—and having again withdrawn them by way of the eastern direction and other gates, he transcended—meaning he passed beyond—the limiting attributes of his own self in the heart, such as having the heart and so forth as its essence.

"I ask you about that person established in his own self—the person of the Upaniṣads who is free from hunger and other such needs, who is to be known through the Upaniṣads alone and is not accessible through any other means of knowledge. If you do not explain him clearly to me—that is, if you will not speak of him—I declare that your head shall shatter," said Yājñavalkya. Śākalya, however, did not know—that is, he certainly did not understand—that person of the Upaniṣads.

His head indeed fell off; it fell away. The narrative is concluded. This is the statement of the Śruti: "He did not recognize him," and so forth. Furthermore, even the bones of this man—being carried by his disciples toward his home for the sake of funeral rites—were plundered (*apajahruḥ*) by thieves (*parimoṣiṇaḥ*, *taskarāḥ*). For what reason? Thinking that some other wealth was being carried. Indeed, a past event is indicated here [in the story].

It is said that in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, a discussion took place between Śākalya and Yājñavalkya that ended in a dispute; there, Yājñavalkya uttered a curse: "You shall die before your guests arrive, and no one shall carry your bones home. He indeed died in that very manner; moreover, thinking they were something else, robbers carried off his bones. Therefore, one should not be a slanderer, for even one who knows this becomes an object of reproach. This narrative is indicated here for the sake of proper conduct and for the praise of knowledge.

Since Brahman has been indicated by means of the negation of everything else through the formula "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), how is its indication to be made by way of affirmation? Thinking that the root of the world must also be explained, he resorts once again to a narrative and says: [27]— "The wealth of cattle should be seized from the Brāhmaṇa who does not know Brahman"—this is the principle [he considers]. Thus, he relates the connection of the narrative.

Then he said: "Now, after the Brahmins had become silent, he spoke, addressing them thus: 'O venerable Brahmins! Whosoever among you desires—wishes—to ask Yājñavalkya, let him come and question me; or let all of you question me; or whosoever among you desires that Yājñavalkya should question him, him I shall question.'"

"I ask you all, indeed, each of you. Those brahmins did not dare; even though addressed in this manner, those brahmins did not become bold enough to utter even a slight reply. When those brahmins had thus become disconcerted, he questioned them with the following verses that are about to be stated. Just as in the world there is a tree, a *vanaspati*—of a tree...

The qualification is "the lord of the forest" (*vanaspati*); likewise, man is not false—this is true, not false. His body hairs are the leaves of that other, the lord of the forest; his outer skin is the bark of that other, the lord of the forest.

From the very skin of this person blood flows out, just as from the bark of a tree a sprout emerges—for it is from the skin itself that [the wound] bursts open. Thus, everything is exactly the same for both the tree and the person. Therefore, when it is pierced—that is, wounded—that blood issues forth, just like sap from a tree that has been struck or cut.

In this way, the flesh of this person corresponds to those "śakarāṇi" of the tree, which means the splinters. The *kināṭa*—the so-called *kināṭa* of the tree, which is the inner layer of bark attached to the wood located within the splinters—that is the sinew (*snāva*) of the person; it is firm—for that *kināṭa* is indeed as hard as a sinew. The bones of the person are like the pieces of wood (*dārūṇi*) inside the *kināṭa*; for just as the bones are situated within the sinews, so too are the pieces of wood situated within the *kināṭa*.

The marrow: the marrow itself is made the likeness for both the tree and the person; "likeness of marrow" means it is comparable to marrow, implying there is no other distinction. As the marrow of the tree is, so is that of the person; as that of the person is, so is that of the tree. (27.4)

If a tree, once cut down or severed, grows again—sprouts forth and manifests from its root, ever newer than before, more fresh than what preceded it—then, prior to this specific qualification regarding the tree and the person, everything was understood as common to both. However, this distinction is observed in the case of the tree: that which is severed sprouts again; but when a person is cut down by death, such re-sprouting is not observed. And yet, there must be some source from which such re-sprouting occurs.
Therefore, I ask you: from what root does a mortal man, once cut down by death, sprout forth again? The meaning is: from where does the rebirth of a dead person originate? (27.5)

If you say, "It grows from semen," do not say so; you ought not to speak thus. Why? Because that semen is produced from a living man, not from one who is dead. Furthermore, there are trees that grow from seeds—seeds being the seed—and a tree may also grow from a seed, not only from a cutting. The word *iva* is meaningless here. Indeed, a tree arises directly and immediately after dying; likewise, after dying, there would be an immediate arising from a seed as well, for the lord of the forest. (27.6)

If they were to uproot, lift up, or tear out a tree together with its root, it would not come back into existence; having returned, it would not grow again. Therefore I ask you: from what root does mortal man—the root of the entire world—sprout when he is cut down by death? (27.7)

If you think, "He is indeed already born," then what is there to be asked here? For it is the possibility of one who is yet to be born that ought to be questioned, not that of one who is already born. If you say, "But since this one is already born, a question regarding this matter is simply not appropriate"—no; why so? Because one who has died is indeed born again, otherwise there would follow the error of [attaining] the results of actions not performed (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and the loss of results of actions performed (*kṛtanāśa*). Therefore, I ask you: who, indeed, would bring him back to life once he is dead?

The Brahmins did not understand that from which the dead man sprouts again; the root of the world was not known by the Brahmins. Consequently, because of their lack of knowledge regarding Brahman, their cows were taken away; the Brahmins were defeated by Yājñavalkya. The narrative is concluded.

The scripture declares to us in its own terms that which is the root of the world, that by which Brahman is directly designated, and that which Yājñavalkya questioned the Brāhmaṇas: "Consciousness"—that is, cognition—and that is "Bliss," not permeated by suffering like the consciousness of sense-objects; rather, it means it is serene, auspicious, incomparable, effortless, eternally satisfied, and of a single essence.

What is that Brahman? It is the "giver" (rāti), possessing both qualifications; the nominative case *rātiḥ* is used in the sense of the genitive, meaning "of wealth" (*dhanasya*). It is the supreme goal (*parāyaṇam*), the ultimate resort, of the performer of rituals, the sacrificer who gives wealth—that is, the giver of the fruits of action. Furthermore, for one who has risen above desires and stands firm in that very Brahman, being a non-performer of rituals and a knower of it (*tadvid*)—meaning, a knower of Brahman—it is the supreme goal. For him who stands [in Brahman] and knows it, it is the supreme goal.

In this regard, the following is considered: the word *ānanda* is well-known in the world as denoting happiness; and here, the word *ānanda* is heard as a qualification of Brahman—namely, "Brahman is bliss" (*ānandaṃ brahma*). And in another scriptural passage: "He understood that Brahman is bliss," "The knower of the bliss of Brahman," and "That which is this space... [and so forth].

There would be no bliss, yet there are such scriptural passages as, "That which is the Plenum (bhūman), that is bliss," and "This is the supreme bliss," and so forth. Furthermore, the word *ānanda* is well-known in common usage to denote a pleasure that is experienced (*saṃvedya*). If the bliss of Brahman were also something experienced, then these uses of the word *ānanda* for Brahman would be appropriate. [Objection: But surely, on the authority of the Śruti, Brahman is of the very nature of experienced bliss; what then is there to be deliberated upon? [Reply: No, because we observe scriptural statements that appear contradictory. It is true that the word *ānanda* is heard in reference to Brahman; however—

And there is the negation of consciousness in the state of oneness: "But where everything has become the Self for him, then by what and whom should he see? By what and whom should he know? "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, knows nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūmā). "Embraced by the conscious Self (prājña-ātman), one knows nothing at all externally," and so forth. Because such contradictory scriptural statements are observed, an inquiry must be conducted. Therefore, it is appropriate to investigate in order to determine the meaning of the Vedic statements.

Furthermore, there is disagreement among those who propound liberation: the Sāṃkhyas and Vaiśeṣikas, being proponents of liberation, disagree by asserting that in liberation there is no pleasure to be experienced; others, however, maintain that there is unsurpassed pleasure to be experienced through self-awareness.

What, then, is the correct position? It is that bliss is to be experienced in liberation, because of scriptural passages such as "eating, playing, and rejoicing," "if he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers," "he who is all-knowing and all-perceiving," and "he enjoys all desires. [Objection: But if there is oneness, there is an absence of the distinction between factors of action (kāraka), and thus consciousness is impossible; moreover, since an action requires multiple factors of action for its accomplishment, and consciousness is itself an action—this objection is not valid. Consciousness regarding bliss can indeed occur through the authority of scripture.

We have already stated that statements such as "Consciousness is bliss" (*vijñānamānandam*) would be untenable if the nature of bliss were not capable of being experienced. Now, one might object: even by means of a verbal statement, the coldness of fire or the heat of water is certainly not produced, for words are merely indicators; nor can it be made known through speech that fire is cold in another place, or that water is hot in an inaccessible region. To this we reply: no, because the realization of bliss and consciousness is observed within the inner self (*pratyagātman*).

Statements such as "Consciousness is bliss" (*vijñānam ānandam*) do not convey a meaning contrary to perception and other means of knowledge, like the sentence "Fire is cold. Rather, their non-contradictory nature is experienced: one personally perceives the Self as consisting of bliss in the form "I am happy. Therefore, they are all the more consistent with perception; thus, Brahman, being blissful and consisting of consciousness, perceives itself.
In this way, the previously mentioned scriptural passages conveying bliss—such as "eating, playing, and rejoicing"—become coherent.

No, because consciousness is untenable in the absence of the body and the instruments [of action]. For liberation is the absolute dissociation from the body; and in the absence of the body, the instruments are untenable due to the lack of a substratum. Consequently, consciousness is untenable because it lacks both body and instruments. Furthermore, if consciousness were to arise in the absence of the body and so forth, it would follow that the acquisition of all bodies and instruments by everyone would be rendered useless. Moreover, there is a contradiction with the doctrine of non-duality: if the Supreme Brahman, being of the nature of bliss, were the Self because it is eternally conscious...

One might think that he should always be known [in this way], but that is not so; for even while transmigrating, one would attain liberation from transmigration and reach his own true nature. Just as a handful of water thrown into a reservoir does not remain separate, so too for the sake of realizing Brahman whose essence is bliss—then the statement "the liberated one experiences the Self whose essence is bliss" would be meaningless. On the other hand, if the liberated one, being distinct, were to experience the bliss of Brahman and the inner Self, thinking "I am of the nature of bliss," then there would be a contradiction with the doctrine of non-duality (*ekatva*).

And this being the case, there would be a contradiction with all the Śruti texts. Furthermore, the third alternative is not tenable. Moreover, if Brahman possesses an uninterrupted cognition of the bliss of the Self, the conceptualization of "knowing" and "not knowing" is purposeless; for if Brahman’s cognition has the bliss of the Self as its uninterrupted object, then that very bliss is His own nature, and thus the conceptualization that "He knows the bliss of the Self" is untenable. Indeed, a conceptualization is meaningful only when there is the possibility of not knowing that [object], as in the case of saying "He knows himself and the other."

For one whose mind is absorbed in an arrow or similar object, the conceptualization of a continuous stream of knowledge or ignorance regarding that arrow serves no purpose. If, on the other hand, one perceives the bliss of the Self as something interrupted—then it would follow that during a gap in the cognition of the Self, consciousness must have another object; furthermore, it would entail that the Self undergoes modification, and from that, the consequence of its impermanence. Therefore, the scriptural statement "Consciousness is bliss" is intended solely as a description of the essential nature [of Brahman], not for the sake of establishing that the bliss of the Self is an object of cognition.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction with scriptural passages such as "eating and playing," because [the liberated soul] would not be perceivable, we say no; for these passages merely restate what is already established given the oneness of the Self of all. When the liberated one has attained the state of being the Self of all, whatever eating and so forth occurs—whether among yogis or among the gods—is simply restated as it is found to occur. This is done for the purpose of praising liberation as the state of being the Self of all, on the grounds that such experiences belong to that very state of being the Self of all.

If it is argued that [the Self] must be subject to suffering because it merely restates what is already obtained—just as in the case of the *yogins* and others who experience [pleasure] such as laughing and so forth, which is already obtained—[we reply: no. This has all been refuted by the fact that the distinctions of being happy or miserable are superimposed through delusion, produced by contact with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the body and organs formed by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Furthermore, we have already explained the scope of the conflicting scriptural passages.
Therefore, all statements regarding bliss should be understood in the same way as the passage, "This is his supreme bliss.
Thus ends the ninth Brāhmaṇa of the third chapter.
Thus [ends] the work of the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsaparivrājakācārya).
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya, the third chapter:
Now, as for that which is the fifth nectar, the Sādhyas subsist upon it through the mouth of Brahmā; indeed, the gods neither eat nor drink, but they are satisfied merely by beholding this nectar. 1.
Then, having risen above that, he neither rises nor sets; he stands alone in the middle. Regarding this, there is this verse:

Now, indeed, this heart has five openings for the gods. That which is its eastern opening is the out-breath (*prāṇa*); that is the eye; that is the sun. One should meditate upon it as "splendor" and "food-eating. He who knows this becomes splendid and an eater of food.
All this, indeed, is Brahman, because [the world] is born from it, dissolves into it, and breathes in it. One should meditate on it with a calm mind. Now, man is indeed composed of resolve (*kratu*).
As is his resolve in this world, so does he become after departing from here. Therefore, let him form a resolve.
The chest has the intermediate space for its belly; it does not decay, having the earth for its base. The quarters are indeed its corners, and the sky is its upper opening.
This is that treasure-chest, the container of wealth; in it all this universe is supported. 1.

Man, indeed, is the sacrifice. His twenty-four years constitute the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*). The *gāyatrī* meter has twenty-four syllables, and the morning libation belongs to the *gāyatra* chant; therefore, the Vasus are connected to it. The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed the Vasus, for they cause all this to dwell (*vasayanti*).

When he is hungry, when he is thirsty, and when he does not find pleasure—these are his initiatory rites (*dīkṣās*). "One should meditate upon the mind as Brahman"—this is with reference to the self (*adhyātma*). Now, with reference to the divine (*adhidaivata*), "Space is Brahman. Thus both have been taught: that which pertains to the self and that which pertains to the divine.
And with respect to the divine... [the teaching is]:
"The Sun is Brahman"—this is the instruction. Its further explanation is as follows: In the beginning, this world was indeed non-existent;
it became existent; it developed; it formed an egg; it lay for the duration of a year; it burst open; those two halves of the eggshell became silver and gold.
Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was a man of faith, a giver of much, a provider of many cooked meals, and one who maintained dwellings on all sides, thinking, "People shall eat my food from every direction. 1.

Janaka of Videha had taken his seat—that is, he had prepared a seat and offered a formal reception for those desiring an audience with the king. Now, at that moment, Yājñavalkya arrived—having come for the sake of his own spiritual welfare (*yogakṣema*), or perhaps out of grace upon seeing the king’s desire to know. Having performed the appropriate honors for the arrived Yājñavalkya, Janaka said to him: "O Yājñavalkya, for what purpose have you come?"

"Do you desire cattle once again, or do you wish to hear from me questions that culminate in the atom (*aṇu*), that end in the subtle (*sūkṣma*), or that conclude with the determination of the nature of subtle reality? [Yājñavalkya asks: "Both, O Emperor—both cattle and questions. "Emperor" (*samrāṭ*) is a title indicative of one who has performed the Vājapeya sacrifice; or, he who governs a kingdom by command is a *samrāṭ*, and this is his address as "O Emperor"; or else, he is the king of the entire land of Bhārata-varṣa.

"But what did someone say to you?"—"For you have served many teachers; let us hear that. The other said: "My teacher, named Jitva, the son of Śilina—Śailini—said to me: 'Speech indeed is Brahman,' meaning the deity of speech is Brahman. The other said: "One who has a mother is called *mātṛmān*—that is, a son for whom there exists a mother who is a proper instructor and a giver of instruction."

From this point onward, he whose father is his instructor is "one who has a father"; from the time of initiation until the return home, he whose teacher is his instructor is "one who has a teacher. Thus, being endowed with these three causes of purification, he is a true teacher himself and never deviates from authority. Just as he would speak to a disciple, so did Śailini, having mastered it, declare: "Speech, indeed, is Brahman."

"For what would happen if one did not speak?"—for indeed, for a mute person, there would be nothing here or in the hereafter. But he said to you the abode and the support of that Brahman—"abode" meaning the body, and "support" meaning the refuge throughout all three periods of time. The other replied, "He did not tell me."

The other said: "If this is so, then this is indeed 'one-footed'—that Brahman which has but one foot. This one-footed Brahman, being worshipped while empty of its three feet, does not lead to any fruit; such is the meaning. If this is so, then you, being a man of knowledge, tell us, O Yājñavalkya."

And he said: "Speech alone is the abode; for the Brahman who is speech, speech itself is the instrument, the abode, the body; and space, called the unmanifest, is the foundation during the times of its origin, persistence, and dissolution. One should worship it as 'Consciousness' (prajñā)—this 'Consciousness' is the secret teaching (upaniṣad) of Brahman, the fourth quarter. Thinking of it as 'Consciousness,' one should worship this Brahman."

"What is the nature of wisdom (*prajñatā*), Yājñavalkya? Is it wisdom itself, or is it that which has wisdom as its cause—just as the abode and the support of Brahman are distinct from it? "No," he replied. "How then? "Speech alone, O Emperor," he said; "speech alone is wisdom," he declared, meaning that wisdom is not something separate.
But how is it said that speech alone is wisdom? "By speech alone, O Emperor, a relative is recognized; when it is said, 'This is our relative,' the relative is thereby recognized."

Likewise, O Emperor, the Rigveda and the other Vedas; the collection of dharmas occasioned by sacrifices (iṣṭa), those occasioned by oblations (huta), those occasioned by the giving of food (āśita), and those occasioned by the giving of drinks (pāyita); this world and this birth, as well as the next world and the birth to be attained, and all beings—these are known through speech alone. Therefore, O Emperor, speech indeed is the supreme Brahman. Speech does not desert this knower of Brahman as described.

All beings offer tributes to him through offerings and the like. Having become a god in this world, he goes to, that is, enters, the gods after the fall of the body, provided he knows this and meditates upon it in this way. "An elephant and a bull" (*hasty-ṛṣabha*) means a bull equal to an elephant; "I give a thousand cows with an elephant and a bull as the [eleventh]," so said Janaka of Videha. Yājñavalkya said: "One should not take wealth from a disciple without having instructed him, without having made him successful."

"My father thought thus; it was my own intention as well. Then, during that very night, as they were passing by, Hrasva addressed Hrasva: "O Ho! O Ho! O Bhallākṣa! The light of Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa is spread out as vast as the sky. Do not touch it; do not burn yourself! 2. (2) — Śrī Śaṅkarācārya did not comment on this verse.
The other replied to him: "Who indeed is this Raikva whom you call 'like Sayugvā'? What, pray, is this Sayugvā Raikva? 3.

Whatever someone told you—namely, Udaṅka by name, the son of Śulba, a Śaulbāyana, who said: "Brahman is indeed breath (prāṇa)"; the deity is Vāyu, as before. Breath itself is the abode, space is the foundation; its secret name (upaniṣad)—one should meditate upon it as "the dear" (*priyam*). But how is it dear? Because for the sake of breath, O Emperor, one performs sacrifices even for those from whom one should not sacrifice, such as outcasts; and one accepts gifts even from those from whom one should not accept them, such as fierce warriors.

In that regard, there is apprehension of being killed—meaning, the fear of death—in whichever direction one goes that is infested with thieves and the like; and in that direction, there is the fear of death. All this occurs because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is dear, O Emperor, for the sake of the vital breath alone. Therefore, O Emperor, the vital breath is indeed the supreme Brahman; it does not desert him. The rest is the same [as before].

Just as when the *kṛta* throw has been won, the lower throws are included therein, even so all that good which creatures perform is gathered together in him who knows what he [the knower] knows; and he who knows that, it was said by me: "He who knows that. 4.

Now, whoever that person was—Barku by name, the son of Vṛṣṇi, a Vārṣṇa—he said: "The eye, indeed, is Brahman. The deity in the eye is the sun. The secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) is "Truth" (*satya*). For while what is heard with the ear might be untrue, what is seen with the eye cannot be so; therefore, O Emperor, when they ask one who has seen, "Did you see the elephant?", if he says, "I saw it," that becomes the truth. But if another were to say, "I heard it," that can be deceptive.
"Whatever is seen with the eye is indeed real, because it is non-deviating.
Now, Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa heard this. As he was rising, he said to his charioteer, "My good man, have you ever spoken of Raikva, who possesses the cart? "Who, pray, is this Raikva with the cart?

He who is named Gardabhīvipīta by name and Bhāradvāja by lineage—[the teacher said]: "Brahman is indeed the ear. The deity of the ear is the quarters (the directions). One should meditate upon it as the Infinite. What is the infinity of the ear? The quarters themselves are the infinity of the ear. Therefore, O Emperor, whatever direction one goes—whether eastward or northward, or any other direction whatsoever—no one ever reaches its end. Thus, the quarters are indeed infinite. The quarters, O Emperor, are the ear; therefore, the infinity of the quarters is itself the infinity of the ear.

Just as when the Kṛta has been won, the lower throws are included therein, even so all that good which people do is gathered together in him who knows what he knows—that is, "this has been declared by me. 6.

Jābāla, by name Satyakāma, the son of Jabālā—Candramas (the Moon) is the deity of the mind; "Bliss" is its secret name (*upaniṣad*). Since bliss is indeed the mind, therefore, O Emperor, when a man desires a woman, he is drawn toward her—that is, he makes his request. Because he is drawn toward the woman he desires, a son resembling and conforming to her is born; that son is the cause of bliss. That mind by which he is brought forth—that mind is bliss.
The steward returned, saying, "I have searched for him, but I did not find him. He said to him, "O man, go where one searches for a Brahmin; there you will find him.

Vidagdha Śākalya said: "The heart, indeed, is Brahman. "The heart, O Emperor, is the abode of all beings. For we have stated in the Śākalya-Brāhmaṇa that all beings—which consist of name, form, and action—have the heart as their support and are established in the heart. Therefore, O Emperor, all beings are indeed established in the heart. Therefore, one should meditate upon the heart as 'the foundation'; and Prajāpati is the deity in the heart. Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa of the fourth chapter.
Then Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, taking six hundred cows, a gold necklace, and a chariot drawn by mules, went back to him and said:

Janaka of Videha—because Yājñavalkya knew all the Brahmanas along with their specific qualifications—therefore, abandoning his role as teacher, rose from his *kūrca* (a special seat) and approached him, meaning he prostrated at his feet, and said: "Salutations be unto you, O Yājñavalkya! Teach me, instruct me! The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the sentence.

Yājñavalkya said: "Just as in the world, O Emperor, one who is about to travel a great and long road would prepare for it—either by taking a chariot to go by land, or a boat to go by water—even so you, being devoted to these sacred texts (*brahmāṇi*) joined with these secret doctrines (*upaniṣad*), are one whose self is concentrated; indeed, you are one whose self is thoroughly united with these secret doctrines. You are not merely concentrated through the secret doctrines alone."

Thus, although you are a leader, worthy of worship, wealthy, and a lord—not a pauper—and although you have studied the Vedas (meaning that by whom the Veda has been studied, he is "one who has studied the Veda"), and the Upanishads have been explained to you by teachers (meaning that by whom the Upanishads have been explained, he is "one for whom the Upanishads have been explained"); even though you are thus endowed with all prosperity, you remain in the very midst of fear and have not yet achieved your purpose without the knowledge of the Supreme Self—this is the meaning—as long as you do not know the Supreme Brahman.

"Being liberated from this body, where—in what place—will you go when concentrated by these [qualities] which stand in the place of a boat or a chariot? What object will you attain? "I do not know that object, O Blessed One, O Venerable One, where I shall go. "Now, if you do not know thus where you have gone to become one who has accomplished his purpose, I shall indeed tell you that, where you will go. "Let the Blessed One speak, if he is pleased with me. "Listen—"
"Here are six hundred cows, this necklace, and this chariot drawn by mules; but, venerable sir, teach me that deity which you worship.

"Indha" is indeed his name. He who was previously described as "the Brahman that is the eye"—that very person residing within the sun—is he who is specifically established in the right eye. And he is "Satya" (Truth) by name. Because of his quality of luminosity, this person's manifest name is "Indha" (the Kindler); though he is Indha, they call him "Indra" cryptically.

For the gods, as it were, love what is hidden and hate what is manifest; they hate the utterance of their own names when spoken aloud. "You have indeed attained Vaiśvānara as your Self," [said the other].

To him the other replied: "Alas! O Śūdra, let this [gift] remain with you alone, along with the cows. Then Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, taking a thousand cows, a gold necklace, a chariot drawn by mules, and his daughter, returned to him.

Now, this form of a person in the left eye is his wife—she who is the food to be enjoyed by this Indra, the enjoyer, whom you have identified as the Vaiśvānara Self. She is Virāj, for she is food precisely because she is that which is to be enjoyed. Thus, this food and the eater constitute a single couple in the dream state. How so? This is their place of assembly—the meeting place where Indra and Indrāṇī come together and converse with one another; that is their "saṃstāva."

The two sheaths? That which is this space within the heart—within the heart, that is, in the middle of the lump of flesh; now, for these two, this food to be eaten, which is the cause of their subsistence, is as follows: what is it? That which is this lump of blood within the heart—that is, blood itself having assumed the form of a lump, a "lump of blood. Food that has been eaten undergoes a twofold transformation: that which is coarse goes downward.

That which remains is further cooked by the fire and undergoes a twofold transformation: the middle essence (rasa) builds up the body—the aggregate of the five elements—by means of the sequence beginning with blood; the subtlest essence is this very mass of blood belonging to Indra, the self consisting of the subtle body (liṅga-ātman), who has entered into union within the heart, whom they call "luminous" (taijasa).

Having entered into the subtle channels within the hearts of Indra and Indrāṇī joined as a couple, he becomes the cause of their maintenance. This is what is expressed by the passage beginning, "Now this is their food," and so forth. Furthermore: "Now this is their covering"—for in the world, there is a covering for those who have eaten and are sleeping, and the Śruti conceives of this similarity.

What is that covering here? It is this [space] within the heart, which, because it possesses many openings for numerous channels, is like a network (*jālaka*). Now, this is the *sṛti*—the path, the way by which one moves along it—and thus it is called the "path of movement" (*saṃcaraṇī*), the route for traveling from the state of dream to the region of waking. What is that path? It is this channel (*nāḍī*) which, starting from the heart—that is, from the region of the heart—proceeds upward and issues forth.

Its measurement is stated as follows: just as in the world a hair split a thousandfold becomes extremely subtle, so too are the channels called *hitā*—so named because they are beneficial—which belong to this body; they are established within the mass of flesh in the heart. Spreading out from the heart, they extend everywhere like the filaments of a *kadamba* flower. Through these exceedingly subtle channels, this food flows—that is, it goes—and thus it is said to "flow" (*āsravati*). It goes.
This very body of the deity, being nourished by this food which serves as its bond, persists.

Therefore—since the physical body (*piṇḍa*) is nourished by gross food, whereas this subtle body (*liṅga*), which is the body of the deity, subsists being nourished by subtle food—even the food that causes the growth of the physical body is "distinct" (*pravivikta*) only in comparison to gross excrement, urine, and so forth; however, the food that sustains the subtle body is even more subtle than that. Consequently, the physical body has distinct food, and therefore this self of the subtle body (*liṅgātman*) becomes even more distinct in its food than the physical body, compared to this [gross] body.

The "bodily" (*śārīra*) is indeed the body; from that bodily self, Vaiśvānara—the *taijasa* [self], which is subtle and not composed of gross food—becomes nourished. Then he said to Raikva: "Here are a thousand cows, this necklace, this chariot drawn by mules, this wife, and this village in which you dwell; O Venerable One, instruct me further.

This very one, having become the heart and being of the nature of light (*taijasa*), while being sustained by the subtle vital breath (*prāṇa*), becomes the vital breath itself. For this knower who has thus reached the state of *taijasa* from the state of *vaiśvānara*, having attained the self of the heart, and having further attained the self of the vital breath from the self of the heart: the eastern direction is his forward-moving vital breaths; likewise, the southern direction is his southern vital breaths; likewise, the western direction is his backward-moving vital breaths; and the northern direction is his upward-moving vital breaths.

The upward direction is the upward vital breaths; the downward direction is the downward vital breaths; all directions are all the vital breaths. One who knows thus, through his action, comes to regard the vital breath—which is the self of all—as his own self. Having withdrawn that universal self into the innermost self, he realizes the fourth state (*turīya*), the self which is the seer’s true nature as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).

That which the knower attains by this sequence has already been explained in the passage beginning with "This Self is 'not this, not this'" and ending with "he is not injured. Indeed, O Janaka, you have attained that which is fearless—devoid of fear caused by birth, death, and so forth. Thus, indeed, Yājñavalkya spoke. This very point was stated: "Now, indeed, I shall tell you that [Self] where you will go."

Janaka, the King of Videha, said: "May fearlessness indeed come to you as well, O Yājñavalkya, venerable sir, since you have made known—brought us to—the fearless Brahman by removing the veil of ignorance created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). What else shall I give for the price of this knowledge, to one who has given me his very self? Therefore, let there be salutation to you! Let these people of Videha be enjoyed by you as you wish."
"And here I am, standing in the state of a slave; you may take me and the kingdom as you wish"—this is the meaning.
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa of the fourth chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya.
Air, indeed, is the absorber. When fire goes out, it goes into air; when the sun sets, it goes into air; when the moon sets, it goes into air.

Yājñavalkya went to Janaka of Videha. While on his way, he thought to himself: "I shall not say anything at all to the king; my purpose in going is merely for the sake of security and well-being. Although Yājñavalkya had made this resolve not to speak, whatever Janaka asked, that he answered. What was the reason for his acting contrary to his resolve? To explain this, the author relates the following narrative.

It is said that previously there was a dialogue between Janaka and Yājñavalkya concerning the Agnihotra sacrifice; having perceived Janaka’s profound knowledge regarding the Agnihotra, Yājñavalkya was highly pleased and granted a boon to him. Janaka chose the boon of asking any question he desired, and Yājñavalkya granted him that boon.

By the power of that boon-granting, King Janaka alone questioned Yājñavalkya first, even though he remained silent and did not wish to speak. The reason for his silence was that the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is incompatible with ritual action (*karman*); furthermore, because knowledge is independent—indeed, the independent knowledge of Brahman is the means to the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) without depending on any other auxiliary means. As it is said:
"When the waters dry up, they merge into the air alone, for the air indeed gathers them all together"—this is with respect to the deities (*adhidaivata*).

Having addressed him as "O Yājñavalkya" in order to draw his attention, [the question is asked]: "What is the light of this person?"—that is, what is the light of this person by which he performs his activities? What is his light? This ordinary person, consisting of an aggregate of body and organs, possessing a head, hands, and so forth, is being questioned: does he perform his activities by means of some external light distinct from the aggregate of his own limbs, or rather, does he perform the functions of light by means of a light that falls within the aggregate of his own limbs?

Thinking that "this person performs [the action]," he asks. What follows from this—whether he performs the function of light by means of a light distinct [from himself] or one non-distinct? Listen to the reason for this: if his nature were determined to be the performance of the function of light solely by means of a distinct light, then even regarding a case where the function of light is not perceived, we would infer that this effect is indeed caused by a distinct light.

Now, if one conducts one's affairs by means of a light that is non-different from one's own self, then even when the light is imperceptible, since the function of light is observed, the light must be inferred as being non-different [from the self]. Alternatively, if there were no fixed rule—that is, if either a distinct or a non-distinct light were the cause of a person’s activity—then there would be no certain determination regarding the nature of the light. Thinking thus, Janaka asked Yājñavalkya: "What is the light of this person?"

Now, one might object: "If this is so, what is the use of questioning the proponent regarding his skill in inference? Why does he not understand it himself? This is true; nevertheless, because the specific relations between the mark (*liṅga*) and the thing marked (*liṅgin*) are extremely subtle, they are considered difficult to comprehend even for many scholars, let alone for a single person. For this very reason, the involvement of an assembly (*pariṣad*) is required for the determination of subtle matters of Dharma, and a specific type of person is also required—whether it be an assembly of at least ten, or three, or even one.

Therefore, although the King was skilled in inference, Yājñavalkya was nevertheless justified in questioning him, because among men there exists a gradation in the proficiency of their knowledge. Alternatively, the Śruti itself, following the human intellect, introduces the path of inference through the guise of this narrative and instructs us. Yājñavalkya, being aware of Janaka’s intention and wishing to demonstrate that the light of the Self is distinct [from the body], accepted from Janaka precisely that indicative mark which establishes its distinctness, saying: "O Emperor, the well-known light of the sun [is for you]."

How so? By means of the sun itself—that light which is distinct from its own collection of parts and which assists the eye—this ordinary person sits, he sits down; he moves about, he goes around to the field or the forest; having gone there, he performs his work; and he returns, he comes back, just as he went. There are multiple qualifiers for the purpose of demonstrating that the nature of being a distinct light is well-known;
and the demonstration of various external lights is for the purpose of showing that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is non-deviant. "It is exactly so, Yājñavalkya."

Now, with reference to the self: breath indeed is the absorber. When one sleeps, speech goes into the breath, the eye into the breath, the ear into the breath, and the mind into the breath; for breath indeed absorbs all these. Likewise, Yājñavalkya, when the sun has set, what light does this person have?—the moon indeed is his light.
These two are indeed the two absorbers (*saṃvarga*): Vāyu among the gods and Prāṇa among the vital breaths. ...
When the sun has set and the moon has set, fire is the light.

Now, while Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni were being served food, a religious student begged from them; they did not give to him. When the fire has been extinguished, speech is the light. By "speech," sound is intended; by the object that is sound, the sense-organ of hearing is illumined. When the sense-organ of hearing is fully illumined, discernment arises in the mind. Through that mind, one engages in external activity—for the Brāhmaṇa says: "For with the mind alone one sees, with the mind one hears."

But how is speech the light? Since its status as light is not well-known, he says: "Therefore indeed, O Emperor," because this person conducts his affairs aided by speech as light, therefore this status of speech as light is well-established.

How so? For instance—at that time, during the rainy season when there is generally the darkness of clouds and all luminaries have set, even one's own hand is not clearly discerned—then, at that time when all physical activity has ceased due to the absence of external light, wherever a voice utters a sound, or a dog barks, or a donkey brays, one approaches right there; by means of that sound as a light, a continuous connection is established between the ear and the mind, and through that...

Speech attains the state of being the light; by means of that speech as light, one approaches—that is, one indeed goes toward and becomes present there—and there one performs action, one acts. In this context, the mention of speech as light is for the purpose of indicating smell and the other [objects of sense]; for when the nose and the other [organs] are assisted by smell and the rest, activity, cessation, and so forth occur; thus, assistance is also provided by those [objects] to the aggregate of the body and the instruments [of perception]. "It is even so, Yājñavalkya."

He said: "The one God has swallowed the four great ones. Who is he, the guardian of the world? O Kāpeya, mortals do not perceive him, though he dwells manifoldly, O Abhipratārin—him for whom this food is intended, yet it is not given to him.

Furthermore, when speech has become quiet and even external supportive objects such as odors and so forth have become quiet, the cessation of all activity is attained by this person. What is meant is this: when the sense organs, such as the eyes and others, which are directed outward toward the objects of the waking state, are supported by the lights of the sun and other luminaries, then the worldly transaction of this person becomes most distinct.

Thus, first of all, it is observed that in the waking state, this person’s accomplishment of the functions of light is effected by a light distinct from the aggregate of his own limbs; therefore, we maintain that even when all external lights have subsided—in the states of dreaming, deep sleep, and likewise in the waking state—his accomplishment of the functions of light is effected by a light distinct from the aggregate of his own limbs.

Furthermore, the accomplishment of the functions of light is observed in dreams—such as the sight of meeting or being separated from kinsmen, traveling to other lands, and so forth—as well as the rising from deep sleep with the recollection, "I slept happily; I knew nothing. Therefore, there exists some light distinct [from the body]. But what indeed is that light which exists when speech has become stilled? It is said: the Self alone becomes his light.

The term "Self" (ātman) refers to a light that is distinct from the aggregate of the body and its constituent parts, which illuminates the body and its organs—just as external lights such as the sun do—and which is itself not illuminated by anything else. Furthermore, it resides within; and by the method of elimination, it is established that this light is indeed distinct from the body and its organs. Moreover, it is observed that a light distinct from the body and its organs, which sustains the aggregate of the body and its organs, is perceived through external instruments such as the eyes.

But that [light] is not perceived by the eyes and other senses in the same way when the lights of the sun and so forth have ceased; yet, since the effect of light is observed, it follows that "he sits, moves about, performs action, and returns, by means of this very light of the Self. Therefore, it is understood that there is certainly a light situated within. Furthermore, that light is distinct from the lights of the sun and so forth, and it is non-material; the same reason applies for its being ungraspable by the eyes and other senses, just like the sun and other celestial lights.

No, because assistance is observed only by that which belongs to the same class. As for the claim that another light, distinct from the sun and so forth, is established [as the eye's light], this is incorrect. Why? Because it is observed that the aggregate of the body and its organs, being material, receives assistance only from a material light such as the sun, which belongs to the same class as that which is assisted; and this must be inferred according to what is observed.

Even if light, like that of the sun and so forth, were indeed distinct from the body and its organs and yet beneficial to them, it would still have to be inferred as belonging to the same class as the aggregate of the body and its organs, because it is beneficial to that aggregate, just like the light of the sun and other luminaries. As for the claim that it differs [from material things] due to its being internal and imperceptible, that argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the lights of the eyes and other senses; for the lights of the eyes and so forth, though imperceptible and internal, are nonetheless composed of the elements (*bhautika*).

Therefore, it is merely a matter of your own fancy that a distinct light of the Self is established. Furthermore, because the light exists only when the aggregate of the body and the organs exists, it is inferred to be a property of that aggregate. Moreover, inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) is unreliable due to its fallibility; for by the force of such general observation, you seek to establish a light distinct from the body and organs, as in the case of the sun and so forth. And direct perception cannot be sublated by inference.

However, it is this very aggregate of causes and effects (the body) that perceives, hears, thinks, and cognizes directly. Even if another light were to assist it, as the sun and other luminaries do, that other light would not be its self, just as the sun and other celestial lights are not the self. Rather, that which performs the acts of seeing and so forth directly must be the self—the aggregate of causes and effects—and none other; for when there is a contradiction with direct perception, inference lacks authority.

Now, if this very aggregate (saṃghāta) is the self that performs actions such as seeing, how is it that the capacity to perform actions like seeing belongs to it only at certain times and not at others, even though it remains entirely unchanged? This is not a fault, because it is actually observed; for indeed, there is nothing that is logically untenable when it is directly perceived. For one does not infer another cause for a firefly simply because it is seen to be both luminous and non-luminous. Furthermore, if everything were to be inferred based on some commonality, then everything would be inferable from everything, which is undesirable.

Nor is it the case that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things does not exist; for the heat of fire or the coldness of water is not caused by any other external factor. If it is argued that these depend on the merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and so forth of living beings, then it follows that merit, demerit, and the rest would themselves have to possess an intrinsic nature dependent upon further causes. If one accepts this, no; for that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), which is undesirable. [Objection: No, because in dreams and memories, one perceives only what has already been perceived. As for what was stated by the proponent of intrinsic nature—that the acts of seeing and so forth belong to the body alone and not to a distinct [self]—that is not correct.

For if the acts of seeing and so forth belonged to the body alone, there would be no seeing of that very thing seen in a dream; a blind man seeing a dream sees only what was previously seen, not something unseen such as the form of Śākadvīpa and other places. From this, it is established: he who sees a previously seen object in a dream is the very same person who saw it previously while his eyes were functional, and not the body.

If the body were the seer, then when the eye by which one saw was extracted, one would not see that very thing previously seen during dream; yet there is a well-known worldly experience—even among the blind whose eyes have been extracted—such as, "I saw the peak of the Himalayas before, and today I saw it in a dream. Therefore, it is understood that even when the eye has not been extracted, he who is the dream-seer is indeed the seer, and not the body.

Likewise, since memory establishes the identity of the seer and the rememberer—such that whoever is the seer is the very same as the rememberer—it follows that when one remembers a previously seen form even with eyes closed, one sees it exactly as if it were being seen. Therefore, that which is closed is not the seer; rather, it is understood that that which perceives the form while remembering even when the eyes are closed was the very same seer when the eyes were open.

Furthermore, because there is an absence of the perception of forms and so forth even when the body is intact [if it were merely the body], if the body itself were the seer, the acts of seeing and so on would persist even in a dead body. Therefore, it is understood that that whose departure from the body results in the absence of seeing—and whose presence results in its occurrence—is the agent of the acts of seeing and so forth, and not the body. If it is argued that the eyes and other organs themselves are the agents of the acts of seeing and so forth, we say no; for if they were distinct agents, the synthesis of "I who saw that, I now touch it" would be impossible.

If it is argued that it is the mind (*manas*), we say no; for since the mind is itself an object, like color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, its status as a seer and so on is untenable. Therefore, it is established that [the light] resides within [the body] yet is distinct from it, like the sun and other luminaries. As for what was stated—that another light must be inferred as belonging to the same genus as the aggregate of the body and the organs, because it is assisted by things of the same genus such as the sun and so on—that is incorrect, for we observe that the relationship between the beneficiary and the benefactor is not restricted to things of the same genus.

How so? It is observed that the assistance for the blazing of fire is rendered by earthly fuels—such as grass, stones, wood, and so forth—which belong to the same genus as earth; yet, one should not infer on that basis alone that the assistance for the blazing of fire must everywhere be rendered only by things of that same genus, since it is also observed that assistance for blazing is rendered even by water, which is of a different genus, in the case of lightning-fire and digestive fire.

Therefore, in the relationship between the beneficiary and the benefactor, there is no rule that they must be of the same or different classes; sometimes beings of the same class, such as humans, are benefited by others of the same class, and sometimes they are benefited by those of different classes, such as stationary objects, animals, and so forth. Consequently, the argument that [the body] is benefited only by luminaries of the same class as the aggregate of its causes and effects—such as the sun—is not a valid reason.

As for what you further said—that the reason "because it is invisible like the light of the sun and so forth by means of the eyes and other organs" does not establish the internal location and distinctness of another light, because it is inconclusive (anaikāntika) with respect to the eyes and other organs—that is incorrect, because the qualification "while being other than the instruments such as the eyes" is logically applicable to the reason. Furthermore, as for what was stated—that the light possesses the nature of the aggregate of effects and instruments—that is not so, because it contradicts inference.

For it has been stated that light is an entity distinct from the aggregate of the body and its organs, just like the sun and other luminaries; this contradicts the proposition that light is a property of the aggregate of the body and its organs. Furthermore, the fact that [the perception of] light exists only when that [aggregate] exists is unproven, because light is not perceived in a dead body. If inference based on general observation were invalid, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the cessation of all worldly activities, such as drinking and eating; and that is not acceptable.

For if one who has already experienced the cessation of hunger, thirst, and so forth through drinking, eating, and the like were to perceive that [cessation] again, the observed undertaking of drinking, eating, and so forth in the world would not occur on the basis of that similarity; yet we see those who have already experienced drinking and eating inferring, by way of generality, the cessation of hunger, thirst, and so forth through other instances of drinking and eating, and proceeding toward them for that purpose.

As for what was stated—that this very body is the agent of actions such as seeing—that has already been refuted at the outset by the argument that the seer is an entity distinct from the body in the cases of dreaming and memory. By this same reasoning, the non-selfhood of any other light-source is also rejected. Furthermore, the claim that fireflies and the like possess an intermittent capacity for illumination and non-illumination is incorrect; for their illumination and non-illumination are caused by the contraction and expansion of parts such as their wings.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that the nature of dharma and adharma must necessarily be accepted as being the bestower of results—since accepting that would entail the abandonment of your own established doctrine (siddhānta). By this, the fault of infinite regress (anavasthā) is refuted. Therefore, there exists a distinct, internal light which is the Self (ātman).

Then Śaunaka Kāpeya, reflecting upon this, returned, saying: "The Self is the progenitor of the gods and of creatures; he is the golden-horned, devouring, and never-failing one. They speak of his greatness as vast, for though he is not being eaten, he eats that which is not food. "O student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), it is indeed him that we worship here. Give him alms! Thus [he spoke]. 7. (7) ---

Although its distinctness and so forth are established, nevertheless, due to the delusion caused by observing that [the senses] assist those of their own kind, one asks out of a lack of discrimination—"Which one?"—whether it is one of the instruments themselves or something distinct from them. Such a delusion is possible because the subtlety of logical reasoning is difficult to discern. Alternatively, even though [the Self] is established as distinct from the body, all the instruments appear as if they possess consciousness, because the Self is not perceived through such discrimination.

Therefore, I ask: "Which one is the self?"—which among the body, the senses, the vital breaths, and the mind is that which you have called the self, by means of which light it is said to sit? Or rather, which among these vital breaths is this self intended by you as consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), since all these vital breaths are, as it were, composed of consciousness? Just as when it is said, "All these Brahmins are learned in the six Vedāṅgas; which among them is the knower of the six Vedāṅgas?"—so too here.

In the first interpretation, the question consists of only this much: "Which is the self? (katama ātmā), and the answer is: "He who consists of cognition" (yo 'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ). In the second interpretation, however, the question extends up to the words "among the vital breaths" (prāṇeṣu).
