Alternatively, the entire passage up to "the person who consists of cognition, the light within the heart" (vijñānamayo hṛdyantarjyotiḥ puruṣaḥ) constitutes the question.

Considering that it is logical for the word "this which consists of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) to have as its object a specific determined meaning, and for the words "which one is the Self? (*katama ātmā*) to serve the purpose of completing the interrogative sentence, it is concluded that the interrogative sentence ends precisely with "which one is the Self?", while everything following from "this which... onwards is the answer.

The phrase "this which" is a designation [of the Self] because the Self is directly perceived. "Consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) means primarily composed of consciousness. It is called "consisting of consciousness" due to the non-discrimination arising from contact with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the intellect and its cognitions—because the Self is indeed perceived only when conjoined with the intellect and its cognitions, just as Rāhu is perceived only when conjoined with the moon or the sun. For the intellect is the instrument for all objects, like a lamp placed before one in the darkness; for it has been said: "For by the mind alone one sees, by the mind one hears."

For indeed, every class of object is perceived as distinguished by the light of the consciousness of the intellect (*buddhi-vijñāna*), just as objects in the dark are perceived when distinguished by the light of a lamp placed in front; the other organs, however, are merely gateways for the intellect. Therefore, it is distinguished by that alone—as "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*). As for those who offer the explanation that [the self] is a modification of the consciousness of the Supreme Self (*paramātma-vijñapti-vikāra*), their interpretation is determined to be non-scriptural (*aśrauta*) because the word "consisting of consciousness" is seen to have a different meaning in such passages as "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) and "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*).

A word whose meaning is doubtful can be determined elsewhere by observing its usage in a context where it is certain, either through the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) or by the force of a certain principle; furthermore, it is read later as *sadhīḥ*. Because of the statement "within the heart" (*hṛdyantaḥ*), it is appropriate that it consists primarily of consciousness (*vijñāna*). The locative case in *prāṇeṣu* is for the purpose of showing distinction—just as in the expression "a stone among trees"—characterizing proximity; for regarding the self, a doubt arises as to whether it is distinct from or non-distinct from the vital breaths (*prāṇas*).

The meaning is that [the Self] is distinct from the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). For whatever exists within something is necessarily distinct from it—just as a tree is distinct from stones. Regarding the phrase "in the heart" (*hṛdi*): one might think that the intellect (*buddhi*) existing among the vital breaths would be of the same nature as them; therefore, he says "within the heart" (*hṛdyantaḥ*). By the word "heart," a mass of flesh shaped like a lotus is meant; because the intellect resides there, the intellect is called "the heart. Thus, "in the heart" means "in the intellect. The word "within" (*antar*) is intended to demonstrate its distinction from the modifications of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*).

The Self (ātman) is called "light" because its nature is luminosity. For by means of that luminous Self, one sits, moves about, and performs action; for this aggregate of body and organs appears as if possessed of consciousness—just like a jar situated in the light of the sun.

Or, just as a gem such as an emerald, when placed in a substance like milk for examination, makes that substance like milk appear as its own reflection, so too this light of the Self—because it is subtler than even the intellect and thus situated within the heart—unifies the aggregate of the body and organs, including the heart itself, and renders them as the reflection of the light of the Self. This occurs through a gradual progression from the subtle to the gross, owing to its being the innermost of all.

First, because of its transparency and immediate proximity, the intellect (*buddhi*) becomes a reflection of the light of the self’s consciousness; for this reason, even among the discerning, the notion of "I" (the identification with the self) arises first in relation to it. Immediately after that, due to its proximity and through contact with the intellect, the appearance of consciousness occurs in the mind (*manas*). Then, it appears in the sense organs (*indriya*) through their conjunction with the mind. Following that, it appears in the body through its contact with the sense organs.

In this manner, through a continuous succession, the Self illumines the entire aggregate of causes and effects by means of the light of its own conscious nature. For it is because of this that the world at large develops, according to its degree of discrimination, the notion of an unstable self-identification with the aggregate of causes and effects and with their various functions. And thus it has been said by the Blessed Lord in the *Gītā*: "Just as the one sun illumines this entire world..."

"O Bhārata, [the Lord] illuminates the field and likewise the knower of the field in their entirety"—as stated in the passage beginning with "The light that resides in the sun... and so forth. Also in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "He is the eternal among the non-eternal, the conscious among the conscious. And: "Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined. And the Vedic mantra says: "By whose fiery splendor the sun burns. Therefore, this Person (puruṣa) is the light within the heart. He is called "Person" (puruṣa) because He is full (pūrṇa), being omnipresent like space.

And its self-luminosity is unsurpassed, because it illumines everything and is itself not illumined by anything else. This very person (*puruṣa*), whose nature is self-luminous, is the one you ask about when you inquire, "Which is the Self? When all external lights that assist the various organs have subsided, the person who is the internal light within the heart—the Self—is the illuminator by means of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

It has been stated, "of the instruments. Even when there is the presence of external lights such as the sun that assist the instruments, since those lights like the sun exist for the sake of another, and since the aggregate of the body and instruments is insentient, it cannot have its own purpose fulfilled; thus, in the absence of the assistance of the Self, who is the light for His own sake, this aggregate of the body and instruments is not capable of worldly activity.

For indeed, all worldly activity always proceeds solely through the favor of the light of the Self, as is known from another scriptural passage beginning with, "That which is this heart and mind, this is consciousness"; for all the worldly activity of living beings is accompanied by self-identification (abhimāna); and we have already explained the cause of this self-identification by means of the illustration of the emerald gem.

Although this is so, nevertheless, because the light of the Self (*ātmajyotis*) is not within the range of any of the instruments during the waking state, and because it is distracted by the convergence of the activities of the internal and external instruments such as the intellect (*buddhi*), that light called the Self cannot be extracted and shown like a stalk from a clump of *muñja* grass. Therefore, wishing to demonstrate it in the dream state, [the text] begins: "Being the same, he moves along both worlds."

That person who is himself the light-self (*jyotirātmā*) is "equal" (*samāna*), that is, similar—to what? To the heart (*hṛdaya*), because it is the subject under discussion and is proximate. Furthermore, by the word "in the heart" (*hṛdi*), the intellect (*buddhi*), which is denoted by the term *hṛd*, is the subject under discussion and is proximate; therefore, the similarity is with that very [intellect]. But what is this similarity? It is the non-perception of a distinction between them, like that of a horse and a buffalo; the intellect is the object of illumination, while that light-self is the illuminator, just like light.

The non-perception of the illuminated and the illuminator through their distinction is well known; for because of its purity, light becomes similar to that which is illuminated. Just as, while illuminating red, light becomes similar to red and takes on a red form, and just as, while illuminating green, blue, or red, light becomes identical to them, so too, while illuminating the intellect, it illuminates the entire field (kṣetra) by means of the intellect—this has been stated by way of the illustration of the emerald gem.

It is identical with all that through the medium of the commonality of cognition; and for this very reason, he will later say, "consisting of all. Because it cannot be extracted from anything else and shown in its own form of light—like a stalk of grass from the *muñja* reed—the entire world becomes utterly deluded regarding the Self, superimposing upon it the activities of name and form, the attributes of light belonging to name and form, and name and form themselves upon the light of the Self, thinking: "This is the Self, this is not the Self; it has such qualities, it does not have such qualities; it is an agent," and so forth.

It is not an agent; it is pure and impure, bound and liberated, stationary, gone, and come, existent and non-existent—by such conceptual constructions. Therefore, being the same [in both states], it sequentially traverses both worlds—the world already reached and the world yet to be reached, namely this world and the next—through hundreds of successions of conjunctions consisting of the abandonment of the current aggregate of body, senses, and so forth, and the taking up of another.

The similarity of the intellect (*dhīsādṛśya*) alone is the cause for wandering between the two worlds, not [the Self] by itself. In this regard, that very similarity caused by the limiting adjuncts of name and form (*nāmarūpopādhi*), which is the basis of delusion, is the cause, not [the Self] by itself—this is what is being stated. Because, being "common" (*samāna*), it wanders through both worlds in succession. He demonstrates that this is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*): because it "as if meditates," as if performing the activity of meditation, as if thinking; for that [Self], by means of the intellect situated within it, appears to possess the activity of meditation.

Illuminating by means of the form of light whose nature is consciousness, being similar to—that is, identical with—that [light], it "meditates," as it were, just like light itself. Therefore, the delusion arises in the world that "it thinks"; yet, in the ultimate sense, it does not meditate. Likewise, it "moves about excessively, as it were," meaning it moves intensely, because while those very instruments—the intellect and so forth—and the vital airs are moving, it is similar to them due to its being their illuminator. Thus, it "moves about, as it were"; but in the ultimate sense, that light of the Self does not possess the property of motion.

But how is this understood—that the delusion of similarity to that [dream] alone is the cause for wandering through both worlds and so forth, and not [the self] by itself? To demonstrate this point, the reason is taught: "That Self, indeed, having become a dream"—that is, by whatever intellect (dhī) it is similar, whatever that intellect becomes, he too becomes as if that very thing;
therefore, when that [intellect] becomes a dream, i.e., enters the state of sleep, then he too enters the state of dreaming; and when the intellect desires to wake, then he too [wakes].

Therefore, he says: having become a dreamer, manifesting the activity of dreaming, and having assumed the form of the state of sleep, it transcends—having passed beyond—this world, which is characterized by the activities of waking, consisting of the aggregate of causes and effects, and serving as the locus for worldly and scriptural transactions; because it remains manifesting the dream-state activity of the intellect by means of its own distinct self-luminosity, it is therefore "self-luminous"—that is its very nature, and it is pure.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is devoid of agent, action, instrument, and fruit; however, the mere similarity of the intellect (*dhīsādṛśya*) is the cause of the delusion regarding worldly transactions, such as the transition between the two worlds. "The forms of death"—death consists of karma, ignorance, and so forth; it has no other form of its own, for its forms are simply the effects and instruments [of action]. Therefore, one transcends those forms of death which are the substrata of action and its fruits. Now, it may be argued that there is indeed nothing else similar to the intellect that could manifest the intellect, namely the light of the Self (*ātmajyotis*), whether perceived directly or through inference apart from the intellect.

Because of non-apprehension—just as another cognition at that very same time [is not apprehended]. As for the claim that there is similarity between the illuminated object and the illuminator because their distinction is not apprehended, as in the case of a jar and light—that may well be so, since light is apprehended as distinct from the jar and other objects; thus, the similarity of two conjoined things exists only between things that are distinct. But here, we do not perceive by either direct perception or inference any other light that illuminates cognition in the manner of a jar or similar objects.

For cognition itself, by virtue of being the illuminator of its own nature, possesses both its own form and the form of the object; therefore, neither through inference nor through perception can a light distinct from cognition be established as its illuminator. As for the example that was stated—that there is a similarity between the illuminated and the illuminator, such as between a jar and light which are distinct and conjoined—that was mentioned by us merely as a concession.

However, in that case, the object manifested as a jar and so forth and the manifesting consciousness are not distinct; for in ultimate reality, the jar and so forth are themselves of the nature of manifestation along with their light. Indeed, one jar and another arise separately; it is consciousness alone that manifests in the form of objects such as jars accompanied by light. When this is so, there is no external example, because everything is merely the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of consciousness.

Thus, having sufficiently imagined that very consciousness to possess the form of the grasped and the grasper, they further imagine its purification. Some maintain that consciousness, being freed from the grasped and the grasper, remains as something momentary and translucent. Others desire even its cessation. Still other Mādhyamikas declare that even that consciousness—when conventionally free from the aspects of the grasped and the grasper—is merely empty, like external objects such as jars and the like.

All these conceptual constructions are opposed to this Vedic path to the highest good, because they deny the existence of the self-luminous light of the Self, which is distinct from the intellect and consciousness. In that regard, it is said to those for whom external objects exist: first of all, jars and the like do not possess the capacity to illuminate themselves.

An object such as a jar, while situated in darkness, is never manifested by its own nature; rather, it is observed to be invariably manifested through conjunction with light from a lamp or other source, such that one perceives "the jar is illuminated. Even though the jar and the light are in contact, they are indeed distinct, because their specific differences are perceived whenever they repeatedly come together and separate, just like a rope and a jar; and since they are distinct, there must be a separate illuminator; an object does not illuminate itself by its own self.

[Objection: But surely a lamp is seen illuminating itself—for people do not resort to another light to see a lamp as they do for a jar or similar objects; therefore, the lamp illuminates its own self. [Reply: No, because there is no difference in its being an object of illumination. Even though a lamp is the illuminator of other things by virtue of its own nature as light, it nevertheless does not escape being illuminated by a distinct consciousness, just like a jar or other such objects.

And since this is so, it follows that being manifested by something distinct is necessarily required. Now, one might object: just as a jar, despite being manifested by consciousness, requires a separate light, a lamp does not require another separate light.

Therefore, [the opponent argues] that although a lamp is illuminated by another, it illuminates both itself and the jar—[we reply: no, because there is no distinction whether [it is illuminated] by itself or by another. Just as the jar is illuminated by consciousness (*caitanya*), so too the lamp’s being illuminated by consciousness is indistinguishable. As for what is said—that the lamp illuminates both itself and the jar—that is incorrect. Why? Because when it does not illuminate itself, what would it be like [then]?

For at that time, no distinction whatsoever is perceived in the lamp, whether from its own side or from another's. Indeed, something becomes an object of illumination only when a distinction is perceived upon the presence or absence of an illuminator; for it is impossible to conceive of the presence or absence of the lamp's own self. And since there is no occasional distinction, the claim that "the lamp illuminates itself" is spoken falsely. Furthermore, the lamp's being graspable by consciousness is no different from that of jars and other such objects.

Therefore, a lamp is not a valid illustration for consciousness being both the grasped and the grasper. Furthermore, consciousness’s state of being graspable by sentience (*caitanya*) is no different from that of external objects; and since consciousness is graspable by sentience, while there remains doubt as to whether it is graspable only by a consciousness that is itself graspable or by a consciousness that is a grasper, it is proper to postulate that principle which has been observed elsewhere, and not one that contradicts what is observed.

And this being so, just as external lamps are seen to be objects of perception by a perceiver who is distinct from them, so too, since consciousness is perceived by sentience (*caitanya*), it is logical to assume—despite its own luminosity—that it is perceived by a distinct sentience, like a lamp, and not that it is perceived by nothing other than itself; and that which is the perceiver of consciousness is the Self, a light distinct from consciousness. If it is argued that this leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), we say no.

For it has been stated according to logic that the mere fact of being an object of cognition (*grāhyatva*) is the mark for the existence of another entity as its cognizer (*grāhaka*); however, no mark for its being exclusively a cognizer or for the existence of yet another cognizer of that cognizer ever arises. Therefore, there is no consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is argued that an infinite regress would follow because consciousness, if it were to have a distinct object of cognition, would require another instrument [of cognition], we say no, because there is no such restriction—indeed, this restriction does not apply in all cases.

Where one object is perceived by means of another object, it cannot be categorically maintained that there must be a separate instrument distinct from the grasped and the grasper, because of the observed diversity [of cases]. How so? A jar, for instance, is perceived by means of a self-nature distinct from its own; in that case, light such as a lamp is an instrument distinct from the grasped and the grasper. For light such as a lamp is neither a part of the jar nor a part of the eye.

Just as in the case of a lamp, even though it is perceptible by the eye like a jar, the eye does not require any other external instrument in the form of light apart from the lamp itself; therefore, it cannot be established as a rule that wherever there is perception of an object distinct [from the perceiver], there must necessarily be another instrument. Consequently, regarding consciousness being perceived by a distinct perceiver, neither an infinite regress via an instrument nor one via the status of being a perceiver can ever be established.

Therefore, it is established that there exists a distinct light of the Self (ātma-jyotis) separate from consciousness. Now, an objection may be raised: external objects such as jars or lamps do not exist at all apart from consciousness; for whatever is not perceived apart from something else is seen to be merely that [consciousness]—just as the objects such as jars and cloths grasped in a dream-consciousness.

Since objects such as the pot and lamp in a dream are not perceived apart from the dream-consciousness, it is understood that they consist of dream-consciousness alone; likewise, since objects such as the pot and lamp in the waking state are also not perceived apart from waking-consciousness, it is logical that they too consist of waking-consciousness alone. Therefore, there is no external object such as a pot or a lamp; rather, everything is consciousness alone.

In this regard, as for what was said—that because consciousness appears as something distinct [from itself], there exists another light separate from consciousness, just as in the case of a jar and so forth—that is false, because if everything were merely consciousness, there would be no example [to support it]. No, for you accept as much as is necessary—namely, that an external object is not absolutely denied by you.

[Objection: "But surely I do not accept this at all. [Reply: No; for as long as there is a distinctness between the word and its object—such as in the cases of "consciousness," "jar," and "lamp"—an external, separate object must necessarily be accepted. If a real entity distinct from consciousness is not accepted, then since words such as "consciousness," "jar," and "cloth" would have the same referent, they would result in being synonyms.

Likewise, if the means of proof (*sādhana*) and the result (*phala*) were one and the same, it would follow that the treatises teaching the distinction between the goal to be proven (*sādhya*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*) would be purposeless; or else, it would follow that their author lacks knowledge. Furthermore, because the disputant (*vādin*), the opponent (*prativādin*), the arguments, and the faults [of those arguments] are accepted as being distinct from consciousness (*vijñāna*); for it is not accepted that the debate between disputant and opponent, or its faults, consists of nothing but the self-consciousness (*ātmavijñāna*) alone, since the opponent and others must be refuted.

For it is not admitted that one's own consciousness is to be negated, nor that the self of anyone exists as such; for if that were the case, there would follow the consequence of the collapse of all worldly transactional activity. Nor is it admitted that opponents and others are apprehended by means of one's own self alone; rather, they are admitted to be objects of apprehension distinct [from the subject].

Therefore, by that same reasoning, every object of apprehension that is distinct [from consciousness] must be real, because it is an object of the waking state, just like the objects of the waking state such as things to be understood and so forth—an easily available analogy being "like another continuum" and "like another cognition. Consequently, even the Vijñānavādin is unable to refute the existence of a light distinct from cognition.

If it is argued that [the example of a dream] is inappropriate because there is no existence apart from consciousness (*vijñāna*), we say no; for even from non-existence, the status of being a distinct entity is established. You yourself have already admitted that the cognition of a jar and so forth in a dream possesses the nature of an existent thing (*bhāva*). Having admitted that, you then state that the non-existence of the jar and so forth is due to its separation from that [cognition]. Whether that jar and so forth, which is the object of the cognition, be non-existent or existent, in either case the cognition of the jar and so forth has indeed been admitted to possess the nature of an existent thing.

But that [emptiness] cannot be overturned, because there is no reasoning capable of overturning it. By this, the emptiness of everything is refuted. Furthermore, the Mīmāṃsaka position—that the self is graspable as the inner self through the notion "I"—is thereby refuted.

As for what was said—that a pot with light arises as one thing and [the same] pot arises as another—that is incorrect, because there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is that very same pot" even at a later moment. If it is argued that this recognition is due to similarity, as in the case of hair and nails that have been cut and grown back, we say no; for even in those cases, momentariness is unproven, and furthermore, the recognition is based on the identity of the genus (*jāti*). In the case of hair and nails that have been cut and grown back again, the cognition of them as "hair" or "nails" is caused by the oneness of the genus *keśatva* (hair-ness) or *nakhatva* (nail-ness), and is therefore not erroneous.

For indeed, in the case of hair, nails, and so forth that are seen to have been cut and grown back, there does not arise the cognition "this is that very same individual" based on its identity; rather, in the case of certain things seen after a long interval of time and which possess the same dimensions, there arises the cognition "these hair, nails, and so forth are similar to those from that time," but not the cognition "these are those very same ones. In the case of jars and the like, however, the cognition "this is that very same one" does arise. Therefore, the illustration is not equivalent.

For when an object is recognized through direct perception as being "that very same thing," it is not logical to infer its difference, since a logical mark (*liṅga*) that contradicts direct perception must be considered fallacious. Furthermore, the cognition of similarity is untenable because cognition is momentary; for a cognition of similarity could only arise in one who perceives a first object and subsequently perceives another object.

However, one who perceives an object does not remain for another moment in order to perceive another object, because consciousness is momentary and its cessation is established by the perception of the object occurring only once. For the cognition of similarity arises in the form, "This is similar to that"; in this, "that" is the recollection of what was seen, while "this" is the cognition of the present; "that" is the recollection of what was seen, and "this" is the cognition of the present.

If, having remembered "that," one were to persist until the present moment "this," then the doctrine of momentariness would be abandoned. Alternatively, if the memory-based cognition "that" is exhausted as soon as it arises, and the distinct present cognition "this" is likewise exhausted, then the cognition of similarity—"this is similar to that"—would be impossible, because there is no single observer who perceives multiple moments.

And there is the impossibility of verbal designation: since consciousness would be exhausted by the very act of seeing the object to be seen, such designations as "I see this" or "I saw that" would be impossible, because for one who has seen, the moment of designation does not persist. If, on the other hand, it were to persist, the doctrine of momentariness would be abandoned.

If, on the other hand, there were designation and the cognition of similarity for one who has not seen [the object], then, like a person blind from birth designating specific forms and having a cognition of their similarity, everything—including the composition of the scriptures of an omniscient being—would result in a mere "blind tradition" (*andhaparamparā*); and this is not accepted. Furthermore, the faults of "attaining what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and "the loss of what was done" (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*) are even more well-known in the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇavāda*).

If it is argued that the cause for the designation of "seen" is a single cognition—comprising both the preceding and succeeding moments—which arises like a chain, such that one says, "this is similar to that," we reply: no, because the present and the past belong to different times. In this case, the present cognition is one link of the chain, and the past is another; these two cognitions exist at distinct times.

If the cognition of a chain were to touch upon both those [adjacent] objects as its referents, then, because a single cognition would span two moments, the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇavāda*) would be lost. Furthermore, since distinctions such as "mine" and so forth would be untenable, there would follow the consequence of the collapse of all worldly transactional activity (*saṃvyavahāra*).

Moreover, if everything were merely self-cognizing consciousness (*svasaṃvedyavijñāna*), and given that consciousness is admitted to have the nature of being nothing but the manifestation of pure awareness, [the aforementioned faults would ensue].

Furthermore, in the absence of another who perceives it, the postulation of various attributes such as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self would be untenable. Nor can consciousness possess multiple contradictory parts like a pomegranate and so forth, because consciousness is by nature a clear manifestation. Moreover, if impermanence, suffering, and the rest were parts of consciousness, then because they are being experienced, it would follow that they are objects distinct from consciousness itself. If, on the other hand, consciousness were essentially identical with impermanence, suffering, and so forth, then the postulation of its purification through separation from those [attributes] would be impossible.

For purity arises from the separation from adventitious impurities, as in the case of mirrors and the like; however, the separation of anything from its inherent nature has never been observed. Indeed, no separation of fire from its inherent luminosity or heat has ever been seen. Even when the separation of qualities such as redness from flowers is observed through contact with another substance, it is inferred that this too was preceded by a conjunction—since we observe the production of different qualities in flowers, fruits, and so forth, through the cultivation of the seed.

Therefore, the conceptualization of the purification of consciousness is untenable. Furthermore, that impurity which is imagined to belong to consciousness by virtue of its appearing as object and subject is also untenable, because there is no association with anything else; for there can be no association of an existing thing with something non-existent. And when there is no association with another, whatever property is observed in a thing cannot be separated from it, because it is of the very nature of that thing—just as heat belongs to fire, or radiance to the sun.

Therefore, it is understood that this conception—that consciousness (*vijñāna*) becomes defiled through association with the impermanent and that its purification occurs—is merely a blind tradition, devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, regarding their conception that the *nirvāṇa* of that consciousness is the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*), there too the impossibility of a locus for the fruit [of action] arises; for the fruit is the cessation of the pain produced by being pierced by a thorn for one who has been pierced by a thorn, but when one pierced by a thorn dies, a locus for the fruit of that cessation of pain is not possible.

Likewise, if all [entities] have ceased and there is no substratum for the fruit, the postulation of a "human goal" (puruṣārtha) is utterly futile. For when the goal is postulated for that being, self, or consciousness denoted by the word "person," once that person has entered nirvāṇa, for whom would there be a human goal? What would it belong to?

Furthermore, for one who maintains that there exists a self distinct from consciousness which perceives multiple objects, everything is logically consistent: namely, the seeing of what was seen, the recollection [of it], and the conjunction with or separation from suffering and so forth. Impurity is caused by conjunction with another, and purification is caused by separation from that. However, as the position of the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) is contradicted by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), no effort is made here to refute it.

They gave it to him. These five and those other five, being ten, constitute the *kṛta* throw; therefore, food indeed exists in all directions as the *daśakṛta*. This is that Virāj, the eater of food; by her everything is seen. Everything here becomes seen by him who knows this; he becomes an eater of food—yea, he who knows this, yea, who knows this. Thus ends the third section. 3. (8)

Just as here, having become a dream within this single body, one transcends the forms of death—the organs and their functions—and abides in the dream state within one's own self-luminosity (*ātma-jyotis*), even so does that aforementioned person, while being born—how is he said to be born?—attaining the body, which is the aggregate of the physical frame and the senses; the meaning is that he assumes the state of the self within the body; he becomes united with "evils," meaning with the effects and instruments consisting of merit and demerit which are the substrata of evil.

He is joined [to them]; that very same one, "departing"—that is, departing upward, going, dying—is explained by the word "departing. He abandons those very things which are conjoined with him, characterized as effects and instruments, consisting of the nature of evil; he becomes disjoined from them, he relinquishes them.

Just as this [self], being identical with the intellect (*dhi*), incessantly migrates within a single body during the states of dreaming and waking by means of the assumption and abandonment of the instruments of action consisting of sin, so too does this person incessantly undergo the assumption and abandonment of the instruments of action through birth and death in both this world and the next, migrating until liberation from *saṃsāra*.

Therefore, it is established that this light of the Self is distinct from the evils consisting of the body and the organs, on account of its conjunction with and separation from them; for if it were of the nature of those very things, its conjunction with or separation from them would not be logical.

Now, one might object: "This Self does not possess both worlds, through which it moves sequentially by means of birth and death, as it does in sleep and waking; for while sleep and waking are perceived directly, the worlds of this life and the next are not apprehended by any means of valid knowledge. Therefore, these two—sleep and waking—are themselves the worlds of this life and the next. To this it is replied: (9) ————

For this very person, there are indeed these two stations, neither a third nor a fourth. Which are they? This one which is entered—the present birth, characterized by body, senses, objects, and sensations—which is experienced through direct perception; and the station of the other world (*paraloka-sthāna*), which is to be experienced at a time subsequent to the separation from the body and so forth. [Objection: But is not even a dream the other world? If that were so, the restriction "only two" would be incorrect. [Reply: No.

How then [is it]? It is "intermediate" (*saṃdhya*). That which exists in the junction (*saṃdhi*) between this world and the next world is "intermediate. That which is the third is the state of dreaming; by that, the restriction to two states is established. For the junction between two villages does not deserve to be counted as a third in relation to those very two villages.

How, moreover, is the existence of that state belonging to the other world understood, in relation to which the dream state would be the intermediate one—since, while staying, being, and existing in that intermediate dream state, he perceives these two states? Which two? This world and the world belonging to the other world. Therefore, both worlds exist apart from the dream and waking states, which he, being common to both, traverses by means of his intellect through the continuous succession of birth and death.

But how, while situated in a dream, does one see both worlds—what is the basis, and by what method? This is being explained: now listen as to how he sees. "Yathākrama" means that by which one ascends (ākrāmati); it is the basis (āśraya), meaning the support. "Yathākrama" refers to whatever kind of basis this person has. The meaning is: when the occasion for proceeding to the world beyond arises, this person possesses such a basis—that is, he is endowed with the means for proceeding to the other world, characterized by knowledge, action, and prior cognition.

Having stepped upon—that is, having seized and relied upon—that state which is oriented toward the world beyond, like a seed that has reached the stage of sprouting, he perceives both. (The plural number is used because the fruits of dharma and adharma are manifold. "Both" means those of both kinds.

Which ones? "Evils" means the fruits of evil deeds—not that the direct perception of evils themselves is possible, but rather that the meaning is the sufferings which are the fruits of evil—and "blisses," meaning the pleasures which are the fruits of merit. He perceives both these evils and blisses, consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from experiences in other births; and he also perceives those minor fruits of merit and demerit pertaining to the birth he is about to enter, either through the grace of the deities impelled by his merit and demerit.

How, then, is it understood that there is a perception of the bliss of those sins while one is situated in the other world during a dream? It is said in response: because in this life one sees many things that are not experienced [in waking], and a dream is not indeed a perception of something entirely new; for a dream is generally a memory of what was previously seen. Therefore, both worlds exist as distinct from the states of dreaming and waking.

It has been stated that in the absence of external lights such as the sun, this person—the aggregate of causes and effects—performs its functions by means of a distinct self that serves as light. However, that very thing does not exist: namely, the reaching of a state where the lights of the sun and so forth are absent, wherein this self-luminous [self] might be perceived in its isolation; for this aggregate of causes and effects is always perceived only as being in conjunction with them.

Therefore, it is either equal to the non-existent or simply non-existent by its own distinct nature as light, which is the Self. Now, if it were perceived anywhere as distinct by its own nature of light, devoid of contact with external or internal elements and elemental products, then all that has been stated would be realized; for this purpose, he says: "He"—the Self under discussion—"where," at which time, "sleeps," meaning he experiences deep sleep.

It is now explained: with what substratum and by what process does he sleep, and how does he attain the intermediate state? Of this "seen world," characterized by waking—this "all-encompassing" (sarvāvan) world, so called because it encompasses everything—is the aggregate of causes and effects, joined with objects and sensations.

Its "possessing all" (*sarvāvattva*) has been explained in the section on the three kinds of food, beginning with the words, "Now, this self indeed..."—meaning that it possesses all the elements (*mātrā*) of the primary and secondary constituents of existence (*bhūta-bhautika*), which serve as the causes for its conjunction; thus it is "all-possessing" (*sarvavān*), and being all-possessing, it is "all-encompassing" (*sarvāvān*). Having taken—that is, having cut off and seized—a portion (*mātrām*), a single part or limb (*ekadeśam*, *avayavam*) of that all-encompassing one; the meaning is: being permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the present life; having himself, by his own self, struck down—that is, caused the body to fall.

Having brought about a state devoid of awakening— for in the waking state, the favor shown by the sun and other luminaries toward the eyes and other senses is for the sake of the body's worldly activity, and that bodily activity is impelled by the self’s experience of the fruits of merit and demerit; since the cessation of that experience of the fruits of merit and demerit within this body is caused by the cessation of the self’s karma, the self is said to be "the destroyer" (vihantṛ) of this [body]. Having itself fashioned—that is, having created—a dream-body consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which is like an illusion (*māyāmayam*), even that creation is dependent upon its own karma.

It is said to have itself as its agent (*svayaṃkartṛka*): by its own light (*bhāsā*), that is, by its own radiance (*dīpti*) or manifestation (*prakāśa*), characterized by the mere appropriation of the Self; the meaning is: by the manifestation of the activity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) consisting of all latent impressions (*vāsanā*). For that [internal organ], consisting of all latent impressions, shines there as the object; thus, it is called "its own light" (*svayaṃ bhā*) there. By that light of its own which has become the object, and by its own light as the subject—which possesses a distinct form and whose nature is unimpaired vision—that [Self] exists in the form of that [object].

Taking that which consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as its object, it dreams. This very process of occurring is what is called "dreaming. In this state, at this time, this person—the Self—becomes a light unto itself; it becomes a light devoid of contact with external or internal elements and elemental products. But surely, only a measure of this world was taken up [as an object]; how then can it be said that while that exists, this person here becomes a light unto itself? This is not a fault.

For that [dream state] is indeed an object; and by means of that very object, this person can here be shown to be self-luminous, but not otherwise when no object exists, as in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*). When, however, that state consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) becomes an object and is perceived, then—like a sword drawn from its scabbard—the Self-luminosity of the soul, whose nature is free from all contact and distinct from the eyes and other instruments of action, being unimpaired vision, is apprehended as it shines forth in its own form.
Thus it is established that "in this state, this person is self-luminous."

Now, how can the person (*puruṣa*) here be self-luminous (*svayaṃjyotis*), given that all worldly activity characterized by the grasped and the grasper is seen just as it is in the waking state, and the lights of the sun and so forth—which assist the eyes and other senses—are likewise seen just as they are in the waking state? In that case, how can this distinction be determined?

"In this state, this person becomes self-luminous. It is said: because of the difference from the perception of dreams. For in the waking state, the light of the Self is intermingled with the operations of the senses, the intellect, the mind, and external light; but here in dream, due to the absence of the senses and the absence of the light of the sun and so forth that assist them, it becomes distinct and isolated. Therefore, it is different. [Objection: But objects are perceived in dream just as they are in the waking state;
how then can it be said that there is a difference due to the absence of the senses? Listen: (10) ————-

In that state, there are no objects characterized by chariots and the like; likewise, there are no "chariot-yokes"—that is, horses and so forth, which are yoked to chariots—and there are no paths, which are the tracks for chariots. Yet, he himself creates chariots, chariot-yokes, and paths. But how can he create these means, such as chariots, in the absence of trees and other materials?

It is said: But has it not been stated, "Having taken a measure (mātrā) from this entire world, having himself struck it out, having himself fashioned it"? The "measure" of this world is the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*), which is its latent impression (*vāsanā*). Having taken that, the modification of the internal organ in the form of impressions of chariots and so forth—being impelled by karma, which is the cause for the perception thereof—stands forth as an object of sight. To this it is replied: "having himself fashioned it"; he says that very thing: "he creates chariots and the like."

But there, neither the instruments of perception, nor the lights such as the sun that assist those instruments, nor the objects such as chariots illuminated by them exist; rather, only their mere impressions (vāsanā) are seen, supported by a modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) aroused and impelled by the karma of perceiving those [objects]. That light of which this is seen, whose vision is unimpaired—that is the light of the Self (ātmajyotis), which here appears entirely distinct, like a sword drawn from its scabbard.

Likewise, there are no joys (*ānanda*)—that is, specific pleasures—nor delights (*muda*), which are joys caused by the acquisition of sons and so forth, nor raptures (*pramuda*), which are those same joys intensified; yet he creates these joys and the rest. Similarly, there are no pools (*veśānta*), ponds (*puṣkariṇī*), lakes (*taḍāga*), or flowing rivers (*sravantī*) there; yet he creates these pools and the rest, existing merely as mental impressions (*vāsanā*). For he is indeed the creator.

We have stated that its agency consists in its being the cause of karma, which is the motive for the arising of mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*) that serve as the substratum for those latent impressions (*vāsanā*); however, action does not occur there directly, because of the absence of means. For action is not possible without a causal factor (*kāraka*), and in that state, instruments of action such as hands and feet do not exist.

But where those [organs] exist, as in the waking state, there action is accomplished by means of the body and instruments illumined by the light of the Self, for the purpose of giving rise to the functions of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which rests upon the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the chariot and so forth; therefore it is said, "He indeed is the agent"; thus it has been stated: "By the light of the Self alone, he sits, moves about, and performs actions."

Even in that case, agency does not belong to the light of consciousness (*caitanyajyotiḥ*) in an ultimate sense by virtue of its own nature, apart from its character as an illuminator—that is to say, when it illuminates the organs and the body through the medium of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) by means of the light of the conscious self, those organs and body, being thus illuminated, become active in their respective functions; it is in this context that agency is figuratively attributed to the Self. What was stated in the passage, "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were," is here reiterated for the purpose of providing a reason: "For it is the agent. (11)

Regarding this—on the subject thus stated, there are these verses, which are mantras: "By means of sleep"—that is, by the state of dreaming—"having struck down the body," having rendered the physical frame motionless, "he who is not asleep"—because his own nature consists of unimpaired powers such as sight and so forth—"beholds" (abhicākaśīti); that is, he sees with his unimpaired self-vision, illuminating all things—both external and internal—which have arisen in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which reside in the functions of the internal organ, and which, though asleep, have been dissolved into their own nature. This is the meaning.

Having taken—that is, having grasped—the pure, luminous semen (*śukra*), which consists of the subtle elements (*indriyamātra*) and form, the golden one—meaning one whose nature is the light of consciousness like gold—the Person (*puruṣa*), the "Single Swan" (*ekahaṃsa*)—so called because he alone goes (*hanti*), or because as the One he travels through the waking state, the dream state, this world, the next world, and so forth—returns again to the place of waking for the sake of action.

Likewise, by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) with its fivefold functions, protecting—that is, preserving—[the body], lest there be the delusion that it is dead; [he goes] to the inferior, lowly nest, which is the body because it is a collection of many impurities and is utterly loathsome; but he himself, having moved outside of that nest—although one sees dreams while remaining within the body, nevertheless, because of the lack of connection with it, he is said to have "moved outside," like space situated within [a vessel]—being immortal, having the nature of immortality himself, he goes (*īyate*).

"Wherever there is desire"—wherever desire arises toward objects, he goes toward that very desire as it has arisen in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*). (13) Furthermore, "in the midst of sleep," that is, in the state of dreaming, he experiences "high and low"—the high being the state of gods and so forth, and the low being the base state of animals and so forth; this is what is meant by "high and low."

Moving, being traversed, and reaching—this radiant deity (*deva*), possessing the power of illumination, brings about or manifests numerous, incalculable forms of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Moreover, as if rejoicing with women, as if laughing with companions, and even as if beholding terrors—terrors being those from which one fears, such as lions, tigers, and the like—he appears as if seeing them.

All people see the garden, the pleasure-ground, and the playground fashioned by this [Self] in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā)—that is, the form of a playground fashioned from impressions such as village, city, woman, food, and so forth; yet they do not see it, for no one sees it.

"Alas! It exists, utterly secluded, even though it has come within the range of vision—oh, the misfortune of the world, that it does not perceive itself, though it is capable of being seen! Thus the Śruti shows compassion toward the world. The intention is that the Self, which is self-luminous, becomes utterly secluded during the dream state. Regarding this, they say, "One should not wake a sleeping person"—a common saying also exists in the world concerning the distinctness of the light of the Self in the dream state.

Who is this [person]? Physicians and others in the world say thus: "One should not suddenly and violently awaken that sleeping person who is stretched out. They surely perceive that [the self], having withdrawn from the waking body through the doors of the senses, exists externally in its isolated state; for this reason they say, "One should not awaken him while he is stretched out."

And they perceive a fault in that: for when he is being strongly awakened—that is, when those doors of the senses are suddenly being roused—he does not comprehend it. This is what is meant by the statement: "It becomes difficult to treat him for whom he does not comprehend."

That region of the sense-organ from which [the vital essence] was taken and departed—that very region of the sense-organ this self does not regain. Sometimes, by way of transposition, it causes the mere sense-faculties to enter; then, upon the occurrence of defects such as blindness or deafness, there arises for this body a state of being difficult to treat—a condition where medical treatment is painful. The meaning is that this body becomes one that can only be cured with great difficulty.

Therefore, even by common experience, its self-luminosity is understood in the dream state. "Having become a dreamer, he transcends mortal forms"—therefore, in the dream, the Self is its own light. Now, moreover, others say: "This dream is merely the waking state for him; it is not an intermediate place distinct from this world and the next world. Rather, it is this very world, the waking state."

If this is so, what follows from it? Listen to what follows: when this dream occurs in the very same place as the waking state, then this Self has not withdrawn from the body and its organs but is mixed with them; therefore, the Self is not self-luminous. For this reason, others, in order to refute its self-luminosity, say: "This [dream] of his occurs in the very place of the waking state."

In this regard, they do not state a reason—namely, that because a person in the waking state perceives various objects such as elephants while awake in the waking place, he perceives those very same things even when asleep. That is incorrect, because of the cessation of the sense organs; for one perceives dreams only when the sense organs have ceased their activity. Therefore, there is no possibility of any other light existing there. Thus it has been said: "There are no chariots there, nor are there draft animals," and so forth.

Therefore, in this state, this person is indeed self-luminous. By means of the illustration of dream, it has been demonstrated that the Self is self-luminous, and that "it transcends the forms of death. Furthermore, as it moves sequentially through this world, the other world, and so forth, it is shown by Yājñavalkya to be distinct from this world and the other world; likewise, it is distinct from the two nests of waking and dreaming, and because of its sequential movement therein, it is eternal. Thus has it been established.

Therefore, Janaka said, "I give you a thousand [cows] as the fee for this knowledge. [Yājñavalkya replied: "Thus enlightened by you, I give a thousand to you, O Blessed One. Furthermore, liberation (*vimokṣa*) through the inquiry into all desires (*kāmapraśna*) is what I intend. This [gift of a thousand] is useful for that purpose, being but a single part of it. Therefore, I shall appoint you to hear the resolution of the entire inquiry into all desires—for the sake of liberation—by saying, 'Speak further from hereon so that, through your grace, I may be completely liberated from transmigratory existence.
The gift of a thousand is for the purpose of resolving even a single portion of the subject matter of liberation."

That which was introduced—"by its own light, this one sits"—has been established through direct perception by the statement, "In this state, this person becomes self-luminous," namely, in the dream state. As for what was said—"Having become a dream, he transcends this world and the forms of death"—therein this doubt arises: he transcends only the forms of death, not death itself; for it is directly perceived that even when one is withdrawn from the body and the senses in a dream, there is still the observation of joy, fear, and so forth.

Therefore, it is certain that this [individual] does not transcend death; for the effects of death, such as joy and fear, are observed to arise from karma. Moreover, if this person were by nature bound by death, then liberation would be impossible; indeed, no one is liberated from their own nature. However, if death is not one's inherent nature, then liberation from it is possible.

In order to demonstrate how that death is not one's own inherent nature (*ātman*), Yājñavalkya— having been questioned by Janaka with the words, "Speak further for the sake of liberation"— proceeded with the desire to reveal that [truth]:

(15) "That very person who is the subject under discussion, the self-luminous (*svayaṃjyotis*) Puruṣa, who was shown in the state of dreaming— in this state of perfect serenity (*saṃprasāda*)," [meaning] "in which he becomes perfectly serene."

It is *saṃprasāda* (perfect serenity). Having abandoned the turbidity born from the collision of hundreds of activities of the body and senses during the waking state, one becomes slightly serene in the dream state; but here, in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), one becomes perfectly serene—therefore, deep sleep is called *saṃprasāda*. For he will say of the Self abiding in deep sleep: "For then he has crossed over all sorrows" and "he is the one seer in the waters. Indeed, this very Self, having become serene through the gradual process, remains in deep sleep within that *saṃprasāda*.

How is it "serene"? Being about to enter deep sleep from the state of dreaming, it remains in deep sleep. How is it serene? While still in the state of dreaming and desiring to enter deep sleep, it has "enjoyed"—that is, experienced pleasure—by seeing friends, kinsmen, and so forth; it has "roamed," meaning it has moved about in various ways, experiencing the exhaustion that is the fruit of such wandering; the sense is that it has merely *seen* merit and its fruit, and sin and its fruit, rather than having actually *performed* them.

However, we have already stated that there is no direct perception of merit and demerit; therefore, one is not bound by merit and demerit. For he who performs meritorious and demeritorious deeds is bound by them; one cannot be bound by them through mere perception. Therefore, having become a dream, it truly transcends death, and not merely the forms of death. Consequently, there is no suspicion that death is the essential nature of the Self; if death were its essential nature, it would manifest even in a dream, but it does not.

If action were its inherent nature (*svabhāva*), there would be no liberation at all; however, it is not its inherent nature, because [action] is absent in a dream, and therefore its liberation from death through merit and demerit is possible. [Objection: But in the waking state, this [self] has action as its very nature. [Reply: No; for that is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*). And this has been established through the analogy [of the scripture]: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were. Therefore, since death is transcended in the dream state in an absolute sense, there is neither the suspicion of it being inherent nor the possibility of non-liberation.

In this context, "having moved" (*caritvā*) means having experienced the exhaustion that is the fruit of moving. Then, after the experience of the state of perfect serenity (*saṃprasāda*), [the soul returns] "back again according to the rule" (*pratinyāyam*); that is, according to the rule (*nyāya*) as it came—where "rule" (*nyāya*) is a certain way (*niścita āyaḥ*). "Way" (*āya*) is a path (*ayana*), meaning a departure. "Back again according to the rule" (*pratinyāya*) refers to the coming back in the reverse order of the previous departure—that is, it returns just as it came. "To its respective place" (*pratiyoni*) means to its corresponding location.

For having departed from the state of dreaming and entered into deep sleep, one returns again to one's very own place—one rushes back to the respective source, namely to the state of dreaming itself, to the place of dreaming itself.

Now, one might ask: "How is it known that in a dream one does not perform merit or demerit, but merely perceives their fruit? For just as in the waking state, one certainly acts even in a dream, since the act of perception is the same in both cases? To this he says: That Self, whatever fruit of merit or demerit it perceives there in the dream, remains unattached (*ananvāgata*)—that is, unbound—by what was seen; it is not at all bound by it. For if indeed something were performed by it in the dream, it would be bound by that.

Even upon waking from a dream, one would be possessed [of the results of that action]; yet such is not the case in the world—there is no established recognition of being possessed by karma performed in a dream. For no one considers themselves a wrongdoer on account of a transgression committed in a dream; nor does the world, having heard of a transgression by a dreamer, censure or avoid them. Therefore, one is indeed not possessed by it; thus, while it is perceived as if one were acting in a dream, there is in reality no action.

The verse beginning with "As if rejoicing together with women" has been stated; and those who report a dream speak using the word "as if"—saying, for example, "I saw elephants today turned into water-jars as if they were running. Therefore, he has no agency. But how is it that he lacks agency? Contact with material effects and instruments is observed to be the cause of action, and that contact belongs to something material; for nothing immaterial is ever seen to possess action. And the Self is immaterial; therefore, [the objection] is groundless.

And because this person is unattached, he is not followed by what was seen in the dream; for that very reason, his status as an agent of action is in no way possible, since agency would exist only through connection with the body and the senses. That connection is attachment, and he has no such attachment, because "this person is indeed unattached"; therefore, he is immortal. "It is exactly so, Yājñavalkya; I give you a thousand [cows], O Blessed One. Speak further only for the sake of liberation."

Because the discernment of action (*karmapraviveka*), which is one part of the category of liberation (*mokṣapadārtha*), has been correctly shown; therefore, [the request is made: "Speak further for the sake of liberation alone.

(16) In that regard, in the statement "For this person (*puruṣa*) is indeed unattached," non-attachment was stated as the reason for non-agency (*akartṛtva*). And it was stated previously: "By the power of karma, he goes wherever he desires"; and desire (*kāma*) is attachment (*saṅga*). Therefore, the reason stated—"For this person is indeed unattached"—is unestablished (*asiddha*). But this is not so.

How then [is it]? It is said that he is indeed unattached—this very person, having returned from the state of serene bliss (*saṃprasāda*) to the dream state, having enjoyed himself and wandered according to his desire, and having seen both merit and evil—all this is as explained before; [he goes] only to the waking state, the place of consciousness. Therefore, this person is indeed unattached; for if he were attached in the dream state, being full of desire, then upon returning to the waking state he would be stained by the defects born of that attachment.

Just as that person, because of his non-attachment (*asaṅga*), is not tainted by the defects arising from the dream-state upon returning to the waking state, even so he is not tainted at all by the defects arising from attachment to the waking state when he reaches the end of the dream (*buddhānta*). This is what is being said: (17) "He indeed, having enjoyed and moved about in this waking state at the end of the dream," and so forth, as before. Whatever he sees there at the end of the dream, he remains untouched (*ananvāgata*) by it—for this person is indeed unattached (*asaṅga*). But how is it determined that he merely sees [and does not act]? For he performs both merit and demerit there.

And he does not perceive that fruit [of action], because agency is established through the Self's nature as the illuminator of the agent. By such passages as "By the light of the Self alone he sits," the aggregate of the body and the organs, illuminated by the light of the Self, performs worldly activity; therefore, its agency is figuratively attributed [to the Self], but there is no agency in itself. Thus it has been said: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were"—this is caused solely by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect, and not by itself.

In this context, however, with reference to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), he is said to be independent of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—namely, "having merely seen merit and demerit, and not having performed them. Therefore, there is no suspicion of contradiction between what precedes and what follows, because from the standpoint of the ultimate reality, being devoid of adjuncts, he does nothing and is not tainted by the fruit of action. And thus it was said by the Blessed One: "O son of Kuntī, because it is beginningless and devoid of qualities, this immutable Supreme Self, even though dwelling in the body, neither acts nor is tainted."

Likewise, the gift of a thousand [cows] is mentioned because the seclusion from desire has been demonstrated. Furthermore, by these two sections—"In this dream state indeed he becomes unattached"—and "In this waking state indeed he becomes unattached," non-attachment itself is established; for since one who has gone to the end of sleep, being serene, becomes unattached due to the non-perception of actions such as theft performed during the waking state, therefore in all three states this Self is inherently unattached. Consequently, it is immortal, being distinct from the characteristics of the three states.

"He runs back to his source for the sake of the end of dream," meaning for the sake of the state of serene composure (*saṃprasāda*). This is because we see that the word "dream" is used here to denote the state of dreaming as a mode of perception, and because the qualification by the word "end" is appropriate; furthermore, the text will later indicate deep sleep with the words, "He runs toward this end."

If, however, it is argued that because of the statement, "Having enjoyed and moved about in the state of dream," and because of the observation, "He moves between these two ends, the state of dream and the state of waking," the word "dream" in the phrase "for the sake of the state of dream" refers simply to the occurrence of seeing—then even so, nothing is wrong; for the very non-attachment one wishes to establish is indeed proven, since having seen both merit and evil while awake, and having enjoyed and moved about, he comes to the state of dream and does not remain followed by the defects of the waking state.

Thus, this person—the Self—is self-luminous and distinct from the body and the organs, and distinct from desire and action which impel them; because "this person is indeed unattached," and because of that lack of attachment—this meaning has been established by these three sections beginning with "Verily, he is in this state of serene bliss."

In this regard, how is the very non-attachment of the Self established? Because one goes from the waking state to dreaming, from dreaming to deep sleep (*saṃprasāda*), and from deep sleep back again to dreaming; and in sequence, from the waking state to the waking state after having been in the dream state—thus, by moving through this successive order, the distinction of the three states has been proven.

This matter was already introduced previously in the passage, "Becoming a dream, he transcends this world and the forms of death"; having explained that in detail, only the illustration remains, and it is now commenced with the words, "I shall state that" (18).

In this regard, with respect to the meaning thus demonstrated, this illustration is adduced: just as in the world a great fish—one that is both large and a fish—cannot be carried away by the river current (meaning it is not swept away by the flow), and yet it obstructs the current, moving according to its own will, and traverses both banks of the river, the eastern and the western, in succession.

Even while moving between the two banks, one who stays in the middle is rendered subject to the power of the current of the water; in exactly the same way, this person moves back and forth between these two extremes. Which two? The state of dream and the state of waking. The purpose of showing this illustration, however, is that the aggregate of the body and the organs—which is of the nature of death—is not a property of the Self, being driven by desire and action; and this Self is distinct from that—this has been explained in detail.

And here, by means of the transition through the three states, the distinctness of the self-luminous Self—which is separate from the aggregate of effects and instruments—from desire and action has been stated; thus, the collective meaning has been declared that this [Self] is not inherently possessed of the attributes of transmigratory existence, but its state of being a transmigrator is caused solely by limiting adjuncts and is superimposed by ignorance.

And in that regard, the three states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep have been described in a scattered manner, rather than being shown collectively in one place—because in the waking state, the Self is perceived through ignorance as being associated with attachment, subject to death, and joined with the aggregate of causes and effects (the body and organs); whereas in the dreaming state, it is perceived as being joined with desire yet free from the form of death; and furthermore, in deep sleep, it becomes serene and unattached, so that its state of non-attachment is also observed.

However, since the fruit being summarized through syntactic unity—that its nature is eternally free, awakened, and pure—has not been shown by gathering it together in one place, this section (*kaṇḍikā*) is commenced to demonstrate that. For such a state of his is described in deep sleep [in the words]: "Now, this is his form which is beyond desire, free from evil, and fearless. Since he wishes to enter deep sleep, which is of such a distinct nature, [the author] asks:
"How so? and says: "The meaning of this matter becomes clear through an illustration"; thus, an illustration is introduced there: (19) ————

It is as follows: in this material space, either a hawk or a "suparṇa"—by the word *suparṇa*, a swift hawk is meant—having flown about and soared in this space, becomes weary, exhausted by the activity characterized by various modes of flight; then, having folded its wings together, having brought them into contact, having fully extended its wings, [it rests]. Completely...

It is called *saṃlaya* because one merges (*līyate*) into it; it is the nest (*nīḍa*). "For the sake of the nest" means it is supported by its own self, held up by itself. Just as this illustration [of the bird], even so this person runs toward that end. This is an epithet of what is expressed by the word "end": in which end, when asleep, he desires no desire whatsoever, nor does he see any dream whatsoever.

By the phrase "no desire whatsoever," every desire is prohibited without distinction between the states of dreaming and waking, because the term "any" (kaṃcana) is used without qualification. Likewise, regarding the phrase "no dream whatsoever"—the Śruti considers even that which is seen in the waking state to be a dream; therefore, it says, "he sees no dream whatsoever. And so another Śruti passage states: "He has three abodes and three dreams."

Just as in the illustration, a bird retreats to its own nest to dispel the fatigue born of flying about, so too for one who is joined with the fruits of actions arising from the union of the body and the senses during the waking and dreaming states, there occurs a fatigue similar to that of a bird’s flight; to dispel that fatigue, he enters his own self—the nest and abode of his own being—which is distinct from all the attributes of transmigratory existence and devoid of the exertion of all actions, instruments, and their results.

If this is its intrinsic nature—namely, the emptiness of all phenomena of saṃsāra—and its state of possessing the characteristics of saṃsāra is caused by external conditions; and if that which causes its state of possessing the characteristics of saṃsāra through external conditions is ignorance (*avidyā*)—then is that ignorance intrinsic, or is it adventitious like desire, karma, and so forth? If it is adventitious, then liberation is possible.

And what is the justification for its adventitious nature, or how is it that ignorance (*avidyā*) is not an inherent attribute of the Self? To determine the true nature of ignorance, which is the seed of all misfortune, the following section is commenced: (20) Indeed, these channels called *hitā* belong to this person characterized by a head, hands, and so forth; they exist with a subtlety and minuteness such that a single hair split a thousandfold would have that same dimension. And they carry white, blue, brown, green, and red fluids.

"Full" means full with these specific qualities of taste, such as sweetness and so forth. Furthermore, these specific colors of the tastes become manifold and diverse due to the particular variations in the mutual combinations and imbalances of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman). Within such subtle channels—measured like the split tip of a thousand hairs, filled with tastes such as the white and others, and pervading the entire body—the seventeen-fold subtle body (liṅga) resides.

All latent impressions (*vāsanā*) resting upon that [subtle body] are produced by the experience of the various phenomena of saṃsāra, high and low. That subtle body, the substratum of the impressions, being translucent due to its subtlety—resembling a crystal gem—is manifested through specific impressions in the forms of women, chariots, elephants, and so forth, owing to its contact with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the essence circulating in the channels (*nāḍī*), and by virtue of the particular modifications (*vṛtti-viśeṣa*) aroused and impelled by merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*).

Now, this being so, when at any time certain enemies or other thieves come and kill me—this notion, which arises from the cause of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and is called ignorance (*avidyā*), is born as a mere falsehood. This is what is meant by the statement: "They seem to kill this dreamer," or likewise, "they seem to conquer him" or "seem to subjugate him. No one at all kills him, nor do they subjugate him; it is merely a delusion caused by the emergence of the latent impressions of ignorance.

Likewise, it means that an elephant, as it were, eclipses him, obscures him, and drives him away, or makes him run; he falls, as it were, into a pit—meaning he perceives himself as falling into something like a dilapidated well. For such a false latent impression (vāsanā) arises within him, which is extremely base, rooted in a mental modification (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) illuminated by unrighteousness (adharma), because it consists of suffering.

In short, whatever fear characterized by elephants and so forth one perceives while awake, that very form of fear is here—in this dream—conceived as false through the arising of the latent impressions of ignorance, even though there is no actual elephant or such object of fear.

Furthermore, regarding the question of what is the object and what is the characteristic of ignorance when it is being diminished and knowledge when it is being increased—it is said: "Moreover, at which time [does this occur]? When, like a god, one becomes oneself—that is, when knowledge having the deity as its object has arisen during the waking state—then, by means of that arisen latent impression (vāsanā), one considers oneself to be like a god.

This is stated even with respect to a dream: like a god, like a king established in his kingdom and consecrated, one who is permeated by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of royalty thinks, "I am the king," even in a dream. In the same way, when ignorance has been utterly destroyed and knowledge regarding the Self of all has arisen, then—even in a dream—one who is steeped in that state thinks, "I alone am all this. That state of being the Self of all is the supreme world of this Self, its supreme, innate nature as the Self.

However, that state in which even as much as the tip of a hair is perceived as something other than the state of being the Self of all—namely, "I am not"—is ignorance (*avidyā*). Those worlds consisting of non-self (*anātman*) which are presented by that ignorance are inferior, extending down to the level of stationary objects. In comparison with those worlds that are the objects of conventional usage, this state of being the Self of all is complete, without interior or exterior; that is his supreme world.

Therefore, when ignorance is being withdrawn and knowledge has reached its culmination, liberation is the state of being the Self of all; the meaning is that the fruit of knowledge is perceived just as self-luminosity is directly perceived in a dream. Likewise, when ignorance is being intensified and knowledge is being obscured, the fruit of ignorance is perceived through direct experience itself—as in the passage: "Now, where they seem to strike him, as it were, or seem to overcome him, as it were."

These two are the effects of knowledge and ignorance: the state of being the Self of all and the state of having a limited self. Through pure knowledge one becomes the Self of all; through ignorance one becomes non-universal. One becomes differentiated from something else; because one is differentiated from that, one comes into conflict with it; and due to this conflict, one is killed, conquered, and cut down. This occurs because there is a state of non-universality and division; but when one is the whole, how could one be divided so as to come into conflict?

In the absence of contradiction, by what could one be slain, conquered, or cut down? Therefore, this true nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) has been stated: it causes that which is the Self of all to be perceived as not the Self of all; it presents as present another non-existent entity distinct from the Self; and it renders the Self incomplete. From that arises desire for that object; from desire, one undergoes division; from that, one undertakes action; and from that, the fruit—this is what has been explained.

And that which will be stated later—"For where there is, as it were, duality, there one sees another," and so forth—this true nature of ignorance has been shown along with its effect; and the effect of knowledge, which is the state of being the Self of all, has been shown by way of the reversal of ignorance.

Furthermore, that ignorance is not an inherent attribute of the Self—for as knowledge increases, ignorance itself diminishes, and when knowledge reaches its culmination in the state of universal selfhood, ignorance ceases entirely, just as the cognition of a snake in a rope vanishes upon the certain determination of the rope.
