And this has been stated: "But where everything has become the Self alone for him, then by what and whom should he see? and so forth. Therefore, ignorance is not an attribute of the Self.
For the destruction of that which is inherent in its own nature is never possible, just as heat and light are inseparable from the sun. Therefore, liberation is logically possible for it.

(21) Now, this state of being the Self of all, which is liberation—the fruit of knowledge devoid of the fruits of action, agent, and object—is pointed out through direct perception, wherein ignorance, desire, and action do not exist. This very point has been introduced: "Where, sleeping, one desires no desire at all and sees no dream whatsoever..."

"He sees"—this very form of his is that which has been described as "the state of being the self of all, the highest world. Regarding the term *aticchandas*: because it refers to a form (*rūpa*), the meaning is *aticchandam* (that which has transcended desire). *Chandas* means desire; that form from which desire has gone beyond is the "form that has transcended desire" (*aticchanda-rūpa*). This word *chandas* is different from the other [homophonous] word ending in a nasal (*sānta*) which denotes meters such as *gāyatrī*; this one, however, expresses desire and therefore ends in a vowel (*svarānta*).

Nevertheless, the reading "aticchandā" (excessive desire) should be regarded as a feature of the Vedic recitation (svādhyāya-dharma); for in common usage, the word *chanda* is employed in the sense of desire, as in "svacchanda" (one's own will) and "paracchanda" (another's will). Therefore, it should be emended to "aticchandam"; in this context, it means "free from desire," that is, devoid of longing. Likewise, [the term] "apahatapāpman" (one whose evil has been struck away): by the word *pāpman*, both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are meant, because it has been stated [elsewhere], "he is joined with evils" (*pāpmabhiḥ saṃsṛjyate*) and "he casts off evils" (*pāpmano vijahāti*).

"Free from evil" means devoid of both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). Furthermore, "fearless"—for fear is indeed the effect of ignorance, as it has been said, "Through ignorance one imagines fear"; this is a negation of the cause by way of its effect. "Fearless form" means devoid of ignorance. This state of being the Self of all, which is the fruit of knowledge, is this form that is beyond desire, free from evil, and fearless—devoid of all the attributes of transmigratory existence; therefore, this is the fearless form.

And this was already introduced previously at the conclusion of the immediately preceding Brāhmaṇa through scripture, in the passage: "O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness"; here, however, it is elaborated through reasoning in order to strengthen the conviction regarding the meaning of the scripture that has been shown. This Self is by its very nature the light of consciousness (*caitanya-jyotis*); it illumines everything by means of its own light of consciousness—it was stated that whatever it sees there, rejoices, moves about, and knows, [is all by means of this light].

And it is established by logic that the eternal nature of the Self is its character as the light of consciousness. If that Self exists here undestroyed, abiding in its own very form, why does it not know—either the Self as "I am" or external things as "these beings"—as it does in the waking and dreaming states? To this it is replied: hear the cause of this ignorance here. Oneness itself is the cause of ignorance. How so? It is explained as follows:

For the intended meaning becomes manifest through an illustration; thus he says: "In this regard, just as in the world a man who is full of desire, being completely embraced by a beloved, desired woman—being thoroughly enveloped by her—he does not perceive anything external to himself, thinking 'there is some object other than me,' nor does he perceive anything internal, such as 'I am this, happy or miserable'; but when not embraced by her, being separated from her, he perceives everything, both external and internal."

But after the embrace, because of the attainment of oneness, he does not know: "It is exactly thus; as in the illustration, this person, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), being separated from contact with the elements like a lump of salt, has entered here into the body and the organs like the reflection of the moon in water; this very person is completely embraced, thoroughly enveloped, and become one with the wise one—the ultimate, natural, and supreme Self, which is the highest light—without any interval."

He is the Self of all; there is no other external object whatsoever, nor any internal [object] within the Self such that one could know, "I am this, happy or miserable. Regarding what you asked—"If his nature is the light of consciousness, why does he not know here?"—the reason for that has been stated by me: it is oneness (*ekatva*), as in the case of a man and a woman in close embrace. By implication, it is stated therein that plurality (*nānātva*) is the cause of specific cognition.

And as for the cause of diversity—it has been stated that ignorance (*avidyā*) is that which presents the Self as a separate entity. When one becomes free from that ignorance, then everything becomes one with this [Self]. Consequently, when the distinction between the factors of action such as the knower and the known no longer exists, how could specific cognition or desire possibly arise within the natural light of the Self, which abides in its own essential nature?

Since its form is thus characterized by universal unity alone, therefore this is the form of this Self—which is by nature self-luminous—known as "one whose desires are attained" (*āptakāma*). Because this [Self] is the totality, all desires are attained within this form; hence it is called *āptakāma*. For that in which desire is differentiated as something other [than itself] is one whose desires are unattained, such as the form of Devadatta and others in the waking state; but this [Self] is not like that, for it is not differentiated from anything whatsoever.

Therefore, that [state] has its desires fulfilled (*āptakāma*). Is it not differentiated from some other distinct entity, or is that other entity the Self itself? To this he says: "There is nothing other than the Self. How so? Because it is one whose desires are fulfilled—desires which are the Self itself in that form where, as in the states of waking and dreaming, they appear as if differentiated elsewhere and are desired as something other; but because of the absence of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the cause for the appearance of otherness, it is "one whose desires are the Self" (*ātmakāma*).

For this very reason, this form is "without desire" (*akāma*), because there is an absence of objects of desire; it is "the end of sorrow" (*śokāntara*), meaning a gap in sorrow or devoid of sorrow—or alternatively, "the midst of sorrow"—in any case, this form is "without sorrow" (*aśoka*), which means it is free from grief.

(22) —It has been stated that the Self under discussion, being self-luminous, is liberated from ignorance, desire, and action, because the Self is unattached and those [factors] are adventitious. In that regard, the following doubt arises: even though its nature is consciousness, it does not perceive due to becoming one [with the body], as was said regarding a man and a woman in close embrace.

In this context, the following incidental point has been stated: "Self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiṣṭva*) is not the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of this Self, just like desire, action, and so forth, because it is not perceived during the state of profound tranquility (*saṃprasāda*). When this doubt had arisen, in order to refute it, the author employed the analogy of a man and a woman; he explained that while self-luminosity exists even in deep sleep, it is not apprehended due to the cause of "becoming one" (*ekībhāva*), and is not adventitious like desire, action, and the rest. Having thus concluded this incidental discussion, [he returns to] what was the original subject.

He proceeds to explain that very point. And this is what is under discussion here: that form of the Self which is perceived directly in deep sleep is indeed entirely free from ignorance, desire, and action; and this has been stated exactly as it is—that this form transcends all connections.

Because in this state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*), this form is characterized by the absence of desire, the destruction of evil, and fearlessness, therefore, here the father—the progenitor—is such that his status as a father toward his son is caused by action (*karman*); and by that action, he is disconnected at this time. Therefore, because the father is liberated from the action that causes the relationship with the son, even the father becomes "no-father"; likewise, it is understood by implication that the son also becomes "no-son" in relation to the father.

For action is the cause of the connection between both [the body and the worlds]; that [action] he has transcended and exists beyond it, as it has been said: "He is one whose evil has been struck away. Likewise, the mother is no longer a mother; the worlds are to be conquered through action and have been conquered—because of the absence of any connection with such action, the worlds are "non-worlds" (alokāḥ). Similarly, the gods are subordinate members of ritual action—due to the passing away of the connection with that action, the gods are "non-gods" (adevāḥ).

Likewise, the Vedas—which declare the relationship between the goal and its means, which possess the characteristics of mantras and constitute limbs of ritual action through their declarative nature, and which have been studied or are to be studied—are connected to a person solely on account of ritual action; because that action has been transcended, at this time even the Vedas become non-Vedas.

He is not only disconnected from the connection with auspicious deeds; rather, he remains entirely unconnected even with extremely terrible inauspicious deeds. To express this meaning, it is said: "In this state, the thief"—one who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa, as is understood from his mention alongside the killer of an embryo—"is liberated at that time from that terrible deed by which he, being a perpetrator of a mortal sin, is called a 'thief. Likewise, the killer of an embryo is one who is no longer a killer of an embryo."

Likewise, the *caṇḍāla* is not liberated merely from his present action, but rather he is indeed liberated even from that which is innate—even from that which causes him to belong to an extremely low caste. A *caṇḍāla* is one born of a *śūdra* father and a *brāhmaṇī* mother; a *caṇḍāla* is simply a *caṇḍāla*. Because he is no longer connected with the action caused by his birth, he becomes a non-*caṇḍāla*. A *paulkasa* is one born of a *śūdra* father and a *kṣatriyā* mother; a *pulkasa* is simply a *paulkasa*.

He also becomes one who is not an *apulkaśa*. Likewise, it is said that he becomes unconnected with the duties characterized by the stages of life (*āśrama*); namely, the ascetic (*śramaṇa*) and the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*). Because he is liberated from whatever constitutes the cause for those [titles], he is "not an ascetic" (*aśramaṇa*); similarly, the forest-dweller ascetic (*tāpasa-vānaprastha*) is "not an ascetic" (*atāpasa*). Both are mentioned here as an illustration representing all the castes (*varṇa*), stages of life (*āśrama*), and so forth.

What more need be said? "Unreached" (*ananvāgatam*) means not reached, that is, unconnected—unconnected with merit (*puṇya*), which is action prescribed by the scriptures, and likewise with evil (*pāpa*), characterized by the non-performance of what is enjoined and the performance of what is prohibited. The neuter gender is used because it refers to "form" (*rūpa*); for the phrase "the form is fearless" (*abhayaṃ rūpam*) follows [as a governing context].

Furthermore, what is the reason for this lack of connection? That cause is stated: because [He] has "crossed over" (tīrṇaḥ), that is, transcended—being of such a nature—at that time, all sorrows (śokān). Sorrows are desires (kāmāḥ); for the longing for a desired object indeed becomes sorrow when there is separation from that object. Indeed, a person, reflecting with anxiety upon a desired object not yet attained or already lost, suffers by dwelling on its qualities. Therefore, sorrow, attachment, and desire are synonyms.

Since he here transcends all desires—having been described as "not desiring any desire at all" and as "one who has transcended desire"—this word *śoka*, occurring in that same context, must indeed be a synonym for desire. And desire is the cause of action, for it will be stated later: "As is one's desire, so is one's resolve; as is one's resolve, so is the action one performs. Therefore, because he has transcended all desires, it is rightly said that he is "unaffected by merit," and so forth.

Regarding "of the heart": the "heart" (hṛdayam) is a mass of flesh shaped like a lotus. The internal organ, the intellect (buddhi), which resides therein, is called the "heart" because of its location there, just as one might say "the bed cries out" [meaning the person on the bed]. The "sorrows of the heart" are the sorrows of the intellect; for they reside in the intellect, since it has been stated, "Desire, resolve, doubt... all this is indeed the mind," and it will be said later, "Those desires which are rooted in the heart."

Indeed, these statements—"resting in the heart" and "the sorrows of the heart"—are intended to dispel the delusion that [the Self] is dependent upon the self. Furthermore, it has been stated that at this time, "he transcends the forms of death," which means he has transcended the connection with the instrument of the heart; and because he has transcended the connection with the instrument of the heart, it is even more logical to say that he transcends the connection with the desires resting upon it.

However, as for those proponents who assert that desires and latent impressions (*vāsanā*) residing in the heart approach and adhere to the Self associated with the heart, and even when separated from the heart, they remain in the Self—just as the fragrance of flowers and the like remains in oil contained within a vessel—for them, statements such as "desire, resolve," "for forms are indeed in the heart," and "the sorrows of the heart" would be entirely meaningless. If it is argued that this is because they are produced by the organ of the heart, we say no, because of the specific qualification "residing in the heart."
For if the heart were merely an instrument, the statement "resting in the heart" would not be appropriate; for it is said, "In the heart alone are forms."

And because the purity of the Self is intended to be expressed, the statement that [desires] "reside in the heart" is indeed appropriate as it stands; for there is no possibility of another meaning for the Śruti passage, "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were. If it be argued that desires also reside in the Self because of the qualification, "those desires which reside in the heart," we say no, because this refers to those not residing [in the heart]. Here, the qualification "which are in the heart" does not depend on some other locus; rather, it is a qualification with reference to those desires which are not residing in the heart.

However, those [desires] which are yet to arise (*aprarūḍha*), as well as those that have already arisen but have been turned back by their opposites (*pratipakṣa*), do not reside in the heart at all; yet they are still possible. Therefore, it is appropriate to apply the qualification with reference to them: "all those [desires] which have grown strong and are currently present regarding the object are liberated. If it is argued that even so, the qualification is useless, we say no; for there is an excess of effort required toward them, as they are what must be abandoned. Otherwise, one would be assuming something neither heard in scripture nor desired—namely, that desires are self-dependent (*ātmāśrayatva*).

If it is argued that because of the prohibition of what has been previously established—namely, "he desires no object whatsoever"—it is indeed heard in scripture that desires have the Self as their locus, we say: no. For, from the statement "having become a dream through the power [of the mind]," it follows that desires have something else as their cause and locus; furthermore, there is the teaching of non-attachment (*asaṅga*). Indeed, the teaching of non-attachment would not be tenable if desires had the Self as their locus, for we have already stated that attachment is desire. If it is argued that because of the scriptural text "desiring the Self" (*ātmakāmaḥ*), desire must have the Self as its object, we say: no, because that text intends to show the absence of any desire distinct [from the Self].

If it is argued that the self's being the substratum of desire and so forth is established by the logic of the Vaiśeṣika and other systems, we say no; for this contradicts specific scriptural texts such as "they are seated in the heart. Those logical arguments from the Vaiśeṣika and other systems are not to be relied upon, because when they contradict scripture, they must be admitted to be fallacious reasonings. Furthermore, they would subvert the self-luminosity of the Self.

Furthermore, since desires and the like in a dream have as their sole object the pure seer alone, the self-luminosity of the Self—which is established and firmly settled—would be sublated. For if they were inherent in the Self, their visibility would be untenable, just like a specific quality residing in the eye; for the object of vision is necessarily distinct from the seer, and thus the seer’s self-luminosity is proven. That [self-luminosity] would be contradicted if one were to postulate that desires and the like are the substratum [of the Self].

And because it would contradict the meaning of all the scriptures: if one were to postulate a mere partial aspect of the Supreme and [conceive of it] as the locus of desire and so forth, the entire body of scriptural teachings would be subverted. We have already explained this in detail in the fourth [chapter]; for indeed, with great effort, the postulations regarding the Self being the locus of desire and so forth must be refuted in order to establish the scriptural teaching of the oneness of the Self with the Supreme. If, however, such a postulation were to be carried out, the very purpose of the scripture would be undermined.

Just as the Vaiśeṣikas and Naiyāyikas, who postulate that desire and the like are attributes of the self, do not accord with the meaning of the Upaniṣadic scriptures, so too this conception is not to be respected, as it contradicts the meaning of the Upaniṣadic scriptures.

It was stated that [the Self] does not see because of its oneness with the woman and the man, and it is called "self-luminous" (*svayaṃjyotis*). Being self-luminous means having consciousness as one's essential nature (*caitanyātmasvabhāvatā*). For if the Self has consciousness as its essential nature—just as heat belongs to fire and so forth—how could it abandon that essential nature even in a state of oneness, such that it would not know? If, on the other hand, it does not abandon it, how is it that it does not see here in deep sleep? This is contradictory: that consciousness is the essential nature of the Self, yet it does not know. It is not contradictory; both of these are indeed possible. How so? (23) ————-

That which one does not see while in deep sleep—one indeed sees that there, yet seeing, one does not see. If you think that one does not see while in deep sleep, you should not grasp it in that way. Why? Because one is indeed seeing there. [Objection: But we know from experience that one does not see in deep sleep, since neither the eye nor the mind—the instruments of perception—is active. For when seeing, hearing, and so forth are active, the conventional usage occurs that "one sees" or "one hears"; and this is not the case here.

"We perceive that the organs are occupied [with their respective objects]; therefore, this [Self] does not see at all. No; rather, it is indeed seeing. How so? Because there is no loss—that is, no destruction—of that vision which belongs to the seer, the agent of seeing. Just as the heat of fire exists as long as the fire exists, so too this Self is the imperishable seer; therefore, because the Self is imperishable, its vision is also imperishable, for it exists as long as the seer exists.

Is it not a contradiction to say this—that "the vision of the seer is never lost," yet "vision is produced by the seer"? For one is called a "seer" precisely because of being the agent of seeing; and it is impossible to say that vision, while being produced by the seer, is never lost. [Objection: But surely, from the statement "it is not lost," it must be imperishable. [Reply: No, for a verbal statement is merely indicative.

For destruction, when it follows from the nature of things as a logical necessity, cannot be prevented even by a hundred statements, because a statement merely makes known an object as it actually exists. This is not a fault, for its manifestation is possible, just like the illumination of the sun and other luminaries; for instance, the sun and others, while being of the very nature of eternal light, illuminate by means of their own natural and eternal radiance.

For it is not said that those whose nature is non-luminous "illuminate" by producing light; rather, they do so by means of their own eternal luminosity. In the same way, this Self is called the "seer" (draṣṭṛ) because of its eternal vision, which is of an unchanging nature. [Objection: Then its status as a seer is secondary (gauṇa). [Reply: No, for its status as primary is established precisely in this way; for if the Self's status as a seer were observed to exist in any other manner, then this status as a seer would be secondary.

But there is no other mode of seeing for the Self; thus, only in this way does primary seership become possible, and not otherwise—just as the luminosity of the sun and so forth consists in their constant, natural, and non-active light, and that alone is their primary luminosity because no other form of luminosity is possible. Therefore, the vision of the Seer is never destroyed, and there is not even a scent of contradiction.

If it is argued: "Is it not observed that the use of a word ending in the suffix *tṛc* refers exclusively to an agent of an impermanent action—as in 'the cutter,' 'the breaker,' or 'the goer'—and thus it must be so here in the case of 'the seer' (*draṣṭṛ*) as well? We reply: No, because [the term] is seen used in the sense of "one who illuminates" (*prakāśayitṛ*). If it is argued: "Let it be so for things that illuminate, since otherwise it would be impossible; but it cannot apply to the Self," we reply: No, because of the scriptural teaching that the vision does not perish (*dṛṣṭyaviparilopa*). If it is argued: "No, because we observe the experience of 'I see' and 'I do not see'," we reply: No, because those experiences depend upon the specific operations of the instruments (the senses).

Furthermore, because those whose eyes have been removed see that their vision of the self is not lost even in a dream, it follows that the vision of the self exists by its very nature as something unimpaired and non-losing. Therefore, through that unimpaired vision, which is of the nature of self-luminosity, one continues to see even while in deep sleep.

How, then, is it said that "he does not see"? It is because that [object] does not exist. What is that? A second thing, which has become an object; what is its qualification? That which is other than the seer, distinguished as something else, which he might see, which he might perceive. For that internal organ, the eye, and form—which are the causes for perceiving specific distinctions—were previously presented as distinct by ignorance; at this time, however, they have become one through the embrace of the Self by the Supreme.

For an observer who is limited, an instrument exists as something distinct in order to perceive specific objects. But this [Self] is completely embraced in its entirety by its own supreme conscious Self—just as a man is embraced by his beloved. Therefore, the instruments and the objects do not exist as separate entities. Because of their absence, there is no perception of particulars; for that [perception] is produced by the instruments and so forth, not produced by the Self. Yet it appears as if it were produced by the Self. Consequently, this is an illusion caused by those [instruments]: namely, that "the vision of the Self is lost. (24–30)

The rest is the same: "Indeed, when it does not smell; indeed, when it does not taste; indeed, when it does not speak; indeed, when it does not hear; indeed, when it does not think; indeed, when it does not touch; indeed, when it does not cognize. Although thinking (*manana*) and cognition (*vijñāna*) possess sight and the other senses as their auxiliaries, they are mentioned separately because they have an activity directed toward objects of the past, future, and present that exists independently of the eyes and the other organs.

Furthermore, is there a difference in properties among vision and the other faculties—just as fire possesses the distinct properties of heat, illumination, and combustion—or rather, is it that for a single, undivided property, its diversity of properties is caused by external limiting conditions (*upādhi*)? On this point, some explain: the reality of the Self possesses both unity and plurality inherently; just as a cow has unity insofar as it is the substance "cow," yet there is a mutual difference among its properties such as the dewlap and so forth.

Just as unity and plurality are observed in gross objects, so too are unity and plurality to be inferred in partless, formless entities; for since this is seen without exception everywhere, it must be the same for the self (ātman) in relation to its functions such as seeing and the rest.

[The opponent claims: "There is diversity [of states] and yet unity through the Self. [The author replies: No, because the passage has another purpose. For this sentence beginning with "That which... (*yadvai tat*) and so forth does not aim at demonstrating a difference in attributes such as seeing and the rest. What then? It is begun—namely, "That which... and so forth—in order to dispel the following doubt: "If the light of the Self is consciousness, why does one not know [anything] in deep sleep? Surely, therefore, the light of the Self is not consciousness. It is for the sake of removing this doubt that the passage "That which... and so forth is commenced.

That nature of the Self as the light of consciousness—which, during waking and dreaming, is characterized by its manifestation through various adjuncts such as the eyes and so forth, and which enters into empirical usage under designations such as "seeing" and the like—is, in deep sleep, not manifested because the activities of the distinct adjuncts have ceased. Thus, although its nature is not perceived there, it is described as existing by way of restating its state as it was previously attained—appearing as if divided by the diversity of adjuncts. Any conceptualization of distinctions among attributes such as "seeing" and so forth in that state arises from a lack of understanding of the intended meaning.

Because it is a solid mass of the single flavor of consciousness (*prajñāna*), like a block of rock-salt (*saindhavaghana*); and because of scriptural contradictions [if it were otherwise], as seen in such Śruti passages as "Consciousness is bliss," "Truth is knowledge," and "Brahman is consciousness. Furthermore, regarding the application of words: common worldly usage of words—such as "one perceives form with the eye," "one perceives sound with the ear," and "one perceives the taste of food with the tongue"—everywhere shows that those things denoted by terms like "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*) are indeed expressible by the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).

The application of words is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as is the logical consistency of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). For instance, in the world, a crystal endowed with a transparent nature assumes various forms solely due to its conjunction with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as green, blue, or red; yet, apart from its transparent nature, it is impossible to conceive of distinct attributes in the crystal characterized by green, blue, red, and so forth. In the same way, [the Self] assumes various forms through its conjunction with the limiting adjuncts of the eyes and other senses.

In the very light of the Self, which is of the nature of a mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*), a differentiation of powers such as seeing and so forth is observed; this is because the mass of consciousness has a transparent nature, like the transparency of a crystal. Furthermore, due to its self-luminosity—just as the solar light, when in contact with various objects to be illumined, appears in their forms (such as green, blue, yellow, or red) while remaining itself undivided—so too does the light of the Self, illuminating the entire world and the eyes and other senses, assume their respective forms.

And so it has been said: "By his own light, he sits," and so forth. Furthermore, it is impossible to conceive of multiplicity of self-nature in things that are partless, for there is no illustrative example [to support such a claim]. As for the differentiation of attributes—such as the all-pervasiveness of space—or the possession of multiple qualities like smell and taste by atoms and the like, even upon close examination, these are found to be caused solely by external limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). To begin with, the so-called "all-pervasiveness" of space is not an inherent attribute of space itself.

For the conventional usage of "all-pervasiveness" everywhere depends upon the existence [of a thing] in its own form in relation to all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); however, space itself does not, by its own nature, go anywhere or not go anywhere. Indeed, what is called "going" is the cause of conjunction with another location for that which is situated in one location; and such action is simply not possible in that which is devoid of distinctions. Thus, no such attributes exist in space. The same applies to atoms and so forth as well.

That which is called an atom (*paramāṇu*) is the most subtle constituent part of earth as a dense mass of fragrance, and it consists of fragrance alone; it is not possible to further imagine that it possesses "fragrance-ness. If it is argued that it might possess taste and other qualities, we say no, because even in those cases, they are caused by contact with water and the other elements. Therefore, there is no example for a partless entity possessing multiple attributes.

By this, the hypothesis of distinct transformations of the various powers of seeing and so forth, corresponding to the distinctions between the eye, form, and the rest, is refuted in the case of the Supreme Self.

It has been stated that what one might perceive as distinct and separate, as in the states of waking and dreaming, does not exist as a second thing differentiated by otherness; therefore, in deep sleep, one does not perceive any particularity. Now, if this [non-perception] is his very nature, for what reason does he abandon that nature to have specific cognition? Or, if specific cognition itself is his nature, why does he not perceive particularity?

It is said: listen—wherein, whether in the waking state or in a dream, something else as it were, like another entity distinct from the Self, is presented by ignorance (*avidyā*); therein, because of that presentation by ignorance, one regards oneself as other, as if distinct. While there is no separate entity apart from the Self, and while there is no separation of the Self from that [entity], one might see or perceive another as other.

And that has been demonstrated through direct perception in a dream: "as if striking, as if conquering. Likewise, one [dreamer] might smell another thing, taste, speak, hear, think, touch, or cognize it.

Furthermore, in deep sleep, that ignorance which presents other objects has been stilled; therefore, because there is no object distinct from it that could be differentiated by ignorance, who could see whom, or smell, or cognize? Thus, embraced by his own wise Self, whose nature is self-luminous, he is unified, serene, and one whose desires are fulfilled; having become as clear as water—like water, he is "salila"—he is alone.

Because of the absence of a second; for by ignorance a second is distinguished, and that [ignorance] is stilled here, therefore it is one. It is the Seer, because the vision whose nature is self-luminosity is never lost; it is non-dual, because of the absence of a second object to be seen. This is the immortal, the fearless; this is the world of Brahman—Brahman itself is the world, hence "the world of Brahman."

"At this time, O Emperor, this very person exists in his own self-luminous light, with all connections stilled and the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts of the body and organs withdrawn"—this is the statement of the Śruti, that Yājñavalkya thus instructed Janaka. How did he instruct him? "This is the supreme goal of this one consisting of consciousness."

But those other states of existence, characterized by the assumption of bodies from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, which are imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*), are inferior to this [state], because they fall within the domain of ignorance. This state, however, consisting of the nature of the universal Self—in which one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and cognizes nothing else—is the supreme and highest among the states such as that of the gods, which are accomplished through ritual action and knowledge. And this alone is the supreme prosperity (*saṃpat*); for among all prosperities and manifestations, this is the supreme, because it is innate (*svābhāvika*).

For other prosperities are indeed produced by effort. Likewise, this is his supreme world; whereas those other worlds which depend upon the fruits of action are inferior to this, this one is not measured by any action because it is innate; thus, this is his supreme world. Likewise, this is his supreme bliss; compared to those various kinds of bliss born from the connection between objects and the senses, this is his supreme bliss because it is eternal, according to another scriptural text: "That which is plenitude (bhūman) is happiness."

Where one sees something other [than the Self] and perceives something other, that is limited, mortal, and secondary happiness; but this [bliss] is the opposite of that. Therefore, this is his supreme bliss. Other beings subsist on but a minute fraction—a mere particle—of this very bliss, which is presented by ignorance and is experienced only at the time of contact between the senses and their objects.

What are they? They are those very things, O Ānanda, whose true nature is differentiated by ignorance; being conceptualized as other than Brahman, these other entities exist and subsist, being manifested through the contact of the objects and the senses.

Desiring to lead one to that Supreme Bliss—the measure (*mātrā*) or parts of which are subsisted upon by all beings from Brahmā down to human beings—He speaks by means of those measures of bliss, just as one might indicate a mountain of salt by means of fragments of rock-salt. He is anyone among men who is "accomplished" (*rāddha*), meaning fully perfected with all his limbs intact, and "prosperous" (*samṛddha*), meaning endowed with all the instruments of enjoyment.

Furthermore, he is the sovereign and independent lord over others of his own kind, not a mere regional ruler; by the phrase "all together," it is meant that these are all human [enjoyments], thereby excluding divine objects of enjoyment and requisites.

Among the very things that are the instruments of enjoyment for human beings—those with which they are endowed—he who is endowed with them to the highest degree is the most fully endowed (*saṃpannatama*). That is the supreme bliss among humans. In this context, because of the instruction on the non-difference between bliss (*ānanda*) and the one who experiences bliss (*ānandin*), there is no state of being a separate entity; for it has been stated in the passage beginning with "where there is, as it were, something else," that this very supreme bliss has issued forth in the form of the object and the subject.

Therefore, this designation of non-difference as "supreme bliss" (parama ānanda) is logical. A king equal to Yudhiṣṭhira and others serves as the illustration here. Beginning with the observed human bliss, it leads upward through a sequence of hundredfold increments until it reaches supreme bliss, wherein all differentiation ceases, and that state is made known.

In this context, Ānanda increases by a hundredfold progression until it reaches its ultimate limit, where the distinction of calculation ceases due to the absence of further seeing, hearing, and reflecting. Desiring to speak of that supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), he says: "Now, whatever constitutes a hundred such varieties of human bliss, that is one [unit] of the bliss of the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*)," with the qualification for them being "those who have conquered the worlds."

Having gratified the ancestors through rites such as the *śrāddha*, those for whom the world is won by that very action are the "conquered-world" ancestors (*jitaloka-pitaraḥ*). Of those conquered-world ancestors, there is one joy whose magnitude is a hundredfold the human joy. That [joy], multiplied by a hundred, becomes one joy in the world of the *gandharvas*. And that, multiplied by a hundred, is one joy of the "deities by action" (*karmadevāḥ*)—those who attain the state of divinity through Vedic rituals such as the *agnihotra*.

In the same way, there is one degree of bliss for the *ājānadevas*. Those gods who are such by birth, that is, by their very origin, are the *ājānadevas*. And as for the learned man (*śrotriya*) who has studied the Vedas, who is free from crookedness—that is, devoid of evil (*vṛjina*), meaning he acts according to what is taught—and who is not overcome by desire, that is, whose thirst has departed, [there is a degree of bliss] regarding all the objects of sense that lie below the *ājānadevas*. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that for such a person, the bliss is equal to that of the *ājānadevas*.

A single bliss of a magnitude increased a hundredfold from that exists in the world of Prajāpati within the body of Virāj; likewise, one who possesses knowledge of that, who is a Śrotriya, who has studied the Vedas, and is free from evil, etc., as described previously. A single bliss of a magnitude increased a hundredfold from that exists in the world of Brahman within the self of Hiraṇyagarbha; "and he who... and so forth, is exactly as before. Beyond this, the calculation ceases.

This is called supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), of which the joys of the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) and other realms are but mere droplets, like drops from the ocean. Thus, the joys that increase a hundredfold at each successive stage reach a state of unity therein. This very bliss, which is directly perceived by one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), is characterized by perfect serenity (*saṃprasāda*). For in that state, one sees nothing else and hears nothing else; therefore, it is the Infinite (*bhūman*), and because it is infinite, it is immortal. All others are the opposite of this.

And here, while being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyatva*) and being free from crookedness (*avṛjinatva*) are equal, the distinction made by being unaffected by desire (*akāmahatatva*) is the cause for the hundredfold increase in bliss. In this context, these means—being learned in the Vedas, being free from crookedness, and being unaffected by desire—are implied as the requirements for the attainment of each respective bliss, just as rituals such as the *agnihotra* are required for the attainment of divinity by the gods.

In this regard, the two qualities characterized by being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyatva*) and being free from crookedness (*avṛjinatva*) are common even to those on the lower stages; therefore, they are not accepted as the means for attaining the higher bliss. However, it is understood that freedom from being overcome by desire (*akāmahatatva*)—given that detachment (*vairāgya*) occurs in varying degrees—is the means for attaining the bliss of each successive higher stage. This very supreme bliss has been realized through the direct perception of a learned person free from thirst. And so says Vedavyāsa: "Whatever happiness exists in the world of desire, and whatever great divine happiness there is—"

"These do not equal even a sixteenth part of the bliss of the destruction of craving for an Arhat" (MBh). "This, O Emperor, is the world of Brahman," said Yājñavalkya. "Thus instructed, I give you a thousand cows, O Blessed One; speak further only for the sake of liberation"—this has been explained. Regarding this statement, "for the sake of liberation," Yājñavalkya became afraid.

The Śruti states the reason for Yājñavalkya’s fear: Yājñavalkya was not afraid due to a lack of skill in speaking, nor out of ignorance; rather, [he feared] because the wise king had "hemmed me in" (udarautsīt)—that is, he had surrounded and obstructed me from all sides at the conclusion of the determination of each question.

"Whatever question I have determined for the sake of liberation, he repeatedly interrogates me by taking each one as merely a single part of the 'question of desire' (*kāmapraśna*), because of his intelligence—this is the cause of my fear: that he intends to acquire my entire knowledge under the pretext of the 'question of desire.

Here, the Self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), which is self-luminous, has been demonstrated in the state of dream; through its transition between the end of the dream and the waking state, its distinction from the body and the organs, as well as its separation from desire and action, have been shown by means of the analogy of the great fish due to its non-attachment. Furthermore, the effect of ignorance (*avidyā*) has been demonstrated in the dream itself through such expressions as "as if killing," and so forth; thus, the true nature of ignorance has been determined as being of the form of superimposing attributes that do not belong [to the Self], and as not being an attribute of the Self.
Likewise, the effect of knowledge has been demonstrated as the state of being the Self of all, perceived directly even in a dream: "He thinks, 'I am Śarva'; that is his supreme world."

Thus it is said; and therein it has been made known that his very nature is the state of being the Self of all, and that his form transcends all worldly phenomena such as ignorance, desire, and karma, and is directly perceived in deep sleep. This Self is self-luminous, this is supreme bliss, this is the object of knowledge (*vidyā*), this is the supreme state of serene composure (*parama-saṃprasāda*), and this is the highest limit of happiness—all of which has been explained by the text ending in this manner.

And all of this serves as an illustration for the subject matter of liberation and bondage; furthermore, these two—liberation and bondage—are taught along with their causes and their manifold elaborations (*prapañca*) as the effects of knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*). Janaka questions him again, saying, "Explain from here on only that which pertains to liberation," because he considers all of that [the previous discussion] to be merely illustrative, while the liberation and bondage along with their causes—which constitute the actual subject of his inquiry—remain yet to be explained by the other.

In this regard, it has been stated that like a great fish, the single Self, which is self-luminous, moves without attachment between the states of dream and waking. And just as that Self, discarding and assuming the organs and bodies that are of the nature of death, moves between the states of dream and waking like a great fish, so too, being born and dying, it is joined with and separated from those very forms of death—this "moving between both worlds" is a description of the movement between the states of dream and waking.

This has been indicated by way of an illustration. Therefore, the transition [of the self] must now be described here in detail along with its cause; for that purpose, this undertaking is begun. In that context, this Self was made to enter from the waking state into the dream state; therefore, the state of deep sleep (*saṃprasāda*) serves as an illustration of liberation. Consequently, the worldly activity of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) must be demonstrated in relation to the preceding waking state; thus, this is the connection between them.

Indeed, having become serene through the sequence from the waking state to the dream state, he remains in this serenity; then, having slightly departed from it—having enjoyed himself and moved about in the dream state, as described previously—he hastens back toward the waking state itself.

From here on, his transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is described. Just as this self has come from the end of a dream to the waking state, so too will he pass from this body to another body; thus [the text] states an illustration for that: "In this regard, just as in the world a cart (*anaḥ*), well-fastened—that is, very firmly secured with its equipment and utensils such as mortars, pestles, winnowing baskets, and cooking pots, and provided with provisions such as food and other supplies—meaning it is laden with these materials."

Just as [a cart], being overcome by a heavy load, would go along making a sound while being driven by a cartwright; even so, according to the illustration mentioned, this "bodily" one—that which exists in the body—is the Self (ātman) whose limiting adjunct is the subtle body (liṅga). It is that which, like [passing between] the states of dreaming and waking, traverses this world and the next world through birth and death, characterized respectively by contact with and separation from evil; following its departure, the vital breaths and other faculties depart. That [Self] is [united] with the Supreme Self, the Prājña.

Mounted upon, presided over, and illuminated by its own nature as self-luminous—just as it has been said, "By this light of his own, he sits and moves about"—he goes forth emitting [his breath]. There, when the subtle body (liṅga), which consists primarily of vital breath, proceeds while being illumined by the light of the conscious Self, the Self, having that as its limiting adjunct, also appears to go; thus says another Śruti passage beginning with "In whom am I? and "He meditates, as it were. For this very reason it is said: "mounted upon by the conscious Self."

Otherwise, being unified with the wise one, how could he go making sounds like a cart? Therefore, the self, having the subtle body (*liṅga*) as its limiting adjunct, goes—that is, moves—making a sound, afflicted by the sensation of pain as the vital points (*marmans*) are being cut. At what time does this occur? It is said: "when this happens. The word "this" (*etad*) is an adverbial modifier for the action; the meaning is: when his state of upward breathing occurs. This description of what is already perceived is for the purpose of inducing dispassion (*vairāgya*).

"Truly, this saṃsāra is so painful that at the time of death, while the vital organs are being torn apart, there occurs a loss of memory for one afflicted by the sensation of pain, and there is an incapacity for the practice of the means to achieve the goals of human life because the mind has been rendered subject to another's power. Therefore, as long as this state has not yet arrived, one should remain vigilant regarding the duty to perform the means for achieving the goals of human life—thus says the Śruti out of compassion.

Regarding this, it is explained as follows: at what time, for what cause, in what manner, or for what purpose does this upward breathing of his occur? This refers to the natural physical body, consisting of the head, hands, and so forth, in which, at a certain time, this [body] attains *aṇimāna*—that is, the state of being minute (*aṇu*), smallness, or emaciation. For what cause? Either through old age, by itself, like a fruit ripened by time, it becomes worn out and reaches emaciation; or by "affliction" (*upatapan*)—that is, by disease such as fever and the like—which afflicts it.

For one who is afflicted by disease, due to a disordered digestive fire (*viṣamāgni*), the food consumed is not digested; consequently, the body-mass (*piṇḍa*), not being nourished by the essence of food (*annarasa*), undergoes emaciation. This is what is meant by "or by being afflicted"; it reaches a state of extreme thinness (*aṇimāna*). When there is extreme emaciation...

When one is overtaken by the signs of old age and so forth, then one becomes gasping for breath; when one is gasping for breath, then one departs emitting sounds like a heavily laden cart. These misfortunes—the conquest of old age, the affliction of disease and the like, and the onset of emaciation—are inevitable for one who possesses a body; this is stated for the sake of cultivating detachment.

When he departs, how does he release the body? To this, an illustration is given: "In that regard, it is like a mango fruit, or a fig fruit, or a pipal fruit. The employment of these various and diverse examples is for the purpose of making known that death has no fixed cause; for the causes of death are indeed indefinite and innumerable.

This too is solely for the sake of detachment: because this [tree] possesses many causes of death, it therefore always remains in the mouth of death. Regarding "from bondage" (*bandhanāt*): that by which it is bound together with its stalk is the sap which is the cause of bondage; or, that in which it is bound is the stalk itself, which is called "bondage. From that sap or from that stalk—the bondage—it is liberated due to various causes such as wind and so forth.

This very person—the subtle body (*liṅgātman*), having the subtle body as its limiting adjunct (*liṅgopādhi*)—having completely released itself from these limbs, that is, from the members of the body such as the eyes and so forth, releasing it thoroughly and without residue—not protecting it by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as occurs at the time of entering deep sleep, but rather withdrawing it along with the wind (*vāyu*)—then proceeds "again according to the rule" (*punaḥ pratinyāyam*). By the word "again," it is indicated that previously also this [self] has repeatedly gone from one body to another, just as one goes again and again between the states of dreaming and waking; thus, "again according to the rule."

"Returning in the same manner as it came" means that [the soul] rushes toward each respective womb according to its karma, sacred learning, and so forth. For what purpose? "For breath alone" means for the very purpose of the arrangement (vyūha) of the vital breaths; for it is indeed accompanied by the vital breaths that it departs, and thus the qualification "for breath alone" would be redundant. Indeed, the departure from one body to another is for the sake of the arrangement of the vital breaths, because through that arrangement alone is the accomplishment of its purpose—the experience of the fruits of karma—achieved, and not by the mere existence of the vital breaths.
Therefore, the qualification "for the arrangement of the vital breaths" is appropriate in order to indicate that specific purpose.

In this regard, for one who departs having abandoned this body, there is no capacity to take up another body, because of the separation from the body and the senses; nor do others exist in the position of servants, like those waiting for a king to build a new house, who might prepare another body and wait for him. This being so, how does he take up another body? It is said: for this entire world has been acquired by him solely as a means for the enjoyment of the fruits of his own karma.

And this [individual self] has set out for the sake of experiencing the fruits of its own karma, desiring to pass from one body to another body. Therefore, the entire world, impelled by its own karma, prepares the means suitable for the experience of the fruits of that karma and simply awaits [the soul], according to the Vedic revelation: "The person is born into a world made [by his own deeds]"—just as one about to pass from sleep into the waking state. To explain how this occurs, an example well-known in the world is stated:

In that regard, it is just as when a king who has been consecrated to the kingdom is approaching his own realm; the fierce classes of people (*ugrā jātiviśeṣāḥ*) or those of cruel deeds, the *pratyenasas*—those appointed to each specific crime or evil deed—and those appointed to the punishment of thieves and so forth, as well as the *sūtas* and *grāmaṇyas*—the *sūtas* being a specific mixed caste and the *grāmaṇyas* being village leaders—they, having already learned of the king’s arrival, [prepare] with foods...

With various kinds of food and edibles, with drinks such as wine, and with dwellings such as palaces, they prepare themselves—that is, they wait with things already ready—saying, "The king is coming," or "He is arriving. Just as in this illustration, so it is with one who knows thus—the one who knows the fruit of action, meaning the transmigrating soul; for the fruit of action is the subject under discussion, and that is what is referred to by the word "thus" (evam).

The meaning is that all beings—the makers of bodies and the sustainers of the instruments, such as the sun and other deities—impelled by those [past] actions, await [the arrival of the self], thinking: "This Brahman, who is both the enjoyer and the agent, is coming to us; thus He approaches. It is in this very manner that they wait.

Who are those who go along with one desiring to go thus? And as for those who do go, are they impelled by that action, or do they go of their own accord due to the power of that karma—the elements which constitute the body for the next world?

To this it is replied: there is an illustration. Just as when a king desires to set out on a journey (*prayiyāsantam*), fierce deputies, charioteers, and village headmen approach him, coming toward him in a unified manner even without being commanded by the king, simply because they know his desire to depart; in exactly the same way, at the time of the end, at the time of death, all the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*), such as speech and the rest, approach this self, the enjoyer.
This has been explained in the passage beginning, "whereupon he becomes one whose breath moves only upward."
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa of the fourth chapter.
Satyakāma Jābāla addressed his mother Jabālā: "Mother, I wish to live as a religious student (*brahmacarya*). Under which lineage (*gotra*) shall I live? What indeed is my lineage? 1. (1)

This very Self (ātman) under discussion, at which time—having entered into, having gone toward, debility (abalyam), that is, the state of weakness—it is metaphorically designated as "having entered into debility," because the weakness of the body is figuratively attributed to the Self itself; for it does not undergo a state of weakness in its own right, being formless (amūrta). Likewise, it enters into, or goes toward, as it were, delusion (saṃmoha)—delusion being a state of bewilderment, a lack of discrimination.

And for this [Self], there is neither delusion nor non-delusion of its own accord, because its nature is that of the eternal light of consciousness; therefore, the word "as it were" is used—meaning "it goes as if into delusion. For at the time of departure, ordinary people perceive a state of agitation in the Self caused by the withdrawal of the organs; and thus people say, "He is deluded, he is deluded."

Alternatively, the use of the word *iva* (as if) should be applied to both cases—as in "having gone as it were to weakness, he goes as it were to delusion"—because there is no difference in both being caused by external conditions (*paropādhi*), and because of the grammatical indication of a common agent. Now, at this time, these vital breaths (*prāṇa*), beginning with speech, gather together toward this Self; then there is a complete departure from the limbs of this embodied self.

How, then, is there liberation, or in what manner does one fully attain the Self? It is said: that Self, taking up these "measures of light"—the measures of light (*tejomātrāḥ*) meaning portions of light, which are the instruments such as the eyes because they illuminate form and so forth—taking them up completely, without leaving any residue, grasping them directly and withdrawing them; this is qualified by the word "peacefully" (*śam*) in relation to the state of dreaming.

However, there is no perfect grasping in a dream by means of something that leaves no trace; rather, there is merely a grasping, as is evident from such scriptural passages as: "Speech is taken," "The eye is taken," "Having taken a measure of this all-encompassing world," and "Having taken the pure essence. The meaning is that he enters—that is, he approaches—the space within the lotus-like heart; that is, his consciousness becomes manifest in the heart when the distractions of the intellect and other faculties have been withdrawn.

For that [Self] has no movement of its own, nor any modification such as distraction or withdrawal, because it is said, "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were. Indeed, all modifications are superimposed upon it only through the medium of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect (buddhi). When, then, does its taking up of the subtle elements of light occur? It is said: "Wherever this person who exists in the eye—the ocular person (cākṣuṣa)—who is a portion of the Sun, impelled by the karma of the enjoyer, remains performing the service of the eye for as long as the body is maintained;"

At the time of death, however, the eye abandons its support and attains its own solar self; this has been stated thus: "When this person has died, speech merges into fire, breath into the wind, and the eye into the sun," and so forth; they will again resort to [their respective elements] at the time of taking up a body, as well as for one who is about to sleep and for one who is waking up.

This is what he says: "The visual person (cākṣuṣaḥ puruṣaḥ), at which time—at which moment—turns away, that is, turns completely and entirely away from the external world; then, at this time, he becomes one who no longer perceives forms; being on the verge of death, he does not recognize form. At that time, this self (ātmā) begins to gather together the subtle elements of light belonging to the eyes and other senses, just as during the state of sleep."

She said to him, "I do not know this, my dear, to what lineage you belong. While I was wandering about as a servant in my youth, I obtained you; therefore, I do not know to what lineage you belong. But I am Jabālā by name, and you are Satyakāma by name. So you should say, 'Satyakāma Jābāla. 2. (2)---

The collection of organs becomes unified with its own subtle body (*liṅga-ātman*); then those standing nearby say of him, "He sees. Likewise, when the deity of the sense of smell has withdrawn, the sense of smell becomes unified with the subtle body; then they say, "He does not smell. The rest is the same. On the tongue, Soma or Varuṇa is the deity; with respect to their withdrawal, they say, "He does not taste. Similarly, they say, "He does not speak, he does not hear, he does not think, he does not touch, he does not discern."

Then the withdrawal of the deities is observed, as well as the unification of the organs within the heart. When the organs have been withdrawn into that heart, the internal activity therein is described: "Of this very heart under discussion—that is, of the cavity of the heart—the 'tip,' which is the opening of the channel and the gateway for departure, flashes forth, as it does at the time of dreaming, by its own radiance produced by the taking up of the subtle elements of light, and by its own light, which is the Self itself."

By means of that light of the Self, by means of that radiance at the tip of the heart, this Self—consisting of consciousness and having the subtle body (*liṅga*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—goes forth, it departs. Thus it is said in the *Atharvaṇa*: "When I have departed, in what shall I have departed? Or when [the body] has been established, in what shall I be established? He created the vital breath (*prāṇa*). And there, the light of the Self's consciousness is always most manifest.

For it is through the medium of those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that all worldly transactions—characterized by birth, death, going, coming, and so forth—occur in the Self. Indeed, the twelvefold instrument consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest is of that nature; it is the thread, it is life, and it is the inner self of both the moving and the stationary world. It is now stated by which path he departs as he goes forth, illuminated by that light at the tip of the heart: either through the eye, if there be knowledge or action leading to the attainment of the world of Āditya.

Whether it be from the head for the purpose of reaching the world of Brahman, or from other parts or members of the body, according to one's karma and according to one's scriptural knowledge—that conscious self (*vijñānātman*) who is departing, having set out for the next world (the meaning being that his intention is directed toward the next world)—the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which stands in the position of a sovereign over all, departs after him, just as [attendants follow] a king; and after that departing *prāṇa*, all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), such as speech and the rest, depart after him.

This is an intention to describe according to the primary importance [of the topics], and not a desire to express a sequential progression with a specific purpose here. At that time, this self becomes endowed with consciousness; it possesses specific cognition like one in a dream due to the power of karma, and is not independent. For if it were independent in its state of being endowed with consciousness, everyone would have accomplished all their goals; yet that is certainly not attained. Therefore Vyāsa said: "At all times, he is permeated by that state."

But by means of the specific cognition consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā) residing in a particular modification of the internal organ, which is manifested through karma, the entire world at this time becomes possessed of that cognition; and it proceeds toward, or follows, that very state to be reached—meaning it proceeds as illuminated precisely by that specific cognition.

Therefore, at that time, those who possess faith, who seek the next world, and who are heedful must practice the duties of yoga, cultivate the habit of discernment (*parisaṃkhyāna*), and accumulate distinguished merit for the sake of autonomy. This is the purpose that must be diligently implemented according to all the scriptures: the cessation from misconduct. For at that time, it is not possible to accomplish anything, since one being led by *karman* lacks autonomy.

It has been said: "One becomes virtuous through virtuous action and sinful through sinful action. Indeed, all the Upaniṣads of every Vedic branch have been composed for the purpose of prescribing the means to pacify this very evil. For there is no means to the ultimate pacification of this evil apart from following the means prescribed therein. Therefore, one must apply oneself with effort precisely to these means prescribed in the Upaniṣads—this is the purport of the present section.

It has been stated that [the soul] departs, having accumulated its provisions like a cart. Now, what is the provision for the journey for one setting out for the next world—corresponding to the cart-driver’s equipment—which he consumes after reaching the next world, and what is that which initiates the body and so forth? This is explained as follows: for that self going to the next world, there are "knowledge and action" (*vidyākarmaṇī*)—that is, knowledge and action. Knowledge is of every kind: prescribed, prohibited, un-prescribed, and un-prohibited.

And likewise, both prescribed and prohibited action, as well as that which is neither prescribed nor prohibited, together initiate [the new existence]; they properly initiate it, they take hold of it, they follow after it. And "prior cognition" (*pūrvaprajñā*)—cognition regarding objects previously experienced is "prior cognition," meaning the latent impression (*vāsanā*) from the experience of the fruits of past actions; and that impression becomes a factor in the undertaking of new actions and in the ripening of the fruits of action; therefore, that too initiates [the new existence].

For indeed, without that latent impression (vāsanā), it is not possible to perform an action or to experience its fruit; for there is no skill of the sense organs in a domain that has not been practiced; however, in the case of sense organs set in motion by the impressions of previous experiences, skill arises here even without current practice.

Moreover, it is observed that some possess skill from birth itself in certain activities characterized by arts such as painting, even without practice in this life, while others possess a lack of skill in those very same activities despite their extreme ease; likewise, skill and lack of skill in the enjoyment of sense objects are seen in some by their very nature. All of this is caused by the emergence or non-emergence of knowledge from a previous life.

Therefore, without that prior cognition (*pūrvaprajñā*), no engagement in either action or the enjoyment of its fruit is possible for anyone. Consequently, this triad—consisting of knowledge (*vidyā*), action (*karman*), and prior cognition—is like the equipment of a cart-driver; it is the provision for the journey to the next world. Since knowledge, action, and prior cognition are the means for attaining and experiencing another body, one should therefore perform only auspicious knowledge, action, and so forth, so that there may be union with and experience in a desired body. This is the meaning of the section.

Thus, one who has accumulated the equipment of knowledge and so forth, when proceeding to another body, leaves the previous body and takes up another body, like a bird moving from one tree to another; or else, by means of an intermediate subtle body (*ātivāhika*), he is led to the place of birth where the fruits of his karma are to be experienced.

Furthermore, does the functioning of the all-pervading organs occur while [the self] remains right here, or do the organs, which are contracted while residing in the body, expand everywhere—like the light from a lamp inside a broken jar—and then undergo contraction again at the commencement of another body? Moreover, does the mind alone travel toward the location where another body is to begin, as in the Vaiśeṣika system, or is there yet another conception in the Vedānta system? To this it is said: "All these... [and so forth].

Thus, it is heard in scripture that "all [the vital breaths] are equal and infinite"; therefore, the instruments (karaṇas) consist of all things, because they depend upon the vital breath which consists of all things. Their limitation to the internal (ādhyātmika) and external (ādhibhautika) realms is caused by the karma, knowledge, and mental impressions (bhāvanā) of living beings. Consequently, although the vital breaths are by nature omnipresent and infinite, their function contracts and expands in accordance with the latent impressions of karma and knowledge, due to the commencement of another body under the influence of those factors.

And so it has been said: "Peace is equal to a gnat, equal to a mosquito, equal to an elephant, equal to these three worlds, and equal to this entire universe. Likewise, the following statement is consistent with this: "He who meditates upon these as infinite," and so forth, as well as "In whatever way one meditates [upon them]. In that regard, the latent impression (*vāsanā*), known as prior cognition (*pūrvaprajñā*), which is governed by knowledge and action (*vidyākarmatantra*), is continuous like a leech; even while remaining within the heart, it initiates the transition from one body to another, produced by karma, as in the case of the time of dreaming.
Furthermore, regarding the point that when one begins another body, one leaves behind the previous abode—the following illustration is adduced:
He approached Gautama Hāridrumata and said, "I shall live as a religious student under your lordship; I would enter upon the service of your lordship. 3.

In that regard, concerning the transition into another body, this is the illustration: just as, in a certain manner, a *tṛṇajalāyukā* (a grass-leech) having gone to—that is, reached—the end or conclusion of a blade of grass, [seizes] another blade of grass, an "approach" (*ākrama*)—so called because it is approached—and having seized—that is, having taken hold of—that approach, it withdraws its own self, its former part, into the place of its final part.

In this very way, this self under discussion—the transmigrating self—having "struck down" this previously acquired body, as one desiring to enter a dream might do; having cast it off, having caused ignorance to depart, and having rendered it insentient by withdrawing its own nature, it takes up another course, like a caterpillar moving to another blade of grass, and grasping another body through an extended latent impression (*vāsanā*), it withdraws itself and initiates its own existence therein—just as in a dream, while still situated within another body, it begins the formation of a new body at the place of its commencement.

When a body—whether moving or stationary—is being produced, the instruments (the senses), having acquired their functional states through the power of karma, coalesce there; and an external body, comparable to grass or clay, is commenced. Then, with reference to that arrangement of instruments, the deities such as Agni resort to it to assist the organs of speech and so forth. This is the process for the commencement of another body.

Regarding whether, in the commencement of another body, one repeatedly destroys the very material already constantly possessed to begin a new body, or whether one takes up entirely new material again and again—in this regard, an illustration is stated:

He said to him, "Of what lineage are you, my dear? He replied, "I do not know this, sir, of what lineage I am. I asked my mother, and she answered me: 'In my youth, while I was wandering about as a servant, I conceived you; therefore, I do not know of what lineage you are. But I am Jabālā by name, and you are Satyakāma by name. So, sir, I am Satyakāma Jābāla. 4. (4) ---

In this regard, for this purpose, it is just as a peśaskārī—a *peśas* is gold, and one who works with it is a *peśaskārī*, a goldsmith—takes a portion of the *peśas*, that is, of the gold, having cut it off and taken it, fashions (*tanute*), that is, constructs, another form, newer than the previous one, more beautiful than the beautiful; "even so is this Self," and so forth, as before.

Having repeatedly destroyed those very five elements—earth and the rest, ending with space—which are eternally appropriated and were explained in the fourth chapter as "two indeed are the forms of Brahman," and which stand in the place of raw material (*peśas*), he fashions another and yet another newer and more beautiful form—a specific configuration, meaning another body—namely, either a *pitrya* form, beneficial for the ancestors, meaning suitable for enjoyment in the world of the ancestors, or a *gāndharva* form.

It creates another body—whether suitable for the enjoyment of Gandharvas, or divine for the gods, or pertaining to Prajāpati, or this [body] belonging to Brahmā, or according to one's karma and according to one's learning, or related to other beings—this is how it connects.

Those limiting adjuncts (upādhi) which are designated as its "bonds," by being joined with which it is perceived as "consisting of that"—those entities are here collectively pointed out together in one place.

He said to him: "A non-Brahmin does not deserve to speak thus. Fetch fuel, my dear; I will initiate you. You have not strayed from the truth. Having initiated him, he drove away four hundred lean and weak cows and said: "Follow these, my dear. As he was driving them forth, he said: "I shall not return until they have become a thousand. He lived away for many years, and when they had become a thousand— Thus ends the fourth section. 4. (5)

This very Self which thus transmigrates is indeed Brahman alone, the Supreme, who is beyond hunger and other such needs; it is "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*)—where *vijñāna* means the intellect (*buddhi*).

Being perceived by that [intellect], he consists of that; for it has been said: "Which is the Self? It is this which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) among the vital breaths. "Consisting of consciousness" means being predominantly consciousness, because its nature as having that quality is discerned in the passage: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were. Likewise, it is "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), being so called due to its close connection with the mind. Similarly, it is "consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*); the breath has five functions, and he consists of that, by which the conscious one appears to move. Likewise, it is "consisting of sight" (*cakṣurmaya*) at the time of perceiving forms.

In this way, at the time of hearing sound, it consists of the ear; likewise, when the activity of each respective sense organ arises, it becomes composed of that very organ. Thus, through the gateway of the intellect and the vital breath, being composed of the instruments such as the eye and so forth, it becomes composed of the elements such as earth that initiate the body; therein, in the initiation of an earthly body, it becomes composed of earth; similarly, in the worlds of Varuṇa and others, in the initiation of a watery body, it becomes composed of water; and similarly, in the initiation of an airy body, it becomes composed of air.

Likewise, at the commencement of a body made of space, one becomes composed of space; in this way, these divine bodies are fiery (*taijasa*); when they are being commenced, one becomes composed of that—that is, composed of fire (*tejomaya*). Therefore, distinct from these are the bodies of animals and the like, as well as the bodies of those in hell or among the *preta*s, which are not composed of fire; with reference to these, he says "not composed of fire" (*atejomaya*).

Thus, while consisting of the aggregate of causes and effects, the self—perceiving objects to be attained, thinking "this has been attained by me" and "that is to be attained by me"—possesses contrary notions and becomes filled with desire (*kāma-maya*). When one perceives the fault in that desire, and through the subsiding of the longing for its objects, the mind becomes clear, stainless, and tranquil; being absorbed in that state, one becomes "filled with the absence of desire" (*akāma-maya*).

Thus, when that desire has been thwarted by someone, one who possesses desire transforms into anger; becoming absorbed in that, he becomes "full of anger. When that anger is turned back by some means, then the mind, being clear and undisturbed, is called "non-anger," and he becomes absorbed in that. Thus, having become absorbed in desire and anger, and in the absence of desire and anger, he becomes full of dharma and full of adharma.

For indeed, without desire, anger, and the like, the engagement in dharma and so forth is not possible, according to the Smṛti: "Whatever action one performs, all that is the movement of desire. Having become composed of dharma and composed of adharma, one becomes composed of everything—that is, the entire effect of dharma and adharma; whatever is manifested, all that is the fruit of dharma and adharma, and by attaining that, one becomes identical with it.

In short, this is established for him: that since he consists of this—that is, he consists of the objects and so forth being perceived—therefore he consists of "that" (*adaḥ*); by "that," the remote is indicated through its effect which is being perceived. For there are infinite particularities of mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); they cannot be specified individually. At each respective moment, they are understood through their effects: "this is present in his heart," or "that is his."

By means of that perceived action, the imperceptible internal activity is designated through its identity with it—as "this person now consists of this. In brief, however, one whose nature it is to act or behave in a certain way is "one who acts and behaves accordingly"; he becomes exactly as he is. The distinction is that "acting" (*kāraṇa*) refers to a fixed action understood through injunctions, prohibitions, and so forth, while "behaving" (*caraṇa*) refers to what is not fixed. The phrase "one who does good becomes good" is a qualification of the term "one who acts accordingly."

Regarding the statement "one who performs evil becomes evil," which refers to the phrase "according to one's conduct" (*yathācārī*), the suffix denoting habitual action (*tācchīlya-pratyaya*) implies that being "consisting of that" (*tanmayatva*) means an absolute dedication to it, and not merely by performing that action once. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "One becomes virtuous through virtuous action and evil through evil action. [The opponent might argue: "Being 'consisting of that' would occur through the mere performance of virtuous or evil actions, and does not depend on habitual practice; however, when there is habitual practice, there is an excellence of being 'consisting of that'—this is the distinction. [The author replies: This is the specific point.

In this regard, the performance of meritorious and non-meritorious deeds preceded by desire, anger, and so forth, is the cause of being composed of everything (sarvamayatva), the cause of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), and the cause of the transition from one body to another body; for it is impelled by these that one assumes various different bodies. Therefore, merit and demerit are the cause of transmigratory existence; indeed, injunctions and prohibitions have these as their subject matter, and herein lies the efficacy of the scripture.
