Furthermore, others who are indeed skilled in the matter of bondage and liberation have said: "It is true that merit and demerit preceded by desire and so forth are the cause for the assumption of a body; nevertheless, it is the person impelled by desire who accumulates meritorious and non-meritorious actions. But when desire is abandoned, action—even if present—does not effect the accumulation of merit and demerit. Moreover, even though merit and demerit have been accumulated, they do not initiate their results in one devoid of desire. Therefore, desire alone is the root of saṃsāra."

And so it is said in the Atharvaṇa: "He who, thinking, desires desires, is born through those desires here and there. Therefore, this person consists of desire alone; as for his consisting of anything else, that is not the cause, even though it exists—hence he determines: "He consists of desire alone."

Because he, being composed of desire (*kāmamaya*), becomes "whatever his desire is" (*yathākāmaḥ*) through whatever desire he possesses, so does he become "resolved upon that" (*tatkratuḥ*). When that desire—which has been manifested by a mere slight longing—arises toward a particular object, it, remaining unimpeded and becoming manifest, attains the state of a *kratu*. A *kratu* is a determination or a resolve, immediately after which action proceeds.

"Whatever his resolve (*kratu*) is"—that is, whatever kind of resolve he has regarding the action to be performed, according to the form of that resolve; "whatever his resolve is"—he performs that action; whatever the object of his resolve may be, he performs and accomplishes that action which is appropriate for the production of its fruit. Whatever action he performs, that he attains—he attains its fruit. Therefore, in his state of consisting of all things and in his state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*), desire alone is the cause. (6)

Regarding that matter, there is this verse, which is also a mantra: "It comes to that very thing; it goes to that very thing"—meaning one who is attached, clinging, and whose desire has arisen for that.

The meaning is "it exists"; how does it go? Together with action—that is, together with that very action which he performed while being attached to its fruit—he goes to that fruit. What is that? It is the subtle body (*liṅga*), namely the mind; because the subtle body has the mind as its primary constituent, the mind is called the "subtle body. Alternatively, it is called *liṅga* because by it one is characterized (*liṅgyate*) or understood—that is, one perceives through it—and that is the mind. In whatever [object] this transmigrating being is firmly attached—meaning fixed with certainty and possessing an arisen desire—for that [object] he goes.

For it was through the desire for that [result] that one performed that action; therefore, it is solely by virtue of attachment of the mind (*manobhiṣaṅga*) to that [object] that one attains its fruit through that action. By this, it is established that desire is the root of saṃsāra. Consequently, even though actions exist, they become like the barren offspring of a woman who has lost her desire, for the knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*); as the Śruti says: "For one whose desires are fulfilled and whose self is perfected, all desires dissolve right here."

Furthermore, "having reached the end of his action"—meaning having reached the end, that is, the conclusion, by experiencing [the fruit] until the completion of the action's result; reaching the end of what action? It is said: of whatever action he performs or accomplishes here in this world, having experienced its fruit and reached its end, he returns again from that world to this world for the sake of action—for this world is indeed characterized primarily by action.

Therefore he says, "for action"—that is, for the performance of action once again. Having performed action again, one goes to this world once more due to attachment to its fruits—in this manner. Thus, indeed, desiring, one transmigrates. Since it is precisely by desiring that one thus transmigrates, therefore, one who does not desire does not transmigrate anywhere. For the destiny of one attached to results has been described; since action is impossible for one who is free from desire, one who does not desire is necessarily liberated.

But how does one become free from desire? He who is without desire (*akāma*) is one who is free from desiring (*akāmayamāna*). How is it said that he is without desire? One who is devoid of desire (*niṣkāma*)—from whom desires have departed—is "devoid of desire. How do desires depart? By being one whose desires are attained (*āptakāma*); he by whom desires have been attained is "one whose desires are attained. How are desires attained? Through the state of desiring the Self alone (*ātmakāmatva*); for him, the Self alone remains, and there is no other object existing as a separate entity to be desired.

The Self alone is without interior or exterior, entirely a mass of consciousness, a single essence. It is neither above, nor across, nor below. There is no other object whatsoever distinct from the Self that could be desired—by whom could one see whom, hear, think, or know, when everything has become the Self? Knowing thus, what could one desire? For it is only an object known as something "other" that becomes an object of desire; and for the knower of Brahman whose desires are fulfilled, there exists nothing else that is other.

He who, through the desire for the Self alone, has attained all desires, is free from desire, devoid of desire, and no longer desiring; thus he is liberated. For him, the Self alone becomes everything; there remains nothing non-Self that could be desired. And it is a contradiction to say that the non-Self is something other to be desired while at the same time everything has become the Self. Since there is no object of desire for one who perceives the Self in all, the performance of ritual action is impossible.

But as for those who, even though they are knowers of Brahman, imagine ritual action to be for the sake of avoiding transgression (*pratyavāya*), for them the Self alone does not become everything, because they intend something other than the Self—that which is to be abandoned, namely, transgression. And we call him a knower of Brahman by whom the Self has been known as transcending hunger and so forth, eternally unconnected with transgression; he perceives the Self as eternally transcending hunger and so forth.

Furthermore, for one who does not perceive anything else as either to be abandoned or to be acquired, action can by no means be connected to him. However, for one who is not a knower of Brahman, action certainly exists for the purpose of avoiding transgression; thus, there is no contradiction. Therefore, due to the absence of desire, one who is free from desire is not born again, but is indeed liberated.

For him who does not desire in this way, since there is an absence of action, there is an absence of a cause for departure; thus his vital breaths—speech and the others—do not depart, nor do they ascend out of the body. And that wise man, having attained all desires through the state of desiring only the Self, becomes Brahman even here. For this form has been shown as an illustration of Brahman, which is the Self of all.

"This, indeed, is his form in which all desires have been attained and which is free from desire"; for this is the point illustrated by the analogy that is summarized in the passage beginning with "Now, being without desire. How is such a person liberated? It is said: he who perceives the Self—which is like the state of deep sleep, devoid of distinctions, non-dual, and whose nature is the light of consciousness that never perishes—for him, being without desire, there is an absence of karma; and due to the absence of a cause for departure, the vital breaths, speech, and so forth, do not depart.

However, that wise one is Brahman even here, although he appears as if possessing a body; being Brahman already, he attains Brahman. Since there are no desires in him—which are the causes for the limitation of non-Brahmanhood—he attains Brahman while still here, being Brahman itself, and not at a time subsequent to the fall of the body. For the deceased knower does not undergo a transition to another state of existence, nor is his state different from what it was while living; rather, he is said to "attain Brahman" solely by virtue of the absence of the reconnection with another body.

For if liberation were the attainment of another state of being, the intended meaning of all the Upaniṣads—namely, the unity of the Self—would be subverted; furthermore, liberation would result from the cause of ritual action rather than from knowledge, which is undesirable. Moreover, impermanence would follow for liberation, because an object produced by action is never seen to be eternal; yet liberation is accepted as eternal, according to the Vedic mantra: "This is His eternal glory."

Furthermore, it is not possible to postulate anything else as eternal apart from an intrinsic nature (*svābhāvika*). If being [of a certain state] were the intrinsic nature of the self, like the heat of fire, then it could not be said to be experienced through human effort; for neither the heat nor the light of fire is experienced subsequent to an operation of the fire. To say that something is both experienced through the operation of fire and is intrinsic in nature is a contradiction.

If it is argued that heat and light are manifested through the operation of burning, we say no; for their manifestation depends upon the removal of the intervention of other perceived objects. Fire preceded by burning is manifested by its qualities of heat and light; this is not due to fire itself. Rather, the two attributes of heat and light belonging to fire are obstructed from being seen by others, yet they remain unconnected [to the observer] until, through the action of burning, the obstruction is removed and they become manifest to the sight.

In relation to that, an error arises: namely, that these two properties, heat and light, have arisen preceded by fire. If even heat and light did not possess an intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikatva*), then we would point out whatever property of fire is intrinsic; for it cannot be said that there are no intrinsic properties whatsoever among entities.

Furthermore, liberation cannot be understood as the cessation of bondage in the manner of the breaking of shackles, which would imply it is a non-existent entity; for we accept the oneness of the Supreme Self, based on the Vedic scripture stating, "One only, without a second. Nor is there any other bound being whose liberation could consist in the cessation of bondage, like the removal of shackles. We have already explained at length that nothing exists apart from the Supreme Self.

Therefore, we have also stated that the conventional usage of the term "liberation" refers merely to the cessation of ignorance, just as the disappearance of a snake occurs when the ignorance regarding a rope or similar object is removed.

As for those who assert that in liberation another consciousness and another bliss are manifested (*abhivyajyate*), they must explain the meaning of the word "manifestation. If the meaning of the word "manifestation" is simply the worldly apprehension that pervades its object, then it must be stated: is something already existing being manifested?

Or [it might mean] "non-existent. If it were existent, then for that liberated one in whom it is manifested, it would necessarily be his very self, because there could be no obstruction to its perception and because it is eternally manifest; thus, the specific statement that "it is manifested for the liberated one" would be meaningless. If, on the other hand, it is manifested only occasionally, then—due to the obstruction of perception—it would not be his self, which entails the consequence that it must be manifested by something else; and in that case, it would depend upon the means of manifestation.

However, if they share the same substratum as their apprehension, then since the postulation of an obstruction is untenable, there would be either perpetual manifestation or perpetual non-manifestation; there is no evidence for postulating an intermediate state. Furthermore, it is not possible for properties that share the same substratum and are identical with its essence to stand in the relation of subject and object to one another.

Furthermore, for one who holds that there is the state of being a transmigrator prior to the manifestation of consciousness and bliss, and the state of liberation subsequent to their manifestation, he would be other than the Supreme Self, whose nature is eternally manifest knowledge, because of their absolute difference—just as coldness differs from heat. Moreover, by postulating a distinction between the individual self and the Supreme Self, the established conclusion of the Vedas would be abandoned.

If it is argued that since liberation is now, as it were, devoid of any distinction, the exertion of greater effort for its sake would be untenable and the scripture would be rendered useless—this is not so, because [the scripture] aims at the removal of the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*). For in reality, there is no distinction between being liberated and being bound, since the Self (*ātman*) is eternally of a single nature; rather, the ignorance concerning it is removed by the higher knowledge (*vijñāna*) produced through the instruction of the scripture. Thus, prior to the attainment of that instruction, the exertion for its sake is indeed entirely appropriate.

If it is argued that there would be a distinction in the Self caused by the cessation or non-cessation of ignorance for one who possesses ignorance, we say no; for we have already stated that there is no fault, since it is admitted that [the distinction] is an object of the imagination of ignorance—just as the distinctions of a snake, water, silver, or impurity are attributed to a rope, a mirage, mother-of-pearl, or the sky respectively. If it is argued that there would be a distinction in the Self caused by being the agent of ignorance or not being the agent, like the difference between seeing with cataracts and seeing without them, we say no; because the agency of ignorance is denied of the Self in its own right by the text: "It meditates, as it were; it vibrates, as it were."

Furthermore, because the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā-bhrama*) arises from the convergence of multiple activities, and because its status as an object is logically established, one who perceives the delusion of ignorance as distinct—just like a jar or other objects—is not himself possessed of that delusion of ignorance. If it is argued that he is indeed possessed of the delusion of ignorance because we observe the cognition "I do not know" or "I am deluded," we say no, for even that [cognition] involves the grasping of a distinction. Indeed, one who perceives something by way of its distinction from another is not said to be deluded regarding that thing.

Furthermore, it is contradictory to say that there is the apprehension of distinction regarding that [state], yet there is delusion regarding that very same thing; for you claim that one sees, "I am deluded," and yet you also say that the ignorance and the state of being deluded are seen by the observer—that they become the object of that seeing, falling into the status of an objective effect.

In that case, how could ignorance—which is itself an object—be the qualifier of the seer (the subject) which is the agent? Or, if those two [ignorance and delusion] are qualifiers of the seer, how could they be objects—that is, how could they be pervaded by the seer? For an object is that which is pervaded by the action of the agent; moreover, the pervaded is one thing and the pervader is another; a thing cannot be pervaded by itself.

Tell me, this being so, how could ignorance and delusion be attributes of the Seer? Furthermore, one who perceives the distinction from ignorance, while apprehending ignorance as something belonging to the Self in the objective case, does not grasp it as an attribute of the perceiver—just as one does not grasp emaciation, form, and so forth in the body. If it is argued that everyone in the world grasps pleasure, pain, desire, effort, and the like [as attributes of the Self], even then, the distinctness of the person who grasps them must be admitted.

If you say, "I do not know what you have said because I am indeed deluded," let it be so that you are ignorant and deluded; however, we recognize as wise and undeluded one who perceives things in this way. Thus it has been stated by Vyāsa: "The Knower of the Field illumines the entire field, including desire and the rest," and "The Supreme Lord abiding in all beings—peaceful while they perish, He does not perish"—and so on, as has been stated hundreds of times.

Therefore, there is no distinction in the Self produced by its own bondage, liberation, knowledge, or ignorance, because it is admitted that its nature is always uniform and of a single essence. As for those who otherwise conceptualize the reality of the Self and reduce the scriptures concerning bondage, liberation, and so forth to mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), they might as well strive to see a bird's footprint in the sky, to seize the sky with their fists, or to wrap the sky like a piece of leather; we, however, are unable to do such things.

"We are indeed Brahman—the reality of the Self which is at all times equal, of one flavor, non-dual, changeless, unborn, undecaying, immortal, deathless, and fearless"—this is the meaning ascertained by all the Vedāntas, and thus we understand it. Therefore, the statement "one attains Brahman" is merely figurative; it refers only to the cessation of the continuity of the body, viewed from the perspective of the fruit of realization, just like the removal of a misconception.

The analogy of going from sleep to waking has been illustrated by the corresponding case of *saṃsāra*. Furthermore, the causes of *saṃsāra*—namely, ignorance (*avidyā*), action (*karman*), and prior cognition (*pūrvaprajñā*)—have been described. Those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the body and the organs, by being enveloped by which one experiences the state of transmigratory existence, have also been mentioned. Having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that merit and demerit (*dharmādharmau*) are the direct motivators of these [adjuncts], it is concluded that desire alone (*kāma eva*) is the cause.

Just as this matter was determined by the Brāhmaṇa, so too has it been [determined] by the Mantra; thus, having explained bondage and the cause of bondage, the section is concluded with the words, "Thus indeed for one who desires. Beginning with "But he who does not desire," liberation—which consists in becoming the Self of all—has been described as the illustration corresponding to the example of deep sleep.

Furthermore, that which was described as "having one's desires fulfilled" (*āptakāmatva*) by virtue of desiring the Self (*ātmakāmatā*) is the cause of liberation. And this, by implication, cannot be the fulfillment of desires through the desire for the Self without the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*). Thus, by implication, it is stated that the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) alone is the cause of liberation. Therefore, although it was said that desire is the root, nevertheless, by the very opposite of the cause of liberation, it is also effectively stated that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of bondage. Here too, both liberation and the means to liberation have been declared in the Brāhmaṇa; to further strengthen that point, a verse—referred to by the word *śloka*—is cited as a mantra: (7) ————
Regarding that very point, there is this verse, which is a mantra: "When—at which time—all desires, which are various forms of thirst, are completely released."

For the knower of Brahman who desires the Self, those well-known objects of pursuit in this world and the next—characterized by the desire for sons, wealth, and worlds—which had taken root and rested in the heart, that is, in the intellect of this well-known person, fall away entirely from the root. Then, at that time, though being mortal and subject to death, he becomes immortal through the total separation from desires. By implication, this means that desires directed toward the non-Self, which are characterized by ignorance, are themselves deaths.

Therefore, through liberation from death, the wise man becomes immortal even while living. Thus, remaining in this very body, he attains Brahman; the meaning is that he realizes the state of Brahman, which is liberation. Consequently, liberation does not depend upon going to another place or similar means. Therefore, the vital breaths (prāṇas) of the knower do not depart; they are simply merged into their own cause, the Person (puruṣa), as they were situated, for only the name remains—so it has been said.

But how is it that when the vital breaths have been completely withdrawn and the body has dissolved into its own cause, the liberated man of knowledge—who exists right here as the Self of all—does not again assume, as before, the state of being embodied characterized by transmigratory existence? To this it is said: in this regard, there is the following illustration.

Just as in the world there is a snake (*ahi*), its slough (*nirlvayanī*), that is, its skin-shedding (*nirmoka*); this slough, having been dead—that is, cast off, thrown away, and abandoned by the snake as no longer its own body—lies or remains in an anthill (*valmīka*), meaning in a place such as an anthill which is the snake's abode; even so, according to this illustration, this body, abandoned by the liberated one as no longer his own body—standing in the place of the snake—lies like something dead.

Now, the other, who corresponds to the snake, being liberated and having become the Self of all, remains in that very place like the snake; yet he is indeed bodiless (*aśarīra*), and does not again become embodied as before. For previously he was embodied and mortal by virtue of identifying with a body impelled by desire and action; through separation from that, he is now bodiless, and for that very reason, immortal.

Prāṇa: that which breathes is prāṇa—as in the verse to be cited later, "the breath of breath," and in another Śruti, "For the mind, O dear one, is fastened to prāṇa. By the force of both the context and the sentence, it is the Supreme Self alone that is denoted here by the word prāṇa; it is Brahman alone, the Supreme Self. What, then, is that? It is light itself, consciousness, the luminosity, by which the world, being illumined by the light of the Self, proceeds without falling away, having consciousness as its guide and possessing the light of discernment.

That question regarding desire (*kāmapraśna*) which was intended for liberation and granted as a boon by Yājñavalkya to Janaka—characterized by its cause, consisting of the nature of bondage and liberation, and existing as both the illustration and the illustrated—has now been determined in detail by the Śruti through the narrative form of the dialogue between Janaka and Yājñavalkya. Thus, the means for the liberation from saṃsāra has been declared for all living beings. Now, the Śruti itself says that Janaka spoke thus for the purpose of paying the fee for this knowledge (*vidyāniṣkraya*).

"How so? 'Having been thus liberated by you, O Blessed One, I give a thousand [cows] to you for the price of this knowledge'—thus indeed did Janaka of Videha speak. Here, since the matter of liberation has already been determined, why does he not offer the kingdom of Videha and his very self, but instead gives only a thousand [cows] as if it were a partial payment? What is the intention behind this?"

Regarding this, some explain as follows: Janaka is a connoisseur of the inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*); therefore, even though he has already heard the meaning, he listens further through mantras. For this reason, he does not disclose everything at once. He thinks, "Having heard what I desire from Yājñavalkya, I shall disclose it all at the end. Furthermore, out of fear that if he were to disclose everything right now, Yājñavalkya—thinking his desire for hearing had ceased—would not speak the verses, he gave a thousand [cows] to signal his intent to listen.

All of this is also incorrect, because it is impossible for the Veda—which, like a person, is an authoritative means of knowledge—to act with deceit; and because there remains a further purpose to be fulfilled. Even though the subject of liberation has been stated, there remains a portion of the subject matter to be explained: namely, the renunciation known as *saṃnyāsa*, which consists in the abandonment of all desires and serves as a means for the knowledge of the Self. Therefore, the assumption that [the text] merely intends to hear a single verse is unwarranted; for to assume a redundant meaning is a resort only when no other way is possible, and that is improper when another way exists.

And we have already stated that this is not mere praise. [Objection: If this were so, it should have been said, "From here on, solely for the sake of liberation. [Reply: This is not a fault; for he considers renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) to be, like the knowledge of the Self, non-necessary (*aprayojaka*) in one alternative, just like a rite of preparatory practice (*pratipattikarma*), as the Smṛti says: "One should cast off the body by means of renunciation. Even in the case where it is a means (*sādhana*), it does not deserve the question "From here on, solely for the sake of liberation," because its purpose is the ripening of the knowledge of the Self which constitutes the means to liberation. (8)

Regarding this matter stated in the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas—that liberation belongs to the knower of Brahman who desires the Self—these verses serve as a detailed exposition. [The Self is] *aṇu*, meaning subtle.

The path is "difficult to discern" because it is hard to understand; it is "stretched out" (vitata) because it is extensive, or alternatively, from the variant reading "vitara," because it is a means for clearly crossing over. It is the ancient (purāṇa), time-honored path of knowledge that is the means to liberation, revealed by the eternal Vedas; it is not a recent path born of the faulty views arising from the intellects of logicians. It has "touched me," meaning it was attained by me; for when something is obtained by someone, it is as if it touches him, being connected to him.

Therefore, because this path to liberation, characterized by the knowledge of Brahman, has been obtained by me, it is said to have "touched me. It was not merely obtained by me, but rather "realized by me alone" (*anuvitta*); realization (*anuvedana*) means the attainment of the finality and consummation of the fruit in accordance with the ripening of knowledge, just as eating results in the finality of satisfaction; the distinction is that previously there was merely a connection with the acquisition of knowledge.

Is it that this seer of the mantra alone attained the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman, and no one else, such that he asserts, "It has been found by me alone"? This is not a fault, because this statement is intended as a praise of the knowledge of Brahman, showing that its fruit is unsurpassed and realized through one's own self-evidence. For thus he praises the knowledge of Brahman: "Self-knowledge, which is witnessed by the conviction of the Self, brings about the realization of having achieved one's purpose; what else could there be beyond this?"

It is not, however, that another knower of Brahman does not attain that fruit, for there is a scriptural text of universal application stating, "Whosoever among the gods... He says this very thing: by that path of the knowledge of Brahman, the wise—meaning other knowers of Brahman as well—attain, they go to, the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman, which is liberation, the world of heaven (*svarga-loka*). Although the word *svargaloka* usually denotes the triple heaven, here, due to the context, it signifies liberation;
[they do so] from here, after the fall of this body, while still living, being liberated.

Regarding that path which is the means to liberation, there is a divergence of opinion among those seeking liberation. How so? Regarding that [path], some seekers of liberation say it is white—pure and stainless; others say it is blue; others say it is tawny, green, or red, according to their respective perceptions. Furthermore, these channels, such as the *suṣumnā* and others, are filled with the essences of phlegm and so forth, because it has been stated that they are "white, blue, tawny," and so on.

Some consider the path to liberation (*mokṣamārga*) to be the Sun, based on other scriptural passages such as, "This is white, this is blue," and so forth; for colors such as white and the like cannot possibly belong to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*). However, in any case, these [colors] such as white are distinct from the path of the knowledge of Brahman under discussion. [Objection: But surely "white" (*śukla*) means pure, referring to the non-dual path (*advaitamārga*)? [Reply: No, because it is followed by words denoting colors such as "blue" and "yellow"; those paths to liberation which the practitioners of yoga (*yogin*) call "white" and so forth are not actually paths to liberation.

For those [rays] belong precisely to the sphere of *saṃsāra*—because of their connection with emerging from parts of the body, as stated in [the passage], "either from the eye, or from the head, or from other parts of the body"—since they lead to the worlds of Brahmā and others.

Therefore, this alone is the path to liberation: since there is no further movement when all desires have perished due to the fulfillment of all desires, the dissolution of the eyes and other organs of action and perception occurs right here, like the extinguishing of a lamp. This is the path of knowledge, which was discovered by a Brāhmaṇa—one who has abandoned all longings—in his very nature as Brahman, the Supreme Self; by that path of the knowledge of Brahman, any other knower of Brahman also goes.

What kind of knower of Brahman goes by that path? It is said: having first been a doer of merit, and then having abandoned the desire for sons and other worldly goals, he unites his self with the splendor of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); having become perfected in That, he becomes of the nature of light (*taijasa*), meaning right here in this world. Such a knower of Brahman goes by that path. We have already stated that those who perform a combination of merit and other such acts are not included here, because of the contradiction; as it is said: "When merit and demerit have ceased, those who are free from the fear of rebirth [go there]."

And from the Smṛti: "The peaceful renunciants go [to that state]; salutation to Him, whose nature is liberation"; and because of the instruction to renounce merit and demerit, such as "Abandon both dharma and adharma"; and: "The gods know him to be a Brāhmaṇa who is free from desire, free from undertakings, free from salutations, and free from praise—one whose karma is exhausted and who is himself undecaying"; and: "There is no wealth for a Brāhmaṇa like this: oneness, equanimity, and truthfulness."

This is also supported by such Smṛti texts as: "Virtue is steadfastness, the laying aside of the rod [of punishment], uprightness, and desisting from activities here and there. Furthermore, in this very context, the text will teach: "This is the eternal greatness of a Brāhmaṇa; he does not increase by action, nor does he become less" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23). Having thus stated the reason for the absence of purpose in ritual action, it teaches the cessation of all activities with the words: "Therefore, knowing this, being calm and self-controlled," and so forth. Therefore, the state of being a doer of meritorious deeds is exactly as previously explained.

Alternatively, "he who knows Brahman goes by that [path]"—this is a praise of the knower of Brahman, implying he is a performer of meritorious deeds (*puṇyakṛt*) and one who is radiant (*taijasa*). In the world, great fortune is well-known to belong to the performer of meritorious deeds and to the yogi who is radiant; therefore, the knower of Brahman is praised here because his great fortune is renowned in the world.

They enter—that is, they fall into—the blinding darkness characterized by non-perception, which governs the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). Who are they? Those who "worship" ignorance—that is, that which is other than knowledge and characterized by the relationship between means and ends; the meaning is that they persist in ritual action (*karman*). From that [darkness], they enter what is even greater, as it were—a much deeper darkness. Who are they? Those who "delight"—that is, take pleasure—in "knowledge," namely in the triple Vedic knowledge (*trayī-vidyā*) intended for ritual action, which sets forth the objects of ignorance. The meaning is: those who disregard the purpose of the Upanishads, holding that the Veda consists solely of injunctions and prohibitions and nothing else. (11)

If they enter into that darkness characterized by non-perception, what is the fault? It is said: those worlds are called "joyless," "devoid of joy," and "unhappy. Enveloped and pervaded by that blind darkness characterized by non-perception, they become the domain of that darkness of ignorance; having died and passed away, they go to them.

They approach [death]; who? Those who are ignorant. Is it by ignorance in general, merely being unlearned? No, it is said: "abuddhaḥ" is a form derived from the root *budh*, meaning "to understand," with the suffix *kvip*; the meaning is those devoid of self-knowledge. "Janāḥ" refers to common people, or those whose nature is subject to birth. (12)

If one should know oneself—both oneself and others—as the knower of the desires of all living beings, abiding in the heart, transcending such attributes as hunger and thirst, then perhaps some among thousands [might do so]. The word "if" (*ced*) shows the rarity of the knowledge of the Self. How so? This supreme Self is the witness of the perceptions of all living beings, who has been described by "not this, not this" and so forth, than whom there is no other seer, hearer, thinker, or knower, who dwells equally in all beings, whose nature is eternally pure, awakened, and free—I am that.

The *puruṣa* is the Supreme Person. Desiring what? Desiring what other object existing apart from His own nature as a fruit; or for the sake of what other desire or purpose belonging to another self distinct from Himself? For there is no fruit to be desired by that Self, nor is there anyone other than the Self for whose sake He might desire anything, since everything has become the Self.

Therefore, desiring what, or for whose sake, would one cause the body to suffer, fall away, or become miserable by following the suffering caused by the limiting adjunct of the body, or burn with the heat of the body? For one who does not perceive the Self, who desires another object distinct from that [Self] and strives thus—"May this be mine," "this be for my son," "this be for my wife"—is bound to the continuous succession of birth and death and is pained by the disease of the body. But for one who perceives the Self as all, such [suffering] is impossible; this is what is stated here.

Furthermore, that Brahmin for whom the Self has been "found" (*anuvitta*)—that is, attained—and "awakened to" (*pratibuddha*), realized directly; how so? Realized as the innermost Self (*pratyagātman*) in the form "I am the Supreme Brahman"—and who has entered this "body" (*saṃdehya*), which is a dense thicket of doubt, a mass of many calamities and difficulties, a treacherous wilderness opposed by hundreds of thousands of obstacles to discriminative knowledge; he, for whom the Self has been found through awakening—that Brahmin is the creator of the universe (*viśvakṛt*).

Anticipating the question, "In what sense is he the maker of all (viśvakṛt), and why is his name 'the Maker of All'? the text says: For he is the creator of everything, not merely in name; he is not only the maker of all acting under the direction of another, but rather, the entire world is his. Is it said that the world is one thing and he is another? No; he is indeed the world itself. By the word "world" (loka), the Self (ātman) is meant; the meaning is that his entire self is everything, and he is the self of everything.

This very Self, which has been realized by the Brahmin through awakening as the innermost Self—that Self who had entered into the dense thicket of the perilous mass of misfortune—is not a transmigrating being, but rather the Supreme alone; for He is the creator of the universe and the Self of all, and all is His Self. The meaning of the verse is that one should contemplate: "I am indeed the one, without a second, the Supreme alone.

Moreover, even here in this world, which is crowded with manifold misfortunes, you virtuous ones, though deluded by the long sleep of ignorance, have somehow, as it were, realized the reality of Brahman as the Self—that very Brahman under discussion; thus the intention is: "Ah, we have achieved our life's purpose!"

If we had not known this Brahman—which we do know—then we would have been "avedi. *Veda* means knowledge; one who possesses *veda* is a *vedī*. That which is to be known (*vedya*) itself is *vedi*; that which is not *vedi* is *avedi*. Thus, I would have been *avedi*. If I were *avedi*, what would be the fault? There would be a great destruction, characterized by birth, death, and so forth, of infinite extent. The meaning is: "Oh, how we have been liberated from this great destruction, in that we have known the non-dual Brahman!"

And just as we, having known Brahman, have been liberated from this place of destruction, so too those who know It become immortal. But those others—meaning those different from the knowers of Brahman, i.e., the non-knowers of Brahman—who do not thus know Brahman, they enter into, that is, undergo, only suffering characterized by birth, death, and so forth; the meaning is that there is never any cessation for the ignorant from that state, for they indeed regard suffering itself as the Self.

But when, having somehow obtained a certain teacher who is supremely compassionate, he gains grace from him and subsequently sees—that is, realizes—his own self as a god (*deva*), one who is luminous or the giver of the fruits of the actions of all living beings according to their respective karma; directly and immediately as the Lord (*īśāna*), the master of the past and the future—that is, of the three periods of time—he does not thereafter feel any particular loathing for himself on account of that divine Lord.

He desires to protect himself. For everyone in the world who perceives duality desires protection from the Lord; but this one, perceiving unity, fears nothing from anywhere. Therefore, he does not feel aversion when he sees the Lord God directly as his own Self. At that time, he does not revile anyone, for he sees everything as the Self; seeing thus, whom would he revile?

(16) Furthermore, because [everything] is prior to the Lord—meaning it has no other object than Him—the year, which is the self of time, is the delimiting factor of all that is born, [and it is He whom...]

Not delimiting [it], it exists only as that which is proximate—by means of "days," that is, its own parts, meaning by days and nights. That is the "light of lights," because it is the illuminator even of the lights such as the sun and others. The gods meditate upon it as "life" (*āyus*) and as "immortal light. Other than this, everything dies; for light does not die. Indeed, this light is the life of all. Since the gods meditate upon that light with the attribute of life, they are long-lived. Therefore, the meaning is that Brahman should be meditated upon with the attribute of life by one who desires longevity. (17)

Furthermore, that Brahman in which the five groups of five—namely, the Gandharvas and others counted as five, or the Pitṛs, Devas, Asuras, Rakṣasas, and Niṣādas as the fifth, or the social orders with the Niṣādas as the fifth—and the unevolved space (avyākṛtākāśa) are woven like warp and woof, and in which [all] is established; that in which, O Gārgī, it was said "the space is woven," that very Self, the immortal Brahman, I consider to be myself, and I do not know myself as being anything other than that.
What then? Being a knower of Brahman, I am immortal; however, through mere ignorance, I was mortal. With the departure of that [ignorance], as a knower, I am indeed immortal.

Furthermore, it is because the vital breath (prāṇa), being illumined by that light of the conscious Self which has become its own essence, breathes; therefore, He is the "breath of the breath. Likewise, He is the "eye of the eye" and the "ear of the ear. For it is only when presided over by the power of Brahman that the eyes and other organs possess the capacity for seeing and so forth; by themselves, they are like wood or clods of earth, devoid of the light of the conscious Self.

Those who know that "the mind is also the mind"—that is, those who know the inner self (pratyagātman), whose existence is inferred from the activities of the eyes and other senses, and who do not know it as an object—they have truly known (nicikyuḥ), that is, they have ascertained with certainty, Brahman, the ancient (purāṇa), the eternal, and the foremost (agrya), existing from the beginning. For it is said in the Atharva Veda: "That which those who know the Self know.

The means for the vision of that Brahman is stated: it is to be perceived by the mind alone, which has been refined by the knowledge of the supreme reality and preceded by the instruction of a teacher. And regarding that Brahman, the object of vision, there is not even the slightest diversity here at all. Since diversity does not exist, one superimposes diversity through ignorance (*avidyā*). Such a person, from death to death—that is, he incurs further death—who sees here as if there were diversity. The meaning is that apart from the superimposition of ignorance, there is no duality in the ultimate sense. (20)

Since this is so, therefore it should be perceived in one way alone—that is, in a single manner, as a mass of consciousness of a uniform nature, continuous like space. For this Brahman is immeasurable (*apramaya*), being beyond measurement because it is the oneness of all; for by one thing another is measured, but this is only one, and therefore it is immeasurable. It is "fixed" (*dhruvam*), meaning eternal, immutable, and immovable. Now, is it not a contradiction to say that it is "immeasurable" and yet "is known"?

The term ‘is known’ (jñāyate) means that it is measured by the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), while ‘immeasurable’ (aprameya) is the negation of that; this is not a fault, because its purpose is to negate being an object of valid cognition through scripture (āgama-pramāṇa) in the same way as other things. Just as other entities are made objects of cognitions independent of scripture, the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) cannot be made an object by any other means of valid cognition in that manner.

If everything were the Self, who could see whom, or what could one cognize? Thus, the scripture (*āgama*) itself makes this known precisely by negating the operations of the knower, the means of knowledge, and so forth, and not by accepting the properties of a sentence characterized by the relationship between signifier and signified. Therefore, it is not established by scripture in the same manner as heaven or Mount Meru; for that [Self] is the very essence of the one who establishes it, since the act of establishing and the establisher both have the object to be established as their domain, which occurs only when there is a distinction [between them].

And knowledge regarding that [Self] is simply the cessation of the conception of another self; one does not need to effect the manifestation of the Self in it directly, because the manifestation of the Self already exists. For the manifestation of the Self is eternal for everyone, yet it appears as if it were not directed toward that [Self]. Therefore, no manifestation of the Self is enjoined in it other than the cessation of the appearance of what is not that [Self]. When the conception of another self ceases, that manifestation of the Self which is innate to itself becomes solitary; thus it is said, "the Self is known."

That it is not an object of knowledge by itself and is not made an object by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—both of these are entirely non-contradictory. "Dustless" (*virajaḥ*) means free from dust; "dust" (*rajaḥ*) refers to the impurities of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), and he is devoid of that. "Supreme" (*paraḥ*) means distinct, subtle, or pervasive, even more so than space known as the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*). "Unborn" (*ajaḥ*) means he is not born; by the negation of birth, the subsequent modifications of being are also negated, since all of them begin with birth. "Self" (*ātman*); "great" (*mahān*) in terms of magnitude, greater than everything. "Firm" (*dhruvaḥ*) means indestructible. (21)

Having understood this very Self as such, through both instruction and scripture, the wise and intelligent Brāhmaṇa should cultivate wisdom—that which has as its object what is taught by scripture and teacher, and which brings the inquiry to completion. Thus, the means for cultivating wisdom are renunciation, tranquility, self-control, withdrawal, forbearance, and concentration.

The meaning is that one should act [in this way]. One should not meditate upon, nor contemplate, many—that is, numerous—words. Since multiplicity is here prohibited, only a few words that establish the absolute oneness of the Self are permitted; as it says in the *Ātharvaṇa*: "Meditate on the Self with the syllable 'Om' alone," and "Abandon other words. For the excessive proliferation of speech (*vāco viglāpanam*) causes exhaustion and fatigue, because such contemplation involves many words.

Bondage and liberation have been declared by both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas to be accompanied by causes; furthermore, the true nature of liberation has been explained in detail through verses. Thus, this section is commenced for the purpose of explaining how the entire Veda is to be applied to this subject of the Self.

And having restated with its purpose that which was declared in this chapter, the passage beginning with "For he is this" (*sa vā eṣa*) serves the purpose of showing the application of the entire Veda—excluding the collection of optional rites (*kāmyarāśi*)—to this very [knowledge]. The word "he" (*sa*) is used for the purpose of referring back to what has been stated. To which two sheaths (*kośau*) does it refer? He points it out: "He who consists of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*). This is said so that there may be no confusion with the understanding expressed in the immediately preceding sentence; it refers to "he who is this."

What is this? It is said: "consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths. This reference to the previously stated sentence is for the purpose of removing doubt, for it was indeed stated earlier at the beginning of Janaka's question: "Which is the Self? That which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths," and so forth.

This is what is meant: this very Self-luminous Self, who was presented by the passage beginning with "consisting of consciousness, among the vital breaths," has been liberated by means of establishing that desire, action, and ignorance are not attributes of the Self, and has been brought to the state of the Supreme Self—it is said that "this is the Supreme itself, not another"; he is explicitly called "the Great Unborn Self. As for the phrase "this one consisting of consciousness, among the vital breaths," its meaning is exactly as previously explained.

This which is within the heart—in the center of the lotus of the heart—is this space that serves as the substratum for the cognition of the intellect (*buddhi-vijñāna*). In that space, accompanied by the cognition of the intellect, he lies or abides. Alternatively, at the time of supreme serenity (*saṃprasāda*), this space within the heart is the Supreme Self itself, free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), the very essential nature (*svasvabhāva*) of that which consists of cognition. He lies in that essential nature, the Supreme Self known as space. This was explained in the fourth chapter as the answer to the question, "Where was he then? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.4).

And he is the controller (*vaśī*) of everything, including Brahmā, Indra, and the rest; for everything remains under his control, as it has been said: "Under the governance of this very Imperishable. He is not merely a controller, but the sovereign (*īśāna*) and ruler (*īśitā*) of all, including Brahmā, Indra, and others. Lest it be thought that his rulership is merely due to birth—as in the case of a prince who rules even over servants more powerful than himself—he says: "The Lord of all (*sarvasyādhipatiḥ*)," meaning one who protects by presiding over all, and thus independent.

He is not dependent on servants such as ministers like a prince. These three—mastery (*vaśitva*) and so forth—are related as cause and effect: because he is the sovereign (*adhipati*) of all, therefore he is the lord (*īśāna*) of all; for it is well known that whoever protects someone by presiding over them is indeed the master of that person; and because he is the lord of all, therefore he is the master (*vaśin*) of all.

Furthermore, this person consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), who is such a one—the inner light within the heart—does not become greater by means of "good" action performed according to the injunctions of the scriptures; he does not increase through any attribute from his prior state. Nor indeed does he become smaller—that is, more diminished—by "bad" action prohibited by the scriptures; the meaning is that he does not decrease from his prior state. Moreover, everyone who performs the protection of subjects and so forth becomes joined with what is called merit and demerit, produced by the favor or injury done to others.

But how is it that there is an absence of that [karma] for him? It is said: because he, being the Lord of all (*sarveśvara*), indeed possesses the nature of being able to govern even karma; therefore, he is not bound by karma. Furthermore, he is the "Lord of beings" (*bhūtādhipati*); this term has the meaning already explained, namely, the Lord of all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. He is the "Protector of beings" (*bhūtānām patiḥ*), their guardian and preserver. He is the "Bridge" (*setu*); to specify what kind of bridge, it is said: "the Sustainer" (*vidharaṇaḥ*), the one who maintains the established order of the castes, stages of life, and so forth.

Regarding this, he says: "For the non-confusion of these worlds, beginning with the earth and ending with the world of Brahmā"—that is, for the sake of their undisturbed boundaries. If they were not held up by the Supreme Lord like a dam, the worlds would have their boundaries broken. Therefore, the Supreme Lord, who is himself the self that is its own light, acts as a dam for the non-confusion of the worlds. He who knows this is the controller of all—this is the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman thus specified.

In this very knowledge of Brahman—which is prescribed in the sixth chapter beginning with "Of what light is this person? and which yields such a fruit—the entire section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*), excluding only those parts pertaining to optional rites, is employed for that purpose. How so? It is said: "They seek to know" (*vividiṣanti*)—that is, they desire to know—"this very person of the Upanishads" (*aupaniṣadaṃ puruṣam*) who is of such a nature, "by means of Vedic recitation" (*vedānuvacanena*), characterized by the constant study of the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas* (the daily recitation of one's own Veda); who [seek to know]? The Brāhmaṇas.

The mention of the *brāhmaṇa* is intended as an illustration; for the qualification [to study] is indeed common to all three castes. Alternatively, they desire to know through the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), consisting of the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas*, and through the recitation of the Vedas. To the question "How do they desire to know?", it is said: "By sacrifice," and so forth.

Furthermore, as for those who explain [the passage] thus: "They desire to know that which is being manifested by the recitation of the Vedas characterized by the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas"—for them, the "recitation of the Vedas" (vedānuvacana) would consist only of the Āraṇyakas; for the Supreme Self is not manifested by the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), given the specific scriptural statement, "That which is based on the Upaniṣads" (tattvaupaniṣadam). Moreover, because the phrase "by the recitation of the Vedas" is unqualified, this expression must be understood as referring to the Vedas in their entirety; and it is not proper to exclude a single part of them. [Objection: But even in your own position, would it not be the case that [the term refers to everything] except the Upaniṣads?

It might be argued that [the term *vedānuvacana*] would refer only to a part [of the Veda]; this is not so, because there is no contradiction in our first interpretation. This fault does not apply to our position: when the constant recitation of one's own Veda (*nitya-svādhyāya*) is enjoined by the word *vedānuvacana*, the Upanishads are thereby included as well; thus, no part of the meaning of the word *vedānuvacana* is abandoned. Furthermore, because of its mention alongside sacrifices and other rites—since the author employs the word *vedānuvacana* while intending to enumerate sacrificial acts and the like—it is understood that the word *vedānuvacana* denotes ritual action alone; for the constant recitation of one's own Veda is indeed a form of ritual action.

But how, again, do they desire to know the Self through such acts as the constant recitation of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*)? For these [acts] certainly do not reveal the Self in the same way that the Upaniṣads do. This is not a fault, because these acts are the cause of purification. For those whose selves have been purified by the refinement (*saṃskāra*) brought about by ritual acts are able to know the Self—revealed by the Upaniṣads—without obstruction. Thus it is said in the Atharva Veda: "But one whose being (*sattva*) is purified then beholds Him who is partless."

"while meditating"; and there is also the Smṛti: "Knowledge arises in men from the destruction of sinful karma," and so forth. But how is it understood that obligatory rites (*nitya-karmāṇi*) are for the purpose of purification (*saṃskāra*)? From such Śruti as: "He indeed is a self-sacrificer (*ātmayājī*) who knows: 'By this [rite] this limb of mine is purified; by this [rite] this limb of mine is established,'" and so on; and because all the Smṛti scriptures declare that rites are indeed for the purpose of purification, in passages such as "the forty-eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*)," and so forth.

And in the Gītā: "Sacrifice, charity, and austerity are indeed the purifiers of the wise. All these are knowers of sacrifice, whose taints have been destroyed by sacrifice. Regarding the phrase "by sacrifice": sacrifices of material objects and sacrifices of knowledge are for the purpose of purification; and for one who has been purified and whose being is cleansed, the arising of knowledge will occur without obstruction. Therefore, they desire to know through sacrifice. Regarding "by charity": charity also, because it is a cause for the destruction of evil and a cause for the increase of merit.

Regarding "by austerity" (*tapasā*): since the term "austerity" (*tapaḥ*) is used without qualification, it might be understood as referring generally to *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such rites; therefore, a specification is provided by the word "fasting" (*anāśakena*). Fasting (*anāśaka*) means the non-eating of desired things, but not the total cessation of eating; for if there were a total cessation of eating, one would simply die, rather than attaining self-knowledge. By the compound "Vedic recitation, sacrifice, charity, and austerity," all obligatory (*nitya*) ritual action is indicated. Thus, the entire collection of obligatory rites, excluding those performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), attains the status of being a means to liberation by way of generating self-knowledge.

Thus, its syntactic unity with the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) is understood. In this way, by the reasoning already stated, having known this very Self as it has been revealed, one becomes a sage (*muni*); "sage" because of his capacity for reflection (*manana*), meaning he becomes a yogi. It is only by knowing this very [Self] that one becomes a sage, not by knowing anything else. Now, one might object: "Could one not become a sage even by knowing something else? How is it determined that it is 'this very' [Self]? Certainly, one could become a sage even by knowing something else.

However, if there were knowledge of anything other than this, one would not be a sage (*muni*); rather, he would be a mere performer of ritual action (*karmī*). But by knowing this very Person taught in the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣada-puruṣa*), one becomes a sage indeed, and no longer a performer of action. Therefore, the author emphasizes that what is intended here is the sagehood that is unique [to this state], by saying "this very one. For when this is known, since activities such as "who could see whom" are impossible, there remains only the state of contemplation (*manana*).

Furthermore, desiring and praying for this very Self as their own world, those who have gone forth—those whose nature is renunciation—go forth; that is to say, they completely renounce all actions. From the restrictive emphasis in the phrase "desiring this very world," it is understood that those who desire the three external worlds have no qualification for the life of a wandering mendicant (pārivrājya); for one who wishes to reach Gaṅgādvāra does not set out facing east while residing in the region of Kāśī.

Therefore, for those who seek the three external worlds, the means [of attainment] are the son, ritual action (*karman*), and the knowledge of the lower Brahman (*aparabrahmavidyā*), according to such scriptural passages as, "By a son this world is to be conquered, not by any other action. Consequently, it is not proper for those seeking that [world] to renounce the means consisting of the son and so forth and instead adopt the life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*), because the life of a wandering mendicant is not a means for that end. Therefore, the restrictive statement, "Desiring this very world, they go forth," is appropriate.

For the attainment of the world that is the Self is simply abiding in one's own Self once ignorance has been removed. Therefore, for one who desires the world that is the Self, the cessation of all ritual action is the primary and internal means for attaining the world of the Self; just as sons and so forth are the means for the three external worlds, since actions such as procreating sons are not means toward the world of the Self. And we have already stated that [action] is contradictory [to this goal] because it is impossible [to achieve it through action].

Therefore, those who desire the world of the Self must indeed go forth as renunciants; the meaning is that they must desist from all ritual actions. Just as for those seeking the three external worlds, specific means such as sons and so forth are prescribed, even so for those seeking the world of the Self, the renunciation of all desires in the form of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) is indeed ordained for the knower of Brahman. But why is it said that those seekers of the world of the Self must go forth? It is stated as follows:

In this regard, he shows the reason by means of an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*): "For indeed, this was so. This is stated as the reason for wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*): "Indeed, it is said that the ancient sages of the past—those who were wise and possessed self-knowledge—[abandoned] progeny, work, and the knowledge of the lower Brahman. For these three, characterized by "progeny," are pointed out as the means for attaining the three external worlds in the passage "progeny" (*prajām*).

"Offspring"—what does this mean? It means they do not desire it; that is to say, they do not practice the means for attaining the three worlds, such as sons and so forth. But surely they do practice the vision of the lower Brahman (*apara-brahman*), for it is by the power of that [vision] that they renounce worldly life—is this not so? No, because of the following sublation (*apavāda*): "Brahman would desert him who knows Brahman as other than the Self," and "Everything would desert him..."—thus even the vision of the lower Brahman is indeed sublated, since everything, including the lower Brahman, is contained within "all"; and also because of the passage: "Where one sees nothing else."

And because of the negation of seeing what is prior or posterior, external or internal—expressed as "without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior"—and because of the statement, "Then by what means could one see whom? What could one know?", therefore, there is no need to depend upon any other cause for emergence apart from the vision of the Self. But what is their intention? It is said: "What purpose, what fruit, what goal shall we accomplish by means of progeny? For progeny is known to be a means for attaining the external world."

And that external world does not exist for us as something distinct from our own self; for everything is indeed our very self, and we are the self of all. Furthermore, because it is the self, the self cannot be produced, obtained, modified, or refined by any means of purification (*sādhana*). As for the claim that ritual action is for the sake of purifying the self-sacrificer, that too pertains only to the view of the self as consisting of the body and the organs, since there are scriptural texts concerning the relationship between limbs and the possessor of limbs, such as: "By this [act], this limb of mine is purified."

For one who perceives the uninterrupted, single-flavored mass of consciousness, the perception of the distinction between the parts and the whole, or the superimposition of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), is impossible. Therefore, we shall achieve nothing by means of offspring and other such instruments; for that fruit which is to be accomplished through offspring and other instruments belongs only to the ignorant. Indeed, it is not reasonable for one who perceives water in a mirage to engage in activity for the purpose of drinking that water, even if he subsequently perceives that there is merely a salt-flat and an absence of water.

The intention is this: for us as well—who perceive the world of the Self from the perspective of ultimate reality—it is not proper to engage in activity directed toward ends such as progeny, which are accomplished by means such as ritual acts, and which are like a mirage and fall within the range of the vision of the ignorant. This is what is being said: for us, who perceive the ultimate reality, this Self is free from hunger and other such needs, is unchangeable by the good or the evil, and this is the world that is intended as the fruit.

Furthermore, no means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) need be sought for this Self, which is entirely free from all the attributes of transmigratory existence such as the goal and the means; for it is only for that which is yet to be accomplished that one seeks a means. To seek a means for that which is not to be accomplished would be like attempting to cross dry land with the idea that it is water, or like searching for the tracks of a bird in the sky. Therefore, having known this Self, the Brahmins should indeed renounce the world; the meaning is that they should not undertake ritual action, because the ancient Brahmins who were thus enlightened acted in this way.

Not desiring offspring, they thus censured the conventional practice of the relationship between means and ends, considering that "this belongs to the realm of the ignorant. What did they do? It is said: "Having indeed risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, they then lived the life of mendicants," and so forth, as has already been explained.

Therefore, the injunction "those desiring the Self and the world should go forth, they should go forth" is consistent with the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); for it is not possible that this [injunction], together with its explanatory passage, should be directed toward the mere praise of the world. Indeed, the subsequent text beginning with "This, indeed, they say... is of the nature of an explanatory passage for the word "they go forth. If it were merely an explanatory passage, it would not require another explanatory passage; however, the phrase "they go forth" does require the explanatory passage beginning with "This, indeed, they say...".

Since the wise men of old, having desisted from activities such as procreation, indeed went forth into the life of renunciation (*pravrajita*), therefore those of the present day also go forth and should go forth—it being construed in this manner, [the text] cannot be intended merely for worldly praise; for we have already stated this by saying, "because of the instruction that they share the same agent as knowledge," and so on, and also because of its recitation together with "the study of the Vedas" (*vedānuvacana*) and other such acts.

Just as the study of the Vedas and other such acts, which are enjoined as means for the realization of the Self, possess literal truth and are not mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), so too it is improper to regard renunciation (*pārivrājya*), which is mentioned alongside them as a means for attaining the world of the Self, as being merely an *arthavāda*. This is also because there is an instruction regarding a distinct division of results.

By the statement, "Having known this very Self as the world," the text distinguishes the Self from any other external world by presenting it as a distinct result—just as it is said, "This world is to be won only through a son, not by any other ritual act; the world of the fathers is won through ritual acts. Nor can the phrase "those who renounce" be taken merely as a praise of the world already attained, nor can it be regarded as a subordinate explanatory passage (arthavāda) dependent on a primary injunction, for if it were so, it would have been mentioned only once. Therefore, the notion that this is merely a praise of the world is simply an error.

Nor is praise appropriate by means of the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) as something to be practiced. If wandering mendicancy, even while being something to be practiced, were intended for the sake of praising something else, then the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) and other such practices would also have to be considered for the sake of praise. Furthermore, no obligation to perform it is known from any other source than this context, such that it could here serve merely as praise. If, on the other hand, an injunction for wandering mendicancy were to be postulated anywhere, it is only here that it can be primary, not elsewhere.

Furthermore, if wandering mendicancy were to be postulated for a subject that is not its proper domain, then even such acts as climbing trees and so forth would have to be postulated as forms of wandering mendicancy, since there is no difference in their being unascertained as duties. Therefore, it is impossible to postulate even a trace of eulogy here.

If this world of the Self is desired, why should one not simply undertake ritual actions (*karmāṇi*) as the means for attaining it, rather than adopting the life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*)? To this it is replied: because this world of the Self has no connection with ritual actions. That Self which they desire and for whose sake they would renounce the world is not connected with ritual actions in any way—neither as a means, nor as a result, nor even as something to be produced or by any other such category.

Therefore, this very Self is characterized as "not this, not this," "ungraspable, for it is not grasped," and so forth; because the Self is thus characterized—being unrelated to the means or fruits of action, distinct from all the attributes of transmigratory existence, beyond hunger and other such states, possessing attributes such as being "not gross" and so on, unborn, undecaying, immortal, deathless, fearless, having the nature of a single essence of consciousness like a mass of salt, self-luminous, one alone without a second, without prior or posterior, without interior or exterior—this has been established through both scripture and reasoning.

This is especially so in this dialogue between Janaka and Yājñavalkya. Therefore, when the Self is known in this manner—as the Self—no undertaking of ritual action is at all appropriate. Consequently, the Self is without distinctions. For one who possesses sight and has set out on a path does not fall into a well or upon a thorn during the day; and because the fruit of the entire range of ritual action is included within the fruit of knowledge, a wise person does not exert effort toward an object that is attained without effort.

"If one should find honey in the hem of one's garment, why would he go to the mountain? When the desired object has been attained, what wise man would exert effort? "O Pārtha, all action in its entirety culminates in knowledge"—thus it is said in the *Gītā*. And here too, it is stated that other beings subsist only on a fraction of this very supreme bliss which is attained by the knower of Brahman. Therefore, those who know Brahman do not undertake ritual action.

Since he has desisted from all desires and, having approached the Self as "not this, not this" (neti neti) by identifying with that very nature, he abides in that form alone; therefore, these two which are about to be mentioned do not overcome—that is, do not reach—him who knows thus and has become the Self characterized as "not this, not this. This is indeed logical, such is the completion of the sentence. What are those two? It is said:

Therefore, on account of this cause—namely, for the purpose of maintaining the body and so forth—I have performed a sinful, non-meritorious act. "Alas, my conduct has indeed been wretched; by this sinful deed I shall fall into hell"—this remorse which arises later in one who has committed a sinful act does not cross over that Self which is of the nature of "not this, not this."

Likewise, because of this cause—the desire for auspicious results—he has performed meritorious and beautiful actions characterized by sacrifice, charity, and so forth, thinking, "Therefore, I shall enjoy the fruit of this, namely happiness, in another body"—this joy also does not transcend him. Indeed, this knower of Brahman transcends both these types of action, characterized by merit and demerit.

Thus, for the knower of Brahman who has renounced, both types of karma are exhausted—those performed in previous births and those performed in this birth—and no new karma is commenced. Furthermore, "neither what is done nor what is left undone" affects him: "done" refers to the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya-anuṣṭhāna*), and "left undone" refers to the non-performance of those very same rites; these two, "done and undone," do not afflict him. For one who does not know the Self, the "done" afflicts by yielding its fruit, and the "left undone" afflicts by producing sin (*pratyavāya*).

But this knower of Brahman reduces all actions to ashes by means of the fire of the knowledge of the Self, according to the Smṛti passage beginning with, "As a well-kindled fire [consumes] pieces of wood"; however, the two [actions] that have already begun to produce a body are exhausted only through experience. Therefore, the knower of Brahman is no longer connected with action.

This very matter has been stated by the Brāhmaṇa and expressed—that is, revealed—by means of a verse (ṛc) and a mantra. This greatness, characterized as "not this, not this" (neti neti), is eternal; whereas other forms of greatness are produced by action and are therefore non-eternal. But this greatness is distinct from them and is eternal because it is innate, belonging to the knower of Brahman, the Brāhmaṇa who has renounced all desires. To provide the reason for its eternity, he says: "It does not increase through action"—that is, by performing auspicious deeds, it does not undergo any modification characterized by growth.

By means of impure action, he does not become diminished, nor does he undergo any transformation characterized by decay; for all transformations are indeed caused by increase and decrease, and these two are here negated. Therefore, because it is immutable, this majesty is eternal. Consequently, one who knows that very majesty—being a "knower of the path" (*padavit*), meaning a knower of the path (*pada*)—[attains it]; for the "path" (*pada*) is the very nature of that majesty, since it is that which is reached, traversed, and known. One who is the knower of that path [is called *padavit*].

What would result from the knowledge of that state? It is said: having known that majesty, one is not smeared—that is, one is not bound—by evil action characterized as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*); for the knower, both are indeed equally evil.

Since this greatness of the Brāhmaṇa—characterized by "not this, not this" and so forth—is thus unrelated to action, therefore one who knows this should be tranquil, being pacified from the activity of the external senses; likewise, self-controlled, having turned away from the thirst of the internal organ; withdrawn, being a renunciant liberated from all desires; patient, enduring the pairs of opposites; and composed, having become concentrated in the form of one-pointedness by turning away from the movement of the senses and the internal organ.

This has been stated previously: "Having become disillusioned with both childhood and panditya. He sees the Self—the inward conscious perceiver—within his own self, that is, within the aggregate of the body and the organs. In that regard, is it merely that much which is delimited? No, it is said: he sees everything, the whole, as the Self alone; he sees that there is nothing else whatsoever distinct from the Self, not even as much as the tip of a hair. Because of this contemplation (manana), he becomes a sage (muni), having abandoned the three states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

Sin, characterized by merit and demerit, does not overcome—that is, does not reach—the Brahmin who sees in this way; rather, this knower of Brahman overcomes all sin, pervades it through his very self-nature, and transcends it. Sin, characterized by what has been done and what has not been done, does not afflict him by producing either the fruits of ritual acts or the consequences of transgressions; instead, this knower of Brahman consumes all sin, reducing it to ashes with the fire of the vision of the Self as the All.

He who knows this thus becomes sinless—free from merit and demerit; stainless—free from stain; free from passion, for passion is stain; free from doubt, with his uncertainty severed; and with the firm conviction, "I am the Self of all, the Supreme Brahman," he becomes a true Brāhmaṇa. Indeed, one who has become such as this in this state is a primary Brāhmaṇa; prior to this abiding in the nature of Brahman, his status as a Brāhmaṇa was only secondary.

"This is the world of Brahman"—the world of Brahman being Brahman itself as the world, the primary and non-figurative state characterized by the nature of the Self of all, O Emperor. "You have reached this world of Brahman, which is characterized as 'not this, not this' and so forth," thus said Yājñavalkya.

Thus, Janaka, having become one with Brahman and having been led to the state of Brahman by Yājñavalkya, replied: "I, who have been led to the state of Brahman by you, give all my kingdom, the Videha lands, to you, O Blessed One; and me, along with the Videhas, for the purpose of service—that is, for the work of a slave. The word "and" (*ca*) is connected [to this]. Thus, the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), together with renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), along with its limbs and its prescribed procedures, has been completed; the supreme goal of man (*paramapuruṣārtha*) has been accomplished.

"This much is to be done by a person; this is the culmination, this is the supreme goal, this is the highest good. Having attained this, a Brahmin becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done; this is the instruction of all the Vedas. (24) — This very Self which was explained in the narrative of Janaka and Yājñavalkya is indeed this great, unborn Self, the eater of food, dwelling within all beings.

The eater of all foods, the giver of wealth—wealth (*vasu*) meaning riches, which is the fruit of the karma of all living beings—he is the giver thereof, meaning he unites living beings with the fruits according to their karma. He who knows this very Self—the unborn eater of food and giver of wealth—as endowed with these two qualities of being the eater of food and the giver of wealth, he, having become the Self of all beings, eats food and finds wealth; that is, he obtains the entire range of fruits of action, precisely because he has become the Self of all, provided he knows as it has been described.

Alternatively, even by those seeking visible results, one who possesses such qualities should be worshipped; by him, the eater of food and the acquisition of cattle are obtained—the meaning is that through this very visible result, his connection with being an eater of food and with cattle, horses, and so forth, comes to pass.

Now, the entire meaning of the Āraṇyaka that has been stated is pointed out in this section by way of summary, to show that "this much is the meaning of the entire Āraṇyaka. That indeed is this great, unborn Self (*ātman*); "unaging" means He does not grow old, which is to say, He does not undergo transformation. "Immortal"—and because He is unaging, therefore He is immortal; He does not die, hence He is immortal. For he who is born and grows old perishes or dies.

But this [Self] is indestructible because it is unborn and undecaying; for this very reason, it is immortal. Since it is devoid of the three modifications of being beginning with birth, it is therefore also devoid of the other three modifications of being and of death in the form of desire, action, delusion, and so forth, which are produced by them.
