It is fearless for this very reason; and since it possesses the aforementioned attributes, it is free from fear, for fear indeed is the effect of ignorance.

The negation of ignorance should be understood as established through the negation of its effects and the negation of the modifications of existence (*bhāvavikāra*). What is this fearless Self, distinguished by such qualities? It is *brahman*, meaning the sovereign, unsurpassed, and great. Indeed, it is well-known in the world that "the fearless is *brahman*. Therefore, it is entirely appropriate that the Self, distinguished by such qualities, is *brahman*.

He who thus knows the Self as the fearless Brahman, as it has been described, indeed becomes that very fearless Brahman. This is the summary of the meaning of the entire Upanishad that has been stated here. For the sake of the perfect awakening to this very meaning, the conceptualization of origin, maintenance, dissolution, and so forth, as well as the superimposition of action, agent, and fruit upon the Self, have been employed; and by means of their removal through the negation "not this, not this," which strips away all superimposed attributes, the true reality is once again made known.

Just as, for the sake of fully understanding the nature of numbers starting from one up to the highest possible count (aparārdha), one employs the superimposition of lines—teaching and making it understood that "this is one line," "this is ten," "this is a hundred," "this is a thousand"—one thereby causes the nature of the number itself to be grasped, yet not that the number consists essentially of the lines themselves.

Just as one who wishes to teach the letters beginning with 'a' employs means such as paper, ink, and lines to communicate the true nature of the phonemes, yet does not cause the letters to be grasped as being identical in essence to the paper or the ink—so too here, by employing various means such as origination and so forth, the single reality of Brahman has been communicated; then, for the purpose of purifying the specific distinctions produced by those imagined means, the summary of the reality was made by saying "not this, not this. That summarized and purified, absolute knowledge alone is presented as the fruit in the final section (kaṇḍikā).

Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa of the fourth chapter. Then a bull addressed him, saying, "Satyakāma! "Sir," he replied. "O dear one, we have now completed our thousand [cows]; take us to the teacher's house. 1.

(1) The word *atha* (now/then) serves to indicate the immediate succession to the instruction on the cause (*hetu*). For the preceding passages were primarily concerned with the cause; immediately following them, the matter proposed is concluded by means of the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa, which is primarily concerned with traditional scripture (*āgama*). The particle *ha* indicates a past occurrence. It is said that the sage Yājñavalkya had two wives—namely, one named Maitreyī and the other named Kātyāyanī.

Of those two wives, Maitreyī was indeed a speaker of Brahman, meaning she was habitually engaged in the discourse on Brahman; whereas Kātyāyanī was at that time one of "womanly wisdom"—that is, her wisdom consisted solely of the kind appropriate for a woman, characterized by the pursuit of household affairs. Now, this being the case, Yājñavalkya, desiring to undertake another mode of life—namely, the state of a wandering mendicant (pārivrājya) as opposed to his previous state of a householder—was about to do so.

"And I shall tell you a quarter of Brahman. "Let the Blessed One tell it to me. He said to him: "The eastern direction is one part, the western direction is one part, the southern direction is one part, and the northern direction is one part. This, my dear, is the four-part quarter of Brahman, named 'The Radiant'."

He addressed his eldest wife, Maitreyī; having addressed her, he said: "O Maitreyī, I am indeed about to depart from this state of household life, intending to embrace the life of a wandering mendicant. O Maitreyī, give me your permission; if you so desire, I shall now bring this [marital] relationship to an end with Kātyāyanī," and so forth, as has already been explained.

He who, knowing it thus, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "The Radiant" becomes radiant in this world; he wins radiant worlds—he who, knowing it thus, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "The Radiant. Thus ends the fifth section.
(3) --- Śrī Śaṅkarācārya did not comment on this.
Thus addressed, Maitreyī said: "If this entire earth were filled with wealth, would I become immortal by it? Or would I not? "No," said Yājñavalkya; the rest is the same as before. (5)

He said: "Truly, you were dear to us before; being so, you have increased our very dearness—you have determined it. Therefore I am pleased. Well then, if you wish to know the means to immortality, O lady, I shall explain that means to immortality to you.

"Verily, Maitreyī, when the Self is seen—how is the Self seen? It is said: first, it is heard through the teacher and the scriptures (*āgama*); then, it is reflected upon through reasoning and logical justification (*upapatti*); and finally, it is known—determined that 'this is so and not otherwise. What happens then? It is said: 'This becomes known. That is, everything other than the Self [becomes known], because there is no existence apart from the Self.
(7–9) *Sri Shankaracharya did not comment on this portion.*

(10) — He would "cast down" that one who perceives incorrectly; he would render him disconnected from absolute liberation (*kaivalya*)—the sense being that this is due to the offense of thinking, "He perceives me through a nature that is not my true Self.
(11) — Śrī Śaṅkarācārya did not provide a commentary on this [portion].

(12) — In the fourth [chapter], the exhalation of the meaning of the worlds and so forth was already stated by implication through the exhalation of sound; therefore, it was not mentioned separately. However, since this [fifth chapter] constitutes a summary of the meaning of the entire treatise, even though the matter is already established by implication, it must be made explicit; thus, it is stated separately.

When all effects have dissolved due to the cause of knowledge (*vidyā*), the Self remains as a single, undivided mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*), without interior or exterior, like a solid block of salt; whereas previously, due to its specific contact with the elements (*bhūtamātra*), it possessed specific cognition. When that specific cognition and its cause—the contact with the elements—have been dissolved by knowledge, there is no longer any perception after death; thus was it stated by Yājñavalkya.

She said: "Right here, on this very matter, the venerable sir has utterly confounded me—confounded at the beginning and confounded in the middle—when you said, 'He is a mass of consciousness alone; there is no consciousness after death. The meaning is that you have bewildered me. Therefore, I do not understand this Self, characterized as described, through discernment. He said: "I do not speak of delusion, for this Self, my dear, is indeed indestructible."

One who has destruction as their nature is *vināśī*; one who is not subject to destruction is *avināśī*. By the word "destruction" (*vināśa*), modification (*vikriyā*) is meant; thus, "indestructible" (*avināśī*) means the Self (*ātman*) is immutable. O Maitreyī, this Self under discussion is of a nature that does not perish (*anucchittidharmā*). "Perishing" (*ucchitti*) means cutting off (*uccheda*); "cutting off" means an end or destruction. One whose nature is perishing is "perishable by nature" (*ucchittidharmā*); one who is not so is "of a non-perishing nature. This means that neither is it characterized by modification, nor is there any destruction for it characterized by annihilation. (15)

In all four chapters, one single Self is determined to be identical—the Supreme Brahman. However, the specific means for its realization differ from one to another. That very Self which is the goal remains the same, whether it is pointed out in the fourth chapter as "Now, therefore, the instruction: not this, not this," or determined in the fifth chapter through the discussion on the wagering of life in the dialogue between Śākalya and Yājñavalkya, again at the conclusion of the fifth chapter, again in the dialogue between Janaka and Yājñavalkya, and once more here at the conclusion of the Upaniṣad.

This concluding section—beginning with "That is this 'not this, not this'" and so forth—is intended to demonstrate that throughout all four chapters, the sole focus is the state of being grounded in the Self (*ātmaniṣṭhatā*), and that no other intermediate subject matter is intended. For when the Reality is examined even by a hundred methods, the final conclusion reached through either reasoning or scripture is only the Self as "not this, not this," and no other [conclusion] is found.

Therefore, wishing to conclude this point—that the very means for attaining immortality is this thorough knowledge of the Self as "not this, not this" (neti neti) along with the renunciation of everything—He says: "So much," that is, merely this much, namely, this vision of the non-dual Self as "not this, not this"; and this, O Maitreyī, is the means for attaining immortality, independent of any other auxiliary causes.

Regarding that which you asked—"Tell me that alone which the Blessed One knows as the means to immortality"—you should understand that it is precisely this much. Having thus spoken of the knowledge of the Self as the means to immortality to his beloved wife, what did Yājñavalkya do? He did that which he had previously promised, saying, "I am about to renounce"; that is, he departed, meaning he became a wandering ascetic (*pravrajita*). Thus, the science of Brahman, culminating in renunciation, is complete.
This much is the instruction, this is the teaching of the Vedas, this is the supreme goal, and this is the end of what must be done for the sake of human purpose.

Now, however, an inquiry is undertaken for the sake of discerning and understanding the meaning of the scriptures, since we observe conflicting statements such as: "One should perform the *agnihotra* as long as one lives," "One should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as long as one lives," "Performing actions here indeed, one should desire to live a hundred years," and "The *agnihotra* is a lifelong sacrificial session (*satra*) ending only with old age," which indicate that there is only one stage of life (*aikāśramya*).

And there are other statements establishing the transition between the stages of life, such as: "Having known [the Self] and having risen above [worldly desires], they go forth into homelessness"; "Having completed the student stage, one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller and then go forth"; "Or otherwise, one may go forth from the student stage itself, or from the house, or from the forest"; and "There are indeed two paths that have emerged: the path of action (kriyā-patha) first, and renunciation (saṃnyāsa) after them. Of these two...

"Renunciation alone excels," as well as such [scriptural] passages as, "Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone some have attained immortality. Likewise, there are Smṛti texts: "One who is observant of celibacy goes forth [into the life of a wandering mendicant]," "One whose celibacy is unbroken may enter whichever [stage] he desires," and "Some speak of an option regarding his stages of life"; likewise, "Having studied the Vedas with celibacy, one should desire sons and grandsons for the sake of purifying one's ancestors."

"Having established the sacred fires according to rule and performed the required sacrifices, one should enter the forest and then desire to become a sage. "Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, for which all one's possessions are the sacrificial fee, and having internalized the fires within oneself, a Brāhmaṇa should go forth from his home as a renunciant. Such are the scriptural and traditional texts that establish various options for renunciation, the sequential order of stages, and the adoption of any stage of life at will; indeed, hundreds of such passages, which appear mutually contradictory, are found, as is the practice of those who know them.

Furthermore, there is a divergence of opinion among those who understand the meaning of the treatise, even among the learned. Consequently, it is not possible for those of dull intellect to discern and comprehend the meaning of the treatise. Indeed, only those whose intellects are firmly established in the logic of the treatise are able to determine the specific scope of these statements. Therefore, in order to make known their respective scopes, we shall investigate them according to the capacity of our own understanding.

Since it is impossible for statements such as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) to have any other meaning, the purpose of the Veda culminates solely in ritual action; this is because of the hearing of the final rites in the text, "They burn him with the sacrificial vessels," and because of the hearing of the phrase "ending with old age" (*jarāmarya*). There is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the text, "The body ends in ashes"; for if the state of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*) were intended, the body would not end in ashes. Furthermore, there is a Smṛti text: "He whose prescribed rule, beginning with conception and ending at the cremation ground, is declared by means of mantras—him alone we recognize as qualified for this scripture, and no one else."

For the Smṛti shows that whatever action is prescribed here by the Veda along with its ritual accessories has the cremation ground as its final limit; and because it demonstrates the absence of qualification [for further rites], it is understood that one who is without action (the renunciant) is absolutely excluded from the qualification for the Śruti. Furthermore, there is a prohibition against extinguishing the sacred fires: "He who extinguishes the fire is indeed a slayer of the heroes of the gods. Now, an objection may be raised: since the injunctions for renunciation and so forth exist, the culmination of the Vedic purpose must be optional. This is not so, because the scriptural texts concerning renunciation and the like have a different purpose.

Since scriptural injunctions such as "One should offer the Agnihotra for as long as life lasts" and "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa for as long as life lasts" have as their sole occasion the mere fact of living, and since it is impossible to conceive of them as having any other purpose, it follows that the passages concerning renunciation and so forth can only apply to those who are not qualified for ritual action.

Furthermore, from the Vedic mantra, "One should desire to live a hundred years performing actions here," and from the statement, "For one is released from this [duty] either by old age or by death," it follows that for those engaged in ritual action (*karmiṇaḥ*), there is no possibility of a gap in their connection to action other than through old age or death; thus, their ending at the cremation ground is not optional. Since even those who are disabled, such as the one-eyed or the humpbacked, are to be favored by the Śruti as being ineligible for ritual action, the injunction of alternative stages of life (*āśrama*) such as renunciation (*vyutthāna*) is not untenable.

If it is argued that there is no room for the injunction regarding the sequence of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*), we say no; for the *Viśvajit* and *Sarvamedha* sacrifices constitute exceptions to the lifelong injunction. The injunction for the lifelong performance of the *Agnihotra* and other rites is indeed set aside by the *Viśvajit* and *Sarvamedha*; and in those cases, the possibility of perceiving a sequence exists—as in: "Having completed the stage of studenthood (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller (*vanī*); and from the forest-dwelling state, one should renounce. This is because no contradiction [between the two sets of injunctions] is logically possible.

For if the scriptural injunction regarding the sequence of stages of life has such a scope [as you claim], there is no contradiction whatsoever in the comprehension of that sequence; however, if one were to imagine another scope for it, the Vedic revelation prescribing [the householder's life] "for as long as one lives" would be restricted from its own proper domain. But since the comprehension of the sequence pertains to the Viśvajit and Sarvamedha sacrifices, there is no sublation at all.

No, because you yourself accept that the knowledge of the Self is the cause of immortality. For you have accepted that the knowledge of the Self—which begins with the passage, "One should meditate upon [the Self] as 'This is the Self,'" and concludes with the section ending, "He is 'not this, not this'"—is the means to immortality. In that case, you simply cannot tolerate the idea that this alone is the means to immortality, independent of anything else. Regarding this, I ask you: for what reason do you tolerate [the efficacy of] the knowledge of the Self?

Listen to the reason for this: just as for one desiring heaven who does not know the means of attaining heaven, the Agnihotra and other rites are taught as the means for attaining heaven; so too here, for one desiring immortality who does not know the means of attaining immortality, the means to immortality—which was sought in the words, "Tell me that alone which the Blessed One knows"—is taught by the Veda in such passages as, "So much, my dear."

In that case, just as the means to heaven such as the Agnihotra and other rites are accepted exactly as they are taught, so too here, it is proper to accept the knowledge of the Self exactly as it is taught—as being the very means to immortality; for the authority [of the scriptures] is equal in both instances. If this is so, what would follow? Since the knowledge of the Self sublates the cause of all ritual actions, there would be the cessation of action upon the arising of that knowledge.

First, those rites connected with wife and fire, such as the Agnihotra and others, are accomplished by means of an objective factor (kāraka) consisting of a recipient (saṃpradāna) that is the object of the notion of difference; for indeed, without a recipient factor such as the deity Agni or others, who is delimited by a distinct cognition, that rite cannot be brought to completion.

For that notion of the recipient (*saṃpradāna-kāraka*) by which the recipient is taught as an instrument for the action is here sublated by knowledge—based on such scriptural passages as: "He who thinks 'this one is one and I am another' does not know"; "The gods abandon him who knows the gods as other than the Self"; "From death to death he goes who perceives here as if there were diversity"; and "It is to be viewed as one alone; he sees the Self as everything. Etc.

Furthermore, knowledge of the Self does not depend on place, time, or instrumental causes, because its object is the eternally established reality that is the Self. Ritual actions, however, being dependent on the person performing them, may indeed depend on place, time, and instrumental causes; but knowledge, being dependent on the reality itself, does not depend on place, time, or instrumental causes—just as fire is hot and space is formless, so too is the realization of the Self. [Objection: But if this were so, there would be a contradiction of the injunctions for ritual action, which constitute a means of valid knowledge.

Nor is mutual annihilation possible between two things of equal authority—no, because [the knowledge of the Self] merely annuls the cognition of inherent difference; for the knowledge of the Self, while annulling other injunctions, does not merely annul the cognition of inherent difference.

If it is argued that, nevertheless, because the cause has been removed, action becomes impossible and there would thus be a cessation of the injunction itself—this is not so. For there is no fault here, just as in the case of the cessation of activity toward a desired object due to the prohibition of desire. Just as when one who is engaged in a sacrifice—a means to heaven—according to the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," the engagement in performing that desired sacrifice is halted once the desire is frustrated by the injunction prohibiting desire; yet, by this much alone, the injunction for the desired sacrifice does not become nullified.

If it is argued that, because the injunction for optional rites is known to be purposeless through the prohibition of desire, its performance becomes untenable and thus the injunction would be effectively nullified—then let there likewise be a nullification of the injunctions for ritual action (*karma*). If it is further argued that, just as the injunction for optional rites is nullified when desire is prohibited, so too would the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the injunctions for action be untenable—if it is claimed that since they cannot be performed (due to the absence of a performer once self-knowledge is attained), the injunctions for performance become useless and thus the injunctions for action lack authority—[we reply]: No, for activity is still possible prior to the knowledge of the Self.

The fact that the innate cognition of distinctions between action, its factors, and its results serves as a cause for ritual action prior to the knowledge of the Self is indeed logical. Just as, in the case of desires, the natural longing for heaven and so forth necessarily serves as a cause for engaging in optional rites prior to the arising of the cognition of their defects, so it is here. If it is argued that, this being the case, the Veda would have both beneficial and harmful purposes—no, for benefit and harm depend upon intention; and because, with the sole exception of liberation, everything else falls within the domain of ignorance (*avidyā*).

For profit and loss depend upon the intention of the person, as is seen in the case of sacrifices performed with the desire for death and so forth. Therefore, ritual action is to be enjoined only so long as there is a lack of orientation toward the injunction for self-knowledge. Consequently, it is established that ritual actions do not coexist with the knowledge of the Self; thus, the knowledge of the Self alone is the means to immortality, as in the passage, "This much indeed, my dear, is immortality," because knowledge is independent of ritual action.

Therefore, renunciation (*pārivrājya*) is established for the wise even without an explicit scriptural injunction, by the mere firm realization of the Self as Brahman—which is immutable and devoid of the factors of action such as the recipient of a gift, as well as genus and so forth—according to the reasoning already stated. This has been explained through the statement of a reason: "For us, this Self is this world," [and] "The ancient wise ones, not desiring offspring, rose above [worldly life]"—thus, renunciation occurs for the wise solely from the awakening to the Self as the world.

And thus, renunciation is established even for one who desires to know (vividiṣu), because of the scriptural statement: "Desiring this very Self as their world, they go forth into homelessness. Furthermore, we have stated that ritual actions pertain to the realm of the ignorant; and since rituals serve the purposes of origination, modification, and purification within the sphere of ignorance, we have also declared that rituals—such as sacrifices—serve as means to the knowledge of the Self by way of purifying the self, in accordance with the text: "They desire to know through sacrifice and other rites."

Thus, this being the case, when considering the relative strength and weakness of the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karman) pertaining to the unenlightened, mental qualities such as humility and the rest—which are dominated by self-restraint—and meditation, knowledge, dispassion, and so forth, are directly contributory (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) toward the production of self-knowledge; whereas others, because they abound in violence, attachment, aversion, and the like, are intermingled with many afflicted actions (*kliṣṭa-karman*). Therefore, they praise the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) for those seeking liberation: "Indeed, renunciation alone [is superior] among all actions, even those already mentioned."

Furthermore, detachment (*vairāgya*) is the ultimate limit of this liberation. As it is said: "O Brahmin, what use have you for wealth, or what use for kinsmen? What use have you for a wife, since you shall die? Seek the Self that has entered the cave; where have your grandfathers and your father gone? Thus, in the Sāṃkhya and Yoga scriptures, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is declared to be proximate to knowledge (*jñāna*); and because of the absence of the impulse toward desire (*kāmapravṛtti*). For the antagonism of knowledge toward the impulse of desire is well-known in all the scriptures.

Therefore, for one who is dispassionate and seeks liberation, the injunctions such as "one should renounce even from the stage of studentship" (*brahmacaryād eva pravrajed*) are appropriate, even without [prior] knowledge. Now, it was argued that because these [injunctions] have room for interpretation (*sāvakāśatvāt*), they refer to those who are not yet qualified [for renunciation], since this would contradict the scriptural texts concerning lifelong [duties] (*yāvajjīva-śruti*). This is not a fault, because those lifelong scriptural texts have even greater room for interpretation. For we have already stated that all ritual actions are to be performed by the ignorant person who possesses desires; however, it is not the case that action must be performed solely on account of life itself, independently [of other motives].

For generally, men are full of desire, and desire has many objects and is to be accomplished by the means of many actions. Vedic rites, which have many fruits as their means, involve a person's connection with a wife and the sacred fires; and when performed again and again, they yield abundant results like agriculture and other such activities, lasting for a hundred years whether in the householder’s life or in the forest. Therefore, with reference to those, there are scriptural injunctions for "as long as one lives," and the mantra-text says, "Performing indeed here [in this world] actions..."

In that view, there is the abandonment of ritual action in the Viśvajit and Sarvamedha sacrifices; and in the view where lifelong performance [of rites] is maintained, then the body ends at the cremation ground and its final state is ashes. Alternatively, the scriptural injunction regarding lifelong performance is with respect to those of other castes; for there is no attainment of the wandering life (pārivrājya) for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. Likewise, such statements as "the rule for whom is declared by the mantras" and "the teachers [hold] that there is only one stage of life" have reference to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.

Therefore, depending on the individual's capacity, knowledge, dispassion, desire, and so forth, the various methods for rising [from worldly life], making choices, following a gradual sequence, and entering the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) are not contradictory. Furthermore, because wandering mendicancy is prescribed separately for those who are not yet qualified [for higher stages] in such passages as, "Whether he be a *snātaka* or not a *snātaka*, whether his sacred fires have been extinguished or he is without fires," it is established that the other stages of life (*āśrama*) are intended only for those who are qualified.
Thus ends the fifth Brāhmaṇa of the fourth chapter.

"Agni will tell you one quarter," [he said]. On the following day, he drove the cows toward [his destination]. When they arrived at the place where they were to stay for the night, he kindled the fire there, penned the cows, added fuel to the fire, and sat down behind the fire, facing eastward.
*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya*, Chapter Four.

The sixth Brāhmaṇa... Now, immediately following this, the lineage (vaṃśa) of the section belonging to Yājñavalkya is commenced, just as the lineage of the Madhu-kāṇḍa was. The explanation, however, is as before. "Brahman, the Self-existent; salutation to Brahman; Om. Thus ends the sixth Brāhmaṇa of the fourth chapter.
Thus [ends] the work of the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācāryas.
In the fourth chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya:
Fire addressed him, saying, "Satyakāma! He replied, "Yes, venerable sir. 2.

"Dear boy, let me tell you a quarter of Brahman. "May the venerable sir tell it to me. He said to him: "The earth is one part, the intermediate space is one part, the sky is one part, and the ocean is one part. This, dear boy, is the four-part quarter of Brahman called 'the Endless'. "Tomorrow I shall tell you the other quarter. When the next day had dawned, he drove out his cows. Wherever they settled for the evening, he built a fire, penned the cows, added fuel to the fire, and sat down behind the fire facing the east.

"Tell him that I have placed my foot upon the water-bird. On the following day, he drove the cows toward home. When they reached the place where they were to stay for the evening, he built a fire, penned the cows, added fuel to the flame, and sat down behind the fire, facing the east.
He arrived at the teacher’s house, and the teacher addressed him, saying, "Satyakāma! "Revered sir," he replied.

Upakosala Kāmalāyana lived as a religious student with Satyakāma Jābāla. For twelve years he tended his fires; yet while he allowed other students to return home after completing their studies, he did not allow him to return.
Then the Gārhapatya fire instructed him: "The earth is Agni; food is the sun. That person who is seen in the sun—I am he; I am indeed he."

"That person who is seen in the eye—that is the Self," he said; "that is the immortal, the fearless; that is Brahman. Even if one pours clarified butter or water into it, it flows only along the eyelashes.

This indeed is the sacrifice, which is this wind that blows; for as it blows, it purifies everything. Because it purifies everything as it blows, therefore it is the sacrifice. Its two paths are mind and speech. Prajāpati brooded over the worlds; from them, as they were being brooded upon, he drew forth their essences: Agni from the earth, Vāyu from the intermediate space, and Āditya from the sky.
He who knows the eldest and the best indeed becomes the eldest and the best. Verily, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the eldest and the best. 1.

The section on supplements (*khilakāṇḍa*) beginning with "Consisting of plenitude" (*pūrṇamaya*) is now commenced. By means of the four preceding chapters, that which is Brahman—direct and immediate; that which is the Self within all, free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), beyond hunger and so forth, designated as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*)—has been determined; and that knowledge of which alone is the means to immortality has been established. Now, however, there are to be described certain meditations (*upāsanā*) upon that very same Self when it is possessed of limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*) and has entered the sphere of linguistic and conceptual usage, such as words and their meanings, which are not contradictory to ritual action (*karman*).

The subsequent section of the text intends to describe those means for attaining supreme worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) which also lead to gradual liberation (*kramamukti*). Furthermore, as supplementary to all forms of meditation (*upāsana*), the syllable *oṃ*, self-restraint (*dama*), charity (*dāna*), and compassion (*dayā*) are intended to be enjoined. "Pūrṇam adaḥ" — "Full is that": it is not excluded from anything, meaning it is all-pervasive (*vyāpin*); the suffix should be understood as denoting the agent (*kartari*). "Adaḥ" is a pronoun expressing what is remote; its meaning is "the Supreme Brahman."

That [Brahman] is complete, all-pervasive like space, continuous, and free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*). This very same [Brahman], when possessed of adjuncts, abiding in name and form, and entered into empirical usage, is "complete" by its own nature as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), pervaded as it were by that [Supreme Self], and not by a particular self delimited by adjuncts. This Brahman, having attained particularity and consisting of effects, "overflows" (*udacyate*), "surges forth" (*udricyate*), or "emerges" (*udgacchati*) from the complete causal self.

Although it overflows in the form of an effect (*kāryātman*), nevertheless, it does not abandon its own nature (*svarūpa*), which is fullness (*pūrṇatva*) and the state of the Supreme Self (*paramātmabhāva*); rather, it is fullness itself that overflows. Having taken—that is, having grasped—the fullness of the full Brahman in the form of an effect, and having attained the state of being of a single flavor with its own essential nature through knowledge (*vidyā*), one sets aside the appearance of otherness born from contact with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the mere elements produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, there remains only the absolute Brahman, which is full, without interior or exterior, and whose essential nature is a single mass of pure consciousness (*prajñānaghanaikarasasvabhāva*).

It remains to be explained. As for what was stated—‘In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself, therefore it became all’—this is the meaning of that mantra. In that context, the meaning of ‘Brahman’ is ‘That [is] full’ (*pūrṇam adaḥ*); and the meaning of ‘This was indeed Brahman in the beginning’ is ‘This [is] full’ (*pūrṇam idam*). And so says another Śruti: ‘What is here, that is there; what is there, that is likewise here.’

Therefore, that which is denoted by the word "that" (*adaḥ*) is the full Brahman; that very same [Brahman] is this full [world] situated in the realm of effects, conjoined with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of name and form, and made prominent by ignorance (*avidyā*). It appears as if different from that supreme essential nature—yet having known the Self alone as the supreme, full Brahman, thinking "I am that full Brahman," one takes up the full [Brahman], casting aside the incomplete nature produced by ignorance through contact with the limiting adjuncts of name and form, by means of this [knowledge].

Through the knowledge of Brahman, only the Absolute remains as the plenum; thus it has been said: "Therefore, that became all. That which is the meaning of all the Upanishads—Brahman—is here restated by this mantra for the sake of connection with what follows. For the practices to be described—namely *oṃkāra*, self-restraint (*dama*), charity (*dāna*), and compassion (*dayā*)—are intended to be the means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman, and, due to their connection with the supplementary section (*khila-prakaraṇa*), they serve as limbs of all forms of meditation.

On this point, some explain as follows: from a full cause, a full effect emerges; that emergent effect, even in the present time, remains full, being the ultimate reality in the form of duality. Then, at the time of dissolution, having taken back the fullness of the full effect and deposited it within itself, only the fullness in the form of the cause remains. Thus, in all three times—origination, persistence, and dissolution—the fullness alone belongs to both cause and effect.

And that single fullness alone is designated through the distinction between cause and effect; thus, Brahman is one, consisting of both duality and non-duality. Just as the ocean is indeed composed of water, waves, foam, bubbles, and so forth, and just as water is real while the waves, foam, bubbles, and the like arising from it are essentially of the nature of the ocean—possessing the properties of manifestation and disappearance yet being ultimately real—so too all this duality is ultimately real.

The waves and so forth are comparable to [the individual soul], while the supreme Brahman is comparable to the water of the ocean. Thus, it is said that if duality were real, the Karmakāṇḍa would possess authority; however, when duality—like a mirage—is unreal, being produced by ignorance as if it were dual, and non-duality alone is the ultimate reality, then the Karmakāṇḍa becomes invalid due to the absence of a subject matter, and thus there would indeed be a contradiction.

The Upaniṣads, being a portion of the Veda, are authoritative because they establish the reality of ultimate non-duality; the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) is not authoritative because its subject matter consists of unreal duality. Desiring to avoid contradiction between these two, the Śruti has stated the reality of both cause and effect through such passages as "That is full" (*pūrṇam adaḥ*), comparing them to the ocean. That is incorrect, because the two alternatives of [the Upaniṣads] being either a qualified object or a negation are impossible. Indeed, this is not a well-conceived hypothesis.

Why? Because, just as in the domain of action an exception (*apavāda*) is made for a specific portion of what has been established by a general rule (*utsarga*), such as "One should not harm any living beings, except at the sacred sites (*tīrtha*)," where the harming of all beings—prohibited by the general rule—is permitted in the specific context of the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices; so too, it is not possible here to first establish non-dual Brahman as a general rule regarding the nature of reality and then subsequently make an exception for a portion of it, precisely because Brahman is non-dual.

Because a partial application [of the analogy] is untenable, and likewise because an alternative (vikalpa) is untenable. For instance, in the case of "one takes up the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice" and "one does not take up the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice," an alternative occurs because the taking up or not taking up depends on the person; however, here in the case of the reality of the object, an alternative such as "is it duality or non-duality? is not possible, because the reality of the Self (*ātmavastu*) is independent of persons, and because there is a contradiction between duality and non-duality within a single thing. Therefore, this conceptualization is not well-conceived.

Furthermore, because it would contradict both scripture and logic: all such scriptural passages as "like a mass of salt, a single mass of the essence of consciousness, without interval, devoid of distinctions between before and after, outer and inner, with and without, unborn, 'not this, not this,' neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, undecaying, fearless, immortal"—passages whose meanings are certain and free from any suspicion of doubt or error—would be cast into the ocean and rendered ineffective, as they would have no bearing [on the doctrine].

Likewise, there is also a contradiction with logic (*nyāyavirodha*), because it is impossible for that which has parts, which consists of multiple constituents, and which possesses activity to be eternal; yet the eternity of the Self is inferred from the observation of memory and so forth, and a contradiction would arise if it were non-eternal. Furthermore, your hypothesis would be rendered purposeless, and in this view, the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) of the Veda would clearly become useless, due to the consequence that one would experience the results of actions not performed (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and that actions performed would perish without result (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*). [Objection: But are there not examples such as the ocean and so forth for Brahman’s nature as being both dual and non-dual?

How can you say that it is contradictory for one thing to possess both duality and non-duality? No, because the subject matter is different. We have stated that the contradiction regarding duality and non-duality applies to an eternal, partless reality, not to an effect that possesses parts. Therefore, this conception is untenable due to its contradiction with Śruti, Smṛti, and reason. It would be better to abandon the Upaniṣads than to accept this conception; furthermore, because it is something to be studied [as a mere intellectual exercise], this conception is not the true meaning of the scripture.

For Brahman—which is like the ocean or a forest, consisting of hundreds of thousands of diverse evils such as birth and death, possessing parts, and having manifold aspects—is not taught by the Śruti as an object of meditation or as an object of knowledge. Rather, the Śruti teaches its nature as a single mass of consciousness (prajñānaghana), stating, "It is to be viewed as one alone," and because it prohibits viewing it as manifold, saying, "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity. And that which is censured by the Śruti must not be performed.

And that which is not to be performed is not the meaning of the scripture; the multiplicity of essence and the multiplicity of constituent parts of Brahman, being of the nature of duality, are censured and therefore should not be viewed as such—hence they are not the meaning of the scripture. However, that which is the single-essence of Brahman is to be viewed as such, and because it is praised, it ought to be the meaning of the scripture.

As for what was said—that a portion of the Veda lacks authority regarding ritual action because of the absence of duality [in that context], while it possesses authority regarding non-duality—that is not so, because the scripture has the purpose of teaching according to what is already established. For the scripture does not first inform a person of the reality of either duality or non-duality as soon as he is born, and only afterwards teach ritual action or the knowledge of Brahman. Nor is duality worthy of being taught, since it is accessible to the intellect of a living being immediately upon birth.

Furthermore, the cognition that duality is unreal could not possibly arise in anyone at the very outset, such that the scripture would first have to teach the reality of duality and only afterwards establish its own authority. Nor would even those established by heretics fail to accept the authority of the scripture [if it were presented in such a manner].

Therefore, having taken for granted the duality produced by ignorance as if it were natural, [the scripture] first teaches action—which is the means for accomplishing the human goals as they are desired—to one who is joined with that very natural ignorance and possessed of defects such as attachment and aversion. Subsequently, for one who perceives the defects inherent in the nature of well-known actions, agents, and results, and who seeks the fruit of abiding in the state of the nature of indifference which is the opposite of that [duality], [the scripture] teaches the knowledge of Brahman, which consists in the realization of the oneness of the Self and serves as the means to that end.

Now, this being the case, when the fruit—which is the abiding in the nature of that very indifference—is attained, one's desire regarding the authority of the scripture ceases. Due to the absence of that [desire], the status of being a "scripture" (śāstratva) also ceases for him. Thus, the scripture is complete for every individual, and there is not even a scent of contradiction with the scripture, because the duality consisting of the scripture, the disciple, and the teaching culminates in the knowledge of non-duality (advaita); for contradiction would only exist if any one of these were to remain [as a separate entity].

However, because the scripture, the disciple, and the teaching are mutually dependent, not even one of them can exist independently; and when everything has reached its consummation in the realization of the non-dual, auspicious, and absolute reality, whose contradiction could possibly be suspected? Nor is there a state of non-contradiction, for that very reason. Now, even granting [the existence of these factors], we say: since the contradiction with the scripture remains equal even if [reality] consists of both duality and non-duality.

Even when we accept that Brahman alone is one, consisting of both duality and non-duality—like the ocean and so forth—and that there is no other distinct entity, even then we are not released from the contradiction with scripture you have mentioned. How so? For the single supreme Brahman consists of both duality and non-duality; because it transcends sorrow, delusion, and the like, it does not require instruction, nor is there any instructor other than Brahman, since we accept that Brahman alone exists in the form of both duality and non-duality.

If it is argued that because the realm of duality is manifold, there is mutual instruction [between individuals], whereas there is no such instruction regarding the realm of Brahman—then this contradicts the position that Brahman alone is the one reality, consisting of both duality and non-duality, and that nothing else exists. Furthermore, the ocean analogy is contradictory: if that in which mutual instruction occurs within the realm of duality is one thing, and duality is another, then the two are distinct. Moreover, just as the water of the ocean is one, if the consciousness of Brahman is one, then the conceptualization of instruction, reception, and so forth, cannot possibly occur elsewhere than in Brahman itself.

For it cannot be imagined that in the case of Devadatta—who consists of both duality and non-duality in his hands and so forth—the organ of speech and the ear (which are parts of Devadatta) function such that the speech is the teacher and the ear is merely the receiver of the instruction, while Devadatta himself is neither the teacher nor the receiver of the instruction; this is because Devadatta possesses a single unified consciousness, just as the ocean has a single nature of water. Therefore, such an interpretation would contradict both scripture and logic, and the intended meaning would remain unestablished.
Consequently, the meaning of the mantra "pūrṇam adaḥ" is exactly as we have explained it.

"Oṃ khaṃ brahma" is the mantra; and this, which is not employed elsewhere, is here enjoined by the Brāhmaṇa for the practice of meditation. In this context, "Brahman" is the substantive (viśeṣya) and "kha" (the ether/space) is the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa). The qualifier and the substantive are indicated in grammatical apposition (sāmānādhikaraṇya), like "blue lotus"—that is, "khaṃ brahma. The word "brahman" refers generally to the vast reality without specific qualification; therefore, it is qualified as "khaṃ brahma" (the ether is Brahman).

That which is the ether-Brahman (*khaṃ brahma*) is either denoted by the word *oṃ* or is of the very nature of the word *oṃ*; in either case, the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not contradictory. Furthermore, the word *oṃ* is employed here for the purpose of serving as a means for the meditation on Brahman, as is evident from other scriptural passages such as: "This is the best support, this is the supreme support"; "One should yoke the Self with the syllable *oṃ*"; "With this very syllable *oṃ*, one should meditate upon the Supreme Person"; and "Thus, meditate upon the Self as *oṃ*," and so forth.

And because no other purpose for the instruction is possible. Just as in other instances—such as "He recites with 'Om'," "He chants the Udgītha with 'Om'"—and at the beginning and conclusion of Vedic study, the employment of the syllable *oṃ* is understood through its specific application (*viniyoga*), and no other purpose is understood there; so too here, no other purpose is understood. Therefore, the instruction regarding the word *oṃ* here is solely for the sake of being a means to meditation.

Although words such as *brahman*, *ātman*, and so forth are denotative of Brahman, nevertheless, according to the authority of the Śruti, the syllable *oṃ* (om) is the most proximate designation of Brahman. For this very reason, it is the supreme means for the realization of Brahman. And that [means] is of two kinds: by way of being a symbol (*pratīka*) and by way of being a name (*abhidhāna*). By way of being a symbol—as a statue of Viṣṇu and others is [regarded] through non-difference—so too the syllable *oṃ* is to be realized as "Brahman."

For thus, Brahman becomes gracious to one who has the syllable *oṃ* as an object of meditation, according to the Śruti: "This is the best object of meditation; this is the supreme object of meditation. Having known this object of meditation, one is glorified in the world of Brahman."

In this context, lest there be a misconception that "space" (*kha*) refers to physical space (*bhautika-kha*), he says: "Space is ancient," meaning it is the eternal space that is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Since that ancient space which is the space of the Supreme Self is beyond the reach of the eyes and other senses, it is without support and impossible to grasp; therefore, through faith, devotion, and a particular state of being, one causes it to enter into the syllable *Oṃ*—just as people [perceive] Viṣṇu in a stone image or the like marked with the limbs of Viṣṇu.

"Vāyuraṃ kham": *vāyuraṃ* means that which contains air (*vāyuḥ asmin vidyate*); *kham* refers to the mere space (*khamātraṃ*), not the "ancient space" (*purāṇaṃ kham*)—thus he spoke. Who was he? Kauravyāyaṇīputra. For the usage of the word *kha* is primarily applied to the air; therefore, he considers it appropriate to understand [the term] in its primary sense.

In this regard, whether the "ancient space" (*purāṇaṃ kham*) is Brahman in its unconditioned nature, or the "wind-filled space" (*vāyuraṃ kham*) is Brahman with attributes, in every case the syllable *oṃ* attains the status of a means as a symbol (*pratīka*), like an image [of a deity]. This is because of another scriptural passage: "O Satyakāma, this *oṃ* is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman. There is disagreement only concerning the meaning of the word "space" (*kha*).

This *oṃkāra* is the Veda; for by means of it one knows (*veda*) that which is to be known, therefore the *oṃkāra* is the Veda—the designator, the name. By means of that name, the practitioner knows and perceives Brahman, which is to be known, being manifested and expressed; therefore the Brahmins know, "This is the Veda. Thus, it is intended that the *oṃkāra* serves as the means (*sādhana*) for the Brahmins by way of being the designator. Alternatively, the passage beginning with "This is the Veda" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

How is the syllable *oṃ* prescribed as a symbol (*pratīka*) of Brahman? Because of the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement "The ether is Brahman" (*khaṃ brahma*), its praise is now given by way of its being the Veda: for this entire Veda is indeed the syllable *oṃ* alone. This *oṃ* is the source of all and constitutes the essence of everything divided into the distinctions of *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman* verses, according to another scriptural passage: "Just as all leaves are [pierced] by a pin," and so forth.

For this reason also, this *oṃkāra* is the Veda: whatever is to be known, all that which is to be known is known by means of this *oṃkāra* alone; therefore, this *oṃkāra* is the Veda. The status of the other Veda [the Ṛgveda, etc. as "Veda" is also due to this very fact; hence, this *oṃkāra* is to be understood as a distinguished means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Alternatively, it is the Veda itself: what is it? That which the Brāhmaṇas know as the *oṃkāra*; for among the Brāhmaṇas, this is to be understood through various applications such as the *praṇava*, the *udgītha*, and so forth.
For when it is employed as a means of accomplishment, the entire Veda becomes employed.

Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa of the fifth chapter. He said, "What shall be my food? They replied, "Whatever there is here, even down to dogs and birds. Now, this is indeed the food of the breath (*ana*); for "breath" (*ana*) is its manifest name. Indeed, for one who knows this, there is nothing whatsoever that is not food. 1. (1)

Now this undertaking is for the purpose of prescribing the three means, beginning with self-control (dama): "Three"—meaning numbering three—"descendants of Prajāpati" (*prājāpatyāḥ*), that is, offspring of Prajāpati; what were they? Being disciples—because of the predominance of the state of studentship (*brahmacarya*) among the duties of a disciple—they lived the life of a student (*brahmacarya*) under their father Prajāpati; the meaning is that they have dwelt there. Who were they? Specifically, the gods, humans, and asuras.

And it is now stated what they did after having lived the holy life (*brahmacarya*): those gods spoke to their father Prajāpati. What was it? "May he speak"—that is, may he tell us—what instruction you have for us. To them, who were thus petitioners, he spoke this syllable, merely a phoneme: "Da. And having spoken, the father asked them: "Did you understand?"—that is, did you grasp the meaning of the syllable uttered by me for the sake of instruction, or not?

The gods said: "We have understood; we have come to know. [Uddālaka said: "If that is so, let it be told what was said by me. The gods said: "'Be self-controlled! You are by nature uncontrolled; therefore, become self-controlled'—this is what you said to us. The other replied: "Om! You have understood correctly. He said: "What shall be my garment? They said: "Water. Therefore, when about to eat, one wraps oneself with water both before and after; thus one becomes a possessor of garments and remains unclothed (unexposed). 2. (2)

The rest is the same. "You are greedy by nature; therefore, distribute and give according to your ability"—this is what you have told us. What else could a man say for our benefit? Having said this to Gośruti Vaiyāghrapadya, Satyakāma Jābāla spoke further: "Even if one were to say this to a withered stump, branches would surely spring up and leaves would grow upon it.

Likewise, [he says] to the Asuras, "Be compassionate"; for you are cruel, devoted to violence and the like, therefore be compassionate—exercise mercy toward living beings. This very instruction of Prajāpati continues even today. He who formerly instructed the gods and others, he still instructs them even now through his divine voice characterized by thunder.

How is this divine voice heard? What is that thunder? It is "da da da," which is an imitation uttered three times to indicate the sentences: "Be self-controlled, give, and be compassionate. It is not that the sound of thunder itself consists of exactly three syllables, for such a restriction of number is not well-known in common worldly usage. Since even today Prajāpati continues to instruct, "Be self-controlled, give, and be compassionate," for that reason these three [virtues] are [to be observed].

What are those three? It is said: one should train in, or adopt, self-restraint (*dama*), charity (*dāna*), and compassion (*dayā*); that is, one should form the thought, "The instruction of Prajāpati must be carried out by us. And so says the *Smṛti*: "These three are the gates to hell, the destruction of the self: desire, anger, and greed; therefore, one should abandon this triad. For this is the preliminary to the injunction.

Nevertheless, those who understand the intentions of others raise this doubt: for what purpose did Prajāpati utter three syllables beginning with *da* when addressing the gods and the rest, each seeking a separate instruction? And how did they individually comprehend Prajāpati’s mental intent through the mere letter *da*, which was common to all? Regarding this, some say: because they were undisciplined, ungenerous, and lacking in compassion, they considered themselves at fault and remained apprehensive toward Prajāpati, wondering, "What will he say to us?"

And for them, by the mere hearing of the syllable *da*, there arose an understanding of its meaning through the influence of their own apprehension of self; for it is well known in the world that sons and disciples, being those who are to be instructed, must be turned away from wrongdoing. Therefore, Prajāpati’s utterance of the mere syllable *da* was appropriate; and because the three qualities beginning with self-restraint (*dama*) share the phoneme *da*, they were understood by the gods and others through discrimination in accordance with their own respective defects.

However, once one has knowledge of one's own defects, it is possible to turn away from those defects even with a brief instruction, just as the gods and others [were turned away] by the mere syllable *da*. Now, an objection is raised: "Is this not an instruction for the three classes beginning with the gods, such that each of these—gods and the rest—should adopt only one [of the three], and even today humans should not train in all three? To this it is replied: These three were practiced by the distinguished beings of old, the gods and others; therefore, they must be trained in by humans alone.

In that case, it might be argued that compassion (*dayālutva*) is not something to be practiced, because it was practiced by the Asuras, who are unworthy. To this we say: no, for all three [groups] are equal. Therefore, there is another intention here: the gods and the others are the three sons of Prajāpati; and a father must teach only what is beneficial to his sons. Since Prajāpati knows what is beneficial, he does not teach otherwise. Consequently, this instruction of his sons is the supreme benefit for Prajāpati.

Therefore, these three must be practiced by humans alone. Alternatively, there are no gods, asuras, or others whatsoever apart from humans. Among humans themselves, those who are unrestrained yet endowed with other superior qualities are "gods"; those dominated by greed are "humans"; and likewise, those cruel ones intent on violence are "asuras. It is precisely these same humans who, in relation to the three defects such as lack of self-restraint, receive the designations of "gods" and so forth, and in relation to the other qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas.

Therefore, these three must be practiced by human beings alone, because it was with reference to them that Prajāpati taught this. For indeed, humans are seen to be undisciplined, greedy, and cruel; and thus says the Smṛti: "Lust, anger, and likewise greed—therefore, one should abandon these three.
This concludes the second Brāhmaṇa of the fifth chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya.
Śvetaketu Āruṇeya went to the assembly of the Pañcālas. There, Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said to him, "Boy, did your father instruct you? "He did, indeed, sir," he replied.

It was stated immediately after that "this is Prajāpati, for Prajāpati instructs the heart. But who is this Prajāpati who instructs? It is said: "This is Prajāpati. Which two? "The heart"; by "heart" is meant the intellect (buddhi) residing in the heart.

In this passage at the end of the Śākalya-Brāhmaṇa, the withdrawal of names, forms, and actions is described by way of the division of the quarters. This very heart—which is the foundation of all beings and which has become the self of all beings—is Prajāpati, the creator of creatures. It is Brahman, because of its vastness (*bṛhattvāt*) and because it is the self of all. It is all this. The all-pervasiveness of the heart was stated in the fifth chapter; since it is all this, therefore the heart, as Brahman, is to be meditated upon.

In this regard, first of all, meditation upon the syllables of the name "Hṛdaya" is taught. This very thing called "Hṛdaya" consists of three syllables; that which has three syllables is "tryakṣaram. Which, then, are those three syllables? They are stated as follows: "hṛ" is one syllable.

"He who knows that the form 'hṛ' belongs to the root *hṛ* (to bring) in the sense of the act of bringing—because for the sake of the Heart, which is Brahman, one's own senses and other objects such as sound and the rest bring their respective functions, and the Heart brings [them] for the sake of the enjoyer—he who knows this syllable 'hṛ' as the name of the Heart—for that knower his own kinsmen and others unrelated to him bring offerings; this is the completion of the sentence."

This fruit corresponds to consciousness. Likewise, *da* is also a single syllable; this *da*, which is a form of the root *dadāti* (to give) in the sense of giving, is fixed as a syllable of the name "Heart. Here too—both one's own organs and other objects give their respective vigor to the Heart, the Brahman; the Heart gives its own vigor to the enjoyer. Therefore, he who knows it thus as the syllable *da*—"it gives" (*dadāti*) to him, both his own [faculties] and others. Likewise, *yaṃ* is also a single syllable.

He who knows that this form "yam" is derived from the root *i*, meaning "to go," and is thus connected to this name, goes to the heavenly world. If such a distinguished fruit is obtained even from the syllables of the name, what need is there to mention the fruit arising from the meditation on the true nature of the heart? Thus, the syllables of the name are introduced for the sake of praising the heart.
This concludes the third Brāhmaṇa of the fifth chapter.
"That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire. The sun is its fuel; the rays are its smoke; the day is its flame; the moon is its embers; and the stars are its sparks. (1)

(1) — Desiring to enjoin the meditation upon that very Brahman called the heart as "the Truth," he says: "That, that. By "that," the heart-Brahman is referred to; "vai" is for the purpose of recollection. One "tat" refers to the fact that the heart-Brahman is being recollected; the second "tat" means "this same thing is now being stated by way of another method. What, then, is this other method? It is connected with the word "this" (*etad*) in the phrase "this is that very thing"; this is the third "tat."

Bringing to mind what is about to be stated with the word "this," he says: "It was" (*āsa*), meaning it existed. But what was that which existed? That which was previously called "the heart is Brahman"—that is "this. The third occurrence of the word *tat* (that) is employed here. He specifies what that is: "Truth alone" (*satyameva*). Truth is both the manifest (*sat*) and the unmanifest (*tyat*), the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*); this is Brahman, consisting of the five elements.

Whoever knows this very Self as Truth—great because of its greatness, a *yakṣa* (to be worshipped), the first-born, born before all that pertains to transmigratory existence, for this Brahman was born at the very beginning and is therefore the first-born—and knows it as "Brahman is Truth," for him this result is declared: just as these worlds have been made one's own and conquered by the Truth that is Brahman, so too he who knows the Self as Truth, as the great *yakṣa*, the first-born Brahman, conquers these worlds.

Furthermore, "conquered" means brought under control; "thus" (*ittham*) refers to how that enemy is [overcome] by Brahman—this is the completion of the sentence. "And the unreal would become unreal" means that this enemy would be conquered. He concludes by stating for whom this fruit belongs: "He who knows this great, first-born Yakṣa as the True Brahman. Therefore, a fruit corresponding to the knowledge is appropriate, because Brahman is indeed the Truth. Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth chapter.

"Parjanya, O Gautama, is indeed the fire; its fuel is the wind, its smoke is the cloud, its flame is lightning, its embers are thunderbolts, and its sparks are the rain-showers. (1) This is stated for the purpose of praising the Brahman that is Truth. It was said [in the previous section] that it is "the great, adorable being, the first-born"; how, then, is its status as the first-born explained? It is said: "In the beginning, this world was only water"; by "water" is meant the oblations of the Agnihotra and other rites which are inherent in ritual action. Because the Agnihotra and other oblations consist of liquid matter, they possess the nature of water.

And those waters, after the completion of rituals such as the *agnihotra*, do not exist in isolation but are accompanied by the other elements, not abandoning their state of inherence in action through a certain subtle, unseen self (*ātman*). Because of this inherence in action, water holds primacy; thus, all the elements, remaining in the undifferentiated state (*avyākṛta*) prior to creation and accompanied by the agent, are indicated by the term "waters. These waters, being the seed of the world, abide in the form of the undifferentiated.

These very waters existed at the beginning as this entire world transformed into name and form; there was nothing else whatsoever born of modification. Those waters, in turn, produced the True (satyam). Therefore, the Brahman that is the True is the first-born. This is the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha, the Thread-Self (sūtrātman), which is the differentiation of the undifferentiated world. Why is that the True Brahman? Because of its greatness. How is it great? He says: because it is the creator of everything.

How so? That which is the Truth, Brahman, created Prajāpati—the Lord of creatures, the Virāj, whose instruments are the sun and other organs; this is to be supplied to the sentence. That Prajāpati created the gods; that Virāj, Prajāpati, created the gods. Since everything has thus been born in this sequence from the Truth, Brahman, therefore Brahman is the Great Truth. But how is it further called a "Yakṣa"?—those very gods, having been thus created, even surpassing their father the Virāj, worship that same Truth, Brahman.

Therefore, this is the first-born Great Yakṣa; for that reason, it should be worshipped with one's whole being. Furthermore, the name of that Brahman which is Truth is "Satyam. This consists of three syllables. He asks: what are those syllables? He says: *sa* is one syllable; *ti* is one syllable—the *ī* in *tī* is an adjunct for the sake of pronunciation; *yam* is one syllable. Among them, the first and last syllables, *sa* and *yam*, are Truth, because they lack the nature of death; in the middle, however, is untruth.

For falsehood is death, because of the commonality of the letter *t* in both "death" (*mṛtyu*) and "falsehood" (*anṛta*). This very falsehood, the syllable *t*, which is of the nature of death, is enclosed on both sides by truth—characterized by the letters *s* and *y*—and is thus pervaded and contained within the two forms of truth. Therefore, it is ineffective; there is only an abundance of truth, a preponderance of truth.
Thus, for one who knows this—the abundance of truth and the ineffectiveness of all death and falsehood—falsehood, even when uttered through negligence, never harms that knower.
Into this very fire, the gods offer King Soma; from that oblation, rain comes into being. Thus ends the fifth section. 5.

Now, the meditation upon this True Brahman in its specific form is being described: "That which... What is that? The True Brahman, the first-born. What is it? That one; who is that one? The Sun. But who is this Sun? He who is this; who is this? The person who is the presiding deity (abhimānin) within this solar orb—that is the True Brahman. And he who is here with respect to the body (adhyātma)—this person who is in the right eye—in the eye; by the word "and" (*ca*), the connection is that he too is the True Brahman.

Since these two persons residing in the sun and in the eye are specific manifestations of the one true Brahman, therefore they are established in each other—the solar person in the ocular person and the ocular person in the solar person—because the individual self (adhyātma) and the divine principle (adhidaivata) stand in a relationship of mutual benefit. How are they established? It is said: by means of its rays and light, this solar person, bestowing favor, is established in this ocular person within the individual self.

And this visual [self], supporting the sun by means of the vital breaths, is established in that sun, which is the deity above. When he, who consists of consciousness and is the experiencer within this body, is about to depart at that time, then this solar person in the eye withdraws his rays and remains in a state of pure neutrality. At that time, this one consisting of consciousness sees it as purely white and devoid of rays, like the lunar orb.

This vision of the *ariṣṭas* (omens of death) is presented as a digression, intended to show how a person might become diligent regarding what ought to be done. It is not the case that these rays—having previously approached for the sake of favoring this visual person (*cākṣuṣa-puruṣa*) by virtue of their master’s duty—now fail to reach him or do not return, as if out of regard for the exhaustion of his karma.
Therefore, it is understood from their mutual relationship of helper and helped that these two are indeed portions of the one true Self.

In that regard, who is this [person]? It is this person within this maṇḍala whose name is Truth (*satya*). The *vyāhṛtis* are his limbs. How so? The *vyāhṛti* which is "Bhūḥ" is his head, because of its priority. Regarding this, the Śruti itself states the point of similarity: the head is one, being possessed of the number one; likewise, this syllable "Bhūḥ" is one. "Bhuvaḥ" is the two arms, because of the commonality of duality; there are two arms, and these two syllables are likewise two. Similarly, "Svar" is the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*).

These two syllables are two supports; they are supports because one stands firm by means of them as feet. The secret name (*upaniṣad*)—the hidden designation—of this very Brahman, which consists of the *vyāhṛtis*, is that by which, when it is uttered, that Brahman becomes manifest, just as in common worldly usage. What is it? He says: "Day" (*ahar*). One who knows that this form [of the word] comes from the roots *han* (to strike) and *hā* (to abandon), and who knows thus, strikes down and abandons evil.

In this same way, regarding this person in the right eye, everything is identical, beginning with "Bhūḥ is his head," and so forth. His secret name (*upaniṣad*) is "I" (*aham*), because he is the innermost self (*pratyagātman*). This is according to the previous rule [of derivation] from the roots *han* or *hā*.

Thus ends the fifth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth chapter. "The earth, O Gautama, is indeed the sacrificial fire. Of that [fire], the year is the fuel, space is the smoke, the night is the flame, the quarters are the embers, and the intermediate quarters are the sparks. (1)

(1) "Consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) means having the mind as its primary constituent, because it is perceived within the mind, and because one perceives by means of the mind; thus this person is "consisting of mind. "Light-true" (*bhāḥsatya*) means that light alone is his truth, his existence, and his essential nature; he is thus "light-true," which is to say, luminous. Because the mind illuminates all objects and because he consists of mind, he possesses this luminosity. "Within that" refers to within the heart, that is, inside the heart.

The meaning is that it is seen by yogins within that inner heart as being of such a size as a grain of rice or a grain of barley. This very one is the ruler of all, the lord of everything belonging to his own differentiated manifestations. Even though he is the master, he is not like some subordinate official such as a minister; rather, he is the sovereign ruler (*adhipati*), the sustainer who presides over all. He governs this entire world—whatever exists, whatsoever it may be—and he rules over all that.

Thus, through the meditation upon the mind-made [self], the fruit is indeed the attainment of that very form. "In whatever way they meditate upon it, that very thing they become"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the sixth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth chapter.
Man, O Gautama, is indeed the fire. His speech is the fuel; his breath is the smoke; his tongue is the flame; his eyes are the embers; his ears are the sparks. (1)

(1) — In the same manner, another meditation concerning the Brahman that is Truth is begun with a specific fruit: "They say lightning is Brahman. The etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of Brahman as lightning is stated: because it pierces (*vidānāt*), that is, because it cleaves through the darkness of the clouds and mists, it shines forth; therefore, it is called *vidyut*.

He who knows that Brahman is lightning, which possesses such qualities—he "lights" (vidyati), meaning he shatters and destroys all evils that have become adverse toward this Self; the meaning is that he shatters all those evils. For him who knows thus that "lightning is Brahman," there is a corresponding fruit, because lightning is indeed Brahman.
Thus ends the seventh Brāhmaṇa of the fifth chapter.

Woman indeed is the fire, O Gautama; her lap is the fuel; when one addresses her, that is the smoke; the womb is the flame; what one does within is the embers; the pleasures are the sparks. Furthermore, there is another mode of meditation on that very Brahman: "Speech is indeed Brahman. Speech means sound; it is the threefold Veda. That speech is a cow—like a cow, for she is a cow. Just as a cow pours forth milk from four udders for her calf, so the cow of speech pours forth food like milk from her udders, as will be described, for the gods and others.

What, then, are those udders? Or what are they from which she flows? Of this cow that is Speech, two udders are lived upon by the gods who stand in the place of calves. Which two? The utterance *svāhā* and the utterance *vaṣaṭ*; for by these two the oblation is given to the gods. Humans [live upon] the utterance *hanta*; for with "Hanta! they bestow food upon humans. The ancestors [live upon] the utterance *svadhā*; for with the utterance *svadhā* they bestow the *svadhā*-offering upon the ancestors.

Of that cow which is speech, the breath (*prāṇa*) is the bull, for by means of breath speech is brought forth; the mind (*manas*) is the calf, for it is milked by the mind; indeed, speech proceeds only toward an object perceived by the mind. Therefore, the mind stands in the place of the calf. Thus, the one who meditates upon speech as the cow attains identity with it. Thus ends the eighth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth chapter. "But as for the statement, 'In the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called man,' [the process is as follows]: having lain within the womb, enveloped by the membrane, for ten or nine months, or for however long it takes, he is then born. (1)

(1) --- This Agni Vaiśvānara; as before, this is another mode of meditation. This Agni is Vaiśvānara. What is this Agni? He says: it is that which is within the person (*puruṣa*). Is it the fire that produces the body? No, it is said: it is that fire called Vaiśvānara by which this food is cooked. What is that food? It is this food which is eaten and consumed by creatures; the meaning is that it is the digestive fire (*jāṭharo 'gniḥ*).

To provide a direct illustration of this, he says: "Of that fire—the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*)—which cooks food, there is this sound. Which sound? It is that sound which one hears when one covers the ears by closing them with the fingers; "this" is an adverbial modifier for the act of hearing. One should meditate upon that as Prajāpati, the Vaiśvānara fire. Here too, the fruit is becoming one with that. In this context, the following sixfold set of omens is mentioned incidentally: when that experiencer within this body is about to depart, he no longer hears this sound.

Thus ends the ninth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth chapter. Now, those who know this thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity—they pass into the light; from the light into the day; from the day into the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight into the six months when the sun moves northward; [from there] into the year... (1) ---

In this section, the destination and the fruit of all these meditations are stated: when a wise person departs from this world—that is, when he abandons the body—he then reaches the wind. In the intermediate space, the wind remains motionless and impenetrable; that wind, for him who has arrived there, opens itself up—it disperses its own parts and makes itself porous; such is the meaning.

What is the size of that aperture? It is said: it is like the opening of a chariot wheel, which is of a well-known dimension. Through that aperture, the knower ascends—he goes upwards. He reaches the sun. The sun stands having blocked the path for one who desires to go to the world of Brahman; yet he too opens the door for the worshipper who knows thus. For him, the sun makes way there.

Just as there is a specific aperture in the hollow of a *lambara* musical instrument, by means of that he ascends upward. He reaches the moon; there too, it makes way for him. Just as the hollow of a drum is well known, by means of that he ascends upward. He reaches the world of Prajāpati—of what nature is it? It is "without sorrow," meaning it is devoid of mental suffering; it is "without cold," meaning it is devoid of bodily suffering.
Having reached that, he dwells there for eternal, perpetual years—that is to say, for many kalpas of Brahmā.
Thus ends the tenth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth chapter.

Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava, Satyayajña Pauluṣi, Indradyumna Bhāllaveya, Jana Śārkarākṣya, and Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi—these great householders and great Vedic scholars, having come together, deliberated: "Who is our Self? What is Brahman? (1)

(1) — This indeed is the supreme austerity. What is that? When one who is afflicted, diseased, or seized by fever and the like undergoes suffering, one should reflect: "This is the supreme austerity," because of the commonality of suffering. For the wise man who reflects thus, that very austerity becomes the cause for the destruction of karma, provided he does not reproach himself and does not despair. And he, having his impurities burnt away by that austerity of knowledge, surely conquers the supreme world—he who knows this.

Likewise, one who is about to die imagines at the very outset: "What is this? This is indeed the supreme austerity—that when I have passed away, the officiating priests carry me from the village to the forest for the funeral rites. Because of the commonality of going from the village to the forest, that will become my supreme austerity. For it is well known that "going from the village to the forest is the supreme austerity. "He who knows thus indeed conquers the supreme world."

"Likewise, this indeed is the supreme austerity: that they place the deceased upon the fire; because of the commonality of entering the fire, he who knows this conquers the supreme world. This concludes the eleventh Brāhmaṇa of the fifth chapter. "Aupamanyava, upon which Self do you meditate? "O Venerable King, I meditate upon the sky alone," he said.
