"This is indeed the Vaiśvānara Self named 'The Radiant' (Sutejas), whom you meditate upon as the Self. Therefore, Soma-pressings—Suta, Prasuta, and Āsuta—are seen in your lineage. 1.

(1) — "Food is Brahman. Desiring to prescribe another such meditation, he says: "Food is Brahman"—that which is eaten is Brahman; thus say some teachers. That should not be accepted as "food is Brahman. Others say: "Breath is Brahman"; that also should not be accepted in that way. For what reason, then, should it not be accepted that "food is Brahman"? Because, apart from breath, food putrefies, becomes moist, and reaches a state of decay; how then can it be Brahman?

That which is indestructible is indeed called Brahman. Let it be, then, that the vital breath (prāṇa) is Brahman; it is not so, because the vital breath indeed withers—it undergoes desiccation—without food. For the vital breath is an eater; therefore, without food as its sustenance, it is unable to maintain itself. Thus, the vital breath indeed withers without food.

Therefore, since the state of being Brahman is not possible for each one individually, these two deities—food and breath—having become one, having attained a single state, reach the highest state, they attain the nature of Brahman. Having determined this thus, Prātṛda by name said to his father: "What indeed?"—the word *svid* expressing doubt or inquiry.

"Just as Brahman has been conceived by me, so what good could I do for the one who knows thus? 'Good' means something auspicious or worshipful; the intention is: 'What kind of worship could I perform for him? Likewise, what evil could I do for this knower? The intention is: 'He has already accomplished all that was to be done. One who knows that food and vital breath together constitute Brahman is neither diminished by the performance of evil, nor is he exalted by the performance of good."

To him who was speaking thus, his father said, restraining him with his hand: "Prātṛda, do not speak so! Who among these two—food and breath—having become unified, attains supremacy? No one at all, even a wise man, attains supremacy through this vision of Brahman; therefore, you ought not to say that these two have accomplished their purpose. If this is so, then let your honor tell me: how does one attain supremacy?"

To him he spoke these words that are about to be mentioned. What were they? "Vi. What is this "vi"? It is said: food (*anna*) is indeed "vi"; for because all these beings are pervaded (*viṣṭa*) by, or supported upon, food, therefore food is called "vi. Furthermore, he said "Ram. And what is this "ram"? Vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed "ram. Why? He says: for when vital breath—the support of strength—is present, all beings rejoice (*ramante*); therefore, the vital breath is "ram."

Food possesses the quality of being the refuge for all beings, and vital breath (prāṇa) possesses the quality of being the delight of all beings. For no one who lacks an abode or lacks support finds delight; nor does one find delight when, despite having an abode, one is breathless and weak. But when one possesses an abode and is endowed with vital breath and strength, then the world, considering itself to have achieved its purpose, finds delight—according to such scriptural passages as, "He should be young, well-youthful, and studious."

Now he declares the fruit for one who knows thus: "Indeed, all beings enter into him because of his knowledge of the qualities of food; all beings rejoice in him because of his knowledge of the qualities of the vital breath—so it is for him who knows thus.

This concludes the twelfth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya. Then he said to Satyayajña Pauluṣi: "O Prācīnayogya, upon which Self do you meditate? "The Āditya alone, O Venerable King," he replied. [The teacher said: "This indeed is the Self known as Vaiśvānara, the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa), whom you meditate upon as the Self. Therefore, many things of universal form are seen in your family. (1)

(1) --- *Uktha* --- is another form of meditation. *Uktha* is a liturgical hymn (*śastra*); for that is the principal element in the Mahāvrata sacrifice. But what is that *uktha*? The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the *uktha*. And the vital breath is the principal among the sense organs, while the *uktha* is the principal among the liturgical hymns; therefore, one should meditate upon it as the *uktha*. How is the vital breath the *uktha*? He says: because the vital breath raises up (*utthāpayati*) all this; since it raises up, the vital breath is the *uktha*; for no one who is without breath rises up.

He states the fruit of that worship: "Verily, from such a knower of this, a son arises who is an *uktha*-knower and a knower of *prāṇa*, a hero. This is the visible fruit; but as for the invisible fruit, he who knows thus conquers union with the *uktha* and residence in the same world as it.

"A chariot drawn by mules will come to you; you will have female slaves and gold coins; you will eat food and see what is pleasing; he eats food and sees what is pleasing, and there is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) in his family—he who meditates upon this Ātman as Vaiśvānara. 'This, however, is only the eye of this Ātman,' he said. 'You would have become blind had you not come to me. Thus ends the thirteenth section. (13) (2)---

One should meditate upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the *yajus*. The vital breath is indeed the *yajus*. How is the vital breath the *yajus*? Because all beings are joined (*yujyante*) in the vital breath; for when the vital breath is absent, no one has the capacity for union with anything. Therefore, because it joins (*yunakti*), the vital breath is the *yajus*.

He states the fruit for one who knows thus: "They are joined"—meaning they exert themselves—for him who knows thus; all beings [exert themselves] for that pre-eminence (*śraiṣṭhya*), for the state of being the best, thinking, "May he be the best among us. "Union with the *yajus*, which is breath," and so forth—all is the same [as before].

One should meditate upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as *sāman*. The vital breath is indeed *sāman*; how is the vital breath *sāman*? Because all beings are united (*samyañci*) and come together in the vital breath, and because it is the cause of attaining harmony (*sāmya*) through this coming together, the vital breath is *sāman*. Indeed, all beings are united and come together for his sake; not only do they come together, but they also become capable and fit for his state of excellence. "Union with *sāman*" and so forth are as explained previously. (4)

One should meditate upon that vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the ruling power (*kṣattra*). The vital breath is indeed the ruling power; this is well known—for the vital breath is indeed the ruling power. How is it well known? He says: because the vital breath protects—that is, preserves—this physical body from being wounded by weapons and the like, and fills it again with flesh; therefore, its status as the ruling power is well known by virtue of its protection against injury (*kṣatatrāṇa*).

He states the fruit for the knower: "He attains the *kṣattra* that is *ātram*. *Ātram* means that which does not protect (*na trāyate*) by anything else; *kṣattra* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The meaning is that he attains that *kṣattra*, the *ātram*—the vital breath. Or, according to the reading in another recension (*śākhāntara*), he attains the *kṣattra-ātram*, meaning he becomes the vital breath. "He who knows thus wins union with and residence in the same world as the *kṣattra*. This is the thirteenth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth chapter.

Then he said to Indradyumna Bhāllaveya Vaiyāghrapadya: "Upon what Self do you meditate? He replied, "Venerable King, upon Vāyu alone. [The teacher said: "This one whom you meditate upon as the Self is indeed Vaiśvānara, the Self whose paths are manifold. Therefore, offerings come to you from various directions, and rows of chariots follow you in various directions.

The meditation upon Brahman as qualified by various limiting adjuncts (upādhi), such as the heart and so forth, has been described; now, the meditation upon it as qualified by the Gāyatrī meter is to be explained, and thus this section begins. For among all meters, the Gāyatrī meter is the most preeminent; he will explain that it is called "Gāyatrī" because it protects (trāṇa) the vital breath (prāṇa) of its user, whereas other meters lack the capacity to protect the vital breath of their user. Furthermore, it is identical with the vital breath, and the vital breath is the self of all meters.

And because it protects the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is called *kṣattra*; furthermore, the *prāṇa* is the *gāyatrī*. Therefore, the meditation upon that very [gāyatrī] is what is intended to be taught. Moreover, because it is the cause of the second birth for the best of the twice-born—as it is said, "He created the Brāhmaṇa from the *gāyatrī*, the Rājanya from the *triṣṭubh*, and the Vaiśya from the *jagatī*"—the second birth of the best of the twice-born is caused by the *gāyatrī*. Consequently, the *gāyatrī* is preeminent.

"Having risen [from worldly life], the Brāhmaṇas address him as a Brāhmaṇa; he becomes a Brāhmaṇa who is free from evil, free from passion, and free from doubt"—thus [the text] shows the connection of the Brāhmaṇa with the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha). And that state of being a Brāhmaṇa has its root in the birth from Gāyatrī; therefore, the true nature of Gāyatrī must be explained. For the best of the twice-born, once created by Gāyatrī, is authorized without restriction to achieve the supreme human goal; hence, the connection with the highest human goal is rooted in her.

Therefore, for the purpose of prescribing its meditation, he says: "Earth, atmosphere, heaven"—these are eight syllables. That which has eight syllables is this "eight-syllabled" [Gāyatrī]. The words *ha* and *vai* are used as indicators of what is well-known. This is the first foot of the Gāyatrī. The number eight is completed by the syllable *ya* itself. This indeed is that very first foot of this Gāyatrī, characterized by earth and so forth, whose nature is the three worlds, because of the commonality of having eight syllables.

Thus, for one who knows this first foot of the Gāyatrī, which consists of the three worlds, this is the fruit: whatever is to be conquered within these three worlds, all that indeed he conquers—the wise man who knows this foot in such a manner.

"You shall eat food and see what is pleasing; he who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self in this way eats food, sees what is pleasing, and there arises in his family a spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). "But this is merely the breath of the Self," he said. "Your breath would have departed had you not come to me. Thus ends the fourteenth section. 14. (2)

Likewise, the syllables of the threefold knowledge—the *ṛc*s, the *yajus*s, and the *sāmans*—are also these same eight. Similarly, one foot of the *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables as its second part; this very [foot] of hers is characterized by the *ṛc*, *yajus*, and *sāman* precisely because of the commonality of having eight syllables. Whoever knows this foot of the *gāyatrī*, which is characterized by the threefold knowledge, wins as much as this entire threefold knowledge extends—that is, whatever collection of fruits is obtained through the threefold knowledge.

Likewise, *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and *vyāna*—these syllables designating the vital breaths are also eight; and that is the third foot of the Gāyatrī. Whoever knows this third foot of the Gāyatrī in this way conquers as much as this entire world of living beings.

Immediately thereafter, the fourth foot of the three-footed Gāyatrī, which consists of sound, is declared to be its referent (the object denoted). Of this aforementioned Gāyatrī, this very fourth, visible foot, "beyond the dust" (*parorajā*), is that which shines yonder. The Śruti itself explains the meaning of the words in the sentence beginning with "the fourth": that which is well-known in the world as "fourth" is here designated by the word *turīya*.

What is the meaning of the phrase "the visible step" (*darśataṃ padam*)? It is said: for this Person within the orb is seen as if he were visible; therefore, he is called "the visible step. What is the meaning of the word "beyond the dust" (*parorajā*)? It is said: for this Person situated in the orb indeed shines over and above the entire, whole *rajas*—that is to say, the entire world born of *rajas*—shining with sovereign lordship over the whole world born of *rajas*.

The repetition "higher and higher" (uparyupari) is for the purpose of making known his sovereignty over the entire world. [Objection: Since this is already established by the word "all" (sarva), the repetition is redundant. [Response: This is not a fault; the repetition is intended to remove the doubt that the word "all" might refer only to those regions above which the sun is visible. For there is another scriptural passage stating, "And he rules over the worlds that are beyond that [sun] and over the desires of the gods. Therefore, the repetition is for the sake of including everything.
Just as that sun shines with glory characterized by universal sovereignty, with fame, and with renown, even so does he who knows this fourth, visible foot shine with glory and fame.

This very Gāyatrī, which is said to have three feet—characterized by the three worlds, the three Vedas, and the vital breath—is established upon this fourth, the visible foot, beyond the dust of the mortal realm (*parorajas*), because the Sun is the essence (*rasa*) of both the formed and the formless. For when its essence is removed, an object becomes sapless and unstable, just as wood and the like are once their core substance is burnt; in the same way, the three-footed Gāyatrī, consisting of the formed and the formless world, is established in the Sun along with its three feet, because that Sun is its essence.

That fourth quarter is indeed established in truth. But what is that truth? It is said: the eye is truth. How is the eye truth? He says: this is well known; for the eye is indeed truth. How is it well known? He says: therefore, if two people should come at this very moment disputing, speaking contradictory things—one saying, "I saw," and the other saying [the opposite]—then...

"I have heard that the object seen by you was not so. Of these two, we should place our trust in the one who says, "I saw it," and not in the one who says, "I heard it. For a false hearing is possible for a listener, but there is no false seeing for the eye. Therefore, we would not trust one who says, "I heard it"; thus, because it is the cause for the attainment of truth, the eye is Truth.

The meaning is that when that Truth exists as the eye, together with the other three feet, the fourth foot is established. And it has been said: "In what is the sun established? In the eye. That Truth, which is the support of the fourth foot, is established in strength (*bala*). What, then, is that strength? He says: "Strength is indeed breath (*prāṇa*); Truth is established in that strength, which is breath. And thus it has been said: "In that thread, this [world] is woven lengthwise and crosswise."

Since truth is established upon strength, therefore they say: "Strength is more powerful than truth"—meaning it is more vigorous and more forceful. Even in the world, it is well known that whatever rests upon something else, the support is stronger than that which is supported; for a weak thing is never seen to be the support of something strong. Thus, by this logic, this Gāyatrī is established in the *adhyātma*, that is, in the vital breath (*prāṇa*); this very Gāyatrī is the vital breath.

Therefore, the world is established in the Gāyatrī; that vital breath (*prāṇa*) in which all the gods become one, as do all the Vedas, rituals, and their fruits—that Gāyatrī, being of the nature of vital breath, is the Self of the world. She indeed protects (*tatre*) the *gayas*; but who are the *gayas*? The vital breaths, such as speech and the rest, are indeed the *gayas*, because they produce sound (*śabda*); she protects them, and thus she is the Gāyatrī. Because she protects the *gayas* (*gayatrāṇāt*), she is celebrated by the name Gāyatrī.

That teacher, having initiated the eight-year-old boy, recites that very Gāyatrī Sāvitrī—whose deity is Savitṛ—first foot by foot, then half-verse by half-verse, and finally the whole verse. This alone is the manifest Prāṇa, the Self of the world, which has now been explained here as being entrusted to the boy, and no other. That teacher, for whichever boy he recites it, protects his vital breaths (*prāṇas*) from falling into hell and other such states.

Regarding this *Sāvitrī*, some followers of certain Vedic branches recite it for the initiated student as an *Anuṣṭubh*—meaning they claim it originates from the *Anuṣṭubh* and possesses the *Anuṣṭubh* meter. He states their intention: "Speech is the *Anuṣṭubh*, and Speech in the body is Sarasvatī; it is that very Speech, Sarasvatī, whom we recite for the young student," so they say. One should not do so, nor should one know it thus; what they say is indeed false. What then? One should recite the *Sāvitrī* as the *Gāyatrī* alone.

Why? Because it has been stated that "the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the Gāyatrī. When the vital breath is mentioned, speech (*vāk*), Sarasvatī, and all the other vital breaths become entrusted to the young student (*māṇavaka*). Furthermore, having said this as a digression, he praises the knower of the Gāyatrī: "Even if one who knows thus should receive much—though for him, who is the Self of all, there is nothing at all that is 'much,' since the knower is the Self of all—nevertheless, that entire mass of gifts is not sufficient even for a single foot (*pada*) of the Gāyatrī. (6)

He who knows the *gāyatrī*—he who might accept these three worlds, beginning with the earth (*bhūr*), which are filled with wealth such as cattle and horses—that acceptance would only cause him to attain this first foot of the *gāyatrī* that has been explained; he would obtain the fruit of knowing the first foot, and by that it would be as if he had already enjoyed it. That acceptance, however, does not produce any further fault.

Furthermore, whoever should receive as much as this threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*) extends, he would thereby obtain this second quarter (*pada*); by him the fruit of knowing the second quarter would have been enjoyed. Likewise, whoever should receive as much as all these living beings (*prāṇin*) extend, he would thereby obtain this third quarter; by him the fruit of knowing the third quarter would have been enjoyed. This is said by way of illustration.

Even if someone were to accept [the gift] equal to three quarters [of the earth], that would only be a cause for the exhaustion of the fruit of the knowledge of those three quarters, and not capable of being the agent of any other fault; neither the giver nor the recipient is like this; [this] is imagined for the sake of praising the knowledge of the Gāyatrī; even if the giver and the recipient are conceived in such a way, that acceptance is not capable of [producing] transgression.

Why? Because even the knowledge of the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*) remains as that which is yet to be attained, being the subject matter of the fourth quarter of the *gāyatrī*. He demonstrates this: "Now, this is its very fourth, visible quarter, 'beyond the dust,' which is that which shines yonder. If it were not so, [the text would have said] it is not to be obtained by any gift whatsoever—that is, it is not to be attained at all—just like the three previously mentioned quarters. Even these [three] are not to be obtained by anyone; this was stated assuming them to be so for the sake of illustration.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), how could one possibly accept [the world] as being equal to the three worlds and so forth? Therefore, the meaning is that the *gāyatrī* itself is to be meditated upon (*upāsyā*) in this manner.

Her worship—her worship, that is, approaching and standing near her, is the act of salutation with this mantra. He states what that mantra is: "O Gāyatrī, you are one-footed by means of the three worlds as your foot; you are two-footed by means of the second, which is the form of the triple knowledge (the Vedas); you are three-footed by means of the third, consisting of the vital breaths and so forth; and you are four-footed by means of the fourth, the *turīya*. Thus, by these four feet, you are approached—that is, known—by the worshippers."

Beyond this, you stand by means of your own supreme, unconditioned Self—you who have no foot (apad), that is, for whom no place exists, by which you are reached; thus you are "footless" (apat), because you are not reached, since your nature is "not this, not this. Therefore, salutations to You, the Fourth (turīya), the visible foot, which transcends the realm of dust (parorajas) and lies beyond the sphere of empirical transaction.

"This enemy is evil, creating an obstacle to your attainment"; "that" refers to the self's own function, namely, being the creator of an obstacle to your attainment; "may he not attain it"—may he certainly not attain it. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the mantra. Regarding "whomsoever one may hate," this means the learned person himself should direct this ritual attendance toward the object of his hatred; he should utter the name, saying, "This enemy is so-and-so by name."

One worships with the thought, "May the desired object for this Yajñadatta not be fulfilled, may it not reach him"; for that desire is indeed not fulfilled for this Devadatta, but rather for whomsoever one worships in this manner. Or one worships with the thought, "I have obtained that which was desired by Devadatta. There is an option according to one's preference among these three mantra-words beginning with "May this [object] not reach him" (*asāv ado mā prāpat*).

An explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) is now spoken for the purpose of prescribing the mouth of the *gāyatrī*: this is indeed recorded in tradition as follows. In that context concerning the knowledge of the *gāyatrī*, Janaka of Videha spoke to one named Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi—the son of Aśvatarāśva. "Now" (*yat nu*) is used in the sense of deliberation; "ho" and "aho" are particles of address. That which you said—namely, "I am a knower of the *gāyatrī*"—is inconsistent with that statement [of yours]. What is this? It is inconsistent with those words.

"Now, how is it so? If you are one who knows the Gāyatrī, why have you become an elephant through the fault of accepting a gift? Being reminded by the king, he replied: "O Emperor, because I did not know—that is, I had not realized—the mouth of this Gāyatrī, my knowledge of the Gāyatrī has become fruitless due to being deficient in one limb. Listen then: fire itself is the mouth of that Gāyatrī."

Just as when worldly people throw even a great deal of fuel into the fire, the fire consumes all that fuel, so indeed does one who knows this—knowing that "Fire is the mouth of Gāyatrī"—become himself the self of Gāyatrī with Fire as his mouth.

Even if he commits much evil, such as the fault of accepting gifts, he consumes and devours that entire mass of evil; being purified and cleansed like the fire, he becomes the self of Gāyatrī, free from the fault of accepting gifts, undecaying, and immortal.
Thus ends the fourteenth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth chapter.

Then Janaka Śārkarākṣya said: "Whom do you worship as the Self? He replied: "The ether alone, O Venerable King. [Yājñavalkya] said: "This Vaiśvānara Self which you worship as the Self is indeed the 'Abundant' (Bahula). Therefore, you are abundant in offspring and wealth. (1) ---

He who performs the combination of knowledge and action prays to the Sun at the time of death; and there is a logical connection here, for He is indeed the fourth foot of the Gāyatrī, and the worship of Him is the subject under discussion; therefore, He alone is prayed to. With a golden vessel—that is, a vessel consisting of light—just as a desired object is covered by a vessel, so too this Brahman called "Truth" is, as it were, veiled by the luminous orb, because it is invisible to those whose minds are not concentrated.

That is explained as follows: "The face of truth"—the face being its primary essential nature—is covered by a covering, which, like a vessel with a lid, is the cause of obstruction to perception. O Pūṣan—so called because you nourish (*puṣ*) the world—you are Savitṛ; remove that covering, open it, meaning: take away the cause of obstruction to perception. "For me, whose nature is truth" (*satyadharmāya*): truth is my *dharma*; such a person as I am is "one whose nature is truth"; for him, who has become one with you, [open it]. "For seeing" (*dṛṣṭaye*): for the purpose of perception.

The names beginning with "Pūṣan" are for the purpose of addressing Savitṛ. "Ekarṣi": he is both one and a seer (ṛṣi), hence Ekarṣi; he is a seer because of his vision, for he, being the Self and the eye of the entire world, perceives everything. Or, he is Ekarṣi because he goes alone, according to the Vedic verse: "The Sun moves alone. "Yama": for the restraint of the entire world is performed by you. "Sūrya": he impels (sūrayate) well the juices, the rays, the vital breaths, or the thoughts of the world.

O Prājāpatya—O offspring of Prajāpati, the Lord, or of Hiraṇyagarbha—withdraw your rays; gather together and contract the splendor of your self, so that I may be able to see. For, with my vision overwhelmed by your splendor, I am unable to perceive your true form directly, just as one cannot see forms during a flash of lightning. Therefore, withdraw your splendor; [reveal] that form of yours which is the most auspicious of all auspicious things.

That [Person] of yours I behold—we behold it, with a change in the grammatical number. That Person who is a constituent part of the *vyāhṛtis* "Bhūḥ," "Bhuvaḥ," and "Svaḥ," who is called "Person" because of his human-like form, he am I; I exist as that. And because it is stated in the Upaniṣads, "Day by day I [enter]," this refers to both the Sun and the one in the eye; thus the connection is: "He am I, the immortal. When my body falls away, let the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the wind residing in the body, go back to the external air alone, to *anila*.

Likewise, let other deities return each to their own respective nature; and now, this body also, having ended in ashes, shall go to the earth. Now, he prays to the deity Agni, who has become his own volition and is established in the mind: "O Kratu! Om! O Kratu!"—these two are indeed for the purpose of address. He is "Om" because he is the symbol of the syllable *oṃ*; and he is "Kratu" because he consists of the mind (*manas*). O Kratu, remember that which is to be remembered.

For at the time of death, by the power of remembering you, the desired goal is attained; therefore, this is prayed for: "Remember what has been done by me"—the repetition is for the sake of emphasis. Furthermore, O Agni, lead us—cause us to reach—by a fair path, that is, by an auspicious way, for the sake of wealth, meaning for the attainment of the fruits of our actions; not by the southern, dark path which involves return, but rather by the bright fair path alone.

O God, you who know all our ways—that is, the various forms of wisdom belonging to all living beings—separate from us, drive away, and remove from us all crooked sin, that is, the entire multitude of evils. Freed from that sin, we shall proceed by the northern path through your grace. However, we are unable to perform service for you.

"We shall offer to you the most abundant, that is, the greatest, utterance of homage—the word of salutation; we shall serve you by means of this speech of homage," meaning that we are unable to do anything else.
Thus ends the fifteenth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth chapter.
Thus [ends the work] of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, Śrī Govinda Bhagavat...
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the worshipful teacher, the fifth chapter [ends].
Now, he said to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi Vaiyāghrapadya: "Whom do you meditate upon as the Self? "Water alone, O Venerable Sir."

"O King," he said, "this indeed is the Vaiśvānara Self that is wealth; since you worship this Self, therefore you are wealthy and prosperous. Then he said to Uddālaka Āruṇi, "Gautama, what Self do you worship? "The earth itself, O Venerable King," he replied. "This indeed is the Vaiśvānara Self that is the foundation; since you worship this Self, therefore you are firmly established with offspring and cattle."

He said to them: "Indeed, you eat food as if you were each knowing this Vaiśvānara Self separately. But he who meditates upon this very Vaiśvānara Self as of the measure of a span, as the all-pervading one—he eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves. Therefore, whatever food comes first, that is to be offered as a sacrifice. The first oblation which he should offer, let him offer it with the words, 'Svāhā to Prāṇa!'; thus Prāṇa is satisfied. (1)

Then, that which he should offer as the second, he should offer with the words, "Svāhā to Vyāna! and Vyāna is satisfied. Then, that which he should offer as the third, he should offer with the words, "Svāhā to Apāna! and Apāna is satisfied. Then, that which he should offer as the fourth, he should offer with the words, "Svāhā to Samāna! and Samāna is satisfied.
Now, that which he should offer as the fifth [oblation], he should offer with the words, "To the out-breath, svāhā! Thus the out-breath is satisfied.

There was once Śvetaketu Āruṇeya. His father said to him: "Śvetaketu, live the life of a religious student; for, my dear, no one from our family has ever been a mere kinsman of the Veda (*brahmabandhu*) without having studied it.

It has been stated that "the vital breath (prāṇa) is the Gāyatrī. But for what reason does the Gāyatrī possess the nature of the vital breath, and not the nature of speech and the other organs? It is because the vital breath is both the eldest (jyeṣṭha) and the best (śreṣṭha), whereas speech and the others do not partake of this priority and excellence. With the desire to determine how the vital breath possesses this priority and excellence, this section is commenced. Alternatively, it may be that the meditation on the vital breath alone—through its aspects as the Uktha, Yajus, Sāman, Kṣatra, and so forth—has been set forth, even though the eyes and other organs also exist.

In this context, the mere cause is connected here by way of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), and not as a continuation of what preceded. However, since this section (*kāṇḍa*) is intended to be a supplement (*khila*), that meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) concerning a specific fruit which was not mentioned previously must now be stated. The words "yaḥ kaścit" (whoever) and "ha vai" serve to emphasize the point: whoever knows the one possessing the qualities of being the eldest and the best, as will be described, he indeed becomes both the eldest and the best.

Thus, being enticed by the fruit [of knowledge], he became intent on asking a question; and to him [the teacher] said: "The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the eldest and the best. But how is it understood that the vital breath is both the eldest and the best? Because at the very time of conception, the connection with the semen and the blood is common to the entire collection beginning with the vital breath. Nevertheless, since the semen does not grow without the vital breath, the first acquisition of function belongs to the vital breath rather than to the eyes and other organs; therefore, the vital breath is the eldest in terms of age.

From the time of conception, it is *prāṇa* that nourishes the embryo; for when *prāṇa* has attained its function, only then do the eyes and the other senses attain their functions. Therefore, it is appropriate that *prāṇa* is the eldest among the eyes and the rest. However, in the world there may be someone who is the eldest in the family but, due to a lack of qualities, is not the best; or the middle one or the youngest may be the best because of his abundance of qualities, rather than the eldest. But it is not so in this case, as the text says: "But *prāṇa* alone is both the eldest and the best."

But how, then, is the preeminence of the vital breath (prāṇa) understood? We shall demonstrate this here by means of a dialogue. In any case, however, he who knows—that is, meditates upon—the vital breath as possessing the qualities of being the eldest and the best, becomes the eldest and the best among his own kinsmen, by virtue of the power of meditating on those qualities of being the eldest and the best.

Moreover, among those who desire to become—that is, who wish to be—the eldest and the best even apart from their own [natural] seniority, one who perceives the Prāṇa as the eldest and the best becomes both the eldest and the best among them. Now, an objection may be raised: "Is not being the eldest caused by age? How then can it come about through mere desire? This is not a fault, because what is intended here is that "being the eldest" refers precisely to the attainment of a functional priority, just like that of the Prāṇa.

Having approached [his teacher] at twelve years of age, he returned at twenty-four years of age, having studied all the Vedas; being high-minded, considering himself a learned scholar, and arrogant, he came home. Then his father said to him:

He who indeed knows the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhā*) becomes the most excellent among his own people. The fruit corresponds to the nature of that vision. And he becomes the most excellent even for those among his kinsmen whom he wishes to excel. Let it then be stated: what is this "most excellent"? Speech indeed is the most excellent. It is "the most excellent" because it causes one to dwell (*vāsayati*) or because it clothes (*vaste*) exceedingly. For through speech, those possessing mental power dwell exceedingly well. Or, *vasiṣṭhā* is derived from the root *vas* in the sense of covering.

For those who have mastered speech indeed surpass others by means of their speech. Therefore, through the thorough knowledge of the quality of being Vasiṣṭha, one comes to possess the quality of being Vasiṣṭha; this is the fruit corresponding to the vision [of the teaching].

"O Śvetaketu, my dear, since you are so high-minded, considering yourself learned in the Vedas, and arrogant, you did not ask that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known. How, O Venerable One, does that instruction come to be?

He who knows the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*)—it is called "foundation" because one stands firm by means of it—he who knows that foundation, which possesses the quality of being a foundation, for him this is the fruit: he stands firm on level ground and at the right time, as well as on difficult, uneven, or inaccessible terrain, or during difficult times such as famine. If it is asked what this foundation is, [the answer is]: the eye indeed is the foundation.

"How is it that the eye has the nature of a foundation? He says: "For having seen both level ground and difficult terrain with the eye, one stands firm. Therefore, there is a corresponding result: he who knows this stands firm on level ground and stands firm on difficult terrain. Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay would be known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply 'clay'—so it is. 4. (4)

Whoever knows the perfection (*saṃpad*), whoever knows that which is endowed with the quality of perfection—for him this result accrues: whatever desire he desires, that desire is fulfilled. But what, then, has the quality of perfection? The ear, indeed, is perfection. How, then, is it said that the ear possesses the quality of perfection? Because when the ear exists, all the Vedas are perfected [in him], since they are to be studied by one who possesses the faculty of hearing; and desires are dependent upon the rituals prescribed in the Vedas.
Therefore, the ear is perfection. Consequently, a fruit corresponding to that consciousness accrues to him who knows this, whatever desire he may desire.
"Just as, my dear, by means of a single ingot of gold, everything made of gold might be known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while 'gold' alone is the truth. 5.

He who knows the abode (*āyatana*)—the abode being the support—he becomes the abode for his own people and the abode for other people as well. What, then, is that abode? It is said: the mind (*manas*) is indeed the abode, the support of the sense organs and their objects. For it is when supported by the mind that objects attain the state of being experienced by the self. Furthermore, the sense organs proceed and withdraw under the influence of the mind's volitions; therefore, the mind is the abode of the sense organs.
Therefore, according to one's vision, the result becomes the abode for oneself and the abode for others, for one who knows thus.

"Just as, my dear, by means of a single nail-cutter, all that is made of iron might be known—[knowing] that the modification is a mere verbal handle, a name, while 'iron' alone is the truth—is this not so, my dear? This, my dear, is the instruction.

(7) These vital breaths (*prāṇas*), beginning with speech (*vāk*), desiring their own excellence—that is, for the purpose of [determining] "I am the best"—entered into dispute, speaking contradictorily, and went to *Brahman*—that is, they approached Prajāpati, who is denoted by the word *Brahman*. Having gone there, they said to that *Brahman*: "Who among us is the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*)? Who among us dwells (*vasati*) and causes others to dwell (*vāsayati*)?"

When that Brahman was thus questioned by them, it spoke as follows: "Among you, when whichever one has departed, having gone out from the body, this body is considered by the world to be more wretched—that is, more sinful—than before. For the body, being a collection of many impurities, is indeed sinful even while living; yet it becomes even more miserable when he has departed. This is stated as 'more wretched' for the sake of generating dispassion."
"He shall be the Vasiṣṭha among you. Although Prajāpati knew who Vasiṣṭha was, he did not say, "This one is Vasiṣṭha," in order to avoid causing displeasure to the others.

(8) Thus addressed by Brahmā, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) departed from themselves one after another in order to test their own power. Thereupon, speech (*vāk*) alone first departed from this body. Having departed and stayed away for a year, having become absent, it returned and said: "How were you able—how did you have the power—to live without me?"

Thus addressed, they replied: "Just as in the world there are those who are without parts (*akalāḥ*), who are mute, not speaking with speech, yet breathing—performing the function of breathing—with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), seeing—performing the function of seeing—with the eye, likewise hearing with the ear, knowing with the mind the objects of what ought and ought not to be done, and procreating—begetting sons by means of semen—in this very way we have lived. Having thus received an answer from the vital breaths regarding its own remaining in this body, Speech indeed entered back in.
Likewise, "the eye departed," and so forth, as before. [The senses are] the ear, the mind, and procreation.

Then, as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) was about to depart—that is, as it was on the verge of departing—the speech and the other organs immediately moved from their own places. To illustrate this, he says: "Just as in the world, when a great and noble horse (*mahāsuhaya*)—an excellent steed endowed with auspicious marks, large in size, and a Saindhava by birth, originating from the Sindhu region—were to simultaneously uproot the pegs of its foot-tethers (*paḍvīśaśaṅkūn*), that is, the stakes used for binding its feet, pulling them out all at once while the rider is mounted."

Having mounted [the body] for the purpose of testing them, he thus indeed tore out these vital breaths, speech and the rest, displacing them from their own positions. Those [breaths], speech and the others, said: "O Venerable One, do not depart! For we shall certainly not be able to live without you. "If this excellence of mine has been recognized by you—if I am the best here—then pay tribute to me, grant me a tax."

And this dialogue among the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) is a contrived instruction on the method for examining who is the best among the wise; for by this very method, the wise man examines, "Who indeed here is the best? This method of examination is described in the form of a dialogue, because otherwise, it would not be possible for these [organs], acting in combination, to have their respective departures and so forth occurring directly over the course of exactly one year.

Therefore, it is only the wise person who, desiring to know the preeminent among speech and the other organs for the sake of meditation, investigates in this manner; and the vital breaths, being requested for their tribute, promised, saying, "So be it.

That Speech, having indeed been the first to offer her tribute, spoke thus: "Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), that which is my excellence belongs to you alone; by virtue of that quality of being most excellent, you shall be 'Vasiṣṭha'. "Insofar as I am the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), you are that foundation; that which is my foundation, you are it"—thus [spoke] the Eye. The rest is the same. They have successively surrendered their qualities of being the assembly, the abode, and procreation.

"If it is so, you have indeed given a worthy offering. Speak—what is the food for him who is distinguished by such qualities as these? And what is his clothing? They replied: "Whatever is known in this world as 'food,' from dogs down to worms and down to insects and moths—whatever is the food of dogs, the food of worms, and the food of insects and moths—all that together, whatever is eaten by living beings, all that is your food.
The instruction here is to cultivate the vision that everything is the food of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)."

However, some who know the doctrine of the food of life (*prāṇānnavid*) claim that there is no fault in eating anything whatsoever. That is incorrect, because it is prohibited by another scripture. If it is argued that this [other scripture] constitutes an option (*vikalpa*) for the present case, we say no, because it is not prescriptive. The statement, "Indeed, nothing that is not food is eaten by him," is intended as a praise for the enjoined knowledge that "everything is the food of the vital breath" (*prāṇa*); for it forms a single syntactical unit with that injunction. It does not have the power to sublate what is enjoined in another scripture, since its purpose is directed elsewhere.

The intended teaching here is that all food belongs to the mere vital breath (*prāṇamātra*), and not that one should eat everything. As for the notion that there is no fault in eating everything, that is entirely false, because there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for it. If it is argued that there is indeed no fault because, by implication, the capacity for all food is possible since the knower is the vital breath itself, we say no; for it is impossible for [the knower] to consume every single bit of food.

It is true that although the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the knower, the consumption of all food—including worms, insects, gods, and so forth—is not possible by means of that aggregate of body and organs (*kāryakaraṇasaṃghāta*) which characterizes one who possesses knowledge. Therefore, the declaration regarding the absence of fault in consuming all food in that state would be purposeless, since the fault of consuming all food has not been reached [as a possibility]. [Objection: But as the vital breath, it certainly does consume even the food of worms, insects, and so on. [Reply: Certainly, but there is no prohibition concerning that.

Therefore—since the *kiṃśuka* flower is naturally red—the absence of fault applies there; hence, indicating the absence of fault by that same form would be purposeless, because the fault of eating all food has not [otherwise] been reached. However, as for the prohibition made in connection with the relationship to the aggregate of the body and its instruments (*kāryakaraṇasaṃghāta*), there is no counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) here in connection with that. Therefore, upon transgressing that prohibition, there would indeed be a fault, because the passage beginning with "Not indeed" (*na ha vai*) refers to a different subject matter.

Furthermore, it is not the case that here the perception of the body of a Brāhmaṇa and others as consisting of all food is being enjoined; rather, it is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone that is intended. And just as, in general, for the vital breath which consists of all food, a certain kind of food serves as the cause of life for some—just as poison is for a worm born in poison—even that very same thing, while being the food of the vital breath of another, is seen to produce a fault characterized by death and so forth. In the same way, even for the vital breath that consumes all food, there is [a fault] in eating prohibited food.

Due to the connection with a body characterized by being a Brahmin and so forth, there would indeed be fault. Therefore, the very false cognition that there is no fault in eating what is not to be eaten is [the issue]. Regarding the statement "Water is your garment": water, when being consumed, stands in the place of a garment for you. And here, the meditation—that water is the garment of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—is enjoined; however, it is not possible to employ water for the actual function of a garment. Therefore, regarding the consumption of water as it naturally occurs, one should merely perform this meditation. For one who knows thus—"Verily, everything is food for this *prāṇa*"—there is indeed nothing that is "non-food" (unfit to be eaten) which, once swallowed and consumed, does not become food.

Although he has eaten what is not edible, it would be as if he had eaten only what is edible, and he is not tainted by the fault caused by that—this, we have said, is a praise of knowledge (*vidyā*). Likewise, he has not accepted what is not to be accepted; although he may have accepted elephants and other things which should not be accepted, even that would be as if he had accepted only what is edible and acceptable, and even in that case, he is not tainted by the fault of accepting what should not be accepted—this too is solely for the purpose of praise.

He who thus knows this food of the breath—the food of *ana*—the fruit is indeed the state of being the very self of the breath (*prāṇātma-bhāva*). However, this is not intended as a statement regarding the fruit [of the meditation], but rather as a statement for the sake of praise. Now, why is this itself not the fruit? It is not so; for one who perceives the self as the breath, the fruit is precisely the attainment of the state of being that very breath-self.

And in that context, for the one whose self is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), who is the Self of all, even what is not to be eaten is indeed to be eaten, and likewise, even what is not to be accepted as a gift is indeed to be accepted; thus, the knowledge (*vidyā*) is praised by taking things exactly as they are encountered. Therefore, the sentence does not have the character of an injunction regarding a result. Since water is indeed the clothing of the vital breath, therefore learned *brāhmaṇas* who are *śrotriyas*—those who have studied the Vedas—sip water when about to eat, that is, when they are going to consume food.

Having eaten, they sip water, and after having finished eating, they consume water at a later time. Regarding this, he asks: what is the intention of those who sip water? He says: they think that they are thereby making this very Prāṇa free from nakedness. And this is indeed so—for when someone gives a garment to another, he thinks, "I am making him free from nakedness. And it has been stated that water is the garment of Prāṇa. This is for the purpose of establishing the realization: "When I drink water, I am giving a garment to Prāṇa."

But surely, one who is about to eat or has already eaten sips water thinking, "I shall become pure"; and in that case, if the purpose were to make the vital breaths "un-naked," there would be a double purpose for the sipping of water. And it is not proper for a single act of sipping to have two purposes: if it is for the sake of purity, it is not for the sake of making [the breaths] un-naked; and if it is for the sake of making them un-naked, it is not for the sake of purity.

Since this is so, [the opponent argues: "Let there be a second rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) for the purpose of making the breath 'unclothed'. [The reply is: No, because two distinct actions are established here. For these are indeed two actions: the rinsing of the mouth prescribed by tradition (*smṛti*) for one who is about to eat and for one who has eaten, which serves the purpose of purification (*prāyatya*) and is merely a ritual act (*kriyāmātra*); in that case, purification does not depend on seeing [the breath] and so forth. And in that context, the perception of the water—which is a constituent part of the rinsing—as being a garment for the breath is enjoined as a subsidiary procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

But when that [meditation] is being performed, the fact that sipping water (ācamana) serves the purpose of purification is not sublated, because sipping water is a distinct action. Therefore, regarding the sipping of water by one who is about to eat or has already eaten, the mere contemplation (*darśana*) that "water is the clothing of the vital breath" is enjoined, since it is not established from any other source.
Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa of the sixth chapter.

In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second. Regarding this, some say: "In the beginning, this was Non-being alone, one only without a second; from that Non-being, Being was produced.

Śvetaketu by name, the son of Āruṇi (the descendant of Aruṇa), specifically his grandson (Āruṇeya); the particle *ha* indicates tradition; *vai* signifies certainty. Having been instructed by his father, he came to the assembly of the Pañcālas for the sake of proclaiming his own glory; the Pañcālas are well-known. Having arrived at their assembly, and thinking with pride, "Having conquered [them], I shall conquer even the assembly of the king," he approached.

[He approached] Jaibali, the son of Jīvala, the King of Pañcāla named Pravāhaṇa, who was being waited upon by his own servants—that is, having them perform service for himself. That king, having previously heard of the pride of that man's learning and thinking, "This man must be disciplined," looked at him and, as soon as he had arrived, addressed him, calling out, "Kumāra!"—the protracted vowel (*pluti*) being for the purpose of reproach. Thus addressed, he replied, "Bho! (O, sir!).

"O! he said, being angry even regarding the three injuries that were improper. The King said: "Have you been instructed? Have you been taught by your father? The other replied: "Yes, indeed; I have been instructed. Ask if you have any doubt. [The King asked: "But how, my dear, could it possibly be so? He said: 'How indeed could the existent be born from the non-existent? 'In the beginning, my dear, this was only the Existent—one only, without a second. (2)

If this is so, do you know—that is, do you understand—in what manner these well-known creatures, when they die and depart, "fall apart"? (The protracted vowel *ā3* is used for the sake of deliberation. For those traveling by a common path, there is a bifurcation of the way at a certain point where some creatures go by one path and others by another; that is their "falling apart. The meaning is: do you know how it is that those creatures fall apart?

"No," said the other. "Then do you know how they return to this world? "They do return; I know how they come back to this world. "No," Śvetaketu replied. "Do you know how that world is not filled up—how, by those who go there again and again, dying repeatedly, that world is not filled up? Do you know that? "No," he replied.

"Do you know at which number of oblations, when each oblation has been offered, the waters come to possess the voice of a person—that is, their speech becomes the very speech of a person, or they become designated by the word 'person'—so that when they have transformed into the form of a person, they then possess the voice of a person, and having risen up, having fully emerged, they speak the truth? "No," he replied.

If you know thus the "pratipad"—the point of entry—of the path leading to the gods (*devayāna*), that by which one enters is the *pratipad*, its point of entry; or the point of entry of the path leading to the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*). He states the meaning expressed by the word *pratipad*: "having performed such a specific action," meaning having performed a particular deed, by means of which action they enter the path leading to the gods or the path leading to the fathers—that action is called the *pratipad*.

"Do you know that path? means "Do you know the means for reaching the world of the gods and the world of the ancestors? Furthermore, we have heard a statement from a seer—a Vedic verse (*mantra*)—that illuminates this meaning; the sense is that there exists a mantra that also reveals this matter. What is that mantra? It is said: "I have heard of two paths, two ways."

Of these two, one leads to the fathers and is connected with the world of the fathers; the meaning is that by that path one reaches the world of the fathers. "I have heard"—this is to be construed with the distant [verb]. And the other belongs to the gods; it leads to the gods. But who are those who go to the fathers and the gods by both paths? It is said: they belong to mortals, to human beings; for it is humans alone who travel by means of the two paths.

By these two paths, this entire universe—everything that moves—goes forth and comes together. And those two paths are "between which," meaning between whom; that is, between the father and the mother. Who are those two, the mother and the father? They are heaven and earth, the two halves of the cosmic egg; for it has been explained by the Brāhmaṇa: "This [earth] is indeed the mother, and that [heaven] is the father."

"Between the two halves of the cosmic egg, within the sphere of *saṃsāra* alone do these two paths exist; they do not lead to the attainment of absolute immortality. The other said: "I do not know even one—nor a single question—from this entire collection of questions," Śvetaketu replied.

"It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It emitted heat (*tejas*). That heat thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It emitted water (*āpas*). Therefore, wherever a person grieves or perspires, from that very heat water is produced. (3)

Immediately thereafter, having removed from him Śvetaketu—who was the subject of the discourse—the pride of his intellectual conceit, the king invited him for the purpose of providing lodging, saying, "May you gentlemen dwell here; let water for the feet and the guest-offering be brought. Having made this invitation, the king [waited]. But disregarding that hospitality, the youth Śvetaketu ran away, returning toward his father.

He went to his father, and having arrived, he said to him: "How is it so? Indeed, indeed, you previously told us at the time of our graduation that we had been instructed in all branches of knowledge. Hearing these reproachful words of his son, the father said: "In what way, by what manner, has suffering arisen for you, O Sumedhas—one whose intelligence (*medhā*) is excellent? Listen to how it happened with me."

"Five"—that is, five questions in number—the kinsman of a royal (rājanyabandhu)—the term "kinsman of a royal" being a word of contempt—asked me. Therefore, I did not know, nor had I understood, even one of them. When his father asked, "Which were those questions asked by the king?", the son replied, "These," and he cited the opening words of those questions.

Those waters thought, "May we become many; may we procreate. They created food. Therefore, wherever it rains, there food becomes most abundant; from water alone that edible food is born. Thus ends the second section. 2. (4)

The father, pacifying his angry son, said: "My dear child, you should know us in this way: that whatever collection of knowledge I know, all of that I have told to you. Who else is dearer to me than you, for whose sake I would protect [anything]? Even I do not know this which was asked by the King; therefore, come."

"Having gone there, let us both live the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*) with the king for the sake of knowledge. He said, "You alone go; I do not venture to look upon his face. He departed—Gautama by lineage, Gautama, the son of Aruṇa—to where the seat, the place of reception, of Pravāhaṇa Jaibali was. (The two genitive endings are used in place of the nominative. For that Gautama who had arrived, having brought a suitable seat, he caused water to be served by his attendants.

Then, having prepared the *arghya* offering with the prescribed mantras and the *madhuparka* for him through his domestic priest, and having thus performed the worship, he said to him: "We grant a boon to you, the venerable Gautama," referring to [boons] characterized by cattle, horses, and so forth. (5) Gautama said: "This boon has already been promised to me by you; make yourself firm in this promise. However, that speech which you uttered in the presence of my son—the boy—in the form of a question, speak that very thing to me; that alone shall be our boon."
(6) The king said: "O Gautama, that which you request among the boons from the gods is indeed [unattainable]; request instead one of the human boons.

Gautama said: "That [wealth] is indeed known to you as being mine; I have no need for that human boon which you wish to give me. For I already possess abundant gold—'I have obtained it' is to be supplied everywhere—and I possess cattle and horses, female slaves, excellent attendants and retinues, and clothing. Furthermore, that which is already in my possession should neither be requested from you nor given by you."

And a boon has been promised by you; you yourself know what is appropriate here, that your promise must be kept. As for me, however, this is my intention: let it not be that you, having been generous toward everyone else, become ungenerous—or rather, miserly—toward us alone, directed specifically against us.

"Of much—that is, abundant—of infinite—that is, having infinite fruit—and of boundless—that is, inexhaustible, extending to sons, grandsons, and so forth—of such wealth as this, may you not be one who gives it to me alone; nor is there anything else that you have not already given away. Being thus addressed, he said: "Therefore, O Gautama, do you indeed seek to obtain knowledge from me by means of the proper way—that is, according to the rule prescribed in the scriptures."

Thus addressed, Gautama said: "I approach, I go unto you as a disciple. For it is said that in former times, Brāhmaṇas seeking knowledge—even when they were Kṣatriyas—would approach Vaiśyas, or Kṣatriyas would approach Vaiśyas in times of distress, doing so merely through the mode of a disciple, not by means of formal entry into discipleship (*upāyana*) or service (*śuśrūṣā*). Therefore, that Gautama dwelt there merely by the mention of his approaching—that is, by the mere act of announcing his arrival—and did not perform the formal entry into discipleship.

When Gautama had thus spoken during this time of distress, the king, considering himself at fault, spoke while seeking forgiveness: "In that manner toward us, do not offend; do not commit an offense"—the meaning is that our offense should not be taken to heart. And just as your ancestors did not take offense against our ancestors, so too should you maintain the conduct of your ancestors toward us. This is the meaning.

"Just as you know that this knowledge (*vidyā*), which you have now requested, has never before dwelt with any Brāhmaṇa since its transmission from me, so too do you know that this knowledge has always come down through a succession of Kṣatriyas. That state of affairs must also be preserved by me, if it is possible. As it was said: 'O Gautama, among the boons [available] for the gods, speak [one] for men'; it does not mean that the boon is not to be given to you. Beyond this point, it is no longer possible to preserve it."
I shall also declare that knowledge to you. For who else indeed would be fit to refuse you while you speak thus—saying "I will not tell you"—as I, however, how could I not tell it to you?

"That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire," and so forth—the fourth question is resolved first; for the resolution of the other questions depends upon the resolution of this one. That heavenly world, O Gautama, is the fire; the perception of fire is enjoined upon the heavenly world, though it is not actually fire, just as [the perception of] a woman or a man [is enjoined upon sacrificial implements]. Of that heavenly fire, the sun alone is the fuel (*samit*), because of its kindling; for by the sun, that world is indeed kindled.

The rays are the smoke, because of the commonality of rising; for from the sun the rays emerge, and in the world smoke rises from the fuel. The day is the flame, because of the commonality of light; the quarters are the embers, because of the commonality of subsiding; the intermediate directions are the sparks, because of their scattering like sparks. Into this very celestial fire, characterized by such qualities, the gods—Indra and the others—offer faith, casting it in as the substance of the oblation.

From that oblation, King Soma arises for the ancestors and the Brāhmaṇas. Regarding this, who are the deities there, how do they offer the oblation, or what is the sacrificial material called *śraddhā*? We have already explained this in the *Saṃbandha* (Introduction) while discussing the six topics, such as "But you [do not know] their departure," in relation to the *agnihotra*.

"They enter the intermediate space"; "they make the intermediate space their *āhavanīya* fire, the wind their fuel, and the rays their bright oblation"; "they satisfy the intermediate space"; "they rise up from there"; "they enter heaven"; "they make heaven their *āhavanīya* fire and the sun their fuel"—thus it has been stated. In that regard, the two *agnihotra* oblations depart together with their implements.

Just as here on earth these specific things are known by their respective means—the Āhavanīya fire, the fuel, the smoke, the embers, the sparks, and the sacrificial materials—so too do they depart from this world to that world.

There, fire remains as fire, fuel as fuel, smoke as smoke, embers as embers, sparks as sparks, and even the sacrificial material, such as milk and the like, remains as the very substance of the oblation; even at the beginning of creation, in the undifferentiated state, it persists through its own subtle self.

That very action characterized as the *agnihotra*, existing together with its means and established in the form of the *apūrva*, undergoes transformation at the time of its manifestation (*vyākaraṇa*), bringing about the state of the intermediate space and so forth as the *āhavanīya* fire and so on; it is exactly the same for the action called *agnihotra* even now.

Thus, the entire world consists of the transformation of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) resulting from the oblations of the *agnihotra*. For the purpose of praising those very oblations, six topics—beginning with the departure [of the soul] and ending with its rising toward the world—were determined previously in the section on ritual action (*karmaprakaraṇa*). However, here, since the intention is to describe the ripening of the fruits of action for the agent, the vision of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*) is introduced, beginning with the heavenly world as fire; this is intended as a means for attaining the northern path (*uttaramārga*) for the sake of experiencing the specific fruits of one's actions. Thus, the vision of the heavenly world as fire and so forth is commenced.

In this regard, those internal vital breaths (*prāṇas*) who here are the offerers (*hotṛ*) of the *agnihotra* become Indra and the other deities when they have been transformed into their celestial counterparts; they are the very ones who serve as the offerers there in the fire of the heavenly world. And it was they who offered the *agnihotra* here for the sake of enjoying its fruit. Even at the time of the transformation of that fruit, because they are the enjoyers of that fruit, they attain the status of being offerers in various places, transforming accordingly and thus becoming denotable by the term "deity" (*deva*).

And here, that substance of milk which served as the substratum for the Agnihotra rite, having been cast into this Āhavanīya fire and consumed by the fire, is transformed into an unseen, subtle form; together with the agent, the sacrificer, it enters that world via the sequence of smoke and so forth—entering the intermediate space from here, and from the intermediate space, the heavenly world.

Those subtle waters, which have become the effect of the oblation, are inherent in the *agnihotra* sacrifice; accompanied by the agent and denoted by the word "faith" (*śraddhā*), they enter the heavenly world to initiate a new body for the agent in the world of Soma, and are thus said to be "offered. Having entered the heavenly world there, they initiate the body of the agent within the lunar orb. This is expressed as: "The gods offer faith; from that offering, King Soma comes into being," because of the Vedic scripture stating, "Faith, indeed, is water."

The question is: "Do you know in which oblation, when offered, the waters, having become human speech, arise and speak? Regarding the determination of that [question], the passage begins, "That world, indeed, is the fire. Therefore, it is concluded that the waters, being associated with ritual action (*karman*), initiate the body of the agent and are denoted by the word *śraddhā*. Because of their predominance, there is the designation "the waters have become human speech," but this does not mean that the other elements are absent; rather, the initiation of the body is impelled by ritual action.

And karma is inherent in water; therefore, water has primacy in the production of the body. By means of this, there is the designation "waters are called man. For everywhere, the commencement of birth is caused by karma. In that regard, although the six topics beginning with departure (utkrānti) were introduced in the context of the Agnihotra by way of praising the Agnihotra oblation, nevertheless, all Vedic rituals beginning with the Agnihotra are indicated [by the term "Agnihotra"].

For, having introduced the fivefold ritual action connected with wife and fire, it was said: "By ritual action [one wins] the world of the ancestors"; and it will be stated later: "Now, those who win worlds by sacrifice, by charity, and by austerity.

"Parjanya, O Gautama, is indeed the second fire, the receptacle for the oblation, according to the sequence of the two oblations' return. Parjanya is the name of the divine self who presides over the instruments of rain. For him, the year is the fuel; for by means of the year—which revolves through its own parts beginning with autumn and ending with summer—Parjanya, the fire, blazes forth. The clouds are his smoke, because they originate from smoke or because they are perceived as being like smoke. Lightning is his flame, due to the commonality of their luminosity."

The thunderbolts are the embers, due to the commonality of being extinguished and hard. The hailstones are the sparks, due to the commonality of scattering and multiplicity. "In this very [fire]" is the specification of the locus for the oblation. Regarding the "gods," they are the very same priests who offer King Soma; that Soma which was produced when the *śraddhā* (faith) was offered into the fire of the heavenly world is offered into the second fire, Parjanya. And from that offering of Soma, rain comes into being. (11)

"This world, O Gautama, is indeed fire. This world refers to the locus for the birth and experience of living beings, characterized by actions, agents, and their fruits; it is the third fire. Of that fire, the earth itself is the fuel (*samit*); for this world is kindled by the earth, which is endowed with the experiences of many living beings. Fire is its smoke, because of the commonality of arising from a support; for fire arises depending on a terrestrial combustible substance, just as smoke arises depending on fuel.

Night is the flame, because of the commonality of arising from connection with fuel; for just as the flame of fire arises through its connection with fuel, so does the night arise through its connection with the earth as fuel, since they call the darkness of the night the shadow of the earth. The moon is the embers, because of the commonality of originating from that; for embers originate from the flame, and likewise the moon appears at night; or else, it is due to the commonality of being tranquil. The stars are the sparks, because of the commonality of scattering, like sparks.

In this very context, "in that [fire]," and so forth, is as explained previously. They offer rain as an oblation; from that oblation, food comes into being, because it is well known that food such as rice and barley originates from rain.

"Man, O Gautama, is indeed fire"—the well-known man, possessed of a head, hands, and so forth, is the fourth fire. His wide-open mouth is the fuel (*samit*); for by means of his open mouth, the man blazes during speech, Vedic recitation, and the like, just as fire blazes with fuel. His breath (*prāṇa*) is the smoke, because of the commonality of its rising; for the breath rises from the mouth. His speech (*vāk*), which is sound, is the flame, because of the commonality of being a manifestor; and just as a flame is a manifestor, so too is speech and sound a manifestor of the objects to be expressed.

The eye is the embers, because of the commonality of tranquility, or because it is the locus of light. The ear is the sparks, because of the commonality of scattering. Into that [fire], they offer food. Now, one might object: "Indeed, gods are not seen here offering food. This is no fault, for the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are rightly established as deities. With respect to the divine sphere (*adhidaiva*), Indra and others are the gods; with respect to the self (*adhyātma*), they are the very same vital breaths. And these are the ones who cast the food into the person. From that oblation, semen comes into being; for semen is indeed the transformation of food. (13)

"A woman indeed is the fire, O Gautama. "Woman" means a female; she is the fire as the locus for the fifth oblation. Her lap is the fuel, for by it she is kindled. The hair is the smoke, because of the commonality of its rising upward. The womb is the flame, because of the commonality of their color. What she does within is the embers; internal activity refers to the act of sexual intercourse, which are the embers, because of the commonality of being the cause for the subsiding of virility; for sexual intercourse is the cause for the subsiding of virility and so forth, just as the state of being embers is the cause for the subsiding of fire.

Delights (*abhinandāḥ*) are mere fragments of pleasure; because they share the quality of being trifling, they are like sparks. Into that [fire] they offer semen. From that oblation, a person (*puruṣa*) comes into being. Thus, the waters denoted by the word *śraddhā*—being offered in succession into the fires of heaven, rain, this world, the man, and the woman, and attaining a progressive degree of grossness through their states as faith, Soma, rain, food, and semen—give rise to what is designated by the word "person."

As for the fourth question—"Do you know at which oblation, when offered, the waters, having become human speech, arise and speak?"—that has now been resolved: at the fifth oblation, when offered into the fire that is the woman, the waters, having become semen, become human speech. That person, born in this sequence, lives; for how long? It is said: as long as he lives, meaning for as long as there exists karma that serves as the cause for his maintenance in this body.
Then, upon its exhaustion, at whatever time he dies. (14)

Then, at that time, the officiating priests carry this dead man for Agni—that is, for the sake of Agni itself—for the final oblation. For him who has become the oblation, the locus of the offering is simply the well-known fire, not a fire to be mentally constructed; the fuel is the well-known fuel; the smoke is the smoke; the flame is the flame; the embers are the embers; the sparks are the sparks—the meaning is that everything is exactly as it is known in common experience. Into that [fire], they offer the person as the final oblation.

From that oblation, when it has been offered, a person of radiant complexion—one possessing extraordinary brilliance—comes into being or is produced, because he has been refined by the rites beginning with conception and ending with the final oblation. (15) Now, for the purpose of resolving the first question, [the text] says: "They. Who are they? They are those who know this aforementioned vision of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*). By the word "thus" (*evam*), the five fires are specified as being characterized by fire, fuel, smoke, flame, embers, and sparks, as well as faith and so forth. The meaning is: "those who know these five fires in this manner."

But is this vision not actually concerned with the observation of the Agnihotra oblation? For it was stated there, in the determination of the six categories beginning with departure (*utkrānti*), that "they make heaven itself the Āhavanīya fire," and so forth; here too, there is much similarity, such as the world over there being the fire and the sun being the fuel, and so on. Therefore...

[Objection: This view is merely a restatement of that [previous position]. [Reply: No, because of the inclusion of the question and its answer regarding "in which [day]. Only as much as is included in the answer to the question "In which [day]? is it proper to refer to by means of the word "this" (*evam*); otherwise, the question would be purposeless. Furthermore, since the number is already known, the fires themselves should be mentioned. If, on the other hand, even what is already known is being restated, it is proper to restate it exactly as it was established, and not as "that world is the fire."

Now, even if it were intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), it would still be appropriate for the first and the last [stages] to serve as the illustration. This is also because of another scriptural passage (*śruti*); for in the Chāndogya, within the same context, the number five alone is mentioned in the statement, "He who knows the five fires," and thus this vision of the five fires is not a subordinate part of the Agnihotra. As for the similarity regarding the fire, fuel, and so forth, we have already stated that this is for the purpose of praising the Agnihotra.

Therefore, the attainment of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*) does not result from the thorough knowledge of the six categories of matters such as departure (*utkrānti*) and the rest, because the injunction for the attainment of the path beginning with light is made by employing the subject matter at hand, namely, "thus" (*evam*).

Who, then, are those who "know thus"? They are householders themselves. But is it not the case that for them the attainment of smoke and so forth is intended to be taught by means of sacrifices and other rites? No; because even for householders who do not know thus, the performance of sacrifices and other rites is possible, and because the mendicants and forest-dwellers are mentioned specifically in connection with the forest, whereas the vision of the five fires is connected to the duties of the householder. Therefore, students (brahmacārins) are also not included among those who "know thus."

Their entry upon the northern path, however, is established by the authority of the Smṛti: "Of the eighty-eight thousand sages who are perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas), the path is to the north of Aryaman; they have indeed attained immortality."

Therefore, those householders who know thus—"I am born from Agni, I am the offspring of Agni"—and who, in this sequence, know themselves as born from the fires and as having the nature of fire; and those forest-dwellers and wandering mendicants in the wilderness who, being endowed with faith, meditate upon the True Brahman, the Self of Hiraṇyagarbha, and do not meditate upon faith itself—all of them attain the light (arcis).

As long as householders do not know the science of the five fires or the true Brahman, they—having been offered as an oblation in the fifth oblation after the sequence of offerings beginning with faith—are born from the fire of woman and, rising again toward the world, become performers of rituals such as the *agnihotra*. By that ritual action, they return again to the world of the fathers by way of smoke and so forth, and then return to this world by way of rain and so forth.

Then again, those born from the fire of women, having performed action once more—in this very manner, like a water-wheel, they revolve again and again through coming and going. But when they know thus, then, being released from the turning of the water-wheel, they attain the *arcis*. By "arcis" (light) is not meant merely a flame of fire; rather, it is the deity presiding over light, denoted by the word *arcis*, who is established as the characteristic of the northern path; they attain that deity.

For there is no direct connection for wandering mendicants with the flame of fire itself; therefore, it is the deity denoted by the word "flame" that is intended. Consequently, [the passage refers to] the deity of the day; since a fixed rule regarding the time of death is impossible, the word "day" also refers to the deity, for death occurs when one's lifespan is exhausted. Indeed, it cannot be said that one who knows this must die on the very day [of his passing], so the day cannot be restricted as the time of death.

And those who have become *pretas* do not wait for the day during the night, because of another scriptural passage stating: "In the time it takes to snap one's fingers, he goes to the sun. From the day, they reach the waxing fortnight (*āpūryamāṇapakṣa*); having been conveyed by the deity of the day, they attain the deity of the waxing fortnight—that is, the deity of the bright half of the month.
