From the waxing fortnight, they reach those six months during which the sun, the illuminator, moves toward the north, the northern direction; having been conveyed by the deity of the bright fortnight, they attain those months.

From the plural "months," it follows that there are six deities presiding over the northern course [of the sun] who move in a group. Having been conducted by those deities of the six months, they reach the deity who presides over the world of the gods (*devaloka*). From the world of the gods, they reach the Sun; from the Sun, they reach the lightning—that is, the deity who presides over lightning. When they have reached the deity of lightning, a certain person residing in the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), created by Brahmā through his mind (*mānasa*), approaches them and leads them to the worlds of Brahmā.

The phrase "to the worlds of Brahman" (brahmalokān) is understood to mean that they are divided according to the distinctions of lower and higher planes, as indicated by the use of the plural number and because it is logical that there should be a gradation in the nature of their meditations. Having been led there by that Person, being supreme—that is, most excellent—in those worlds of Brahman, they dwell for many years, for themselves being supreme (*parāvataḥ*) and excellent; the meaning is that they dwell for many *kalpas* of Brahmā.

For those who have gone to the world of Brahman, there is no returning again to this saṃsāra, nor is there a coming back "here"—for the reading "here" (iha) occurs in another recension. If it is argued that the word "here" refers merely to the general form [of the world], like the expression "on the morrow, the full moon day," we say no; for the qualification "here" would otherwise be purposeless. Indeed, if they did not return at all, the inclusion of the word "here" would be entirely redundant.

Regarding the phrase "on the day after tomorrow [the full moon]," since the fact that the full moon occurs on the day after tomorrow is not explicitly stated, it is appropriate to provide a qualification. For in that case, the word "tomorrow" (*śvas*) does not possess the form of "tomorrow" as its primary lexical meaning; thus, the word *śvas* is employed even though it appears redundant. However, when a qualifying word is used and, upon investigation, no fruit of that qualification is perceived, then it is proper to discard the qualifying word as being purposeless. But this is not the case when the fruit of the qualification is indeed understood.
Therefore, it is understood that there is a recurrence [of the ritual] after this kalpa. (16)

On the other hand, those who do not know at all—namely, the mere performers of ritual action who are knowers only of the six items connected with the Agnihotra, beginning with its departure (utkrānti)—[attain their results] through sacrifice, such as the Agnihotra; through charity, characterized by the distribution of goods to those begging outside the sacrificial altar; and through austerity, which is distinct from the initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth, such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances performed outside the sacrificial altar.

They conquer the worlds; by the use of the plural "worlds," a gradation of results even therein is intended. They attain the smoke; as in the case of the northern path, here too the deities themselves are denoted by the words "smoke" and so forth—the meaning is that they reach the deity of smoke—and the nature of these deities as guides (ātivāhika) is likewise the same.

From smoke they go to the night, the deity of night; from there to the waning fortnight, the deity of the waning fortnight; from there they reach the six months during which the sun moves toward the southern quarter—those specific deities of the months. From the months they go to the world of the fathers, and from the world of the fathers to the moon. Having reached the moon, they become food.

When they have become food there, just as the officiating priests consume King Soma at this sacrifice with the words, "Swell up! Wane away!", so do the gods consume—meaning they enjoy—those performers of ritual action who have reached the moon, like masters consuming their servants. The phrase "Swell up! Wane away! is not a mantra; rather, its meaning is that having repeatedly caused [the Soma] in the cup to swell, and having brought about its waning through consumption, they consume it again and again.

In this way, the gods also—resting again and again those performers of ritual action who have obtained bodies in the world of Soma and granting them fruits according to their karma—enjoy those beings as instruments, just as they enjoy the swelling of the Soma, for that indeed is their nourishment.

When, at whatever time, that karma characterized by sacrifice, charity, and so forth which led them to the world of Soma "passes away"—meaning it is completely exhausted—then they emerge into this very well-known space (ākāśa).

Those waters denoted by the word "faith" (śraddhā), which were offered into the fire of the heavenly world and transformed into the form of Soma—by means of which a watery body was commenced for the enjoyment of the performers of rites in the world of Soma—those waters, upon the exhaustion of karma, dissolve like a lump of snow through contact with heat; having dissolved, they become subtle, as if having become the element of space (ākāśa). This is what is expressed by the statement: "They emerge into this very space."

Furthermore, those performers of action, possessing that body, travel through the atmosphere and are led here and there by the east wind and other winds; thus it is said: "From space they go to the air. From the air they reach rain; as it has been stated: "They offer King Soma into the fire of Parjanya. Then, having become rain, they fall upon this earth. Having reached the earth, they become food such as rice, barley, and so forth.

As it has been said: "In this world, people offer rain into the fire; from that oblation, food comes into being. Those [beings] are then offered into the fire of man, having become food, into the shedder of semen; then, having become semen, they are offered into the fire of woman; from that they are born. Rising up toward the world, those who rise up toward the world perform rituals such as the *agnihotra*."

Then, by means of smoke and so forth, they go again and again to the world of Soma and back again to this world. Thus these performers of ritual actions revolve like a water-wheel; the meaning is that they wander in a cycle until they know Brahman, for the sake of the northern path or immediate liberation. As it has been said: "Thus, desiring, he transmigrates."

Furthermore, those who do not know these two paths—the northern and the southern—meaning they do not practice either knowledge or action for the sake of attaining the northern or the southern path—it is said what becomes of them: they become worms, moths, and that which is biting, namely gadflies and mosquitoes. Thus indeed is this course of transmigratory existence miserable; for one submerged in it, a further emergence is difficult to obtain.

And so says another Śruti passage: "These small beings that return again and again come into being, saying, 'Be born and die. Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that one should, with all one's energy and according to one's ability, abandon natural actions and ignorance, and practice either scriptural action or knowledge, which are the means for attaining the southern and northern paths.

And so it has been said: "Therefore, indeed, it is difficult to escape from that; one should therefore feel aversion [to it]. From this other scriptural passage (śruti), the meaning is that one should strive for liberation. Here too, it is understood that a great effort must be made precisely toward the means for attaining the northern path, because it has been stated, "In this very way they revolve. Thus, all the questions have been resolved.

The fourth question—beginning with "That world indeed... and ending with "...the person comes into being"—is presented first; the fifth, however, is presented second by way of explaining the means for attaining either the path of the gods (*devayāna*) or the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*), that is, the northern and southern routes. By that same [fifth question], the first [question] is also addressed: namely, the disagreement regarding whether some, starting from the fire, attain the flame (*arcis*), while others attain the smoke (*dhūma*).

The second question—namely, that they return to this world by way of the sequence beginning with space—is likewise resolved by that same [passage]. Furthermore, the third question—why that world is not filled up, and why some attain the state of worms, moths, and so forth—is also determined.
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa of the sixth chapter.
Now, for these beings, there are indeed only three origins: the egg-born, the viviparous, and the soil-born. (1)

(1) --- He who might desire this: The course of knowledge and action has been stated; therein, knowledge is independent, whereas action depends upon the two kinds of wealth—divine and human. Therefore, for the sake of action, wealth must be acquired, and that by means which do not cause spiritual downfall (*pratyavāya*). To that end, the rite called *mantha* is commenced for the attainment of greatness; for when greatness is achieved, wealth is indeed established as a matter of course. This is what is said: "He who might desire"—that is, he who is qualified for ritual action and desires wealth.

What [is meant]? "May I attain greatness," that is to say, "may I become great. In this regard, the time for the rite of churning which is intended to be performed is specified: during the northern course of the sun; and within that, since it would otherwise apply everywhere, during the waxing fortnight, i.e., the bright fortnight; and even within that, since it would otherwise apply everywhere, on an auspicious day, meaning one favorable to oneself that ensures the success of the rite.

For twelve days: starting from the very day that is auspicious and favorable for the rite he intends to perform, and continuing for twelve days prior to that, he is one who observes the *upasad* vow. The *upasad* vow consists of subsisting on milk; this vow is well known in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, where it involves consuming milk by means of increasing and decreasing the quantity of the "teats" (milk portions). In the present context, however, because that specific ritual action is not included, only the mere act of subsisting on milk is prescribed, devoid of its specific procedural details (*itikartavyatā*).

Now, if the analysis [of the compound] is "the vow of the Upasad," then everything consisting of the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) should be included; why, then, is it not accepted? It is said: because the rite is based on tradition (*smārta*). For this rite of churning (*manthakarma*) is indeed based on tradition. But how can that which is enjoined by direct revelation (*śruti*) be considered based on tradition? This *śruti* merely restates what is already established in tradition; for if it were directly revealed (*śrauta*), there would be a relationship of archetype and modification (*prakṛti-vikārabhāva*), and consequently, the modified rite would have to adopt the properties of the archetypal rite.

But here there is no status as being based on direct Vedic revelation (*śrauta*); for this very reason, this rite is prescribed to be performed in the *āvasathya* fire, and the entire procedure (*āvṛt*) is indeed *smārta* (based on tradition). "Having become one who observes the *upasad* vow" means being one who observes the milk-vow (*payovrata*). [The vessel is] made of *udumbara* wood—that is, consisting of the *udumbara* tree—in either a bronze cup (*kaṃsa*) or a wooden bowl (*camasa*); its specific qualification is that it must be made of *udumbara* wood whether it is in the shape of a bronze cup or the shape of a wooden bowl. There is an option regarding the shape, but not regarding the material being *udumbara*.

In this context, "all medicinal herbs" (*sarvauṣadham*) means a collection of all herbs as far as possible and according to one's capacity; having gathered all these herbs, among them, ten domestic ones—such as *vrīhi*, *yava*, and so forth, which will be mentioned later—must necessarily be taken. However, there is no fault in taking more than that. One should also take the fruits of domestic plants as far as possible and according to one's capacity. The word "iti" is intended to indicate the accumulation of the entire collection of materials; the meaning is that one should gather everything else that is required for the preparation.

In this matter, the procedure (*krama*) stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* is to be observed. The preparation of the ground consists of sweeping and smearing it. By the statement "having established the fire," it is understood that this refers to the domestic fire (*āvasathya-agni*), because of the singular number and because the act of "establishing" (*upasamādhāna*) is heard [in the injunction]; the establishment is of a fire that is already present. Having strewn darbha grass around it; by the term "according to the ritual procedure" (*āvṛtā*)—since the rite belongs to the *Smṛti* tradition—the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* (pot-cooking) is adopted; having prepared the clarified butter (*ājya*) according to that procedure;

Under a male lunar mansion (nakṣatra), under a male-named lunar mansion conjoined with an auspicious day, one should pour the stirred drink (mantha)—ground grains mixed with all medicinal herbs—into a vessel made of Udumbara wood containing curds, honey, and ghee; having stirred it with a single stirring-stick, having brought it together and placed it in the center, he offers oblations of clarified butter at the place of insertion with these mantras beginning with "As many gods as there are... This very deity thought: "Come now, let me enter these three deities with this living self and differentiate name and form. (2)

(2–3) Beginning with "To the eldest, svāhā! To the best, svāhā!", he offers two oblations at a time and pours the residue into the mash; he causes the ghee adhering to the *sruva* spoon to flow into the mash. Precisely because of these marks of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—beginning with "to the eldest" and "to the best"—only one who knows the vital breath as the eldest, the best, and so forth, is qualified for this rite. Beginning with "To the seed," he offers each oblation one by one and pours the residue into the mash; then, with another churning-stick, he churns again.
"Of these, he made each one threefold. Now, my dear, learn from me how each of these three deities becomes threefold. Thus ends the third section.
(4) Then he touches him with this mantra: "Thou art the whirlpool."
(5) Then he lifts it up; he takes hold of it with his hand together with the vessel, using this [formula]: "We shall honor thee greatly.

Then he sips and eats it: with the first foot of the Gāyatrī, one verse containing the word *madhu*, and the first *vyāhṛti*, he sips the first morsel; likewise, with the second foot of the Gāyatrī, the second *madhu* verse, and the second *vyāhṛti*, the second morsel; and likewise, with the third foot of the Gāyatrī, the third *madhu* verse, and the third *vyāhṛti*, the third morsel.

Having recited the entire Sāvitrī and all the Madhumatī verses, and having uttered at the end, "May I indeed become this entire universe," he consumes the whole [substance] with the formula, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā. He should determine beforehand so that the entire substance is finished with four mouthfuls. Having washed the entire vessel that was smeared with the substance, he should determine it [for consumption]. Having washed the entire vessel that was smeared with the substance, he should drink silently.

Having washed his hands and sipped water, he lies down behind the fire with his head toward the east. Having performed the morning twilight devotion (*prātaḥsaṃdhyā*), he worships the sun with the mantra, "Thou art the unique lotus among the quarters. Having returned by the same way he came, and having sat down behind the fire, he recites the *vaṃśa* (the lineage).

"Regarding this very [instruction], Uddālaka... and so forth. Having spoken thus to his pupils, Satyakāma Jābāla said: "Even if one were to pour this [mixture] upon a withered stump, branches would surely spring up and leaves would grow upon it. Having thus related this entire procedure of the churning-stick (mantha)—which had been handed down in succession from each teacher beginning with Uddālaka—Satyakāma, the teacher, spoke to his many pupils.

What else did he say? It is said: "Even if one were to sprinkle this churned mixture (*mantha*), prepared for consumption, upon a dry stump—even one whose life-force has departed—branches, that is, the limbs of the tree, would surely grow upon this stump, and leaves (*palāśa*) would sprout, just as they do from a living stump; how much more so would desire be fulfilled by this rite! This is intended as praise for the ritual, signifying that its fruit is certain. Regarding the acquisition of knowledge, there are six sacred seats (*tīrtha*).
In this matter, for the attainment of that knowledge of the churning-stick which includes the vision of the vital breath, only two types of disciples are authorized: the son and the pupil.

It has been explained that there are four [types of] *udumbara* wood. There are ten kinds of cultivated grains; we have stated that ten of these cultivated grains must necessarily be taken. Which ones are they? They are specified as follows: rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*); sesame (*tila*) and beans (*māṣa*); *aṇu* and *priyaṅgu*—where *aṇu* refers to those things designated by the word *aṇu*, which in some regions are well known by the name *kaṅgu*; *khalva* and *niṣpāva*—the latter being designated in common usage by the word *valla*; and *khalakula* and *kulattha*.

Apart from these, one should take all medicinal herbs and fruits according to one's ability—so we have said—excluding those not prescribed for sacrifice. Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa of the sixth chapter. That which is the red color of fire is the color of heat; that which is white is the color of water; that which is black is the color of food. The "fire-ness" of fire has departed; it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name. Only the three colors are real. 1.

(1) — Since a son, according to his birth, the manner of his procreation, and the qualities with which he is distinguished, becomes the savior of both himself and his father in the next world, this Brāhmaṇa section is commenced for the purpose of bringing about that result. One who has perceived the Prāṇa and performed the Śrīmantha rite is qualified for the Putramantha. When he desires to perform the Putramantha, he should first perform the Śrīmantha and then wait for his wife’s fertile period; this is understood from the praise of semen as being the most excellent essence of herbs and other substances.

Of these moving and non-moving beings, the earth is indeed the essence (*rasa*), the substantial core; for it has been said that [the earth] is the honey (*madhu*) of all beings. Of the earth, water is the essence, for the earth is woven across and through water. Of water, plants are the essence, because plants and so forth are effects [of water], and thus possess the nature of being its essence. Of plants, flowers are the essence; of flowers, fruits; of fruits, man; and of man, semen—according to another Vedic text: "It is the radiance (*tejas*) produced from all his limbs."

That which is the red form of the sun is the form of fire; that which is white is the form of water; that which is black is the form of food. The "sun-ness" has departed from the sun; it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name. Only the three forms are real. 2. (2)---

Since this semen is thus the most essential element of all beings, the creator Prajāpati reflected: "What indeed would be a suitable receptacle for it? Having reflected, he created a woman. And having created her, he performed worship toward her—that is, he engaged in the act known as sexual union, which is called *adha-upāsana*. Therefore, one should worship a woman by means of sexual union (*adha-upāsīta*); for offspring follow after the excellence of their progenitor.

In this context, he describes the general application of the Vājapeya sacrifice: He produced for himself that "prāñc" (forward-moving) pressing-stone, which—due to its common quality of hardness—is like the generative organ and serves as the stone for pressing Soma; he brought it forth toward the female organ (*strīvyañjana*). By means of that, he emitted her—that is, he effected union with that woman.

That which is the red form of the moon is the form of fire; that which is white is the form of water; that which is black is the form of food. The "moon-ness" has departed from the moon; it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name. Only the three forms are real. 3. (3) ---

Everything beginning with "her altar" is well known as being common [to all sacrifices]. The kindled fire is in the middle of the woman's sexual organ; those two testicles are connected, by way of a syntactical ellipsis, to the two pressing-boards. The world that is well known to belong to one who performs the Vājapeya sacrifice—just so great is the world, the fruit, of the wise man who engages in the act of sexual intercourse. This is a praise [of the act] meaning: "Therefore, one should not feel loathing. He who, knowing this, practices sexual dalliance, takes away—that is, appropriates—the merit of these women.

Furthermore, if one who is ignorant does not know the perfection of the Vājapeya sacrifice, nor the fact that the essence of semen is identical [to it], he behaves with contempt toward women; his women take away the merit of that ignorant man. That which is the red form of lightning is the form of fire; that which is white is the form of water; that which is black is the form of food. The nature of lightning has departed from the lightning; it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name. "The three forms"—that alone is the truth. 4. (4) ---

Indeed, it was knowing this—that the act of sexual intercourse known as "laughing at" (adhopahāsa) is perfected by the Vājapeya sacrifice—that Uddālaka Āruṇi said; likewise [said] Nāka Maudgalya and Kumārahārita.

What did they say? It is explained as follows: "Many *maryāḥ*—that is, mortal men subject to death; *brāhmaṇāyanāḥ*—those for whom the Brahmins are their refuge, meaning mere kinsmen of the Brahmins who subsist on their caste alone; *nirindriyāḥ*—those whose senses are impaired; *visukṛtaḥ*—those from whom meritorious deeds have departed; *avidvāṃsaḥ*—meaning those attached to the act of sexual intercourse. What of them? They depart from this world, having fallen away from the next.
He demonstrates that the act of sexual intercourse is an extreme cause of sin: "Those ignorant ones who practice this downward laughter (*adhopahāsa*)."

Having performed the *śrīmantha* rite, he observes his wife’s fertile period while practicing celibacy. If this semen is spilled—whether much or little, whether in sleep or while awake—due to the intensity of passion, those who knew this in the past, the great householders and great Vedic scholars, used to say: "Nothing today shall be uttered by us that has not been heard, thought, or known. For they understood it thus. 5.

He should touch it, or consecrate it with mantras—that is, he should recite them over it. When he touches it, he takes up that semen with his ring finger and thumb using the mantra ending with "I take it up" (*ādade*). With the mantra "Again [to] me," he should wipe it away either between the eyebrows, or on the eyebrows, or on the breasts, or on the nipples. "That which appeared as if red, they knew to be the form of fire; that which appeared as if white, they knew to be the form of water; that which appeared as if black, they knew to be the form of food. (6) ---

Now, if at any time he should see his own reflection in water, there too he should consecrate it with this mantra: "May splendor be in me. For she who is among women a wife is indeed Śrī (Prosperity), because she is *malodvāsāḥ*—one whose soiled garments have been removed. Therefore, having approached that illustrious and prosperous woman whose soiled garments have been removed, he should address her thus: "Today we have a task to perform, namely the procreation of a son," [to her] after she has bathed at the end of three nights.

"That which seemed as if unknown was actually the combination of these very deities; they understood it thus. "Now, my dear, understand from me how each of these three deities, upon reaching a person, becomes threefold. Thus ends the fourth section.

If she does not grant him sexual union, he may, if he so desires, purchase her by means of ornaments and the like, thereby making his intention known. Even if she still does not grant it, he may, if he so desires, strike her with a staff or with his hand and pass her for the sake of sexual union, having proclaimed: "I shall curse you; I shall make you unfortunate. Approaching her with this mantra—"I take away your glory with my own glory"—she becomes, as a result of that curse, barren, notorious for her misfortune, and indeed devoid of glory.

If she should give herself to him, it would be entirely agreeable to the husband; then he should approach her with this mantra: "I bestow glory upon your glory through my own glory. Then both of them become glorious indeed.

(9) — He who should desire his own wife, thinking, "May she love me," should fix his generative organ upon her, place his mouth against her mouth, touch her private parts, and mutter this mantra: "From limb to limb... [and so forth].

(10) Now, if she whom he desires—meaning, "may she not conceive," may she not bear a child—he should perform the ritual as before: first performing *abhiprāṇana* (blowing into her mouth), he should afterwards exhale (*apānyāt*) with this mantra: "With my organ, I take away your seed. The meaning is that she becomes indeed seedless; she does not become pregnant.

Now, if she should desire, "May she conceive a child," then for her [the procedure] is as before, beginning with the word "the purpose" (*artham*). Having performed the reverse of the previous [breathing], he should breathe upon her [with the words]: "With my faculty, I place seed in your seed. She indeed becomes pregnant.

Now, furthermore, if one should have a lover or paramour for his wife, and if he should hate him and think, "I will practice sorcery against him," this is the ritual for him: having established fire in an unbaked clay vessel, he should perform everything in reverse order; in that fire, he should offer these reed-shafts—reeds with their tips intact, reversed, and smeared with clarified butter—as oblations, beginning with the words, "In my kindled fire you have sacrificed," and so forth; at the end of each, he should utter the name of the person [the rival], saying "So-and-so."

He who knows this, whom a Brahmin curses, departs with his merit exhausted, that is, deprived of the fruits of his virtuous deeds. Therefore, one who knows this should not seek even a joke with the wife of a learned Śrotriya, nor should he engage in playful banter, much less in sexual dalliance; for even such a person remains an outsider, meaning he remains an enemy.

Now, the passage beginning with "If one should find his wife in her menses, he should enter upon the state of the *ṛtu*," should be seen as occurring before the section starting with "For she is indeed the glory (*śrī*) of women," due to the logical connection (*sāmarthya*). [The injunction is: "She should drink from a bronze vessel for three days and wear unwashed clothes; neither a low-caste man (*vṛṣala*) nor a low-caste woman (*vṛṣalī*) should approach (*upahanyāt*) her—that is, touch her—whether she has bathed or not. At the end of the three nights, when the vow of the three nights is completed, the connection with the separated word is: "having immersed herself—that is, having bathed—she should wear unwashed clothes."
When she has bathed, one should have her thresh rice; one should employ her specifically for the threshing of the rice.

(14) He who should desire: "May a son be born to me white in complexion, may he recite a single Veda, and may he reach a full lifespan"—for a hundred years—having cooked milk-rice with clarified butter, the two of them, being capable, should eat it in order to procreate.
(15) Having cooked rice with curd and a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) with curd; if he desires a son learned in the two Vedas, then this is the rule for his food.
It is exclusively boiled rice prepared naturally. The inclusion of the word "exclusively" (*kevalam*) is for the purpose of precluding any other possibility.

(17) --- The daughter’s proficiency pertains only to the domain of household management, as she lacks authority regarding the Veda. *Tilaudana* is rice mixed with sesame seeds; *kṛsara* is rice cooked with sesame and meat.

(18) "Vividha" means sung in various ways, that is to say, celebrated; "samitim-gamaḥ" means one who goes to an assembly, that is to say, one who is bold, since "pāṇḍitya" (scholarship) is mentioned separately; "bhāṣitā vācam" means one who speaks speech that is desired to be heard or beautiful, that is to say, one who speaks refined and meaningful language. "Māṃsaudana" is rice mixed with meat. To specify the type of meat, he says: "with the meat of an ox" (*aukṣeṇa māṃsena*); an "ox" (*ukṣan*) is a bull capable of impregnation, its meat being that;
"ṛṣabha" is one of even greater age than that, its meat being "ārṣabha."

(19) Then, at the very time of dawn, having taken rice grains that have been husked, he performs the rite according to the procedure for the *sthālīpāka*—having prepared the clarified butter (*ājya*), performed the consecration of the clarified butter, and cooked the sacrificial porridge (*caru*)—he offers oblations of the *sthālīpāka*, taking portions repeatedly with the formula "To Agni, Svāhā! and so forth. Every domestic rule (*gārhya-vidhi*) should be observed here; having offered the oblations and drawn out [the remainder], he eats the rest of the porridge.

Having eaten himself, he gives the remains to his other wife. Having washed his hands and sipped water, he fills a water-vessel and sprinkles her three times with that water while reciting this mantra, "Arise from here," pronouncing the mantra only once. (20) Then, having consecrated her [with mantras], the sequence should be understood as follows: they eat milk-rice and so forth according to their desire for offspring. At the time of sexual union, he approaches her while reciting the mantra beginning with, "I am he (Ama), she is she (Sā)."

(21) Then he causes her thighs to part with the mantra, "May Heaven and Earth part. In that [act], the purpose and so forth are as before. He strokes her three times from the head downwards, following the direction of the hair, with each mantra beginning with, "Viṣṇu [prepared] the womb.
First, he calls her by name, saying "So-and-so.

(23) At the time of delivery, he sprinkles the woman about to give birth with water for the sake of an easy birth, using this mantra: "Just as the wind stirs a lotus pond on all sides, so may your fetus stir."

(24) Now, the birth-rite (*jātakarman*). When [the son] is born, having kindled the fire and placed the son on his lap, he pours together the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*)—having mixed curds and ghee—in a bronze vessel (*kaṃsa*), and offers it as a portion of the speckled butter at the point for the insertion [of the *yājyā*], beginning with the verse "In him a thousand... (RV 3.1.23).

Then, placing his own mouth near the child's right ear, he should mutter three times, "Speech! Speech! Then, having brought together curd, honey, and ghee, he makes him eat them with a piece of gold that is uncut and unadulterated, using these mantras for each one individually.
(26) Then he gives him a name, saying, "You are Veda. That becomes his secret name—namely, "Veda."
(27) Then, having handed him over to his mother and placed him on her lap, she gives him the breast with the mantra beginning, "That breast of yours...

Then he consecrates his mother with the mantra, "Thou art *ilā*. Regarding this, they say: "A son born according to this rite surpasses his father and grandfather; he attains the highest perfection through prosperity, fame, and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*)"—the meaning is that he thus becomes worthy of praise. And for that Brāhmaṇa who possesses such knowledge, if a son is born, he too becomes worthy of praise; this is to be supplied to complete the sense. Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa of the sixth chapter.

Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts. That which is its coarsest constituent becomes feces; that which is middling becomes flesh; and that which is finest becomes the mind. Now, the lineage of the entire tradition is set forth, for it has been introduced that a son is born endowed with qualities through the preeminence of the woman. Therefore, by means of the specific qualifications of the woman alone, the succession of teachers is glorified. "These are the white ones" means they are unmixed by a Brāhmaṇa. Alternatively, those Yajus formulas which exist are "white," meaning pure.

Beginning from Prajāpati down to Pautimāṣīputra, this lineage—descending in order through fixed teachers—is uniform up to Sāṃjīvīputra. This is the lineage of the Veda known as the *Pravacana* (the Oral Tradition). And this very Brahman, having come down through the succession of the lineage of Prajāpati, has spread manifold among us. This self-existent Brahman is eternal, without beginning or end. Salutation to that Brahman. Salutation to the teachers who follow it. Thus ends the fifth Brāhmaṇa of the sixth Adhyāya.
Thus [ends the work] of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya...
The Commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, is complete.
"My dear, when curd is being churned, that subtle essence which rises upward becomes ghee.
"My dear, man consists of sixteen parts. Do not eat for fifteen days; drink water at will. Life-breath (*prāṇa*) consists of water; it will not be cut off from one who drinks water.

Uddālaka Āruṇi said to his son Śvetaketu: "My dear, learn from me the state of deep sleep (*svapnānta*). When a person here is said to 'sleep,' then, my dear, he has become united with Being (*sat*); he has gone to his own (*svam apītaḥ*). Therefore, they say of him 'he sleeps' (*svapiti*), for he has gone to his own."

"Just as, my dear, honey-makers collect the juices from trees of various kinds and, having brought them together, reduce them to a single essence; even so, my dear, these rivers—the eastern ones flowing eastward and the western ones flowing westward—flow into the ocean and become the ocean itself. Just as those [rivers] do not know there, 'I am this one,' or 'I am that one'..."

"Place this salt in water, and then come to me in the morning. He did accordingly. Then he said to him, "My dear, bring that salt which you placed in the water last evening. Having searched for it, he did not find it. "My dear, it is just as if a man were brought from the Gandhāras with his eyes blindfolded, and were then left in a place where there are no people. Just as he might wander there toward the east, or the north, or the south, or the west—having been brought with his eyes blindfolded and being left with his eyes blindfolded—[so it is with one who knows only the scriptures]."

"My dear, when relatives sit around a man who is suffering from illness, saying, 'Do you know me? Do you know me?', he knows them as long as his speech has not merged into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into heat, and the heat into the supreme deity. (1)

"O Somya, suppose they bring a man, seized by the hand, saying, 'He has stolen, he committed theft; heat the axe for him. If he is the doer of that deed, then he makes himself false. Being one whose intention is rooted in falsehood, having concealed himself with falsehood, he grasps the heated axe; he is burned and then he is slain. (1)
